title: Will Trump attend the Alabama-Georgia game amid Hurricane Isaias threat? Here’s what he said
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The midterm elections are looming and the first hurricane of the Atlantic Season is menacing the Gulf Coast.
But President Donald Trump is really, really hoping the weather doesn’t stop him from going to another big college football game — this one in Alabama on Saturday night.
“Well, hurricane and football? I love Alabama. I gotta go to the game. It’d be awfully hard,” Trump said Wednesday, when asked if Hurricane Isaias — and a forecast track which has parts of Alabama, Mississippi and Florida bracing for significant impacts — might alter his plans.
Trump had been set to visit Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa when Alabama hosts Georgia in a Top 10 matchup, following an afternoon rally in Tennessee.
Officials are still discussing how the storm might affect the game. But if it happens and Trump is there, it would be the 10th college football game he’s attended as president since 2017 — including the late September game in Knoxville when Texas topped Tennessee 20-17.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday “if there’s a hurricane, I don’t want to do anything” to take the focus of first responders and law enforcement away from the storm, saying he wanted people to be safe.
“We’ll have to see,” he said.
It’s unusual to mix football and midterm politics
A president trying to give his party a midterm boost typically wouldn’t even contemplate going to two college football games so close to Election Day. But Trump’s longtime love of sports — and big crowds — are often key factors in his travel schedule.
Live sports — especially big games that attract casual fans nationwide — are one of the few televised programs that can still draw large, real-time audiences. But mixing sports and politics can be tricky: Trump received cheers but also boos when he was shown on Tennessee’s jumbotron, despite being in a deep red state.
“I think what they’re trying to do is get this broadcast: trying to raise enthusiasm, particularly among young men,” said University of Richmond political scientist Dan Palazzolo, who has researched, written and taught about the intersection of politics and sports.
Tennessee and Alabama are “safe turf,” Palazzolo said, and Trump “clearly sees sports as a kind of way to connect with a certain part of the base.”
While presidents usually visit key swing states leading up to elections, Trump’s sinking approval ratings mean some GOP candidates may be looking to distance themselves from the increasingly unpopular Iran war and the higher gasoline prices it’s caused.
The White House says Trump attending football games — even in reliably Republican states — can energize his core supporters around the country. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers described the president as “the greatest champion of college sports in American history” and said that Trump has used his executive powers and championed congressional efforts to try to overhaul how the sport is governed.
Trump is now a week into what he said would be 32 days of travel ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3 — including a visit last week to Alabama and other stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Ohio and Nebraska. Swings in coming weeks will take him to Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Kansas and Alaska, among other places.
Presidents have used sports for political gains before. But not like this
Richard Nixon publicly leaned into his fierce love of football to ”make a difference politically by capturing the Midwest, working class values," Palazzolo said. His successor, Gerald Ford, was a standout University of Michigan center and used his playing days as a key component of his folksy personal style when campaigning.
But Trump has made sporting events a big part of his second term. A onetime owner of the USFL’s New Jersey Generals, Trump recently attended the Presidents Cup and flew to his golf course for the Irish Open.
He was at the World Cup final, the NBA finals and the NCAA football championship game, while marking his 80th birthday with a UFC extravaganza on the White House lawn.
In 2025 alone, Trump went to the Super Bowl, the Daytona 500, the Ryder Cup, a New York Yankees game and the U.S. Open men’s final, as well as UFC fights and the NCAA wrestling championships.
“I think it helps the brand more than anything else. Because, I think his brand is ‘Sports Guy,’” said Dave Mowery, an Alabama-based consultant who has worked on campaigns for both parties.
“I know everything is political,” Mowery said. “But it almost puts him above politics and into that type of guy that is seen in the box with the people.”
In some states, there’s the risk of backlash
Mowery, a Georgia fan who plans to attend Saturday’s game against Alabama, said a presidential visit means fans have to cope with additional security and arriving early to sit in the stands long before the game begins.
He said not everyone there will support Trump, though few will be frustrated enough about the disruptions to vote for Democrats on that issue alone. Seeing the president flash on the scoreboard, or wave to the crowd from a private box, probably won’t win him votes from the crowd, either, Mowery said.
Palazzolo said he thinks it’s a “time-drain” for a president to go to a football game when there’s no evidence it can sway voter behavior — and he said it risks backlash, especially in parts of the country where football remains bipartisan with “conservatives and liberals finding common ground at the ballpark.”
Mowery said the difference between attending a big game in the South versus other parts of the country is that college football is the top attraction. That’s in contrast to NFL games, which might be bigger draws in other, more northern battleground states.
He also said it’s no accident that Trump has stuck to attending marquee college matchups.
“If ‘Sports Guy’ helps drive the brand, then you want to be at the top of that food chain,” Mowery said. “He wants to go to the best game on the board. He wants to go to the top of the pops.”

title: Martha Raddatz of ABC News in Maine ahead of midterm election
text:
Martha Raddatz of ABC News in Maine to speak with voters ahead of midterm election
The U.S. Senate race in Maine, one of the most closely watched in the country, will take center stage in the WMTW Channel 8 studio Thursday night, and Maine's Total Coverage got the chance to speak with one of the top political minds about it.
ABC News chief global affairs correspondent Martha Raddatz is in Maine to speak with voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Raddatz said debates like the one between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson are still a big and important part of how voters make decisions. Maine's Senate race, a key to Democrats' goal of flipping the balance of power, has captured national attention.
"Obviously, the Graham Platner story got a lot of attention," Raddatz said. "They look at Maine now wondering whether that will tip the balance in favor of the Democrats and what will happen. It's a very key state at this point, like several others. I think in regards to that, about how voters are looking at Maine, it's a beautiful place but ooh, they have a lot of sway this year."
The Senate debate between Collins and Jackson starts at 8 p.m. on WMTW Channel 8 and can be livestreamed on WMTW.com and the WMTW app (iOS and Android). The debate can also be streamed on Very Local, the WMTW-TV YouTube channel and the WMTW-TV Facebook page. After the hourlong debate ends, it will be available to watch in its entirety on all platforms.
The Maine's Total Coverage debate will be the second debate of the week for Collins and Jackson, who had their first debate Tuesday night.
Raddatz is also the co-anchor of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" on ABC. She got her start in television at WMTW sister station WCVB in Boston, where she was the chief correspondent.

title: Obituary: Sage L. Ingalls
text:
PORTLAND – Family, friends and the Portland community are mourning the loss of 15-year-old Sage L. Ingalls, a talented musician, artist and Deering High School Sophomore who passed away unexpectedly in their sleep Sept. 29, 2026.
Born on Jan. 20, 2011 to Portland residents Nancy L. Cartonio and Jason Ingalls, Sage brought a deep joy and happiness to their parents; their two older sisters, Nevyn and Norah; “twin” stepsister Isobel, and many other family members and friends.
In all of their interests, Sage found their own unique ways, both small and large, to connect with family and friends they loved. All are left to wonder what heights they would have reached in their many passions. To read more about Sage’s life, visit dignitymemorial.com and search Sage Ingalls.
A memorial service will be held at the Jones, Rich and Barnes Funeral Home on Saturday, Oct. 10. The service starts at 11 a.m., followed by visitation hours from 12:30-3 p.m.

title: We need a public, nonprofit universal healthcare system now
text:
Paul F. Kando lives in Damariscotta.
Maine’s newspapers are full of articles and reader comments about the terrible shape of our healthcare. Not only is our business-modeled “healthcare” expensive, lately it has been even difficult to find a doctor; and essential hospital departments are being closed, based on their lack of profitability.
I am afraid capitalist ideology is at the root of what, in these United States, including Maine, passes for “healthcare.” But health, illness and knowledge are not commodities on which to legitimately profit.
At age 90, I still miss the “circuit doctors” of my teenage years. As a teenager in postwar Europe, my family and I were beneficiaries of a simple, decentralized universal healthcare alternative — which could serve as an alternative model to our failing system.
My whole native country was divided into circuits, to each of which a resident “circuit doctor” was assigned. At his/her disposal, as needed, were a pool of home visiting nurses and other assistants, as well as other doctors to consult.
The circuit doctor was paid a decent salary plus expenses and provided an office and subsidized family housing in the community. His job was to keep visiting his circuit, to (1) counsel healthy ways of living, (2) diagnose illnesses, (3) distribute or prescribe (no cost) medicines as required, (4) treat and help heal sick people in their homes and (5) arrange for pubic, nonprofit hospital or sanatorium care (including transportation), if needed.
Our family’s beloved circuit doctor routinely stopped by to see us once or twice every week. Our healthcare was free from a public nonprofit system. It was also economical: with people’s homes doubling as healthcare facilities, the cost of most hospital/nursing home rooms was eliminated. Even very ill people were cared for at home by our circuit doctors who often taught family members to do home care.
Of course, such a free public healthcare system was made possible in part by universal access to housing and tuition free education. We had no homeless people, and our doctors received their education without becoming indebted. But the most important feature was the absence of (capitalist) ideology. And in such a nonprofit system insurance companies had no legitimate role— certainly not in selecting medical procedures.
Such a system could be painlessly tax-financed through fair, progressive taxation that set the income tax rate according to a person’s real income (the standard throughout the sadly bygone, civilized era of the post-World War II liberal consensus in American politics). Alternatively, everyone could be charged a given percentage (say 2-3%) of his/her income.
Having lived with much better options in several civilized countries, I consider corporate “business” healthcare an oxymoron. Civilized countries have affordable, universal healthcare systems. Americans seem to be intellectually paralyzed when it comes to alternatives to our own failing health system, even though good alternatives abound.

title: Maine House speaker says lawmakers will aim to ease federal healthcare cuts, heating oil spikes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
House Speaker Ryan Fecteau on Thursday said that lawmakers will try to lessen the impact of federal healthcare cutbacks and the spike in heating oil prices.
Work requirements for Medicaid are set to start in 2027 and are expected to result in over 31,000 additional uninsured Mainers, according to state estimates. Those cutbacks stem from the 2025 budget bill, which also cut into the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Thousands of Mainers are also paying much higher Affordable Care Act premiums after some of the program’s subsidies expired at the end of 2025.
Fecteau and Rep. Gary Friedmann, D-Bar Harbor, participated in a news conference on Thursday with Defend America Action, a progressive advocacy group.
“We’re going to have to stand ready to provide some immediate relief when we return to Augusta,” said Fecteau, referring to heating oil cost increases and also possibly tapping into a $30 million SNAP contingency fund. The legislative session will begin in January.
The contingency fund was set up this year to continue SNAP payments during government shutdowns. Fecteau said presuming the government doesn’t shut down this winter, the state money could be used to boost the SNAP program, formerly known as food stamps.
Meanwhile, heating oil prices have reached $6 per gallon. Politicians including Gov. Janet Mills, and all three major gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett, have called for helping Maine residents afford heating oil this winter.
Friedmann said that when the Legislature convenes in January, a top priority will be figuring out “how to keep our constituents from freezing.”
The federal Low Income Heating Assistance Program helps about 40,000 Maine people with their heating costs. But the roughly $27 million in heating oil funding expected this winter won’t begin arriving until late this month and about $4 million leftover from last winter will be used to jumpstart the program for those who are most vulnerable and applied early, MaineHousing announced this week.
About 23,000 fewer Mainers had SNAP benefits in August 2026 compared with July 2025, when the budget bill was passed, according to an analysis by the Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Friedmann said Maine will do what it can to help, but state government will not be able to restore cuts made by the federal government to programs like Medicaid and SNAP.
“The state of Maine doesn’t have the resources of the federal government,” Friedmann said. “We can’t make up for the billions in healthcare cuts that the feds are passing on to us.”
James Myall, policy analyst for the Maine Center for Economic Policy, said the state is facing about $350 million in cutbacks to Medicaid and SNAP.
Myall said the state can do some things to reduce negative impacts, such as providing a few extra months of SNAP benefits for people who are about to lose SNAP eligibility.
“It’s a matter of trying to find a way to provide extra help for people, and balancing that with the state having enough money to do it,” Myall said.
Fecteau said state lawmakers are also looking at ways to help hospitals, which are struggling financially, cutting services like birthing centers or closing. That’s before funding losses begin next year under the Medicaid cutbacks.
Fecteau said “we obviously need serious help from Washington,” but there’s also a “real urgency” for the state Legislature to help Maine’s hospitals.
“We need to have all parties at the table having a real earnest conversation about what the future of healthcare delivery looks like across the state,” Fecteau said.
Medicaid work requirements that start in January 2027 will mandate that some recipients work, volunteer or attend school 80 hours per month or lose their Medicaid insurance.
Fecteau said one of his priorities will be to ensure that people who are eligible for Medicaid maintain their benefits and “don’t get discouraged and don’t walk away from the process because they can’t make sense of these new requirements.”
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services hired 35 staffers to help administer the new work requirements, with a goal of ensuring eligible people maintain Medicaid enrollment, state officials have said.

title: Maine native among astronauts who returned to Earth after 8 months in space
text:
Maine native Jessica Meir among astronauts who returned to Earth after 8 months in space
Four astronauts, including one who grew up in Maine, returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
NASA’s Jessica Meir, a Caribou native, and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”
All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX's recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston.
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the United States, Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.

title: Family demands answers after video display board falls on 5-year-old boy at school, killing him
text:
PALM BAY, Fla. (WESH) - A Florida family is demanding answers after a 120-pound video display board fell on a 5-year-old boy at school, killing him.
The victim was identified by his family as 5-year-old Bellamy Dawkins-Morris, who had autism.
Brevard Public Schools says Bellamy was seriously injured after a Promethean video display board fell on him around 11:36 a.m. Wednesday at Riviera Elementary School. School staff called 911 and began lifesaving measures before the boy was taken to the hospital, where he later died.
Family members say they are devastated by Bellamy’s death and searching for answers.
“We’re expecting him to be safe. He didn’t return to us,” said Bellamy’s great-aunt, Miriam Rodriguez. “My emotions, my sadness has subsided, and I am angry. We need answers, and we need them immediately.”
Brevard Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Mark Rendell says he met with Bellamy’s family shortly after the boy’s death.
“We lost a life today, a precious young life. There are no words to describe that loss,” Rendell said. “I’ve been doing this for over 30 years, and I really couldn’t find the words to share with them my grief and the grief that all of us have.”
According to Bellamy’s family, his mother was told he was moving the display board back and forth before it tipped over and fell on him. The family is now questioning whether the board was properly secured and whether enough supervision was provided.
Another great-aunt, Melissa Rodriguez, says they believe Bellamy’s death could have been prevented.
“I’m angry because it could have been prevented if they were paying attention to him. I’m not saying he doesn’t do things that he shouldn’t do, but this child did not deserve to not be here anymore,” she said.
The Palm Bay Police Department’s Special Victims Unit and Major Case Unit are investigating.
As investigators work to determine exactly what happened, Bellamy’s family says they are seeking accountability and legal counsel.

title: Uneasy about Susan Collins’ backers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am writing to express my concerns regarding Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection campaign receiving at least $50,000 from Marc Rowan, CEO of Apollo Global Management, through supporting PACs.
Apollo Global Management purchased and sold off the assets of paper mills in Bucksport and Jay, resulting in the loss of more than 1,000 jobs for working-class Mainers. Furthermore, the current proposal to build an AI data center at one of these sites will only offer temporary construction work, with very few permanent positions created.
Given this track record, I question whether representation tied to these interests truly serves Maine’s working class. That’s why Troy Jackson has my vote for U.S. Senate this November.
Timothy Stevens
Kennebunk

text:

title: SeniorsPlus: Free, unbiased Medicare counseling is available
text:
LEWISTON, ME – With Medicare’s Annual Open Enrollment Period running October 15 through December 7, SeniorsPlus is reminding residents of Androscoggin, Franklin, and Oxford counties that free, unbiased Medicare counseling is available through its certified counselors.
As new, for-profit Medicare-focused businesses open across the region, SeniorsPlus wants the public to understand a key distinction: as a nonprofit, SeniorsPlus does not sell insurance, does not represent any insurance company, and does not receive any financial benefit based on which plan a person chooses. Its only role is to provide accurate, unbiased information so individuals can make the choice that works best for their own health needs and budget.
SeniorsPlus Medicare counselors can help people who:
are new to Medicare;
need assistance understanding Medicare;
currently have Medicare and want to review their options;
are concerned about paying for health insurance; and/or
need help understanding when they can change their health insurance, or whether changing is the best idea.
Counselors can answer questions on Medicare, Medicare Savings Programs, supplemental insurance, prescription drug programs, and related health insurance, helping people compare Medicare Advantage and prescription drug plans and navigate enrollment.
“Meeting with a counselor helped me understand my options and what plan changes are coming for the following year,” said one person who contacted SeniorsPlus for Medicare counseling. “This helped support me in choosing which plans work for me.”
SeniorsPlus counselors commonly help clients identify opportunities to reduce prescription drug and healthcare costs, in some cases saving hundreds or even thousands of dollars per year, while ensuring they understand the coverage and provider access that comes with each option.
To speak with a Medicare counselor, call SeniorsPlus at 1-800-427-1241.

title: Mr. Drew Steps Back From Poland Education Center To Focus On Family, Will Continue Animal Outreach
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Saying Goodbye…For Now…To Mr. Drew & His Animals Too
It's the end of one chapter and the beginning of another for one of Maine's most well-known and well-loved animal attractions.
The History:
Families across Maine have come to know the name Mr. Drew, as the man with all the cool animals.
Aside from the hundreds of talks he's done with his exotic critters to school kids across the Pine Tree State, Drew Desjardins, (know to most of us now as Mr. Drew) has also operated his "Natural Science Hands-on Museum and Exotic Rescue/Reptile Zoo" out of a few different locations in Maine over the last decade.
For years, he was set up in the Lewiston Mall. Most recently, this past January, he and his many volunteers moved the entire operation of the Mr. Drew and His Animals Too Education Center to their latest location of Poland, Maine.
Mr. Drew has not only been educating the public on the animals he has, but he's been rescuing them as well, often taking in animals that humane societies will not.
What's Happening Now?
With his new facility up and running this year, and Mr. Drew appearing at speaking engagements around the state, things seemed to chugging right along.
But, as is often the case in life, sometimes challenges arise and force you to change your focus.
This year has been a tough one for many, economically, and that is certainly affecting many small businesses and nonprofits throughout Maine.
Another thing that often has an impact on people is when a loved one unexpectedly becomes ill. And when it's your child, and they end up in the hospital for an extended period of time, the world just stops, and your priorities shift, as they should.
It is this combination of recent challenges that led Mr. Drew and his team to make the very difficult decision to close the doors to their new facility, permanently.
He made the announcement over the Mr. Drew and His Animals Too Facebook Page earlier this week.
"Mr. Drew and His Animals Too Education Center in Beautiful Poland, Maine is OFFICIALLY CLOSING OUR DOORS FOREVER ON SATURDAY OCTOBER 31st. Please know Mrs. Drew and I have accepted this decision and we are NOT seeking a 'Hail Mary', any public financial support or a GoFundMe...Many of you will suggest other locations like the Auburn Mall but we do not have the finances for another move nor do we have the mental capacity to start over again...With everything going on in our lives, Mrs. Drew and I are getting older and stretched way too thin to continue at this pace."
How Will The Closure Work?
Drew says for the remainder of the month, the facility will stay open from 10 AM to 4 PM, 7 days a week, so that those who have purchased passes can use them, as they will not be able to offer refunds. They will also be open on Indigenous Peoples Day and are planning to go ahead with the Pokemon Event they had planned in advance of the decision to close. They are also in the process of reaching out to those schools and individuals who had book out for parties and field trips past the October 31st date.
What's next for Mr. Drew and His Animals Too?
The Drews sold their home of 20 years to make the move to Poland, so they don't plan to leave the community, especially after all the community did to welcome them in the first place. But they cannot sustain maintaining the facility, all of the animals and their duties to their family all at the same time.
Mr. Drew says that they plan to return to their roots of animal education and outreach, and will continue to book out traveling exhibits for birthday parties, homeschool or scouting functions and community events.
For those who had already booked Mr. Drew for the rest of this year, 2027 or 2028, he plans to honor those engagements, as well.
As for the animals, Mr. Drew says his team is working on that right now, but assures everyone that they will all end up in safe places.
"We cannot move all my animals into my home but many will come with me as I continue to do my outreach, the remaining will be move to educational facilities or sanctuaries that I fully trust. No animal will be euthanized and we are NOT adopting animals out publicly nor taking animals it but you email, I may be able to direct you to other resources."
Mr. Drew says he will be taking a step back from social media for a while, to focus on family and rebrand in a simpler way. If you wish to book him for an event, you can email a request to mr.drewsanimals2@yahoo.com.
We wish Mr. Drew, his family, his crew and all the animals all the best in this next chapter they will write.

title: Watch: Yarmouth cross country is Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Boys Team of the Week: Yarmouth cross country
As the defending Class B state champion, the Yarmouth High boys cross country team knew in preseason it had the returning talent to strive for even higher levels of performance.
On Saturday at the Festival of Champions, the Clippers showed what they could achieve, running to a convincing victory in a field of 79 teams from across New England. Yarmouth also won the event at Belfast’s Troy Howard Middle School in 2025.
Bowen Mitchell (sixth), Jackie Chalmers (eighth), Eli Chalders (13th) and Jesse Canfield (17th) were in the top 20 and just 22 seconds apart in a field with 940 finishers. Yarmouth’s next two runners, freshman Joel Kiander and junior Jasper Keller, finished 72nd and 73rd, providing enough depth to complement the strong top four. Kiander ran fast enough as a solo runner in the freshman race to edge Keller for the Clippers’ final scoring position.
This year’s field was deeper and larger because the New England Championships will also be held on the same course on Nov. 14.
Yarmouth coach Sarah Carrigan said her top four “crushed it.”
“They went in wanting to repeat, but nervous about the competition,” Carrigan said. “But in that top four, all of them PR’d by 20 to 30 seconds. They ran it really strategically, too. That course goes out wicked fast, and they stayed kind of middle of the pack in the first mile and then really turned it on and moved up and executed really well.”
“It obviously feels amazing,” Mitchell said. “I knew all the work we’ve put in was going to pay off. I know that we trusted in the process.”
Yarmouth is the clear favorite to win the Class B championship Oct. 31 at Cony High School in Augusta. Carrigan said the goal for the rest of the season is “taking that pack and moving it up.”
“We definitely have an amazing shot to win states,” Mitchell said. “That doesn’t mean we’re going to stop training. We’re going to train harder, and we want to win.”

title: Trump’s $90 Medicare rebate rolls out, but millions aren’t eligible
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Less than one-third of all Medicare recipients are eligible for the payments, which are expected to be sent out this week. Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
The election-year promise that the Republican president made over the weekend comes as the Nov. 3 midterms are fast approaching, with the cost of living and healthcare expenses among the top issues for voters.
Some questions and answers about the payouts:
Who will benefit?
Some 20.8 million people in the original Medicare Part B who are living in the United States, not receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or not paying an income-related monthly adjusted amount.
Medicare Advantage enrollees, who make up more than half of the eligible 64.2 million Medicare beneficiaries, will not receive a payment, according to KFF, a healthcare research nonprofit. Nor will 12 million low-income older adults and people with disabilities who get premium assistance.
The Part B program covers expenses such as doctor’s visits, ambulance services and lab tests. Total monthly costs generally start at about $200 and vary with income.
Allison Schuster, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that the administration “is enabling Americans to take control of their health by putting money directly back in the hands of Medicare patients.”
When will the payments go out and how will they be disbursed?
According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit on or around Friday. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, said the payment will be automatic.
“As far as a benefit goes, people don’t have to call or sign up — it’s just money they receive directly, but not everybody on Medicare will receive this money.”
A White House fact sheet says people can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to check on their eligibility for the premium rebate. To check on payment status, people should call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213.
What is the source of the money?
Payments will come out of the Medicare Improvement Fund created by Congress in 2008 and intended to make improvements to the Medicare fee-for-service program.
The fund was created to improve program management and conduct oversight of contracts and contractors, according to the Congressional Budget Office, but its purpose has expanded after various legislative changes.
This is not the first time the fund has been used.
Democratic President Barack Obama’s administration, along with Congress, redirected $20 billion to expand healthcare coverage through the Affordable Care Act.
But under Trump, it is the first time that the fund has been used to directly pay recipients.
What are critics of the plan saying?
Critics of Trump’s promise characterize the $90 payments as a preelection stunt designed to sway voters rather than address structural problems in healthcare costs and administration.
The top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, said in a statement that “this is another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans’ revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas.”
Trump recently promised $500 rebate checks to an estimated 1 million Obamacare enrollees across 30 states whom the White House alleged were overcharged by the Biden administration for some fees.
Cubanski said the Medicare rebate payments were being doled out when Americans were feeling the bite of higher food, energy and gas prices. Surging healthcare costs are only compounding those pressure, she said.
“This might be helpful for people but it might not go very far.”

“It’s something that I’ve had set in my sights my whole pro career, so it’s one of the bucket list checks. I don’t think there’s any mysteries. He’s a wrestler, I’m a striker. title: High schools Thursday: Cony football rams Camden Hills
text:
Drew Lindquist threw four first-half touchdowns, and the Cony football team cruised to a 37-0 win over Camden Hills on Thursday night in Augusta.
Cony, the ninth-ranked team in the Varsity Maine poll, bounced back from a 35-27 loss to Lawrence last week, to improve to 5-1. Camden Hills is 1-5.
Lindquist, who finished with five TD passes, first threw a 44-yard scoring strike to Tyson Horne less than two minutes into the contest, then added a 9-yard TD pass to Jacob Fifield with 55.2 seconds left in the first quarter.
Lindquist threw scoring passes of 2 yards to Austin Bucknam and 6 yards to Landen Perry in the second quarter. Fifield caught an 18-yard TD pass from Lindquist in the third, and the Rams added a safety in the fourth.
GIRLS SOCCER
SKOWHEGAN 5, MESSALONSKEE 1: Lydia Herrick and Vivian Hart each scored twice, and the River Hawks extended their winning streak to eight games by defeating Messalonskee in Skowhegan.
Mya Robinson also scored for the River Hawks (9-1-1), who led 4-0 at halftime. Herrick, McKaela McLaughlin and Joslyn Hart each had an assist. Chloe Cyr and Ellie Quirion shared goalkeeping duties, combining for nine saves.
Messalonskee (3-9) got a second-half goal from Grace McKay.
MT. ABRAM 1, WINSLOW 0: Lya Pepin scored off an assist from Evelyn Pepin in the first half to lift the Roadrunners (11-0) past the Raiders (7-3) in Salem Township.
Edna Bilodeau made four saves for Mt. Abram, while Isabella Loubier stopped 12 shots for Winslow.
FIELD HOCKEY
SKOWHEGAN 4, EDWARD LITTLE 0: Charlotte Haynie set up two goals and scored the final goal as the River Hawks (11-0) defeated the Red Eddies (4-8) in Skowhegan.
The No. 2 team in the Varsity Maine Top 10 grabbed a 2-0 lead in the first quarter on goals by Avery Farnham and Kaitlyn Dufour. Sydney Perkins made it 3-0 in the third, and Haynie scored in the fourth.
The River Hawks did not allow a shot on goal.
HALL-DALE/MONMOUTH 8, TELSTAR 0: Hannah Rauch collected three goals and two assists for the Bulldogs (3-7) in a win over the Rebels (0-10) in Farmingdale.
Avery Croll, Sidney Keleher and Rylee Rowe all chipped in with a goal and an assist. Keleher converted a penalty stroke. Emmerson Ellis and Zoe Lacasse also scored, and Katie Murphy had two assists.
BOYS SOCCER
MT. BLUE 2, BREWER 1: Luc Walker scored off an assist from Mason Kellett in the second overtime to lift the Cougars (6-2-2) past the Witches (1-7-1) in Farmington.
Kellett also set up Avery Kangas’ goal in the second half for Mt. Blue, while Paxton Snow scored in the second half for Brewer.
Ollie Cormier made six saves for the Cougars. Landon Baker stopped 10 shots for the Witches.

title: ICE detained a Maine immigrant’s wife, then let him trade places
text:
Pedro, a carpenter, was at a job site when his wife called. Immigration agents had pulled her over, but they were looking for him.
The couple, who are asylum-seekers from Angola, had discussed what to do if one of them got arrested. The scenario they feared most was leaving their 10-year-old son without his parents. On that warm July morning, his wife had just dropped the boy off at summer school classes.
Over speakerphone, Pedro asked the officers if they would come to him and let his wife go, he said, and gave them his exact location.
“But they said they would only free her [when] they got me,” he said.
It took a few hours and some negotiating by a lawyer for Pedro to strike that deal. At approximately 4 p.m. on July 8, he walked into Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Scarborough office and traded places with his wife.
As ICE activity surged over the summer, the agents employed a range of methods to detain a record number of immigrants across the country. In Maine, the agency zeroed in on a small immigrant population that has largely followed the law.
ICE repeatedly pursued immigrants like Pedro, who came to the United States legally on a visa, applied for asylum and got a work permit. The Bangor Daily News identified about a dozen such cases in federal court records filed this summer in Maine and Massachusetts. They were arrested outside of their homes or their jobs or named as surveillance targets in arrest reports or warrants, according to immigration lawyers across New England.
Arrests like Pedro’s have stood out more in Maine than in other New England states, they said. They saw few explanations beyond a push to arrest as many people as possible in a state with few immigrants, many of whom have lived openly on the government’s radar. The pattern comes as the agency ramps up more discreetly following blowback over aggressive tactics. Just days after Pedro’s quiet arrest, a rookie agent’s killing of a man in Biddeford sparked fresh outrage.
“I don’t think in Massachusetts they are doing this camping outside someone’s home thing,” said Jacob Binnall, a Massachusetts-based lawyer who helped file a habeas corpus petition challenging Pedro’s detention. “In Maine, that does seem to be happening.”
The trend also undercuts the agency’s claim that it is targeting the “worst of the worst” criminals who came here illegally. An ICE spokesperson repeated that line to the BDN in a statement that did not answer pointed questions about its enforcement strategy.
“Our message is clear: if you come into our country illegally and break our laws, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you,” the spokesperson wrote.
Pedro, his wife and their son flew into John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City on tourist visas in late 2021, then applied for asylum. His application describes his fear of being tortured over his Christian faith and political beliefs, according to a copy included in his habeas petition. He spoke through an interpreter on the condition that the BDN use only his first name because of his immigration status.
Asylum-seekers can wait years for a decision in the backlogged system, and the federal government lets them work in the meantime. One man arrested in July outside his job at a company that serves adults with disabilities had been waiting more than a decade, his petition said. A state report published last month found that foreign-born workers participate in the workforce at higher rates than Mainers as a whole.
The state’s unique immigrant composition — only about 4% of residents — prompted a study by the Washington D.C.-based Migration Policy Institute last year. It highlighted how an influx of new arrivals over the last decade, many asylum-seekers from Africa, have integrated into a more established population who tend to have citizenship or a green card.
“The number of immigrants is small, but we were struck by the impact particularly on the economy,” said Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, one of the authors. “[My co-author] and I have both been surprised in ways that Maine has now become part of the larger target of ICE.”
When Pedro got to Maine, he took English classes and joined the carpenters union. His family attended church twice a week and his son enrolled in public school. He never expected to be arrested because he had his documents, paid his taxes and committed no crimes. He and his wife only began to grow frightened in recent months, when they realized that didn’t matter anymore.
When he hung up with his wife on the day she was stopped, his mind immediately went to his son. Though he had told agents to find him at the job site, he decided he needed to get the boy somewhere safe and he left, he said.
He then holed up at a friend’s house and found a lawyer, Shannon McKinnon. On the phone with an ICE supervisor, she helped work out the deal for Pedro’s surrender. By then, hours had passed, and Pedro learned that officers had already taken his wife to a field office in Burlington, Massachusetts.
“I said a lot of caring words about my wife, that I would give my life for her, that I was willing to swap and go in her place,” Pedro said. His account matches a federal court petition, including that the agent agreed to the deal so their son would have a parent to care for him. Binnall, his other former lawyer, said the bargaining in his case demonstrated ICE’s focus on numbers.
Visa entrants are entitled to a bond hearing before an immigration judge, so they are less likely than many other detainees to file federal petitions seeking one. When they do, their lawyers often have argued that ICE never explained why their clients needed to be detained, according to the BDN’s review.
One petitioner said he had lived openly for years at the address he gave the federal government when he applied for asylum, so he was not a flight risk. A Rwandan mother said her toddler was a U.S. citizen. Another man worked for a nonprofit that helps asylum-seekers settle in Maine.
None was accused of being a danger to public safety. Most immigrants who have been detained by ICE in Maine since Trump returned to office lack a criminal record, according to the Deportation Data Project. After a five-day operation in January and this summer’s surge, Maine saw the nation’s third-largest jump in arrests of people without convictions, according to a Maine Public analysis. Angolans have accounted for the greatest number of ICE detainees here, the data show.
Jamie Wagner, a Maine-based immigration lawyer, has represented more than a dozen asylum-seekers detained only for overstaying a visa. All were released once they went before an immigration judge, he said, and several said the agents who arrested them had told them they would be. ICE did not respond to a question about those statements.
“You spent $50,000 in bonuses to hire ICE agents to arrest people that they know they’ll be released in a couple weeks at their bond hearing?” Wagner said. “That seems insane from a taxpayer perspective, putting aside the inhumanity of it.”
Even hardline conservatives have struggled with the politics of arresting working immigrants. Former Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican candidate in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, has decried “illegal immigration” in campaign ads. Last month, he revealed that his son’s father-in-law had been deported.
“That’s not right. He has a work permit. He should be allowed to stay,” LePage said at an Augusta press conference.
He also told WMTW that “anybody who came in under the Biden years should be deported,” a group that includes many asylum-seekers with work permits who make up some of Maine’s newest immigrant communities. A LePage strategist did not respond to a question about his position.
When Pedro arrived at the Scarborough office, he saw his wife for the first time that day. He had left early for work that morning, and she had still been asleep. Pedro, usually reserved in his demeanor, held her and cried. Then he went to get fingerprinted.
The officer who oversaw this process seemed to notice his anxiety. “The ICE agent said, ‘Don’t worry. You will see a judge soon and everything will be resolved,’” Pedro said.
Months later, Pedro said he still lives in a constant state of worry. But the officer was right. Nine days after his arrest, he went before a judge and was freed.

title: Millions of SAVE plan borrowers getting 90-day notices to switch
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Borrowers who have been in the SAVE forbearance plan for the past several years are now receiving notices requiring them to leave the plan and choose a new repayment option.
The personalized 90-day notices come from loan servicers and began going out in July, with new notices rolling out roughly every two weeks through the end of the year. Robert Farrington, with The College Investor, said once a borrower receives the notice, a 90-day clock begins.
“When you get your notice, you have to take action and choose a new repayment plan,” Farrington said. “For borrowers that don’t choose a new repayment plan, you will be automatically enrolled in the standard or tiered standard repayment plan at the end of that 90-day mark, which may or may not be the best plan choice for you.”
What happens if payments are missed
Once a borrower is moved into a new plan, payments begin coming due. Farrington said failing to make those payments can lead to delinquency and eventually default on federal student loans.
Farrington said borrowers are not required to wait until they receive a notice to act.
“It’s also important to note that borrowers don’t have to wait for their notice,” Farrington said. “A lot of borrowers might benefit from moving earlier, especially if you are pursuing public service loan forgiveness and you’re ready to start making payments that count again for public service loan forgiveness.”
Borrowers can begin the process at any time by visiting studentaid.gov and selecting “Enroll in a repayment plan.” Farrington also recommends using a student loan calculator now to estimate a future monthly payment and begin budgeting ahead of time.

title: Office of Maine Attorney General accidentally shares confidential case information
text:
The Office of the Maine Attorney General on Thursday accidentally sent a report containing sensitive details about active criminal cases to an external mailing list that includes local media outlets.
The 45-page Criminal Division Report contains information on homicides, missing person cases, financial crimes and more. Many of the details contained are confidential and have not been previously disclosed.
The incident raises questions about the potential implications on the cases — which include some of the state’s most high-profile homicides — as well as how such sensitive material was inadvertently sent to dozens of people outside the attorney general’s office. Danna Hayes, a spokesperson for the office, said in a written statement Thursday evening that the report was accidentally sent to a media distribution list.
“The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that. … We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine,” Hayes said.
Frayla Tarpinian, executive director for the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services, said in an interview that she was “shocked to hear about a release of this magnitude.”
“I don’t know exactly what’s on it,” Tarpinian said of the document, “but if it involves precharge information or investigatory information that has not yet been brought forward … that information is very sensitive.”
The document contains updates on active cases, recent pleas and sentences. It’s broken into numerous categories, including: murder and manslaughter cases; drug, tax and healthcare crimes; and election and public corruption violations. The first page notes in all capital letters that it “may contain confidential information including attorney work product.”
While much of the information has been included in public court records and police reports, some of the case descriptions in the document include explicit descriptions of causes of death in homicides, specific dollar amounts in financial cases, and names of suspects not yet charged in missing persons investigations.
For example, cases involving a healthcare company disclose “potential” amounts of money involved, including an instance where more than $1.5 million is suspected of being stolen. One missing person case notes that a relative was interviewed multiple times and describes their demeanor with investigators. Some case updates also include anticipated outcomes, such as how a defendant is expected to plead.
Such sensitive details becoming public can impact active investigations in a variety of ways, Tarpinian said.
“It could make pursuing a suspect harder, it could make collecting evidence more difficult and it could make it, ultimately, more difficult to bring cases forward,” she said.
It can also raise issues surrounding the justice system’s integrity, she added, by disclosing the names of individuals who may eventually be determined to have not been involved in a crime.
Kristy Winslow, a senior paralegal and supervisor for the criminal division of the attorney general’s office, sent the email at about 2:50 p.m. Thursday. A follow-up email attempted to recall the message several minutes later.
About half an hour after the original email was sent, Hayes, the attorney general’s spokesperson, asked anyone who received it to delete the message and destroy any printed copies of the report.
“Any disclosure could endanger the integrity of the criminal investigations and the safety of the individuals,” she wrote.
The list of recipients included dozens of state employees — but also journalists and email addresses for the Portland Press Herald, Morning Sentinel, Kennebec Journal, Sun Journal and Bangor Daily News, as well as WGME, WVII and WMTW owner Hearst.
Tarpinian said she feels for those involved in Thursday’s incident.
“I think we all can sympathize with sending information that we didn’t intend to,” she said. “This is just on a larger scale than I think usually happens.”

title: Leavitt field hockey tops Cony for key Class B North win
text:
TURNER — For all the good field hockey the Leavitt Hornets have played this year, moving up the Heal point standings in a strong Class B North field has proved difficult.
A win over another top squad in the region, then, was just what fifth-ranked Leavitt needed. The Hornets got one Thursday against second-ranked Cony.
Leavitt owned the game from start to finish and claimed a 4-0 victory. Calee Libby, a senior, scored three goals for the Hornets, who remain unbeaten against Class B teams, having lost only to Class A powerhouse Skowhegan.
“It was a really important win,” Libby said. “I think it’s a game that really shows what we’ve got and what we’re going to put out for some of the hard games we have coming up. … We have a lot of grit, and when we want something, we’re really going to put it forth.”
HOW THEY DID IT
• Possession dominance: Leavitt (9-1) didn’t really let Cony see much of the ball in the first half. The game was played primarily in Cony’s defensive zone, allowing the Hornets to launch a barrage of shots.
• Structure: Leavitt’s offensive success, coach Cathy Marston said, was due in part to the Hornets’ ability to keep their shape in attack. With players in the right place at the right time, Leavitt made the most of its opportunities.
“When we’re locked in, we really do keep the structure well, and the girls can finish,” Marston said. “They get a little feisty in the circle, and when they’re on, they’re on. We had our sticks down and out in front of our bodies, and we were ready.”
WHAT IT MEANS
• Leavitt jumped from fifth to second in Class B North. With two of the Hornets’ four remaining games against other contenders — Belfast and Gardiner — there’s room for them to cement their position near the top of the region.
• Cony (7-3-1) had a four-game winning streak — all via shutouts — and a six-game unbeaten streak snapped. Although the four goals allowed were the most by the Rams this season, coach Jenny Evans said a game against one of the region’s top teams was what her squad needed.
“I’m glad we had a team like Leavitt as we get geared up for the playoffs, because we can’t come off these 6-0 or 7-0 wins and expect it to be given to us,” Evans said. “It’s definitely a good reminder that we have to work for all of the balls that we need.”
UNSUNG HERO: AINSLEY BARRY
Libby’s hat trick will get the most acclaim, but fellow senior and forward Ainsley Barry was no less impactful for Leavitt. The Hornets’ second goal came on an assist from Barry, who caught the Cony defense napping with a speedy run and found Libby for a tap-in.
“She’s really the rock to our whole team,” Libby said. “She’s always looking for us and doing a great job of watching the field and knowing what’s best. It really shows how selfless she is that she passed it to me. We have a good connection going on.”
NOTABLE QUOTABLE
“We have a core of four or five who have been with us for a while, but we’ve added (four) freshmen (Grace Bilodeau, Aquinnah Chretien, Kameo Cote and Adalyn Williams) to the mix. They’ve really stepped up this year, and I’m grateful for that.” — Cathy Marston
STAT LEADERS
• Cony: Courtney Ramage (seven saves)
• Leavitt: Calee Libby (three goals), Brylee Emmons (goal), Ainsley Barry (assist), Savannah Boulay (assist), Riley Millett (two saves)
UP NEXT
• Cony: at Oceanside, 3:30 p.m. Tuesday
• Leavitt: at Belfast, 3:30 p.m. Tuesday

title: Remembering a beloved family farm dog
text:
In 1948, my maternal grandparents, Florian and Lucille Yeaton, brought home Bonnie, the runt of a border collie litter purchased in Farmington. This scrappy pup caught Grampa’s attention by fearlessly wrestling with littermates twice her size.
They took her to their Mercer farmhouse, where she slept on a horsehair blanket behind the wood cookstove. However, their hopes for a collie to herd sheep and dairy cows dimmed as Bonnie’s weight plummeted.
As a last resort, Grammy Lue wrapped Bonnie in the blanket and, in a gamble, placed her in the pigpen with a 250-pound sow nursing six piglets.
“We’ll know by day’s end whether the sow takes to her,” Grammy said to Grampa.
For 10 days, Bonnie nursed alongside the pink piglets, thriving under her unlikely foster mother’s warmth and care. Her weight — scarcely three pounds — more than doubled. Within two months, she was racing between the farmhouse and the barn.
My grandparents initially wondered if such an unusual start would leave a lasting mark. It did, but not the one they feared. Bonnie matured into an extraordinarily intelligent working dog, consistently proving her capabilities in protecting her family and livestock.
One summer afternoon in 1953, my 5-year-old brother, Robert, came face-to-face with a rabid fox behind the barn. Bonnie didn’t attack. Instead, she steadily nipped at Robert’s heels, driving him back toward the farmhouse while keeping her body between him and the fox. Grampa killed the fox with his shotgun.
A year later, Robert and our cousin, Cheryl, accidentally started a barn fire while playing with matches. Bonnie’s frantic barking alerted the family before anyone smelled smoke. Grampa fought the flames with pails of rainwater from the cistern, Mother smothered them with wet blankets, and Grammy herded the frightened livestock into the pasture. Together, they saved the barn.
But Bonnie’s greatest feat occurred on a sweltering August day in 1958.
While wading in the Sandy River to cool off, my 6-year-old twin brother, Don, was swept into the deep channel. Mother dove in after him but couldn’t dog-paddle fast enough to close the gap as he drifted downstream.
Bonnie understood the river’s currents better than either of them. Instead of immediately jumping in, she sprinted along the high bank, tracking Don as he fought to keep his head above water. Nearly 300 feet downriver, she launched off the bank, entered the current just ahead of the hairpin rapids, clamped onto his shirt collar, and hauled him onto a gravel bar.
The next morning, Don, still shaken, sat beside Grampa in the milking parlor. From his three-legged stool, Grampa squirted warm milk to the waiting barn cats and Bonnie, as he did every morning. Watching Bonnie lick her whiskers, my twin laughed through his tears and pulled her close.
The day before, she had saved his life — that morning, she helped restore his spirit.
Age never dulled her instincts. Shortly after midnight in October 1961, Don and I woke to growls rising from the pumpkin pine floorboards at the foot of our bed.
“Why’s Bonnie growling?” we yelled into the dark.
“Might be a bear in the barnyard,” Grampa answered from the adjacent bedroom. “She found fresh tracks in the orchard yesterday.”
He lit a kerosene lantern and retrieved the 12-gauge from above the kitchen door. Bonnie paced and whined at the latch. The second it lifted, she shot through the doorway and bolted toward the pigpen, her dark silhouette framed by a huge harvest moon.
“You boys go back to bed,” Grammy barked.
We obeyed but opened our bedroom window to listen. The hogs were squealing, Bonnie was barking, and a single shotgun blast cracked across the farm. Then everything went deadly quiet.
The next 10 minutes felt like an hour before Grampa and Bonnie returned to the kitchen.
“She chased a bear clean out of the pigpen,” he said, still catching his breath. “The pen door’s stove to hell, but the hogs are fine.”
Two nights later, a few miles from our farm, Ralph True shot the same bear after it killed one of his sheep. The boar weighed 490 pounds.
“Its front paws,” he told Grampa, “were the size of dinner plates.”
When cancer took Bonnie in April 1962, Grampa wrapped her one last time in the ratty horsehair blanket she’d slept on her entire life and carried her up the knoll to the apple orchard — her favorite spot on the farm. He dug her grave that night by moonlight, working past the frost line with a pickaxe and shovel. The next afternoon, my three siblings and I picked yellow daffodils from the south side of the farmhouse and planted them on her grave.
That evening, my heartbroken 5-year-old sister, Gale, barely ate her supper. When the meal was over, she quietly walked behind the cookstove and scraped her plate into Bonnie’s enamel bowl.
In the morning, her eyes lit up at the sight of an empty bowl.
Years later, E.B. White gave me the words for what Bonnie meant to our family: “A really companionable and indispensable dog is an accident of nature. You can’t get it by breeding for it, and you can’t buy it with money.”
Ron Joseph of Sidney is the author of “Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist,” published by Islandport Press.

title: Mia Goth files for divorce from Shia LaBeouf nearly 10 years after the actors married
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Mia Goth has filed for divorce from Shia LaBeouf nearly 10 years after the two actors were married.
The petition filed Tuesday in Los Angeles County Superior Court says the 32-year-old Goth and the 40-year-old LaBeouf have been separated since July 2025.
The two met and became a couple while filming “Nymphomaniac: Vol. II” in 2012, and married in 2016. They had previously split and said they were divorcing in 2018, but remained legally married, reunited in 2020 and had a daughter in 2022.
Goth is seeking primary legal and physical custody of the 4-year-old, with visitation rights for LaBeouf. She also asked the court to deny either party spousal support. It was the first marriage for both.
As with most U.S. divorces, irreconcilable differences were cited as the reason for the split.
Representatives for Goth and LaBeouf did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
The actor, born Mia Gypsy Mello da Silva Goth in London, most recently appeared as the unfaithful servant Melantho in this summer’s “The Odyssey,” and had a dual role in last year’s “Frankenstein.” She previously starred in the horror trilogy “X,” “Pearl” and “MaXXXine.”
LaBeouf was a child star on the Disney Channel’s “Even Stevens” and in the 2003 film “Holes.” He later starred in “Indiana Jones and the Crystal Skull” and director Michael Bay’s first three “Transformers” films.
The day before Goth filed for divorce, LaBeouf, for the second time, settled a lawsuit with singer, songwriter and actor FKA Twigs, whom he dated when he was split from Goth.
FKA Twigs, whose legal name is Tahliah Barnett, had alleged in a suit filed in 2020 that LaBeouf emotionally and physically abused her during their relationship that began when she had a supporting role in the semi-autobiographical film “Honey Boy,” which he wrote and starred in.
The two settled the lawsuit and had it dismissed last year, but she sued him again in March, saying nondisclosure provisions in the settlement illegally silenced her under California law.
On Monday, she moved to dismiss the second lawsuit, saying in court documents that LaBeouf had agreed to void those provisions.
In June, LaBeouf was sentenced to probation after pleading guilty to punching three people outside a New Orleans bar during Mardi Gras.

title: Time for Angus King to endorse Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In a recent newsletter, Sen. Angus King noted that he joined with Sen. Susan Collins in support of Rep. Jared Golden’s bill that would delay restrictions aimed at protecting the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale. The senator correctly described the economic importance of lobstering to Maine’s economy. However, he failed to acknowledge that the greatest threat to lobstermen is climate change and the warming oceans.
His fellow senator, Susan Collins, voted to confirm two climate deniers as heads of the EPA and the Department of Energy. Collins is the only member of the Maine delegation who takes meaningful money from fossil-fuel PACs. I do not believe Collins will support the necessary transition from fossil fuels.
It is time for Sen. King to endorse Troy Jackson, a candidate who is not beholden to the fossil fuel industry. It’s time for him to stand up for future generations, including his own grandchildren.
Tom Mikulka
Cape Elizabeth

title: Bangor Police Respond To Six Incidents Involving Glenburn Resident Over Two Days
text:
Glenburn Man Becomes ‘Frequent Flier’ At Penobscot County Jail After Multiple Arrests In One Week By Bangor PD
Officers from the Bangor Police Department were kept quite busy by the alleged antics of one Glenburn man this week.
Read More: Ellsworth, Maine Crash Kills Orrington Man, Injures Dedham Man
38-year-old Ryan Sawyer was arrested twice and involved in no less than six criminal incidents after his arrival in the Queen City, having been transported to Bangor after giving another law enforcement agency some trouble.
According to Sgt. Jeremy Brock of the Bangor PD, these incidents ranged from disorderly conduct to obstructing a public way.
The first encounter Bangor PD had with the man was Tuesday evening (October 6th) when they received calls from a local hospital that a man was taking his clothes off and acting aggressively. Officers, in the process of issuing him a trespass warning, watched him move out into the roadway, when he had to be told to move out of the way of traffic. He was issued a criminal trespass warning, left for a while, but then came back and blocked the emergency entrance to the hospital. Because this meant ambulances could not safely enter that space, cops were called back to the scene, and Sawyer was arrested.
He was out of jail by the next day, and allegedly spent Wednesday evening causing issues for Bangor residents and business again.
The first call Bangor PD received was on Clinton Street, just after 7:30 PM "for a disorderly complaint of a man throwing apples at a car whilst screaming. Sawyer
was warned for disorderly conduct." He received another warning from the police and moved on from there.
Sawyer ended up, less than an hour later, at a business on Hammond Street, where he was allegedly screaming profanities, scaring patrons and those around the business, and breaking windows. So the police were called out again.
"The business owner was still visibly upset from the encounter and told officers that she had asked Sawyer to leave when he began asking patrons of the store to use their phones. The owner said Sawyer then began hitting the windows with his fists and yelling vulgarities at the business owner. Others who witnessed the outburst were
also frightened by it."
Officers caught up with Sawyer, who had moved away from that scene after the alleged chaos he created, and arrested him again.
Read More: Fatal Crash On Bar Mills Road In Hollis Claims One Life
Ultimately, Sawyer was arrested twice in two days, and charged with 3 Bail Violations, Obstructing a Public Way, Aggravated Criminal Mischief, Disorderly Conduct and Terrorizing.
