title: UNE gets green light from Biddeford for pier project, Decary Hall renovations
text:
After roughly two years of debate, the city of Biddeford has given the University of New England the green light to move forward with its proposed research pier, as well as a building renovation project.
The city and university have been at loggerheads over development for months, with each side taking legal action against the other, city officials denying requests to begin work and passing a development moratorium, and UNE’s president decrying misinformation surrounding the situation and the erosion of the two sides’ long-standing relationship.
But a late August ruling from the Saco River Corridor Commission effectively removed any possible routes to legally blocking the pier, and soon after, the city dropped its appeal for the state’s highest court to review the matter. Now, both parties appear to be mending ties and moving forward.
On Tuesday, the City Council voted to lift an ongoing moratorium on UNE development to allow for the pier project and the renovation of Decary Hall. A day later, the city’s planning board voted to extend the university’s pier project permit.
In a joint news release Thursday morning, UNE spokesperson Sarah Delage said the actions by the council and planning board are a milestone in the collaborative effort between the city and university. UNE’s goal, she added, is to advance projects that will support education, research, economic vitality and the long-term interests of the Biddeford community.
“We are proud to call Biddeford home and look forward to continuing our investment in this city,” UNE President James Herbert said in a written statement.
The moratorium on other future UNE projects is still in place while the city’s Institutional Zone Review Committee continues its work to review relevant ordinances. Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain on Thursday encouraged residents to stay engaged as the revived committee works toward establishing clearer standards for future development.
The pier is planned to be located at the Arthur P. Girard Marine Science Center on UNE’s Biddeford campus and would provide students and professors with year-round access to research opportunities on the Saco River. The project has drawn some backlash from residents concerned about the pier’s possible impacts, particularly on those who hold moorings in the portion of the river that the university has targeted for the pier.
Any moorings impacted by the pier will be moved by the city at the university’s expense, Thursday’s news release says. The number of moorings that would need to be moved has remained unclear throughout the process: UNE has said only one would be affected, while the city has said it could be anywhere from two to six.
“Biddeford officials have taken residents’ concerns about institutional development along the Saco River seriously, including through the city’s prior court appeal and its recent testimony before the Saco River Corridor Commission,” LaFountain said in the release. “The council’s vote addresses these two previously approved projects, while the moratorium remains in place for future proposals.
“This decision shows that we can address concerns thoughtfully while still supporting projects that enhance learning, research and local opportunity.”
Biddeford and university leaders both said Thursday that the decision to lift the ongoing moratorium to allow the two projects to proceed is also a signal of the city and UNE’s shared commitment to working constructively on important issues.
“As Biddeford grows, careful planning and strong partnerships are essential,” LaFountain said. “UNE plays a meaningful role in Biddeford’s future, and we look forward to continued collaboration that strengthens both the university and our community.”

title: ‘Genocide’ or not, US must seek an end to the suffering in Gaza
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
Israel’s continuing attacks on Gaza roiled Maine’s U.S. Senate race last week, as Democratic nominee Troy Jackson apologized for remarks he made in a TV interview. He said it was “unfortunate” that there are “people here in Maine that don’t like that term” — genocide — “only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
Like “racism” and “imperialism,” the term “genocide” has become more a weapon used to batter political opponents than anything descriptive of the facts or the truth. It was indeed unfortunate that Jackson indulged his knack for plain-speaking over carefully approaching an issue that, in American as in world politics, has become a powder keg.
As we often do, we’re debating the wrong question. What Israel, led by its longtime leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done in response to the horrific attack by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, has long since degenerated into a campaign of retribution, without any coherent military or political strategy.
Through three long years, Israel has destroyed most of Gaza’s infrastructure, repeatedly put its people to flight and brought the populace to the edge of famine without really settling anything. Some 1,200 Israelis lost their lives on Oct. 7. Since then, an estimated 70,000 Palestinians have died. Depending on your definition of genocide, this may or may not qualify, but surely Israel’s response has been utterly disproportionate, and has gotten us nowhere near a future for the Palestinians that doesn’t produce destitution and endless suffering.
Normally, in a democracy like Israel, these issues would be settled by elections, but that may not be the case here. Just a week before our midterm elections, Israeli voters will choose a new government on Oct. 27, implicitly the first referendum on Netanyahu’s preparedness, or lack of it, for the Oct. 7 attacks — and the absence of any coherent plan for Gaza’s future. We must also recall that Israel withdrew from Gaza in 2005, removing settlers and leaving the power vacuum that Hamas ended up filling.
Americans often complain about our two-party system, but Israel struggles with too many parties, which come and go with each election, often built around a particular political figure. A party with as little as 3.5% of the vote can be represented in the 120-member Knesset, and throughout Netanyahu’s record tenure, serving almost continuously since 2009, his party has never held a majority.
In recent years, Netanyahu’s centrist allies spurned him, forcing him to rely more and more on Orthodox religious parties, which see all the territory now held by Israel as its by right. In reality, the West Bank and Gaza have been, since 1967, Israeli-occupied territories. They also represent the only homeland Palestinians will ever have.
The coalitions of both Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former defense chief, who represents the largest opposition party, are both short of a majority, meaning a half dozen small parties may be needed to form a government. Whether the 2026 election is any more decisive than previous ones isn’t yet known, but if Netanyahu is finally ousted, the atmosphere, if not policies, could shift.
None of Israel’s leading parties favor anything approaching reconciliation with the roughly equal numbers of Palestinians under Israeli rule, let alone negotiations for a two-state solution. Yet suffering in Gaza could be ameliorated, primarily through a U.N. peacekeeping force overseeing restoration of public services while Israel withdraws its troops.
Donald Trump has again done this country a grave disservice by throwing in his lot with Netanyahu’s vainglorious military schemes that imagine Israel subduing Iran. He followed Israel’s lead by bombing suspected nuclear enrichment facilities in June 2025, then launched “Operation Epic Fury” on Feb. 28, which seems to have petered out, despite occasional Trumpian threats of “annihilation.”
Regardless, Congress has a responsibility to bring Trump back to reality, and ensure the U.S. cuts support for Israel’s continuing attacks. Much of the weaponry used in Gaza represents American military aid.
On this issue, Troy Jackson said the U.S. should stop sending “blank checks” to Israel, an entirely sensible idea. Sen. Angus King, no radical, said essentially the same thing months ago, vowing to oppose any further military aid.
We should recognize that nothing Americans do will greatly shape the future of Gaza. Israel, unfortunately, is in control. Demonstrations on college campus won’t make much difference, nor will debating the word “genocide.”
Yet we can stop enabling the excesses of an important ally in the Middle East. We can, as Trump has not, make it clear there are limits — and firmly establish that criticism of Israel’s current government does not equate to antisemitism.

title: The Best Films and Shows By Rod Serling That Aren’t ‘The Twilight Zone’
text:
The Underrated Rod Serling Films Every ‘Twilight Zone’ Fan Should Watch
Before there were David Chase, Vince Gilligan, and Taylor Sheridan, there was Rod Serling.
In an era when television was referred to as a “vast wasteland” by government officials and critics, Serling’s work helped prove otherwise. He became so well-known for his tough, thoughtful television plays that he not only received the opportunity to create his own sci-fi anthology, he got to host it as well.
Serling’s The Twilight Zone ran for five seasons on CBS. More than 60 years after it ended its initial run, it remains one of the most beloved TV shows in history. So beloved, in fact, that when I got the opportunity to talk to Alan Sepinwall about his terrific new biography Serling: A Journey Into The Twilight Zone With TV’s First Visionary, I thought it would be a more valuable use of my time to discuss some of Serling’s other great work that doesn’t get the attention or scholarship of The Twilight Zone.
I asked Sepinwall to pick three underrated Serling projects we could discuss; anything, I said, except episodes of The Twilight Zone. His picks, and our conversation about them, follows below.
Requiem For a Heavyweight (1956)
Serling won a Peabody Award (and his second straight Emmy Award for writing) for this live TV play about an aging boxer (Jack Palance) who must decide what to do with his life after a doctor declares him unfit to fight. The play was remade as a theatrical film six years later, starring Anthony Quinn in the Palance role.
Singer: Why the TV version, rather than the film version?
Sepinwall: I picked this one because, first of all, it's really important. You want to factor in Sterling's time as a writer of ’50s scripted live television. That's this huge part of his career that’s almost completely unknown now. People think “Oh, he's The Twilight Zone guy.” They know that he was on camera. That's what he's famous for.
[Serling’s television play from 1955] Patterns is the thing that made him famous. And I think there's good stuff in Patterns [but] I don't think a lot of it holds up hugely well when you watch it all these years later. Requiem, I think, is still really good. I think the story, the characterization, the performances, especially by Jack Palance, are wonderful.
And Serling wrote a lot of different variations on it over the years. He wrote this short story in college called “The Good Right Hand” about a boxer who breaks his hand, and then “What am I gonna do?” He did another thing called The Twilight Rounds. Because the thing Rod was obsessed with besides boxing — which he did himself in the Army — was, ‘What am I gonna do when one day I can't write anymore?”
The the TV play aspect of it is is interesting to revisit. It's an art form that is basically non-existent today. It was born of technological limitations, obviously, but you see here that when it's done well, it can be very powerful. And it was making me think “Maybe somebody should should do a live TV play?” And I remember there have been some examples of people trying to resurrect it in the ’90s? Didn’t they do Fail Safe with George Clooney?
Clooney is huge into live TV. He made them do the live ER episode. He did live Fail Safe. They did a Good Night, and Good Luck for television at some point.
I definitely think the idea of it is great. Even just a filmed play. It doesn't have to be a pro shot. Just “Hey, we're gonna have a playwright come in and do the sort of thing they would do for the stage,” but as a TV movie.
Part of it is just the death of the TV movie, you know? I guess we have them now, with films that go straight to streaming ... the technology is primitive, but also theater at the time was considered by far the highest art form available in America. So, hey, we can do a play for television and that will make you feel a little classier for owning a TV set.
And yet one of the things that you talk about in the book was that Serling was one of the most famous TV play writers, but he didn't really have a lot of success on Broadway. Why do you think that is?
I talked to Anne Washburn, who did The Twilight Zone play in London about a decade ago. And she said [the stage] is just a different kind of muscle. He also struggled, frankly, writing for movies other than the one we're going to talk about. And I think it's just a different set of skills. Both of them are filmed entertainment, or in the case of a live teleplay and then a play.
Yet the things that he was good at seem to really work well in a TV context versus as a play, and I don't know that he necessarily put enough of the effort into ‘How am I different if I'm writing a play? How am I different if I'm writing a screenplay? How am I different from writing a novel?’ He tried doing all of these other kinds of writing, and some of it's really interesting, but a lot of it just doesn't work because he didn't already have that skill set, and he was ultimately an impatient guy who [thought] “I know how to do this thing. That's what I'm gonna do.”
You mentioned in the Acknowledgments of your book that you liked The Twilight Zone and some other things, but you were not a Serling scholar or anything like that when you started the project. So I'm curious if there was anything that was particularly revelatory to you during the process? I know from writing books myself that you start out with certain expectations, and then through the research, there are discoveries you do not anticipate along the way.
One of the big appeals to me of getting to do this book was I'd always heard about Requiem for a Heavyweight; I'd heard about Patterns. I knew about Serling's pre-Twilight Zone rep. But I’d never had an excuse to watch the stuff, and a lot of it's on YouTube. So that was cool.
But the big discovery was seeing how much of his stuff was autobiographical, which was, frankly, a godsend for me because I'd never written a biography before. And I just went in thinking, “How am I going to structure this? How is this going to work?” And when you start learning about him, and then you watch the stuff at the same time, you're like “Oh, this comes from this part of his life. This comes from this part of his life.” And it gave me the whole way that the book is shaped.
I like reading biographies, but I'm a really impatient reader sometimes, I guess like Serling. And I'm like, “I understand that this person's childhood is important. I understand that the early parts of their career are important. I really want to get to reading about the thing that they're already famous for.” And so I thought, “Well, how am I going to get people to read about Serling as a kid in Binghamton or Serling in the war, Serling in college, and not feel the same way I do?” And I realized I'm just gonna take the famous writing and use that to sort of draw parallels. So you're reading about Twilight Zone long before you actually get to The Twilight Zone.
Seven Days in May (1964)
Almost all of Serling’s most popular and acclaimed work in his lifetime was all on television, but he did write a number of film scripts, including the one for this Oscar-nominated 1964 thriller, directed by John Frankenheimer, about an attempted coup of the U.S. government by the hawkish Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (Burt Lancaster), who is disgusted by the President of the United States (Frederic March) and his plan to sign a disarmament treaty with the Soviet Union.
Why did you pick this one?
Because it's the best movie he wrote. He wrote a bunch of films that actually got released, and he wrote a lot of others that didn't — and I read some of those scripts. The movies were a struggle for Serling. Several of the movies he wrote are just god awful. [The 1958 Western] Saddle the Wind is bad. I think he said it should have been called Saddle the Fart.
[The 1966 thriller] Assault on a Queen with Frank Sinatra; such a good premise, and it's the most boring goddamn thing. Everyone failed on that, including him. And even Planet of the Apes, which is by far the most successful movie he was associated with, most of his work was rewritten. I've read his draft, and it’s very good too, but I don't know if that version would have been the enduring hit that the Michael Wilson is. [Wilson rewrote Serling’s Planet of the Apes script.]
I also think the Requiem for a Heavyweight movie is good too, although I prefer the TV version, in part because I like Palance more, in part because I like the ending more. I'm not in love with the dark ending that he went with for the movie. But Seven Days in May is like the one where it's like “This is Rod Serling, screenwriter.” It all works.
At least half of that is just Frankenheimer, because Frankenheimer was a great director. They worked together a bunch. The thing that Frankenheimer was better at than almost any director who ever lived was, “What's an interesting visual way I can show this?” And so you have a movie that's super talky, like almost all of Serling's stuff, but it's being done by this hugely dynamic visual stylist. And so you're never bored as you're just getting monologue after monologue after monologue, because it's being shot really well. So it's exciting, even though it's just philosophical arguments about pacifism versus war.
You mentioned reading some of his scripts. I'm sure you've read lots of scripts by lots of writers over your career. What do you make of Serling's scripts? How do they compare to watching the actual films or TV shows?
The TV shows, when you read those, they're good. Most of the movie scripts that I read were written for stuff that didn't get made. And sometimes I would listen to him dictate them, and that was cool. Because he's just saying, like, “Name, line of dialogue, punctuation, spelling,” and he's going a mile a minute. I have no idea how anybody could work that way. Obviously you're writer, I'm a writer, and when you're really feeling it, the words are flowing out of you. But that’s at a keyboard. I feel like the keyboard is sort of this necessary intermediate step to make sure it makes sense. He’s just talking, and it’s great.
But in terms of the scripts themselves, I read a couple in great detail. One was The Salamander. It is this Italian conspiracy thriller. And eventually, it was made [in 1981], cheaply, and it's a 90-minute movie. And his script was, like, 180 pages. He did not cut anything out of the book, whatsoever, and it's also him sort of struggling to do, “more adult content,” which mostly meant like he could have people curse and someone's looking at a Playboy centerfold, that kind of thing. It felt like, “All right, I'm trying to do this thing that is not necessarily in my comfort zone.” So that's not great.
And [1970’s] RPM — revolutions per minute — is about liberal activism on college campuses and, you know, hippies and all of that. It's almost entirely, again, monologues and speechifying. And on the page, it's not that exciting. But maybe if somebody like Frankenheimer had directed it as opposed to Stanley Kramer ... and he got Erich Segal from Love Story to write it. [Serling’s work on the film was uncredited.] And it stars Anthony Quinn.
Anthony Quinn was in The Salamander too.
There you go. They kept crossing paths.
When you're listening to those dictated scripts, does he sound like the Rod Serling that I imagine The Twilight Zone? Does he speak differently when he's not on camera?
He's a little bit older, because most of the ones that have been like preserved are from like the last seven, eight years of his career. You can hear him do a Night Gallery, and his voice is a little bit older. His daughters would say he didn't talk that way in real life. But every interview you watch with him, that's how the guy talks! He sounds like the host of The Twilight Zone, and every character he wrote talked like him. So you hear him dictating and it sounds like it's a Twilight Zone intro.
With regard to Seven Days in May, I had not seen the movie before. I haven't read the novel, so I don't know how it compares to the novel. But watching the movie, it does feel like Rod Serling. It has a lot of his themes. I don't know if you agree, I don't know if you read the book, but I could feel the Serling-ness of it, which maybe you can't feel in some of those less successful films, which I admit I haven't seen.
That's part of why it's good. Saddle the Wind or Assault on a Queen, that's just genre stuff. That was not really his interest. Even when he did a Western himself, like the TV show The Loner, that was an excuse for him to work through the same philosophical and sociological questions he was always interested in. This and Planet of the Apes are really the only two movie scripts he did that got made that feel like Rod Sterling, and the kind of thing he cares about.
And structurally, [the released film of] Planet of the Apes is largely what he wrote. The ideas are there. It's more Michael Wilson changing dialogue and changing characterization. But Serling cared a lot about nuclear disarmament. He had fought in World War II and cared passionately about that, but he became more and more anti-violence as he got older. By the ’60s, he quickly turned against Vietnam. He felt it was a mistake for us to be there. So he's writing about something with passion, and you can feel that in the writing, whereas a lot of these other things, it feels like he's going through the motions.
When you hear the description, if you don't necessarily know that it's Rod Serling, you hear, “Oh, it's about a military coup,” you imagine something more violent and more action oriented. And then you see the movie and the big climax is two guys sitting in the White House talking. The end of the movie is a press conference. When you know it’s a Rod Serling script, that does make sense because, as you said, he enjoyed his speechifying. Where does that love come from?
Some of it is just the stuff he grew up reading. I don't really touch on it in the book, but I know just from like reading letters back and forth between him and Nolan Miller, who was the writer in residence at Antioch when he went to college, that Serling loved these radio plays, which are just people talking and giving speeches because you're not seeing any of the action.
So that was his thing. He liked words on the page, and he certainly couldn't resist, I guess, because he was a guy who monologued. You watch interviews with him, and Mike Wallace asks him a question, and it's five minutes before Mike Wallace gets to interject again. So I think that was just the way he talked. He thought in monologue, and so he wrote in monologue.
And I guess that makes sense when you watch The Twilight Zone. He gives monologues in every episode, and he's so good at it. Even though he wasn't an actor, he's the perfect host and introducer of these stories, often giving these very flowery monologues, explaining the theme of whatever you are about to watch or have watched.
Yeah. I did the audiobook for [Serling], which meant I had to read aloud a number of Serling Twilight Zone monologues. And it ain't easy! Because again, he wrote the way he talked and nobody else ever talked like him. For instance, I'm just going to read this aloud. I'm not even going to try to do it right, but [adopts a Serling-esque cadence]: “In just a moment, that hope chest will be opened, and an improbable phantom will try to bedeck the drabness of these two people's failure-laden lives with the gold and precious stones of fulfillment.”
Who the hell talks like that? Nobody, except Ron Sterling. When he does it with a cigarette in his hand and in the suit, he pulled it off.
READ MORE: Every Episode of The Twilight Zone, Ranked
The last thing I wanted to ask before we talk about the last show you picked is something you mentioned, which was that you read Serling’s script for Planet of the Apes. I have always been very curious about that because I love that film, and I love The Twilight Zone, but I’ve always heard that Apes was heavily rewritten after he left the project. Do you think if they had produced his script it would have still been a success? Do you understand why they decided to rewrite him?
The main reason they revised it was for budget because his script is set in what looks like a contemporary city with apes wandering around wearing suits and ties and driving cars. For whatever reason, it was felt like dressing an entire city to look like apes live there would be prohibitively expensive. It was simpler to do it, and cheaper to do it, if they were living in a more primitive society. By the time they wanted to do that, Serling had written, I think, four or five drafts, and he was always overcommitted to different projects, and he just said, “I can't do it anymore. You guys get somebody else.”
His version of the script is a lot talkier. It's a lot more philosophical, but I think the biggest change — because the Statue of Liberty is his drafts — is the main astronaut character is a man who is arguing on behalf of humanity and is thoughtful and empathetic and all of that. And Heston’s character is like a misanthrope who hates everyone and is cynic and realizes when he winds up in this terrible situation “Oh, I have to argue on behalf of humanity because I'm literally the only one who can do it.” And that's sort of a fun idea, and that's not really present in the Serling thing.
But also, the Sterling script is not nearly as action-oriented as the Michael Wilson version. Maybe [Planet of the Apes director] Franklin Shaffner would have added some of those elements anyway, and he would have asked Rod to do it, or he would have, like Frankenheimer, just figured out stuff on his own. But the Wilson script also has stuff like “Get your paws off me, you damn dirty ape!” which is hugely quotable and not at all the sort of thing that Rod would write.
“They’re Tearing Down Tim Riley’s Bar” (1971)
Six years after The Twilight Zone ended, Serling created a similar anthology series called Night Gallery, with less successful results; the show only survived for three tumultuous seasons, with Serling given far less creative control than he’d had on its predecessor. Serling did contribute a number of Night Gallery scripts, including this one about a washed-up businessman (William Windom) on the precipice of an unwanted retirement.
I have seen the pilot or the TV film of Night Gallery. But that might be the only Night Gallery I had ever seen before this. With admittedly very little experience of watching it, I have always seen it as kind of like an inferior Xerox copy of The Twilight Zone. Would you say that's fair?
That's fair. I think there are some episodes — and “Tim Reilly's Bar” is one of them — that I think are really, really good. It’s not even so much episodes, as it is segments, because the way that the show was structured was there would be multiple stories per episode, and some of them are really good. Some of them are just awful. Some of those are ones Rod wrote, some of them are from other writers.
The guy who ran the show, Jack Laird, hated Rod. Rod hated him. It was constant fight for control. Rod was not good at writing comedy, but Jack Laird was somehow worse and he kept doing these vaudeville-style sketches in between the segments. It’s like Cesar Romero as Dracula, and he comes to a blood bank, and he's like, “You don't understand. I don't want to make a deposit. I come for a withdrawal!” It completely kills the mood.
But there are some segments that are very good, and [Serling] did a lot of good adaptations. That’s an area where he's underrated a little bit, because when he's doing an adaptation, the characters are not Rod Serling. He's working with material that other people gave him, and he would make very smart choices in how to adapt them. There's this one called “The Caterpillar.” And in “The Caterpillar,” a man is jealous, he's in love with a woman, the woman's gonna marry another guy, and this guy, Lawrence Harvey, decides, “I'm going to murder my rival so that she will have to marry me.” And he hires someone to put this brain worm in the other guy's ear. And for whatever reason, the brain worm instead winds up in Lawrence Harvey's ear, and it crawls inside and it's driving him mad and it's clearly going to kill him. It will make you never want to put anything else in your ear for the rest of your life.
I forget how the original story ends, but Sterling came up with this great new ending, which is Lawrence Harvey somehow survives the initial attack of the brain worm, and he's like, “Okay, all right. This was a bad idea. I shouldn't have done it, but I guess I'm doing okay now.” And the doctor treating him says, “Just so you know, that worm was a female, and females lay eggs.” That's a great ending. It's the perfect little knife twist and he came up with that.
The point being, Night Gallery is more up and down. It looks super ’70s in a way that Twilight Zone does not always look super ’60s. The washed out colors and the fashions; even when they're doing period pieces. It hasn't aged as well. But some of it is very good.
When we were talking about Requiem for a Heavyweight, you alluded to this, but there is this theme that runs through so much of Serling’s work going all the way back to those TV plays: This terror about getting older and becoming obsolete. It makes sense to me on a certain level in “They're Tearing Down Tim Riley's Bar.” That was written at the tail-end of Serling’s career. He's been through ups and downs. But we were talking about Requiem for a Heavyweight from 1956 and it’s present in that film as well. Why was he so fixated on this even as a young man?
It's even in the stuff he wrote in college when he was in his mid 20s. And I think part of it is his father died young, and that really scarred him. His father died in his early 50s, not too much older than Rod was when he died. He knew his grandfather had, on that side, also died young. So part of it is that Mickey Mantle thing of, “I'm not gonna live that long. I'm a ticking time bomb. What can I do with the time?”
He was also an acutely self-conscious person. Despite being really charismatic and outgoing and popular, he was always judging himself and worrying that what he did wasn't good enough, or if it was good, he was doing it for the wrong reasons. So he lived with this acute fear of “Things are working now, but eventually it's gonna fall apart and then what?” I mean, I feel that way too! I don't know how to do anything but be a TV critic and eventually there's gonna come a day where nobody's gonna pay me for that and then what? So I can absolutely relate to that.
But yeah, he was sort of an old man before he was an old man. They called him “TV's angry young man,” but he was really TV's youngest old man. He thought a lot about “What's coming later? What happens if this fails?” His dad ran a grocery business that was very successful for a while when he was a kid, and then it went bust, and they had to downsize and live in an apartment. So that was an acute thing for him as well.
The other thing about Night Gallery that I found interesting — because again, I’m certainly familiar with the concept but I didn’t know anything about the behind the scenes drama before your book — is that while Serling is the host and wrote a lot of it, he was not the guy in charge in the same way he was on The Twilight Zone. He’s working with that producer who hates him, doesn't really respect him, and doesn't always agree with his choices. And in your book, you go into how the show was butchered in syndication. And it’s fascinating to look at how shabbily people would treat television shows back then, even by a respected writer. Serling was one of the most famous writers in TV history, and this is what they did to his show!
It did make me think about how Serling dies in 1975, so he doesn’t live to see the rise of cable television. He’s only 50 years old. If he had survived for another decade or two, how do you think he would have adapted? How do you think his career would have continued if he had lived a little bit longer?
He was really struggling to find his way in the early to mid ’70s until he passed away. What would happen if he was alive for like five more years? Spielberg, Lucas, Landis, all of these guys who grew up like idolizing him would have like said “All right, Rod, please come write me a script and I will try to make that script.” There were all of these Serling fans who grew up on his stuff, were inspired to do what they did by him, and I imagine they would have recruited him in some ways. It would have been easier for him to do stuff in the movies again, working with these more adventurous filmmakers.
Once cable TV started, I think he would he would have written for that and it would have gone well for him. He would have been a much older man by the time we get to the ’90s, but I think he could have done some interesting stuff there. Frankenheimer was directing HBO movies basically until he died.
Sure, and he makes Ronin in the ’90s. He has a bit of a resurgence. And The Twilight Zone Movie, which is a misbegotten object for other reasons, is only like eight years after Serling passed away. He could have written that.
He could have. He was kind of a man out of time when he passed away. If he had held on another ten years, he would have had a whole third act. It's kind of a bummer. But he did have the incredible timing to be born when he was, in terms of breaking into television to begin with.
Right.
Because if he was even born five years later, TV as the Wild West, it would have been settled by the time he started trying to write for television, and the opportunities that he had living in Cincinnati, mailing scripts to New York, would not have been there, right? But at the same time, then he lingers long enough to get past the point where TV wants his kind of stuff, and he dies before his acolytes come into enough power that they could have given him that third act.
Alan Sepinwall’s Serling: A Journey Into the Twilight Zone With TV’s First Visionary goes on sale on October 13.

title: Trump says US will not resume military strikes on Iran before the midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States.
Trump, while stumping for Republicans this week, has hinted that was confident that at endgame to the war cold come in the days before or after the election, while also hinting that he remained open to resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
But Trump in a social media post on Thursday said the U.S. “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”
Trump added that his team has been “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Negotiations had appeared at a standstill since Trump late last month publicly rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the U.S. met certain conditions.
Iran, however, said last week they had received a U.S. counterproposal. And Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Thursday said he expected Tehran would offer a formal reply within days.
Trump’s post comes as the military has dispatched more resources to the region. U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could arrive as early as the end of October.
Trump’s announcement was made the same day the USS Abraham Lincoln was due to arrive to its home port in San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war. There have been reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
The USS George Washington, which is usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August. The other aircraft carrier in the Middle East, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

title: PVC pipes swept away by Hurricane Helene flooding still dominate cleanup of North Carolina river
text:
WOODFIN, N.C. (AP) — They’re piled on river banks, lodged in uprooted trees, embedded in sediment and jammed under logs. Many are tangled in mounds of debris up to two stories high.
Two years after Hurricane Helene leveled forests, bulldozed houses and filled western North Carolina rivers with everything from cars to refrigerators, the work of cleaning up the debris goes on. And along the iconic French Broad River, known for its whitewater rapids, one item stands out among the rest: massive numbers of PVC pipes that washed away from a factory north of Asheville.
“Just the amount of time and energy that we put into removing all this pipe is exhausting,” said Jon Stamper, operations director at MountainTrue, the nonprofit conducting cleanup on several rivers affected by Helene. “We still have stretches of river that haven’t been touched.”
MountainTrue estimates its crews have pulled hundreds of thousands of pipes from the river — most of which went to landfills — with an untold number still littering the river for 70 miles (113 kilometers), to a large lake at the Tennessee border.
Canada-based IPEX would not say how many pipes were stored at its Woodfin, North Carolina, site before the storm or share results of a company-funded study of how much remains in the river, calling the information “commercially sensitive.” Officials did say 60% of pipes stored outdoors at the site, sandwiched between railroad tracks and the river, were swept away in the 2024 flood, but most were recovered fairly quickly.
But the company acknowledged that the remaining debris was significant and has agreed to pay MountainTrue $500,000 toward continued cleanup on the French Broad, which will allow the organization to continue working into next year.
A $10 million state grant awarded to MountainTrue in 2025 to clean up debris in several western North Carolina rivers that was set to expire in December has been extended to February. The organization said there’s still a long way to go, and estimates that it’s spent 50,000 work-hours and over $1.5 million just on pipe removal, which is only in the French Broad.
PVC pipe comprises 80% of the debris in some areas, according to MountainTrue, posing risks to rafters and kayakers, changing water flow and altering the ecosystem.
“We understand the ongoing challenge,” IPEX CEO Colleen Pritchett said. “We recognize that … recovery efforts are complex, they’re resource-intensive, and it’s constantly shaped by the river conditions.”
Epic flood took everyone by surprise
Hurricane Helene hit western North Carolina in late September 2024, dumping more than 30 inches (76 centimeters) of rain in some areas, triggering landslides, toppling trees, pushing buildings off their foundations and choking waterways.
At IPEX, an earthen berm was the only thing separating tall stacks of pipes from the French Broad River. Company officials said they expected a so-called 100-year flood — meaning it has a 1% chance of occurring in any given year — and moved pipes out of that flood zone.
But the flooding from Helene was 10 times worse.
“We secured the site as best we could and we sent people home a day before the flooding was expected,” said Johnny Drummond, vice president of manufacturing. He said the company did not anticipate a 1,000-year flood, which has a 1-in-1,000 chance of occurring.
The company closed the factory for a couple of months afterward, with losses “well over $100 million,” Pritchett said. It since has invested over $100 million to repair and strengthen the buildings, and now is studying ways to contain the pipes in future floods — something MountainTrue had publicly urged for months.
Though there’s much more than IPEX debris still in the waterways, the pipes are so ubiquitous that “there are places where you go that it makes up almost everything that we remove,” said Stamper, who formerly worked for a whitewater river outfitter and now oversees 10 cleanup crews totaling about 100 people — many of them former river or fishing guides who lost their livelihoods after the hurricane.
Removing the pipe is especially vexing because it binds with other debris and has embedded in the river bottom, where fish and other creatures have taken up residence inside. Stamper said he also worries about long-term environmental and health effects from the pipe, which can degrade and become brittle, leaving microplastics in the river.
“We want to avoid that stuff sitting there forever and just slowly deteriorating and breaking into smaller and smaller pieces,” said Stamper. “Some of the pipe that’s been sitting out since Hurricane Helene that has been exposed to the sun all the time is getting to the point where you could crack it when you grab it.”
Removing pipes is tedious, sometimes dangerous
Some of the pipes — both straight, rigid plastic and flexible coils that have unraveled — are under huge piles of tangled logs topped by other debris, often in mounds 20 feet (6 meters) high. Cleanup crews “just sort of picture it as a jungle gym” that they must climb and balance on as they clear the pile, said Jemima Filiss-Cook, who leads the cleanup in Madison County, where most of the pipe is concentrated.
She said many crew members were already cleaning up the river before MountainTrue hired them, as a way of “trauma bonding” over what had happened.
They include avid outdoorspeople, including rock climbers, because the cleanup is “quite a tedious and technical process” that requires a comfort with the rigors of the job, said Anna Alsobrook, MountainTrue’s French Broad Riverkeeper.
Crews saw longer pipes into smaller chunks, load them on a boat, then take it downstream to a landing spot where it’s loaded onto a truck. Almost all of the pipe goes to a landfill, though some in good condition are given to community members, because there are no good recycling options, MountainTrue said.
“I truly don’t think anybody else could do this work except for our debris team members,” said Alsobrook, noting they must be able to navigate whitewater rapids with a boat full of pipes and saws.
The first priority was removing pipes that could pose an immediate danger or entrapment hazard to tubers or kayakers, and much of the remaining debris stranded in flood plains and on banks, especially around riverbends and corners and vulnerable to being washed away in another flood, Stamper said.
But it becomes apparent that many pipes are still in the river whenever the water levels change, he said.
MountainTrue is applying for other grants to help extend its program after state and IPEX funding run out, Stamper said, because it could take years to remove all the debris.
“We’re going to do our best as long as the funding allows,” he said. “But there’s going to be pipe out there that we can’t get ever.”
___
Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan.

title: Phillips-area school district discusses possible school consolidation at forum
text:
Maine School Administrative District 58 residents were presented Oct. 6 with three options that could decide which district campuses stay open in the coming years.
At a community forum on future planning at Mt. Abram High School in Salem Township, representatives of Oak Point Associates, an architecture firm, explained their findings on possible renovations, consolidations or closures for its campuses across the district.
The district includes Avon, Kingfield, Phillips and Strong, with elementary schools in Kingfield and Phillips, an elementary and middle school in Strong, and a high school in Salem Township.
Voters in Kingfield and Strong will decide Nov. 3 whether to withdraw from MSAD 58, with many citing gaining local control of their schools.
The architect said the firm’s projections assume all four towns will remain as members.
Tyler Barter, an architect and principal at Oak Point Associates, presented three potential options, from the least expensive to the most.
None of the options came with exact costs associated with them.
Under option one, the district would move students pre-K through third grade to Kingfield Elementary School. Fourth through eighth graders would attend Day Mountain Regional Middle School in Strong. Mount Abram High School would remain, but the district’s central offices in Phillips would relocate to the school.
Option two would also reconfigure the schools, with additional renovations. Kingfield Elementary would see renovations and an addition of the main offices serving pre-K through fourth grades. Day Mountain and Mount Abram schools would remain largely as is with some renovations to update the buildings.
Option three would see a single, combined pre-K through grade eight school next to Mount Abram High School. This option would carry the highest cost.
Barter said although it would certainly be the most expensive in up-front costs, in the long term, a single campus could be the least expensive when deferred maintenance and other costs associated with options one and two were taken into account.
In every option, Oak Point recommended the closure of Phillips Elementary School due to the cost of upkeep compared to Kingfield and Day Mountain schools.
Barter said if one or both towns did withdraw … “we would have enough data now to help the district with that discussion in November.”
Closing one of the schools would act as a cost-saving measure by immediately ceasing the daily operational costs. Oak Point did not calculate the exact savings made by closing each school, but Barter said it would be significant.
“This is the very beginning of kind of a longer process, so as we start to get more information, we will work with your school board to really refine these,” Barter said.
The three options will be presented at the next school board meeting Oct. 15 for feedback.

title: Cash App settlement payments are coming in October. Here's who qualifies
text:
Cash App settlement payments are coming in October. Here's who qualifies
Users who filed approved claims in a Cash App $15 million data security settlement could receive payments this month.
This story originally appeared in The Dallas Morning News, a Hearst publication.
Cash App users who filed claims in a $15 million class-action settlement over alleged security failures are expected to receive payments in October, according to the official settlement website.
The settlement stems from a lawsuit alleging that Cash App and its parent company, Block Inc., failed to adequately protect customers’ information following security incidents in 2022 and 2023.
Current and former users whose accounts or personal information were accessed without authorization, or who experienced fraudulent transactions between Aug. 23, 2018, and Aug. 20, 2024, were eligible to submit claims.
Those eligible could seek up to $2,500 for documented out-of-pocket losses related to the incidents. Actual payments will depend on approved claims and the settlement terms, the statement said.
The court granted final approval on March 27, 2025. The deadline to file a claim was Nov. 18, 2024, and new claims are no longer being accepted.
According to the settlement administrator, payments to approved claimants are scheduled for sometime in October. More information is available at cashappsecuritysettlement.com.

title: Cooper Flagg and New Balance unveil logo with nod to Maine
text:
After nearly two years of professional partnership, Maine native Cooper Flagg and New Balance unveiled a new logo Thursday that will be used on all collaborative product lines.
The video announcement includes multiple nods to the Pine Tree State, including a shot of the basketball court at Nokomis Regional High School in Newport and a Maine license plate reading “FL4GG.”
The logo itself is a stylized “CF,” with the C resembling a pine tree, another nod to Flagg’s home state.
Flagg attended Nokomis as a high school freshman, earning Maine’s Gatorade Player of the Year in 2022 and helping the Warriors win the school’s first Class A championship. He then played two years at Montverde Academy in Florida and then a year of college basketball at Duke University.
In June 2025, Flagg was selected with the No. 1 overall pick in the NBA Draft by the Dallas Mavericks. He was named Rookie of the Year last season after averaging 21 points, 6.7 rebounds, 4.5 assists and 1.2 steals per contest.
Flagg’s second season tips off Oct. 21 when the Mavericks play at the Houston Rockets.

title: Barack Obama boosts Troy Jackson in Maine Senate race against Susan Collins
text:
Former President Barack Obama is wading into Maine’s closely watched U.S. Senate race between Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
On Thursday, the Democrat’s campaign released video of the former president urging voters to pick Jackson, a former state Senate president.
Obama, speaking directly to the camera while sitting in a chair, said he’s “proud to be on board” as a Jackson supporter, citing the candidate’s prior work as a logger and a political leader.
“In this economy, we need a fighter like Troy,” Obama said. “A fifth-generation logger, Troy worked 80 hours a week and still struggled to get by. So as Maine’s Senate president, he fought to raise wages, lower the cost of prescription drugs and provide free lunch to every student in the state. After Roe was overturned, Troy helped protect the right to an abortion in Maine.”
“And now we need Troy to deliver for us in the Senate,” Obama continued. “So do not sit this one out. Get out there and vote for Troy Jackson.”
The 50-second video is one of about two dozen Obama has recorded in key battleground races for U.S. Senate and governor. Politico reported that Obama — arguably the most prominent spokesperson for the Democratic party — is targeting races where he can “move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters, particularly in states with key races.”
The video seeks to consolidate moderate Democrats and independent voters behind Jackson by focusing on economic issues.
Those voters have proven to be fickle in Maine. A CNN exit poll in 2020 found that Collins earned the support of 13% of Democrats, and that she had a three-point edge with independents in her polls-defying win over former House Speaker Sara Gideon.
Obama’s pro-Jackson message comes only days before progressive U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is slated to hold three rallies with Jackson over the weekend.
Jackson said in a written statement that he was honored to have Obama’s support.
“The momentum we’re seeing in Maine is something I’ve never seen before,” Jackson said. “Working people are sick and tired of a government that works for the wealthy and well-connected while they struggle to get by. They’re ready for change, and together, we’re going to bring that change to Washington.”
Blake Kernen, a spokesperson for Collins, criticized the video, noting that everyday Mainers are more important to Collins than high-profile politicians.
“The fact that Troy Jackson is endorsed by Obama, funded by Chuck Schumer, and campaigning with Bernie Sanders this weekend tells you how much the national Democratic machine wants to control Maine’s Senate seat,” Kernen said in an emailed statement.

title: Susan Collins does, in fact, answer the call
text:
Letter writer Earle Wingate of Peru recently asserted that he has written to Sen. Susan Collins “for more than eight years” and that he has “never” received a response from her. (“Country over party means time’s up for Susan Collins,” Sept. 30).
It is true that Wingate has written to the senator many times, but it is false that he has never received a reply to his correspondence.
Our office last received an email from Wingate on Jan. 28, 2025, urging Sen. Collins to oppose the confirmation of certain executive branch nominees.
Wingate received a written response from Collins informing him of her decision to oppose Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel to their nominated positions. Over the past eight years, Wingate has received seven responses to his messages, writing on topics including the following: support for Ukraine (she does), support for convicting Donald Trump during his impeachment trial (she did), opposition to withdrawing U.S. troops from Syria (she did), opposition to the 2019 partial government shutdown (she led the work to end it) and a message approving of her vote to confirm Justice Kavanaugh. Other messages to Collins from Wingate indicated that he did not wish to receive a response.
The truth is that Sen. Collins welcomes hearing from Mr. Wingate and all Mainers and our office strives to respond quickly. We also believe readers deserve an accurate account of the facts.
Katie Brown
Chief of Staff, Sen. Collins
Washington, D.C.

title: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had described it as being “public.”
The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice on Wednesday, said, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the U.S., especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Experts offer mixed reactions on the plan
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike’s botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.
When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, “I don’t recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government,” she said.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Trump has spoken out against public executions in Iran
Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on Feb. 28.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on Jan. 14. “It’s stopping, and there’s no plan for executions.”
In his State of the Union address just days before launching the Iran war, Trump reiterated, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on Dec. 3.”
It’s not clear if Hasan will try to appeal
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan began his portion of the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence.
The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed him telling military mental health workers that he could “ still be a martyr ” if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, spoke with Hasan on Wednesday but is barred from offering much detail about that conversation. He is not representing Hasan in his criminal case but said he’s worried about his physical health under the plan laid out by officials, and that Hasan has not yet had access to legal counsel.
Galligan said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain but no attorney from either the Trial Defense Service or from his civilian defense when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution. Galligan called that a breach of Army regulations.
A spokeswoman for the Army said Thursday that multiple attempts were made to contact Trial Defense Service attorneys, saying they made every reasonable effort and adhered to policy.
“The civilian counsel was not reasonably available to be physically present for the notification on the 5th,” the spokeswoman said, adding that counsel was located in Virginia but did not provide a name.
The spokeswoman also said Hasan has not been kept from contacting and communicating with his counsel.
Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Amnesty International said in its report on executions in 2025 that it knew of at least 17 public executions — 11 in Iran and 6 in Afghanistan.
___
Lauer reported from Philadelphia. Associated Press writers Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix, Josh Boak and Michelle L. Price in Washington, and Gene Johnson in Seattle contributed to this report.

title: If Susan Collins wins, Donald Trump wins
text:
Earlier this week, Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign summed up Tuesday’s debate between her boss and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson: “It was clear from the beginning that Sen. Collins is running to serve Maine, and Troy Jackson thinks he’s running against Donald Trump.”
It doesn’t bother me at all if Jackson thinks he’s running against the president. You know who else shares that notion? The president.
The way I see it, Jackson also has an agenda to serve Maine that’s at least as good as what Collins envisions, even if, as a new senator, he would have far less ability to deliver on his priorities.
More important, though, is that hindering President Trump is the best thing any Maine senator can do for our state, nation and the wider world.
There are many reasons to retire Collins. And just as many to keep her on Capitol Hill funneling federal dollars back home to Maine. But looming over every calculation is a more stark reality: an unfettered president who is enabled by a spineless Congress.
Collins has occasionally offered polite objections to Trump’s most egregious actions but she has failed to rally her party to stand for something beyond loyalty to a would-be tyrant.
For Collins supporters, her civility and seniority are what’s crucial. They insist, correctly, that her presence and status in the nation’s capital benefits Maine.
We need to ask ourselves: At what point does her institutional clout come at the expense of the democracy we cherish? Voters have to weigh whether Collins has grown too entrenched, too distant from her constituents and too beholden to her party and the president.
That’s what matters.
During last month’s Republican Midterm Convention in Texas, Trump said at least three times that voters this fall need to pretend “I’m on the ballot.”
What Trump meant by his insistence that he is “on the ballot” is that voters should send GOP politicians — including Collins — to the Capitol to continue to do his bidding … or at least stay out of his way. For him, sadly, the measure of a senator is how compliant she is to the whims of the White House.
During this week’s debate, Collins said she is “not exactly” Trump’s favorite senator, to which there is some truth.
It is equally true, however, that the president wants her to secure another term. Like everyone else, Trump recognizes that a “concerned” Collins is far better for him than a dedicated foe like Jackson.
Collins wants Mainers to see her as a moderate, reasonable and independent leader in the mold of former Sens. Olympia Snowe and William Cohen. That vision has grown ever more hollow as Collins faced the difficult task of dealing with Trump. As he runs amok in Washington, she has, sadly, proved that she isn’t up to the challenge of protecting the prerogatives of the Senate and defending the laws it has enacted.
We can appreciate that Collins has delivered plenty of federal help to Maine without sending her back into a crucial fight in which she has already capitulated.
If Collins wins, Trump wins.

title: Characters of the County: Andy Rogers perfects his craft one oyster at a time
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Andy Rogers takes his oysters seriously.
The 30-year-old co-owner of Jolie Rogers Raw Bar in Wiscasset serves up freshly shucked oysters for customers at the restaurant and during catered events. He is also a champion oyster shucker who has competed and placed in some of the most prestigious shucking contests around the country and in Canada.
Rogers can shuck a dozen oysters almost perfectly in less than a minute.
Since taking an interest in oysters during college, Rogers has become an expert on oysters and the art of shucking them, brainstorming and analyzing the best methods to get the meat out of the shell.
“I really like the craft of shucking,” Rogers said. “Craft is something that speaks to me. Like if there’s one thing that you can just steadily improve at, it’s a very addictive process.”
Rogers grew up in Hopkinton, Mass., and studied hospitality management and ecogastronomy at the University of New Hampshire.
Rogers said it was after completing his first year in college in May 2015 that he first became interested in oysters. That was when he had a summer job at Row 34, an oyster bar in Portsmouth, N.H., that was just opening. The eatery was owned in part by Island Creek Oysters, a large oyster farm operation in Duxbury, Mass.
“They took their oysters really seriously,” Rogers said. “There’s a serious education component to the service. They wanted everyone to be really knowledgeable about oysters, beer, wine, whatever it was. And so I sort of dug into that.”
Rogers said he requested a reading list about the shellfish and started his oyster education. He also frequently found himself working at the oyster bar, where he got plenty of practice shucking thanks to the restaurant’s daily dollar oyster special.
That was the start of his love for oysters, though Rogers said it took some time.
“It wasn’t necessarily like fireworks and love at first sight with oysters, but I always appreciated them,” he said. “And they grew on me over time, in a big way.”
The genesis for what eventually became Jolie Rogers Raw Bar began after Rogers graduated in May 2018. At an internship in revenue management and sales at Cliff House Resort in Ogunquit, he saw a lot of potential in the event contracts.
“I was kind of shocked at how much money there was in events,” he said. “It seemed like there was so much money just in what they had booked out that if I had 1% of all their jobs just to shuck oysters really well for those events, I could have a living off that.”
Rogers and his colleague Ryan Jolie, whom he met at work the year before, knew by then they wanted to start a business. They collaborated well, and their last names, Jolie and Rogers, fit together neatly, he said. The duo established the business at the end of 2018 and started working events in New Hampshire in 2019 as Jolie Rogers Traveling Raw Bar.
“We did a lot of brewery pop-ups and then we were able to book a bunch of weddings off that,” Rogers said.
The end of 2018 was also when Rogers attended the Wellfleet Oyster Shuck-Off, held during the annual Wellfleet OysterFest in Massachusetts. The shuck-off pits 28 oyster shuckers against each other and claims to be the largest shucking contest in North America. The website advises potential contestants that it is not open to amateurs.
Rogers said he was inspired by the competition, especially by seeing William “Chopper” Young compete. Young is a world champion oyster shucker who won the international shucking championships in Ireland. He also won the U.S. national championships three times and the Wellfleet Shuck-Off six times.
“I got to see how good you can get at this skill,” he said. “And that was really eye-opening. I was really fired up to go back and figure out how to do it.”
Rogers competed the next year and made it to the finals, placing ninth overall.
“I was pretty proud of that,” he said. “First competition at that level, and to be in the top 10 was pretty cool.”
Since then, Rogers has competed in countless shucking competitions in larger and smaller formats.
He took first place in Wellfleet in 2021, sixth place in the 2022 U.S. National Oyster Shucking Championship Contest in Maryland, and in October 2023, after opening the brick-and-mortar Jolie Rogers Raw Bar in Wiscasset, he earned fourth place at the national championship.
On Sunday, Sept. 27, Rogers won first place at the Pemaquid Oyster Festival shucking contest in Boothbay Harbor for the third year in a row, just a week after taking second place at the Raspberry Point International Oyster Shucking Championship in Prince Edward Island.
Rogers said he is always looking for ways he can improve his shucking technique.
“That’s, for me, what makes it addictive, to see how I improve year-over-year,” he said.
Because these competitions are judged both on time and on performance, Rogers has started experimenting with different ways to improve his results, such as incorporating meditation into his training and using various levels of force.
As part of that drive to improve, Rogers started developing his own oyster knife in 2020, with help from friends and collaborators, and plans to do an initial run of 100 knives to see how sales go.
“I just had this sense that I needed to have control over the tool,” he said. “Because there were a lot of knives that were good, but they weren’t quite right, and then you end up modifying the knife anyways.”
Rogers said his knife design uses a higher-grade steel so the blade will not bend, a frequent issue he had during shucking. He redesigned the grip to give him more control and keep the knife in his hand. The knife also features an asymmetrical blade, with one flat side and one curved side. He said this design matches the shape of an oyster.
Rogers is experimenting with names for his knife, but likely the name will be something related to swords.
Looking ahead, Rogers said he would like to find more of a balance between work and life to work on ceramics, which is his other passion. He suspected it was just his personality to “go all in” and not allow himself that space, though.
Rogers said he would also like to pass on what he has learned on another decade or so, to offer a smoother journey for the next generation of oyster shuckers
Jolie Rogers Raw Bar, at 8 Railroad Ave. in Wiscasset, is open from 5-10 p.m. on Thursdays, 1-7 p.m. Fridays through Mondays, and is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. The business continues to offer event and catering services.

title: Llewellyn Estes Bridge Removal Work Starts Tuesday, Temporary Crossing Closes For Demolition
text:
Closures Ahead For Temporary Bridge In Old Town; Clean Up Of Collapsed “Llewellyn Estes” Bridge To Begin
It's been two months since the Llewellyn Estes Bridge in Old Town partially collapsed into the water as crews worked to replace it.
The Maine DOT, which has been investigating the bridge failure since it fell as workers began pouring concrete on the deck on August 13th, is now ready to begin removing the collapsed sections of the structure.
How Will The Cleanup Take Place?
To safely remove the debris from the collapse, contractors with Reed & Reed, along with folks from the Maine DOT, will have to close down the temporary bridge for a short while throughout the next two weeks. The temporary bridge was constructed so that motorists could travel along Stillwater Avenue over the river while the original bridge was being replaced.
According to ME DOT officials, the closure is necessary due to how close these two bridges are to one another, and because of the large equipment that will need to be brought in to remove the broken sections, one part at a time.
"Closure timing will depend on demolition operations, construction progress, weather conditions, and other site-specific factors...The work will include crews carefully separating the span from the pier and abutment, reducing it into smaller pieces, and lifting those pieces from the river for processing on land. This work will proceed slowly and carefully to protect workers and the public while minimizing damage to the pier and abutment."
When Will The Bridge Be Closed?
Officials say that the closures will begin Tuesday, October 13th between the hours of 9 AM and 3 PM. It will happen, they say, intermittently throughout that week, and they estimate the work could lead into the next week as well.
What Will Drivers Do When Llewellyn Estes Temporary Bridge Is Closed?
With plenty of messaging via message boards in the vicinity, motorists will be guided along a familiar detour (this is the same one that's been used in former instances when the bridge has been closed).
This will take them up Bennoch Road to North Main Street and connect them with College Ave in Orono, which will hook back up with Stillwater, just past the bridge. The detour does add about an extra 10 minutes max to that drive, so folks should plan accordingly.
Read More: Maine Musician Writes Song About Stillwater Bridge Collapse
Maine DOT officials say they hope that if the weather, the demolition and deconstruction efforts all line up, and no other major challenges arise, the temporary bridge will reopen to a regular traffic pattern by the end of the week of October 19th.

title: Texas carries out nation's first execution since Christa Pike's failed lethal injection
text:
Texas carries out nation's first execution since Christa Pike's failed lethal injection
A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee's failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. Wednesday after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was convicted of the killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery caught on surveillance video.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to members of his victim's family, who watched through a viewing window just feet from the death chamber.
"I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness," he said, shortly before the injection got underway. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."
Texas has executed six people so far in 2026 and plans two more executions later this year.
Earlier Wednesday, Howard's attorneys unsuccessfully sought to block the execution by arguing that he was intellectually disabled and that he faced risks similar to those in Pike's case because both states use pentobarbital for lethal injections.
Pike's lawyers are seeking more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old woman survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. Her lawyers said she was unconscious at a hospital after the attempt but was awake and speaking by Tuesday.
Inmate remained 'chatty' on drive to the death chamber
Earlier Wednesday, Howard was "chatty" during the 45-mile drive from the death row prison to the Huntsville Unit, where executions are carried out, said Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.
"He made small talk with the officers through the whole trip" before being taken to a holding cell near the death chamber, she said. "He was asking questions and was very engaged in the process."
Store clerk's killing was caught on surveillance video
Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during the robbery. Evidence presented at trial included surveillance video showing Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in Silsbee, a small, rural town about 100 miles northeast of Houston, according to court records.
Man's attorneys filed late appeals bidding to stop execution
In bidding to halt Howard's execution, his attorneys filed a motion before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals raising concerns about the quality of Texas' execution drugs. The court denied that request and a second filing involving the drugs without comment.
His attorneys also argued unsuccessfully to the U.S. Supreme Court that Howard's execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities.
The state told the court that Howard's lawyers did not present evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
The high court late Wednesday declined to intervene, without comment, clearing the way for the execution.
Florida leads the nation in executions this year
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.
Tennessee's Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution that was scheduled to be carried out in his state this year.
___
Stengle reported from Fort Worth, Texas.
