title: 'You deserve to be safe': Bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
text:
'You deserve to be safe': Bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
On Thursday, Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Florida, introduced bipartisan legislation, known as the Campus Accountability and Safety Act, aimed at changing how colleges handle sexual violence allegations and protect students.
'You deserve to be safe': Bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
On Thursday, Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Florida, introduced bipartisan legislation, known as the Campus Accountability and Safety Act, aimed at changing how colleges handle sexual violence allegations and protect students.
A renewed proposal on Capitol Hill could address sexual violence allegations, like those recently brought to light on the campus of Cornell University.
On Thursday, Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Florida, reintroduced the Campus Accountability and Safety Act, a bipartisan bill aimed at changing how colleges and universities address sexual assault on their campuses.
Frankel said the legislation is based on three pillars: transparency, support and prevention.
"To every student and survivor, you deserve to be safe," Frankel said in a Thursday morning press conference. "You deserve to be heard and you deserve justice, because students are going to pursue their dreams and not to become victims of sexual violence."
The bill would require colleges and universities to publish their campus safety policies, provide instructions for filing complaints, and disclose statistics on sexual misconduct allegations on their websites.
It would also mandate "violence specialists" at institutions to serve as confidential aides for survivors.
The bill also seeks to expand a federally mandated grant program to improve campus safety, including funding for survivor services, campus law enforcement training, and student prevention and awareness education.
Institutions that fail to meet the bill's standards could face financial penalties. The legislation included a provision allowing fines of up to 1% of a college or university's annual operational budget for each year the institution fails to comply.
This was not the first time the Campus Accountability and Safety Act was introduced in Congress. Lawmakers have said that they will reintroduce the bill in the future if it does not pass this year

title: Susan Collins has put too many lives at risk
text:
Hillary Shende lives in Brunswick.
Sen. Susan Collins directs federal funding toward some Maine projects: a fire station here, a library there, etc.
But recent analysis by the Maine Center for Economic Policy found that while Collins brought in $3.45 billion over the last 10 years, her procedural vote on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last summer negated all of that and then some, leaving Mainers with a net loss of $675 million.
We must stop the financial bleeding as soon as possible. The first step is to flip Congress by firing Collins and hiring Troy Jackson.
If economics doesn’t convince you, perhaps the loss of human life will. Yes, you read that right.
On abortion, Collins cast a critical vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who predictably cast the deciding vote overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022. So far, the ensuing state abortion bans led to the deaths of 59 women who suffered from miscarriage-related sepsis, ectopic pregnancies and other medical conditions for which the only lifesaving care is abortion. Still, Collins doesn’t regret voting for Kavanaugh and just recently voted for openly anti-choice judge Matthew Byrne, erasing any doubt that she is willing to let Americans die if her party needs her vote.
On ICE/CBP, the number of people dying in ICE/CBP custody has more than doubled since Donald Trump took office in 2025. And that doesn’t even count the horrific ICE/CBP killings in our streets, some of which happened before Collins allocated $70 billion to immigration enforcement. Unsurprisingly ICE went on to kill more people, including our fellow Mainer, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Center for American Progress projects that 70,0000 Americans could die by 2040 as a result of SNAP cuts, and 51,000 more per year could die from Medicaid cuts, both of which became law as part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. This is the bill that also drains $4.1 billion from Maine. Collins advanced the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to the Senate floor, where, as I have seen so many times, the senator voted against the bill once it was evident it could pass without her.
On ceding congressional authority over war, the Iran war has caused at least than 8,000 deaths, at least 22 of which were American service members, and at least 2,100 of which were civilians. Worse, a U.N. fact-finding mission found that the U.S. likely engaged in war crimes by striking Iranian civilian structures like a school in Minab, where 120 schoolchildren were killed. Imagine being the parent of the child I saw in a photo, her severed arm sticking out from the tons of concrete rubble that crushed the rest of her to death. I am enraged at Collins’ unwillingness to stop these reckless atrocities.
These numbers are enormous, and each one is a person somebody loved. The collective grief Collins has caused, through both action and inaction, is incomprehensible to me.
Given Collins’ record of voting with Trump 95% of the time, it would be foolhardy to think she will ever meaningfully rein the president in. That’s especially true now that we know that Trump’s FBI abandoned a corruption investigation into Collins. I believe that he owes him, and he owns her.
In any other job, a record like this would get you fired yesterday.
The good news is that we can turn grief into justice. Maine voters have the power to turn the tide of this nightmare, and it is time to use it. Let’s make the lifesaving decision to vote out Susan Collins.

title: This nonprofit throws birthday parties for children living in shelters
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (InvestigateTV) — A nonprofit is bringing birthday parties to children experiencing homelessness so they can celebrate their special day while living in shelters.
Extra-Ordinary Birthdays organized a party for Yalina, who turned 7, at a shelter in Washington, D.C. The celebration included a cake, a personalized card, decorations and gifts chosen in her favorite color, pink.
Founder started organization in 2010
Schinnell Leake founded Extra-Ordinary Birthdays in 2010 to throw personalized parties for children living in shelters in the D.C. area on their birthdays.
“Personalization, individual, and the fact that we really do cater to that child’s interest, their needs, their special needs,” Leake said, describing what makes a birthday an extraordinary birthday. “But it’s also just about, just that pure, unadulterated joy that happens.”
Leake, a former professional party planner, said she started the organization because of a loss of empathy.
“The world has just lost empathy. They’ve lost everything,” Leake said. “And I’m kind of being a little defiant right now and saying that for me, the joy, you can’t erase joy.”
More than 1,700 parties organized
More than a million children across America are considered homeless, according to federal data.
Leake and volunteer “birthday angels” have thrown more than 1,700 parties across D.C., Maryland and Virginia.
Parents fill out a form selecting colors, gifts, decorations and the cake. A week before each party, volunteers wrap, pack and decorate.
Yalina’s mother, Nicole Berry, said her daughter likes princess-themed items and the color pink.
“It’s really special because right now, you know, it’s hard since we’re in the shelter,” Berry said. “So I just wanted her to have, you know, at least her birthday celebrated. Because, you know, being in this situation is not easy.”
Berry and all three of her children are living in the shelter in D.C.
Personalized touches include birthday cards
Leake said another volunteer mother makes personalized birthday cards for each child.
Berry said the volunteers “have good hearts to help people like this, you know, to make their kids day special.”
Leake said volunteers spend about an hour at each party.
“We’re here for an hour and in that hour, we are pouring in. We’re giving them snacks. We’re, you know, a cake based on what they want, gifts based on what they want. Doing the activities. Giving them goody bags,” Leake said.
Extra-Ordinary Birthdays gives each child at least one book, and offers a book for parents as well.
Those interested in donating money or time can visit extraordinarybirthdays.org.

title: Jails, prisons can now bill MaineCare for some clinical services, including addiction treatment
text:
Maine’s jails and prisons will finally have a way to pay for addiction treatment and other services for incarcerated individuals before release, thanks to a federal waiver granted late last month.
Androscoggin County Sheriff Eric Samson said Thursday he was looking forward to being able to take advantage of the waiver next year and reduce the financial burden on the jail, but didn’t yet know how much help it would provide.
The Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services approved Maine’s request to allow correctional facilities to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for certain clinical services provided up to 60 days from an individual’s expected release date.
Those services include medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorder, physical and behavioral health case management, treatment for HIV and hepatitis C, family planning services, diagnostic services and a 30-day supply of prescription medications provided upon release.
It’s a turning point for the jails, which have been required to provide medication-assisted treatment since a 2019 ruling, but shoulder the costs for those services on a local level.
Many jails have leaned on grants, opioid settlement funds and local fundraising, according to a January 2026 report from the Maine County Corrections Professional Standards Council.
Maine’s counties spent more than $12.6 million on medication-assisted treatment and mental health services across 15 correctional facilities last year, the report said.
Samson is among the state’s county sheriffs who have been struggling with rising costs and pressure from the towns and cities ultimately paying those costs. He said Thursday his department has been preparing for the federal waiver since 2024, meeting with federal agencies and state representatives as they prepare for the roll out.
That roll out will initially involve county jails that are most ready for the new system, Samson said, and it is expected Androscoggin County Jail will be among the first.
Samson said he is cautiously optimistic about the arrangement.
“It should provide savings due to the reimbursement, but until we get this implemented, we won’t know how advantageous it will be,” he said. “But it should provide some relief financially.”
MaineCare officials say correctional facilities will start billing for services on July 1, 2028.
Staff Writer Mark LaFlamme contributed to this report.

title: Live tonight: Ossoff, Collins take the stage as Georgia Senate race heats up
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - Georgia’s U.S. Senate candidates, incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and U.S. Rep. Mike Collins (R), will debate live Thursday in a broadcast streaming across Gray Media stations nationwide.
The one-hour debate will begin at 7 p.m. ET and take place at Assembly Studios, Gray Media’s studio production facility. It will air on Atlanta News First and Gray Media television stations in Georgia, with a stream available across Gray Media stations nationwide.
Gray Media will also offer pre- and post-debate coverage. “On the Record: Live,” hosted by Doug Reardon, begins at 6:30 p.m., with post-debate analysis airing at 8 p.m.
Atlanta News First anchor Rick Folbaum will moderate. A panel of journalists will ask the candidates about key issues facing Georgia and the nation.
The election cycle between Collins and Ossoff has already been a heated one. They’ve traded barbs in interviews and online.
As for what they might do on the debate stage, Collins said he plans to attack Ossoff for his voting record in the Senate chamber.
“Not just what we say, but our records,” Collins said earlier this year. “I look forward to the people seeing just what I’ve been able to deliver for the State of Georgia, how I’ve been able to bring things back to help improve people’s lives and the fact that Jon Ossoff, my opponent, has made people’s lives less safe, more expensive.”
Ossoff said he plans to attack Collins for his policy record and close alignment with President Donald Trump. Ossoff also pressed Collins to release alleged text and phone communications between his office and several high-profile white nationalist influencers.
“On the Record: Live” begins at 6:30 p.m. and the post-debate analysis airing immediately following the debate.

title: Augusta City Council finalizes Kennebec Arsenal settlement
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Augusta City Council has approved a settlement with Main Street I LLC, the owner and developer of the Kennebec Arsenal, outlining the next steps in the redevelopment of the riverfront property on the city’s east side.
The settlement, which requires Main Street I, owned by Tom Niemann, to finalize a funding plan in the next 90 days and complete the redevelopment of six of the eight granite buildings within a year after that. Main Street is also required to pay the city $75,000.
According to the terms, Neimann Capital LLC, the sole managing member of Main Street I, will be replaced with a panel of three co-managers: Mike Scholtz, an investor; Richard Parkhurst, a local developer focused on renovating old buildings in Augusta; and Niemann Capital.
If the terms of the new settlement agreement are met, the litigation will be resolved.
“I have absolutely zero faith that Mr. Niemann will get this done,” At-Large Councilor Courtney Gary-Allen said before the Oct. 1 council vote. “However, I do have 100% faith in the other two co-members in this agreement, particularly Richard Parkhurst. May God be with him if he can get this done.”
Other councilors similarly expressed low confidence in Niemann and were thankful for the addition of Parkhurst to the project.
“I’m hoping that a year from now, we’re not sitting here discussing this issue anymore other than (that) it’s almost done,” Ward 3 Councilor Michael Michaud said.
Niemann did not respond to requests for comment this week.
If Main Street I fails to obtain certificates of occupancy for the buildings within one year of finalizing funding, the city would obtain a court order requiring the company to address any remaining violations within three months, and Main Street I would be required to pay the city $60,000.
A third-party construction manager will be appointed to oversee the redevelopment, and Parkhurst will serve as clerk of the works for the project. Main Street I is also required to provide a weekly progress report and will be responsible for paying the cost of the clerk of the works.
In August 2022, the Augusta City Council declared the property dangerous and gave Niemann 90 days to address the building concerns before pursuing further legal action. Niemann filed a complaint shortly thereafter requesting the dangerous building determination be reviewed in the Kennebec County Superior Court.
The Kennebec Arsenal was built by the federal government between 1828 and 1838 and is a National Historic Landmark. Niemann bought the property in 2007 with plans to turn it into a mixed-use site with retail, office space, a boutique hotel and residences, but little progress was made over the past 20 years as the buildings continued to deteriorate.

title: Letter to the Editor: Scott Landry has the know-how we need
5 notable moments from Susan Collins and Troy Jackson’s second debate
text:
Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson ran the gamut from personal attacks to policy disagreements.
It was the second time this week the 73-year-old Collins and the 58-year-old Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president, squared off. Their final two debates will take place next week.
On Tuesday, Jackson put in a strong performance, delivering a couple zingers that took on lives of their own on social media. Those quips included comparing Collins to an arsonist and telling her that “you can’t eat road salt” after she claimed she got the material exempted from tariffs.
Collins was largely on the defensive as she tried to distance herself from President Donald Trump, who is deeply unpopular in Maine, and from corruption allegations amplified by Democrats. But she also displayed her experience and knowledge of the issues.
On Thursday, Jackson was a bit shakier, struggling at times to find his talking points on the fly while Collins continued to hold her own.
Polls continue to show a close race, with Jackson having a slight edge. But Republicans have more money than Democrats and have been flooding the airwaves with ads attacking Jackson in the closing final weeks of the campaign.
Here are five takeaways from their second meeting, which was broadcast on WTMW.
1. Both candidates got personal
The candidates brought each other’s families into the debate.
Collins went on the attack first. She accused Jackson of changing his position on accepting donations from corporations. In his U.S. Senate campaign, Jackson has said he would not — but as state Senate president, his leadership PAC accepted those types of donations.
“It usually has to do with issues that his son has been hired to lobby him on,” Collins said of instances where Jackson has changed his positions over the years.
Later, Jackson took aim at Collins’ husband while discussing high energy prices. Jackson repeatedly blamed the Iran War for increasing fuel and electricity prices, saying that Collins voted five times against stopping it. (Collins noted she has voted nine times to end it.)
“She could use her leverage to stop this war,” he said. “But instead … Sen. Collins and her husband are making money off this war and so is a whole bunch of other people and that’s why this doesn’t stop.”
Jackson was referring to Collins’ husband, Tom Daffron’s, vast stock portfolio, which includes holdings in natural gas and Boeing. (Boeing’s stock price has fallen since the start of the war.)
Collins called Jackson’s charge of her family profiting off the conflict “absolutely outrageous” and demanded an apology.
“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson replied.
2. A rare moment of agreement
When the debate turned to protecting Social Security, Jackson and Collins found a rare point of agreement — both agreed that people who earn more money should pay more into the system.
Social Security taxes are currently capped at a percentage of the first $184,000 you make, regardless of your income. Jackson said that cap should be scrapped so that wealthy people would pay more into the system.
“Here is something where I actually agree with Troy,” Collins said.
But Collins didn’t go as far as Jackson. Instead, she said, she would assemble a panel of independent financial experts to provide recommendations.
“We are simply going to have to adjust the cap,” Collins said.
3. Jackson hits Collins’ strength
Collins has made her experience and seniority a central theme of her campaign. Again, she referenced the $1.5 billion she has helped bring to Maine in recent years as chair of the Appropriations Committee — the first Mainer to hold that position in 92 years.
But Jackson wasn’t impressed. He continued to describe Collins as kowtowing to Trump’s demands.
“She’s powerful during election time but she’s weak every time we need her to stand up and fight for us,” Jackson said.
4. Collins tried to flip the script on abortion
Abortion has been a big issue this campaign, especially Collins’ vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, which led in part to the overturning of Roe v. Wade.
But Collins tried to flip the script by noting that Jackson had been longtime opponent of abortion until he ran for Congress in 2014. She specifically pointed to a bill he opposed that would have allowed for abortions if a pregnancy threatened the mother’s health.
“He was an extremist when it comes to abortion,” Collins said, noting she has always been pro-choice.
Jackson, however, was ready. He acknowledged that he changed his views on abortion after speaking with women — something he said Collins didn’t do when Mainers traveled to D.C. to urge her to oppose Kavanaugh.
“Our records have changed,” said Jackson, who is endorsed by Planned Parenthood. “Mine has gotten better — hers has gotten worse.”
5. Collins recasts voting record with Trump
Jackson has repeatedly accused Collins of voting with Trump 96% of the time. The claim comes from CQ Roll Call analysis of the first seven months of 2025, which found the percentage was closer to 95%.
Collins said using the same approach to analyze her votes under former President Joe Biden would have shown her siding with the Democrat 91% of the time. And a more expansive look at Collin’s voting record in Trump’s second term shows she has sided with him 72% of the time, she claimed.
Collin said she has voted against Trump 137 times.
“But it didn’t matter,” Jackson shot back.

title: Boy, 5, killed after video board falls on him at Florida school
text:
Boy, 5, killed after video board falls on him at Florida school
A Florida family is demanding answers after a 120-pound video display board fell on a 5-year-old student at an elementary school Wednesday, killing him.
Brevard Public Schools said the boy, who was identified by his family as Bellamy Dawkins-Morris, was seriously injured after the large display board fell on him at Riviera Elementary School just before noon.
School staff immediately called 911 and began emergency lifesaving measures before Bellamy was taken to Holmes Regional Medical Center, where he later died.
Family members said they are devastated and searching for answers.
"We're expecting him to be safe. He didn't return to us," Bellamy's great-aunt, Miriam Rodriguez, said. "My emotions, my sadness has subsided, and I am angry. We need answers, and we need them immediately."
Palm Bay Police Deputy Chief Nicholas Szczepanski said the department's Special Victims Unit and Major Case Unit is investigating.
"Our thoughts and prayers go out to everybody that was involved in this tragic accident," Szczepanski said.
Brevard Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Mark Rendell said he met with Bellamy's family shortly after the child's death.
"We lost a life today, a precious young life. There are no words to describe that loss," Rendell said. "I've been doing this for over 30 years, and I really couldn't find the words to share with them my grief and the grief that all of us have."
According to Bellamy's family, his mother was told he was moving the display board back and forth while other students were lining up before it tipped over and fell on him. The family said Bellamy had autism and questioned whether the display board was properly secured and whether enough supervision was provided.
"He's on the spectrum. When he sees things in motion, he's gonna keep pushing it to keep it in motion. That's just something that children on the spectrum do," Miriam Rodriguez said. "Obviously, the monitor was not secure, and that's a huge issue. That could have been anybody's child. (...) There's no reason that that is not bolted to the wall or however. There is no reason there should be any movement."
Bellamy's grandmother, Christy Rodriguez Bruno, said the family believed he should have been safe at school.
"He was supposed to be in a safe place enjoying his little five-year-old self. And now we don't have him coming home, and my daughter shall never be the same," she said.
Another great-aunt, Melissa Rodriguez, said the family believes Bellamy's death could have been prevented.
"I'm angry because it could have been prevented if they were paying attention to him. I'm not saying he doesn't do things that he shouldn't do, but this child did not deserve to not be here anymore," she said.
As investigators work to determine exactly what happened, Bellamy's family said it is seeking accountability and legal counsel.
"This is not a slap on the wrist. This is not a broken leg. We lost our baby today because of this, and I need everybody to understand the severity of this. He's not coming back," Miriam Rodriguez said.
In a statement, Brevard Public Schools said, in part, "We are devastated by this unimaginable loss. Our deepest condolences are with the student's family, loved ones, classmates, and everyone in our school community who is grieving."
The district said counseling and additional support services will be available for students and staff in the coming days.

title: New US indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
text:
New US indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations.
Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
The updated indictment “alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable,” New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power.
“This is the epitome of corruption,” McDonald said.
The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro’s behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.”
Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.
The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.
Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.
Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores’ lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.
Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.
Alleged torture victims included US citizens
The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela’s feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro’s co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.
While the indictment doesn’t name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.
Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.
Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.
In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed “El Tigrito.”
“It’s incredible to see a dictator in court,” Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. “The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations.”
Former first lady denied release for medical treatment
Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during her capture.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an “extreme” flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.
U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores’ request. He noted, among other things, that she’s unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.
He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she’s already on medication for that.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

title: Maine heating oil prices near $6 a gallon
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices are again approaching $6 a gallon.
The average cost for a gallon of heating oil is $5.97, up from $5.96 last week, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
That’s down from last month’s record high of $6.02.
Still, this time last year the average cost for a gallon of heating oil was $3.34, meaning this week’s price is about 79% higher.
That means it will cost Mainers an additional $725 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank, the Department of Energy Resources has said.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.50 to a high of $6.30.
The skyrocketing cost of heating oil has been fueled by President Donald Trump’s ongoing war against Iran, which effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies.
Maine is particularly vulnerable to such price shocks, because the state is heavily reliant on heating oil to keep warm during the winter.
Last week, Gov. Janet Mills called on Congress to approve additional funds for low-income fuel assistance.

title: Letter to the Editor: Knowing Trevor Doiron
Barack Obama endorses Troy Jackson
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Former President Barack Obama has endorsed Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate.
That endorsement came hours ahead of the Democrat’s second debate with incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. It’s among nearly two dozen endorsements that Obama has rolled out in recent days for U.S. Senate and gubernatorial races, according to Politico. In 2020, Obama endorsed Collins’ Democratic challenger, Sara Gideon, who ultimately lost by several points.
In a 49-second video, released Thursday morning, Obama praised Jackson for his work in the Maine Senate to boost wages, lower prescription drug costs and provide free lunch to students.
“In this economy, we need a fighter like Troy,” the former two-term president said.
Jackson said in a Thursday statement that he’s “honored” to get Obama’s endorsement.
“Working people are sick and tired of a government that works for the wealthy and well-connected while they struggle to get by. They’re ready for change, and together, we’re going to bring that change to Washington,” the former Allagash logger said.
A Collins campaign spokesperson said Thursday that the endorsement shows that national Democrats are pushing heavily for control of the Maine Senate seat.
“The fact that Troy Jackson is endorsed by Obama, funded by Chuck Schumer, and campaigning with Bernie Sanders this weekend tells you how much the national Democratic machine wants to control Maine’s Senate seat,” Blake Kernan said while highlighting the senior senator’s work to boost Social Security benefits for retired public sector employees and to bring down insulin prices.
Jackson has generally been leading Collins in recent public polling since he became his party’s nominee after Graham Platner dropped out in July when an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape. In one poll last month, Collins had a 3-point edge over Jackson, her first lead over him in a public poll.
It will be an uphill battle for Democrats to unseat Collins, who officially announced her historic bid for a sixth term in February. The Republican has handily beaten back challengers, including in 2020 when she defied polls and expectations to secure a fifth term in the Senate. But Collins, who has been ranked the country’s most bipartisan senator and relied on cross-party appeal to carry her to victory, has seen her popularity slump since Trump’s first term in the White House.
If Collins is successful in winning a sixth term, she would be Maine’s longest-serving U.S. senator.

title: Gardiner soccer is Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week​
text:
Girls Team of the Week: Gardiner girls soccer
Gardiner High’s girls soccer team is atop the Heal point standings in Class B North, a rare position for a team that has been solid but seldom a title contender.
“It’s honestly a bit of a surprise,” said Jess Prince, the Tigers’ sixth-year head coach.
Gardiner won its first nine games, including crossover games last week against Morse from Class B South (2-1 victory) and Messalonskee from Class A North (3-0 victory). On Tuesday, the Tigers remained unbeaten but settled for a 1-1 tie at Erskine Academy.
After graduating six seniors from a team that went 10-5-1 in 2025, Gardiner spent the preseason working through multiple player combinations, settling on a lineup with three freshmen and several returners in new positions.
When linchpin senior center back Sara Mansir was injured, more juggling followed.
Center midfielder Molly Takatsu shifted to the back line in place of Mansir (who could return later this season). Lexi Dyer moved from outside midfielder to center mid, and senior Kaetlyn Stevens, a key reserve, moved into Dyer’s spot.
Freshmen Olivia Ketner, Evalyn Grover and striker Riley Antognoni have strengthened the lineup. Antognoni leads a balanced scoring attack.
“She’s crazy fast and bothering other team’s backs all day long,” Prince said.
Adela Ricker, a junior first-year starter, has three shutouts and heads a veteran back line of Takatsu, junior Zoey Epperson and seniors Cheyenne Goodman and Lilah Serber that has held opponents to nine goals. Gardiner has scored 25 goals.
The past three seasons, the Tigers have lost on the road in the quarterfinals. This season, they’re looking good for a top-four finish and a home quarterfinal game.
“It’s somewhat of a surprise,” Goodman said. “At the same time, we’re working really hard. We’re excited, because my whole high school career, we’ve never been undefeated this far in.”
Predicting Gardiner’s playoff performance is difficult. The Tigers do not play any of the other current top-six teams in the regular season.
“The past three seasons, we’ve been knocked out by a team that didn’t even have a common opponent,” Prince said. “That’s why that home-field advantage is huge when you get deeper in the playoffs.”

title: Margaret Hamilton, who led a software team for NASA's Apollo program, dies at 90
text:
Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90.
Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at MIT and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university’s communications office.
“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”
In recent years a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. And a Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
She graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.
After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”
“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

title: 1 dead, another seriously injured in Lovell crash
text:
A 25-year-old woman was killed Thursday morning when her SUV collided head-on with a pickup truck on Main Street.
Police said the driver of the pickup truck sustained life-threatening injuries and was taken by LifeFlight helicopter to a hospital.
Police did not identify either driver as they continued to investigate the 11:45 a.m. crash in the 600 block of Main Street.
Neither driver was traveling with passengers when they collided, police said. They said the 25-year-old was dead when rescue crews first arrived at the scene.
The crash was being investigated by the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office, which was assisted at the scene by Fryeburg police, Fryeburg rescue and crews from the Lovell Fire Department.

title: In Winthrop, new helmet tech provides impact data for coaches, medical staff
text:
Thanks to a generous gift, the Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale football program has 50 state-of-the-art Riddell helmets that include impact sensors, giving coaches and athletic trainers access to immediate feedback when a player absorbs a blow to the head.
Coach Joel Stoneton also receives daily emails with an impact report for the entire team. He said that has already helped him correct improper tackling technique for a varsity player who was inadvertently dropping his head during tackling drills, resulting in impacts to the crown of his helmet. Riddell football helmets are considered one of the best in the country.
“I was able to spend extra time with that varsity player, show him the data, and fix it. Get his head up and see your target,” said Stoneton. “More importantly, medically, my athletic trainer can look that up and tell where that impact was on the student.”
Stoneton said he had already worked with the player on his tackling form. But it wasn’t until the player saw the data that his habits changed.
“Sometimes you don’t really understand it until you have a neutral piece of information. Then you can see very clearly that you’re not using the correct part of your body,” Stoneton said.
Stoneton believes having the impact data helps to protect his players this season and widespread use could further the study of how head impacts cause concussions and CTE in football players. CTE is a progressive brain disease caused by repeated blows to the head.
“The more of these helmets that are out there recording data the more we’ll be able to hone in on, maybe get to those thresholds when a concussion happens,” Stoneton said. “It’s just more information to keep our kids safer.”
The Ramblers are using the Riddell Axiom helmet. Those helmets, with an individual retail price just over $1,000, come equipped with five impact sensors. The analytic software that allows coaches to glean the sensors’ information, and is normally an optional add-on subscription, was also part of the gift. The software is sold as a team-wide product. Riddell does not publicize the cost.
Before the season, each helmet was custom fit to individual players’ heads. The helmet will stay with them through their Winthrop career. When new players join the program, they will go through the same fitting process.
“These are fantastic helmets but what takes them further as a coach and working with the trainer are the five different sensors,” said Stoneton, adding that the Riddell rep trained the Winthrop staff on how to utilize and interpret the head impact results.
Riddell is the only football helmet manufacturer that builds impact sensors into their products but the concept is not new. The NFL had a trial, voluntary program it suspended in 2015, citing data inaccuracies and potential infringement on players’ medical privacy rights.
Winthrop’s new helmets were a gift from Walter Wiacek, a part-time Winthrop resident and the chief financial officer of private equity firm Fenway Partners, the primary owner of Riddell. Wiacek and Stoneton were introduced through a mutual acquaintance. Riddell has a community outreach program that includes helmet donations. Wiacek decided Winthrop was a worthy candidate.
“He said he’d been to a couple of our games and liked the local vibe,” Stoneton said. “He donated 50 helmets and wrote a check for $30,000 to cover them.”
As a small-town athletic director, Stoneton said he needed to be sure the helmet fitting and continued use of sensor analytics would be affordable in the future. Football helmets are routinely sent back to the manufacturers after each season to be reconditioned.
Stoneton said the cost of reconditioning and updating the Riddell system for the next season or a new player is “not much different,” than it would be for any other helmet.

title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego
text:
SAN DIEGO (AP) — The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”
He said that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”
Hegseth told the crew that President Donald Trump “tracked your activities from day one and couldn’t be more proud of what you executed.”
The Navy initially downplayed problems on the carrier
The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.
The Navy initially downplayed any problems, and Trump commented in August that the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough.”
The carrier had left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln’s crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Long deployments can tax service members
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.
The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.
Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.
___
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio.

title: In Augusta, the Mill Park Pétanque Club teaches its game to a new generation
text:
AUGUSTA — Eric Ayotte picked up the nuances of pétanque quickly. A golfer, the Mattanawcook Academy junior studied the way the ball spun and broke on the crushed stone court the way he studies a green before a putt.
Where do I want to toss this ball so it not only ends up closest to the cochonet, the smaller target ball, but also prevents my opponents from getting a clean shot? Where’s the break? Is there a divot in the stone that will mess everything up?
“You really have to think about your shot. There’s a lot of moving parts,” Ayotte said between games Thursday morning at Augusta’s Mill Park. “It would be sick to get one of these in Lincoln.”
That’s exactly the kind of thing Raymond Fecteau wants to hear. He calls pétanque, “the best game nobody’s heard of,” and he’s trying to change that.
Fecteau, 82, is one of the founders of the Mill Park Pétanque Club. Since he retired from his career as a barber 17 years ago, Fecteau’s goal has been to play pétanque as much as possible, and pass the game on to anyone who wants to learn how to play.
“What I like best is teaching kids how to do it,” he said, “but we don’t get a lot of kids.”
On this overcast Thursday morning, with the trees along the nearby Kennebec River hitting their fall color peak, that meant giving a lesson to 16 students from a Mattanawcook French class who made the 250-mile round trip from Lincoln.
This was the second time French teacher Melanie Turner brought one of her classes to Augusta for a day of pétanque. It’s a chance for the students to learn a game they can play the rest of their lives, as well as find a touchstone to the Franco culture many of them share, Turner said.
“I think it’s important for them to make that connection,” she said. “I’d like to see if we can bring it back to Lincoln.”
Pétanque’s rules are easy to learn. Standing inside a ring, players try to get their balls closest to the cochonet. The balls are hollow and metal, about the size of a baseball, the perfect size to fit into your palm.
“I think it’s pretty fun,” Gracie Averill, a Mattanawcook junior, said an hour after playing the game for the first time. “We do get competitive. It’s just a fun game that’s not too strenuous.”
At Mill Park, the club has 10 courts, and lighting to play in the evening. Right around the time he retired, Fecteau learned the game on a trip to France. He bought a set of balls and played where he could, introducing friends to the game.
With enough people looking for a place to enjoy a few rounds of pétanque, Fecteau and the club approached the city of Augusta and asked for a space to build courts. The club raised $50,000, and the courts at Mill Park were the result.
The Mill Park Pétanque Club currently has 71 members, Fecteau said. The membership skews older. Seniors come during the day to play. As Fecteau and a handful of club members taught the students, a group of senior women played their weekly games on one of the courts.
Last year, Fecteau had open heart surgery. He thought maybe his pétanque playing days were over. After a couple months of rest of rehab, he was back on the courts. Dan Howard took over as club president, taking a little off Fecteau’s plate.
Teaching the game to younger players, passing the game along, is important.
“I think the baby of our crowd is around 47,” Fecteau said, “but see, these people, they take to it.”
Fecteau pointed to Ayotte and three of his classmates getting instruction from club member Gary Golden. They studied the lay of the court before making their throws. They cheered when somebody made a good throw. He pointed to a court where Howard coached another group of students. The same thing was happening there.
“In the time they’ve been here, you see how much progress they’ve made. It’s satisfying,” Fecteau said.
Fecteau smiled. When you pass on something you love, satisfying isn’t a strong enough description.

title: Orrington man dies after vehicle rams into Ellsworth home
text:
An Orrington man died Thursday after the vehicle he was a passenger in rammed into the corner of a downtown Ellsworth home.
Paul Meservey, 23, sustained fatal injuries after the 2018 GMC Sierra he was riding in lost control near the intersection of Bucksport and Surry roads just before 1:30 a.m., striking two buildings, according to the Ellsworth Police Department.
The driver of the eastbound truck, 19-year-old Landon Rockwell of Dedham, was ejected from the vehicle and taken to Northern Light Maine Coast Hospital in Ellsworth, according to police. He was later transferred by LifeFlight to Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor.
The corner of one of the homes, at 5 Main St., had a gaping hole following the crash. A fireplace inside the home was visible from the street Thursday morning. The area was cordoned off by caution tape and “uninhabitable structure” signs posted on both of the affected homes.
The Hancock County district attorney’s office was notified of the fatal crash, according to police.
The crash remains under investigation.
Ellsworth police and fire responded to the crash, as well as a Northern Light ambulance and the Bangor Police Department.

title: ‘Genocide’ or not, US must seek an end to the suffering in Gaza
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
Israel’s continuing attacks on Gaza roiled Maine’s U.S. Senate race last week, as Democratic nominee Troy Jackson apologized for remarks he made in a TV interview. He said it was “unfortunate” that there are “people here in Maine that don’t like that term” — genocide — “only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
Like “racism” and “imperialism,” the term “genocide” has become more a weapon used to batter political opponents than anything descriptive of the facts or the truth. It was indeed unfortunate that Jackson indulged his knack for plain-speaking over carefully approaching an issue that, in American as in world politics, has become a powder keg.
As we often do, we’re debating the wrong question. What Israel, led by its longtime leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done in response to the horrific attack by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, has long since degenerated into a campaign of retribution, without any coherent military or political strategy.
Through three long years, Israel has destroyed most of Gaza’s infrastructure, repeatedly put its people to flight and brought the populace to the edge of famine without really settling anything. Some 1,200 Israelis lost their lives on Oct. 7. Since then, an estimated 70,000 Palestinians have died. Depending on your definition of genocide, this may or may not qualify, but surely Israel’s response has been utterly disproportionate, and has gotten us nowhere near a future for the Palestinians that doesn’t produce destitution and endless suffering.
Normally, in a democracy like Israel, these issues would be settled by elections, but that may not be the case here. Just a week before our midterm elections, Israeli voters will choose a new government on Oct. 27, implicitly the first referendum on Netanyahu’s preparedness, or lack of it, for the Oct. 7 attacks — and the absence of any coherent plan for Gaza’s future. We must also recall that Israel withdrew from Gaza in 2005, removing settlers and leaving the power vacuum that Hamas ended up filling.
Americans often complain about our two-party system, but Israel struggles with too many parties, which come and go with each election, often built around a particular political figure. A party with as little as 3.5% of the vote can be represented in the 120-member Knesset, and throughout Netanyahu’s record tenure, serving almost continuously since 2009, his party has never held a majority.
In recent years, Netanyahu’s centrist allies spurned him, forcing him to rely more and more on Orthodox religious parties, which see all the territory now held by Israel as its by right. In reality, the West Bank and Gaza have been, since 1967, Israeli-occupied territories. They also represent the only homeland Palestinians will ever have.
The coalitions of both Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former defense chief, who represents the largest opposition party, are both short of a majority, meaning a half dozen small parties may be needed to form a government. Whether the 2026 election is any more decisive than previous ones isn’t yet known, but if Netanyahu is finally ousted, the atmosphere, if not policies, could shift.
None of Israel’s leading parties favor anything approaching reconciliation with the roughly equal numbers of Palestinians under Israeli rule, let alone negotiations for a two-state solution. Yet suffering in Gaza could be ameliorated, primarily through a U.N. peacekeeping force overseeing restoration of public services while Israel withdraws its troops.
Donald Trump has again done this country a grave disservice by throwing in his lot with Netanyahu’s vainglorious military schemes that imagine Israel subduing Iran. He followed Israel’s lead by bombing suspected nuclear enrichment facilities in June 2025, then launched “Operation Epic Fury” on Feb. 28, which seems to have petered out, despite occasional Trumpian threats of “annihilation.”
Regardless, Congress has a responsibility to bring Trump back to reality, and ensure the U.S. cuts support for Israel’s continuing attacks. Much of the weaponry used in Gaza represents American military aid.
On this issue, Troy Jackson said the U.S. should stop sending “blank checks” to Israel, an entirely sensible idea. Sen. Angus King, no radical, said essentially the same thing months ago, vowing to oppose any further military aid.
We should recognize that nothing Americans do will greatly shape the future of Gaza. Israel, unfortunately, is in control. Demonstrations on college campus won’t make much difference, nor will debating the word “genocide.”
Yet we can stop enabling the excesses of an important ally in the Middle East. We can, as Trump has not, make it clear there are limits — and firmly establish that criticism of Israel’s current government does not equate to antisemitism.

title: Watch tonight’s high stakes debates for governor, senate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The candidates running in Maine’s two highest profile races are debating tonight, back-to-back.
First, at 7 p.m., the candidates for governor — Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and Independent Rick Bennett — will meet in Bangor for a debate hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public, and NEWSCENTER Maine.
Then, at 8 p.m., Senate candidates Troy Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins will square off in their second debate in three days on WMTW.
We will stream both debates, back-to-back, right here — along with live updates starting at 6:30.
We’ll see you there.
And just like that, it’s over!
Thanks so much for following along with us tonight. It was a marathon double debate session. See you at the next one.
-Kirby Wilson
-Both candidates essentially said they don’t use artificial intelligence for major daily tasks
-The candidates said they disagree on term limits for senators and Supreme Court justices. (Jackson is in favor of both, Collins is opposed to both.)
-Kirby Wilson
Collins countered by saying appropriations doesn’t have jurisdiction over tariffs, but she’s working with the Trump administration to try to get some of them lifted.
-Drew Johnson
Collins said ICE does need reforms, including restrictions on where the agency should conduct arrests. But she said the agency shouldn’t be abolished. A similar exchange happened last debate as well.
-Kirby Wilson
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better, hers has gotten worse.”
“She’s made sure that, I think she’s put 55 anti-abortion judges onto the courts, including Brett Kavanaugh, that she knew that he was anti-abortion and that was what he was going to do when he got there, and he did.” Jackson continued.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
“When Donald Trump wants something, Sen. Collins will not stop him,” he said.
-Kirby Wilson
The candidates agree on something!
Jackson and Collins agree that high earners should pay a greater share of their income to Social Security. This may be the first moment of agreement all night.
-Kirby Wilson
This is another familiar theme: Collins says Jackson and Augusta leaders are to blame for Maine’s cost-of-living woes. Jackson says D.C. politicians and Collins are.
-Drew Johnson
Collins shot back that policies that Jackson advocated for have caused premiums to spike in Maine.
-Kirby Wilson
“To say that my husband and I are making money off the war in Iran is absolutely outrageous,” Collins said.
This was one of the most striking moments of the debate so far.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
“I have been the leading proponent” of the program in Congress, argued Collins, and said they could expand the program.
Collins also emphasized that “we have a supply problem” and that the United States needs to become “energy independent.”
-Drew Johnson
“People are going to freeze to death this winter because they can’t afford to heat their home,” Jackson said.
-Kirby Wilson
“He’s in jail today, where he belongs,” Collins said.
Jackson insisted the allegations aren’t false, before turning to what he said was Collins’ proximity to Donald Trump, who he emphasized is “a convicted felon.”
-Drew Johnson
Collins keeps it much more positive, noting some of her signature legislative accomplishments, and saying they came because of her seniority and her connections.
-Kirby Wilson
The Senate debate is underway!
We don’t have a moment to rest. It’s time for Troy Jackson vs. Susan Collins, round two.
Bennett and Pingree played their closing statements much straighter, asking viewers for their vote.
-Kirby Wilson
Charles said he opposed late-term abortions but attempted to sidestep the question somewhat, saying “there are a ton of issues that are confronting us” and that “this is not the number one issue.” When pressed for an answer, he again said he opposes late-term abortions.
“There is only one Bobby Charles, and he is perfectly consistent,” Charles said, noting that he’s long been critical of Trump’s Canada tariffs, for example.
Then he pivoted to criticizing Pingree some more. He’s staying on the attack.
-Kirby Wilson
Bennett on why he left the GOP
When asked why he left the Republican party to run as an independent, Bennet said he once believed that parties were “a vehicle for participation” in the political process, but that is no longer the case.
“Both parties are more interested in keeping us fighting with each other than actually resolving issues,” Bennett said.
“Hannah talks more about Trump than Trump talks about himself,” Charles said.
-Kirby Wilson
A $1 billion budget shortfall?
This part of the night could make news: What are the candidates’ plans to fight the state’s potential $1 billion budget shortfall? Not sure we’ve heard from the candidates on this point.
-Kirby Wilson
Charles said he does not support the expansion.
“I would say we made a fundamental error,” Charles said of expanding MaineCare, noting that able-bodied Mainers are taking advantage of the program, which has become underfunded.
-Kirby Wilson
“I would argue that Biddeford probably wouldn’t have had happened if the sanctuary state law didn’t exist here, because the comms, they were sidelined. The comms between local and state and feds would have been clear,” Charles said.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
He argued that “Biddeford probably wouldn’t have had happened” if the various law enforcement agencies involved if there were better lines of communication.
-Drew Johnson
The candidates start with substance
Quite a substantive start, so far! Bad times for those who want to see name calling.
-Kirby Wilson
Among other priorities, Pingree said DEP permits should get a 90-day “shot clock,” noting that Maine needs to incentivize more housing on the supply side. She plugged her housing plan, which you can find here.
And Bennett said the state should reduce down payments for first time home buyers. He also said the state should assist with mortgage payments.
He addressed the supply side challenges of housing as well, arguing the state should increase factory-build housing.
-Kirby Wilson
And we’re off!
The gubernatorial debate has started. This debate is brought to you by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine.
-Kirby Wilson

title: Maine attorney general’s office accidentally shares confidential case information
text:
The Office of the Maine Attorney General on Thursday accidentally sent a report containing sensitive details about active criminal cases to an external mailing list that includes local media outlets.
The 45-page Criminal Division Report contains information on homicides, missing person cases, financial crimes and more. Many of the details contained are confidential and have not been previously disclosed.
The incident raises questions about the potential implications on the cases — which include some of the state’s most high-profile homicides — as well as how such sensitive material was inadvertently sent to dozens of people outside the attorney general’s office. Danna Hayes, a spokesperson for the office, said in a written statement Thursday evening that the report was accidentally sent to a media distribution list.
“The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that. … We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine,” Hayes said.
Frayla Tarpinian, executive director for the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services, said in an interview that she was “shocked to hear about a release of this magnitude.”
“I don’t know exactly what’s on it,” Tarpinian said of the document, “but if it involves precharge information or investigatory information that has not yet been brought forward … that information is very sensitive.”
The document contains updates on active cases, recent pleas and sentences. It’s broken into numerous categories, including: murder and manslaughter cases; drug, tax and healthcare crimes; and election and public corruption violations. The first page notes in all capital letters that it “may contain confidential information including attorney work product.”
While much of the information has been included in public court records and police reports, some of the case descriptions in the document include explicit descriptions of causes of death in homicides, specific dollar amounts in financial cases, and names of suspects not yet charged in missing persons investigations.
For example, cases involving a healthcare company disclose “potential” amounts of money involved, including an instance where more than $1.5 million is suspected of being stolen. One missing person case notes that a relative was interviewed multiple times and describes their demeanor with investigators. Some case updates also include anticipated outcomes, such as how a defendant is expected to plead.
Such sensitive details becoming public can impact active investigations in a variety of ways, Tarpinian said.
“It could make pursuing a suspect harder, it could make collecting evidence more difficult and it could make it, ultimately, more difficult to bring cases forward,” she said.
It can also raise issues surrounding the justice system’s integrity, she added, by disclosing the names of individuals who may eventually be determined to have not been involved in a crime.
Kristy Winslow, a senior paralegal and supervisor for the criminal division of the attorney general’s office, sent the email at about 2:50 p.m. Thursday. A follow-up email attempted to recall the message several minutes later.
About half an hour after the original email was sent, Hayes, the attorney general’s spokesperson, asked anyone who received it to delete the message and destroy any printed copies of the report.
“Any disclosure could endanger the integrity of the criminal investigations and the safety of the individuals,” she wrote.
The list of recipients included dozens of state employees — but also journalists and email addresses for the Portland Press Herald, Morning Sentinel, Kennebec Journal, Sun Journal and Bangor Daily News, as well as WGME, WVII and WMTW owner Hearst.
Tarpinian said she feels for those involved in Thursday’s incident.
“I think we all can sympathize with sending information that we didn’t intend to,” she said. “This is just on a larger scale than I think usually happens.”

title: Atlantic hurricanes starting with ‘I’ typically bring death and destruction. Here’s why
text:
(AP) - Be wary of hurricanes that start with the letter “I.”
The ninth letter of the alphabet leads all others in the number of named Atlantic storms that have been retired over the decades due to their destruction or high death tolls. The names may be out of circulation, but storms including Ian, Ida, Igor, Ike, Inez, Ingrid, Iota, Irene, Irma, Isabel and Ivan left lasting legacies.
Next up is Isaias, which became the first hurricane of the Atlantic season on Wednesday night. Whether it lives up to the misery of others whose first letter it shares remains to be seen. The latest forecast suggested Isaias could be less dramatic, but still “extremely dangerous.”
“It’s the ‘I’ storm, which usually we have a lot earlier in the year,” said Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of atmospheric and environmental sciences at the University at Albany. “It’s always the ‘I’ storms that seem to cause problems.”
Isaias was expected to make landfall on the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
Atlantic hurricanes have been given names since 1953, and 100 of them are no longer used. There have been 14 storms with “I” names retired, including 12 this century. When eastern and central Pacific hurricanes are considered, that retired “I” list grows to 20.
Ten Atlantic storm names starting with “F” have been retired, followed by “C” with nine, and “D” and “M” with eight apiece, according to a list compiled by the hurricane center.
Why I is such a foreboding letter
Hurricanes starting with “I” typically occur in the middle of the June 1-Nov. 30 season, when warming ocean waters can supercharge a storm’s energy.
The timing of Isaias is an exception to this trend, due to the current super El Niño weather pattern, which stunted Atlantic hurricane formations through September while cranking out storms throughout the Pacific region.
Isaias came one day shy of tying a 121-year-old record for the latest-forming initial hurricane of the Atlantic season.
‘I’ storms prove to be costly
Of the 55 costliest hurricanes to hit the United States, a dozen began with the letter “I”, including four in the top 10.
Category 4 Ian in 2022 came in at No. 3 with $119.6 billion in damage. Ian hammered Florida with such ferocity that it wiped out whole neighborhoods, tossed boats onto highways, swept away beaches and swamped homes in roof-deep waters.
Category 4 Ida, devastating parts of Louisiana in 2021, was the sixth-costliest hurricane at $84.6 billion. Category 4 Irma tore through the Florida Keys in 2017 for No. 8 at a cost of $64 billion. Category 2 Ike made landfall near Galveston, Texas, in 2008 for No. 10 at $43.2 billion. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said it based these figures on the 2024 Consumer Price Index adjusted cost.
In 2020, they ran out of names. Then came Iota
The 2020 hurricane season exhausted that year’s alphabetical list of storm names by mid-September, so later storms were identified using Greek letters, including Iota, the 30th named storm of that record-breaking year.
Category 4 Iota decimated Nicaragua and Honduras in November 2020 only two weeks after another hurricane had passed through the region.
The World Meteorological Organization, which oversees storm naming, later decided not to use the Greek alphabet for future storms, citing potential confusion when translated into other languages. Instead, a supplemental list of names will be used when the standard list is exhausted in a particular season.
Ivan spawned 118 tornadoes in a destructive loop
Ivan tore through Grand Cayman island in 2004, damaging or destroying an estimated 95 percent of the buildings there, the National Weather Service said. Then it slammed into the United States, spawning 118 tornadoes from Florida to Pennsylvania, more than any other tropical system since modern-day records have been kept starting in 1950, the weather service said. The storm was blamed for 124 deaths, including 57 in the United States.
Ivan formed during an El Niño, and churned a loopy path. After coming ashore near Gulf Shores, Alabama, it went up to Virginia, then back down through southeast Florida, returning into the U.S. Gulf and to Texas.
Irene was among the costliest in its category
In 2011, Hurricane Irene sent cars bobbing down rivers, swept away covered bridges, put millions in the dark and killed dozens of people. It made landfall along the North Carolina coast, then veered north along a densely populated corridor. New York City took a direct hit, but the heaviest rains were further inland.
In Vermont, the storm killed six people, washed homes off their foundations and damaged or destroyed more than 200 bridges and 500 miles (805 kilometers) of highway. It was the costliest Category 1 U.S. hurricane on record since at least 1980, with estimated total damage of $18.8 billion.
___
AP Science Writer Seth Borenstein in Kensington, Maryland, contributed to this report.

title: Did Maine state senators represent counties until the mid-1960s?
text:
Yes.
Until the mid-1960s, Maine senators represented counties rather than today’s population-based districts. Under the state constitution in effect in 1965, every county received one to five senators, depending on its population.
That system changed amid a national reapportionment revolution. In 1964, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Reynolds v. Sims that both chambers of state legislatures generally must be apportioned by population, establishing the principle commonly known as “one person, one vote.”
Maine voters responded in November 1966, approving a constitutional amendment that replaced county representation with senatorial districts centered around roughly 30,000 residents.
When lawmakers failed to agree on a map, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court stepped in and drew 32 districts in 1967.
Counties still played a role under the new maps, as the amendment instructed mapmakers to follow county lines as much as possible.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Letter: Troy Jackson would be a sorry replacement for Susan Collins
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
At 80 years of age I have seen a lot of elections. This one however takes the cake, I believe, for being the nastiest and probably the most costly.
What bothers me the most are the attacks on Sen. Susan Collins. I believe the claim that she caves to President Donald Trump is absurd.
