She has stood up in support of issues that she felt would benefit her constituents, whether from the left or the right.
Why would the left complain that a Republican supports a Republican president 95% of the time? I would venture that Sen. Angus King votes against Trump most of the time.
Trump will be gone in about two years. I think the self-described lumberjack who has been in politics for 20 years would be a sorry replacement for Collins.
Remember, Trump is not on the ballot. Be careful who you vote for.
Leo H. Mazerall Jr.
Stockton Springs

title: Julie A. Witzell
text:
Julie Ann (Dow) Witzell, of Edgecomb, Maine, formerly of Upton, Massachusetts, passed away peacefully on July 29, 2026, surrounded by her loving family, at the age of 79.
Julie, the daughter of Edward and Eleanor Dow, grew up in Natick, Massachusetts.
In 1970, Julie married the love of her life, William Witzell, sharing 56 wonderful years of marriage.
Julie is survived by her devoted husband, William Witzell; her daughter, Lynne McLain and her husband, Brian; her son, Greg Witzell; and her cherished grandchildren, Michael McLain, Cody McLain, and Katie Witzell. She also leaves behind four sisters, one brother, and many nieces and nephews.
She was predeceased by her parents Edward and Eleanor Dow, her daughter-in-law, Rebecca (Vincent) Witzell, and niece Kristina Bartlett.
Family was the center of Julie's world. Nothing brought her greater joy than spending time with those she loved. She had a heart of gold, an unforgettable sense of humor, and an artistic eye for both painting and writing.
Julie loved browsing yard sales and thrift shops in search of hidden treasures, especially cookbooks to add to her ever-growing collection. She enjoyed reading and completing crossword puzzles. It was these simple joys, along with her generous spirit and gentle kindness, that made her so special.
Though our hearts are heavy with her loss, we are grateful for the love, laughter, and countless memories she gave us. Julie's kindness, warmth, and unwavering love for her family will continue to inspire all who were fortunate enough to know her.
We are deeply grateful for the wonderful staff at St. Andrews Retirement Home for their care and love for Julie.
A Celebration of Life will be held on Saturday, Sept. 26 from 1 to 4 p.m. at The American Legion, 25 Industrial Park Road, Boothbay.
Julie will be deeply missed and forever remembered with love.

title: Big brother’s bone marrow donation offers hope to 9-year-old sister with sickle cell disease
text:
ALABASTER, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - An older brother’s bone marrow donation will offer a second chance at life for his 9-year-old sister, who has sickle cell disease.
Alexa Turner, a 9-year-old student at Thompson Intermediate School, is dealing with more than homework. She has sickle cell disease. Her 13-year-old brother, Amari Rose, is a bone marrow match for a transplant surgery set for January.
Now, the siblings are learning to process medical terms including blood transfusion, surgery and lifesaving. Their mother, Jennifer Turner, said she struggles with the vocabulary, too.
“Honestly, the attitude, the positive attitude that they have... they encourage me because I’m the one that needs help when it comes to those big words,” Turner said.
Alexa’s struggle has been difficult for the family
Sickle cell disease causes blood cells to take on an irregular shape, which causes pain and can threaten Alexa’s life.
“When you have sickle cell, it’s not just the one thing that’s being hard. It’s just that you just got to keep on going and keep on walking through that path and let God walk you through it and keep on being brave,” Alexa said.
Amari said watching his sister’s struggle has been difficult.
“It’s been sad to watch my sister get hurt and, like, in pain,” he said.
Alexa’s mother said sickle cell disease brings additional risks beyond blood and pain crises. Her daughter is at risk for acute chest syndrome, a form of pneumonia in the lungs that she experiences every year.
“So, every year, we’re watching her fight for her life with no oxygen. I mean, her lowest is like 70, and we were fighting,” Turner said.
The family is also fighting against silent strokes. Alexa receives monthly blood transfusions to try to restore proper blood flow to her brain and prevent a major stroke.
‘Fight through your fear’
Amari is a bone marrow match for his sister, and the transplant surgery is scheduled for January. The process will include chemotherapy and radiation.
Afterward, the family will need to quarantine. They will isolate for 9 to 12 months to protect Alexa from infection while her immune system rebuilds.
“You have to be brave when anything that you’re afraid of. You have to just fight through your fear and go through it. ‘Cause like how I said with God, if he’s right there beside me... then, I guess he’s just going to be walking me through that path,” Alexa said.
Turner said her daughter’s story underscores the need for people to give blood, which is crucial for Alexa and others with sickle cell disease.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help the family because Turner will not be able to work during the quarantine period.

title: Maine AG's Office accidentally shares confidential case info with media outlets
text:
Maine Attorney General's Office accidentally shares confidential case information with media outlets
A supervisor within the Criminal Division of the Maine Attorney General's Office accidentally emailed a document that included confidential case information to a number of media outlets, including WMTW.
The 45-page document, which was sent at 2:50 p.m. Thursday, featured information about dozens of homicide and manslaughter cases in Maine, including the names of suspects who have not yet been charged.
The document also includes details about alleged crimes and evidence gathered that have not been released publicly.
The supervisor who sent the email recalled it at 2:53 p.m., three minutes after it was sent.
At 3:21 p.m., the Attorney General's Office sent another message asking everyone who received the email to delete it, along with the attached document.
"The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that," the Maine Attorney General's Office said in a statement shared at 6:12 p.m. Thursday. "Unfortunately, a distribution list reserved to push public information out to the media was accidentally used. We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine. We respectfully request our partners in the media help us by not compounding our error."
It appears the intent of the email was to get lawyers and investigators to update their reports for internal use.

title: Border crossing between Maine and New Brunswick to close for 6 weeks
text:
Border crossing between Maine and New Brunswick to close for 6 weeks
The Ferry Point Bridge port of entry between Calais and St. Stephen, New Brunswick, will close for six weeks starting next week so that the Maine Department of Transportation (MaineDOT) can make repairs to the bridge.
The Ferry Point Bridge carries traffic over the St. Croix River.
MaineDOT says the project includes deck rehabilitation and bridge joint repair on the Maine side of the international border crossing.
The bridge will close on Oct. 13 and work is expected to be done by the end of November.
Drivers traveling between Calais and St. Stephen should use the Milltown International Bridge between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. (9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Atlantic Daylight Time) about two miles away, or the International Avenue Bridge/St. Stephen Third Bridge, which is open 24-7 and is about 2.5 miles away.
Commercial traffic must use the International Avenue Bridge, also known as Third Bridge.

title: DNC sues Trump administration over taxpayer-funded TV ads
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Democratic National Committee has filed a federal lawsuit accusing the Trump administration of illegally spending millions of taxpayer dollars on television advertisements promoting President Donald Trump just weeks before the midterm elections.
The lawsuit, filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., alleges the ads were designed to boost the president’s public image and help Republicans maintain control of Congress.
The commercials began airing in late September, featuring major moments from Trump’s second term, including his administration’s immigration enforcement efforts and military operations.
According to media-tracking firm AdImpact, the administration has spent more than $12 million airing the commercials. The money comes from Department of Homeland Security funding, with $20 million allocated for the advertising campaign.
The White House has defended the commercials as public service announcements, arguing that previous administrations have used government funds to promote their policies.
But Democrats believe the ads cross a legal line.
“Congress has banned spending taxpayer dollars on publicity or propaganda,” said Dan Freeman, litigation director for the Democratic National Committee. “These ads are flagrantly illegal, and in the run-up to an election, we thought it was just vital that the Democratic National Committee stand up for free and fair elections, fight back against these autocratic tactics.”
The DNC’s lawsuit asks a federal judge to declare the administration’s spending illegal and block the government from using additional taxpayer money to air the advertisements.
After days of criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, Trump announced Monday that future advertisements would be paid for using money from his super PAC, MAGA Inc., rather than taxpayer funds.
However, the president has not committed to reimbursing the government for the millions already spent.
“The ads were really good. They were promotion for the country. Done by presidents before, so we’ll decide,” Trump told reporters Tuesday when asked whether the government would be reimbursed.
In a September 25 statement, the White House rejected accusations that the commercials were intended to influence the midterm elections. The administration argued that Trump is not on the ballot and that the advertisements do not explicitly ask Americans to vote for Republican candidates.
The White House also pointed to campaigns for government programs under previous presidents, including George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden, as examples of government-funded public messaging.
The controversy has also prompted calls for congressional oversight.
Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, has called for an investigation into the advertising campaign and for taxpayer money spent on the commercials to be returned to the government.
Friday, the DNC filed a further request - a Temporary Restraining Order against the Trump administration to immediately stop them from using more taxpayer dollars to air blatantly illegal campaign-style TV advertisements.

title: Public executions in the US were once a community spectacle and then they stopped
text:
For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. The stunning Pentagon announcement Thursday that the first military execution in more than 65 years will be livestreamed could change that.
Allowing the world to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan face the firing squad in December would make it the first public execution since two hangings in the 1930s in Kentucky and Missouri drew crowds.
In 1936, a man who reportedly confessed to the rape and murder of a woman was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a man in Missouri be hanged.
Proposal harkens back to a bygone era
A livestreamed execution is reminiscent of a bygone period in America’s history in which public executions were seen as deterrents to crime as well as popular ceremonies, said Michael L. Radelet, professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on executions.
Parents and teachers would often bring children along to teach them a lesson. The events would sometimes feature a choir, a preacher giving an “execution sermon” and the condemned, who was typically a man being hanged, giving a long speech to the crowd.
In an execution in Leadville, Colorado, in the late 1800s, Radelet said Cyrus Minich, who was being put to death, told the crowd, “Therefore I apologize and I’m ready to go. Goodbye, goodbye.”
The crowd reportedly responded: “Goodbye Cy, goodbye Cy.”
“This is in the days before TV, so not much going on often in big cities, certainly in rural areas, too, so they were there just for the spectacle,” Radelet said, adding that sometimes it would draw a crowd because the person was so hated.
Thousands watched country’s last public execution
The 1936 hanging in Kentucky of Rainey Bethea is often considered the last public execution in the country, said Radelet.
Bethea was a Black man who reportedly confessed to the rape and killing of a 70-year-old white woman, but was never charged with murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thousands of people attended the event, which was held in a parking lot so the courthouse lawn wouldn’t be damaged by the crowd, according to the center.
But there was also one the following year in which Roscoe “Red” Jackson in Missouri was hanged. The Los Angeles Times reported that some people were given passes to watch, while others climbed trees or cut peepholes to catch a glimpse of the morning execution.
States started to change the policy as an increasing number of people witnessed botched hangings and as broader concerns grew over the events, Radelet said.
“Instead of promoting the sanctity of life and how solemn the circumstance was, with people applauding and having a carnival-like atmosphere, that really turned people off,” he said.
Oklahoma City bomber’s execution was on CCTV
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said they have no record of any execution being livestreamed.
The closest came in 2001, when Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed at a federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana. Then-U.S. Attorney General John Ashcroft announced that victims could attend in person or view it through a closed-circuit television
But will the Army’s announcement about livestreaming the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding many others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, change the situation?
Maher said she sees Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s comments as “simply aspirational.”
“There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public,” she said in a statement.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
Execution would raise both legal and social questions
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said the announcement raises many legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when a botched execution in Tennessee has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.

title: Susan Collins’ campaign needs to be more forthcoming
text:
In his recent op-ed column (“Susan Collins’ donors are the people we need to be worrying about,” Nov. 9) Maurice Cunningham makes a valid point that the bigger scandals in politics are the perfectly legal pay-to-play dark money contributions.
Cunningham cites, among others, Peter Thiel’s Palantir, which he characterizes as “a virtual partner of the government” with millions in contracts, including $200 million with ICE, and whose employees have given $117,000 to Collins’ political committees.
But legal scandals should not deter us from scrutinizing and holding accountable illegal ones.
Collins’ campaign officials object to reports of a $150,000 illegal campaign contribution from the CEO of the defense contractor Navatek and alleged reciprocation through government contract awards worth millions, claiming that the FBI investigated and dropped its inquiry. But they tend to fail to note that Trump’s FBI later backed off, and, meanwhile ProPublica’s reporting has presented receipts, including in the form of a check to a Collins-affiliated entity.
The Collins campaign needs to be more forthcoming. Voters heading to the ballot box have a right to know whether this “Navagate” scandal is real and what is says about who Collins’ true constituents are.
Nelson Checkoway
Ogunquit

title: Trump attitude to AI should give voters pause
text:
The catalog of serious problems for our nation caused by the current president is breathtaking. As recent polls show, a clear majority of Americans do not approve of where he has been taking us across a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues.
The most recent troubling action occurred last month when the Trump team reportedly worked with the Russians to weaken a U.N. agreement designed to create guardrails around the development of AI systems involving the use of autonomous lethal weapons. This at a time when even CEOs of the companies that are racing headlong to develop AI are sounding warnings about the high potential threat to humanity this new technology could present.
We need to remember that while this president is the main driving force behind all of these destructive initiatives, he would not be able to follow through on many of them without the support of a Republican-led House of Representatives and Senate.
Whatever one’s political persuasion, if people want to put the brakes on this reckless, damaging and potentially dangerous leadership, they should be voting blue.

title: Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the US
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to crack down on foreign enrollment.
A proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years.
Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student’s initial application to the program, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal.
Change would be a blow to higher education and some businesses
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. Tech companies and other industries also hire many international students for technical roles.
The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education.
“Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership,” Aw said in a written statement.
In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a “pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it.
Trump administration puts pressure on international students
The proposed rule is part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education. Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them.
This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September.
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, predicted that the fee would be struck down in the courts, as was a $100,000 fee for the H-1B work visas that many tech companies and universities rely on to fill openings for skilled jobs.
The Trump administration is now trying a different way to raise the fee for the visas to more than $100,000.
Rand said fees are not the answer.
“When we educate international students at our universities, and they want to work and apply their talents here after graduating, of course we should embrace them -- not use an exorbitant fee as a pretext to send them packing,” Rand said in an email.
Enrollment concerns mount among education groups
Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said international enrollment has suffered.
Last fall, the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 17%, the sharpest decrease since the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall numbers for this fall are not yet available, but Spreitzer said some individual colleges are reporting drops of 30% to 40%.
She said the new Trump plan will not help.
“We know that OPT is one of the reasons that international students choose to study in the United States because they’re able to have that post-graduation work experience,” she added.
A similar program that allowed international students to participate in internships and practicums also has faced scrutiny from the Trump administration. New guidance from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that the program, Curricular Practical Training, should only be authorized when the work experience is a degree requirement led to a lawsuit Monday.
Education groups, including the Association of American Universities and NAFSA, said that in the past that program was allowed if it was “directly related to the student’s major area of study.” The groups also said ICE was threatening college university officials with criminal prosecution if they did not comply.
“We know the administration has been trying to hinder legal employment-based immigration through numerous means,” said Steven Brown, a Houston-based immigration lawyer. “I think this is the next level of attack, and I think it’s a design to kill the program without killing the program. I don’t see too many schools wanting to pay $70,000 for a student to get OPT.”
___
Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kan.

title: In Augusta, the Mill Park Pétanque Club teaches its game to a new generation
text:
AUGUSTA — Eric Ayotte picked up the nuances of pétanque quickly. A golfer, the Mattanawcook Academy junior studied the way the ball spun and broke on the crushed stone court the way he studies a green before a putt.
Where do I want to toss this ball so it not only ends up closest to the cochonet, the smaller target ball, but also prevents my opponents from getting a clean shot? Where’s the break? Is there a divot in the stone that will mess everything up?
“You really have to think about your shot. There’s a lot of moving parts,” Ayotte said between games Thursday morning at Augusta’s Mill Park. “It would be sick to get one of these in Lincoln.”
That’s exactly the kind of thing Raymond Fecteau wants to hear. He calls pétanque, “the best game nobody’s heard of,” and he’s trying to change that.
Fecteau, 82, is one of the founders of the Mill Park Pétanque Club. Since he retired from his career as a barber 17 years ago, Fecteau’s goal has been to play pétanque as much as possible, and pass the game on to anyone who wants to learn how to play.
“What I like best is teaching kids how to do it,” he said, “but we don’t get a lot of kids.”
On this overcast Thursday morning, with the trees along the nearby Kennebec River hitting their fall color peak, that meant giving a lesson to 16 students from a Mattanawcook French class who made the 250-mile round trip from Lincoln.
This was the second time French teacher Melanie Turner brought one of her classes to Augusta for a day of pétanque. It’s a chance for the students to learn a game they can play the rest of their lives, as well as find a touchstone to the Franco culture many of them share, Turner said.
“I think it’s important for them to make that connection,” she said. “I’d like to see if we can bring it back to Lincoln.”
Pétanque’s rules are easy to learn. Standing inside a ring, players try to get their balls closest to the cochonet. The balls are hollow and metal, about the size of a baseball, the perfect size to fit into your palm.
“I think it’s pretty fun,” Gracie Averill, a Mattanawcook junior, said an hour after playing the game for the first time. “We do get competitive. It’s just a fun game that’s not too strenuous.”
At Mill Park, the club has 10 courts, and lighting to play in the evening. Right around the time he retired, Fecteau learned the game on a trip to France. He bought a set of balls and played where he could, introducing friends to the game.
With enough people looking for a place to enjoy a few rounds of pétanque, Fecteau and the club approached the city of Augusta and asked for a space to build courts. The club raised $50,000, and the courts at Mill Park were the result.
The Mill Park Pétanque Club currently has 71 members, Fecteau said. The membership skews older. Seniors come during the day to play. As Fecteau and a handful of club members taught the students, a group of senior women played their weekly games on one of the courts.
Last year, Fecteau had open heart surgery. He thought maybe his pétanque playing days were over. After a couple months of rest of rehab, he was back on the courts. Dan Howard took over as club president, taking a little off Fecteau’s plate.
Teaching the game to younger players, passing the game along, is important.
“I think the baby of our crowd is around 47,” Fecteau said, “but see, these people, they take to it.”
Fecteau pointed to Ayotte and three of his classmates getting instruction from club member Gary Golden. They studied the lay of the court before making their throws. They cheered when somebody made a good throw. He pointed to a court where Howard coached another group of students. The same thing was happening there.
“In the time they’ve been here, you see how much progress they’ve made. It’s satisfying,” Fecteau said.
Fecteau smiled. When you pass on something you love, satisfying isn’t a strong enough description.

title: Tracking Isaias: Storm becomes the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
text:
Isaias weakens but flash flooding threat persists as hundred of thousands grapple with power outages
Isaias weakened overnight and was no longer considered a hurricane, but flash flooding threats and the potential for tornadoes persisted Saturday as the storm moved inland across Alabama.
The storm, now considered a post-tropical cyclone, made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply to 35 mph. But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with a potential for 4 to 8 inches of rain across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend over the weekend.
Early Saturday, Isaias was about 25 miles south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama and nearly 105 miles south of Birmingham, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph, the NHC said Saturday. It is expected to move into the Tennessee Valley later Saturday and Sunday.
All tropical storm and storm surge warnings have been discontinued. But forecasters warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard "throughout the region.”
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
Satellite images of Isaias
Many are braving Isaias at home
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
“As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate,” Mowry said.
Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.
Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often serves as a measure of a storm’s severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace and no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.
“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier.
DeSantis warned residents to expect gasoline shortages and bridge and highway closures.
The state's National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search-and-rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.
Video above: Communities prepare for Hurricane Isaias
The whole region could get soaked
Isaias was already slowing after landfall, and it was expected to weaken further and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the center said.
Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.
Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
Isaias was expected to miss the oil industry's biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast, but fuel prices could rise if power outages shut down refineries for processing crude, industry experts said.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Hurricane Simon became a Category 4 storm early Saturday, ahead of a projected landfall in Mexico this weekend.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.
___
Megnien reported from Panama City, Florida, and Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. title: We need a public, nonprofit universal healthcare system now
text:
Paul F. Kando lives in Damariscotta.
Maine’s newspapers are full of articles and reader comments about the terrible shape of our healthcare. Not only is our business-modeled “healthcare” expensive, lately it has been even difficult to find a doctor; and essential hospital departments are being closed, based on their lack of profitability.
I am afraid capitalist ideology is at the root of what, in these United States, including Maine, passes for “healthcare.” But health, illness and knowledge are not commodities on which to legitimately profit.
At age 90, I still miss the “circuit doctors” of my teenage years. As a teenager in postwar Europe, my family and I were beneficiaries of a simple, decentralized universal healthcare alternative — which could serve as an alternative model to our failing system.
My whole native country was divided into circuits, to each of which a resident “circuit doctor” was assigned. At his/her disposal, as needed, were a pool of home visiting nurses and other assistants, as well as other doctors to consult.
The circuit doctor was paid a decent salary plus expenses and provided an office and subsidized family housing in the community. His job was to keep visiting his circuit, to (1) counsel healthy ways of living, (2) diagnose illnesses, (3) distribute or prescribe (no cost) medicines as required, (4) treat and help heal sick people in their homes and (5) arrange for pubic, nonprofit hospital or sanatorium care (including transportation), if needed.
Our family’s beloved circuit doctor routinely stopped by to see us once or twice every week. Our healthcare was free from a public nonprofit system. It was also economical: with people’s homes doubling as healthcare facilities, the cost of most hospital/nursing home rooms was eliminated. Even very ill people were cared for at home by our circuit doctors who often taught family members to do home care.
Of course, such a free public healthcare system was made possible in part by universal access to housing and tuition free education. We had no homeless people, and our doctors received their education without becoming indebted. But the most important feature was the absence of (capitalist) ideology. And in such a nonprofit system insurance companies had no legitimate role— certainly not in selecting medical procedures.
Such a system could be painlessly tax-financed through fair, progressive taxation that set the income tax rate according to a person’s real income (the standard throughout the sadly bygone, civilized era of the post-World War II liberal consensus in American politics). Alternatively, everyone could be charged a given percentage (say 2-3%) of his/her income.
Having lived with much better options in several civilized countries, I consider corporate “business” healthcare an oxymoron. Civilized countries have affordable, universal healthcare systems. Americans seem to be intellectually paralyzed when it comes to alternatives to our own failing health system, even though good alternatives abound.

title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, has dies at 90
text:
Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, dies at 90
Margaret Hamilton, the groundbreaking researcher who helped create the field of software engineering and whose code helped land NASA’s Apollo astronauts on the moon to win the 20th-century space race, has died. She was 90.
Hamilton’s former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, confirmed her death in a post from the department of aeronautics and astronautics. The cause of her death was not disclosed.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
It was during her time working at MIT, where she took a job in 1959 and remained until the mid-1970s, that Hamilton managed the Software Engineering Division of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory. The division landed a contract with NASA in 1961. She ultimately led a team of 100 engineers that designed the software to guide NASA’s Apollo missions.
Through her work, Hamilton is also credited as one of the founders of the field of software engineering — a term she coined — by helping to establish it as a professional practice.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”
Hamilton was honored in 2016 with the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama for her contribution to science and space travel.

title: Walk a half mile in your shoes, in Brunswick and beyond
text:
Leave the car parked for a 1-mile round trip and you prevent about 0.9 pounds of tailpipe carbon dioxide—and skip the cold-start minutes when a gasoline car pollutes most.
There’s probably a trip in your week that’s almost too short to call a trip: the post office, the pharmacy, the library, school.
Those little drives don’t use much fuel, but they’re short enough to walk and often begin with a cold engine, when a gasoline car is least efficient and its pollution controls haven’t warmed up.
This week, pick one trip of about a half mile that you’d normally drive, and walk it instead.
This is a step along the Movement pathway: how we and our things get from place to place. Some changes along this pathway take money and years. This one saves you a little money for a little time and effort.
GOOD WEEK TO RECONSIDER A SHORT TRIP
The first Wednesday in October is National Walk and Roll to School Day in the United States, coordinated by the National Center for Safe Routes to School. Thousands of schools participate, encouraging families to walk, bike, or roll instead of driving. It’s a good prompt for the rest of us, too.
A half mile is roughly a 10-minute walk for many adults, and distance shapes habits. The National Household Travel Survey shows that more than 80% of children living within a quarter mile typically walk to school, as do more than half of those a quarter to a half mile away.
The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that an average fuel-burning passenger vehicle emits about 400 grams of carbon dioxide per mile from its tailpipe. That’s about 0.9 pounds of CO2 for a 1-mile round trip. Walk that round trip weekly for a year and you’ve prevented dozens of pounds of pollution without buying anything.
Modern gasoline cars control some air pollution well once their engines and catalytic converters are hot, but engines don’t start hot. In one study of trips under 5 kilometers that began with a fully cooled engine, the cold start accounted for more than 90% of carbon-monoxide emissions and more than 80% of particle-number emissions in some conditions. The numbers vary by vehicle and weather, but the pattern is consistent.
Fuel economy suffers, too. The U.S. Department of Energy and EPA report that several short cold-start trips can use roughly twice the fuel of one warm-engine trip of the same distance, even more in cold weather.
So the day’s first trip, which begins with a cold engine, is an especially good one to replace with walking.
SCHOOL IS ONE DESTINATION. WHAT IS YOURS?
If you have children in school, check whether their school is participating in Walk and Roll to School Day. If it isn’t, suggest it to a teacher for next year.
Otherwise, look at the trips you make without thinking.
Maybe you drive half a mile to get coffee on Saturday morning.
Maybe your nearest post office is eight blocks away.
Maybe you drive to a neighborhood trailhead so you can… go for a walk.
Look, too, for trips where the walk itself adds something: meeting a friend, lunch with a coworker, or walking grandchildren or young neighbors to school.
THE HALF-MILE EXPERIMENT
Think of a place about half a mile away where you’d normally grab the car keys but could walk. Next time, go on foot.
Then notice the details. How long did it really take? Was it pleasant? Did you dress for the weather? Did 10 minutes outside beat 10 minutes behind the wheel?
There are legitimate reasons not to walk some trips: ability, road safety, weather, heavy loads, tight schedules, or missing sidewalks. Your challenge is finding the ones that work for you.
YOUR CHALLENGE THIS WEEK
Choose one destination about a half mile away that you would ordinarily reach by car. Walk there instead.
If you’re connected to a school, Walk and Roll to School Day is a ready-made opportunity. Check participation at walkbiketoschool.org.
No school connection? Establish your own Walk and Roll Day: coffee, lunch, the library, an appointment, a friend’s house.
If the experiment works, do it again next week. Turn “a trip I could walk” into simply “a place I walk to.”
Expand your positive impact on Earth by becoming a sustainable practitioner today!
Sustainable Practice empowers you to protect our planet in practical ways. Share this article with someone who has a short trip they might enjoy taking on foot.
Fred Horch and Peggy Siegle are principals of Sustainable Practice. You can pick up their new 2026 edition of “Your Earth Share: Seven Pathways to Sustainable Living” or any of their other publications at SustainablePractice.Life. Join their community of sustainable practitioners at that address for both benefits and books.

title: Case dismissed against 1 of 4 adults after 16 children found in ‘deplorable’ home, looked like ‘feral animals’
text:
VINTON COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - A judge has dismissed the case against one of the four adults charged in an Ohio child endangerment case where 16 children were found in “deplorable conditions.”
The case against Gary Siders Sr. was dismissed after he was found not competent to stand trial, according to court records.
Gary Siders Sr. is one of four adults who were charged after 16 children were found living in an Ohio home that officials called “third world” and “deplorable.”
Gary Siders Jr., Elizabeth Siders and Christina Siders were all indicted by a grand jury in August. Elizabeth Siders and Christina Siders were indicted on 19 charges. Gary Siders Jr. was indicted on 16 charges.
The raid at the home
The adults were arrested after Vinton County Sheriff’s Office and the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation executed a search warrant at the home in Hamden, Ohio.
Officials said they were there for an unrelated investigation when they found the children.
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson said if authorities had waited another 24 hours to raid the home, some of the children may have died.
Conditions of the children
Several of the children were in serious condition and two were flown to hospitals due to the severity of their conditions, Wilson said.
“Some of the children could not even speak and looked like feral animals,” he said.
The children ranged in age from 1 to 18. All 16 of them had to be medically evaluated.
“The number one priority is to make sure that these kids are taken care of physically, mentally and emotionally,” Wilson said.

title: Collapsed span of Old Town bridge to be demolished, traffic impacts expected
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - A bridge in Old Town that collapsed during construction nearly two months ago will be partially demolished starting next week.
The replacement Llewellyn Estes bridge, which spans the Stillwater River, collapsed in August when crews were pouring concrete as part of a years-long construction project. Three workers were injured.
The Maine Department of Transportation said the temporary bridge that was carrying traffic was not damaged.
Crews will begin removing the impacted spans of the bridge on Tuesday between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., according to the Maine DOT. The work could continue into the following week.
The temporary bridge will be closed for periods while crews work, though exact times are fluid.
Workers will separate the damaged span from the pier and abutment, making the pieces smaller before removing them from the river.
Motorists should expect delays while the work is ongoing. The MaineDOT says drivers should follow detour signs for Bennoch Road, North Main Street, and College Avenue to return to Stillwater Avenue.

title: Adult education enrollment surges as programs expand
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — Franklin County Adult & Community Education is seeing strong enrollment growth as it expands workforce training, college and career preparation and community education programs under new Director Donna Seppy.
Seppy told the Regional School Unit 9 board of directors Sept. 22 that overall enrollment is up sharply from last year and nearly 80% from two years ago. “We’re up 70.7% to be exact from last year in terms of overall enrollment,” Seppy said. She attributed much of the growth to the program’s college and career offerings and work center.
The program’s September newsletter shows community education enrollment increasing from 177 in 2025 to 330 in 2026, while workforce program enrollment rose from 30 to 73. High school completion enrollment increased from 73 to 75.
Seppy also highlighted a summer welding partnership with Bath Iron Works. About 14 people participated in the July program, and nine received job offers from BIW. “They were so pleased with the program up here that they already come and talked to us about trying to do something again next summer,” Seppy told the board.
The program is also exploring development of an emergency medical technician program with support from Foster Career and Technical Education Center and emergency management partners. Seppy said offering EMT training locally could reduce the need for students to travel to Auburn, Portland or Waterville.
Adult education is offering more than 65 community programs this fall, including financial literacy, foster care and adoption basics, birth doula training and homeschool support.
The Maine College & Career Access program provides free or low-cost academic support, career planning, financial aid guidance and college preparation. Services include help with resumes and cover letters, LinkedIn profiles, the FAFSA, career exploration and college preparation.
Eight participants advanced to college last year.
Seppy said the program has also expanded evening and testing opportunities, with drop-in hours during the week and HiSET testing and assessments available on multiple days, including Saturdays.
Another new effort is homeschool support. Seppy said the program recently held its first information session for homeschool students and families, drawing about 18 people. “We’re going to be doing some services and supports there for all ages and help out not only the students, but the parents that are trying to lead and support the students in the community,” Seppy said.
The RSU 9 board appointed Seppy director of Franklin County Adult Education at the end of June, and she began serving July 13.
Seppy holds a doctorate in education and has nearly 30 years of experience in education, workforce development and community service. Her background includes work in clinical and correctional settings, K-12 and higher education, the University of Maine System, and educational settings in the United States, Europe, East Asia and the Pacific Islands.
She has also served on a local school board, including two years as chair, and spent about 10 years with the American Red Cross as a disaster mental health and mass casualty provider. She has operated the Monmouth Fair’s main office for more than eight years.
In her new role, Seppy said she plans to build on the program’s foundation while strengthening partnerships with schools, businesses and community organizations and expanding outreach in rural parts of Franklin County.
“I’m excited to get to know the communities we serve and learn from the people and organizations already doing great work across Franklin County,” Seppy said.
She said adult education can help people earn credentials, prepare for careers, continue their education or learn something new. “I believe FCAE is where education, work, and community meet, and paths come together,” Seppy said.
Two new staff members have also joined the program. Michael Mercier is serving as a commercial drivers license instructor, while Kevin Brodeur is working with students at the Somerset and Franklin County correctional facilities.

title: Baby bath seats sold on Amazon recalled over drowning risks
text:
Baby bath seats sold on Amazon recalled over drowning risks
A popular baby bath seat sold on Amazon has been recalled over a potential drowning risk, federal officials announced Thursday.
About 2,140 ONTHEWEI baby bath seats are being recalled because they can tip over and put children at risk of drowning, officials with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said.
Related video above | How to stay ahead of recalls
The seats violate the mandatory safety standard for infant bath seats because they are unstable, the agency said.
No incidents or injuries have been reported.
The recall covers gray, pink, blue and mist green seats with detachable restraint arms and suction cups on the underside. The label on the back lists “Model No: MY002” and a manufacturing date of Jan. 10, 2026.
The seats were sold on Amazon in April for $40 to $50. They were made in China by Hubei Youhong Trading Co., which does business as ONTHEWEI.
Consumers should stop using the seats immediately and contact ONTHEWEI for a full refund. For more information on the recall, click here.

title: High schools Thursday: Falmouth, Portland boys soccer play to draw
text:
Jack Verville scored the tying goal for Falmouth midway through the second half as the Navigators played to a 2-2 draw against Portland in a Class A South boys soccer game Thursday at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
Falmouth (3-7-2) twice erased a one-goal deficit. Conor Kirkham tied it in the first half after an early goal by Portland’s Charlie Lavertu, which was assisted by Marcelo Malonda.
Lavertu then set up a goal by Malonda that put the Bulldogs (6-3-2) ahead 2-1 early in the second half.
Falmouth keeper Wyatt Binnette made 11 saves. Mateo Pulaski had six saves for Portland.
FRYEBURG ACADEMY 9, SACOPEE VALLEY 1: The Raiders (8-2-1), paced by two goals apiece from Joaquim Peres and Felix Merckens, rolled to a win over the Hawks (2-7-1) in Fryeburg.
Rafael Zanchi, Oriol Font, Pedro Barata, Hudson Hagan and Gabriel Kosnitzer were the other Fryeburg goal scorers.
Cooper Berkowitz scored for Sacopee.
WELLS 5, SPRUCE MOUNTAIN 1: Aiden Thibodeau and Logan Desper combined for five goals as the Warriors (3-8-1) defeated the Phoenix (0-9) in Jay.
Thibodeau recorded a hat trick and Desper scored twice. Wells keeper Josiah Leighton made 14 saves.
Jonathan Hines scored for Spruce Mountain.
THORNTON ACADEMY 3, NOBLE 0: Enzo Mugisha scored twice to lead the Trojans (9-0-2) past the Knights (2-6-3) in North Berwick.
Santiago Macias Olivar also scored, while David Moyemade, Griffin Ayers and Melvin Moyemade each had an assist. Lucas Stolf mad four saves for the shutout.
Noble’s Hunter Michaud stopped 11 shots.
FOOTBALL
OLD ORCHARD BEACH 66, TRAIP ACADEMY 0: The Seagulls (6-0) scored on three consecutive offensive plays in the first quarter, then added four second-quarter touchdowns on their way to a win over the Rangers (1-5) in Old Orchard Beach.
Evan Moody opened the scoring with a 23-yard catch from Matthew Charron. Old Orchard then recovered the kickoff at the Traip 40, and Moody broke free on the next play for another touchdown.
Traip nearly answered moments later when Matt Long caught a pass from JV Blanco and headed toward the end zone for what would have been a 66-yard touchdown. Charron, though, chased him down from behind and stripped the ball from Long just before he crossed the goal line, resulting in a touchback when the ball went through the end zone.
The Seagulls again scored immediately, on an 80-yard run by Brayden Koelker. Charron’s conversion rush made it 22-0.
Cooper Gallant ran for two TDs in the second quarter, sandwiched around touchdown runs by Charron and Koelker. Gabe Jefferds rushed for the conversion after each touchdown, bringing the halftime score to 54-0.
Two freshman added touchdowns in the second half. Brandon Costa scored on a 52-yard run, and Oscar Stanton had a 5-yard TD run.
CONY 37, CAMDEN HILLS 0: Drew Lindquist threw four first-half touchdown passes, and the Rams cruised to a win over Camden Hills in Augusta.
Cony, the ninth-ranked team in the Varsity Maine poll, bounced back from a 35-27 loss to Lawrence last week and improved to 5-1. Camden Hills is 1-5.
Lindquist, who finished with five TD passes, first threw a 44-yard scoring strike to Tyson Horne less than two minutes into the contest, then added a 9-yard pass to Jacob Fifield with 55.2 seconds left in the first quarter.
Lindquist threw scoring passes of 2 yards to Austin Bucknam and 6 yards to Landen Perry in the second quarter. Fifield caught an 18-yard TD pass from Lindquist in the third, and the Rams added a safety in the fourth.
MORSE 40, POLAND 6: The Shipbuilders (4-2) took advantage of short fields and rolled to a Class D South victory over the Knights (1-5) in Bath.
Morse’s first four touchdown drives began at the Poland 12, 27, 12 and 28. The fifth TD was a 73-yard run by Jack Trask midway through the final quarter.
Trask also caught one of Dylan Root’s three touchdown passes. Trask’s was a 20-yard reception, Oscar Gallant’s TD went for 12 yards, and Nathan Spaulding’s was a 28-yard touchdown.
Root completed all 10 of his passes for 120 yards and also rushed for 70 yards on 11 carries.
Junuh Hays scored the Shipbuilders’ first touchdown on a 1-yard run.
Poland’s touchdown was a 5-yard pass from Lucas Gayton to Lucas Verrill. Verrill also took a short pass 64 yards to the end zone, but it was called back because of a penalty.
Gallant and Nathan Trask each had an interception for Morse.
GIRLS SOCCER
MARSHWOOD 3, MASSABESIC 0: Tiegan Boisvert scored a pair of goals and the Hawks (5-5-1) shut out the Mustangs (1-11) in Waterboro.
Brooklyn Smith also scored.
FREEPORT 6, LINCOLN ACADEMY 2: Ella Tracy had two goals and an assist to power the Falcons (7-3) past the Eagles (8-3) in Newcastle.
Isla Pattershall and Emily Kelsh each added a goal and an assist, while Ada Shirley, Emily Kelsh and Lexi Ritcheson also scored for Freeport. Joanie Sacks was credited with two assists and Karleigh Costello made four saves.
Brea Lafranaya and Samantha Lopp scored for Lincoln, while Natalie Hanna stopped 12 shots.
SPRUCE MOUNTAIN 3, WELLS 2: The Phoenix (6-3-2) got goals from Lexus Hebert, Adalia Scarbrough and Natasha McDonald in a win over the Warriors (0-9-1) at Wells.
Ashley Nelson set up two goals and Jocelyn Melanson also had an assist for the Phoenix.
Aleah Bouchard converted a penalty kick for Wells. Eva Talevi got the other Warriors goal.
DEERING 6, SANFORD 0: Matilda Freeman scored three goals to spark the Rams (6-5-1) past the Spartans (3-7-1) in Portland.
Natalie Cameron added a goal and an assist. Zoe Noonan and Moriya Nguema Mve also scored.
Abbie Forest made nine saves for Scarborough.
FIELD HOCKEY
FRYEBURG ACADEMY 1, YORK 0: Kendall Valente scored from a scramble in the circle in overtime, lifting the Raiders (2-7) over the Wildcats (1-9) in York.
Sophia Carone earned the shutout with nine saves. York’s Sarah Orso had five saves.
VOLLEYBALL
PORTLAND 3, NOBLE 1: Asanti Bendasta recorded 16 kills, Cece Waring added nine kills, and the Bulldogs (6-5) beat the Knights (2-9) in four sets at North Berwick, 15-25, 25-14, 25-23, 25-17.
FALMOUTH 3, BIDDEFORD 0: Olive Clark had three aces and 15 kills to lead the Navigators (8-3) to a 25-14, 25-10, 25-12 sweep of the Tigers (0-10) in Falmouth.
Lyla Gagnon added two aces and seven kills, Megan Gilbert had an ace, two kills and 15 assists, and Rosie Clement had three aces and 10 digs.
Also for the Navigators, Ava Draeger recorded four aces and seven assists, and Embury Williams had three kills and two blocks.
MARSHWOOD 3, WINDHAM 0: Julia Sudol finished with nine kills and two blocks, Hannah Tuttle had 16 digs and Taylor Airey contributed 20 assists and three aces, helping the Hawks (6-5) beat the host Eagles (3-9) in three sets, 25-19, 25-19, 25-12.

title: Bucksport approves temporary data center ban
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bucksport’s town council approved a six-month moratorium on potential data center developments in a divided vote Thursday after weeks of discussion on the subject.
The temporary ban is intended to give the town time to do more research and add regulations without the pressure of any official proposal on the table. Even some councilors who voted in favor said they wanted to avoid “foot-dragging” on making updates and indicated the move wasn’t a blanket effort to keep such potential developments out of town.
The conversation has higher stakes in Bucksport than some other Maine towns adopting such pauses because the former Verso paper mill remains mostly vacant and appealing for redevelopment; at least two data center-related companies have eyed it in the last year, though no applications have come to the town.
Residents have also generally prioritized bringing industry to town since the mill closed in 2014, and moratorium opponents have said they think a temporary ban would send a hostile message to potential deep-pocketed developers.
Data centers to support AI growth have often met with bipartisan opposition in other states for their resource demands that increase local utility costs, along with other concerns including noise and environmental consequences.
Bucksport’s mill site is mostly owned by Whole Oceans, which proposed a land-based fish farm there but never broke ground — meaning the town’s say over what happens there lies in its local regulations.
The company says it’s still moving ahead with that project, Rich Rotella, the town’s economic and community development director, told the Bangor Daily News last week.
But it’s also taking meetings with other companies interested in buying the mill site for other projects, according to Rotella. Beacon Data Centers contacted him in 2025 but appeared to drop out after talks of a statewide moratorium last fall, which was later vetoed by Gov. Janet Mills to protect a proposal for Jay’s former paper mill site.
This summer, a representative of Kratos Data Centers met with town officials and toured the mill site, he said, and was last in contact with him in August. The company appears to be a site selector for developers, according to Rotella.
Those visits weren’t widely public knowledge until last month, and councilor Tracey Hair previously said she didn’t know developers had already come knocking when she proposed the moratorium idea at a resident’s suggestion.
After two readings and a favorable public hearing, the council voted 5-2 Thursday to enact the moratorium. Ed Rankin and Teri Doty were opposed. The pause could be rescinded in less than six months if regulations are updated, multiple councilors have noted. Moratoriums can also be extended.
Rankin said he couldn’t support the version advanced Thursday because it covered all data center proposals instead of only larger ones. Councilor Mark Eastman, who did vote in favor, agreed that smaller projects appeared to be less problematic.
Size has been one theme of the local data center conversation, with some saying they haven’t found much evidence of problems with existing projects under 10 megawatts. Moratorium supporters counter that there are still unknowns about the projects regardless of size, and that even “small” projects come with large electricity demands.

title: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had described it as being “public.”
The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice on Wednesday, said, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the U.S., especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Experts offer mixed reactions on the plan
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike’s botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.
When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, “I don’t recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government,” she said.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Trump has spoken out against public executions in Iran
Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on Feb. 28.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on Jan. 14. “It’s stopping, and there’s no plan for executions.”
In his State of the Union address just days before launching the Iran war, Trump reiterated, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on Dec. 3.”
It’s not clear if Hasan will try to appeal
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan began his portion of the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence.
The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed him telling military mental health workers that he could “ still be a martyr ” if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, spoke with Hasan on Wednesday but is barred from offering much detail about that conversation. He is not representing Hasan in his criminal case but said he’s worried about his physical health under the plan laid out by officials, and that Hasan has not yet had access to legal counsel.
Galligan said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain but no attorney from either the Trial Defense Service or from his civilian defense when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution. Galligan called that a breach of Army regulations.
A spokeswoman for the Army said Thursday that multiple attempts were made to contact Trial Defense Service attorneys, saying they made every reasonable effort and adhered to policy.
“The civilian counsel was not reasonably available to be physically present for the notification on the 5th,” the spokeswoman said, adding that counsel was located in Virginia but did not provide a name.
The spokeswoman also said Hasan has not been kept from contacting and communicating with his counsel.
Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Amnesty International said in its report on executions in 2025 that it knew of at least 17 public executions — 11 in Iran and 6 in Afghanistan.
___
Lauer reported from Philadelphia. Associated Press writers Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix, Josh Boak and Michelle L. Price in Washington, and Gene Johnson in Seattle contributed to this report.

title: One Bangor spa is blending witchcraft with wellness
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - When you think of witches, brooms, black cats and pointy hats may come to mind.
Instead of a bubbling cauldron, one Bangor witch is using a spa basin to put patrons under a spell of serenity.
The Beauty Artist, located at 268 State Street, offers services including red-light therapy, infrared sauna and a head spa.
What sets these services apart from their TikTok-viral counterparts is the infusion of owner Crystal French’s witchcraft practice.
“I’ve identified as a witch for quite some time, but not necessarily public-facing. And about three years ago was when I decided that I wanted to, we call it, ‘coming out of the broom closet.’ So, I came out of the broom closet and incorporated it into my work,” French describes. “I was a little nervous at first because of a lot of like misconception with what a witch is and a lot of it’s like Hollywood stereotypes unfortunately.”
As witchcraft spans centuries and continents, French calls the practice “a very personal experience.”
“What it means to me is that everything is with intention. The energetic part is what resonates the most with me,” explains French. “How that translates to my services is the same concept, with everything is energy, helping people understand their bodies better energetically and looking at traditional beauty services is something significantly deeper than surface level.”
For French, offerings like the Enchanted Head Spa or Ember Room red-light therapy sauna transcend one-time treats. Instead, she promotes them as rituals, another term she says is frequently misunderstood.
“Rituals can be everyday things that we do just by habit, but it’s the intent that we have behind it that’s important. So, creating these rituals, it gives people a place to feel seen,” French says.
Since incorporating her witchcraft practices into her services, French says the spa has helped her feel seen, too.
“I wouldn’t even have to necessarily outwardly label myself as a witch to have had that experience, but allowing myself permission, I connected so much deeper with the work that I was doing, and the people that were receiving the work,” reflects French. “It’s just been really beautiful.”
French says the practices can benefit anyone, regardless of belief. Through guided meditations and giving clients crystals to hold during facials and massages, she says her magic touch lies in giving patrons the tools and space to truly relax.
The Beauty Artist is open for spa appointments Monday through Friday with an occasional Saturday.
Upstairs at the same address, The Ember Room is a self-serve infrared sauna with red light therapy and a massage chair. This is open seven days a week.

title: Bodycam footage shows moments after 6-year-old shoots teacher
text:
Newly released bodycam footage shows moments after 6-year-old shoots teacher
Police body camera video released this week shows the moments after a 6-year-old shot his teacher inside a Virginia elementary school in January 2023.
Warning. The video above may contain imagery that could be disturbing to some viewers. Viewer discretion is advised.
The first-grade student shot his teacher, Abby Zwerner, inside a classroom on Jan. 6, 2023, according to police.
The body camera footage shows officers interacting with the child at Richneck Elementary School after the shooting. Reading specialist Amy Kovac can be seen holding the child as he shouted profanities at officers.
"Both of y'all want a [expletive] piece of me [expletive]," the boy said.
The boy said, "I don't care if you call backup. I don't care if I go to jail, [expletive]."
Zwerner was shot in the hand and chest while sitting at a reading table in her classroom. "I thought I was dying. I thought I had died," Zwerner testified in a civil case against ex-assistant principal Ebony Parker.
The lawsuit claimed Parker ignored repeated warnings that the child had a gun. In November 2025, a Virginia jury awarded Zwerner $10 million. A criminal case against Parker was dismissed earlier this year.
The student's mother was sentenced to nearly four years in prison for felony child neglect and federal weapons charges. Her son told authorities he got his mother’s handgun by climbing onto a drawer to reach the top of a dresser, where the firearm was in his mom’s purse.
The 6-year-old boy was not criminally charged because of his age. His identity was not released.

title: How volunteers step up to help when elderly or disable adults are reported missing
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - For families caring for someone with dementia, it’s a constant concern that they may get disoriented, walk out of their house, and struggle to get home or find safety.
That behavior is known as “wandering.” It’s an umbrella term that can mean everything from escape to repetitive pacing or getting lost.
If a person isn’t found within 24 hours, half are either severely injured or found dead.
In many states, officials use emergency alerts and resources for missing, at-risk adults like silver alerts. In Georgia, it’s known as Mattie’s Call. It was named after 67-year-old Mattie Moore, who had Alzheimer’s and wandered from her home and was found dead months later.
The struggle for normalcy
Ernestine Merritt was known as “Ernie” to her church family at Greenforest Community Baptist Church, where she served as an usher greeting members and guests at the front doors each Sunday.
Gayle Allen and Felecia Prince, fellow ushers at Greenforest Community Baptist, became caregivers when Merritt began losing her memory.
“She knew something was happening but she didn’t give in to the fact that it was dementia,” Prince said. “I never heard her say that.”
Late last year, what was once uncertain became evident to her church family. “We had to just take it one day at a time and just treat her as she was, each day,” Allen said. “We still loved her, no matter what.”
Prince said one of the hardest moments was when a doctor told Merritt she couldn’t drive anymore.
“She was so independent,” she said. “It was hard for her to accept that.”
The 79-year-old woman with dementia left her Ellenwood home at 4 a.m. on Jan. 4, 2026, determined to get to church on her own. She never made it.
Doorbell footage revealed when Merritt left her house. DeKalb County police and volunteers searched the woods, the neighborhood and nearby highway bridges for four days before locating her body in a nearby creek.
Because Merritt told her friends hours earlier she wanted to go to worship, search crews were intentional about mapping out the possible walking route to the church.
Searching for hope
Angel Alonso was one of the volunteers who led the search with his nonprofit Georgia Emergency Search & Rescue. He said his nonprofit assists any Georgia police department on Mattie’s calls, an emergency missing alert for a person who is disabled, special needs, elderly or has dementia.
There have been 69 Mattie’s Calls issued in the first four months of 2026. Last year, there were 213.
“If you find them alive, you did a great thing,” Alonso said. “But if you find them deceased, you still did a great thing because you brought them closure. They don’t have to wonder.”
The Georgia Emergency Search and Rescue nonprofit operates on donations when helping on cases. The dollars spent by law enforcement for each search climb to five figures for each operation.
A typical search and rescue can cost $1,500 per hour with low-tech operations, according to an Alzheimer’s initiatives report from the International Association of Chiefs of Police. In a nine-hour work day, that’s $13,500 in taxpayer dollars on one search alone.
Law enforcement agencies welcome the free assistance from groups like Alonso’s.
His nonprofit is made up of neighbors, retired officers, investigators and volunteers. From drones to dogs to four-wheelers, they expand police resources that would be otherwise limited.
“I can’t put a price on a life,” Alonso said. “God has put us in a good place to help others.”
The International Association of Chiefs of Police advises departments have a voluntary dementia registry that provides critical information about the loved one prior to the actual emergency.
Georgia has a growing statewide registry after state lawmakers increased funding for it last year. When a patient is formally diagnosed, their medical professional adds them to the registry.
