title: Trump’s $90 Medicare rebate rolls out, but millions aren’t eligible
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Less than one-third of all Medicare recipients are eligible for the payments, which are expected to be sent out this week. Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
The election-year promise that the Republican president made over the weekend comes as the Nov. 3 midterms are fast approaching, with the cost of living and healthcare expenses among the top issues for voters.
Some questions and answers about the payouts:
Who will benefit?
Some 20.8 million people in the original Medicare Part B who are living in the United States, not receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or not paying an income-related monthly adjusted amount.
Medicare Advantage enrollees, who make up more than half of the eligible 64.2 million Medicare beneficiaries, will not receive a payment, according to KFF, a healthcare research nonprofit. Nor will 12 million low-income older adults and people with disabilities who get premium assistance.
The Part B program covers expenses such as doctor’s visits, ambulance services and lab tests. Total monthly costs generally start at about $200 and vary with income.
Allison Schuster, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that the administration “is enabling Americans to take control of their health by putting money directly back in the hands of Medicare patients.”
When will the payments go out and how will they be disbursed?
According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit on or around Friday. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, said the payment will be automatic.
“As far as a benefit goes, people don’t have to call or sign up — it’s just money they receive directly, but not everybody on Medicare will receive this money.”
A White House fact sheet says people can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to check on their eligibility for the premium rebate. To check on payment status, people should call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213.
What is the source of the money?
Payments will come out of the Medicare Improvement Fund created by Congress in 2008 and intended to make improvements to the Medicare fee-for-service program.
The fund was created to improve program management and conduct oversight of contracts and contractors, according to the Congressional Budget Office, but its purpose has expanded after various legislative changes.
This is not the first time the fund has been used.
Democratic President Barack Obama’s administration, along with Congress, redirected $20 billion to expand healthcare coverage through the Affordable Care Act.
But under Trump, it is the first time that the fund has been used to directly pay recipients.
What are critics of the plan saying?
Critics of Trump’s promise characterize the $90 payments as a preelection stunt designed to sway voters rather than address structural problems in healthcare costs and administration.
The top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, said in a statement that “this is another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans’ revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas.”
Trump recently promised $500 rebate checks to an estimated 1 million Obamacare enrollees across 30 states whom the White House alleged were overcharged by the Biden administration for some fees.
Cubanski said the Medicare rebate payments were being doled out when Americans were feeling the bite of higher food, energy and gas prices. Surging healthcare costs are only compounding those pressure, she said.
“This might be helpful for people but it might not go very far.”

title: Wilton board approves $70,407 police truck purchase
text:
WILTON — The Wilton Select Board unanimously approved the purchase of a 2027 Ford F-150 police truck for $70,407 on Tuesday, Oct. 6, replacing an aging patrol cruiser and providing the Police Department with additional capabilities for training, towing and emergency response.
The purchase includes $48,841 for the truck from AutoFair and $21,566 for police equipment and installation through ITS. The money will come from the town’s Vehicle Capital Improvement account.
Police Chief Ethan Kyes recommended the pickup over a Ford Police Interceptor, citing its ability to transport equipment, tow heavier loads and support off-road operations. The truck will also be used for routine patrol duties.
The department received bids for both vehicle types, with some alternatives carrying lower purchase prices. During the meeting, board members questioned the additional expense of choosing a truck.
Kyes said the department relies on officers’ personal vehicles to transport equipment for firearms training because the equipment does not fit easily into cruisers.
“When we go to training, firearm training, we will take a personal truck that someone owns and put the equipment in it and drive it to the range,” Kyes told the board.
The truck would also be able to tow a speed trailer expected to arrive in late November. Kyes identified disaster response, evidence transportation and higher resale value as additional reasons for choosing the pickup.
The new vehicle will replace a black 2017 cruiser with about 132,000 miles and 16,000 engine hours. According to Kyes, the next-highest engine-hour total among the department’s vehicles is about 6,000, despite that vehicle having about 163,000 miles.
The four-door F-150 will enter the department’s regular patrol rotation and be equipped with a partition for transporting people in custody.
Board members also questioned the visibility of the department’s vehicles, particularly dark-colored cruisers with markings that can be difficult to distinguish.
Kyes said the department intends to add more visible, reflective lettering to several vehicles. He explained that lettering decisions had been delayed while the department awaited developments concerning a possible merger with the Jay Police Department.
Installation scheduling and costs have also contributed to the delay. Kyes said one vendor quoted about $1,300 to letter a single cruiser, not including the time required for officers to transport the vehicle.
The board approved Kyes’ recommendation without opposition.

title: Trump attitude to AI should give voters pause
text:
The catalog of serious problems for our nation caused by the current president is breathtaking. As recent polls show, a clear majority of Americans do not approve of where he has been taking us across a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues.
The most recent troubling action occurred last month when the Trump team reportedly worked with the Russians to weaken a U.N. agreement designed to create guardrails around the development of AI systems involving the use of autonomous lethal weapons. This at a time when even CEOs of the companies that are racing headlong to develop AI are sounding warnings about the high potential threat to humanity this new technology could present.
We need to remember that while this president is the main driving force behind all of these destructive initiatives, he would not be able to follow through on many of them without the support of a Republican-led House of Representatives and Senate.
Whatever one’s political persuasion, if people want to put the brakes on this reckless, damaging and potentially dangerous leadership, they should be voting blue.
Tom Berry
Kennebunk

title: Taliban firmly in control in Afghanistan 25 years after US-led invasion to oust them
text:
Taliban firmly in control in Afghanistan 25 years after US-led invasion to oust them
Dr. Nigar Nangrahari was on a night shift in a Kabul hospital when the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan began 25 years ago — an event that would shape her and her country’s future for decades to come.
Video from 2022 above: Afghan girls face uncertain future about education
As she walked home the next morning, Nangrahari saw Kabul residents taking revenge on members of the Taliban, whose harsh, repressive rule had seen public stonings, limb amputations of alleged criminals and women obliterated from public life.
“Along the way, I saw ordinary people killing anyone they caught who was a Taliban member. I witnessed with my own eyes the people of Kabul capturing and killing Taliban fighters. Some had climbed trees to hide,” she said.
Afraid of what was to come, Nangrahari and her family stayed home for about a month. Eventually, she was called back to the hospital and returned to work as an obstetrician-gynecologist. She no longer had to wear a burqa in the street.
“They granted us freedom — but not the kind that Afghans could truly benefit from,” said Nangrahari, 58.
Afghanistan is a deeply conservative Muslim society, and the U.S. culture that came with the American presence in the country often rankled some segments of society.
“Afghans should neither be completely unrestricted nor subjected to the kind of severe constraints imposed by the Taliban,” she said. “There needs to be a moderate balance.”
A bitter legacy
Under U.S. President George W. Bush, the American-led coalition launched Operation Enduring Freedom with the stated goal of dismantling al-Qaida, the terrorist organization whose leader, Osama bin Laden, had orchestrated the Sept. 11 attacks in the United States from his base in Afghanistan.
The invasion was to mark the start of a 20-year war that killed tens of thousands of Afghan civilians, along with thousands of coalition service members, U.S. contractors, aid workers and journalists.
The legacy of that war, and of the successive U.S.-supported Afghan governments during that time, endures today.
“Their stated goals were to bring good governance to Afghanistan and to combat narcotics and terrorism,” said Muin Gul Chamkanai, a former doctor who now heads a humanitarian organization, the Shkula Charitable Foundation, and also works as a political analyst. “The reality turned out to be the exact opposite.”
At a massive cost, both financial and in lives, the American presence brought certain freedoms, particularly for the media and in women’s education and employment opportunities. But pervasive corruption and often heavy-handed military tactics soon bred deep resentment.
Sitting at home on Oct. 7, 2001, Chamkanai switched on his television. The sight of his country being invaded enraged him.
“Had I been struck by their bombs, I would have considered martyrdom far preferable. I was not afraid,” he said. “I wanted to fight against them in Afghanistan using both the pen and the gun.”
The return of the Taliban
Now, 25 years after the invasion and five years after the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from the country, the Taliban are firmly back in control of Afghanistan. Although not quite as extreme as their previous government, when they ruled the country from 1996-2001, they have reinstated many draconian restrictions, particularly on women and girls.
Security has improved without question since the Taliban seized power in August 2021. Gone are the endless devastating bombings and attacks, the vast majority of them carried out by the Taliban themselves during the two-decade-long war.
“After a long and arduous struggle, jihad and great sacrifices, Afghans succeeded in liberating their country,” deputy government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat said in a statement on the 25th anniversary of the invasion. “This struggle demonstrated that Afghans will never submit to foreign occupation or external coercion.”
He said that Oct. 7, 2001, was “a dark day in the country’s history that resulted in thousands of Afghans being martyred, wounded, imprisoned, displaced and left homeless.”
But for a generation who grew up under U.S.-supported governments, the loss of personal freedoms, especially for women, who face restrictions on everything from what they wear to where they can go, has been a brutal blow.
After the Taliban took over, “gradually … restrictions were imposed, and the normal life we had known was taken away. Things became very difficult for us,” said Tahmina Mangal, a 33-year-old woman who saw her hopes of continuing her studies dashed by the shuttering of high schools and universities for girls and women.
“The burden is immense. It weighs heavily on my own spirits and psyche,” she said.
A perilous future
Now, Tahmina owns and runs a store selling traditional Afghan clothing for women. Although women face multiple restrictions and are barred from most jobs, the Ministry of Commerce does issue business licenses to women, she said. She viewed that as the only avenue open to her.
But with women barred from education and participation in any form of governance, she worries deeply about the future.
“If this situation persists, Afghanistan’s future is perilous,” Tahmina said. “Without women pursuing their studies or receiving an education, we will lack doctors, teachers and literate women, including mothers capable of raising healthy children for society. I view Afghanistan’s future as bleak and dire if this trend continues.”
For Nangrahari, although the Taliban government’s emphasis on improving infrastructure in the country is welcome, its emphasis on religious education for boys, and its ban on higher education for girls, “sets Afghanistan back by a century.” Afghanistan already is among the world's poorest countries.
“Roads have been improved and high-rise buildings constructed. Indeed, infrastructure is the foundation of the economy, and we acknowledge all of this,” Nangrahari said. “But a society lacking education is zero.”
Still, sitting in her clothing shop in Kabul, Tahmina said that women shouldn’t give up hope, and should continue pursuing their studies, even if it is only online.
“Governments inevitably come and go, collapses happen, and no government lasts forever,” she said. “I always say: ‘Remain hopeful for the future. Study, pursue professional training alongside your regular schooling, and seek higher education.’”

title: Former Scarborough police lieutenant accused of felony theft appears in court
text:
A former Scarborough police lieutenant accused of stealing from the town made his initial appearance in court Thursday morning. He pleaded not guilty.
Timothy Barker, 55, is accused of stealing more than $10,000 by falsifying overtime records while he was employed with the police department. He was charged with felony theft by deception, tampering with public records or information, and official oppression.
When the value of a stolen item exceeds $10,000 in value, theft is elevated to a Class B crime, according to state statute. Class B theft is a felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $20,000.
From February 2021 to September 2025, Barker authorized overtime payments for traffic details he did not perform, prosecutors allege.
Barker worked with the department for 31 years.
He was released on his own recognizance without additional bond conditions. Barker’s next court appearance is scheduled for March 10, 2027.

title: Remembering a beloved family farm dog
text:
In 1948, my maternal grandparents, Florian and Lucille Yeaton, brought home Bonnie, the runt of a border collie litter purchased in Farmington. This scrappy pup caught Grampa’s attention by fearlessly wrestling with littermates twice her size.
They took her to their Mercer farmhouse, where she slept on a horsehair blanket behind the wood cookstove. However, their hopes for a collie to herd sheep and dairy cows dimmed as Bonnie’s weight plummeted.
As a last resort, Grammy Lue wrapped Bonnie in the blanket and, in a gamble, placed her in the pigpen with a 250-pound sow nursing six piglets.
“We’ll know by day’s end whether the sow takes to her,” Grammy said to Grampa.
For 10 days, Bonnie nursed alongside the pink piglets, thriving under her unlikely foster mother’s warmth and care. Her weight — scarcely three pounds — more than doubled. Within two months, she was racing between the farmhouse and the barn.
My grandparents initially wondered if such an unusual start would leave a lasting mark. It did, but not the one they feared. Bonnie matured into an extraordinarily intelligent working dog, consistently proving her capabilities in protecting her family and livestock.
One summer afternoon in 1953, my 5-year-old brother, Robert, came face-to-face with a rabid fox behind the barn. Bonnie didn’t attack. Instead, she steadily nipped at Robert’s heels, driving him back toward the farmhouse while keeping her body between him and the fox. Grampa killed the fox with his shotgun.
A year later, Robert and our cousin, Cheryl, accidentally started a barn fire while playing with matches. Bonnie’s frantic barking alerted the family before anyone smelled smoke. Grampa fought the flames with pails of rainwater from the cistern, Mother smothered them with wet blankets, and Grammy herded the frightened livestock into the pasture. Together, they saved the barn.
But Bonnie’s greatest feat occurred on a sweltering August day in 1958.
While wading in the Sandy River to cool off, my 6-year-old twin brother, Don, was swept into the deep channel. Mother dove in after him but couldn’t dog-paddle fast enough to close the gap as he drifted downstream.
Bonnie understood the river’s currents better than either of them. Instead of immediately jumping in, she sprinted along the high bank, tracking Don as he fought to keep his head above water. Nearly 300 feet downriver, she launched off the bank, entered the current just ahead of the hairpin rapids, clamped onto his shirt collar, and hauled him onto a gravel bar.
The next morning, Don, still shaken, sat beside Grampa in the milking parlor. From his three-legged stool, Grampa squirted warm milk to the waiting barn cats and Bonnie, as he did every morning. Watching Bonnie lick her whiskers, my twin laughed through his tears and pulled her close.
The day before, she had saved his life — that morning, she helped restore his spirit.
Age never dulled her instincts. Shortly after midnight in October 1961, Don and I woke to growls rising from the pumpkin pine floorboards at the foot of our bed.
“Why’s Bonnie growling?” we yelled into the dark.
“Might be a bear in the barnyard,” Grampa answered from the adjacent bedroom. “She found fresh tracks in the orchard yesterday.”
He lit a kerosene lantern and retrieved the 12-gauge from above the kitchen door. Bonnie paced and whined at the latch. The second it lifted, she shot through the doorway and bolted toward the pigpen, her dark silhouette framed by a huge harvest moon.
“You boys go back to bed,” Grammy barked.
We obeyed but opened our bedroom window to listen. The hogs were squealing, Bonnie was barking, and a single shotgun blast cracked across the farm. Then everything went deadly quiet.
The next 10 minutes felt like an hour before Grampa and Bonnie returned to the kitchen.
“She chased a bear clean out of the pigpen,” he said, still catching his breath. “The pen door’s stove to hell, but the hogs are fine.”
Two nights later, a few miles from our farm, Ralph True shot the same bear after it killed one of his sheep. The boar weighed 490 pounds.
“Its front paws,” he told Grampa, “were the size of dinner plates.”
When cancer took Bonnie in April 1962, Grampa wrapped her one last time in the ratty horsehair blanket she’d slept on her entire life and carried her up the knoll to the apple orchard — her favorite spot on the farm. He dug her grave that night by moonlight, working past the frost line with a pickaxe and shovel. The next afternoon, my three siblings and I picked yellow daffodils from the south side of the farmhouse and planted them on her grave.
That evening, my heartbroken 5-year-old sister, Gale, barely ate her supper. When the meal was over, she quietly walked behind the cookstove and scraped her plate into Bonnie’s enamel bowl.
In the morning, her eyes lit up at the sight of an empty bowl.
Years later, E.B. White gave me the words for what Bonnie meant to our family: “A really companionable and indispensable dog is an accident of nature. You can’t get it by breeding for it, and you can’t buy it with money.”
Ron Joseph of Sidney is the author of “Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist,” published by Islandport Press.

title: Leftover federal funds provide early fuel aid to Maine households
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 4,000 of Maine’s most vulnerable households will receive early fuel assistance due to the release of nearly $4 million in federal funding leftover from the 2025-2026 heating season.
MaineHousing has issued Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, payments to fuel vendors amid expectations of a challenging winter heating season and record-high heating oil prices.
The funding will help about 4,400 of Maine’s most vulnerable households receive fuel before cold weather sets in. Priority households include those with older adults, young children and people with disabilities.
Maine is waiting for its annual federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, grant from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which usually arrives in late October or early November. Once the funding is available, MaineHousing will pay fuel vendors serving approved applicants.
The state said HEAP, Maine’s largest component of LIHEAP, helps approximately 40,000 households pay a portion of their home energy costs each season.
So far, Congress has flat funded the program for next year.
Monica Grady, senior director of Community Services for Kennebec Valley Community Action Program, said a lot of people will still be turned away.
“For the state of Maine flat funding is not enough to cover everyone that applies. We typically serve 35,000 people statewide a year, but we’re now getting 75,000 applications. That’s a big difference. That tells you what’s going on in this state,” Grady said.
Income eligibility for LIHEAP changed this month from about $70,000 a year to just over $73,000 a year for a family of four.
Maine’s congressional delegation and Gov. Janet Mills have asked for increased LIHEAP funding. U.S. Sen. Angus King’s office said the program is awaiting funding from the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Maine receives approximately $38 million to $42 million annually through LIHEAP, with about $26 million going to direct heating assistance distributed statewide through community action agencies. The remaining funds are used for energy-related programs, including central heating improvements, emergency fuel intervention and weatherization.
“We encourage anyone who expects to struggle with heating costs this winter to apply for HEAP now,” said Dan Brennan, director of MaineHousing. “Do not wait until you are facing a heating crisis or emergency. If you have not started the application process, now is the time.”
To review eligibility information and begin the application process, visit mainehousing.org. Mainers may also contact their local community action agency or call 211 for help.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Deadly attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi airports highlight widening fallout from Yemen conflict
text:
Deadly attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi airports highlight widening fallout from Yemen conflict
Houthi rebels attacked two Saudi airports, killing three people and injuring 36 others this week, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said Wednesday, as the conflict in Yemen increasingly spills across the border into the kingdom.
In a statement, GACA said Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport came under attack on Oct. 6 and 7.
The attacks prompted a security alert from the U.S. Mission in Saudi Arabia, warning American citizens of potential drone and missile attacks and cautioning that the conflict could escalate.
“The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate,” the mission said Wednesday. “US citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.”
The Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of northern Yemen including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015.
The conflict flared up in July 2026, shortly after the US-Iran ceasefire unraveled, with Houthi missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in an expansion of the Middle East war. Riyadh has responded with airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces.
According to GACA, the attack on Abha International Airport on Tuesday killed two female residents, one Moroccan and one Algerian national, and wounded 28 others, including Saudi citizens as well as Bangladeshi and Filipino residents.
A separate attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh on Wednesday killed a Sudanese resident and wounded eight people, including five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents and one Pakistani resident, the authority said.
The Houthi-controlled armed forces claimed responsibility for both attacks. The group said it had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile and claimed the strike disrupted air traffic in Riyadh.
Saudi military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said Saudi forces had destroyed the ballistic missile launcher used in the attack on Riyadh. In a post on X, al-Maliki said the launcher was destroyed in Sanaa while preparations were underway for “another imminent attack against Saudi Arabia.”
A day earlier, the Houthis said they had carried out a ballistic missile attack on Abha International Airport and similarly claimed it had disrupted airport operations.
The group also renewed its warning to international airlines against operating flights through Saudi airspace, saying it had become “a theater for our military operations,” while excluding the airspace around the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
Saudi authorities did not immediately comment on the Houthi claims.
The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press ahead with Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at rolling back recent gains made by the Iran-backed Houthis.
The escalation has also prompted Saudi Arabia to strengthen defense cooperation with regional allies. Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to move forward with the implementation of collective defense measures under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, often referred to as the Mecca Alliance.
In a joint statement following an emergency meeting in Riyadh, the three countries said they would move immediately to implement collective defense commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Pakistan’s military confirmed to CNN on Wednesday that Pakistani forces are already stationed in Saudi Arabia as part of the alliance. Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security was “absolute” and described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense and deterrence. He added that the pact includes a NATO-style provision under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all.
The United States has also increased its support for Saudi Arabia’s campaign. More than 100 U.S. military advisers are currently in Saudi Arabia providing intelligence and targeting support to the kingdom’s military operations against the Iran-backed Houthis, CNN reported last month citing multiple sources familiar with the effort.
The assistance comes as fighting intensifies on the Arabian Peninsula and raises concerns that the conflict could expand further, potentially threatening a second major maritime corridor in the Middle East in addition to the Red Sea.
In recent days, Yemeni government forces have claimed advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia.
The strikes on airports in both southern Saudi Arabia and the capital underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign.
With civilian infrastructure now coming under renewed attack, the hostilities are showing signs of expanding beyond the battlefield in Yemen and posing a growing challenge to Saudi security and transportation networks.
The activation of the Mecca Alliance and confirmation that Pakistani forces are already deployed in the kingdom suggest Saudi Arabia and its allies are preparing for the possibility of a broader regional security confrontation.

title: David Pastrnak scores twice to lead Bruins past Mammoth
text:
BOSTON — David Pastrnak scored his first two goals of the season and added two assists as the Boston Bruins routed the Utah Mammoth 6-1 on Thursday night.
Matthew Poitras, Casey Mittelstadt, Mason Lohrei and Morgan Geekie also scored for the Bruins, who led 3-0 after one period and 6-0 after two. Jeremy Swayman made 36 saves.
Pastrnak scored his first goal with 5:38 left in the first period on a power-play wrist shot, assisted by Frederic Brunet and Geekie. He tacked on a power-play slap shot 4:40 into the second period, assisted by Geekie and Hampus Lindholm.
Jack McBain scored for the Mammoth midway through the third period to spoil Swayman’s shutout bid.
Karel Vejmelka stopped 11 of 14 shots he faced before he was replaced by Sebastian Cossa, who made five saves.
The Bruins scored three power-play goals, while the Mammoth went scoreless on the power play. The Bruins blocked 23 shots.

title: Man pleads not guilty in attack that left woman dying along Maine highway
text:
A Portland man has pleaded not guilty in the stabbing that left a 21-year-old dying along the side of Interstate 295.
Glen Rodney, 58, who faces a murder charge in the death of Julian Nadeau of Portland, entered his plea Wednesday, according to the Portland Press Herald.
Julian Nadeau was walking with friends on Aug. 5 on the path near Tukey’s Bridge, which carries I-295 over the entrance to Back Cove.
Rodney approached them on a bicycle, and an argument broke out, during which Rodney allegedly stabbed Nadeau in the chest, according to ABC affiliate WMTW, which cited a police affidavit.
Before the stabbing Rodney allegedly threatened to kill someone, WMTW reported, citing the police document.
Police found Nadeau in the breakdown lane along the southbound side of the highway about 9:47 p.m. Nadeau was taken to Maine Medical Center but didn’t survive.
Rodney, who had fled on the bicycle and has claimed he was attacked, was arrested without incident just minutes later on Presumpscot Street in the city’s East Deering neighborhood.
His defense attorney, James Howaniec, on Wednesday suggested that Rodney didn’t initiate the conflict. He has asked a judge to grant Rodney bail, while prosecutors have pushed for Rodney to remain at the Cumberland County Jail, characterizing the attack as a “stranger-on-stranger assault,” the Press Herald reported.
Friends who spoke with the Press Herald over the summer described Julian Nadeau, or Juju, as an energetic and goofy person. The night she died she was heading to a colorful graffiti wall under Tukey’s Bridge to hang out with friends and open Pokemon cards, the newspaper reported.
She frequented furry conventions in the area, which her partner, 22-year-old Kasper DeWitt, told the Press Herald was a big part of her life.
“I just want to spread her love and carry that part of her for the rest of my life. I need to channel her energy forever,” DeWitt told the Portland newspaper.

title: GRAPHIC: Bodycam footage reveals moments after 6-year-old boy shot his first grade teacher
text:
NEWPORT NEWS, Va. (CNN) - Newly unsealed body camera footage shows the moments after a 6-year-old Virginia boy shot his elementary school teacher in January 2023. test
Bodycam footage from Newport News Police shows the 6-year-old boy being restrained by a reading specialist at Richneck Elementary School. The boy, who was described by his mother’s attorney as having “extreme emotional issues,” is seen cursing at points in the video.
Abby Zwerner, his first grade teacher, was shot and suffered gunshot wounds to her hand and chest in the January 2023 shooting. Police say the boy had taken the unsecured gun from his mother’s purse and brought it to school in his backpack.
According to prosecutors, the boy stood on a dresser drawer to get the gun from the purse.
The boy’s mother, Deja Taylor, apologized to Zwerner and accepted responsibility for the shooting. She pled guilty to a state charge of felony child neglect and was sentenced to two years in prison in December 2023. She was released from state custody to community supervision in May 2026.
A jury awarded Zwerner $10 million in damages following a civil trial against the school’s former assistant principal, Ebony Parker, who Zwerner said failed to act on concerns that the boy brought a gun to school in the hours before the shooting.
The boy is now in the custody of his great-grandfather. He was not criminally charged in the case, according to Commonwealth’s Attorney Howard Gwynn.

title: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration announced Thursday it was suspending Microsoft and several other firms from a program allowing foreign workers to apply for green cards as it also lashed out at universities that bring international students to the U.S. on exchange programs.
The announcement by Vice President JD Vance marks the latest swing from the Trump administration at employers and universities that welcome foreign students and workers into the country.
Such programs have frequently been targeted by some Trump supporters who argue they undercut American students and workers. Supporters say they allow the U.S. to attract the best talent from around the world and fill important hiring gaps.
Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like H-1B visas — which Vance accused Microsoft of abusing — essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In the wide-ranging announcement, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms.
The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies.
Vance says US workers are replaced with ‘foreign indentured servants’
Vance said the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.”
Microsoft is No. 5 among U.S. employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No. 1.
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.” Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, the company said 80% were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“These were not to hire new people,” Microsoft said in a statement. “The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.”
The company added that it only files H-1B petitions for “those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category.”
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at USCIS during the Biden administration, called Vance’s announcement “incoherent.”
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” he said. “Once you have a green card, you’re no longer dependent on your employer for your immigration status — you’re a permanent resident who can change jobs and negotiate higher wages without fear.”
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position.
H-1B program has been scrutinized
The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
Trump last year attempted to ratchet up the fee for H-1B work visas to $100,000, saying it would protect American workers from losing their jobs to lower-paid foreigners, but a federal judge struck that down in June.
The administration has since tried a different tack, announcing plans in August for a $103,265 fee. The proposed regulation described the new fee as a “dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system.” The rule isn’t yet final and is expected to face a legal challenge, like the one before it.
Ron Hira, a Howard University political science professor and longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.” Hira noted the White House last month issued a little-noticed executive order directing government agencies to “implement appropriate measures to protect American workers from abuse of the H-1B program and ensure that the program serves the national interest.’’
“There are supposed to be protections for U.S. workers that say: If you hire an H-1B, you are promising that you are not adversely affecting similarly employed U.S. workers,’’ Hira said. “That’s never been enforced.’’
Besides Microsoft, Vance said the government was similarly suspending Adobe and tech consulting firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. The companies did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
Trump also has targeted foreign students
The Vance announcement came a day after Trump’s administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practical Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.
Vance also called out universities, suggesting that they were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. In most cases, to get the visa, students must receive the majority of their funding from an institution, such as a fellowship-granting organization, rather than paying for their tuition personally.
Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT. Stanford said it would cooperate with the investigation. The other universities did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ___
Associated Press writers Heather Hollingsworth in Mission, Kansas and Paul Wiseman and Annie Ma in Washington D.C. contributed. Ortutay reported from Oakland, Calif.

title: 5 notable moments from Susan Collins and Troy Jackson’s second debate
text:
Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson ran the gamut from personal attacks to policy disagreements.
It was the second time this week the 73-year-old Collins and the 58-year-old Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president, squared off. Their final two debates will take place next week.
On Tuesday, Jackson put in a strong performance, delivering a couple zingers that took on lives of their own on social media. Those quips included comparing Collins to an arsonist and telling her that “you can’t eat road salt” after she claimed she got the material exempted from tariffs.
Collins was largely on the defensive as she tried to distance herself from President Donald Trump, who is deeply unpopular in Maine, and from corruption allegations amplified by Democrats. But she also displayed her experience and knowledge of the issues.
On Thursday, Jackson was a bit shakier, struggling at times to find his talking points on the fly while Collins continued to hold her own.
Polls continue to show a close race, with Jackson having a slight edge. But Republicans have more money than Democrats and have been flooding the airwaves with ads attacking Jackson in the closing final weeks of the campaign.
Here are five takeaways from their second meeting, which was broadcast on WTMW.
1. Both candidates got personal
The candidates brought each other’s families into the debate.
Collins went on the attack first. She accused Jackson of changing his position on accepting donations from corporations. In his U.S. Senate campaign, Jackson has said he would not — but as state Senate president, his leadership PAC accepted those types of donations.
“It usually has to do with issues that his son has been hired to lobby him on,” Collins said of instances where Jackson has changed his positions over the years.
Later, Jackson took aim at Collins’ husband while discussing high energy prices. Jackson repeatedly blamed the Iran War for increasing fuel and electricity prices, saying that Collins voted five times against stopping it. (Collins noted she has voted nine times to end it.)
“She could use her leverage to stop this war,” he said. “But instead … Sen. Collins and her husband are making money off this war and so is a whole bunch of other people and that’s why this doesn’t stop.”
Jackson was referring to Collins’ husband, Tom Daffron’s, vast stock portfolio, which includes holdings in natural gas and Boeing. (Boeing’s stock price has fallen since the start of the war.)
Collins called Jackson’s charge of her family profiting off the conflict “absolutely outrageous” and demanded an apology.
“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson replied.
2. A rare moment of agreement
When the debate turned to protecting Social Security, Jackson and Collins found a rare point of agreement — both agreed that people who earn more money should pay more into the system.
Social Security taxes are currently capped at a percentage of the first $184,000 you make, regardless of your income. Jackson said that cap should be scrapped so that wealthy people would pay more into the system.
“Here is something where I actually agree with Troy,” Collins said.
But Collins didn’t go as far as Jackson. Instead, she said, she would assemble a panel of independent financial experts to provide recommendations.
“We are simply going to have to adjust the cap,” Collins said.
3. Jackson hits Collins’ strength
Collins has made her experience and seniority a central theme of her campaign. Again, she referenced the $1.5 billion she has helped bring to Maine in recent years as chair of the Appropriations Committee — the first Mainer to hold that position in 92 years.
But Jackson wasn’t impressed. He continued to describe Collins as kowtowing to Trump’s demands.
“She’s powerful during election time but she’s weak every time we need her to stand up and fight for us,” Jackson said.
4. Collins tried to flip the script on abortion
Abortion has been a big issue this campaign, especially Collins’ vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, which led in part to the overturning of Roe v. Wade.
But Collins tried to flip the script by noting that Jackson had been longtime opponent of abortion until he ran for Congress in 2014. She specifically pointed to a bill he opposed that would have allowed for abortions if a pregnancy threatened the mother’s health.
“He was an extremist when it comes to abortion,” Collins said, noting she has always been pro-choice.
Jackson, however, was ready. He acknowledged that he changed his views on abortion after speaking with women — something he said Collins didn’t do when Mainers traveled to D.C. to urge her to oppose Kavanaugh.
“Our records have changed,” said Jackson, who is endorsed by Planned Parenthood. “Mine has gotten better — hers has gotten worse.”
5. Collins recasts voting record with Trump
Jackson has repeatedly accused Collins of voting with Trump 96% of the time. The claim comes from CQ Roll Call analysis of the first seven months of 2025, which found the percentage was closer to 95%.
Collins said using the same approach to analyze her votes under former President Joe Biden would have shown her siding with the Democrat 91% of the time. And a more expansive look at Collin’s voting record in Trump’s second term shows she has sided with him 72% of the time, she claimed.
Collin said she has voted against Trump 137 times.
“But it didn’t matter,” Jackson shot back.

title: Father speaks after 1-month-old’s mom accused of slamming baby’s head against the floor
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) — A baby girl is continuing to fight for her life after suffering a number of serious injuries that could have ended it.
The month-and-a-half-old child has been recovering at Children’s Hospital in Omaha.
According to police, the infant suffered life-threatening injuries at the hands of her mother, 20-year-old Kayleigh Lowe.
Court records showed Lowe likely slammed the baby’s head against the floor of their home, threw her in the air and squeezed her ribs.
As a result, police said the baby suffered seven broken ribs and bleeding on both sides of her brain.
The young girl was taken to a Lincoln hospital before being transferred to Children’s Hospital on Sept. 13.
After a few weeks of uncertainty, doctors said they believed the girl would survive, a relief to her father, 20-year-old Cooper Miller.
“She is doing better than she had the last couple of days, so that is giving me better hope,” Miller said. “Her ribs are healing miraculously. Her bruising is gone on her face. She just, she’s so beautiful.”
Miller, who now lives in Hastings, said he was in a relationship with Lowe until the beginning of this year. They learned she was pregnant in late 2025 and the two had kept in touch as she closed in on her due date.
An arrest affidavit showed that Lowe searched “shaken baby syndrome” on her phone on Sept. 2, just 12 days after her daughter was born. She later took the infant to an emergency room on Sept. 10 but left against medical advice, police reported.
A doctor with Children’s Hospital told police that the infant had suffered permanent brain injuries. Miller said that a large portion of his daughter’s brain was full of fluid and threatening to claim her eyesight.
As for a prognosis, Miller said his little girl’s future remained unclear. He is, however, hopeful as doctors expect to know much more by the end of the month.
“They will evaluate from there as to whether or not she’s going to go into rehabilitation, which I am really hoping for because she’s a great candidate for it,” Miller said. “And honestly she could really use it right now given what she’s been through.”
In the meantime, Miller said his daughter has gotten back to eating from a bottle, and he’s eager to see what the future holds.
“There’s been a lot of prayers and a lot of miracles answered. And this one’s one of them,” Miller said. “It’s gonna be a story to tell in the future, too, because the night I got that call I took work off the whole week. I wasn’t going nowhere until I knew my little girl was OK.”
Court filings show the state is working to remove custody from Lowe. Miller expects to know more about his bid for custody this week.

title: People in addiction often fear law enforcement. In Biddeford, they met on a softball field.
text:
BIDDEFORD — Tia Lavigne stood in the dugout waiting to take the field. At 26, she said it would be the first time she had ever played softball sober.
She said she had played under the influence of substances even as a kid in Buxton. She could throw from home plate to second base without hitting the ground, so she found her place as a catcher. But at just 9 years old, she said, she was given alcohol by an adult and became addicted. Lavigne said she made a lot of “not great choices” and was later arrested on a gun purchasing charge.
By the time she put on the red uniform shirt at Rotary Park in Biddeford on a damp Wednesday night at the end of September, she had been sober for two years, seven months and 16 days, with help from ENSO Recovery in Sanford, and had put herself on a better path by starting her own cleaning business.
“This is the only time I felt comfortable playing ball. All the co-ed teams out there, there are substances around,” she said.
This game, which has become an annual tradition, was unusual: It was built for people in various stages of drug and alcohol recovery to be together — and to play alongside law enforcement officers.
The Recovery Softball BBQ was created by Ryan and Cynthia Paige and their organization AccessDirect Recovery Network in order to break down stigma on both sides.
Lavigne used to see a cop car and bolt in the other direction, she said. On the night of the game, the cars and trucks squeezed into the parking lot and lining the road to the softball field included a lot of police and sheriff’s department vehicles.
“There’s a person out there who might’ve been sober for nine days,” Ryan Paige said, pointing to the field during warmups. “When you look it might be hard to tell who’s who — law enforcement or a person in recovery. That’s the whole point.”
Day to day, he
He stood near the pitcher’s mound before the ceremonial first pitch and said into the microphone that the rate of overdose deaths in Maine was dropping, that recovery was possible and that support from peers mattered. About 150 people stood in the dugouts and along the fences and cheered.
Ryan Paige is in recovery, too, and like some of the people he invited to participate, he said he surprised himself.
“I never thought a life like this was possible for me,” he said, scanning the scene.
He was always social and now he had something productive to channel it toward. So much so that he was too busy to play in the game. He bounced between the barbecue, the vendors and service providers who had set up information tables, the softball field, and the dunk tank, which was a new addition this year.
York County Deputy Sheriff Matthew Cummer, in full uniform, got dunked dozens of times for about an hour. Ryan
QUIETING JUDGMENT
Auburn Police Sgt. Nick Gagnon jogged up to the plate.
“I haven’t hit a ball in 10 years, but I’m hitting this one!” he boldly told the catcher.
Gagnon took a big swing and
He said he’s seen fentanyl and methamphetamine come into Maine over his 17-year career.
“First, like a lot of young officers, you judge people,” he said. “Over time with age and maturity, you learn empathy.”
Asked what he would tell a younger version of himself, he said he would try to explain how important it is to have compassion.
“If you become cynical and judge people in the wrong way,” he said, “ there’s too much hostility between law enforcement and the community.”
By the second inning, the blue team, the Resilient Riders, appeared to be way ahead, though there was no scoreboard and several players said no one was keeping track. It didn’t lessen the effort or enthusiasm in the dugouts.
“It’s so fun to listen to them cheer each other on,” Auburn Police Lt. Matt Dailey said of the players who’d come from sober houses and long-term care facilities to play in the game.
“As law enforcement we need people in recovery to help their friends and get people out of drugs,” he said.
York County Sheriff Bill King walked along the left field fence, blending into the crowd in a sweatshirt.
“I’ve met people who’ve served time in our jail,” he said. “That’s the most fulfilling, to see them working on their substance issues.”
Scott Brockelbank said he played in adult softball leagues for years around Maine and traveled to Disney World for games. During the sixth inning of the game last week, as his team pulled ahead, he said it was the first time he had played sober.
“I always thought I played better messed up, but I actually think I play better sober,” he said. He was proud to play in front of his wife and, in his words, not make a fool of himself.
Brockelbank, who said he first took crack cocaine at age 11 when it was given to him by an adult relative,
“I used to hate law enforcement for a long time. Today I realize they were doing their jobs and I was the problem,” he said. “It’s nice to share the field and not be worried.”
He added that he’d been sober for 90 days.
Brockelbank later said the event may help him get back into softball without it being a trigger to use drugs.
Fog settled onto the field as Gagnon, from the Auburn Police Department, smacked a ball to right center field. His teammate, Austin McAlister, walked up to the plate. McAlister said he got addicted to heroin during his third prison stint, and he used to run away from police and firefighters.
Now he said he’s been sober for 10 months and is in treatment court, where he gets random drug tests.
“Law enforcement changed my life by getting arrested,” he said. “I’m super grateful.”
“When I hear them say going to jail saved my life it feels good,” Gagnon said.
Soaking in the fresh air and freedom of the softball field, McAlister tried out his home run swing and ran down the base path. A few plays later the second baseman fielded a grounder and acrobatically tipped it to the shortstop for an out. Everybody laughed. “It’s like Banana Ball!” someone yelled near home plate, likening it to the wacky, up-tempo baseball that’s getting popular in the U.S..
In the last inning the players decided the red team, the Hope Hustlers, would bat through the order. They were almost certainly losing by a lot but no one was really sure. Dailey, the lieutenant, hit the game’s final pitch a long way out in right field and rounded the bases.
Both dugouts cheered as he came around third, then got tagged out at the plate.
Dailey and his Auburn Police colleagues were the last to leave the field, and they walked away talking about plans for next year’s game.
Nicholas Toth was also thinking ahead. He’d come from a nearby men’s facility in Biddeford to play. At 45, he’d lost toes to frostbite and had other serious health problems, he said. He’s six and a half years sober and credited Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous for helping him.
The night’s game wore him out — he had panted coming around the bases and was emotional as he walked up to Ryan Paige to thank him for organizing everything. Paige had picked him up at a homeless shelter earlier this year.
Just like the players from all backgrounds that night who had whiffed at arcing pitches, lost their footing, and eventually reached base, Toth said his recovery has been bumpy, not linear and not as easy as it looks.
By next year’s game he plans to be living in his own place.
And Ryan Paige has plans to expand the dunk tank.

title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
text:
CORONADO, Calif. (AP) — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.
The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.
Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
“It feels amazing,” he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.”
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.
“It feels really overwhelming,” she said about being seeing her mom again. “She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday.”
She added that she’s happy her mom won’t be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship’s commanding officer, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
“It’s a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet,” he said.
The Navy has downplayed problems on the carrier
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough.”
Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth told the crew that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”
USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals
The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln’s deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
“She’s our deployment baby,” said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship’s conditions while she was pregnant, she said. “I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn’t sure if he was OK or not,” she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was “pretty bad,” but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
“I couldn’t grasp the reality of it,” he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, “seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me,” Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.

title: Remembering a beloved family farm dog
text:
In 1948, my maternal grandparents, Florian and Lucille Yeaton, brought home Bonnie, the runt of a border collie litter purchased in Farmington. This scrappy pup caught Grampa’s attention by fearlessly wrestling with littermates twice her size.
They took her to their Mercer farmhouse, where she slept on a horsehair blanket behind the wood cookstove. However, their hopes for a collie to herd sheep and dairy cows dimmed as Bonnie’s weight plummeted.
As a last resort, Grammy Lue wrapped Bonnie in the blanket and, in a gamble, placed her in the pigpen with a 250-pound sow nursing six piglets.
“We’ll know by day’s end whether the sow takes to her,” Grammy said to Grampa.
For 10 days, Bonnie nursed alongside the pink piglets, thriving under her unlikely foster mother’s warmth and care. Her weight — scarcely three pounds — more than doubled. Within two months, she was racing between the farmhouse and the barn.
My grandparents initially wondered if such an unusual start would leave a lasting mark. It did, but not the one they feared. Bonnie matured into an extraordinarily intelligent working dog, consistently proving her capabilities in protecting her family and livestock.
One summer afternoon in 1953, my 5-year-old brother, Robert, came face-to-face with a rabid fox behind the barn. Bonnie didn’t attack. Instead, she steadily nipped at Robert’s heels, driving him back toward the farmhouse while keeping her body between him and the fox. Grampa killed the fox with his shotgun.
A year later, Robert and our cousin, Cheryl, accidentally started a barn fire while playing with matches. Bonnie’s frantic barking alerted the family before anyone smelled smoke. Grampa fought the flames with pails of rainwater from the cistern, Mother smothered them with wet blankets, and Grammy herded the frightened livestock into the pasture. Together, they saved the barn.
But Bonnie’s greatest feat occurred on a sweltering August day in 1958.
While wading in the Sandy River to cool off, my 6-year-old twin brother, Don, was swept into the deep channel. Mother dove in after him but couldn’t dog-paddle fast enough to close the gap as he drifted downstream.
Bonnie understood the river’s currents better than either of them. Instead of immediately jumping in, she sprinted along the high bank, tracking Don as he fought to keep his head above water. Nearly 300 feet downriver, she launched off the bank, entered the current just ahead of the hairpin rapids, clamped onto his shirt collar, and hauled him onto a gravel bar.
The next morning, Don, still shaken, sat beside Grampa in the milking parlor. From his three-legged stool, Grampa squirted warm milk to the waiting barn cats and Bonnie, as he did every morning. Watching Bonnie lick her whiskers, my twin laughed through his tears and pulled her close.
The day before, she had saved his life — that morning, she helped restore his spirit.
Age never dulled her instincts. Shortly after midnight in October 1961, Don and I woke to growls rising from the pumpkin pine floorboards at the foot of our bed.
“Why’s Bonnie growling?” we yelled into the dark.
“Might be a bear in the barnyard,” Grampa answered from the adjacent bedroom. “She found fresh tracks in the orchard yesterday.”
He lit a kerosene lantern and retrieved the 12-gauge from above the kitchen door. Bonnie paced and whined at the latch. The second it lifted, she shot through the doorway and bolted toward the pigpen, her dark silhouette framed by a huge harvest moon.
“You boys go back to bed,” Grammy barked.
We obeyed but opened our bedroom window to listen. The hogs were squealing, Bonnie was barking, and a single shotgun blast cracked across the farm. Then everything went deadly quiet.
The next 10 minutes felt like an hour before Grampa and Bonnie returned to the kitchen.
“She chased a bear clean out of the pigpen,” he said, still catching his breath. “The pen door’s stove to hell, but the hogs are fine.”
Two nights later, a few miles from our farm, Ralph True shot the same bear after it killed one of his sheep. The boar weighed 490 pounds.
“Its front paws,” he told Grampa, “were the size of dinner plates.”
When cancer took Bonnie in April 1962, Grampa wrapped her one last time in the ratty horsehair blanket she’d slept on her entire life and carried her up the knoll to the apple orchard — her favorite spot on the farm. He dug her grave that night by moonlight, working past the frost line with a pickaxe and shovel. The next afternoon, my three siblings and I picked yellow daffodils from the south side of the farmhouse and planted them on her grave.
That evening, my heartbroken 5-year-old sister, Gale, barely ate her supper. When the meal was over, she quietly walked behind the cookstove and scraped her plate into Bonnie’s enamel bowl.
In the morning, her eyes lit up at the sight of an empty bowl.
Years later, E.B. White gave me the words for what Bonnie meant to our family: “A really companionable and indispensable dog is an accident of nature. You can’t get it by breeding for it, and you can’t buy it with money.”
Ron Joseph of Sidney is the author of “Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist,” published by Islandport Press.

title: Karl’s Kids Annual Fundraiser Oct. 18
text:
From noon to 6 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 18 the Damariscotta-Newcastle Rotary Club will host the annual Karl’s Kids community fundraiser at Lakehurst Lodge, 30 Lakehurst Lane in Damariscotta.
Karl’s Kids helps kids and teens in Lincoln County participate in sports or physical activities by providing shoes, equipment, uniforms, and other necessary items. The goal is to make sure children have the opportunity to be involved in athletics and pursue an active lifestyle.

Donations are encouraged. All money raised will help kids in Lincoln County. There will also be a 50/50 raffle.

title: Damariscotta Artist Featured at Carey Gallery
text:
The work of Damariscotta artist Mark Lazzari is on display for the month of October at the Carey Gallery in Skidompha Public Library.
This show is titled “Aquatics” and highlights creatures that live in the sea. Lazzari is a self-taught painter working in acrylics and pastels. In his work career, Lazzari was an ichthyologist, a biological scientist specializing in the study of fish.
Lazzari loves the beauty, color and variety of the creatures that live in the watery world. He has exhibited in solo and group shows throughout Maine.

title: Brooks woman accused of trafficking cocaine and fentanyl
text:
Aimee Brown, 41, of Brooks is in jail facing multiple charges after allegedly turning over drugs to police following a traffic stop.
The Maine Drug Enforcement Agency and Waldo County Sheriff’s Office had been conducting a drug investigation in Brooks for several months prior to the arrest, the MDEA said on Thursday.
The investigation included undercover purchases of cocaine from Brown, the agency said.
On Wednesday, MDEA agents were surveilling Brown in anticipation of arresting her on charges related to the undercover purchases. Agents stopped her in Burnham after identifying her as the driver of a Subaru Outback, the MDEA said.
The agents placed Brown under arrest and searched the car but didn’t find any drugs or evidence. However, Brown indicated that she “was secreting drugs on/in her person,” according to the agency.
At the Waldo County Jail, the MDEA said Brown voluntarily turned over the drugs: 83 grams of cocaine and 20 grams of suspected fentanyl.
She was charged with two counts of trafficking Schedule W drugs and one count of violating conditions of release. She was not granted bail because she had been released after an earlier drug trafficking indictment, the MDEA said.
The agency said it anticipates more arrests in this case.

title: Damp start in Maine but showers move out quickly
text:
Damp start in Maine but showers move out quickly
Winds pick up and the temperature is on the rise but not for long.
Damp start in Maine but showers move out quickly
Winds pick up and the temperature is on the rise but not for long.
A cold front crossing our region this morning will bring a quick round of showers followed by clearing skies, breezy west winds gusting to 30 mph, and highs reaching the upper 60s. We will see even stronger northwest winds on Friday, gusting 20 to 30 mph, before high pressure builds in to deliver a beautiful, fair-weather Saturday with highs around 60.
As we head into Sunday evening, our attention shifts to moisture from Isaias merging with an approaching frontal boundary. This setup will bring increasing chances for beneficial rainfall late Sunday night through Monday, accompanied by highs in the upper 60s. Conditions quiet down briefly Monday night into early Tuesday, but another cold front arrives Tuesday night.
That system will trigger shower chances with high-elevation snow possible and usher in much cooler temperatures to round out the middle of next week.

title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
text:
CORONADO, Calif. (AP) — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.
The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.
Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
“It feels amazing,” he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.”
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.
“It feels really overwhelming,” she said about being seeing her mom again. “She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday.”
She added that she’s happy her mom won’t be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship’s commanding officer, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
“It’s a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet,” he said.
The Navy has downplayed problems on the carrier
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough.”
Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth told the crew that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”
USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals
The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln’s deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
“She’s our deployment baby,” said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship’s conditions while she was pregnant, she said. “I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn’t sure if he was OK or not,” she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was “pretty bad,” but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
“I couldn’t grasp the reality of it,” he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, “seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me,” Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.
Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.
He had told his wife about “the lack of food and showers” on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln’s crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

title: McDonald’s sued over AI tool that recommends prices to US franchisees
text:
(AP) - McDonald’s is facing a federal lawsuit that alleges its AI-enhanced pricing tool violates antitrust laws because it shares nonpublic data with franchisees who might be competing in the same market.
The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in Illinois, said McDonald’s pricing tool uses artificial intelligence to collect data that competing franchises wouldn’t normally share, like store-level sales. The Chicago-based burger giant has said it makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.
The lawsuit also blames the pricing system for raising McDonald’s U.S. prices.
“McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of U.S. restaurants,” the lawsuit states. “The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”
McDonald’s said Tuesday that the lawsuit is “filled with inaccuracies” and it would vigorously defend itself.
“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” the company said in a statement. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”
The lawsuit was filed on behalf of a consumer, Michael Thomas, of DeKalb, Illinois. According to the lawsuit, Thomas frequently visits McDonald’s and orders a Quarter Pounder with cheese, french fries and a Coke. The lawsuit said Thomas noticed price differences between McDonald’s stores near his home.
McDonald’s said it has used an AI-enhanced pricing tool for more than a decade. The program determines the optimal price for menu items based on a store’s sales, location and other factors, including competitors’ prices.
McDonald’s said that long before adopting the AI-enhanced tool, it collected data and recommended prices to its franchisees, who own and operate 95% of McDonald’s 14,000 U.S. stores.
“All we do is provide the context of what’s going on,” a McDonald’s spokesman told The Associated Press. “We don’t have any way to affect the menu pricing in a restaurant.”
But the lawsuit said McDonald’s has “significant leverage over its franchisees” and can pressure them to follow its pricing recommendations.
The Associated Press left a message Tuesday with the National Owners Association, which represents McDonald’s franchisees.
McDonald’s has been experimenting with various value strategies in the U.S. and other markets for several years as it tries to win back lower-income consumers, whose visits to fast-food chains have dropped.
But franchisees don’t always follow its guidance. During a conference call with investors in August, McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering McDonald’s proposed menu of 10 items for under $3.
“As you know, in our system, that’s not something that we just flip the switch on,” Kempczinski said. “It requires conversations with franchisees.”
The lawsuit asks the judge to certify the case as a class action and to require McDonald’s to pay damages to the class. It also seeks to prevent McDonald’s from enforcing agreements that restrict competition.
