title: Maine seeks settlement in generic drug price-fixing scheme
text:
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey on Thursday joined a coalition of 45 states and territories seeking court approval of settlements with three generic drug makers over allegations that they colluded to artificially inflate prices and reduce competition.
Under the settlement, Ascend Laboratories will pay $400,000 to the states and Mayne Pharma will pay $650,000. Settlement from the third company, Citron Pharma, “only includes non-monetary terms” because it has ceased operations, Frey’s office said in a news release.
The companies also each agreed to “meaningful injunctive terms including a series of internal reforms to ensure fair competition and compliance with antitrust laws,” AG’s office said.
Connecticut is leading a coalition of most U.S. states and territories in a series of antitrust cases, dating to 2016. The latest settlements come as the states prepare for the first trial to be held in Hartford, Connecticut, next February.
The states previously reached settlements with Sandoz, Glenmark, Lannett, Bausch, Apotex, Heritage, and Heritage’s parent company, Emcure, totaling $496.5 million.
The cases stem from investigations based on evidence from cooperating witnesses “at the core of the conspiracies,” along with a database of more than 20 million documents, and a phone records database containing millions of call records.
According to the AG’s office, the complaints lay out “an interconnected web of competing industry executives that met with each other during industry dinners, ‘girls’ nights out,’ lunches, cocktail parties, golf outings, and communicated via frequent telephone calls, emails, and text messages that sowed the seeds for their illegal agreements.”
“Defendants use[d] terms like ‘fair share,’ ‘playing nice in the sandbox,’ and ‘responsible competitor’ to describe how they unlawfully discouraged competition, raised prices, and enforced an ingrained culture of collusion,” the AG’s office said.
If you bought a generic prescription drug between May 2009 and December 2019, you may be eligible for compensation. To determine your eligibility, call 866-290-0182, email info@AGGenericDrugs.com or visit AGGenericDrugs.com. You can submit a claim for compensation here.
States that are not party to the case are: Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Missouri and Texas.

title: 49th case reported in Penobscot County HIV outbreak
text:
A new HIV case was reported in Penobscot County this week, raising the total number of cases associated with the outbreak to 49, according to the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
The outbreak began in October 2023. Nearly all of the people infected have reported injecting drugs or being homeless within one year of their diagnosis, according to the Maine CDC.
The new diagnosis is the first reported this month following three that were reported in September. Public health officials have emphasized that the actual number of cases in the outbreak is likely higher than what’s been detected.
The Maine CDC now updates its public-facing dashboard tracking HIV case counts every other week instead of weekly. The agency also expanded its criteria in April for counting a case as part of the outbreak, now including cases linked to the outbreak through molecular surveillance, which allows scientists to identify particular strains of a disease and track transmission networks.
Community organizations across the state have ramped up testing and prevention efforts as the outbreak continues, and the Maine CDC identified a set of five cases in November that had been detected in Cumberland County last year among people who inject drugs.
HIV attacks a person’s immune system and interferes with their body’s ability to fight off infection and disease, according to the CDC. There is no known cure, although there is medication that can control the disease.
Penobscot County typically has two new HIV cases per year, according to the Maine CDC.
In nearly all of the reported cases in Penobscot County, the people affected also tested positive for hepatitis C, the Maine CDC reported.
Hepatitis C is a liver disease that can be a mild, short-term illness for some people but can cause more serious, long-term issues for others, including liver cancer, according to the CDC.
Seventy-six percent of HIV patients in the Penobscot County outbreak were connected to care within 30 days of their diagnosis, and 70% of the 47 people currently living in Maine had reached viral suppression — meaning they can’t transmit HIV to others — at their most recent test, the Maine CDC reported.

title: Maine heating fund, even with leftover money, won’t go as far this winter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating assistance program plans to use about $4 million left over from last winter to kickstart aid for vulnerable households across the state, MaineHousing announced this week.
This initial round of Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) funding will go to households who applied early to the program with adults over 60 years old, children age 6 and under, and people with disabilities. The $4 million is about 13% of the total heating fuel assistance money expected to be distributed this year.
About 4,400 families will begin receiving credits on their heating accounts in the next week or so, said Scott Thistle, MaineHousing’s spokesperson.
Maine is expecting to receive about $41 million in HEAP funding from the federal government this year — of which about $27 million will be for heating fuel — but that money won’t start arriving until late this month.
“We know this assistance will not fully offset the outsized heating burden many Mainers are facing, but acting now means some of our most vulnerable households can begin the winter with fuel in their tanks,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said in a news release.
Even with the $4 million injection, the heating assistance won’t go as far this winter.
With heating oil costs hovering around a record high, set last month at more than $6 per gallon, the average HEAP award will have less purchasing power than it did last year.
“The benefit amount will just not be as deep,” Thistle said. “It ultimately means less oil for them.”
MaineHousing also used carryover funds to kickstart its HEAP program last year. That was during the six-week government shutdown, when MaineHousing wasn’t sure if the federal government would be providing funding at all, Thistle said.
Last year’s $2 million in extra money provided help for about 4,000 households. This year, $4 million is providing help for 4,400.
The average HEAP award was set this summer at about $700, Thistle said. But after oil costs skyrocketed at the end of the summer and into the fall, the value of that help has fallen significantly, he said.
Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation last week demanding that the federal government allocate more money for heating assistance. Congress kept heating assistance funding level this year.
Prices as high as they are — $5.97 per gallon, as of Monday — demand action from the federal government, Mills said. Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, could be particularly hard-hit if the federal Low Income Heating Assistance Program funds aren’t increased, she said.
Mills blamed record heating costs on President Donald Trump and the war in Iran, where the constriction of the Strait of Hormuz has reduced the worldwide oil supply and driven up costs.
“Federal funding levels appropriated for LIHEAP this winter did not fully consider the drastic impacts of the president’s war that has sent fuel prices skyrocketing and are now insufficient for the circumstances that Maine and other cold-climate states now face,” Mills said.
Meanwhile, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies announced last week their plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, lauded the G7 announcement Friday. She said the release should put “immediate downward pressure on energy prices.”
MaineHousing’s carryover funding will begin with households who applied when the program opened in August, but applications remain open on the agency’s website. Federal funds will go to all eligible applicants as long as there is money available.
Thistle said the number of applications is up about 5% over last year, but are actually substantially far below average in some parts of the state.
Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Lewiston boys soccer wins top-2 showdown with Brunswick in overtime
text:
BRUNSWICK — Lewiston boys soccer coach Dan Gish said, in a game like this, all a player needs is one opportunity.
Blue Devils midfielder Khalil Ibrahim capitalized on his opportunity Thursday against Brunswick.
After an Abdirauf Hersi free kick from midfield, Ibrahim controlled the ball in the box and fired a shot that deflected off a Dragons defender into the goal with 1:39 remaining in overtime to give Lewiston a 1-0 win.
“It was slow motion for me,” Ibrahim said. “As soon as I heard my teammate Nathan (Dimandja) say shoot, everything was in slow motion. I took a touch (and) shot it. I didn’t really know what to do. I just shot it, and it took a huge deflection.”
Brunswick became the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll after defeating the second-ranked Blue Devils 3-2 last week in Lewiston. The Blue Devils (10-1) returned the favor Thursday, dealing the Dragons (9-1) their first loss of the season on their home field, in what was another classic Lewiston-Brunswick hard-fought showdown.
“One opportunity and having the composure to finish it, and not backing off for a single minute by either team,” Gish said. “So, it’s a great confidence booster. If you can win away, especially in overtime, that’s quite a feat. And we’re not done by any means.”
Corner chances
Both teams had plenty of corner-kick opportunities throughout the game. Lewiston finished with eight and Brunswick had six. On the Dragons’ second chance, in the 15th minute of the first half, the ball was loose in the box and went toward the goal, but a Lewiston defender stopped it.
Dimandja almost finished on a corner kick in the 25th minute, but his header went over the crossbar.
“He finds a way to get open,” Gish said. “He is great at tracking the ball and putting shots on target (and) headers on target.”
Both teams had several more corner kicks opportunities throughout the game, but neither capitalized. For the Dragons, even getting shots on goal was difficult.
“We were spinning (our) wheels a little bit,” Brunswick coach Mark Roma said. “I feel like we started the game well. We had a grip. Then we got away from it a little bit, which happens sometimes.”
What it means
Lewiston is first in the Class A North Heal point standings by more than 20 points over Brunswick. The Blue Devils have three games remaining, while the Dragons have four. Both teams face No. 3 Edward Little (sixth in the Varsity Maine poll) — Brunswick on Saturday in Auburn, while the Blue Devils host the Red Eddies in the regular season finale Oct. 20.
Unsung hero
Hersi took many of Lewiston’s free kicks, including the one in overtime that set up the game-winning goal. Hersi said the Blue Devils were determined to bounce back from last week’s loss to the Dragons.
“I was just thinking of putting it in a dangerous place … last (week against Brunswick), I did the same thing and we almost capitalized,” Hersi said. “But, thank God, this game, we capitalized off this long ball. All game, I’ve been trying to create something, a goal or assist. I’m happy I’m able to contribute to my team.”
Statistical leaders
Lewiston: Khalil Ibrahim (goal), Abdirauf Hersi (assist), Farhan Mohamed (three saves)
Brunswick: Declan Theberge (four saves)

title: Christa Pike survived a failed execution. So did 7 other inmates in recent decades
text:
Tennessee’s bungled attempt to execute Christa Pike was not the first time a state has failed to carry out a lethal injection over problems in the death chamber.
Pike, 50, has regained consciousness and is speaking a week after Tennessee gave her two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee has ordered a review into what went wrong and the state has not said whether they will again try executing her, which experts say could wade into uncharted legal waters.
Pike, who was sentenced to die for torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995, is one of at least eight condemned inmates in the U.S. who left their state’s execution chamber still alive because of problems carrying out the punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Pike is the only one who was actually administered lethal drugs before the process was halted, according to the organization.
Not all have faced execution a second time. Three of the inmates would die years later in prison, two remain alive and two were executed after another attempt.
Lethal injection failures in Ohio
Ohio unsuccessfully tried to put Romell Broom to death by lethal injection in September 2009. The execution was called off after two hours when technicians could not find a suitable vein, and Broom cried in pain while receiving 18 needle sticks.
Broom died in December 2020 of possible complications of COVID-19 while on Ohio’s death row.
Ohio also failed to execute another inmate, Alva Campbell, in November 2017 by lethal injection. The execution was halted after executioners couldn’t find a usable vein.
Campbell was found unresponsive in his death row cell in March 2018. It was determined that he died from natural causes.
Alabama executed inmates a second time after failed attempts
Alabama called off the execution of Doyle Lee Hamm in February 2018 because of problems getting the intravenous line connected. A doctor hired by Hamm’s legal team later wrote in a report, filed in court, that Hamm had to be carried back to his cell by correctional officers after the execution was called off because he was in so much pain.
Hamm died of natural causes on death row in November 2021.
In September 2022, Alabama unsuccessfully executed Alan Eugene Miller by lethal injection when executioners spent more than an hour trying and failing to properly insert the catheter, repeatedly puncturing Miller with needles trying to find a vein. At one point, they left him hanging vertically on a gurney before state officials made the decision to call off the execution, according to news coverage at the time.
Miller had originally asked for nitrogen gas, but the Alabama Department of Corrections told a federal district court that they could not complete the execution that way.
The state successfully executed him two years later in September 2024 with nitrogen gas.
Almost two months after failing to execute Miller, Alabama had a second failed execution, when executioners did not have enough time to get a second IV line in before the death warrant expired at midnight for Kenneth Eugene Smith.
Smith was the first person to die by nitrogen gas as an execution method in January 2024.
Idaho prisoner remains alive
Idaho halted the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in February 2024 after medical team members repeatedly failed to find a vein to carry out the lethal injection. In some cases, they couldn’t access the vein, and in others they could but had concerns about vein quality. They attempted sites in his arms, legs, hands and feet. At one point, a medical team member left to gather more supplies.
After eight attempts, the prison warden told them to give up. Creech remains alive and on death row.
Pike was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year
Four months before Pike’s execution went awry, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after his executioners tried and failed for over an hour to establish an intravenous line.
Lee announced soon afterward that the state would not try to execute Carruthers again for at least a year. Tennessee prison officials have said medical personnel had quickly established a primary IV line but were unable to find a suitable vein for a backup line as required by the state’s execution protocol. Efforts to insert a central line also failed.
Carruthers remains alive and on death row.

title: Acoustic Grateful Dead tribute band to perform at Bath’s Chocolate Church
text:
Dead to the Core is a collective of singer-songwriters and acoustic musicians, led by musician/author Jeffrey Pepper Rodgers, with a shared love of the Grateful Dead. In intimate concerts, the musicians celebrate the band’s music not through note-for-note re-creations but by playing the songs their own way — letting them grow and evolve collaboratively in the true spirit of the Dead.
Interspersed with the music are clips from Rodgers’ own interviews with Jerry Garcia and Bob Weir, in which they reflect on the roots and evolution of the music.
The band will perform at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, at the Chocolate Church Arts Center. Tickets are also available for a pre-concert workshop and jam session, singing and playing classic Grateful Dead songs. Bring any acoustic instrument, or just your voice. The band will supply lyric and chord charts and go through the basic form and rhythm of each song.
Get tickets at chocolatechurcharts.org, $22.99 general admission for the concert, $20.72 for veterans, students and seniors, and $17.35 for the jam session. The Chocolate Church is located at 804 Washington St. in Bath.

title: David Pastrnak scores twice to lead Bruins past Mammoth
text:
BOSTON — David Pastrnak scored his first two goals of the season and added two assists as the Boston Bruins routed the Utah Mammoth 6-1 on Thursday night.
Matthew Poitras, Casey Mittelstadt, Mason Lohrei and Morgan Geekie also scored for the Bruins, who led 3-0 after one period and 6-0 after two. Jeremy Swayman made 36 saves.
Pastrnak scored his first goal with 5:38 left in the first period on a power-play wrist shot, assisted by Frederic Brunet and Geekie. He tacked on a power-play slap shot 4:40 into the second period, assisted by Geekie and Hampus Lindholm.
Jack McBain scored for the Mammoth midway through the third period to spoil Swayman’s shutout bid.
Karel Vejmelka stopped 11 of 14 shots he faced before he was replaced by Sebastian Cossa, who made five saves.
The Bruins scored three power-play goals, while the Mammoth went scoreless on the power play. The Bruins blocked 23 shots.
Up next
Utah: Visits the Buffalo Sabres on Saturday night.
Boston: Hosts the Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday.

title: Collins and Jackson to square off in Senate debate
text:
Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in Maine Senate debate on WMTW Channel 8
The hourlong debate aired Thursday, Oct. 8, on WMTW Channel 8
Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in Maine Senate debate on WMTW Channel 8
The hourlong debate aired Thursday, Oct. 8, on WMTW Channel 8
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, faced off in an hourlong debate hosted by Maine's Total Coverage on Thursday. Below is a summary of how Collins and Jackson responded to the questions they were asked during the debate.
A recap of the debate from Maine's Total Coverage reporter Bonnie Bishop and analysis from the In the Arena podcast team is featured in the video player at the top of this page.
You can watch the debate in its entirety in the video player embedded below, or on the WMTW-TV YouTube channel.
WMTW's partners at PolitiFact conducted a fact-check of the claims made by both candidates. PolitiFact's blog is embedded below. Click here to read an article featuring fact-checks of several key claims made during the debate.
Collins is seeking to win her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. She was uncontested in the June 9 primary, as she was the only candidate to qualify for the Republican primary ballot.
Jackson has only been in the Senate race for just over two months. The former Maine Senate president finished third in the gubernatorial primary, but was chosen as the Democratic Senate nominee on July 25 at a special nominating convention. The Maine Democratic Party had to find a replacement candidate for the Senate primary winner, Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race on July 8 following allegations of sexual assault.
Jackson's political experience
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Fort Kent, led a weeklong blockade along the border with Quebec in 1998, when Maine loggers were protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into Maine and driving down pay rates. The standoff ended with Jackson being escorted away by police, and he went on to fight for better logger and wood hauler protections as a state lawmaker.
In 2000, Jackson ran for the Maine House of Representatives as a Republican but lost out on the House District 151 seat. He ran for the same seat as an independent two years later and was victorious, and became a Democrat in 2004 before the end of his first term. Jackson was elected later that year to serve the new House District 1, and was reelected in 2006.
In 2008, Jackson ran for the State Senate and was elected to represent District 35. He won reelection in 2010 and 2012 before running to represent Maine's 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House in 2014. Jackson lost the 2014 Democratic primary to Emily Cain, who wound up losing the CD2 general election to Republican Bruce Poliquin.
Jackson led U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential campaign in Maine in 2016 and helped the independent from Vermont win the state's caucus. Sanders will be campaigning with Jackson in Maine this weekend.
In 2016, Jackson was reelected to the Maine Senate to represent the 1st District and then chosen by fellow Democrats to be the Senate's minority leader. He was reelected in 2018 and became Senate president after Democrats won a majority in the chamber, and he held that role while being reelected two more times in 2020 and 2022. Jackson left office in December 2024 due to term limits.
More on Collins' experience
Collins grew up in Caribou, where her family runs a sixth-generation lumber business. Both of her parents served as mayor of Caribou, and her father served in both chambers of the Maine Legislature.
After graduating from St. Lawrence University in 1975, Collins began working as a legislative assistant for U.S. Rep. Bill Cohen, a Republican from Maine. Cohen was eventually elected to the U.S. Senate in 1978 and in 1981, Collins was promoted to staff director of the Oversight of Government Management Subcommittee of the Committee on Governmental Affairs.
Collins remained on Cohen's staff until 1987, when Maine Gov. John McKernan appointed her as commissioner of the Maine Department of Professional and Financial Regulation. In 1992, President George H.W. Bush appointed Collins as director of the Small Business Administration's New England regional office. After President Bill Clinton took office in January 1993, Collins served as deputy state treasurer of Massachusetts.
In 1994, Collins won the Republican primary for Maine governor, becoming the first woman to be nominated for the office. She wound up finishing third in the election behind Democrat Joseph E. Brennan and the winner, independent Angus King, who is now Collins' fellow U.S. senator from Maine. Collins was named the founding executive director of the Center for Family Business at Husson University after the 1994 gubernatorial election.
Two years later, Collins ran for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Cohen, her former boss, and went on to defeat Brennan in the 1996 general election. Collins was reelected in 2002, 2008, 2014 and most recently in 2020, when she became the first Republican woman to win a fifth term in the Senate.
Collins, the most senior Republican woman in the Senate and the seventh-most senior senator, currently serves as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. She previously chaired the Committee on Governmental Affairs (2003-05), Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (2005-07) and Special Committee on Aging (2015-21).
The Maine's Total Coverage debate was the second debate of the week for Collins and Jackson, who had their first debate Tuesday night.

title: Trump tries to smooth over controversial remarks about Iran striking San Diego, Los Angeles
text:
(Gray News) – President Donald Trump fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton Wednesday night, but his remarks were not only focused on Paxton.
Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.
“You want to see trauma? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country.”
People at the rally cheered when the president clarified the controversial statements he made earlier in the week at a political rally in Nebraska.
How are California leaders responding?
“Trump thinks he will scare people into voting for MAGA candidates by threatening the bombing of over 16 million Americans. He has lost his mind,” Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X in response to Trump’s most recent comments at the rally in Texas.
Los Angeles is the most populous city in California and the second most populous in the United States. It has one of the busiest container ports in the Americas and is home to the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command Headquarters.
LA Mayor Karen Bass reacted to Trump’s statement on X saying, “We should not be in a position where we are questioning whether or not the President of the United States is threatening cities in his own country.”
Bass said on X that she called Congressman Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, “to investigate the dangerous threats the President has encouraged this week against Angelenos.”
“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” Bass said on X earlier in the week.
“Seriously, again? How many times do we have to say it? San Diego is not a prop. San Diego is not a target. San Diego is not your applause line,” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote on X in response to Trump’s remarks in Texas.
“We are a proud military city full of real people. Stop using us in your reckless war talk.”
San Diego is home to Naval Base San Diego, where the Navy SEALs train. There is a large military presence in the city with 70,000 civilians and active-duty service members living and working in the area.
The president’s message was interrupted in Texas repeatedly by protesters, including one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.
Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.
“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”

title: How volunteers step up to help when elderly or disable adults are reported missing
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - For families caring for someone with dementia, it’s a constant concern that they may get disoriented, walk out of their house, and struggle to get home or find safety.
That behavior is known as “wandering.” It’s an umbrella term that can mean everything from escape to repetitive pacing or getting lost.
If a person isn’t found within 24 hours, half are either severely injured or found dead.
In many states, officials use emergency alerts and resources for missing, at-risk adults like silver alerts. In Georgia, it’s known as Mattie’s Call. It was named after 67-year-old Mattie Moore, who had Alzheimer’s and wandered from her home and was found dead months later.
The struggle for normalcy
Ernestine Merritt was known as “Ernie” to her church family at Greenforest Community Baptist Church, where she served as an usher greeting members and guests at the front doors each Sunday.
Gayle Allen and Felecia Prince, fellow ushers at Greenforest Community Baptist, became caregivers when Merritt began losing her memory.
“She knew something was happening but she didn’t give in to the fact that it was dementia,” Prince said. “I never heard her say that.”
Late last year, what was once uncertain became evident to her church family. “We had to just take it one day at a time and just treat her as she was, each day,” Allen said. “We still loved her, no matter what.”
Prince said one of the hardest moments was when a doctor told Merritt she couldn’t drive anymore.
“She was so independent,” she said. “It was hard for her to accept that.”
The 79-year-old woman with dementia left her Ellenwood home at 4 a.m. on Jan. 4, 2026, determined to get to church on her own. She never made it.
Doorbell footage revealed when Merritt left her house. DeKalb County police and volunteers searched the woods, the neighborhood and nearby highway bridges for four days before locating her body in a nearby creek.
Because Merritt told her friends hours earlier she wanted to go to worship, search crews were intentional about mapping out the possible walking route to the church.
Searching for hope
Angel Alonso was one of the volunteers who led the search with his nonprofit Georgia Emergency Search & Rescue. He said his nonprofit assists any Georgia police department on Mattie’s calls, an emergency missing alert for a person who is disabled, special needs, elderly or has dementia.
There have been 69 Mattie’s Calls issued in the first four months of 2026. Last year, there were 213.
“If you find them alive, you did a great thing,” Alonso said. “But if you find them deceased, you still did a great thing because you brought them closure. They don’t have to wonder.”
The Georgia Emergency Search and Rescue nonprofit operates on donations when helping on cases. The dollars spent by law enforcement for each search climb to five figures for each operation.
A typical search and rescue can cost $1,500 per hour with low-tech operations, according to an Alzheimer’s initiatives report from the International Association of Chiefs of Police. In a nine-hour work day, that’s $13,500 in taxpayer dollars on one search alone.
Law enforcement agencies welcome the free assistance from groups like Alonso’s.
His nonprofit is made up of neighbors, retired officers, investigators and volunteers. From drones to dogs to four-wheelers, they expand police resources that would be otherwise limited.
“I can’t put a price on a life,” Alonso said. “God has put us in a good place to help others.”
The International Association of Chiefs of Police advises departments have a voluntary dementia registry that provides critical information about the loved one prior to the actual emergency.
Georgia has a growing statewide registry after state lawmakers increased funding for it last year. When a patient is formally diagnosed, their medical professional adds them to the registry.

title: Trump says he’ll award pitcher Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom
text:
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump announced Wednesday night that he would award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to fireballer Roger Clemens, calling the seven-time Cy Young winner “maybe the greatest pitcher of all time.”
Addressing a rally in San Antonio, Trump renewed his calls for Clemens to be inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame. That’s an honor the pitcher known as “The Rocket” has yet to receive because of suspicions he used steroids during a 24-year career that featured time with the Boston Red Sox, Toronto Blue Jays, New York Yankees and Houston Astros.
“We’re giving him the Presidential Medal of Freedom,” Trump said. “And, along with the Congressional Medal of Honor, it’s the highest award bestowed upon anyone.”
The president continued: “He’ll be in the Hall of Fame someday, but he deserves it. One of the greatest athletes, and maybe the greatest pitcher, of all time.”
He added that the medal “is a big step up from the Hall of Fame.”
Trump has given the medal to various athletes during his two terms in the White House, including golfing legend Tiger Woods, former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Roger Staubach, famed Yankees closer Mariano Rivera and Lou Holtz, former coach of Notre Dame football.
He’s bestowed the same honor on Elvis Presley posthumously and on Rush Limbaugh the year before the conservative radio host died.
Wednesday’s surprise revelation came near the end of a Trump speech that lasted more than 100 minutes, and with the crowd having lost some of its enthusiasm. Clemens was attending the event, and the president called him to the stage, where the retired right-hander offered, “Well, I’m stunned.”
“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” Clemens said. “And to get it from this man, this president, there wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from.”
Clemens, who was raised in Houston, said he was honored that the announcement came in Texas and added of Trump: “You’re talking about a winner. That’s a winner right there.”
Clemens, like slugger Barry Bonds and many other stars widely suspected of using performance-enhancing drugs, was repeatedly rejected by baseball writers in his bid for the Hall of Fame. There are other avenues where Clemens and others could eventually make it, but the road is not easy.
Clemens isn’t the first star baseball player Trump has made a Hall of Fame case for. The president issued a posthumous federal pardon last year for the late Pete Rose, which led to Major League Baseball lifting its ban on the all-time career hits leader.
Trump has called for Rose to be inducted in the Hall of Fame too — also, so far, unsuccessfully.
__
Weissert reported from Washington.

title: 3 takeaways on the 2nd Maine gubernatorial debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The second of four debates in Maine’s three-way race for governor was mostly a substantive affair — and, to some extent, a repeat of the candidates’ first meeting last week.
The debate was hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine at the Gracie Theatre on Husson University’s campus in Bangor. The three candidates went back and forth for an hour on housing, immigration, healthcare and more.
Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree remains the race’s strong favorite, having dominated fundraising and holding a steady double-digit lead in polling since she won a competitive ranked-choice primary this summer.
Bobby Charles, a Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, won the Republican nomination in a similarly competitive — but more bruising — primary. His campaign has tried to link Pingree to higher electricity prices and property taxes under Democratic Gov. Janet Mills.
Rick Bennett, the independent, is a state senator from Oxford County who left the Republican Party when he joined the race last summer. He’s tried to position himself as a middle-ground candidate, but has failed so far to pick up widespread support, polls show.
After the trio’s second debate, here are a few takeaways.
1. Charles talked about Pingree about as much as himself.
Charles began his participation in the debate, and ended it, by attacking Pingree.
The first question posed to the candidates was about housing affordability, and — before spinning into a list of policy proposals that included reducing property taxes for disabled veterans and raising the Homestead Exemption — Charles said housing costs have doubled under Mills and Pingree, who served in Mills’ administration.
That’s been his strategy since he won the Republican nomination: Link Pingree to Mills, and point the finger.
And this approach was typified by Charles’ closing statement. After a brief moment of emotion, Charles pointed the finger at Pingree once again.
“Who in their right mind, charged with affordable housing by a governor, would give $840,000 to her own nonprofit, one that employs her husband and her family?” Charles said, alluding to state funding awarded to a nonprofit Pingree once led, before being cut off by Maine Public host Jennifer Rooks.
Charles’ time was up.
2. The second debate was pretty similar to the first.
As in the first debate, Charles, behind in polls by double digits, went on the attack and positioned himself as an outsider with new ideas. He again attempted to distance himself from President Donald Trump on tariffs and said he has appealed to Trump to return to the negotiating table, calling Canada a “friend.”
As in the first debate, Pingree stuck to her message, avoided addressing Charles’ constant attacks and linked Charles on tariffs and the war in Iran to Trump — whose approval ratings are well underwater in Maine, recent polling shows.
And as in the first debate, Bennett swung with his independence. He called the two-party system, which he abandoned last year, the “political industrial complex,” calling out both Democrats and Republicans for stifling debate and encouraging the explosion of campaign money.
3. There were a few areas of policy agreement.
On the first question of the night, all three candidates acknowledged housing production in Maine is too slow, and that rolling back regulations may help ease the state’s 80,000-unit shortfall.
Pingree called for a 90-day environmental permitting “shot clock,” Charles said he would encourage municipalities to speed up permitting and Bennett said he would audit the state’s housing bottleneck to understand where delays are coming from.
All three candidates acknowledged Maine is struggling to retain its healthcare workforce and its rural hospitals. Bennett and Charles agreed that reimbursement rates need to increase, and Pingree and Bennett agreed that Maine should be working toward universal health insurance coverage.
In fact, Pingree and Bennett agreed on quite a bit: that immigration enforcement has gone too far, that data center development should pause and that the Indigenous tribes in Maine should have sovereignty.
Bennett — ever the middleman — and Charles agreed that the state budget shortfall was due to overspending, and that the state budget deserves a thorough comb-through.
Watch the full debate on Maine Public’s YouTube channel. The candidates will meet on stage again in a CBS13 and FOX23-hosted debate on Tuesday, and on Wednesday in a debate hosted by WMTW.

title: Ketamine: What to know about the sedative drug some college students are using recreationally
text:
Ketamine: What to know about the sedative drug some college students are using recreationally
Known as special K, key and K, ketamine is both a psychoactive club drug similar to acid or ecstasy and a promising option for treating depression or substance use disorder.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
With its dueling profile, the anesthetic ketamine has made lots of headlines in recent years.
It was scrutinized for its role in “Friends” actor Matthew Perry’s 2023 death. During the 2024 election, billionaire and business owner Elon Musk said he used ketamine to treat depression while others reported he may have misused it.
Now, a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit alleging she was gang raped by a group of fraternity members in 2024 includes numerous descriptions of ketamine use by her and her attackers.
As recreational ketamine use rises and researchers continue to explore ways the drug could help people in clinical settings, here’s a primer on this drug, its uses and its risks.
What is ketamine?
It is a dissociative drug, meaning it makes users feel detached from their body, pain and the physical environment, according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. It can also cause hallucinations and sedation.
The Food and Drug Administration approves of ketamine for anesthesia purposes, as it can help block pain and cause unconsciousness. For this purpose, it is typically administered intravenously or injected into a muscle.
The FDA has also approved the nasal spray esketamine, a ketamine derivative, to treat depression in very controlled circumstances.
Under federal law, ketamine is classified a Schedule III drug, which means it has a “moderate to low” potential for physical and psychological dependence and less potential for abuse than Schedule II drugs such as cocaine and methamphetamine.
It has a reputation as a party, club and rave drug. Its other nicknames include ket, super K, vitamin K or super acid. Liquid ketamine is injected, mixed into drinks or evaporated into crystals that are then ground into powder that can be snorted or smoked. It has been used to facilitate sexual assault.
Ketamine is legal with a prescription for medical use, including for off-label uses such as treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder.
But its status as a Schedule III drug means that it is illegal to possess and distribute or traffic ketamine for recreational use.
What is ketamine used for in clinical settings?
Before and during a surgical procedure, it can be used at high doses to cause drowsiness, promote sleep and render a person unconscious.
Esketamine, sometimes also simply called ketamine, is used to manage depression that’s unresponsive to other treatments and can offer rapid relief. The spray is administered in a hospital or clinic and healthcare providers monitor patients for at least two hours before they are allowed to leave.
Ketamine therapy is when medical professionals administer low doses of the drug. Some people describe esketamine spray for depression as ketamine therapy, but the term also refers to doctors prescribing ketamine infusions off-label to treat conditions such as chronic pain, depression, obsessive compulsive disorder and PTSD. Medication being prescribed “off-label” means it isn’t FDA approved for that purpose.
Early research has also found short-term benefits to using ketamine as a substance use disorder treatment, but more research is needed.
How is ketamine misused or abused?
The drug is sometimes used recreationally because it can cause an out-of-body experience or produce hallucinations that last about 30 minutes to a few hours. Some people describe a dissociative state or experiencing oblivion, sometimes called a “k-hole.”
Ketamine can cause immobility, sedation, amnesia and distort a person’s sense of sight and smell. Overdosing on ketamine can cause unconsciousness and dangerously slowed breathing.
What are side effects and other risks of ketamine?
Side effects can include headache, dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, poor memory, confusion, anxiety, agitation, a spike in blood pressure and shortness of breath.
People can develop an addiction to ketamine, and that risk is higher for people who have a history of addiction.
Long-term ketamine abuse also carries risks such as poor memory and concentration, abnormal liver or kidney function and ketamine bladder syndrome (weakened bladder, incontinence and bladder ulceration), according to the Alcohol and Drug Foundation in Australia.
How does it mix with alcohol?
As a central nervous system depressant, alcohol slows brain activity. Mixing alcohol with ketamine increases the sedative effects of both drugs, increasing a person’s risk of losing consciousness.
At lower doses of combining the two, a person risks nausea and vomiting and at higher doses the risk of passing out and then aspirating vomit increases.
“Even on relatively small doses, you’re very detached from things,” New York University ketamine researcher Joseph Palamar told The New York Times. “You’re not as in touch with your emotions.” As the dose increases, it becomes harder to communicate, he said.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Obituary: Patricia Ann (Davies) Fleshman
text:
YARMOUTH – Patricia Ann (Davies) Fleshman, known to family and friends as “Pat”, of Freeport, Maine, died Oct. 2, 2026, at the age of 83. She was born on Dec. 4, 1942, to William and Mary Davies.
Pat graduated from Texas Christian University in Fort Worth, Texas, where she worked at a movie theater—fitting for someone whose lifelong love of old movies began as a girl sending away for autographed photographs of movie stars.
After college, Pat taught middle school English in Texas and Indiana. She later lived for many years in Bluefield, W.Va., where she worked as a medical secretary, before eventually returning to teaching.
Pat and her husband, Walter “Bud” Fleshman, made their home in Troutdale, Va., in a cabin at the end of a mile-long gravel drive, complete with a lovely pond. Pat navigated the winding mountain roads to teach English first at Oak Hill Academy and later at Grayson County High School. She delighted in teaching literature, writing and grammar and cared deeply for her students. At Oak Hill, she was an enthusiastic supporter of the school’s basketball team, and at GCHS, she was honored to serve as a commencement speaker.
Pat’s classrooms changed with the seasons, with Bud serving as her patient co-decorator, assisting with the logistics behind each month’s collection. Pat was known for her fashion coordination, matching her outfits from head to toe, including earrings, necklace, watch and shoes, and, at times, a seasonally appropriate flower in her hair.
Pat’s love of language followed her home. Laura credits her mom with making her a better writer, beginning with childhood draft thank-you notes finalized following gentle lessons in spelling and grammar. Pat’s frequent cards for family and friends and her annual Christmas letter were legendary. Her family long suspected it was no coincidence that the local Hallmark store closed after she left Bluefield.
Pat dearly loved her grandchildren and treasured being Grandma. When they were young, visits included gifted books read aloud; as they grew, she enjoyed holidays and special occasions with them whenever she could. Birthdays brought a phone call and Grandma proudly singing “Happy Birthday.”
Pat was predeceased by her parents; her brothers William Davies Jr. and James Davies; and Bud.
She is survived by her sisters Barbara (David) Coleman of Haslet, Texas, and Judy Mattingly of New Castle, Ind.; her children, David Doyle of Croton-on-Hudson, N.Y. and Laura Doyle Sanborn (Greg) of Yarmouth; her grandchildren, Christopher and Jonathan Doyle and Matthew, Evelyn and Benjamin Sanborn; and Valerie Doyle, mother of Chris and Jon.
Pat’s family is deeply grateful to the staff of Freeport Place for their kindness and care. Laura is especially grateful to her husband and children for the errands, appointments, visits and, of course, monthly seasonal decor changes Pat eagerly anticipated.
A celebration of Pat’s life will be planned at a later date.
Arrangements and guidance are in the care of Stetson’s Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 12 Federal St., Brunswick.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Stetson’s Funeral Home website, http://www.stetsonsfuneralhome.com
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to Food Independence with information available at https://graysonlandcare.org/product/food-independence-donation

title: Former Maine police officer pleads not guilty in alleged overtime fraud scheme
text:
A former Scarborough police officer has pleaded not guilty in an alleged overtime fraud scheme.
Timothy Barker, 55, entered his plea on charges of theft by deception, tampering with public records or information, and official oppression Thursday morning, according to CBS affiliate WGME.
Prosecutors allege that Barker conspired to submit fraudulent time records for traffic details he didn’t work from March 5 to Sept. 19, 2025, the TV station reported.
He allegedly tried to collect as much as $10,000 in overtime from Scarborough.
Scarborough police informed the Maine attorney general’s office in December of the alleged theft, and Barker retired as a lieutenant on Feb. 2 after 31 years with the department.
Barker will next appear in court in March.

title: $1,600 stolen in July from Leavitt Area High School in Turner
text:
Androscoggin County sheriff’s deputies are investigating the July theft of $1,600 from a storage area at Leavitt Area High School in Turner.
The majority of the Maine School Administrative 52 board of directors learned about the theft Oct. 1 during a report from the district’s Finance Committee.
“I can confirm that we did take a report, however there are no suspects and the area it was stolen from does not have cameras,” Sheriff’s Chief Deputy William Gagne wrote in an email.
It happened sometime during a four-week period, he wrote.
The money was from bottle returns earmarked for staff and the faculty Sunshine Fund and athletic cash box, Superintendent Cari Medd wrote in an email.
The money from the Sunshine Fund is used to support a staff colleague who needs it: flowers or food or other things. The athletic funds were from a game ticket box, she wrote.
“We did not submit this to insurance because the amount was small enough that it didn’t warrant it,” Medd said Monday. “We believe it was locked in the main office storage closet.”
Director Jenny Maheu who is on the Finance Committee, said steps have been taken to make sure it doesn’t happen again. Money will be deposited nightly, she said.
The board will also be informed quicker if such an incident happens again.
If anyone has any information about the theft, they are asked to call the Androscoggin County Regional Communications Center at 207-753-2599.

title: Maine House speaker says lawmakers will aim to ease federal healthcare cuts, heating oil spikes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
House Speaker Ryan Fecteau on Thursday said that lawmakers will try to lessen the impact of federal healthcare cutbacks and the spike in heating oil prices.
Work requirements for Medicaid are set to start in 2027 and are expected to result in over 31,000 additional uninsured Mainers, according to state estimates. Those cutbacks stem from the 2025 budget bill, which also cut into the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Thousands of Mainers are also paying much higher Affordable Care Act premiums after some of the program’s subsidies expired at the end of 2025.
Fecteau and Rep. Gary Friedmann, D-Bar Harbor, participated in a news conference on Thursday with Defend America Action, a progressive advocacy group.
“We’re going to have to stand ready to provide some immediate relief when we return to Augusta,” said Fecteau, referring to heating oil cost increases and also possibly tapping into a $30 million SNAP contingency fund. The legislative session will begin in January.
The contingency fund was set up this year to continue SNAP payments during government shutdowns. Fecteau said presuming the government doesn’t shut down this winter, the state money could be used to boost the SNAP program, formerly known as food stamps.
Meanwhile, heating oil prices have reached $6 per gallon. Politicians including Gov. Janet Mills, and all three major gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett, have called for helping Maine residents afford heating oil this winter.
Friedmann said that when the Legislature convenes in January, a top priority will be figuring out “how to keep our constituents from freezing.”
The federal Low Income Heating Assistance Program helps about 40,000 Maine people with their heating costs. But the roughly $27 million in heating oil funding expected this winter won’t begin arriving until late this month and about $4 million leftover from last winter will be used to jumpstart the program for those who are most vulnerable and applied early, MaineHousing announced this week.
About 23,000 fewer Mainers had SNAP benefits in August 2026 compared with July 2025, when the budget bill was passed, according to an analysis by the Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Friedmann said Maine will do what it can to help, but state government will not be able to restore cuts made by the federal government to programs like Medicaid and SNAP.
“The state of Maine doesn’t have the resources of the federal government,” Friedmann said. “We can’t make up for the billions in healthcare cuts that the feds are passing on to us.”
James Myall, policy analyst for the Maine Center for Economic Policy, said the state is facing about $350 million in cutbacks to Medicaid and SNAP.
Myall said the state can do some things to reduce negative impacts, such as providing a few extra months of SNAP benefits for people who are about to lose SNAP eligibility.
“It’s a matter of trying to find a way to provide extra help for people, and balancing that with the state having enough money to do it,” Myall said.
Fecteau said state lawmakers are also looking at ways to help hospitals, which are struggling financially, cutting services like birthing centers or closing. That’s before funding losses begin next year under the Medicaid cutbacks.
Fecteau said “we obviously need serious help from Washington,” but there’s also a “real urgency” for the state Legislature to help Maine’s hospitals.
“We need to have all parties at the table having a real earnest conversation about what the future of healthcare delivery looks like across the state,” Fecteau said.
Medicaid work requirements that start in January 2027 will mandate that some recipients work, volunteer or attend school 80 hours per month or lose their Medicaid insurance.
Fecteau said one of his priorities will be to ensure that people who are eligible for Medicaid maintain their benefits and “don’t get discouraged and don’t walk away from the process because they can’t make sense of these new requirements.”
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services hired 35 staffers to help administer the new work requirements, with a goal of ensuring eligible people maintain Medicaid enrollment, state officials have said.

title: South Portland parents voice opinions on school reconfiguration options
text:
South Portland parents voice opinions on school reconfiguration options
The second in a series of community forums on school reconfiguration options was held in South Portland on Wednesday night following the closure of Kaler Elementary at the end of the 2025-2026 school year in June. Plans to reconfigure the city's four elementary schools were delayed back in April until the 2027-2028 school year. On Wednesday, proposals for reconfiguration were weighed out.
"The biggest thing, what has come out on top from parents is having schools that are close to their home," said South Portland School Board Chair Rosemarie De Angelis.
De Angelis said the decision to close Kaler was difficult, and that a majority of parents and students did not want it, but students have been adjusting well overall to classrooms in different buildings across the district — many at Brown Elementary School. She said the hope is to not move students again.
Five models were presented on Wednesday, and some were not as popular as the district anticipated.
"There is less weight put on balancing the socioeconomic, which is what we have tried to do in the schools," said De Angelis.
Other ideas included the district purchasing more small buses and vans to transport students and minimize traffic across the city. There is also an idea to centralize Pre-K programs, potentially in the former Kaler building. That would take up half of the building, and the district would lease the other half to private parties.
De Angelis said she wants to keep costs as low as possible for South Portland residents, including those who do not have any children in the school system.
"Everything isn't answered by more money. You know we can't be making decisions that increase spending and drive people out of their homes," said De Angelis.
The school board is set to vote on a set of plans for reconfiguration on Nov. 9.

title: The song remains the same, but Lez Zeppelin brings a whole lotta rock ‘n’ roll
text:
In the summer of my 15th year, I worked as a camp counselor. My fellow counselors and I spent our lunch breaks engaged in two great debates of the era: What is the best way to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich? (More jelly than peanut butter, obviously, and always spread on opposite slices of bread.) And which Led Zeppelin album was the greatest?
The second question was considerably more contentious. I was born in 1976, the year Led Zeppelin released “The Song Remains the Same,” their legendary live album and concert film recorded over three nights at Madison Square Garden in 1973. Fifty years later, this monumental document of rock ‘n’ roll history is coming roaring back to life at the Chocolate Church Arts Center.
On Nov. 6 (two days after my 50th!) at 7:30 p.m., Lez Zeppelin, the internationally acclaimed, all-female Led Zeppelin tribute band, will perform “The Song Remains the Same” in its entirety.
And here’s the kicker: Lez Zeppelin is the only Led Zeppelin tribute band to have received the personal endorsement of Jimmy Page himself. After attending their London performance in 2013, Page praised the group’s “extraordinary sensuality” and the “energy and passion” of their musicianship. That’s quite an endorsement from the man who practically invented the vocabulary of hard rock guitar.
“The Song Remains the Same” captures Zeppelin at the height of its powers. From the opening explosion of “Rock and Roll” to the epic grandeur of “Stairway to Heaven,” the psychedelic adventures of “Dazed and Confused” and the irresistible swagger of “Whole Lotta Love,” this is rock music operating on a truly mythological scale.
The expanded soundtrack also includes “Black Dog,” “Over the Hills and Far Away” and other unforgettable classics. There’s something wonderful about celebrating the 50th anniversary of this album with four women who have made this music entirely their own. It’s both a loving tribute and a reminder that great music belongs to every generation willing to pick it up and make it roar.
As most of you know, I try to bring at least one amazing tribute band a season. From the Doors to the Eagles to Tom Petty, we’ve had some amazing shows that bring us back to our favorite tunes. Lez Zeppelin fits that bill and more. Founded in 2004, these rockers are no ordinary tribute act. These four extraordinary women (Steph Paynes, Dana Athens, Joan Chew and Hillary Blaze) don’t simply impersonate Robert Plant, Jimmy Page, John Bonham and John Paul Jones. They inhabit the music, unleashing its thunderous riffs, blues-drenched improvisations, hypnotic rhythms and occasionally otherworldly beauty with astonishing precision and ferocity. They have an incredible stage show to boot, so at a time when we all need to blow off some steam, I am genuinely thrilled about this act.
I can’t remember which Zeppelin album won those lunchtime debates 35 years ago. I suspect we never reached a consensus. But I do remember the pleasure of arguing passionately about music that mattered to us. On Nov. 6, we can dispense with the arguments, gather together and let the music do the talking. And believe me, it’s going to rock.
Matthew Glassman is executive and artistic director of the Chocolate Church Arts Center in Bath.

title: New US indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. authorities charged former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with conspiring to torture his fellow citizens in order to maintain his hold on power. The new indictment, unsealed Thursday, adds pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking offenses.
Maduro, who was previously charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., is now also facing allegations of human rights abuses during his reign as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
“He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition,” says the revised indictment, which newly charges Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, with torture conspiracy.
The revised indictment accuses the couple of staying in power by “terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence,” saying thousands of Venezuelans were “harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed” by people acting at the behest of the government he controlled.
The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro’s behest. The indictment accuses the ex-president of signing off on methods of torture and personally threatening the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.”
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro’s lawyer; Flores’ attorney was due in court for a previously scheduled hearing. Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.
Both have pleaded not guilty in the criminal case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They had already been facing potential life prison sentences if convicted.
Flores was scheduled to be in court Thursday, where her lawyers will urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail, and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she has “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital, when care was needed.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence.”
___
Associated Press writers Larry Neumeister and Jennifer Peltz in New York and Josh Goodman in Miami contributed to this report.

title: Award-winning actor comes to Portland to highlight Jewish diversity
text:
Tony and Grammy award-winning actor and writer Ari’el Stachel hopes to challenge binaries and highlight the diversity of Jewish culture during his visit to Portland next week, hosted by the Maine Jewish Museum.
“Right now, the Jewish community is facing spiraling anti-Semitism with roots in the toxic binaries that are polarizing our society,” said Maine Jewish Museum Executive Director Dawn LaRochelle. “Ari’el’s work is urgent (because) he uses theater to challenge the assumptions that allow anti-semitism to root.”
Stachel will take part in three events on Oct. 16 and 17: a performance and conversation with Maine public school students as part of the museum’s Delet Program, which educates K-12 students about Jewish culture to challenge stereotypes; a pescatarian Yemenite-inspired Shabbat dinner; and a performance of “Other,” his autobiographical one-man show that recreates pivotal moments of his life centered around his struggles with anxiety and his embracing of his identity.
Stachel won the 2018 Tony Award for Featured Actor in a Musical for his role in “The Band’s Visit,” and a Grammy the same year for Best Musical Theater Album.
“I don’t do this to just wave a political wand; I do it to connect with people on a very deep level,” said Stachel. “The goal of this art form is for people to enjoy a story and, afterwards, reflect on their own lives and feel a little moved and refreshed.”
Stachel, the son of a Yemenite-Israeli father and an Ashkenazi-American mother, said that his cultural identity had been a point of tension for him in part due to a perception that Jews are white and European; Stachel’s skin is darker, like his father’s, he said. Stachel said this stereotype, combined with anti-Arab sentiment in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, resulted in years of him trying to hide his dual identities. He credits the theater as the place where he found a sense of belonging and meaning in his teenage years.
Stachel said he is much more comfortable in his cultural identity now and the fact that it doesn’t have to be tied to a single truth.
“I’m trying to preach for peace, co-existence, and unity, so I always like to be a voice that is both the proud son of a Yemenite Israeli and someone who is tolerant and not hateful,” he said. “I live in that grey area that a lot of people think is impossible.”
Recently, Stachel has been hard at work on Shalom Habibis, an initiative that aims to bring ethnicities perceived to be at odds with one another, such as Jews, Arabs, and Muslims, together through conversations and Shabbat dinners, which he said will “showcase our shared humanity.”
“It is all about seeing people beyond the boxes, beyond the labels that we often put on them,” said Stachel.
LaRochelle hopes that Stachel’s visit will appeal to non-Jewish Mainers as well.
“This is compelling theater, not just a homework assignment,” said LaRochelle. “Anyone, regardless of their background, who has been misjudged, told they don’t belong, or felt pressure ot conceal part of their identity, will recognize something in his story that resonates with them.”
IF YOU GO
‘At the Table with Ari’el Stachel: A Yemenite-Inspired Shabbat,‘ Oct. 16, 6- 8 p.m., Maine Jewish Museum, 267 Congress St., Portland. The event is a Yemenite-inspired pescatarian Shabbat feast prepared by Maine Jewish Museum Executive Director Dawn LaRochelle and conversation with Ari’el Stachel, tickets $75. Get tickets at eventbrite: eventbrite.com/e/at-the-table-with-ariel-stachel-a-yemenite-inspired-shabbat-tickets-1999214091164?aff=oddtdtcreator.
