title: Russia says no epidemic risk as WHO pushes for transparency on plague lab death
text:
Russia says no epidemic risk as WHO pushes for transparency on plague lab death
Russia’s health watchdog said Wednesday there is no risk of an epidemic following the death of a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Siberia, even as the World Health Organization (WHO) made a plea for more information about the concerning episode.
Related video: Secretary of State Marco Rubio urges Russia to share more information about the death of a lab worker in Siberia.
In a statement Wednesday, Rospotrebnadzor said it is winding down a set of preventative measures in Russia’s Irkutsk region where the laboratory is located. Medical monitoring has been completed for “over 90%” of contacts of the deceased worker, and no dangerous pathogens have been found, it added.
The death of the lab technician, who worked at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in Russia’s southeast, has sparked international concern and speculation in recent days about the cause of her illness.
Russian authorities sought to alleviate those worries on Wednesday, with the country’s watchdog saying, “As of October 7, 2026, medical monitoring has been completed for over 90% of contacts. No health issues related to infectious disease were detected, and the results of nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.”
Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease, also denied reports of a second case of illness linked to the deceased worker following speculation in a small number of Western media outlets.
Local authorities have previously introduced disease-control measures at local hospitals in Irkutsk, a move that fueled questions among some local residents about whether authorities were being transparent.
Global health experts urge greater transparency
But despite the positive statement from Russian authorities, global health experts are still urging caution, and asking for more transparency from Moscow.
WHO chief Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that a “full risk assessment” has not been possible following the death of the Russian worker, adding that “timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
WHO’s experts also updated their early evaluation that the lab worker’s death posed “low” risk to public health, saying that because she may not have died of pneumonic plague — a bacterial infection that can be transmitted from person to person, but doesn’t spread easily — the risk from the event was now undetermined.
Meanwhile, Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, director of the WHO’s department of epidemic and pandemic management, said the organization had reached out to colleagues in Russia’s Ministry of Health and expected “further answers.”
“So we do reach out to them to ask very detailed questions about what tests were done, the results of those laboratory tests,” she said. “What further analysis is being done if the cause is not yet known, what contacts were put under quarantine or under follow up.”
“What we have been told is that they had no case of plague registered in this area, and that no high-threat pathogens were detected,” Van Kerkhove said. “So clearly, we would like more information to understand which laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, and if this individual didn’t die from plague, then how did she die?”
The Kremlin has dismissed the concerns and said that it has kept the WHO informed “in accordance with established practice.”
Under its International Health Regulations, designed to prevent the cross-border spread of disease, WHO member states are obliged to notify it of “events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern.”
On Thursday, Rospotrebnadzor said reports of a second case of illness linked to the lab worker are “incorrect,” after WHO earlier asked for clarification on media reports.
“In response to fake information circulating on social media regarding a second case of illness involving a person who had contact with an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute who was previously diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia, Rospotrebnadzor states that this information is incorrect,” the watchdog said in a statement to Russia’s state news agency TASS.
Tedros on Tuesday said WHO was seeking clarity regarding “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause,” without specifying which news reports he was referring to.
US presses for more info
The Trump administration is also struggling to get clear answers about the incident from Moscow, though Trump said Wednesday that the US does not believe that Shipilova died from exposure to a bioweapon, adding that the Kremlin has since insisted the situation at an anti-plague institute is “under control.”
“We don’t think so,” Trump said. “We’re going to find out soon enough, but we don’t think so.”
The US has escalated its request for information, issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, a source familiar told CNN late Tuesday.
“We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson said. “We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.”
“It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.”
Nonetheless, Trump said Russia is “very sophisticated, very smart, and they’re saying it’s very much under control,” even as he allowed that Russian officials had not disclosed much so far.

title: Fact-checking 6 claims that dominated the Susan Collins-Troy Jackson debate
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic opponent Troy Jackson went toe-to-toe Tuesday in the first of four debates over 10 days in a race that may decide which party controls the Senate.
The pair challenged each other over their stances on abortion, ethics, President Donald Trump, housing, healthcare, taxes and more, with a few inaccuracies and misleading statements coming from both. The five-term incumbent talked up her experience and accused Jackson of repeating falsehoods, while the former Maine Senate president tried to hammer home the message that Collins hadn’t done enough to blunt Trump’s agenda.
Here are a handful of fact-checks of key moments as the candidates prepare for another debate Thursday on WMTW.
‘Votes with Trump 96% of the time’
Jackson repeated the figure at least four times, and it’s been a mantra throughout the campaign. He cited a Bangor Daily News story, but the claim is rooted in a CQ-Roll Call analysis from last year that looks at only a subset of bills that Trump has taken an explicit position on.
The report stands at 95% for the first seven months of 2025, and the outlet has noted the total was due in part to party leaders mostly bringing up measures the president agrees with in the first year of his second term. That makes it incomplete and out of date.
During the debate, Collins argued the 96% figure was misleading and pointed to another analysis from the same outlet that looks more broadly at party unity. That put her at just over 72% with fellow Republicans.
Iran war votes
Jackson, who blamed high fuel and energy prices largely on Trump’s unpopular war with Iran, said Collins had voted “five times” against ending the war. Collins said she has voted “nine times to end” it. In this case, both numbers are right.
Of the 14 times Democrats forced the Senate to vote on Iran war powers measures since the conflict began in February, Collins voted five times against failed resolutions. She said after the first vote on March 4 that the move “would send the wrong message to Iran and to our troops.”
But she also said she would not approve of the president exceeding a 60-day threshold for congressional approval under the War Powers Act. As the deadline hit on April 30, she voted with Democrats in support of ending the war. She has continued to back such resolutions through late September.
The distinction on Iran votes marks a key theme throughout the race: Just as Collins looks to distance herself from Trump on Iran, tariffs or his signature tax law, Jackson makes the case that her moves come too late, citing votes that either advanced or did not stop Trump’s overall plans.
$70 billion for ICE
Jackson suggested Collins did not regret approving $70 billion this summer for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, despite the fatal shooting of Colombia native Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero by federal agents in Biddeford in July. Guerrero was not the target of an ICE warrant, and his death sparked protests and calls for greater oversight and reform.
While Jackson didn’t specifically say the entire $70 billion went only to ICE, he and his campaign have said so in the past in making the case that Collins and the Republican-controlled Congress failed to push back against the agency. Collins challenged Jackson over the figure going to ICE, saying it’s about half that amount over four years.
The law signed in June allocated about $38 billion to ICE, $26 billion to CBP and another $5 billion to the Department of Homeland Security through 2029. The amounts marked dramatic increases, especially when considering the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year injected $75 billion into ICE, nearly tripling its annual budget.
Collins was right about the figures, but Jackson argued that whatever amount went to ICE, it was too much. He wants the agency disbanded. She said reforms are needed but disbanding it would undercut federal agents deporting dangerous criminals or handling drug traffickers.
Jackson’s bill record
Collins argued Jackson would face an uphill battle getting things done as a freshman in Washington based on his Augusta track record. Along with citing 100 combined vetoes of his bills by Govs. Janet Mills and Paul LePage, she said more than a third of Jackson’s bills in 20 years in the Legislature died after being unanimously rejected in committee.
We replicated this number in a search of legislative records. During his career, nearly 36% of bills he led died this way, although the number relies mostly on his less-successful early days in the Legislature. He was at 19% during his final two years, well below the average.
But Jackson had a point in his retort, noting that lawmakers hold hearings on all bills and many that are killed see their parts rolled into other vehicles. For example, a 2019 bipartisan workers’ overhaul had pieces of two dead Jackson bills in it, according to a digest.
Energy costs
During an election year dominated by high costs, Collins looked to shift blame to the state level while Jackson pointed to Trump’s tariffs and healthcare overhauls. In this vein, the senator said Maine has the fourth-highest electricity rates “due to how Troy has voted in Augusta.”
She was keying in on Maine’s solar subsidies enacted under Mills and Jackson. An attention-grabbing estimate from a watchdog in 2023 said the program would balloon to a cost of $225 million per year if lawmakers didn’t act. Democrats shot down Republican attempts to end the program but made a notable reduction to it after Jackson left office in 2025.
So Jackson does own a piece of that. But it is only a sliver of electric bills. The market can’t be untangled from wider factors. Natural gas makes up more than 40% of generation here, according to state data. Heavy natural gas reliance, a lack of regional production and pipelines are often pointed to as reasons for New England’s high electricity prices.
Medicaid autism audit
Collins argued Jackson failed to police Maine’s Medicaid program, citing a federal audit under the Biden administration that found “$42 million in improper payments and fraud … and Troy did nothing about that.”
The comment overstated auditors’ findings. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services inspector general flagged about $45.6 million in Medicaid payments for autism services for Maine children, but it did not call those payments fraud. The report labeled them “improper” or “potentially improper,” citing missing documentation and oversight.
Additionally, Democratic-led Maine was not singled out, as Jackson noted. The same multiyear audit, also overstated by Vice President JD Vance, revealed at least $56 million in improper payments in Republican-led Indiana and $18.5 million in Wisconsin.

'Unexpected K-9 applicant': Dog reunited with owner after wandering to police station
An "unexpected K-9 applicant" was reunited with its owner after the furry friend was caught on camera making a stop at a police station in Tampa, Florida.
The Tampa Police Department shared a video on Facebook, capturing the moment the four-legged friend wandered up to the station's District 2 office last month.
"This four-legged visitor was ready to join the team, but unfortunately, our K-9 roster is currently full," the post said, with a video showing the dogs meeting with officials. "We made sure our hopeful recruit was safely reunited with his owner instead. He may not have gotten the job, but he definitely stole our hearts."

The video showed the dog being reunited with his owner, with an officer saying the animal was checked at the vet. Officials said the owner was tracked via the dog's chip.

title: College GameDay moving indoors for Alabama-Georgia amid Hurricane Isaias
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - As Hurricane Isaias remains on track for a potential Alabama landfall, the University of Alabama announced that ESPN’s College GameDay is moving indoors.
Hurricane Isaias is projected to make landfall late Friday night or early Saturday morning.
The weekly pregame show will take place inside Alabama’s Coleman Coliseum from 8 a.m. to 11 a.m. Saturday and will feature a familiar face as its guest picker.
Pat McAfee announced on The Pat McAfee Show Wednesday morning that Heisman Trophy winner Bryce Young will serve as GameDay’s guest picker.
In recent years, College GameDay has aired from The Quad on Alabama’s campus. The move to Coleman Coliseum comes as Isaias strengthened overnight into a Category 2 storm.
ESPN told WBRC Tuesday that only severe weather would force College GameDay to change its plans.
University officials said there will be no overnight camping allowed and that fans can begin lining up at the north and east doors of Coleman at 5:15 a.m. Doors will open at 5:30 a.m.
A clear bag policy will be in effect for fans attending College GameDay, and bags will be inspected as fans enter the building.
Raffle tickets for Pat McAfee’s “Kicking is Easy” contest will be distributed at both entrances, and no tickets will be given out before 5:15 a.m.
Fans attending College GameDay and Saturday’s Alabama-Georgia game are encouraged to monitor weather conditions and visit @UA_Athletics and @UAGameday for the University of Alabama’s latest information.

title: Raymond Brown found guilty in 1984 murder of Linda Maxwell
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - Raymond Brown, 67, has been found guilty in the 1984 murder of 18-year-old Linda Maxwell.
The jury returned the guilty verdict Thursday afternoon after deliberating for about an hour.
Jurors heard more testimony Thursday morning. A cold-case investigator outlined the renewed investigation, and witnesses gave differing accounts about evidence and Maxwell’s class ring.
Sgt. Chad Lindsey of the Maine State Police testified that investigators began revisiting the case in 2021, paused while the agency addressed nine homicides in Washington County, and resumed work in March 2024. The team consulted agencies involved in the original investigation, conducted 35 interviews and exhumed Maxwell’s body for a second examination in May 2024, Lindsey said.
Jurors also heard a recording of Lindsey’s July 2024 interview with Brown. In the interview, Brown recalled drinking and driving with Maxwell and friends but said he could not remember many details. He denied sexual contact, disputed accounts about wet boots and his return time, and accused a former detective of targeting his family, according to the testimony.
Maxwell’s naked body was found in the St. Croix River.
Lindsey testified that earlier interviews placed Brown dropping off two friends at about 12:15 a.m. He also said in the interview that three witnesses reported hearing screams from the river. Lindsey testified he did not consider a bra and undergarment found in 1984 credibly connected to Maxwell and did not seek additional testing. He also discussed changes to evidence-handling procedures.
Witnesses offer differing accounts of class ring
Defense witnesses gave differing accounts about Maxwell’s high school class ring. A friend testified that Maxwell had been in his car with friends and left her ring there. He said he later retrieved it from the car and an officer took it from him, though he could not recall how it first ended up in the vehicle.
A former Maine State Police detective who helped with interviews and canvassing testified that he saw the ring but did not take it. Earlier, another witness testified she had told police she knew a different man had the ring, but said that was not based on her own observation.
Testimony revisits 1984 investigation
A former Maine State Police detective previously testified that Brown said he took Maxwell to Milltown and returned to Calais. The defense questioned why police did not search a burn barrel on Brown’s property and challenged the thoroughness of the original investigation.
A Maine game warden testified that, based on the river conditions he reviewed, it would have been essentially impossible for a body to travel 14 miles down the St. Croix River.
Earlier testimony included a cousin’s account that Brown said his pants were wet after Maxwell’s body was found, that he burned clothing and was frustrated with the investigation. A jailhouse witness also testified that Brown described trying to have sex with Maxwell, holding her underwater after an argument, leaving her body at a boat landing and later burning clothing. The defense challenged that witness’s credibility, citing a recorded call in which he said he might lie if his bail request was denied.
Prosecution and defense reflect on trial
Defense attorney Steven Smith said after the trial that he does not believe there was enough evidence to convict his client, and that his legal team plan to appeal the verdict.
“After 42 years, We don’t think Ray deserved this. We absolutely intend to appeal. There was absolutely no physical evidence, and nobody can tell what happened to Linda in the 36 hours between the time she left the party to the time she was found,” Smith said.
“Testing the statements against the evidence and once you looked at the physical geography of the scene, once you looked at what he was saying and where he was saying it, it was incredible,” Assistant Attorney General Leanne Robbin told WABI. “Did not pass the straight face test, and it was that analysis that brought us here today.”
Robbin says it’s sad Linda’s parents were not alive to see justice served, but they hope this gives the family a sense of closure.
Brown will be sentenced at a later date is being held without bail.

title: Former Lawrence girls basketball coach Greg Chesley moves on to KVCC
text:
It wasn’t an easy decision, but for Greg Chesley, it was the right one.
Chesley stepped down as the girls basketball coach at Lawrence last month after 15 years with the program, including nine as the head coach. He led the Bulldogs to a Class B championship in February. He is now the head coach for the Kennebec Valley Community College women’s basketball team, which began last season.
Chesley said family reasons led to his decision to switch jobs. Chesley is a grandfather after his son, Keith (the associate head coach of the men’s team at Division I Mount St. Mary in Maryland), and daughter-in-law, Jamie (a former Richmond High and UMaine-Augusta women’s basketball standout), had their first child a year ago. The schedule with his new job at the Fairfield community college allows Greg more time to visit with family in the summer.
“Too much of my summer, Christmas and holidays were taken up with high school basketball, which I loved,” Chesley said. “But it became a matter of, ‘Do I (keep coaching in high school), or do I (spend more time with family)?'”
Still, Chesley struggled with the decision. He is a Lawrence alum and led the Bulldogs to two state championships in the last four seasons, including a 52-41 win over Oceanside in the Class B final last season.
“It was an emotional decision,” Chesley said. “I played at Lawrence 150 years ago. I always have been and always will be a Bulldog. That community is amazing in the support they show all their athletes and coaches. That’s a pretty hard thing to replicate anywhere.”
Chesley was originally hired at KVCC to be an assistant under Rusty Mercier. But Mercier stepped down as head coach so he could focus on his administrative duties as athletic director, and he handed the job to Chesley.
“I’m really excited,” Chesley said. “It’s a new chapter, a new level (of basketball). It’s all going to be about, eventually, recruiting in the area. Rusty did a nice job recruiting this past year. We have a good foundation to build on and I’m looking forward to practice and then hitting the recruiting road.”
The Lynx, a member of the Yankee Small College Conference along with the UMA, Central Maine Community College and Southern Maine Community College, have a scrimmage against UMaine-Farmington on Oct. 18.
UMA women’s soccer off to a strong start
UMaine-Augusta, which brought back its women’s soccer program four years ago,is enjoying success this fall. The Moose are 4-3-2 overall and 3-1 in the YSCC, good for second place.
“We got out of the gate real strong. To be sitting where we are right now, I couldn’t be happier,” said UMA coach Larry Thornton. “We’re doing well, I can’t complain.”
Temple Academy graduate Dixie Szabo leads the Moose, with 13 goals and four assists. She’s the top scorer in the United States Collegiate Athletic Association’s Division II.
UMA roster is a mix of central Maine talent and players from outside the state. Defender Kuhle Madlokazi, a native of Cape Town, South Africa, and center halfback Jazmine McCallum of Henderson, Nevada, have both made an impact.
Colby women’s soccer continues strong pace
The Colby women’s soccer team is 8-1-1 and has not lost since falling to Tufts, 2-1, on Sept. 12. During their 6-0-1 stretch, the Mules earned a 1-0 win over Williams, ranked 12th in the IWSOC NCAA Division III coaches poll, and a 2-2 tie with Middlebury.
Abigail Jarvi, a senior, leads the Mules with four goals, and junior Ella Caraluzzi has three goals and one assist. Sadie Gardner is 5-1-1 with a .77 goals-against average.
The Mules reached the NCAA Division III tournament each of the past two seasons, including a trip to the Sweet 16 in 2024.
Colby is third in the New England Small College Athletic Conference standings with a 4-1-1 record and 13 points, trailing only Williams (6-1) and Tufts (4-0-2).
Thomas men’s soccer leads NAC standings
The Thomas College men’s soccer team is 7-2 overall and leads the North Atlantic Conference with a 4-0 record.
Senior forward David Ivarsson, a native of Reykjavik, Iceland, has four goals and three assists. Forward Cody Robinson of Warwick, Bermuda, also has four goals.
The Terriers have won three straight, including a 4-1 victory over Husson on Tuesday. They are at Worcester State next Tuesday.

title: Southport Junior Yacht Club
text:
Time seems to keep flying by at SYC this year as we are through yet another week of this wonderful summer!
We had three swimmers brave the cold cozy harbor waters, Casey Boudrow, Violet Fauver and Annabelle Fauver, all passed their swim test.
The morning class had quite an eventful week with a handful of cruises, working on mooring landings and for a Friday fun day, the instructors took out the kids in 420s, where they raced and had a blast.
The afternoon Turnabout program had a week filled with cruises to places such as Reid State Park, Five Islands and the Roundhouse, while also working on solo sailing skills such as mooring landings.
The afternoon Opti program took part in their final race days for the August series and took part in a cruise to Five Islands and ended off the week with a swim in the harbor.
The afternoon 420 program held two race days, and an activity on Friday that many would consider a “Wild Goose Chase” where they had to swim to the 420 dock from the Junior Dock and then rig their boat and sail it around the Red Nun, Cedarbush Island, and other miscellaneous locations.
There were many extracurricular events this week outside of sailing, the first being the Tuesday Night sibling regatta, where all of the boats must be sailed by a pair of siblings. The Turley brothers eventually came out victorious. Shortly after the sibling Regatta, there was a spikeball tournament, which was won by Nathan Phippen and Liam Donahue, who didn’t win a single match by less than four in the double elimination style tournament.
On Thursday, the club held its annual prize bingo, where stores from around the community donate bingo prizes so the event can be ran for the club. Thank you very much to all of the stores who participated or donated!
We are unfortunately looking into our final week of sailing, where we will look forward to decommissioning and the banquet on Friday night!

title: Obituary: Terrance Wells Tucker
text:
DAYTON – Terrance Wells Tucker, 74, passed away on Oct. 6, 2026, at Maine Veterans Home in Scarborough, with Julie, his loving wife of 52 years, by his side.
“Terry” was born Nov. 8, 1951, in Saco, the youngest son of Wyman and Doris Tucker. He weighed less than three pounds when he was born and liked to tell people he had slept in a shoebox as a baby. He grew up in Old Orchard, where he starred in baseball, football, and basketball, while spending many days on the beach in the summer. He attended the University of Maine Fort Kent, where he met the love of his life, Julie. He enlisted in the Army in 1973 and was stationed in Germany, and he and Julie were married on Sept. 7, 1974. During their time in Germany, they traveled widely throughout Europe.
Terry knew everyone in Old Orchard, and everyone seemed to know Terry. He had a way of making friends wherever he went and seemingly never met a stranger. While he loved to win and was fiercely competitive and tenacious when it came to sports, that competitive streak was mostly reserved for the playing field. In everyday life, Terry was friendly, generous, and easygoing. He was the life of the party and could light up a room simply by being in it. Some people suck the oxygen out of a room; Terry brought it with him and kept it flowing. His laughter was infectious, he was always quick with a joke or a good-natured jab, and he had a remarkable ability to make the people around him feel welcome and loved.
While serving in the Army, Terry suffered a spinal injury that would impact his mobility for the rest of his life. Throughout all the challenges he faced, Terry kept his sense of humor and his fierce loyalty to the people he loved and cared about.
Sports played a big part in Terry’s life. He loved the Bruins, Celtics, Red Sox, Patriots, and UMaine sports. For several years, he had UMaine hockey season tickets and religiously made the trek north to Orono with his father-in-law, Jamie Waterhouse (and whoever else was feeling particularly adventurous) whenever the Black Bears played at home. He was also involved in kids’ sports, whether that was coaching teams, serving on boards, refereeing basketball games, or anything else that needed to be done. Terry loved to compete, but he loved being part of the community even more.
Terry was an avid fly fisherman who tied many of his own flies and went on many fishing trips with his high school friend, Jamie Mullen and Bill Pinette. Together they made many visits to the Moosehead area and an epic bucket list trip to fish in Argentina. He loved music, and could often be heard singing Bob Dylan and Harry Chapin. He was a longtime member of the Goodwins Mills Advent Christian Church, where he served on the board and as a deacon for many years.
One of Terry’s favorite roles in life was Grampa to his five grandchildren. Even when in poor health, he would light up when they visited.
Terry is survived by Julie, his wife of 52 years; daughter, Erin and her husband Derek Rice of Kennebunk, son, Christopher and his wife Greta of Yarmouth; grandchildren Juliet and Henry Rice, and Scarlett, Samson, and Agnes Tucker; and many extended family members and good friends, all of whom will miss him very much.
He was predeceased by his parents; and brothers Tom and Timothy.
Terry will be buried with his beloved dog, Scruffy, who was a faithful companion for many years.
The family would like to thank the caretakers at the Maine Veterans Home in Scarborough who made his final years there more comfortable, especially Tim, who also became a good friend.
Funeral services will be held at the Goodwins Mills Advent Christian Church at 1 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10, followed by internment at Goodwins Mills Village Cemetery and a luncheon at the church mill.

title: Millions of SAVE plan borrowers getting 90-day notices to switch
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Borrowers who have been in the SAVE forbearance plan for the past several years are now receiving notices requiring them to leave the plan and choose a new repayment option.
The personalized 90-day notices come from loan servicers and began going out in July, with new notices rolling out roughly every two weeks through the end of the year. Robert Farrington, with The College Investor, said once a borrower receives the notice, a 90-day clock begins.
“When you get your notice, you have to take action and choose a new repayment plan,” Farrington said. “For borrowers that don’t choose a new repayment plan, you will be automatically enrolled in the standard or tiered standard repayment plan at the end of that 90-day mark, which may or may not be the best plan choice for you.”
What happens if payments are missed
Once a borrower is moved into a new plan, payments begin coming due. Farrington said failing to make those payments can lead to delinquency and eventually default on federal student loans.
Farrington said borrowers are not required to wait until they receive a notice to act.
“It’s also important to note that borrowers don’t have to wait for their notice,” Farrington said. “A lot of borrowers might benefit from moving earlier, especially if you are pursuing public service loan forgiveness and you’re ready to start making payments that count again for public service loan forgiveness.”
Borrowers can begin the process at any time by visiting studentaid.gov and selecting “Enroll in a repayment plan.” Farrington also recommends using a student loan calculator now to estimate a future monthly payment and begin budgeting ahead of time.

title: Susan Collins backs raising Social Security taxes on high earners in debate with Troy Jackson
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins said Thursday that high earners should pay more into Social Security, siding with Democrat Troy Jackson on an idea most Republicans have avoided in a second debate that turned personal over money and influence.
It was a surprising shift. As recently as Thursday morning, a Collins spokesperson told NBC News she had not taken a position on lifting the cap. The spokesperson pointed only to her call for an independent commission of experts. On the WMTW stage, she went further.
“I don’t think someone who makes $40 million a year as a movie star should pay the same rate of social security taxes as someone who’s earning $184,000 a year,” she said. “We simply are going to have to adjust the cap.”
It was a rare moment of agreement in a debate that was arguably sharper than Tuesday’s opener, which centered on abortion and ethics. Jackson got further off honed talking points and made an unfounded claim that Collins and her husband profited from the Iran war, drawing a demand for an apology.
Earnings above $184,500 a year aren’t taxed for Social Security. The program’s trust fund is projected to run short in late 2032, which would trigger a large benefit cut unless Congress acts. Jackson wants to scrap the cap and expand benefits. Collins did not specify whether adjusting it means eliminating the cap, raising it or taxing income above a higher threshold.
The rest of the hour ran through the central argument of a race that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Collins pledged in 1996 to serve only two terms and is now seeking a sixth, citing the $1.5 billion she has secured for Maine projects as the top Senate appropriator while Jackson continued to try to tie her to the unpopular President Donald Trump.
“She’s powerful towards election time, but she’s weak every time that we needed her to stand up and fight for us,” Jackson said.
Jackson, who has rejected corporate PAC money during his campaign like many Democrats, was asked about a Washington Post report. It found that under his leadership, the Maine Senate’s Democratic campaign arm took money from tobacco, drug and gambling companies while he was listed as one of its principal officers from 2017 to 2024.
He said he didn’t decide which donations it took, even though he told reporters in August he was “one of a number of people that made those decisions.”
“I have never accepted any donations from Big Tobacco. Troy has,” Collins said.
Her 2020 campaign took nearly $12,000 from tobacco industry PACs and employees, according to OpenSecrets. Federal law bars companies from giving directly to candidates. Maine law allowed the tobacco company Altria to give $12,000 to Jackson’s PAC.
Jackson’s charge that Collins profits from the Iran War echoed a September report by a liberal news site promoted by the Maine Democratic Party. It found that her husband, longtime political strategist and former lobbyist Tom Daffron, owns stock in the defense contractors Boeing and RTX. But RTX stock is down since the war began, and Boeing has traded sluggishly.
“That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology,” Collins said.
On abortion, both candidates said they would vote for federal protections. Under fire from Democrats for her 2018 vote for Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, she noted that she co-sponsored a 2022 bill to write Roe v. Wade into law and pointed to Jackson’s opposition to abortion rights earlier in his career.
He acknowledged voting “the wrong way” and turned it back to the Kavanaugh vote, which Collins has stood by even though she opposed the court’s vote to end federal abortion rights.
“I can admit when I was wrong,” Jackson said. “Sen. Collins can’t.”

Bangor police say the man fled from the caller but continued throwing things. The caller told police he had also assaulted her by hitting her in the torso. title: Cornell gang-rape accuser has been receiving death threats, attorney says
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — The woman accusing several men of raping her at a Cornell University fraternity party was “misled” about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday.
Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell’s internal disciplinary process, the university’s police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press.
In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police.
Van Houten has said that he asked Cornell’s police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer.
Giuffra said the woman was told that the criminal investigation was ongoing.
“I think she was misled. She was told it was still — they weren’t going to prosecute, but they were still investigating,” Giuffra said. “I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren’t doing anything.”
Giuffra added that at the time, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.
“But nothing was being done, and we didn’t know that,” Giuffra said.
A message seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell’s media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university’s police department.
The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident that no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman’s account, written by a police officer.
Summary left out key details, lawyer says
Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman’s participation in drug use and sex was “voluntary, conscious and consensual.”
That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month.
Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available.
Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, The New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten’s office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed.
“At first I thought these police were incompetent,” Giuffra said. “It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down.”
Giuffra said that while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support, including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults.
Students rally against sexual violence
Some Cornell students staged a sit-in at a dining hall and vowed not to spend money on campus Wednesday to protest sexual violence and how the university has handled complaints, in the latest expression of outrage over an alleged 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
A handwritten sign reading “Justice for Jane Doe” — the name under which the accuser is suing — was propped on an empty table in the dining hall in the afternoon. Some students sat around the room without eating, while others lunched. Another small group sat outside holding signs with messages such as “we are Jane Doe.”
The demonstrations were meant to spotlight complaints that the university is slow to respond to reports of sexual assault while quick to protect its reputation. Among other demands, the groups want the university to retool disciplinary procedures for addressing complaints and expel or revoke the degrees of anyone involved in the alleged October 2024 sexual assault.
Jane Doe, who was a student then, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month.
Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.
Man in lawsuit wants attorney general removed
The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, Van Houten said he was reopening the investigation. Days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul took the case away from him and appointed the state’s attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor.
Giuffra applauded the move, saying he was troubled by Van Houten’s plan for conducting the reopened investigation and “didn’t think he was up to the task.” Giuffra said the district attorney wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel within two weeks.
That timeline, leaving little time to review evidence or interview witnesses, suggested that Van Houten may have been trying “to go take a dive and not really give it his best effort and not do any investigation,” Giuffra said.
James hasn’t said how long her investigation might take, but she suggested it would take months.
On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit filed a court petition seeking James’ removal from the case, arguing she showed bias by posting on social media a few days before her appointment: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.”
A spokesperson for James declined to comment.
Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.
This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.
___
Sisak reported from New York.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off on WMTW
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic opponent Troy Jackson meet at 8 p.m. Thursday for their second debate of their race, hosted by WMTW.

title: Media attorneys ask court for help in preventing White House ban until legal case is resolved
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An attorney for three news organizations told a federal judge Thursday that the Trump administration must be prevented from barring their reporters from the White House, saying the ban is a classic example of “viewpoint discrimination” that is punishing people for what they say — and restricting the media outlets’ First Amendment rights.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly said he intended to rule by Tuesday, possibly sooner, on whether to extend an order that preserves White House access for journalists from MS NOW, CNN and Politico.
The case has been going on since last month, shortly after President Donald Trump banned the outlets from the White House grounds, saying he objected to their reporting.
Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the media plaintiffs, said the government was continuing to discriminate against viewpoints and reporting it doesn’t like.
“He doesn’t like scrutiny of his policies, he doesn’t like the reporting, he wants more good press,” Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the media organizations, said in court. That’s a content-based restriction on speech and a clear violation of the First Amendment, he said.
The government countered, as it has before, that what it called false reporting can impact policy and adversely affect national security.
“He doesn’t mind negative press stories if he deserves them. he has problems with trafficking verifiable falsehoods,” said Michael Velchik, the administration’s attorney, said of the president.
Velchik said some of the issues the White House has with the banned news organizations’ reporting include “quotations that are not actually said,” the use of anonymous sources and splicing interviews to insert different questions than what the interviewee was actually asked. “I do think that we’ve identified specific allegations for each individual outlet,” he said.
It was the latest development in the escalating drama between the Trump administration and the news media, which has raged in various arenas during his second term as president. At its core, though, are multiple First Amendment questions. The dispute has produced sanctions and restrictions on White House and Pentagon reporter and led to several lawsuits that are progressing through the federal court system.
The news organizations want longer-term relief until the entire case is resolved, and a temporary restraining order was due to expire on Thursday. But the judge extended it until Tuesday and said he intends to rule by then on whether to issue a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo pending the outcome of the litigation.
Three-week saga continues
The hearing before Kelly came nearly three weeks after CNN, MS NOW and Politico were abruptly banished from White House grounds, with the president decrying their “fake news.”
Kelly granted a two-week temporary restraining order against the ban, but it expires Thursday. The outlets have asked the court to halt the ban until the case is resolved, saying the administration has “persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban” despite the restraining order — including selectively keeping CNN from participating in White House pool duties.
“The White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity,” lawyers for the networks wrote in a filing on Sept. 28.
At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is “viewpoint discrimination” forbidden by the First Amendment’s free-speech protections.
Trump insists that he doesn’t have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds. “When it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said on ABC recently, invoking an argument the administration has made since the beginning. “It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there.”
The news organizations say that approach violates the Constitution’s amendments protecting free speech and due process.
The requested preliminary injunction would extend the White House access until the case is finally resolved.
___
Noveck reported from New York and Boone from Boise, Idaho. Laurie Kellman in London contributed.

Former clerk of court accused of bumping his salary on 44 paychecks, police say
text:
LORIS, SC. (WMBF/Gray News) - A former clerk of court in South Carolina is accused of secretly increasing his own pay rate 44 times over about a year and a half.
Todd Keith Massey turned himself in Wednesday morning as he faces charges of breach of trust with fraudulent intent, grand larceny valued at $5,000 or more, and a violation of the state Ethics, Government Accountability and Campaign Reform Act.
From June 2021 through January 2023, Massey, while employed as clerk of court, allegedly gradually increased his own hourly pay rate across 44 consecutive biweekly pay periods, according to the warrants.
The warrants stated that Massey’s real approved salary was $16.98 an hour as of July 2021, but he fluctuated his hourly rate between $22.82 and $46.26 over the following months, without city council or mayoral approval.
This led to him making about $55,183.02 more than his approved salary.
In addition to serving as clerk of court, the city of Loris told WMBF News that Massey held several positions with the city, including police officer, city clerk and city treasurer. The city said it is still working to confirm the dates Massey held each position.
Massey was treasurer of Giving Hope Gardens, a nonprofit in the Loris area that helps support people with disabilities by teaching them life skills.
In April 2025, Massey pleaded guilty to embezzling roughly $70,000 from Giving Hope Gardens.
Massey transferred or wrote $35,000 in checks to “All Star Pest” and nearly $14,000 to “KEM Management.” Both are companies that he owns, according to filings with the South Carolina Secretary of State.
The loss of funds led to staff cuts and fewer interns at Giving Hope Gardens.
A judge then sentenced Massey to five years in prison, suspended to five years’ probation. The 15th Circuit Solicitor’s Office said Massey also paid back $34,000 in restitution.
In December 2025, WMBF News aired an investigation into allegations from customers of Massey’s former North Myrtle Beach business CabinetWorks who say he botched their home remodeling projects.
Multiple complaints of ditching cabinet renovations led to his arrest by North Myrtle Beach police in February 2026.
Arrest warrants stated Massey provided fake invoices, company logos and even staged calls to make customers think their cabinets were on the way but never arrived.
At the time of the February arrest, the news came as a sigh of relief for several customers who shared their complaints during WMBF News’ investigation.
Massey told WMBF News in January that he stepped away from his business to let someone else take over after several customers canceled orders following our investigation.
Massey faces three counts of breach of trust in the North Myrtle Beach case.
WMBF News also learned that Massey previously oversaw finances for Providing Hope VA, another Loris-based charity whose CEO pleaded guilty to money laundering in 2024. Massey was never charged or named in that case.
Massey remains booked at the J. Reuben Long Detention Center as of Thursday morning.

title: DNC sues Trump administration over taxpayer-funded TV ads
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Democratic National Committee has filed a federal lawsuit accusing the Trump administration of illegally spending millions of taxpayer dollars on television advertisements promoting President Donald Trump just weeks before the midterm elections.
The lawsuit, filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., alleges the ads were designed to boost the president’s public image and help Republicans maintain control of Congress.
The commercials began airing in late September, featuring major moments from Trump’s second term, including his administration’s immigration enforcement efforts and military operations.
According to media-tracking firm AdImpact, the administration has spent more than $12 million airing the commercials. The money comes from Department of Homeland Security funding, with $20 million allocated for the advertising campaign.
The White House has defended the commercials as public service announcements, arguing that previous administrations have used government funds to promote their policies.
But Democrats believe the ads cross a legal line.
“Congress has banned spending taxpayer dollars on publicity or propaganda,” said Dan Freeman, litigation director for the Democratic National Committee. “These ads are flagrantly illegal, and in the run-up to an election, we thought it was just vital that the Democratic National Committee stand up for free and fair elections, fight back against these autocratic tactics.”
The DNC’s lawsuit asks a federal judge to declare the administration’s spending illegal and block the government from using additional taxpayer money to air the advertisements.
After days of criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, Trump announced Monday that future advertisements would be paid for using money from his super PAC, MAGA Inc., rather than taxpayer funds.
However, the president has not committed to reimbursing the government for the millions already spent.
“The ads were really good. They were promotion for the country. Done by presidents before, so we’ll decide,” Trump told reporters Tuesday when asked whether the government would be reimbursed.
In a September 25 statement, the White House rejected accusations that the commercials were intended to influence the midterm elections. The administration argued that Trump is not on the ballot and that the advertisements do not explicitly ask Americans to vote for Republican candidates.
The White House also pointed to campaigns for government programs under previous presidents, including George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden, as examples of government-funded public messaging.
The controversy has also prompted calls for congressional oversight.
Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, has called for an investigation into the advertising campaign and for taxpayer money spent on the commercials to be returned to the government.
Friday, the DNC filed a further request - a Temporary Restraining Order against the Trump administration to immediately stop them from using more taxpayer dollars to air blatantly illegal campaign-style TV advertisements.

title: Man with a gun and knife is fatally shot by security at Nashville federal courthouse, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — A man armed with a pistol and knife was fatally shot by a security officer Thursday just inside the busy entrance of a federal courthouse in Tennessee’s largest city, authorities said.
The man in his 40s tried to fire his gun but failed and then pulled out a knife at around 9:30 a.m., said Don Aaron, spokesperson for Metro Nashville Police.
“The security individual fired on the armed individual,” Aaron said, adding that the man was taken to a hospital where he was pronounced dead.
The man was from out of state. Investigators didn’t immediately know why he was at the courthouse, and a search of his car found “nothing threatening,” Aaron said.
Courthouse visitors must go through a security checkpoint, which is common at all federal courts. The entrances are typically staffed by armed former police officers contracted by the U.S. Marshals Service.
“That’s the entrance that most people in this courthouse use,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Rob McGuire told reporters outside.
The library next door was closed as a result, and officers with dogs were circling the perimeter while workers in nearby buildings gathered to watch.
McGuire noted that the local U.S. Attorney’s Office is inside the courthouse, as are the offices of Tennessee’s U.S. senators.
There have been “security instances where a person acts up or acts inappropriately and has to be removed from the premises, but nothing even approaching this kind of situation,” he said.
Reports of the shooting immediately stirred anxiety and concern.
“People are calling their families to let them know they’re OK,” McGuire said. “I called my wife, called my son, called people that I knew were wanting to know if I was OK. We’re all doing that.”
___
White reported from Detroit.

title: Maine’s Jessica Meir, 3 other astronauts return to Earth
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — Maine’s Jessica Meir and three other astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the American, French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
Meir and her NASA colleague Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
“We are so excited to be back on planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down.
While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”
Meir, who is from Caribou, was on her second trip to the space station. Her previous mission, in 2019, lasted 205 days and featured the first all-female spacewalk.
This time, she and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA’s Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA’s first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
Meir’s seventh career spacewalk, on Sept. 1, moved her into third place for total spacewalks by women at NASA and brought her career spacewalk time to more than 49 hours.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef’s toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA’s count.
Meir has been an astronaut since 2013 and was the first Maine woman to travel to space. After graduating as valedictorian from Caribou High School, she studied biology at Brown University. She then earned a master’s degree from the International Space University in France and a doctorate in marine biology from Scripps Institution of Oceanography in San Diego.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

Severe conditions spread north, coastal Maine sees no relief
Passing showers fail to ease drought conditions as severe drought expands north.
Severe conditions spread north, coastal Maine sees no relief
Passing showers fail to ease drought conditions as severe drought expands north.
The latest U.S. Drought Monitor update highlights severe drought spreading into more of northern Maine this week, with severe and extreme drought holding a tight grip along the coast. While much of central and inland Maine remains under moderate drought, more dry weather pushed harsher conditions further north while offering no relief to hard-hit shoreline towns.
Simply put, the dry stretch is worsening in the North Woods while coastal areas remain in the bulls eye.
River flows and well levels are dropping from the shoreline to the Canadian border, and light, passing showers aren't sinking deep enough to replenish groundwater. That leaves farmers, homeowners, and local crews dealing with heightened wildfire risks and shrinking water supplies until a major, multi-day storm moves in.

title: Somerset County Jail gets $3M boost for addiction treatment program
text:
SKOWHEGAN — A $3.1 million federal grant will keep afloat — and spare taxpayers the cost of — a medication-assisted treatment program for opioid addiction at the Somerset County Jail that has garnered national attention, county officials announced this week.
The U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration award comes as the federal government separately approved a long-anticipated waiver in Maine’s Medicaid program that, among other rule changes, will allow correctional facilities to bill MaineCare for such treatment in certain situations.
The new grant is a bridge to keep the opioid addiction treatment program running until the new Medicaid rules are implemented, likely in 2028 or 2029, county officials told the Board of Commissioners at its meeting Wednesday.
It also frees up what Somerset County can do with its funds from state settlements with pharmaceutical companies that fueled the opioid epidemic. The county had been conserving most of its funds, which will continue to be paid out through
“We are saving many lives with this medication,” said Somerset County Sheriff Dale P. Lancaster in a statement Thursday. “And this grant provides the ongoing funding we need to purchase it, which saves the county taxpayers money.”
WHAT IS THE TREATMENT PROGRAM?
In 2022, the Somerset County Jail in Madison switched from offering inmates with opioid addiction a daily medication to monthly injections of an extended-release version of the drug buprenorphine. The medication is also known by its brand name, Sublocade, and, more recently, Brixadi.
The monthly administrations have been found to reduce the risk of overdoses after people are released and make it significantly more likely people continue receiving treatment after their release. The switch also helped cut down on illicit activity among inmates related to the daily version of the medication, Suboxone, Lancaster said previously.
A scientific study of the jail’s early success administering the extended-release buprenorphine drew national attention, including from The New York Times.
According to a news release, the grant will fund the medication program; support developing a program to address a sharp rise in methamphetamine-involved overdoses; expand outreach, referrals and reentry support; and allow addiction medicine staff to provide technical assistance to other county jails.
Lancaster credited Dr. Alane O’Connor, director of addiction medicine at the jail, for working with his staff to secure the funds.
“We are incredibly excited to receive this grant and to be able to build upon the remarkable work the jail is already doing,” O’Connor said in a statement.
HOW MUCH DOES IT COST?
Maine jails are required to provide medication-assisted treatment.
The costly endeavor largely falls on counties to pay for through property taxes or other funding sources.
In fiscal year 2025, Maine’s 16 counties spent $9.1 million on medication-assisted treatment, according to a January report from the County Corrections Professional Standards Council. Lancaster and Somerset County Administrator Tim Curtis are members of the board.
The cost to buy the drugs and run the program in Somerset County varies based on how many inmates are receiving treatment at any given time, Curtis said.
The cost is typically about $1 million per year, he said. Waldo County, which contracts with Somerset County to board its inmates, reimburses Somerset County for the costs of the medication for its inmates.
To date, Somerset County has used a combination of grants and opioid settlement funds to pay for its extended-release buprenorphine program.
That included $3.2 million more in grants, figures from county Finance Director Patrick Dolan show. Nearly all of the previous grant money has been spent.
WHAT IS THE NEW FUNDING?
The SAMHSA grant will provide Somerset County with $729,380 this year and next year, $635,164 in 2028, $557,414 in 2029 and $479,664 in 2030, according to figures Curtis prepared for the commissioners.
It comes from a batch of federal funding totaling $68 million that was expected to be awarded to 91 applicants, a SAMHSA grant database shows.
County officials estimate the grant, at least in its first years, will cover most of an estimated $161,000 in labor costs and $600,000 in medication costs. Program staff are O’Connor for medical oversight, a care coordinator from Somerset Public Health who works within the jail and a project manager.
Somerset County also has about $665,000 available in one-time funding the state gave jails for medication-assisted treatment programs, Curtis’ figures show. Meanwhile, the county is waiting to hear back about an additional $1.2 million requested through the office of U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican.
HOW DOES THE MEDICAID WAIVER COME INTO PLAY?
Officials described the SAMHSA grant as a bridge of sorts to when the MaineCare policy changes allowing coverage for medication-assisted treatment will be in effect a few years from today.
Until now, one’s MaineCare benefits would be suspended upon incarceration.
The slew of changes, technically known as a section 1115 waiver, include a new provision that Maine jails and prisons can bill MaineCare for certain services, including medication-assisted treatment, within 60 days of an inmate’s release.
The change is expected to be implemented first at state prisons, Curtis said. At county jails it will be more difficult to put into practice, he said, because many people being held are pre-trial and do not have a set release date. County jails generally hold those serving sentences of less than a year.
“The 1115 waiver is not the magic dust that’s going to solve all of the problems,” Lancaster told the commissioners. “There’s a lot of things that are attached to that. It will help in the big picture, and it’s still a long ways away.”
AND WHAT ABOUT THE OPIOID SETTLEMENT FUNDS?
Somerset County is slated to get a share of the more than $230 million in funds from settlements with pharmaceutical companies, distributors and retailers that played a role in the opioid epidemic. The state started receiving settlement payments in 2022 and is expecting to receive the funds through 2038.
Somerset County’s allocation is estimated to total about $2.5 million, according to the Maine Office of the Attorney General.
So far, the county has used a portion of its funds to supplement the cost of the Somerset Public Health care coordinator position, which will now be covered by the SAMHSA grant. It also gave $6,250 to Kennebec Behavioral Health.
Otherwise, county officials have mostly been saving the settlement funds received so far amid the uncertainty of getting more grant funding for the extended-release buprenorphine program. Right now, the settlement funds in the bank total approximately $837,000, records show.
“If you’re asking me my recommendation,” Curtis told the commissioners, “I’d say we keep the money that we have in the bank just in case something falls apart in this particular (medication-assisted treatment) program for the jail, and maybe allocate the money that comes in” to a grant program for community organizations.

title: Who pays for Christa Pike’s medical care as she remains hospitalized after botched execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Christa Pike is awake and “speaking limitedly” after her botched execution in Tennessee.
On Wednesday, Pike’s legal team said she was declared brain dead Monday night and was expected to be taken off life support, but she woke up and started talking on Tuesday.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning but I do know she has a long road to recovery,” attorney Randy Spivey said.
Pike has a blood clot, cannot swallow and has not eaten, according to her attorneys. Her arms and hands are swollen, and it is unknown at this time if she will regain function in her arms. They also said she has pneumonia.
“The swelling was extraordinary,” Spivey said.
Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to The Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike remains hospitalized. Her feet and right arm are shackled to her hospital bed, and medical staff and her attorneys have asked for some of the restraints to be removed.
Who pays for Pike’s medical care?
Pike is still a Tennessee inmate, and Vanderbilt Law School professor Christopher Slobogin said that means the state remains responsible for her medical care.
“Governor Lee would have to commute her sentence, and the state would have to care for her like any prisoner who’s got medical problems. Now, sometimes the care isn’t all that great, but at least in theory, the state has to provide her full medical care,” he said.
A constitutional barrier
If Pike does not fully recover or suffers permanent brain damage, Slobogin said that creates a possible constitutional barrier to another execution.
“We’ve never seen anything quite like this,” he said. “We’ve certainly had botched executions before, and the state has then subsequently executed the person who survived the botched attempt. But her case is unique in that they tried twice.”
Slobogin said the United States Supreme Court has ruled that the Eighth Amendment prohibits states from executing someone who is incompetent.
“Because to be competent to be executed, she has to understand that she will die and why she’s being killed,” he said.
If Pike’s brain is permanently damaged to the point where she cannot understand that, Slobogin said trying to execute her again is off the table.
“If she’s got a brain injury, if she’s got cognitive problems, then she will not be competent to be executed and they simply cannot kill her,” he said.
What happens if Pike fully recovers
If Pike makes a full recovery and Tennessee wants to move forward with executing her, Slobogin said that is where the legal picture gets more complicated.
Under Tennessee law, Pike’s death sentence remains in effect, and the U.S. Supreme Court has said states can try to execute an inmate on death row a second time after a failed first attempt.
But Slobogin believes if the state tried it, Pike’s lawyer would have a good argument that lethal injection can’t be used.
“Given what we know now, how she responds to lethal injection and given what happened to her, Christa Pike’s lawyers have a pretty good argument that it would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment to execute her using that method,” Slobogin said.
Can Christa Pike be executed using another method?
Slobogin said the state could try another way of executing Pike. The electric chair is still available in Tennessee.
But he said because Tennessee has technically tried to kill her twice already through lethal injection, and it was clearly painful, causing serious medical injury, that may be an uphill legal battle for the state as well.
“There might be the possibility the state could execute her constitutionally,” Slobogin said. “But I think her lawyers would also have an argument that it would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment to execute her considering what’s happened.”

title: Who pays for Christa Pike’s medical care as she remains hospitalized after botched execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Christa Pike is awake and “speaking limitedly” after her botched execution in Tennessee.
On Wednesday, Pike’s legal team said she was declared brain dead Monday night and was expected to be taken off life support, but she woke up and started talking on Tuesday.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning but I do know she has a long road to recovery,” attorney Randy Spivey said.
Pike has a blood clot, cannot swallow and has not eaten, according to her attorneys. Her arms and hands are swollen, and it is unknown at this time if she will regain function in her arms. They also said she has pneumonia.
“The swelling was extraordinary,” Spivey said.
Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to The Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike remains hospitalized. Her feet and right arm are shackled to her hospital bed, and medical staff and her attorneys have asked for some of the restraints to be removed.
Who pays for Pike’s medical care?
Pike is still a Tennessee inmate, and Vanderbilt Law School professor Christopher Slobogin said that means the state remains responsible for her medical care.
“Governor Lee would have to commute her sentence, and the state would have to care for her like any prisoner who’s got medical problems. Now, sometimes the care isn’t all that great, but at least in theory, the state has to provide her full medical care,” he said.
A constitutional barrier
If Pike does not fully recover or suffers permanent brain damage, Slobogin said that creates a possible constitutional barrier to another execution.
“We’ve never seen anything quite like this,” he said. “We’ve certainly had botched executions before, and the state has then subsequently executed the person who survived the botched attempt. But her case is unique in that they tried twice.”
Slobogin said the United States Supreme Court has ruled that the Eighth Amendment prohibits states from executing someone who is incompetent.
“Because to be competent to be executed, she has to understand that she will die and why she’s being killed,” he said.
If Pike’s brain is permanently damaged to the point where she cannot understand that, Slobogin said trying to execute her again is off the table.
“If she’s got a brain injury, if she’s got cognitive problems, then she will not be competent to be executed and they simply cannot kill her,” he said.
What happens if Pike fully recovers
If Pike makes a full recovery and Tennessee wants to move forward with executing her, Slobogin said that is where the legal picture gets more complicated.
Under Tennessee law, Pike’s death sentence remains in effect, and the U.S. Supreme Court has said states can try to execute an inmate on death row a second time after a failed first attempt.
But Slobogin believes if the state tried it, Pike’s lawyer would have a good argument that lethal injection can’t be used.
“Given what we know now, how she responds to lethal injection and given what happened to her, Christa Pike’s lawyers have a pretty good argument that it would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment to execute her using that method,” Slobogin said.
Can Christa Pike be executed using another method?
Slobogin said the state could try another way of executing Pike. The electric chair is still available in Tennessee.
But he said because Tennessee has technically tried to kill her twice already through lethal injection, and it was clearly painful, causing serious medical injury, that may be an uphill legal battle for the state as well.
“There might be the possibility the state could execute her constitutionally,” Slobogin said. “But I think her lawyers would also have an argument that it would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment to execute her considering what’s happened.”
