title: Escaped peacock returned to Gray animal sanctuary
text:
The peacock simultaneously known as “George” and “Rambo” was recaptured and safely returned to the Maine Wildlife Park last month after becoming a local sensation when it escaped about five months ago.
Ben Barrett, assistant superintendent at the park, said Rambo, who was first spotted in Thayer Brook Preserve in Gray early this summer, was recaptured without much fanfare on private land.
Rambo escaped from the park in May by flying over the park’s perimeter fence.
Peafowl have a long history at the wildlife park, which previously served as a game farm. At both the game farm and wildlife park, the resident peacocks have historically served as sentries and natural pest control.
At one point during his travels, Rambo joined a group of turkeys at a site the wildlife park had been monitoring since shortly after it escaped, Barrett said.
During the three-month search, the park received multiple reports of sightings, many of which contradicted the whereabouts and confirmed locations of Rambo. Barrett said this was because multiple people in the region own domesticated peacocks; Rambo was positively identified by the bands the park attaches to the legs of its peafowl.
Rambo went viral on social media during his time on the run, with members of the Gray-New Gloucester community board posting photos of his travels.
Barrett said he and one of the park’s wildlife keepers used a small garden to create a cage trap, which they slowly encouraged the peacock to enter.
While quarantined after being returned to the park, Barrett said Rambo was doing “fantastic.” Since Rambo’s return, the park’s peafowl population, which formerly roamed the grounds freely, has been confined to an enclosure to prevent them from escaping again.
Barrett said Rambo’s recapture was a bright spot in an otherwise tough season for the wildlife park, amid the deaths of the park’s resident moose and black bear.
“We’re happy to hear that the peacock has finally been caught and returned home after its extended summer vacation in the Gray woods, just in time for winter,” said Hanae Garrison, stewardship director at Royal River Conservation Trust, which manages Thayer Brook Preserve.

title: Susan Collins has put too many lives at risk
text:
Hillary Shende lives in Brunswick.
Sen. Susan Collins directs federal funding toward some Maine projects: a fire station here, a library there, etc.
But recent analysis by the Maine Center for Economic Policy found that while Collins brought in $3.45 billion over the last 10 years, her procedural vote on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last summer negated all of that and then some, leaving Mainers with a net loss of $675 million.
We must stop the financial bleeding as soon as possible. The first step is to flip Congress by firing Collins and hiring Troy Jackson.
If economics doesn’t convince you, perhaps the loss of human life will. Yes, you read that right.
On abortion, Collins cast a critical vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who predictably cast the deciding vote overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022. So far, the ensuing state abortion bans led to the deaths of 59 women who suffered from miscarriage-related sepsis, ectopic pregnancies and other medical conditions for which the only lifesaving care is abortion. Still, Collins doesn’t regret voting for Kavanaugh and just recently voted for openly anti-choice judge Matthew Byrne, erasing any doubt that she is willing to let Americans die if her party needs her vote.
On ICE/CBP, the number of people dying in ICE/CBP custody has more than doubled since Donald Trump took office in 2025. And that doesn’t even count the horrific ICE/CBP killings in our streets, some of which happened before Collins allocated $70 billion to immigration enforcement. Unsurprisingly ICE went on to kill more people, including our fellow Mainer, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Center for American Progress projects that 70,0000 Americans could die by 2040 as a result of SNAP cuts, and 51,000 more per year could die from Medicaid cuts, both of which became law as part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. This is the bill that also drains $4.1 billion from Maine. Collins advanced the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to the Senate floor, where, as I have seen so many times, the senator voted against the bill once it was evident it could pass without her.
On ceding congressional authority over war, the Iran war has caused at least than 8,000 deaths, at least 22 of which were American service members, and at least 2,100 of which were civilians. Worse, a U.N. fact-finding mission found that the U.S. likely engaged in war crimes by striking Iranian civilian structures like a school in Minab, where 120 schoolchildren were killed. Imagine being the parent of the child I saw in a photo, her severed arm sticking out from the tons of concrete rubble that crushed the rest of her to death. I am enraged at Collins’ unwillingness to stop these reckless atrocities.
These numbers are enormous, and each one is a person somebody loved. The collective grief Collins has caused, through both action and inaction, is incomprehensible to me.
Given Collins’ record of voting with Trump 95% of the time, it would be foolhardy to think she will ever meaningfully rein the president in. That’s especially true now that we know that Trump’s FBI abandoned a corruption investigation into Collins. I believe that he owes him, and he owns her.
In any other job, a record like this would get you fired yesterday.
The good news is that we can turn grief into justice. Maine voters have the power to turn the tide of this nightmare, and it is time to use it. Let’s make the lifesaving decision to vote out Susan Collins.

title: Obituary: Joan Santomango Goulette
text:
LEWISTON – Joan Santomango Goulette, 84, a longtime resident of Lewiston, passed away peacefully at Nevins Hospice House, Methuen, Mass., surrounded by her loving family on Oct. 3, 2026.
A beloved wife, mother, grandmother, sister, and aunt, Joan was the devoted wife of Marcel for 64 years. He survives her.
She was born in Melrose, Mass. and her family moved to Maine when she was in elementary school, finally settling in Lewiston as a teenager. She raised her family in Lewiston. After retirement, she spent her time between Brettuns Pond in Livermore (and later Bear Pond – Turner) and Florida.
Among her many interests, Joni enjoyed playing tennis in her earlier years and, more recently, golf. Joan and Marcel spent their winters in Florida, where they enjoyed playing many rounds of golf together. She was very proud to be a member of the Hole-in-One Club. Nothing brought her more joy than cooking an Italian dinner (especially her lasagna) for her family and friends and teaching her grandchildren how to play cards.
In addition to her husband, Marcel, Joan is survived by her sons, Michael and his wife Kathleen, and Christopher and his wife Joanne; and her three grandchildren, Liam, Owen, and Galen, who affectionately called her “Noni.”
She was predeceased by her parents, Michael and Rose Santomango, and her sisters, Marie and Toni.
Services were private.

title: Randy Cabral's 100th Pavement win highlights NEMA Night at Wiscasset Speedway
text:
While tracks across New England canceled or postponed their racing events on Saturday due to unfavorable weather, Wiscasset Speedway took a chance on the probable window and ultimately won, successfully hosting all Group 1 divisions plus the lightning-fast NEMA Lites and Midgets.
The night kicked off with a 25-lap feature for the County Truss 4-Cylinder Pros. Brody Picard took off with the early advantage, but Chassidy Shorty was on the move, claiming the top spot on lap 5 as Max Parlin followed in succession. Parlin made his way to Shorty's door on lap 8, challenging for the top spot. A lap car slowed the leader shortly thereafter, catapulting Parlin into the lead. While battling for position, Sam Fogg and Darren Miranda made hard contact on lap 22, resulting in a red flag with just 3 laps to go. Max Parlin maintained command on the restart, scoring his second win of the season while Chassidy Shorty and Rowdy Romano rounded out the podium.
Matt O'Brien led the field to green in the night's Pepsi Spotlight feature: a 30-lap bout for the NEMA Midgets. Avery Stoehr was quick to steal it away as Joey Bailey lingered closely behind. Randy Cabral was on the charge early, overtaking second before abruptly coming to a slow on lap 10, resulting in a caution. Avery Stoehr got a good jump on the restart and began to pull away. Meanwhile, third place driver Mike Horn faced mechanical problems, pulling to the infield with just two laps to go. While Avery Stoehr scored his first win of the season, Joey Bailey and Brayden Egan completed the top 3.
Andy Gilbert hopped out to the early lead in the 40-lap feature for the T&L Automotive Modifieds. Kelly Moore was also on the move early, diving to Andy Gilbert's inside on lap 8. The two drivers went door-to-door for a couple of laps before Moore pulled ahead on lap 11. Defending champion Nick Hinkley came to life as the laps wound down, overtaking second on lap 29. Although he was quickly tracking him down, he was unable to catch Kelly Moore, who picked up his third victory of the season. Andy Gilbert followed, completing the podium.
Jeff Farrington took off with the early lead in the 20-lap feature for the Maine Army National Guard Thunder 4 Minis. Ricky Austin made a bold crossover move on lap 2, powering to the top spot just two laps later. Shane Webber was quickly climbing the leaderboard, overtaking second on lap 6 as Derek Cook rode his coattails. Cook got bent out of shape on lap 8, handing third back over to Farrington. He ultimately regained composure, reclaiming the spot on lap 13. Shane Webber was all over Ricky Austin in the closing laps of the race, but Austin was able to hold him off, securing his third straight victory in the division. Derek Cook followed, rounding out the top 3.
Josh Hall took off from the point in the 30-lap feature for the Darling's Brunswick Ford Super Streets. Bubba Pelton peeked to his inside on lap 8 while David Greenleaf joined the fray, making it a 3-way battle for the top spot. Bubba Pelton powered to the lead on lap 11 while David Greenleaf remained glued to his quarter. While duking it out for the top spot, the two drivers made contact on lap 13, catapulting third-place driver Noah Haggett into the lead. It didn't last for long as Greenleaf straightened it out, overtaking the top spot. He sailed into his third victory while Noah Haggett and Bubba Pelton followed, completing the podium.
*Results from the Super Street race are still unofficial and pending engine inspection on the winner's car.
Calvin Bennett took off with the early lead in the 40-lap feature for the NEMA Lites. Randy Cabral was on the move early, overtaking second from Tiana Kibbe on lap 2. Jack Dumas went for a wild ride on lap 13, flipping onto his side in turn 1 after collecting fluid on the track from another competitor. This resulted in an extended red flag and although Calvin Bennett got a strong restart, Randy Cabral seemingly came out of nowhere, clearing him for the top spot. Cabral stretched his lead out to over 2 seconds in clean air, securing his 100th career pavement win as Tiana Kibbe and Zack Martinez rounded out the top 3. Cabral, who was joined by his family in Victory Lane, lovingly dedicated his victory to his dogs, who were also on-site on Saturday.
The night concluded with a 30-lap feature for the Davis Erector Group 207 Crate Modifieds. Ryan Phillips powered to the early lead over Allen Moeller. Travis Buzzell made his way to Moeller's outside on lap 5, challenging for second. Buzzell quickly took over the spot as Nick Hinkley lingered closely behind. Hinkley made way to Buzzell's door on lap 8 and the two drivers battled it out until Hinkley claimed sole possession on lap 12. Travis Buzzell backed down before giving it another go as the laps wound down, stealing the spot back with just two laps to go. Defending champion Ryan Phillips was too far gone at the front of the field, securing the victory as Travis Buzzell and Nick Hinkley completed the podium.
Saturday night's program brought endless excitement and new driver milestones. Team Wiscasset hopes to see even more of this as they host their Group 2 Fan Appreciation Night on Saturday, Aug. 15.
The driver meet and greet will take place on the front stretch at 4 p.m., followed by kid's bike races and qualifying heat races.
As always, adult grandstand admission is just $5 while kids 6 & under get in for free.
For the official track schedule, race results and more, please visit http://www.wiscassetspeedway.com.

title: Scattered Showers Today... Drier & Brighter Friday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front will cross the state this afternoon accompanied by some scattered showers. The showers will be most numerous across the north. A few thunderstorms can’t be ruled out as well. Not expecting anything in terms of severe weather but any thunderstorms that develop could produce some heavier rainfall and even some small hail. Skies will brighten this afternoon... especially south of Greenville and Millinocket. Temperatures will be warmer with highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s this afternoon. Shower chances will taper off early this evening as the cold front exits followed by clearing skies for the night tonight. Overnight lows will drop to the 40s.
Cooler air will move in behind the front for the end of the week. We’ll see a drier and brighter day Friday with a mix of sun and clouds. An upper-level disturbance crossing the state could trigger a few isolated showers anytime from late morning through the afternoon. High temperatures on Friday will be in the 50s to near 60°. High pressure will build in to bring us a nice weekend. Saturday looks absolutely beautiful with sunshine and highs in the 50s. Sunday is looking good too with warmer temperatures. Morning sunshine will give way to increasing clouds as the da progresses. A gusty west/southwest wind will usher warmer air into the region with high temperatures climbing to the 60s to near 70° Sunday afternoon. We’ll keep an eye on the chance for some showers Sunday night into Monday... especially closer to the coast... depending the track of the remnants of Hurricane Isaias.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly cloudy with scattered showers and possibly a few thunderstorms. Highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s. Southwest wind 5-15 MPH becoming west.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy. Lows in the 40s. West wind 5-10 MPH.
Friday: Mix of sun and clouds. Isolated showers possible from late morning through the afternoon. Cooler with highs in the 50s. West/northwest wind 10-20 MPH.
Saturday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s.
Sunday: Increasing clouds. Breezy and warmer. Highs in the 60s.
Monday: Mostly cloudy with morning showers possible then brightening skies during the afternoon. Highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s.

title: College football player dies in rollover crash; teammate accused of driving while intoxicated
text:
SHERMAN, Texas (KXII/Gray News) - An Oklahoma football player has died in a rollover crash, with his teammate arrested in connection with the collision.
Dylan Sebock, a Southeastern Oklahoma State University football player, was killed in the crash that occurred early at about 1 a.m. Thursday on U.S. Highway 75.
Sherman police officers said Sebock and the driver of the vehicle, later identified as 23-year-old De’Taurean Johnson, were ejected from the car.
According to police, Sebock was pronounced dead at the scene and Johnson was found lying in the roadway.
Officers said Johnson attempted to take off from the scene before being taken into custody and transported to an area hospital for his injuries from the crash.
Investigators noted that they collected evidence establishing that Johnson was intoxicated while driving, which contributed to the death of the 23-year-old Sebock.
Johnson, listed as a senior linebacker for Southeastern Oklahoma State University, was released from medical care and arrested for intoxication manslaughter.
“We are deeply saddened to confirm that one student has died as a result of the accident. The other student was hospitalized. Our hearts are with their families, friends, teammates, and all those affected by this tragic loss,” the university shared.
Loved ones have since set up a GoFundMe to help support Sebock’s family.

His fellow senator, Susan Collins, voted to confirm two climate deniers as heads of the EPA and the Department of Energy. title: Army finds systemic failures behind DC midair collision and calls for safety fixes
text:
(AP) - The U.S. Army found many systemic breakdowns that led to last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended numerous steps the military should take to prevent future tragedies.
Families of some of the 67 people who died have been pressuring the Army for months to release the report, which was completed in May. The Associated Press obtained a copy from them Thursday morning, a few hours before the Army made it public.
The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River.
The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Reagan National Airport could have prevented the crash, but also acknowledged the military’s own failings and other contributing factors.
The Army and victims’ families both say they want transparency
Former Army Black Hawk pilot Tim Lilley, whose son Sam Lilley was the first officer on the American Airlines jet, said he needs more details from the military. Some information in the report was redacted, and the military assigned responsibility for its shortcomings broadly across the Army.
“The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again,” said Lilley, who is a commercial jet captain today.
The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday afternoon.
“We recognize the families’ need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army’s review,” the Army said.
The report identifies key factors in the crash
While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board’s conclusions, the civilian investigation was broader and emphasized years of warning signs missed by the Federal Aviation Administration, along with a weak military safety culture.
The Army report recommended that the military look beyond Washington to make sure similar risks aren’t present in every major city where its helicopters operate. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the situation.
The lieutenant general who authored the report said “breakdowns across all layers of conflict management caused this accident,” but, “the most salient contributing factor was the two broken radio transmissions” that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying Flight 5342 as it was circling to land on the airport’s alternate runway. The military pilots were wearing night-vision goggles that limited their field of vision and made it difficult to spot the plane amid the lights of the city.
The poorly designed helicopter route in use at the time of the crash provided only a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on Reagan’s secondary runway, and that was only true if the helicopter stuck to the riverbank. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk’s altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read.
NTSB says the Army is making progress on safety
The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that the agency is pleased with the progress being made on seven of the eight recommendations to the Army. That contrasts with the FAA, which the NTSB has faulted for failing to implement roughly one-third of the recommendations to that safety regulator.
The Army report said the controller should have provided the helicopter crew with more details about exactly where the plane was to help the pilots spot it, and the controller should have warned the plane about the helicopter headed toward it. The FAA has prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace since this crash.
The Army said it strengthened its training for helicopter crews after the crash. Once it became apparent that the ADS-B Out system on the Black Hawk that can broadcast its location was inoperable, all 3,585 affected Army helicopters were inspected and reconfigured. The Army is also working to improve the way it monitors safety concerns and reach an agreement with the FAA to share information about close calls.
Victims’ families push for aviation safety reform bill
The main group of families of passengers on the plane, who were flying from Wichita, Kansas, said the report reinforces their call for Congress to pass aviation safety reforms and require aircraft to be equipped with systems that will help pilots know where traffic in the air is.
“It’s a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing,” the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday.
“We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for,” they said.
Both the House and Senate passed different aviation safety bills, but lawmakers are still working on a compromise piece of legislation to bring up for a vote in both houses of Congress.
___
Associated Press Writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.

title: Jurors begin deliberating in Raymond Brown murder trial
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - Raymond Brown, 67, has been found guilty in the 1984 murder of 18-year-old Linda Maxwell.
The jury returned the guilty verdict Thursday afternoon after deliberating for about an hour.
Jurors heard more testimony Thursday morning. A cold-case investigator outlined the renewed investigation, and witnesses gave differing accounts about evidence and Maxwell’s class ring.
Sgt. Chad Lindsey of the Maine State Police testified that investigators began revisiting the case in 2021, paused while the agency addressed nine homicides in Washington County, and resumed work in March 2024. The team consulted agencies involved in the original investigation, conducted 35 interviews and exhumed Maxwell’s body for a second examination in May 2024, Lindsey said.
Jurors also heard a recording of Lindsey’s July 2024 interview with Brown. In the interview, Brown recalled drinking and driving with Maxwell and friends but said he could not remember many details. He denied sexual contact, disputed accounts about wet boots and his return time, and accused a former detective of targeting his family, according to the testimony.
Maxwell’s naked body was found in the St. Croix River.
Lindsey testified that earlier interviews placed Brown dropping off two friends at about 12:15 a.m. He also said in the interview that three witnesses reported hearing screams from the river. Lindsey testified he did not consider a bra and undergarment found in 1984 credibly connected to Maxwell and did not seek additional testing. He also discussed changes to evidence-handling procedures.
Witnesses offer differing accounts of class ring
Defense witnesses gave differing accounts about Maxwell’s high school class ring. A friend testified that Maxwell had been in his car with friends and left her ring there. He said he later retrieved it from the car and an officer took it from him, though he could not recall how it first ended up in the vehicle.
A former Maine State Police detective who helped with interviews and canvassing testified that he saw the ring but did not take it. Earlier, another witness testified she had told police she knew a different man had the ring, but said that was not based on her own observation.
Testimony revisits 1984 investigation
A former Maine State Police detective previously testified that Brown said he took Maxwell to Milltown and returned to Calais. The defense questioned why police did not search a burn barrel on Brown’s property and challenged the thoroughness of the original investigation.
A Maine game warden testified that, based on the river conditions he reviewed, it would have been essentially impossible for a body to travel 14 miles down the St. Croix River.
Earlier testimony included a cousin’s account that Brown said his pants were wet after Maxwell’s body was found, that he burned clothing and was frustrated with the investigation. A jailhouse witness also testified that Brown described trying to have sex with Maxwell, holding her underwater after an argument, leaving her body at a boat landing and later burning clothing. The defense challenged that witness’s credibility, citing a recorded call in which he said he might lie if his bail request was denied.
Prosecution and defense reflect on trial
Defense attorney Steven Smith said after the trial that he does not believe there was enough evidence to convict his client, and that his legal team plan to appeal the verdict.
“After 42 years, We don’t think Ray deserved this. We absolutely intend to appeal. There was absolutely no physical evidence, and nobody can tell what happened to Linda in the 36 hours between the time she left the party to the time she was found,” Smith said.
“Testing the statements against the evidence and once you looked at the physical geography of the scene, once you looked at what he was saying and where he was saying it, it was incredible,” Assistant Attorney General Leanne Robbin told WABI. “Did not pass the straight face test, and it was that analysis that brought us here today.”
Robbin says it’s sad Linda’s parents were not alive to see justice served, but they hope this gives the family a sense of closure.
Brown will be sentenced at a later date is being held without bail.

title: People in addiction often fear law enforcement. In Biddeford, they met on a softball field.
text:
BIDDEFORD — Tia Lavigne stood in the dugout waiting to take the field. At 26, she said it would be the first time she had ever played softball sober.
She said she had played under the influence of substances even as a kid in Buxton. She could throw from home plate to second base without hitting the ground, so she found her place as a catcher. But at just 9 years old, she said, she was given alcohol by an adult and became addicted. Lavigne said she made a lot of “not great choices” and was later arrested on a gun purchasing charge.
By the time she put on the red uniform shirt at Rotary Park in Biddeford on a damp Wednesday night at the end of September, she had been sober for two years, seven months and 16 days, with help from ENSO Recovery in Sanford, and had put herself on a better path by starting her own cleaning business.
“This is the only time I felt comfortable playing ball. All the co-ed teams out there, there are substances around,” she said.
This game, which has become an annual tradition, was unusual: It was built for people in various stages of drug and alcohol recovery to be together — and to play alongside law enforcement officers.
The Recovery Softball BBQ was created by Ryan and Cynthia Paige and their organization AccessDirect Recovery Network in order to break down stigma on both sides.
Lavigne used to see a cop car and bolt in the other direction, she said. On the night of the game, the cars and trucks squeezed into the parking lot and lining the road to the softball field included a lot of police and sheriff’s department vehicles.
“There’s a person out there who might’ve been sober for nine days,” Ryan Paige said, pointing to the field during warmups. “When you look it might be hard to tell who’s who — law enforcement or a person in recovery. That’s the whole point.”
Day to day, he
He stood near the pitcher’s mound before the ceremonial first pitch and said into the microphone that the rate of overdose deaths in Maine was dropping, that recovery was possible and that support from peers mattered. About 150 people stood in the dugouts and along the fences and cheered.
Ryan Paige is in recovery, too, and like some of the people he invited to participate, he said he surprised himself.
“I never thought a life like this was possible for me,” he said, scanning the scene.
He was always social and now he had something productive to channel it toward. So much so that he was too busy to play in the game. He bounced between the barbecue, the vendors and service providers who had set up information tables, the softball field, and the dunk tank, which was a new addition this year.
York County Deputy Sheriff Matthew Cummer, in full uniform, got dunked dozens of times for about an hour. Ryan
QUIETING JUDGMENT
Auburn Police Sgt. Nick Gagnon jogged up to the plate.
“I haven’t hit a ball in 10 years, but I’m hitting this one!” he boldly told the catcher.
Gagnon took a big swing and
He said he’s seen fentanyl and methamphetamine come into Maine over his 17-year career.
“First, like a lot of young officers, you judge people,” he said. “Over time with age and maturity, you learn empathy.”
Asked what he would tell a younger version of himself, he said he would try to explain how important it is to have compassion.
“If you become cynical and judge people in the wrong way,” he said, “ there’s too much hostility between law enforcement and the community.”
By the second inning, the blue team, the Resilient Riders, appeared to be way ahead, though there was no scoreboard and several players said no one was keeping track. It didn’t lessen the effort or enthusiasm in the dugouts.
“It’s so fun to listen to them cheer each other on,” Auburn Police Lt. Matt Dailey said of the players who’d come from sober houses and long-term care facilities to play in the game.
“As law enforcement we need people in recovery to help their friends and get people out of drugs,” he said.
York County Sheriff Bill King walked along the left field fence, blending into the crowd in a sweatshirt.
“I’ve met people who’ve served time in our jail,” he said. “That’s the most fulfilling, to see them working on their substance issues.”
Scott Brockelbank said he played in adult softball leagues for years around Maine and traveled to Disney World for games. During the sixth inning of the game last week, as his team pulled ahead, he said it was the first time he had played sober.
“I always thought I played better messed up, but I actually think I play better sober,” he said. He was proud to play in front of his wife and, in his words, not make a fool of himself.
Brockelbank, who said he first took crack cocaine at age 11 when it was given to him by an adult relative,
“I used to hate law enforcement for a long time. Today I realize they were doing their jobs and I was the problem,” he said. “It’s nice to share the field and not be worried.”
He added that he’d been sober for 90 days.
Brockelbank later said the event may help him get back into softball without it being a trigger to use drugs.
Fog settled onto the field as Gagnon, from the Auburn Police Department, smacked a ball to right center field. His teammate, Austin McAlister, walked up to the plate. McAlister said he got addicted to heroin during his third prison stint, and he used to run away from police and firefighters.
Now he said he’s been sober for 10 months and is in treatment court, where he gets random drug tests.
“Law enforcement changed my life by getting arrested,” he said. “I’m super grateful.”
“When I hear them say going to jail saved my life it feels good,” Gagnon said.
Soaking in the fresh air and freedom of the softball field, McAlister tried out his home run swing and ran down the base path. A few plays later the second baseman fielded a grounder and acrobatically tipped it to the shortstop for an out. Everybody laughed. “It’s like Banana Ball!” someone yelled near home plate, likening it to the wacky, up-tempo baseball that’s getting popular in the U.S..
In the last inning the players decided the red team, the Hope Hustlers, would bat through the order. They were almost certainly losing by a lot but no one was really sure. Dailey, the lieutenant, hit the game’s final pitch a long way out in right field and rounded the bases.
Both dugouts cheered as he came around third, then got tagged out at the plate.
Dailey and his Auburn Police colleagues were the last to leave the field, and they walked away talking about plans for next year’s game.
Nicholas Toth was also thinking ahead. He’d come from a nearby men’s facility in Biddeford to play. At 45, he’d lost toes to frostbite and had other serious health problems, he said. He’s six and a half years sober and credited Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous for helping him.
The night’s game wore him out — he had panted coming around the bases and was emotional as he walked up to Ryan Paige to thank him for organizing everything. Paige had picked him up at a homeless shelter earlier this year.
Just like the players from all backgrounds that night who had whiffed at arcing pitches, lost their footing, and eventually reached base, Toth said his recovery has been bumpy, not linear and not as easy as it looks.
By next year’s game he plans to be living in his own place.
And Ryan Paige has plans to expand the dunk tank.

title: U.S. Army finds systemic failures behind DC midair collision and calls for safety fixes
text:
US Army finds systemic failures behind DC midair collision and calls for safety fixes
The U.S. Army found systemic safety breakdowns behind last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended changes to prevent future tragedies.
The Army report — completed in May and released publicly Thursday after months of pressure from the victims' families — identified failures involving air traffic control, helicopter routes, training and safety practices. The Associated Press obtained a copy of the report hours before it was released.
Related previous coverage above: "Unacceptable action:" victim's families, transportation officials push for aviation safety changes
The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River and killing 67.
The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Reagan could have prevented the crash, but it also acknowledged the military’s own failings and other contributing factors.
Families demand answers from the Army
Tim Lilley, a former Army Black Hawk pilot whose son Sam Lilley was the airliner's first officer, said the report leaves important questions unanswered. Parts were redacted, and responsibility for the Army's failures was assigned broadly rather than to individuals.
“The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again,” said Lilley, now a commercial jet captain.
The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday.
“We recognize the families’ need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army’s review,” it said.
Report identifies key factors in the crash
While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board's conclusions, the civilian investigation was broader and emphasized years of missed warnings by the Federal Aviation Administration along with a weak military safety culture.
The Army faulted the air traffic controller for not giving the helicopter crew more precise information about the approaching jet and for not warning the jet’s pilot about the helicopter. After the crash, the FAA prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace.
The report recommended looking beyond Washington to examine military helicopter operations in other major cities for similar risks. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the situation publicly.
The lieutenant general who authored the report cited “breakdowns across all layers of conflict management” but singled out two failed radio transmissions that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying the jet. The military pilots' night-vision goggles also restricted their view and made it hard to spot the plane amid the city lights.
The poorly designed helicopter route allowed a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on the airport's secondary runway, assuming helicopters stayed near the riverbank, which the route didn't require. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk’s altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read.
NTSB says the Army is making safety changes
The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that it was pleased with the Army's progress on seven of its eight safety recommendations. That contrasts with the FAA’s failure to implement roughly a third of the recommendations aimed at the agency.
The Army said it has strengthened helicopter crew training and has inspected and reconfigured 3,585 helicopters after discovering the crashed Black Hawk's ADS-B Out system, which broadcasts its location, hadn't been working for some time.
The military is also improving its monitoring of safety risks and working with the FAA to share information about close calls.
Victims' families push Congress for safety reforms
Families of the crash victims said the Army's findings strengthen their case for legislation requiring aircraft to have technology that helps pilots detect nearby traffic.
“It’s a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing,” the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday.
“We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for,” they said.
The House and Senate have passed separate aviation safety bills but have yet to agree on a final version.
___
Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.

title: This nonprofit throws birthday parties for children living in shelters
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (InvestigateTV) — A nonprofit is bringing birthday parties to children experiencing homelessness so they can celebrate their special day while living in shelters.
Extra-Ordinary Birthdays organized a party for Yalina, who turned 7, at a shelter in Washington, D.C. The celebration included a cake, a personalized card, decorations and gifts chosen in her favorite color, pink.
Founder started organization in 2010
Schinnell Leake founded Extra-Ordinary Birthdays in 2010 to throw personalized parties for children living in shelters in the D.C. area on their birthdays.
“Personalization, individual, and the fact that we really do cater to that child’s interest, their needs, their special needs,” Leake said, describing what makes a birthday an extraordinary birthday. “But it’s also just about, just that pure, unadulterated joy that happens.”
Leake, a former professional party planner, said she started the organization because of a loss of empathy.
“The world has just lost empathy. They’ve lost everything,” Leake said. “And I’m kind of being a little defiant right now and saying that for me, the joy, you can’t erase joy.”
More than 1,700 parties organized
More than a million children across America are considered homeless, according to federal data.
Leake and volunteer “birthday angels” have thrown more than 1,700 parties across D.C., Maryland and Virginia.
Parents fill out a form selecting colors, gifts, decorations and the cake. A week before each party, volunteers wrap, pack and decorate.
Yalina’s mother, Nicole Berry, said her daughter likes princess-themed items and the color pink.
“It’s really special because right now, you know, it’s hard since we’re in the shelter,” Berry said. “So I just wanted her to have, you know, at least her birthday celebrated. Because, you know, being in this situation is not easy.”
Berry and all three of her children are living in the shelter in D.C.
Personalized touches include birthday cards
Leake said another volunteer mother makes personalized birthday cards for each child.
Berry said the volunteers “have good hearts to help people like this, you know, to make their kids day special.”
Leake said volunteers spend about an hour at each party.
“We’re here for an hour and in that hour, we are pouring in. We’re giving them snacks. We’re, you know, a cake based on what they want, gifts based on what they want. Doing the activities. Giving them goody bags,” Leake said.
Extra-Ordinary Birthdays gives each child at least one book, and offers a book for parents as well.
Those interested in donating money or time can visit extraordinarybirthdays.org.

title: 'They're seen': Students use GPS to locate graves that have gone unmarked for generations
text:
'They're seen': College students use tech to help locate unmarked Black Catholic graves in Kentucky
At first glance, part of St. Louis Cemetery in Louisville, Kentucky, may look like an empty field. But beneath the grass are the final resting places of many Black Catholics whose graves have gone unmarked for generations.
“This is some way that we can restore dignity to people and restore dignity to families,” said Michele Abee Biskis, assistant professor of environmental studies at Bellarmine University.
Now, Bellarmine University students are using skills they learned in the classroom to help locate those graves and preserve the history of the people buried there.
“It's important for them to know that their family members are here and they're seen,” Bellarmine student Sam Safly said.
The work is part of the Unmarked Graves Project, led by Deacon Ned Berghausen and Linda Fitzgerald in partnership with Bellarmine University. 
For years, Berghausen has worked to identify Black Catholics buried at St. Louis Cemetery.
Last year, Bellarmine students studying geographic information systems helped map the cemetery’s East Plot and Section X, two historically segregated areas.
This week, students returned to the cemetery to take the next step.
Using a grid, they are working to pinpoint the locations of graves and make sure no graves are missed.
For the students, the project is more than a classroom assignment.
“It would be really hard to know that you have someone in your family who was buried out here, but not know where they actually ended up, and/or having a place to visit,” student Deen Hooper said.
Biskis said the work is also about restoring dignity to the people buried there and their families.
The students will return to St. Louis Cemetery Wednesday to continue using GPS units to help locate and mark the graves.
They are expected to complete this portion of the Unmarked Graves Project by the end of the semester.
You can visit findagrave.com to search for your family members and learn more about where they're buried.

title: Did Maine state senators represent counties until the mid-1960s?
text:
Yes.
Until the mid-1960s, Maine senators represented counties rather than today’s population-based districts. Under the state constitution in effect in 1965, every county received one to five senators, depending on its population.
That system changed amid a national reapportionment revolution. In 1964, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Reynolds v. Sims that both chambers of state legislatures generally must be apportioned by population, establishing the principle commonly known as “one person, one vote.”
Maine voters responded in November 1966, approving a constitutional amendment that replaced county representation with senatorial districts centered around roughly 30,000 residents.
When lawmakers failed to agree on a map, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court stepped in and drew 32 districts in 1967.
Counties still played a role under the new maps, as the amendment instructed mapmakers to follow county lines as much as possible.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Billionaires and corporations have the money, but we still have the vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Joel Clement, the first federal whistleblower of the first Trump administration, is a 10th-generation Mainer who lives in Wayne.
It’s all blowing up. The TV, the radio, even my phone, with shrill political demands for my attention and my dollars. For a midterm election, this year feels a little more bonkers than usual, and the numbers bear it out; hundreds of millions of dollars for advertising in the state and one billionaire, the mercurial Elon Musk, has alone committed up to $120 million to support Susan Collins and other Republican candidates. Why have the warring voices risen to such a pitch in 2026?
There is always a lot at stake in the combative back and forth between political parties; power, business investment, social priorities and ideological influence to name a few. This time around, though, it feels like there is something else at stake, and it’s not about political games or who gets to lead agencies and make laws. This time it feels like it’s about us, about our ability to buy a house or rent an apartment, to afford a car or cover healthcare surprises. Finally, the focus seems to be landing where it belongs — the well-being of those who live in this state and this country.
As voters, we should keep it there.
The playing field has tilted toward corporations and billionaires for decades now, and they have a strong interest in keeping it that way. They also have seemingly endless resources to convince us that it’s in our best interests for them to get richer. The ruse was that if they get richer, we get richer. Well the first part held up — they got richer. According to Forbes, in 1982 there were 13 billionaires in the U.S. In 2026, there are 989.
Meanwhile, the middle-class share of the nation’s wealth has declined steadily. In 1990, the bottom 90% of American households owned substantially more wealth than the top 1%. Today, the top 1% owns more than the bottom 90% combined. Combined.
To make matters worse, tax cuts for the wealthy have led to dramatic cuts in services for the rest. Wonder why there was a dangerous cyclospora outbreak this year? Look to cuts at public health agencies. Wonder why the IRS is not chasing down sophisticated tax dodgers? Look to the IRS budget cuts. Wonder why disaster response has gotten worse as natural disasters increase in ferocity and impact? Look to the cuts to FEMA and the federal science agencies. Wonder why there is a national outcry against the proliferation of energy-sucking data centers? Look to cuts at the EPA and other agencies that would normally require permitting.
The data center invasion is emblematic of corporate influence. It’s a wild west out there for big tech as they build “hyperscale” data centers that consume the equivalent of entire cities — raising household electricity bills, fouling water supplies and turbocharging climate change. All this while providing comparatively few jobs and opportunities.
While big tech is getting handouts, it’s nearly impossible to find an affordable apartment in any of the larger cities in Maine, let alone buy a house. Wealthy investors are outbidding families and renters to buy up Maine’s real estate inventory for investment properties dedicated to short term rentals. As a result, historic Maine towns like Boothbay Harbor have become ghost towns in the winter while families and workers have long commutes from homes wherever they can find them.
All this while real wages are down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, and a doctor’s visit, if you can get one, costs so much that people are using the nearest emergency room as their primary care provider and hoping for the best.
So yeah, there’s a lot at stake in this election. The House, Senate, and governor’s races feature candidates who have Donald Trump’s endorsement, Elon Musk’s dollars and the support of billionaires and megacorporations. I don’t belong to a political party, but I sure don’t want the billionaires to think they can have Maine, and it seems these Republican candidates are ready to sell us out for pennies on the dollar. My dad, a lifelong Republican and fiscal conservative, is rolling in his grave.
So far our votes still matter, though. It’s the one thing the wealthy class hasn’t yet managed to take away, and it puts a lot of power in our hands. Voter fatigue is real this year, and it’s getting out of hand with all this advertising, but if all Mainers will make a plan to vote, and follow through, we can send the message that in 2026 the people, the 90%, expect more from our leaders.

title: 27K forested acres in western Maine are now protected for outdoor recreation
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
More than 27,000 acres of forest in western Maine are now permanently protected from development, The Conservation Fund announced Thursday.
The protected lands are centered around Bethel and include the former Chadbourne Tree Farm, along with properties added to existing preserves and public lands across the region.
The forests will remain working forests and open to the public, protecting wildlife habitat, clean water and outdoor access. The lands include portions of the Crooked, Androscoggin and Kezar rivers, and a new Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife boat launch at Songo Pond.
Chadbourne Tree Farm sits at the headwaters of the Sebago Lake watershed, which supplies drinking water to more than 200,000 people in the greater Portland area.
This conservation project also secures some of the remaining large pieces needed to connect Sunday River Resort and Mt. Abram with a continuous trail network for hikers, skiers and cyclists. The connected outdoor destination will provide year-round recreation between the two Bethel-area mountains.
The effort began in 2020, when The Conservation Fund and the Malone Family Land Preservation Foundation acquired 14,898 acres of Chadbourne Tree Farm. The purchase kept the large working forest intact while partners worked toward permanent conservation.
Since then, a coalition that includes Mahoosuc Land Trust, Greater Lovell Land Trust, Western Foothills Land Trust, Inland Woods + Trails, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands and the U.S. Forest Service has helped permanently protect additional lands across the region.
Those lands include 560 acres added to the Inland Woods + Trails Bethel Community Forest, more than 1,300 acres added to Western Foothills Land Trust preserves, more than 328 acres added to Greater Lovell Land Trust’s Kezar Corridor Lands, 600 acres added to White Mountain National Forest and 12,000 acres added to Mahoosuc Land Trust holdings. The Mahoosuc holdings include an 11,000-acre Crooked River Headwaters easement and a nearly 1,000-acre Tumbledown Dick Preserve in Gilead.
The permanent protections were made possible through the Land for Maine’s Future Program, the federal Forest Legacy Program and more than $10 million in private philanthropic support.

title: Obituary: Sarah Olive Perkins
text:
OXFORD – Sarah Olive Perkins, born March 19, 1931, died peacefully on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, at Market Square Health Care Center, where she had lived for the past four years.
Sarah was born and lived her entire life at the family farm in Oxford, Maine. She was a favorite aunt of dozens of nieces and nephews who lived locally and visited often from Connecticut, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Washington and Texas.
She was predeceased by eight siblings, Harrison, Ida (McMorran), Betty (Hunnewell), Elna (Marsh), Ray, Dorothy, Thomas and Ina (Brown). She is survived by many nieces, nephews; grand nieces and grand nephews. Her parents were Merle and Olive (Marcotte) Perkins.
Sarah worked at the Oxford Post Office for 26 years before becoming Post Master in September, 1980. She retired in September, 1986. Sarah’s hobbies included gardening, reading, walking in the woods, quilting and baking. She and her sisters Betty, Dorothy and Ina were active for many years in the Oxford Historical Society.
There will be a graveside service at 11 a.m. on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, at Highland Cemetery, Megquier Hill Rd., West Poland.
Arrangements are under the care of Chandler Funeral Home, 45 Main St., South Paris. Online condolences may be shared at http://www.chandlerfunerals.com.

donations may be made to:

title: US newlyweds tour Croatia after fans photobomb their wedding shoot
text:
SPLIT, Croatia (AP) — It began with a hijacked wedding photo shoot and turned into a very unexpected but exciting trip across the world.
Ashton and Zachary Smith from Philadelphia are guests in Croatia this week after the couple accidentally celebrated their wedding in June with a crowd of joyful Croatian soccer fans during the FIFA World Cup in the United States.
The Smiths had just gotten married and came out of Philadelphia City Hall to take photos when hundreds of Croats in red-and-white chequered jerseys joined in. Photos and videos of the couple kissing among the fans became popular on social networks and paved the way for a new friendship.
“It was so crazy, we just finished our ceremony, we went outside to take some pictures in front of City Hall,” Ashton Smith recalled. “We were warned that the road was taken over but we’re like, oh, let’s just try it anyway.”
It was “the best decision that we ever could have made” despite the initial shock, she said.
“Everyone stormed us,” Ashton Smith added. “At first we were like, oh my gosh I hope everyone is with us. But everyone was there, everyone was celebrating with us and it was just amazing how welcoming they were to complete strangers.”
Months later, the couple received an equally warm welcome in the Croatian town of Split, located on the Adriatic Sea coast. The Croatian National Tourist Board and the Mi Hrvati, or We Croats, fan group invited the Smiths over for a “second honeymoon.”
“I feel amazing,” Ashton said in an interview earlier this week. “We learned a lot of history about Croatia and now the vibes are immaculate.”
Ashton and Zachary joined the fans’ march along the city’s waterfront ahead of Croatia’s UEFA Nations League match against Spain on Tuesday. A band played, the fans sang and the couple quickly fitted in. Later in the evening, they also attended the match.
“The fans are so energetic,” Ashton said. “They brought the same energy that they did in Philly.”
Daniel Pedisic of the Mi Hrvati association said the spontaneous way Croatian fans reacted to the wedding in Philadelphia showed “the kind of people we are, warm, hospitable people.”
“We were with them that day and now we brought them to Croatia,” Pedisic added, whose association follows the team worldwide and is known for carrying a 100-meter Croatian flag.
The trip also took the Smiths to the coastal town of Sibenik and included a sailing trip and a tour of the stunning Krka National Park. On Friday, the couple will travel to the famous medieval walled city of Dubrovnik in the southern Adriatic, before ending their trip in the capital, Zagreb.
“Technically, this is our second honeymoon because we had a pre-planned one before the wedding,” Ashton said. “The first one was laid back and relaxing, and this one is kind of go, go, go, and we absolutely love it.”
Zachary Smith said he had never expected to visit Croatia, which is located in southeastern Europe.
“I knew all about Croatia, where it was, the country obviously,” he said. “But (I) never really thought that I would ever make it here, so it’s amazing.”

title: Susan Collins’ campaign needs to be more forthcoming
text:
In his recent op-ed column (“Susan Collins’ donors are the people we need to be worrying about,” Nov. 9) Maurice Cunningham makes a valid point that the bigger scandals in politics are the perfectly legal pay-to-play dark money contributions.
Cunningham cites, among others, Peter Thiel’s Palantir, which he characterizes as “a virtual partner of the government” with millions in contracts, including $200 million with ICE, and whose employees have given $117,000 to Collins’ political committees.
But legal scandals should not deter us from scrutinizing and holding accountable illegal ones.
Collins’ campaign officials object to reports of a $150,000 illegal campaign contribution from the CEO of the defense contractor Navatek and alleged reciprocation through government contract awards worth millions, claiming that the FBI investigated and dropped its inquiry. But they tend to fail to note that Trump’s FBI later backed off, and, meanwhile ProPublica’s reporting has presented receipts, including in the form of a check to a Collins-affiliated entity.
The Collins campaign needs to be more forthcoming. Voters heading to the ballot box have a right to know whether this “Navagate” scandal is real and what is says about who Collins’ true constituents are.
Nelson Checkoway
Ogunquit

Army finds systemic failures behind DC midair collision and calls for safety fixes
text:
(AP) - The U.S. Army found many systemic breakdowns that led to last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended numerous steps the military should take to prevent future tragedies.
Families of some of the 67 people who died have been pressuring the Army for months to release the report, which was completed in May. The Associated Press obtained a copy from them Thursday morning, a few hours before the Army made it public.
The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River.
The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Reagan National Airport could have prevented the crash, but also acknowledged the military’s own failings and other contributing factors.
The Army and victims’ families both say they want transparency
Former Army Black Hawk pilot Tim Lilley, whose son Sam Lilley was the first officer on the American Airlines jet, said he needs more details from the military. Some information in the report was redacted, and the military assigned responsibility for its shortcomings broadly across the Army.
“The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again,” said Lilley, who is a commercial jet captain today.
The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday afternoon.
“We recognize the families’ need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army’s review,” the Army said.
The report identifies key factors in the crash
While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board’s conclusions, the civilian investigation was broader and emphasized years of warning signs missed by the Federal Aviation Administration, along with a weak military safety culture.
The Army report recommended that the military look beyond Washington to make sure similar risks aren’t present in every major city where its helicopters operate. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the situation.
The lieutenant general who authored the report said “breakdowns across all layers of conflict management caused this accident,” but, “the most salient contributing factor was the two broken radio transmissions” that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying Flight 5342 as it was circling to land on the airport’s alternate runway. The military pilots were wearing night-vision goggles that limited their field of vision and made it difficult to spot the plane amid the lights of the city.
The poorly designed helicopter route in use at the time of the crash provided only a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on Reagan’s secondary runway, and that was only true if the helicopter stuck to the riverbank. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk’s altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read.
NTSB says the Army is making progress on safety
The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that the agency is pleased with the progress being made on seven of the eight recommendations to the Army. That contrasts with the FAA, which the NTSB has faulted for failing to implement roughly one-third of the recommendations to that safety regulator.
The Army report said the controller should have provided the helicopter crew with more details about exactly where the plane was to help the pilots spot it, and the controller should have warned the plane about the helicopter headed toward it. The FAA has prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace since this crash.
The Army said it strengthened its training for helicopter crews after the crash. Once it became apparent that the ADS-B Out system on the Black Hawk that can broadcast its location was inoperable, all 3,585 affected Army helicopters were inspected and reconfigured. The Army is also working to improve the way it monitors safety concerns and reach an agreement with the FAA to share information about close calls.
Victims’ families push for aviation safety reform bill
The main group of families of passengers on the plane, who were flying from Wichita, Kansas, said the report reinforces their call for Congress to pass aviation safety reforms and require aircraft to be equipped with systems that will help pilots know where traffic in the air is.
“It’s a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing,” the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday.
“We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for,” they said.
Both the House and Senate passed different aviation safety bills, but lawmakers are still working on a compromise piece of legislation to bring up for a vote in both houses of Congress.
___
Associated Press Writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.

title: Did Maine state senators represent counties until the mid-1960s?
text:
Yes.
Until the mid-1960s, Maine senators represented counties rather than today’s population-based districts. Under the state constitution in effect in 1965, every county received one to five senators, depending on its population.
That system changed amid a national reapportionment revolution. In 1964, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Reynolds v. Sims that both chambers of state legislatures generally must be apportioned by population, establishing the principle commonly known as “one person, one vote.”
Maine voters responded in November 1966, approving a constitutional amendment that replaced county representation with senatorial districts centered around roughly 30,000 residents.
When lawmakers failed to agree on a map, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court stepped in and drew 32 districts in 1967.
Counties still played a role under the new maps, as the amendment instructed mapmakers to follow county lines as much as possible.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: How the Senate race in Texas could impact the balance of power in Congress
text:
How could the Senate race in Texas impact the balance of power in Congress?
President Donald Trump visited Texas for the second time in a week, urging voters to support Republicans in the midterms as a competitive Senate race and low approval ratings pose challenges.
How could the Senate race in Texas impact the balance of power in Congress?
President Donald Trump visited Texas for the second time in a week, urging voters to support Republicans in the midterms as a competitive Senate race and low approval ratings pose challenges.
President Donald Trump returned to Texas for the second time in less than a week, rallying voters to support Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections on Nov. 3.
The Senate race in Texas is highly competitive, with Republican and former Attorney General Ken Paxton facing off against Democrat James Talarico. A win for Talarico could have a major impact on the policies the Trump administration is trying to carry out.
"It's basically one vote. It's so important. Forget about 'for Texas,' it's still just one vote. It's a killer in Congress because we have a very close majority. We can't let that happen," Trump said.
The president is on the road for a 32-day campaign blitz, but his efforts come amid challenges, including the Iran war in its seventh month, rising gas prices, and a rocky approval rating.
A recent NBC News poll found that 39% of Americans approve of the job Trump is doing, while 59% disapprove. The same poll showed that 52% of Americans prefer a Congress controlled by Democrats, while 43% want Republicans to hold the balance of power.
Trump is scheduled to continue campaigning this weekend, with multiple reports indicating he will host another rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday.

title: MDI summer residents complain about construction noise
text:
Towns on Mount Desert Island often have occasional noise complaints. In Bar Harbor (and last year in Tremont), those complaints tend to be about live music being played in restaurants.
The town of Mount Desert, though, is a bit different.
The complaints in Mount Desert tend to be about construction noise.
This summer most of those complaints focused around Seal Harbor, where there were multiple projects. There was blasting, drilling and other construction noise.
At least one property owner affected by the construction would like the town to have a noise ordinance to help with communication around the disruptions.
“I understand that up to this date, September 20, 2026, there is no noise ordinance or rules around dynamiting for the Town of Mt. Desert. Communications about concerns are managed by the residents, both those under construction and their neighbors,” Marnie Phillips wrote.
An ordinance is needed for the town, she explained, so that there are rules to help property owners navigate the situations.
“Some folks will send out a letter to neighbors advising them of their plans and providing a phone number if there is an issue. Other folks under construction have no regard for neighbors and the disruption. I am a summer resident of Seal Harbor, and there are currently a minimum of six on-going construction projects. There is no guidance given as to the level of noise or the time of noise. While I understand that construction projects are a reality, many of us are trying to enjoy this beautiful place and work from our homes,” she said.
The construction, she wrote, “would be tolerable with rules for everyone.”
She asked for an ordinance with guidelines for timeframes for different types of work.
“It would be beneficial to all to have noise ordinance guidelines which covers both timeframes for regular work, shorter timeframes for noises over a given decibel level e.g. jackhammering ledge, and notification of all dynamiting. Over the last 4-5 years, our house has shaken and doors have slammed due to dynamiting. On some occasions we received notification of the dynamiting and a company came and inspected our premises prior to the event. In other cases, the dynamiting just occurred. Given the small area in which this dynamiting is occurring, it would be difficult to prove which project caused what damage. There could be structural issues to homes with no ramifications for the people doing the dynamiting. Residents and their homes should be protected,” she wrote.
No action on her request was taken during the Tuesday Mount Desert Select Board meeting.
“So, the comment I guess I would make is that as much as last summer may have been a lot about traffic and parking, this summer was definitely the summer of noise complaints and people. This is about the third or fourth request for a noise ordinance that I received over the course of the summer. This is just the first one where she wanted to put it into the minutes. Every one of them is related to construction noise, every single complaint,” Town Manager Alex Kimball told the Select Board.
“And it’s tricky because in the grand scheme of things that tend to follow the law of unintended consequences, there’s noise ordinances first and foremost above all else. Noise ordinances can quickly turn into something other than their intended use: two neighbors who just start checking each other’s decibel levels incessantly and coming back and forth after each other and stuff like that. But that being said, it’s really been all about the construction noise. Seal Harbor in particular, but in some of the places in Northeast Harbor, blasting and requests for time limits on when those noises can occur. So, [it’s a] tricky thing because noise ordinances can run amuck very fast if we’re not careful with them. But I did want to mention this isn’t the only one. It’s been a pretty regular series of comments on it over the summer,” Kimball added.
Vice Chair Wendy Littlefield asked if there were rules and regulations around blasting.
Public Works Director Brian Henkel said he wasn’t sure of the details of exactly how far the radius is for notifications of adjacent landowners, but there are requirements that they have to do with noise and also potential damage to other structures close to the blasting site.
“No matter what a person does and goes through all those things and no matter how much you hear the blast and how much you know it’s coming, and then it happens and your whole house shakes, it’s always going to be upsetting no matter what,” Kimball said.
A primary problem has been construction noise starting before 7 a.m. Kimball suggested that if the board picked one aspect of the situation to tackle that this might be the one.
He said he’d be hesitant on nighttime caps.
“That’s where things tend to get ugly sometimes,” he said.
Nighttime caps exist in Bar Harbor’s ordinance on special amusement permits and its general noise ordinance. The special amusement ordinance regulates amplified music decibel levels for special amusement permitholders. The general noise ordinance regulates many other types of noise, including construction, and generally prohibits them from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m.
Member David MacDonald said he was sympathetic to Phillips’ plight.
“It seems to be that we’ve reached a bit of a tipping point in terms of the old systems no longer doing what they were intended to do, as informal as they might have been,” MacDonald said.

title: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be “public.”
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego.
When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3rd.”
Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan.
Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action. Those warnings preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran at the end of February over its ballistic missiles and the risk of it developing nuclear weapons.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on Jan. 14 of this year. “It’s stopping and there’s no plan for executions.”
He repeated that claim on Jan. 20 at a White House press briefing, saying: “We let them know that if that happens, that will be a very bad day for them. And they decided not to do it. They didn’t hang the people.”
Slightly more than a month later in his State of the Union address, Trump said, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”
The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
However, experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.
During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor.
Soldiers later testified that Hasan’s rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting. Investigators recovered 146 shell casings inside the building and dozens more outside, where Hasan shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a servicemember by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

title: Man allegedly threatened 3 women with a gun in South Thomaston
text:
SOUTH THOMASTON, Maine — A South Thomaston man was arrested Tuesday after allegedly threatening three women with a gun.
Aiden J. Woodward, 23, was charged with one count of felony domestic violence criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and two counts of felony criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon.
Justice Sarah Gilbert set bail Wednesday at $2,000 cash for Woodward during his initial appearance in the state court in Knox County. Assistant District Attorney Christopher Fernald sought $2,500 in bail, while defense attorney for the day Gregory Snow requested $1,000 bail.
According to an affidavit filed in court by the Knox County Sheriff’s Office, a woman said she and two other women went to a house in South Thomaston where Woodward was. When the women arrived, Woodward was outside by his truck, reached into the truck and pulled out a pistol, and racked the slide. He then pointed the gun at the women and at the car they came in. Inside the vehicle was an 18-month-old child.
A friend of Woodward came out of the house wielding a metal pipe. When the woman told Woodward her child was in the car, Woodward backed off and the women left, according to the affidavit.
They then went to Rockland and contacted police.
Woodward denied to police that he pulled back on the slide of the pistol and denied pointing it at anyone.
