title: Fatal Ellsworth crash damages recovery home, displacing six men early Thursday
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - A man died and another was seriously injured early Thursday after authorities say their vehicle crashed into two homes in Ellsworth.
One of the homes was vacant. The second was home to six men with Refuge Recovery Housing.
Nobody in the recovery house was injured, but the crash left the home uninhabitable.
“That was my first thought, just the safety of the people in the program,” said Daniel Stewart, executive director of Refuge Recovery Housing.
Stewart said he searched overnight for hotel rooms during peak leaf-peeping season.
“I was up all night trying to find a hotel. This time of year is a very difficult thing to do in that in this area. So, we were actually after picking them up at 1:00 in the morning, we probably spent several hours driving to every hotel motel that we could find in the area and every single place was booked up,” Stewart said.
Stewart said he eventually found a hotel on Mount Desert Island and later found a temporary place for the men to stay while the organization rebuilds.
“I think that as terrible as this is, I do believe that things, the good things can come from this and seeing the community come together is just, it’s always good to see even under the worst circumstances,” Stewart said.
Stewart said he is nearing 10 years sober and that incidents like this remind him why his work matters.
“I mean, sometimes I just wonder how am I one of the lucky ones, right? Because so many people don’t make it. And so my takeaway that I hope that the people in recovery, especially the men in our program who are seeking recovery right now is just that this really is, this is a life or death. Our decisions matter,” Stewart said.
Stewart said the damage to the house is a setback for the organization but called it a motivator to continue its work.
“We’re not going to let this stop us or even slow us down. If anything, we’re going to use this to motivate us, to open up more homes, to provide more resources, to get the community even more involved in supporting one another because we know this can happen. But, it’s going to take everybody coming together and saying, we’ve had enough of this. We’ve had enough of just watching just addiction and all of just the drugs and alcohol running rampant in our communities, just the destruction and everything that it’s caused. We’ve had enough, and we’re going to do everything we can and save as many people as possible,” Stewart said.
Police said a passenger in the car that hit the house, 23-year-old Paul Meservey of Orrington, was killed in the crash.
The driver, 19-year-old Landon Rockwell of Dedham, was flown to a Bangor hospital. There has been no update on his condition.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: ‘Medieval Times’ Restaurant Will Get Its Own Movie
text:
‘Medieval Times’ Restaurant Will Get Its Own Movie
Welcome to Medievaaaaaaaaal Tiiiiiiiiiimes! (The movie.)
In news that will make you wonder “Is everything IP now?” comes word that Paramount is in “early development” on what is described as a “live-action, four-quadrant, family comedy” based on the Medieval Times themed restaurant. That’s the one where guests show up to a building that looks like a castle, and then dine on rustic fare with zero utensils (you gotta slurp your soup straight out of the bowl) while watching a performance featuring knights on horseback competing in various ancient games of sport.
The first Medieval Times opened in Florida in 1983 and there are now ten of them in the United States and Canada. The film version, according to Deadline, will take a fantasy/time travel approach to the material:
When a struggling employee at the Orlando Medieval Times accidentally unleashes a real 9th-century knight, along with an ancient evil necromancer, he has to team up with the feral warrior to save the castle, then the world, and finally win the respect he’s always craved.
The project will be directed by Eric Appel, who made the “Weird Al” Yankovic biopic spoof Weird and recently directed Nate Bargatze’s The Breadwinner. The project’s screenplay was written by Blaise Hemingway.
I went to Medieval Times a couple of (medieval) times as a kid, and I saw this television commercial growing up in suburban New Jersey about 6,000,000,000 times.
READ MORE: A Brief History of Movie Tie-In Foods and Products
While many children of the ’80s and ’90s have fond memories of the jousts and sword fights and paper crowns at Medieval Times, the brand’s biggest pop culture legacy remains its inclusion in the Jim Carrey movie The Cable Guy, where Carrey’s character takes his buddy for a night out to the restaurant, and then manages to get the two of them inserted into the show
Believe it or not, this is not the first time that the Hollywood trades have reported about a potential Medieval Times movie in development. Way back in 2013, we got word of a similar Medieval Times project that never got off the ground. Will this batch of filmmakers have more luck? They might; Hollywood’s even more IP crazy than they were 13 years ago.
All I have to say is: I am already sweating bullets about the potential tie-in menu opportunities.

title: Nearly 43,000 mowers recalled for fire risks. What to do if you have one
text:
(CPSC/CNN) - Nearly 43,000 DR Power Equipment Pilot and Premier trimmer mowers have been recalled due to a fire risk.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission said grass and debris can accumulate in the mowers and ignite into flames.
The issue could lead to injury, burn hazards, and even death from a fire.
The recall affects eight models of trimmer mowers.
They were sold at hardware stores nationwide and online from November 2022 through July of 2026.
There have been 19 reports of the product catching fire, with two reports of minor burn injuries.
Customers are urged to stop using the products.
The company is offering free repair kits or installations from an authorized dealer.

title: Obituary: Thomas R. Carter
text:
BETHEL – Thomas R. Carter died on his wood lot near home on Sept. 29, 2026. He was in his favorite place, doing his favorite activity. He was born on April 27, 1939, in Berlin, NH to T. Richard and F. Lyndell (Cotton) Carter.
After graduating from Gould Academy in 1958, he joined the army and served in the reserves until 1965. While in high school, he drove a school bus and bought his first car. He was employed as a driver and a mechanic for all of his life. He worked for his uncle, Paul Carter’s Garage before going to work for Maine D.O.T. In his retirement, he drove buses for the Appalachian Mountain Club and the Sunday River Shuttle.
His hobbies centered on the outdoors or mechanics. He had trucks, cars, motorcycles, boats, and snowmobiles. He enjoyed gardening, hiking, fishing, cross-country skiing, and working in the woods with his bulldozer and backhoe. He shared his hobbies with his children and grandchildren and encouraged them to get outside as often as possible. He loved a good home-cooked meal, especially if it included pie and coffee.
Thomas is survived by his daughters, Pamela Carter and her husband Bill Allen of Bethel, and Lorna Lee Dunn and her husband Jeff of Raymond; his grandchildren, Cameron Stephen Taylor and his wife Kelly of Saco, Joshua Taylor and his partner Hannah Maxbauer of Edmunds, Wash., Benjamin Taylor of Portland, Nicholas Taylor and his wife Kelsey of Durham, NH, Trevor Saremi of Lewiston, Audrey Saremi of Auburn; and four great-grandchildren, Sam, Andrew, Emery, and Liam.
He was predeceased by his parents and three brothers, Timothy, David, and Stephen.
A celebration of life will be held in the spring of 2027. Coffee and pie will be served.
Arrangements are under the care of Chandler Funeral Home and Cremation Service, 45 Main St., South Paris. Online condolences may be shared at http://www.chandlerfunerals.com.

title: Woman arrested after 6 children found unsupervised in ‘unlivable’ home, barely clothed, police say
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV/Gray News) - A Florida woman is facing several charges after officers say they found a half-dozen children unsupervised and living in deplorable conditions.
Jamie Jakes, 30, was arrested by the Tallahassee Police Department over the weekend on six counts of child neglect.
Authorities said the situation started when patrolling officers noticed a vehicle turn and swerve onto the curve early Sunday morning to barely avoid hitting a child.
Officers said they made contact with the child and took them home. But that’s when they found children who appeared to be unsupervised at the residence, with one wearing only pants and others wearing soiled diapers.
Tallahassee police said they tried to locate clothes, but only found shoes and parts of clothing because the rest were wet and smelled of mildew.
The responding officers reported finding the home to be “unlivable,” with feces, urine and spoiled food, without having anything edible in the refrigerator.
Jakes was said to have left the home a few hours before officers arrived. Police said they came into contact with her when she returned to the house at about 6 a.m.
Jakes told officers she paid someone $150 a week to watch the children, but that person told officers that this was not true, police said.
Court documents stated that Jakes also claimed that the house was clean the day prior, but officers said the feces and urine on the floor did not match that timing.
Jakes was taken into custody and booked into jail by Tallahassee police.

title: Watch tonight’s high stakes debates for governor, senate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The candidates running in Maine’s two highest profile races are debating tonight, back-to-back.
First, at 7 p.m., the candidates for governor — Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and Independent Rick Bennett — will meet in Bangor for a debate hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public, and NEWSCENTER Maine.
Then, at 8 p.m., Senate candidates Troy Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins will square off in their second debate in three days on WMTW.
We will stream both debates, back-to-back, right here — along with live updates starting at 6:30.
We’ll see you there.
And just like that, it’s over!
Thanks so much for following along with us tonight. It was a marathon double debate session. See you at the next one.
-Kirby Wilson
-Both candidates essentially said they don’t use artificial intelligence for major daily tasks
-The candidates said they disagree on term limits for senators and Supreme Court justices. (Jackson is in favor of both, Collins is opposed to both.)
-Kirby Wilson
Collins countered by saying appropriations doesn’t have jurisdiction over tariffs, but she’s working with the Trump administration to try to get some of them lifted.
-Drew Johnson
Collins said ICE does need reforms, including restrictions on where the agency should conduct arrests. But she said the agency shouldn’t be abolished. A similar exchange happened last debate as well.
-Kirby Wilson
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better, hers has gotten worse.”
“She’s made sure that, I think she’s put 55 anti-abortion judges onto the courts, including Brett Kavanaugh, that she knew that he was anti-abortion and that was what he was going to do when he got there, and he did.” Jackson continued.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
“When Donald Trump wants something, Sen. Collins will not stop him,” he said.
-Kirby Wilson
The candidates agree on something!
Jackson and Collins agree that high earners should pay a greater share of their income to Social Security. This may be the first moment of agreement all night.
-Kirby Wilson
This is another familiar theme: Collins says Jackson and Augusta leaders are to blame for Maine’s cost-of-living woes. Jackson says D.C. politicians and Collins are.
-Drew Johnson
Collins shot back that policies that Jackson advocated for have caused premiums to spike in Maine.
-Kirby Wilson
“To say that my husband and I are making money off the war in Iran is absolutely outrageous,” Collins said.
This was one of the most striking moments of the debate so far.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
“I have been the leading proponent” of the program in Congress, argued Collins, and said they could expand the program.
Collins also emphasized that “we have a supply problem” and that the United States needs to become “energy independent.”
-Drew Johnson
“People are going to freeze to death this winter because they can’t afford to heat their home,” Jackson said.
-Kirby Wilson
“He’s in jail today, where he belongs,” Collins said.
Jackson insisted the allegations aren’t false, before turning to what he said was Collins’ proximity to Donald Trump, who he emphasized is “a convicted felon.”
-Drew Johnson
Collins keeps it much more positive, noting some of her signature legislative accomplishments, and saying they came because of her seniority and her connections.
-Kirby Wilson
The Senate debate is underway!
We don’t have a moment to rest. It’s time for Troy Jackson vs. Susan Collins, round two.
Bennett and Pingree played their closing statements much straighter, asking viewers for their vote.
-Kirby Wilson
Charles said he opposed late-term abortions but attempted to sidestep the question somewhat, saying “there are a ton of issues that are confronting us” and that “this is not the number one issue.” When pressed for an answer, he again said he opposes late-term abortions.
“There is only one Bobby Charles, and he is perfectly consistent,” Charles said, noting that he’s long been critical of Trump’s Canada tariffs, for example.
Then he pivoted to criticizing Pingree some more. He’s staying on the attack.
-Kirby Wilson
Bennett on why he left the GOP
When asked why he left the Republican party to run as an independent, Bennet said he once believed that parties were “a vehicle for participation” in the political process, but that is no longer the case.
“Both parties are more interested in keeping us fighting with each other than actually resolving issues,” Bennett said.
“Hannah talks more about Trump than Trump talks about himself,” Charles said.
-Kirby Wilson
A $1 billion budget shortfall?
This part of the night could make news: What are the candidates’ plans to fight the state’s potential $1 billion budget shortfall? Not sure we’ve heard from the candidates on this point.
-Kirby Wilson
Charles said he does not support the expansion.
“I would say we made a fundamental error,” Charles said of expanding MaineCare, noting that able-bodied Mainers are taking advantage of the program, which has become underfunded.
-Kirby Wilson
“I would argue that Biddeford probably wouldn’t have had happened if the sanctuary state law didn’t exist here, because the comms, they were sidelined. The comms between local and state and feds would have been clear,” Charles said.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
He argued that “Biddeford probably wouldn’t have had happened” if the various law enforcement agencies involved if there were better lines of communication.
-Drew Johnson
The candidates start with substance
Quite a substantive start, so far! Bad times for those who want to see name calling.
-Kirby Wilson
Among other priorities, Pingree said DEP permits should get a 90-day “shot clock,” noting that Maine needs to incentivize more housing on the supply side. She plugged her housing plan, which you can find here.
And Bennett said the state should reduce down payments for first time home buyers. He also said the state should assist with mortgage payments.
He addressed the supply side challenges of housing as well, arguing the state should increase factory-build housing.
-Kirby Wilson
And we’re off!
The gubernatorial debate has started. This debate is brought to you by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine.
-Kirby Wilson

title: Lapse in federal funding for traumatic brain injury research leaves millions without support
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Aging Untold) — A traumatic brain injury, or TBI, can change a life in seconds.
Between 1 and 3 million people visit emergency rooms each year with a concussion — a mild form of TBI — according to the Cleveland Clinic. While TBIs are especially common in young athletes, experts say they often occur far outside of sports.
The number of TBI cases is rising, approaching 3 million per year. Older adults 75 and up account for nearly a third of TBI-related hospitalizations, largely due to fall risk.
A law that expired
The Traumatic Brain Injury Act, first signed in 1996, provided federal funding for research, resources and advocacy. But the act expired in 2024.
“The pause in federal funding is very scary,” Maureen Cunningham, executive director of the Brain Injury Association of America’s Missouri chapter, said. “There’s going to be limited research, so the advances that have been made in research related to brain injury and living life with brain injury are going to stop.”
Survivors speak out
At a TBI survivor camp in Kansas City, the stakes are personal. Mike Caton, who survived a workplace accident in 2005 when a rod went through his head, lost much of his memory and can no longer work. His wife, Mary, said the injury changed him profoundly.
“They tell me it went through his brain and came back out,” she said.
Steven Garman, 39, sustained his TBI in a car crash and still deals with seizures and speech difficulties. His mother, Barbara, said the camp offers her a rare moment of relief.
“I can relax. I don’t have to be on guard all the time,” she said.
Kate Hwang, a former Kansas City, Missouri, police officer, suffered a TBI in 2003 after being attacked while writing a ticket. The injury forced her into early retirement.
“I had seizures, headaches, there was personality change in the beginning and depression,” Hwang said. “These programs mean a lot to people like me, the people behind me, and we need assistance past the initial injury.”
A bill in Congress
Rep. Frank Pallone is sponsoring the TBI Reauthorization Act, which he introduced in February 2025. Despite bipartisan support, it did not pass. He is hopeful it will advance in 2026.
“I think a lot of it is that people don’t recognize this as a disorder,” Pallone said. “And so an important part of it is not only providing services to people and advocacy, but also recognizing that traumatic brain injury exists as a phenomena.”

title: Straw vote on exploring regional high school takes next step
text:
The non-binding question on exploring a regional high school got its second nod Aug. 4. Wiscasset selectmen last month decided to put the question on the Nov. 3 ballot. And last week, they approved the municipal officers' order to make that happen.
The question reads: "Should Wiscasset explore the possibility of a single regional high school serving students from multiple area towns?"
By Maine law, the town clerk needed the order at least 60 days before Election Day.
The order passed 5-0, with no new comment from the board or public. Selectman Sarah Whitfield has said those who'd helped Boothbay Region Schools and Wiscasset pursue a state grant for a consolidated grades nine through 16 school sense the towns still want to explore an option. The grant try ended when a win looked unlikely. Whitfield has described the November question as a survey.
Also Aug. 4, Economic Development Director Aaron Chrostowsky announced a 3 p.m. Aug. 25 workshop at Scout Hall, on the local strategic energy planning being aided by the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project. Selectmen's Chair Alissa Eason told residents, "Your voice and your opinions and your thoughts and your questions will help shape this project."
Selectmen nodded business licenses for Kindred Kneads Massage, 80 Main St.; Restore & Thrive Massage Therapy, 239 Birch Point Road; and Zachari Dalton, 16 Shady Lane. Dalton’s license request describes the business as “retail of my own commercially dug clams.”

title: Bangor police arrest alleged rock-throwing Presque Isle man
text:
Bangor police arrested a Presque Isle man on Wednesday for assault and resisting arrest.
A caller reported that Benjamin Brigman, 24, was throwing rocks at a vehicle outside a Main Street restaurant at about 6:35 a.m.
A woman called the Bangor Police Department about the man and reported he hit her and ran away, but continued to throw things, police said.
Officers arrived to find a man matching the description “screaming and flailing,” police said. The man ran from them, but they caught him and identified him as Brigman, whom they described as a transient.
Brigman was charged with disorderly conduct, assault and refusing to submit to arrest.
Assault, a Class D misdemeanor, carries a punishment of up to one year of incarceration and up to a $2,000 fine. On the other two charges, which are Class E crimes, Brigman could face up to six months imprisonment and up to a $1,000 fine for each.

title: Curtis Flowers, a Black man whose death sentence was tossed by Supreme Court, dies in Mississippi
text:
Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the U.S. Supreme Court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died. He was 56.
Flowers’ family confirmed that he died Wednesday at his home in Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told The Associated Press Thursday.
No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers’ legal team.
Flowers was 26 when he was arrested several months after the July 1996 shooting deaths of four people inside a Winona, Mississippi, furniture store.
At the time, prosecutors described him as a disgruntled former employee who sought revenge against the store’s owner because she fired him and withheld most of his pay to cover the cost of merchandise he damaged. Nearly $300 was found missing after the killings.
Flowers was tried in the killings six times. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the high court’s 7-2 decision in 2019 that the removal of Black prospective jurors deprived Flowers of a fair trial.
During the sixth trial in 2010, Flowers was sentenced to death. There were 11 white jurors and one Black juror who considered the case after District Attorney Doug Evans struck five Black prospective jurors.
Flowers remained in prison for six months after the Supreme Court ruling because he was still under indictment. He finally was released in December 2019 after a judge set bond.
Mississippi dropped charges against Flowers in September 2020.
“Today, I am finally free from the injustice that left me locked in a box for nearly twenty three years,” Flowers said in a statement. “I’ve been asked if I ever thought this day would come. I have been blessed with a family that never gave up on me and with them by my side, I knew it would.”
The legal team that represented Flowers for more than two decades said Thursday in a statement that each member feels “privileged to have called him a client.”
“Later, in the years after his release and exoneration, we felt equally honored to call him a friend,” the legal team said. “No matter where he was — on death row, at home on his parents’ porch with his feet up, singing in church, or fishing in a local pond — Curtis shared his light.”
The trials stretched back more than 20 years. The records showed Evans’ “relentless, determined effort to rid the jury of black individuals,” with the goal of an all-white jury, Kavanaugh wrote.
In the earlier trials, three convictions were tossed out, including one when the prosecutor improperly excluded African Americans from the jury. In the second trial, the judge chided Evans for striking a juror based on race. Two other trials ended when jurors couldn’t reach unanimous verdicts.
Kavanaugh noted that Evans had removed 41 of the 42 prospective Black jurors over the six trials.
Flowers filed a lawsuit in 2021 against Evans and three investigators who worked with the district attorney. The suit claimed Evans and the investigators engaged in misconduct, including “pressuring witnesses to fabricate claims about seeing Mr. Flowers in particular locations on the day of the murders” and ignoring other possible suspects.
Earlier that year, a judge ordered the state of Mississippi to pay Flowers $500,000 for wrongful imprisonment — the maximum under a state law that allows up to $50,000 a year for 10 years.
Evans retired in 2023 after more than 30 years as district attorney. His jury selection tactics had been scrutinized for years.
Flowers’ name is “etched into U.S. Supreme Court jurisprudence — about what it means to fight for a fair trial free from racial bias in the selection of jurors,” Flowers’ legal team said. “And also for that, but for so many other reasons, his name is etched into our memories, too — professional and personal. We will miss him.”
___
Williams is a member of AP’s Race & Ethnicity team. He reported from Detroit.

title: Scarborough girls soccer scrapes past South Portland
text:
SCARBOROUGH — There isn’t much that can happen in 14 seconds, but momentum in a soccer game can certainly shift in that short amount of time.
South Portland thought it had seized momentum Thursday against Scarborough when sophomore Sasha Neff scored to tie the Class A South girls soccer match. The Red Storm, though, quickly regained the upper hand, as Molly Igneri scored the winning goal just 14 seconds later in a 2-1 victory.
“We know South Portland is a good team,” said Igneri, a junior forward. “We know we’re gonna get the next (goal).”
When the whistle blew to resume play after Neff’s goal, Scarlett Floyd quickly took possession and passed it to Igneri, who scraped a shot past Maizie Savage.
The first half was quiet in comparison, with Scarborough (10-0-1), the four-time defending Class A South champion, holding South Portland (7-2-2) without a shot.
“Our halftime talk really helped us,” Scarborough back Amarine Laine said. “ We talked about what we need to work better on, playing different runs, keeping our minds cleared, focusing on what we have to do.”
The Red Storm, ranked No. 2 in the Varsity Maine Top 10, took the lead when forward Abby Roberts scored less than four minute into the second half.
“ I haven’t been having the best shots recently,” Roberts said. “It really helped with my confidence, and I’m just lucky to be at the right place at the right time.”
The Red Storm knew, despite their limited chances, they would take advantage of what opportunties they had.
“Sooner or later, those shots are going to go in,” Igneri said. “We just worked really hard as a team to make it happen.”
Unsung heroes
• South Portland: Rylin Small single-handedly stopped multiple runs from Scarborough and was a key reason why the Red Storm only had three shots in the first half.
• Scarborough: Laine stopped multiple potentially fruitful runs by South Portland and clogged the passing lanes.
Stat leaders
• South Portland: Sasha Neff (goal), Charlie Savage (assist), Maizie Savage (six saves)
• Scarborough: Abby Roberts (goal), Molly Igneri (goal), Gwen Martin (assist), Scarlett Floyd (assist), Vera DiSotto (three saves)

title: Knowing your family health history matters more than you may think
text:
(Aging Untold) — At almost every doctor’s visit, you’re asked about your family health history. But if you don’t know the answers, or you rush through the form, you might be missing one of the most powerful tools available for predicting and preventing disease.
Why family history matters
“Family history can give you a clue years before disease becomes obvious,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers said people often confuse two different questions when thinking about family history: what diseases run in the family, versus what a relative ultimately died from.
“Are you asking what diseases run in your family? Or are you simply just saying, this is what my relative died from, that disease,” Rogers said. “And those two are not necessarily the same.”
She said it’s important to identify patterns in conditions such as heart disease and strokes, particularly when they occur at a very early age, as well as cancers, autoimmune disorders, depression and thyroid diseases.
“All those different things can become significant if you see a pattern of them,” Rogers said.
Genes, genomics and epigenetics
Most diseases, Rogers said, are not caused by a single gene, which is why genetic testing can add another layer of information. She pointed to inherited variations such as BRCA 1 and BRCA 2, linked to breast and ovarian cancer, and other pathogenic variations tied to cholesterol.
“We all inherited these different variations in our DNA, and some of those inherited variations can increase our risk for disease,” she said.
Genetic testing can be especially useful for people who don’t have access to their family history, including those who are adopted, Rogers said.
“That’s where genetics might be important, or genomics,” Rogers said. “That’s tells you how is your environment interacting with the genes that you have? How’s your nutrition, lifestyle, all those different things.”
She distinguished between genetics, which she described as a person’s DNA blueprint, and epigenetics, which determines how those genes turn on or off.
“Your DNA is your blueprint. Epigenetics says how those genes turn on or off,” Rogers said.
Environmental exposure plays a role too
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said family health history isn’t only about what’s passed down from parents to children. Environmental exposure during childhood can also affect long-term health.
“Did you grow up with smokers? Did you grow up with somebody that had fried food all the time? Did you grow up in an area where there were chemicals and the pesticides?” O’Rourke said. “What were the other things that you were raised around and with that would also affect your health?”
She said the National Institute on Aging offers a family health history worksheet that can help people begin building a record of their genetic family history, since genetic testing alone may not catch everything.
“People are not familiar with genomics, but these are all the variations that tell you within your blueprint what is your exposure and what is the susceptibility to other things,” Rogers said.
Katherine Ambrose, an aging well coach, said common household and environmental risks include mold, which people are sometimes unaware is present, and radon gas, a naturally occurring radioactive gas. And it is good to test for those.
Lifestyle changes can help offset genetic risk
O’Rourke said while people cannot change their genetic blueprint, they can take steps to reduce risk once they know what they’re predisposed to.
“You can’t change the genetic blueprint, but you can mitigate with a lot of lifestyle, exercise and eating right, and just knowing what you’re at high risk for,” O’Rourke said.
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said knowing a family history of colon cancer or breast cancer, for example, can lead to earlier screening. She also noted that genetic testing is now available for dementia risk.
“If we can circumvent it, then great,” Cradduck said.
A gift for future generations
Ambrose described written family health history as a lasting gift from one generation to the next.
“One of the greatest gifts an older generation can possibly provide to the generations behind them is this knowledge, this written down information that can be accessed when they need it,” she said. “It can be very much more important than an heirloom.”
Resources
Key takeaways
- Family history can reveal disease risk years in advance. Patterns in conditions like heart disease, strokes, cancers, autoimmune disorders, depression and thyroid disease are especially significant, particularly when they occur at an early age.
- Know the difference between “what runs in the family” and “what a relative died from.” These are not always the same thing and confusing them can lead to incomplete health pictures.
- Genetic testing can fill in the gaps, especially for people who are adopted or don’t have access to their full family medical history.
- Environmental exposure during childhood counts too — things like secondhand smoke, diet, pesticides and chemicals in the home can shape long-term health risk alongside genetics.

title: Time for Angus King to endorse Troy Jackson

text:
In a recent newsletter, Sen. Angus King noted that he joined with Sen. Susan Collins in support of Rep. Jared Golden’s bill that would delay restrictions aimed at protecting the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale. The senator correctly described the economic importance of lobstering to Maine’s economy. However, he failed to acknowledge that the greatest threat to lobstermen is climate change and the warming oceans.
His fellow senator, Susan Collins, voted to confirm two climate deniers as heads of the EPA and the Department of Energy. Collins is the only member of the Maine delegation who takes meaningful money from fossil-fuel PACs. I do not believe Collins will support the necessary transition from fossil fuels.
It is time for Sen. King to endorse Troy Jackson, a candidate who is not beholden to the fossil fuel industry. It’s time for him to stand up for future generations, including his own grandchildren.
Tom Mikulka
Cape Elizabeth

title: 2,400-panel solar array coming to Gorham farm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A 7-acre solar array will be built on the western portion of Martin-Place Farm on Fort Hill Road in Gorham.
Perennial Renewables, a Hallowell-based energy development and consulting firm, is signing a 30-year lease to develop the project on a 10-acre plot from Norman Martin, the farm’s owner. The 2,400-panel development, called Perennial Gorham Solar, will produce 1 megawatt of electricity, enough to power roughly 200 homes, through a contract with Central Maine Power, said company partner Nick Lacasse.
After receiving planning board approval this week, Lacasse said he plans to break ground on the $3 million project in the spring and energize by the end of 2027.
The project is part of Perennial Renewables’ effort to expand its solar production outside of Kennebec County, Lacasse said. The new array will join a 30-acre solar farm already built by Gorham Solar on Fort Hill Road.
U.S. Energy Information Administration data show solar energy accounted for nearly 18% of Maine’s electricity in 2025.
The site will be accessed by an approximately 1700-foot access drive from Fort Hill Road. No residential properties abut the parcel.
“This site is naturally buffered by the topography of the farm itself,” Lacasse said. He estimated paying $20,000-$25,000 per year to the town in taxes.
Martin said the lease will create more revenue streams for his roughly 150-acre farm as property taxes rise. The land for the project is not suitable for farming high-value crops like vegetables, he said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Finding solutions for food deserts
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an inside look at food deserts, where fresh groceries are out of reach, healthier options are limited, and prices can be even higher.
Also, a dementia patient’s disappearance before dawn sparks a massive search, highlighting the wandering risk caregivers fear and resources that can be activated.
Fighting for food access
In communities across the country, more families are getting pushed farther away from fresh, affordable food.
The people who help search
For families caring for someone with dementia, it’s a constant concern that they may get disoriented, walk out of their house, and struggle to get home or find safety.
If a person isn’t found within 24 hours, half are either severely injured or found dead.
Escaping quicksand
As kids playing outside, a lot of us were afraid of running into quicksand. But as it turns out, quicksand is not a bottomless pit like in the movies. It is a mixture of sand and water that appears solid.
According to Scientific American, quicksand can look solid, but the moment a person steps on it, the sand grains lose their grip and the ground turns “soupy.”
Letting kids celebrate birthdays
A nonprofit is bringing birthday parties to children experiencing homelessness so they can celebrate their special day while living in shelters.

title: Mia Goth files for divorce from Shia LaBeouf nearly 10 years after the actors married
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Mia Goth has filed for divorce from Shia LaBeouf nearly 10 years after the two actors were married.
The petition filed Tuesday in Los Angeles County Superior Court says the 32-year-old Goth and the 40-year-old LaBeouf have been separated since July 2025.
The two met and became a couple while filming “Nymphomaniac: Vol. II” in 2012, and married in 2016. They had previously split and said they were divorcing in 2018, but remained legally married, reunited in 2020 and had a daughter in 2022.
Goth is seeking primary legal and physical custody of the 4-year-old, with visitation rights for LaBeouf. She also asked the court to deny either party spousal support. It was the first marriage for both.
As with most U.S. divorces, irreconcilable differences were cited as the reason for the split.
Representatives for Goth and LaBeouf did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
The actor, born Mia Gypsy Mello da Silva Goth in London, most recently appeared as the unfaithful servant Melantho in this summer’s “The Odyssey,” and had a dual role in last year’s “Frankenstein.” She previously starred in the horror trilogy “X,” “Pearl” and “MaXXXine.”
LaBeouf was a child star on the Disney Channel’s “Even Stevens” and in the 2003 film “Holes.” He later starred in “Indiana Jones and the Crystal Skull” and director Michael Bay’s first three “Transformers” films.
The day before Goth filed for divorce, LaBeouf, for the second time, settled a lawsuit with singer, songwriter and actor FKA Twigs, whom he dated when he was split from Goth.
FKA Twigs, whose legal name is Tahliah Barnett, had alleged in a suit filed in 2020 that LaBeouf emotionally and physically abused her during their relationship that began when she had a supporting role in the semi-autobiographical film “Honey Boy,” which he wrote and starred in.
The two settled the lawsuit and had it dismissed last year, but she sued him again in March, saying nondisclosure provisions in the settlement illegally silenced her under California law.
On Monday, she moved to dismiss the second lawsuit, saying in court documents that LaBeouf had agreed to void those provisions.
In June, LaBeouf was sentenced to probation after pleading guilty to punching three people outside a New Orleans bar during Mardi Gras.

title: Driver killed, another seriously injured in Oxford County head-on crash
text:
Maine woman killed, man seriously injured in Lovell head-on crash, officials say
Oxford County Sheriff's Office has identified drivers involved
Maine woman killed, man seriously injured in Lovell head-on crash, officials say
Oxford County Sheriff's Office has identified drivers involved
A Maine woman is dead following a crash in Lovell that left a Maine man seriously injured, according to authorities.
The Oxford County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened shortly before 11:45 a.m. Thursday in the 600 block of Main Street, where a 2003 Chevrolet Silverado pickup truck and a 2015 Ford Flex SUV collided head-on.
The driver of the SUV, 25-year-old Ivy Thomson, of Lovell, was found dead at the crash scene by first responders.
The driver of the pickup truck, 66-year-old Mark Farrington, of Andover, was stabilized at the scene and transported by LifeFlight to Maine Medical Center in Portland with life-threatening injuries, officials said.
Officials said there were no passengers in either vehicle.
The crash is under investigation. Officials said the investigation may take some time to complete.
Authorities are asking anyone who has any information about the events of the crash to call the Oxford County Sheriff's Office at 207-743-9554.
The Sheriff's Office said deputies were assisted by the Lovell Fire Department, Fryeburg Police Department and Fryeburg Rescue.

title: Things to do at Rockland Public Library next week
text:
Crafting Community, Oct. 14
Crafting Community meets at 2 p.m. the second Wednesday of the month, Wednesday, Oct. 14, in Rockland Public Library’s Community Room. Adults of all ages are invited to an afternoon of casual crafting and conversation.
This month, Deputy Library Director Patty King will lead an exploration of autumn and Halloween upcycled book crafts. Supplies will be provided. The library also has adult coloring pages and other basic materials, but participants are welcome and encouraged to bring their own projects. For all skill levels.
For more information or with questions, call 594-0310 or email [email protected].
The Rockland Public Library is located at 80 Union St.
Middle School Book Club, Oct. 15
Children in grades 4–8 are invited to read, snack and chat during Middle School Book Club from 3:45-4:45 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, in the library’s Board Room. New members are always welcome. RSVP with Miss Katie at [email protected].
Join Miss Katie to explore all kinds of fun books through the Maine Student Book Award reading list (sites.google.com/view/mainestudentbookaward/home). Kids get to pick their own book from the list every month and book talk it to the group at the next meeting. Book list books are found on the teal cart in the Children’s Room. This list covers recent fiction and nonfiction in all genres. The list is chosen by Maine librarians. Middle schoolers around the state read as many of the books of the list as they would like, and in March everyone votes for the best book of the year.
Past kids’ choice awards have gone to: “Refugee” by Alan Gratz, “Hoops” by Matt Tavares and “Alone” by Megan E. Freeman.
The next two Middle School Book Club meetings are from 1:30-2:30 p.m. on Nov. 18 and Dec. 10.
Book talk, Oct. 15
Ron Romano will discuss his book, “Stories from Maine Cemeteries – Lives Cut Short,” from 6-7:30 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, in the Community Room.
Romano will share stories of Mainers whose lives were cut short by lightning, shipwreck, disease and even murder. He will also discuss local cemeteries and tombstones from the 1800s. Come find out why the tombstones from that time were decorated the way they were. Books will be available for autographing and sale.
All are welcome to attend. For more information, contact Jeannie Sullivan at [email protected].
AquaTots, Oct. 16
Join Herring Gut Coastal Science Center for stories, songs, movement, a craft and live sea animals at this mini biology lesson for children from 10:30-11:30 a.m. Friday, Oct. 16, at the library. Each visit will have a different theme, with a different sea animal to touch. This month’s visit will focus on sea snails. Come meet the snails and learn about what makes them unique.
For ages 3-6 and siblings. The program will take place in the Community Room at Rockland Public Library. No sign-up is needed.
The next AquaTots events are on Nov. 13 and Dec. 11.
Music Together, Oct. 17
The final Music Together event of the year is 10:30 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 17. Space is limited and is first come, first served. Sign-in starts at 10 a.m. at the front desk. No registration in advance.
Music Together is a free, 45-minute early childhood music and movement for families sponsored by First National Bank. Shannon Burns, talented music teacher, leads families in circle songs, instrument play and rhythm.
This Music Together of Midcoast Music Academy class is for ages 0–5 with caregiver(s). The class follows the recommendations of child development researchers — grouping children of a variety of ages to foster natural, family-style learning. Each child participates at his or her own level. Any caregivers — parents, grandparents, nanny — can bring the children. The whole family is welcome for this important family music experience. Midcoast Music Academy is a community music school that was founded in 2012.

title: Obituary: Brian M. Nelson
text:
NORTH ANSON – Brian M. Nelson, 52, of North Anson, sadly lost his battle with cancer on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026.
He was born on Jan. 3, 1974, in Skowhegan, to Patsy L. (Berry) Collins of North Anson and Byron Nelson of Anson. He was predeceased by his grandfather, Roland “Rasty” Berry, and grandmother, Elizabeth “Bucky” Berry, of North Anson; his mother, Patsy L. Collins of North Anson; and his stepfather, John Collins of North Anson.
Brian leaves behind his sons, Gage M. Nelson and Connor J. Nelson of North Anson; his father, Byron Nelson of Anson; his sister, Meghan Lightbody of Embden; and many family and friends.
Brian was a lifelong resident of North Anson, where he attended Carrabec High School. He served as class president his junior and senior years and graduated with the class of 1992.
He went on to Eastern Maine Community College, where he graduated with a marketing degree. Brian worked as an evening manager at Hannaford until 1998, when he moved on to Madison Paper Industries and began his lengthy career in the paper industry. He transferred to Sappi in 2015 and continued working there until the summer of 2023.
On top of his employment, Brian was a proud business owner who started and ran many businesses with his sons. He was an inspiration to them, encouraging them to start businesses of their own.
He loved what he did and the friends he made along the way. He enjoyed NASCAR on Sundays, listening to his classic rock, kayaking, decorating for the holidays, continuing family traditions, hunting with his son Connor, and spending time with his family and Nelson, his “Ole Boy.”
He had four white German Shepherds that he loved: Nelson, Elouise, Stellar, and Gracie.
On his days off, you’d always see Brian outside mowing, gardening, boiling sap, or grilling a steak with a can of Coors Light in his hand. Every summer, you’d find him with his family at Happy Horseshoe Campground.
He was heavily involved in his community as a member of the Freemasons, a board member of the Madison/Anson Water District, and a board member of Sunset Cemetery in North Anson.
He grew up as a Cub Scout and Boy Scout, so naturally he stayed involved with the BSA as an adult, carrying on that tradition with his own two sons.
A special thank you to Shaun Swain for being there for him and praying with him through this difficult time. Thank you to all the doctors and nursing staff who assisted him in every way possible through his illness, serving as his steadfast lifeline during his most difficult treatments. A service will be held on Saturday, October 10, at 11 a.m., at St. Sebastian Church in Madison, followed by burial at Sunset Cemetery. A celebration of life will be held at the Masonic Hall in North Anson at 1 p.m.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Giberson Funeral Home and Cremation Services. To leave a condolence for the family and to view the online obituary, please visit http://www.gibersonfuneralhome.com.

title: School’s therapy dogs crowned homecoming king and queen
text:
(KCNC) - A Colorado high school crowned two therapy dogs, Polenta and Norene, as its first-ever canine homecoming king and queen.
Evergreen High School created a “puppy homecoming court” for the dogs, who ran uncontested and won.
Dogs support students and staff
Amy Wells, lead counselor at Evergreen High School, said the dogs’ job is simple.
“Their duty is to lie there and just be pet and hang out,” Wells said.
The dogs arrive at school early and stay until after the last bell. Wells said she stands at the front of the building every morning with the principal and lets students greet the dogs.
“I stand in the front of the building every single morning with my principal, and we let the kids come up and pet them or just talk to them,” Wells said.
Jackson Thomas, an Evergreen High School senior, said seeing the dogs affects his mood.
“I light up whenever I see them,” Thomas said.
Support since the shooting
Evergreen was the site of a school shooting one year ago.
“It just felt very vulnerable, you know,” Thomas said.
Wells said research shows cortisol levels can calm with a dog present.
“Research says that cortisol levels will calm down a little bit with a dog,” Wells said.
The dogs can be found in the counselor’s office, walking the hallways or offering support during tests.
Quinn McEvers, an Evergreen High School senior, said students can interact with the dogs without having to talk about what they’re going through.
“You don’t need to talk about what’s going on in your life or how something is affecting you. You can just get the love from the dogs, and it really helps,” McEvers said.
Crowned under the Friday night lights
Thomas said the dogs have made an impact on the school.
“They brought so much joy to this school,” Thomas said.
Polenta and Norene were announced as homecoming king and queen during the homecoming football game.
McEvers said the dogs are more than pets to the school community.
“They make a difference in our community, and I think that it’s really great that they’re getting honored for that because they are a lot bigger than just dogs. They’re really a part of our community,” McEvers said.

title: Belfast council declares former church a ‘dangerous’ building
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Belfast City Council has unanimously designated the building at 333 High St. as dangerous, giving the city authority to intervene and recover its expenses if the owner fails to bring the property into compliance with a court judgment and settlement agreement.
The decision does not trigger immediate demolition. City officials will continue working with owner James Constable and engineer Jeffrey Kingsbury on rehabilitation, while retaining the ability to secure the building, correct dangerous conditions or have the structure demolished if the agreement’s requirements are not met.
The vote followed a presentation and public hearing that brought years of enforcement history before the council, along with Constable’s insistence that the building can be saved and Kingsbury’s assessment that it is ready for additional work.
Councilor Neal Harkness described the decision as a demand for completion, while expressing a preference for rehabilitation.
“What we’re saying here is, ‘get it done,’” Harkness said. “If not, eventually we’ll have to do something about it.”
He added that councilors would “really like to see the house [rehabilitated] and not torn down.”
For the city, the designation establishes a way to enforce the property’s repair obligations and recover public money spent addressing its condition. For Constable, it leaves a route to rehabilitation, but with the possibility of city intervention if that effort fails.
Under the settlement, Belfast must give Constable a 30-day notice before exercising its authority to demolish the structure. The rehabilitation process also requires proper permits, appropriate financing and a qualified contractor acceptable to the city.
Constable told councilors he is working with Kingsbury and other contractors to bring the property into compliance.
“It’s a house we’ve gone to significant lengths to save,” he said.
Constable maintained that the building can be restored and challenged the characterization of its current condition.
“We intend to do so,” he said of saving the house, adding, “it is not a dangerous building.”
Kingsbury offered a more qualified assessment. Although the structure was “not ready for occupancy,” he does not consider it unsafe to work in.
“It’s ready for the remaining work to be done,” Kingsbury told the council.
Those statements underscored a distinction running through the hearing: Whether the building can be rehabilitated is a different question from whether it presently meets the requirements for safe residential occupancy. The council’s designation allows the city to enforce those requirements while repair efforts continue.
The property’s enforcement history stretches back several years. According to City Manager Erin Herbig’s report, the building served as the New Covenant Apostolic Church from 2002 until its sale in 2010. Constable purchased it in 2011 through 333 High Street LLC.
City officials described the structure as primarily empty and inadequately maintained over the ensuing years, apart from an electrical service upgrade and some exterior work. They also identified work undertaken without required permits or inspections.
Code Enforcement Officer Stephen Wilson issued a violation notice in 2022 concerning exterior property maintenance. Subsequent inspections and correspondence expanded the city’s concerns to include structural conditions and unpermitted electrical work.
An engineering report dated April 3, 2024, identified foundation and drainage problems, inadequate ventilation, dry rot in timbers, insufficient structural support and mold. The report described the home as a “significant life safety hazard to occupants” and recommended development and implementation of a comprehensive structural repair or replacement plan.
On Feb. 4, 2025, the council authorized court enforcement proceedings seeking to have the building brought into a safe condition or demolished.
An April 2, 2026, District Court judgment found the structure unsafe, unsanitary and unfit for human occupancy. The court’s findings described progressive deterioration, failing structural members, bowed walls, water intrusion, unsafe wiring, deteriorating porches and steps, and missing essential utility services.
The judgment acknowledged Constable’s repair efforts, including a new foundation costing approximately $45,000, but concluded that those improvements addressed only part of the building’s deficiencies. Engineering testimony recounted in the judgment estimated that approximately 70% to 85% of the structure would require replacement.
The court ordered Constable to finish work covered by an existing permit by June 30, 2026, and obtain the permits needed for the remaining remediation by Aug. 31. It required completion of compliance work within two years of permit issuance, with diligent progress during that period.
Occupancy remains prohibited until the code enforcement officer issues a certificate of occupancy.
The judgment also assessed $144,000 in civil penalties and awarded the city legal fees and costs. Constable appealed, and the parties subsequently reached a July 23 settlement under which he agreed to continue bringing the property into compliance and dismiss the appeal.
The settlement offers a substantial financial incentive to finish the work: the city will waive the court-ordered fines once the code enforcement officer certifies compliance. Constable also agreed to pay $20,000 in legal fees incurred to that point, plus additional legal expenses incurred until compliance is confirmed.
City staff reported before the October meeting that Constable had failed to obtain all necessary permits by Aug. 31 and was therefore in violation of both the judgment and settlement.
The council’s action adds the municipal dangerous-building designation to that enforcement framework. Although the court found serious safety and property-maintenance violations, it did not adjudicate the city’s separate statutory dangerous-building claim, determining that such a claim would need to be heard in Superior Court.
At the hearing, city attorney Kristin Collins said Constable had already agreed to the council’s entry of the order through the settlement.
“The dangerous building order has already been stipulated to,” Collins told councilors. “[Constable] won’t appeal the entry of this order.”
That agreement concerns the legal order, even as Constable continues to dispute whether the building’s present physical condition warrants the dangerous-building description.
In a Sept. 30 submission included in the council materials, Constable asserted that more than $100,000 in structural remediation had been undertaken under a licensed Maine engineer’s oversight. He cited chimney removal, structural work, recent inspection approvals and electrical work he described as approximately 90% complete.
Those assertions presented his account of progress since the court proceedings. They did not establish that all required work, permits and approvals had been completed.
Wilson explained to councilors that the designation allows Belfast to recover expenses if the city ultimately must address the building itself.
Under the order, city expenses must be repaid within 30 days after a demand for payment. Otherwise, the city may assess a special tax against the property. Recoverable expenses can include securing the structure, correcting dangerous conditions, demolition and removal, and related legal and administrative costs.
No immediate demolition date was announced. The code office will continue working with Constable and Kingsbury to oversee the building’s return to compliance.
The council’s unanimous vote leaves rehabilitation as the preferred outcome, backed by an enforceable alternative if the owner does not complete the required work. As Harkness’ remarks made clear, councilors want the house repaired, and expect the effort to produce a safe, compliant building.

title: Maine heating fund, even with leftover money, won’t go as far this winter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating assistance program plans to use about $4 million left over from last winter to kickstart aid for vulnerable households across the state, MaineHousing announced this week.
This initial round of Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) funding will go to households who applied early to the program with adults over 60 years old, children age 6 and under, and people with disabilities. The $4 million is about 13% of the total heating fuel assistance money expected to be distributed this year.
About 4,400 families will begin receiving credits on their heating accounts in the next week or so, said Scott Thistle, MaineHousing’s spokesperson.
Maine is expecting to receive about $41 million in HEAP funding from the federal government this year — of which about $27 million will be for heating fuel — but that money won’t start arriving until late this month.
“We know this assistance will not fully offset the outsized heating burden many Mainers are facing, but acting now means some of our most vulnerable households can begin the winter with fuel in their tanks,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said in a news release.
Even with the $4 million injection, the heating assistance won’t go as far this winter.
With heating oil costs hovering around a record high, set last month at more than $6 per gallon, the average HEAP award will have less purchasing power than it did last year.
“The benefit amount will just not be as deep,” Thistle said. “It ultimately means less oil for them.”
MaineHousing also used carryover funds to kickstart its HEAP program last year. That was during the six-week government shutdown, when MaineHousing wasn’t sure if the federal government would be providing funding at all, Thistle said.
Last year’s $2 million in extra money provided help for about 4,000 households. This year, $4 million is providing help for 4,400.
The average HEAP award was set this summer at about $700, Thistle said. But after oil costs skyrocketed at the end of the summer and into the fall, the value of that help has fallen significantly, he said.
Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation last week demanding that the federal government allocate more money for heating assistance. Congress kept heating assistance funding level this year.
Prices as high as they are — $5.97 per gallon, as of Monday — demand action from the federal government, Mills said. Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, could be particularly hard-hit if the federal Low Income Heating Assistance Program funds aren’t increased, she said.
Mills blamed record heating costs on President Donald Trump and the war in Iran, where the constriction of the Strait of Hormuz has reduced the worldwide oil supply and driven up costs.
“Federal funding levels appropriated for LIHEAP this winter did not fully consider the drastic impacts of the president’s war that has sent fuel prices skyrocketing and are now insufficient for the circumstances that Maine and other cold-climate states now face,” Mills said.
Meanwhile, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies announced last week their plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, lauded the G7 announcement Friday. She said the release should put “immediate downward pressure on energy prices.”
MaineHousing’s carryover funding will begin with households who applied when the program opened in August, but applications remain open on the agency’s website. Federal funds will go to all eligible applicants as long as there is money available.
Thistle said the number of applications is up about 5% over last year, but are actually substantially far below average in some parts of the state.
Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Trump attitude to AI should give voters pause
text:
The catalog of serious problems for our nation caused by the current president is breathtaking. As recent polls show, a clear majority of Americans do not approve of where he has been taking us across a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues.
The most recent troubling action occurred last month when the Trump team reportedly worked with the Russians to weaken a U.N. agreement designed to create guardrails around the development of AI systems involving the use of autonomous lethal weapons. This at a time when even CEOs of the companies that are racing headlong to develop AI are sounding warnings about the high potential threat to humanity this new technology could present.
We need to remember that while this president is the main driving force behind all of these destructive initiatives, he would not be able to follow through on many of them without the support of a Republican-led House of Representatives and Senate.
Whatever one’s political persuasion, if people want to put the brakes on this reckless, damaging and potentially dangerous leadership, they should be voting blue.
Tom Berry
Kennebunk

title: 🚆🏀🏒 MAINE FANS, LET’S GO! Take Amtrak to Celtics & Bruins Games This Season!
text:
Maine Fall Fun: Take Amtrak to Celtics & Bruins Games
For me, the best part of this time of year is fall! Every major sport is going on at once, and it’s pretty darn exciting.
If you’re from Maine and just happen to be a huge Celtics or Bruins fan, there’s a pretty easy way to get to TD Garden without spending hours behind the wheel.
This past spring, I headed to TD Garden to see the final regular-season Boston Celtics game. Normally, that would mean the usual stress-filled four-hour drive from Maine, but this time, we decided to switch things up and try something different: the Amtrak Downeaster. After the quick 90-minute drive from Bangor to Brunswick, I got to kick back, relax, and leave the stress of driving behind.
And honestly? I’m glad we did.
The Downeaster runs between Brunswick and Boston, with stops along the way in places like Portland, Saco, Exeter, New Hampshire, and Haverhill, Massachusetts. The final stop is Boston’s North Station, which just happens to be right underneath TD Garden.
That makes it pretty hard to beat if you’re heading to a Celtics or Bruins game. ??????
Our round-trip ticket was about $50, and the ride took around 3 hours and 20 minutes. Yes, that’s a little longer than driving from Brunswick, but for me, it was absolutely worth it.
Instead of worrying about traffic, parking or navigating Boston, we could sit back, enjoy the scenery, grab some food and a drink, and let someone else do the driving.
Read More: Bangor Waterfront Concerts 2027: Must-See Artists On Our Wishlist
And there’s another cool option for game nights:
They offer an Event Night Train for select Celtics and Bruins games and TD Garden concerts. For qualifying events that start at 8 pm or later, the special train can leave Boston North Station at 11:25 pm, for the trip back toward Maine.
One important thing to remember: the train won’t wait if your game runs late, so check the schedule carefully before making your plans.
Schedules can change, so be sure to check the Amtrak Downeaster website for the latest information before your trip.
For Maine sports fans, though, this is a pretty fun alternative: no Boston traffic, no downtown parking headache, and you can step off the train practically underneath TD Garden. Not a bad way to spend a fall game day!

title: New Balance unveils Cooper Flagg's official logo
text:
New Balance unveils Cooper Flagg's official logo, which pays tribute to his Maine roots
Cooper Flagg is in China with the Dallas Mavericks to take part in the 2026 NBA China Games, and the Maine native made a big reveal on Thursday.
Flagg's official logo was unveiled at a New Balance event at the NBA China store in Macao. The logo is a "CF" with pine tree edging, an homage that pays tribute to his home state.
"The logo design represents me. It connects to my name, but also to my roots, which is something that was really important to me," Flagg said in a statement shared by New Balance. "Where I'm from, there are a lot of trees, so you'll see the pine tree cutouts on the side as a reminder of staying true to who I am and where I grew up. I wanted to include hints of Maine while keeping the design clean and something that feels like me."
Flagg, 19, won the 2025-26 NBA Rookie of the Year award after leading all rookies with an average of 21.0 points per game. He also ranked in the top five among rookies in rebounding (6.7 per game, 4th), assists (4.5 per game, 2nd), steals (1.2 per game, 2nd) and blocks (0.9 per game, 5th). In addition, Flagg became the youngest player to score at least 35 points, 40 points, 45 points and 50 points in an NBA game at different points during his first professional season.
New Balance signed Flagg to an endorsement deal in August 2024, before the start of his freshman year at Duke University. After leading the Blue Devils to the Final Four, Flagg was selected by the Mavericks with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2025 NBA draft.
As part of the NBA China Games, the Mavericks will play a pair of preseason games against the Houston Rockets in Macao. The first game starts at 8 a.m. ET on Friday. The second game is scheduled for 6 a.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Straw vote on exploring regional high school takes next step
text:
The non-binding question on exploring a regional high school got its second nod Aug. 4. Wiscasset selectmen last month decided to put the question on the Nov. 3 ballot. And last week, they approved the municipal officers' order to make that happen.
The question reads: "Should Wiscasset explore the possibility of a single regional high school serving students from multiple area towns?"
By Maine law, the town clerk needed the order at least 60 days before Election Day.
The order passed 5-0, with no new comment from the board or public. Selectman Sarah Whitfield has said those who'd helped Boothbay Region Schools and Wiscasset pursue a state grant for a consolidated grades nine through 16 school sense the towns still want to explore an option. The grant try ended when a win looked unlikely. Whitfield has described the November question as a survey.
Also Aug. 4, Economic Development Director Aaron Chrostowsky announced a 3 p.m. Aug. 25 workshop at Scout Hall, on the local strategic energy planning being aided by the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project. Selectmen's Chair Alissa Eason told residents, "Your voice and your opinions and your thoughts and your questions will help shape this project."
Selectmen nodded business licenses for Kindred Kneads Massage, 80 Main St.; Restore & Thrive Massage Therapy, 239 Birch Point Road; and Zachari Dalton, 16 Shady Lane. Dalton’s license request describes the business as “retail of my own commercially dug clams.”

title: Trump repeatedly interrupted by protesters during rally in Texas
text:
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation’s most populous red state.
But Trump’s remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.
Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.
“You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country.”
The president’s message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.
Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.
“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Texas has become an unexpected battleground for Republicans
The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.
Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.
Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.
In a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.
He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.
Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.
“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”
Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primary
While the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.
Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”
“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state’s GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “He’s a fantastic man.”
Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.
He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.
Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.
The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.
The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution.
Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here.”
Trump makes a big announcement, but not about the Senate race
While Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball’s Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.
Trump brought him onstage and said he’d be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame.
Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.
“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. ... You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.”
___
Peoples reported from New York and Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed.

title: Trump promised a trio of payouts to Americans, from $90 to $5,000. Should you expect one?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump promised a trio of payouts to Americans, from $90 to $5,000. Should you expect one?
With less than a month until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump has promised Americans a trio of government payments, with amounts ranging from $90 to $5,000.
If a government payout sounds good, you should first know that not everyone is guaranteed to benefit — and the biggest payment is far from certain.
Related video above | President Trump’s $5,000 dividend could cost more than $1 trillion. Could it actually happen?
Polls show the economy and affordability are top of mind for voters as they prepare to cast ballots in the Nov. 3 elections. At the same time, Trump’s approval ratings are low, with survey respondents reporting displeasure with his economic policies.
The White House’s plans aim to buffer some of that sentiment. Here’s what to know about the payments.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
The $5,000 dividend check
This might have garnered the most headlines when Trump first announced it, but making the $5,000 checks a reality faces enormous obstacles. Trump said every adult U.S. citizen would receive the payment if Republicans win control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. But the administration has announced no formal plan for such checks and fiscal experts cast doubt on the plan during a time of existing economic challenges.
When will I receive it? That’s unclear. Aside from this promise being tied to an election’s outcome, the White House press release about this dividend provided no details on how Americans would receive it.
Where will the money come from? Trump cited tariff revenues as a potential funding source, but lawmakers did not include a separate tariff dividend in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tax and spending bill that became law in 2025. The payout first would require Congress’ approval. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said he would introduce legislation to fund the proposal. But political analysts say such legislation is unlikely to attain the required 60-vote supermajority in the Senate. The payment could cost the federal treasury more than $1 trillion.
One-time $90 payment for some people on Medicare
On Oct. 2, the administration said it will send one-time $90 payments to certain enrollees in the Medicare Part B government insurance program. The program covers medically necessary services and preventive services — such as ambulance use and medical equipment — for people 65 and older and others with certain disabilities. Part B eligibility requirements vary based on whether a person has to pay a premium for Part A, which covers hospital insurance.
Trump said the money is to help ease the cost of rising Medicare Part B premiums, which cost about $203 for most people.
Do I qualify? More than 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible, according to the White House. People are not eligible if their premiums are covered by Medicaid, if they pay income-related adjustments or if they are enrolled in Medicare Advantage. In 2026, around 64.2 million people are enrolled in Part B.
When and how will I receive the money? The payments are expected to go out in October, through direct deposit or by check through a Medicare-registered mailing address, the White House said.
Where will the money come from? The Medicare Improvement Fund, a fund Congress created in 2008 to make improvements to the original Medicare.
How can I check my eligibility and payment status? To check eligibility, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). To check payment status, call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213.
$500 for some Affordable Care Act enrollees
On Sept. 10, the White House said the government would issue a $500 per person “refund” to some Affordable Care Act enrollees.
Where will the money come from? The White House says the payments will be drawn from what it called “overcharges.” It said the Biden administration charged excess “user fees” passed on to consumers in the form of higher premiums, meaning consumers were charged more than what was needed to operate the federal exchange. User fees cover the expenses of services such as the Healthcare.gov website and its call center, Reuters reported, citing the healthcare think tank KFF.
The Biden administration finalized a 1% rate increase from 2025 to 2026 to offset a projected drop in enrollees following the government’s discontinuation of certain subsidies, Reuters said.
Nearly 1 million Americans will receive the $500 payment, the Trump administration said. The payments come as ACA marketplace health insurance premiums rose by hundreds or thousands of dollars this year.
When will the refunds be issued? October 2026, through checks.
Am I eligible? People who do not receive Affordable Care Act premium assistance, specifically in 30 federal-exchange states: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
The White House told PolitiFact the recipients will mainly be people above 400% of the federal poverty line.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
