title: Collapsed span of Old Town bridge to be demolished, traffic impacts expected
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - A bridge in Old Town that collapsed during construction nearly two months ago will be partially demolished starting next week.
The replacement Llewellyn Estes bridge, which spans the Stillwater River, collapsed in August when crews were pouring concrete as part of a years-long construction project. Three workers were injured.
The Maine Department of Transportation said the temporary bridge that was carrying traffic was not damaged.
Crews will begin removing the impacted spans of the bridge on Tuesday between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., according to the Maine DOT. The work could continue into the following week.
The temporary bridge will be closed for periods while crews work, though exact times are fluid.
Workers will separate the damaged span from the pier and abutment, making the pieces smaller before removing them from the river.
Motorists should expect delays while the work is ongoing. The MaineDOT says drivers should follow detour signs for Bennoch Road, North Main Street, and College Avenue to return to Stillwater Avenue.

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was sexually assaulted while fixing campaign signs
text:
SUN CITY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - A Democratic candidate for Arizona’s 8th Congressional District reported she was knocked unconscious and sexually assaulted by two men while fixing campaign signs in August.
A police report obtained by Arizona’s Family states Bernadette Greene-Placentia was fixing campaign signs Aug. 14 in Sun City. While walking back to her car, she was hit in the head and knocked unconscious, according to the report.
Greene-Placentia reported when she woke up, she was being held down and sexually assaulted by a man. She said another man then sexually assaulted her while she fought back by kicking her feet.
During the assault, the report states Greene-Placentia heard one of the men saying “Democratic b---h.” She reported the two men left her face down in the parking lot, and she doesn’t remember much afterward.
Greene-Placentia told her husband about the assault two or three days later and reported the assault to law enforcement two weeks later, according to the report. She told investigators she did not get a medical exam after the assault.
Authorities were not able to collect DNA or other physical evidence in the case.
The investigation is ongoing.
Political leaders respond
Greene-Placentia is running against Trump-backed GOP incumbent Abraham “Abe” Hamadeh in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District. Hamadeh’s campaign gave the following statement regarding his opponent’s reported assault and called for an investigation:
“I have read the disturbing story and call upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law. No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community.”
Several other Arizona political leaders also expressed their support for Greene-Placentia after news of the reported attack, including Gov. Katie Hobbs and Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego.
“Governor Hobbs is outraged by the sexual assault against congressional candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia,” a statement from Hobbs’ office read. “This was a cruel and cowardly attack, and it has no place in Arizona. No one should have to fear for their safety, or the safety of the people they love, while serving their community. Violence of any kind, against anyone, will not be tolerated in our state. Our hearts are with Bernadette and her loved ones.”
“What happened to Bernadette Greene-Placentia is an outrage,” Kelly posted on social media. “It took real courage for her to speak publicly about something so painful. The criminal who did this must be found and held fully accountable.”
“I’m absolutely heartbroken to hear this news, and I’m thinking of Bernadette and her loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” Gallego said. “We cannot tolerate political or sexual violence in any form. Those responsible must be held accountable. Thank you for speaking out, Bernadette. We’re with you.”
Note: Arizona’s Family does not typically name victims of sexual assault, but Greene-Placentia has publicly come forward with her claims.
Copyright 2026 KTVK/KPHO via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Maine CDC encourages tick bite prevention this Fall
Portland Hearts of Pine eliminated from USL1 playoff chase
text:
The Portland Hearts of Pine are officially eliminated from USL League One playoff contention.
Eight teams in the 17-team league will advance to the quarterfinal round. Wednesday night in Texas, eighth-place Fort Wayne FC beat Corpus Christi, 3-1, to improve to 11-9-9, good for 42 points. Portland (7-12-10) has 31 points with three matches remaining. Even if the Hearts won three straight — something they have not done all season — their maximum point total would be 40.
Portland has been well below the playoff line for most of the season and is 14th in the league standings. In the franchise’s inaugural 2025 season, Portland finished seventh and came within a penalty kick shootout loss of reaching the final.
This season, Portland has been undone by its inability to close out games.
Portland has blown a lead in 10 USL1 matches, mostly because of nine conceded goals in the 90th minute or extra time. Six times Portland settled for a tie. Four times it gave up a second goal and lost. Add in a 2-1 home loss to Chattanooga when they had tied the game with a second-half goal before allowing the winner in the 90th minute, and the Hearts have squandered 25 potential points.
Portland has four comebacks of its own (two ties, two wins), including a 3-3 tie Saturday at Spokane, when it trailed 3-1.
Portland has continued to play in front of packed crowds even in inclement weather. It has averaged 6,234 fans per match at Fitzpatrick Stadium where it is 5-6-3 in league play.
Portland hosts Athletic Club Boise (14-8-7) at 5 p.m. Saturday. Boise, which has announced it will play in USL Championship next season, is in fifth place with a chance to reach the top four and earn a home quarterfinal game. Portland is at third-place Forward Madison (15-7-7) on Oct. 17 and concludes its season Oct. 24, hosting Charlotte Independence (18-5-6), which is one point out of first place.

title: Study: 1 in 4 NFL players will contract a brain disease. How does this impact Maine high school football?
text:
A recent study revealed that over 90% of NFL players’ donated brains were wracked with CTE, the neurodegenerative disease that leads to depression, mood swings and even dementia, and can only be definitively diagnosed after death.
So why would a co-author suggest youth and high school football players should “play like the pros” if they want to protect their brains?
That’s because NFL players today have strict limits on contact during practices thanks to the league’s collective bargaining agreement with the NFL Players Association.
“We have not seen that trickle down to lower levels of football,” said Charlotte Luster, a co-author of a study published in late August that found CTE in 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021.
A total of 878 NFL players died in that time frame. Lead author Dr. Daniel Daneshvar’s attention-getting takeaway is, at minimum, 1 in 4 NFL players will contract CTE. That rate could be much higher. Previous studies have also found CTE in over 90% of studied brains. But researchers acknowledge there is a bias toward donating brains when a player is suspected to have suffered from brain disease.
Many Maine high school football coaches say they, too, have moved away from full-speed, full-contact practices. The vast majority of Maine high school football coaches have been thinking safety first for more than a decade.
“We go full pads one practice a year, the day before our first scrimmage. And that’s just to try the pants on and make sure they fit,” said Kevin Kezal, who has led Thornton Academy to seven Class A championships since 2012.
First-year Portland coach Dylan Rottkov said, “I think I’ve seen one helmet collision in a practice this season and it was accidental.”
Added Joel Stoneton, head coach and athletic director at Class D champion Winthrop: “In the state of Maine, this is the norm. There are a lot more safety protocols. In my opinion, it is safer now through improvements in equipment, the protocols and what coaches are doing.”
But the coaches do not dismiss the significance of this or other studies. They know there is a direct link between football, at least at the highest levels, and CTE.
“Obviously, our high school players and a group of former NFL players are two very different populations,” Stoneton said. “But I do think the findings reinforce why football programs need to continually look at what we can do better when it comes to reducing unnecessary head impacts and taking care of our players.”
WHAT IS CTE?
CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a progressive brain disease where proteins break down and kill brain cells.The spread of the disease is categorized from Stage 1 (least) to Stage 4 (most).
Common symptoms, based on players’ behaviors and medical reports while they were living, include headaches, depression, changes in behavior or thinking, speech difficulties, mood swings that can be violent, and dementia in late-stage development.
Daneshvar’s most recent study showed a high correlation between players diagnosed with dementia having Stage 3 and 4 CTE. Several high-profile NFL players who died by suicide, including former New England Patriots Aaron Hernandez and Junior Seau, were found to have the disease.
Luster said understanding how CTE is caused — by repetitive head impacts, not isolated concussions — is the important message for high school players.
“Ninety-two percent of football players stop playing in high school. We’re not able to say 1 in 4 high school players will develop CTE. That’s not what we’re studying,” Luster said. “But the exposure of repetitive hits that these NFL players absorbed did not begin when they started playing in the NFL.”
While preventing concussions remains a key safety goal, “CTE forces us to think about repetitive blows,” Luster said.
She called it a dose-response relationship. The head impact is the dose, CTE is the response.
“We did not look at that dose-response relationship in this study, but two studies previously have shown that risk of CTE increases with each additional year you play football,” Luster said.
Another paper published by Daneshvar showed the odds of getting CTE increased 21% with every additional 1,000 head hits.
Dr. Chris Lutrzykowski of MaineGeneral Health is the medical liaison adviser to the Maine Principals’ Association Sports Medicine Committee. Lutrzykowski said, at this point, there is no “established threshold at which risk of CTE is clearly defined.” However, Lutrzykowski agreed that the available data indicates that, when it comes to head impacts, “frequency and duration matter.”
Lutrzykowski added, “reducing the number and amount of time devoted to contact can reduce the number of head impacts considerably.”
WHAT DO PLAYERS KNOW ABOUT CTE?
Before a recent Portland High practice at Deering Oaks, seniors Dom Huntington, a two-way lineman who has been a varsity starter since his freshman season, and receiver/defensive back Maddox Meas said they don’t know a lot about CTE. But they are conscious about their own brain health and safety.
“I want to be able to go to school after high school, be able to get a good job, just to be able to still function normally,” Meas said.
Meas chooses to wear a Guardian cap, an extra padded layer that is attached to the exterior of a helmet. There is debate on whether the caps actually reduce impact levels. But players who wear them say it helps. Guardian caps are increasingly seen in practices and games at all levels of football.
“Sometimes the worst impact is when your head hits the ground. I’ve done that a few times and get a little dizzy sometimes. The Guardian cap, I think it might help out a little bit,” Meas said. “My mom also wants to make sure I don’t get hurt.”
Football helmets have improved in their design, with an emphasis on lessening the force of an impact. Some helmets, like those being worn this season by Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale have impact sensors that send real-time head-impact warnings to athletic trainers and coaches.
Huntington stressed that he doesn’t think he’s absorbed a significant head impact from an on-field hit.
Huntington and Meas both said learning that over 90% of the examined NFL players’ brains show CTE damage is “a little scary.”
They also were both quick to point out that playing high school football is not the same as playing in the NFL.
“Those guys play a lot more, their whole life,” Huntington said. “They practice hard. They go to those big colleges and stuff, so I feel like they’re way more at risk than a high school player. And on our team we don’t have anyone who is going to the NFL, realistically. It doesn’t scare me personally.”
REDUCING HEAD IMPACTS
For more than a decade, coaches in Maine have realized that they need to make their game as safe as possible — especially in practice. It benefits the players’ long-term health. It also assures that schools, many with rosters hovering in low to mid-30s, can actually play their scheduled games.
“At least in my neck of the wood, teams are running with 35 to 45 kids, and for me it has never made sense to go out and bang my kids in practice,” said Stoneton, in his 31st season as a high school coach. “We do a ton of tackling drills, but it’s on pads. We work on technique. One of the first things we do in preseason is to walk through tackling technique.”
This July, the National Federation of State High School Associations called for the elimination of several types of heavy-contact drills, including one-on-one tests of strength in a confined area; blocking, tackling, drills where players begin more than 4 yards apart; and any drill — like the infamous Oklahoma Drill — designed to create head-on collisions. The NFHS statement, posted on the MPA site, is guidance, not mandatory.
Those drills have been long gone in Maine high schools, many coaches and players said.
“Honestly, I don’t think we did drills like (the Oklahoma Drill) back at Livermore Falls in the ’90s because we had about 30 players and couldn’t afford to lose anybody in practice,” said Kezal, who started his coaching career as a Livermore Falls assistant in 1990.
But a quick internet search reveals that high-impact “drills,” with teammates and coaches cheering wildly for big hits, are still common in other parts of the country, particularly at the youth level.
Back in Maine, coaches say there are a variety of ways they can reduce the risk of brain injury. Those include emphasizing better tackling and blocking techniques to “take the head out of the game”; never taking a player to the ground when doing a tackling drill; and avoiding any full-contact drill.
Kezal and Stoneton both stressed the importance of having an athletic trainer at practices and games, and improved concussion protocols.
Rule changes have also helped. Once-accepted practices — like the blind-side crackback block or a defender launching themselves to make a tackle — are now penalized.
“That’s good for the game. Kids know they can’t do that,” Kezal said.
Stoneton has another suggestion, one he knows is unpopular: No tackle football until middle school. At the earliest.
That would eliminate years of unnecessary impacts to developing brains. Stoneton believes it would also increase participation at the high school level.
“Those young kids’ bodies are not ready for that type of play,” Stoneton said. “I’ve seen so many get lit up and it hurt and it didn’t feel good and they decide football’s not for them.”
WILL CHANGES MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
The mean age at death of the NFL players whose brains were studied in the 2016-2021 cohort was 66.5 years.
Most played their final NFL game when artificial turf was more like concrete, helmets were viewed as weapons not protection, and big hits were celebrated and encouraged. As recently as 2008, ESPN ran a weekly segment called “Jacked Up” with studio announcers gleefully glorifying the five most vicious hits of the week.
When a 65- to 70-year-old first started playing football, if a player had his “bell rung,” they might be encouraged to take a couple of plays off. Maybe. In those days, if you weren’t knocked unconscious, you didn’t have a concussion.
In 30 years, will a similar study show a decrease in CTE? It stands to reason that the significant limitations on practice collisions, rule changes, improved equipment and overall awareness of brain injuries will reduce the risk of football players contracting CTE.
“Unfortunately, we don’t know yet,” Luster said. “It could be lower but, at the same time, players are bigger, faster and stronger.”

title: Halloween window painting in downtown Farmington
3 takeaways on the 2nd Maine gubernatorial debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The second of four debates in Maine’s three-way race for governor was mostly a substantive affair — and, to some extent, a repeat of the candidates’ first meeting last week.
The debate was hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine at the Gracie Theatre on Husson University’s campus in Bangor. The three candidates went back and forth for an hour on housing, immigration, healthcare and more.
Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree remains the race’s strong favorite, having dominated fundraising and holding a steady double-digit lead in polling since she won a competitive ranked-choice primary this summer.
Bobby Charles, a Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, won the Republican nomination in a similarly competitive — but more bruising — primary. His campaign has tried to link Pingree to higher electricity prices and property taxes under Democratic Gov. Janet Mills.
Rick Bennett, the independent, is a state senator from Oxford County who left the Republican Party when he joined the race last summer. He’s tried to position himself as a middle-ground candidate, but has failed so far to pick up widespread support, polls show.
After the trio’s second debate, here are a few takeaways.
1. Charles talked about Pingree about as much as himself.
Charles began his participation in the debate, and ended it, by attacking Pingree.
The first question posed to the candidates was about housing affordability, and — before spinning into a list of policy proposals that included reducing property taxes for disabled veterans and raising the Homestead Exemption — Charles said housing costs have doubled under Mills and Pingree, who served in Mills’ administration.
That’s been his strategy since he won the Republican nomination: Link Pingree to Mills, and point the finger.
And this approach was typified by Charles’ closing statement. After a brief moment of emotion, Charles pointed the finger at Pingree once again.
“Who in their right mind, charged with affordable housing by a governor, would give $840,000 to her own nonprofit, one that employs her husband and her family?” Charles said, alluding to state funding awarded to a nonprofit Pingree once led, before being cut off by Maine Public host Jennifer Rooks.
Charles’ time was up.
2. The second debate was pretty similar to the first.
As in the first debate, Charles, behind in polls by double digits, went on the attack and positioned himself as an outsider with new ideas. He again attempted to distance himself from President Donald Trump on tariffs and said he has appealed to Trump to return to the negotiating table, calling Canada a “friend.”
As in the first debate, Pingree stuck to her message, avoided addressing Charles’ constant attacks and linked Charles on tariffs and the war in Iran to Trump — whose approval ratings are well underwater in Maine, recent polling shows.
And as in the first debate, Bennett swung with his independence. He called the two-party system, which he abandoned last year, the “political industrial complex,” calling out both Democrats and Republicans for stifling debate and encouraging the explosion of campaign money.
3. There were a few areas of policy agreement.
On the first question of the night, all three candidates acknowledged housing production in Maine is too slow, and that rolling back regulations may help ease the state’s 80,000-unit shortfall.
Pingree called for a 90-day environmental permitting “shot clock,” Charles said he would encourage municipalities to speed up permitting and Bennett said he would audit the state’s housing bottleneck to understand where delays are coming from.
All three candidates acknowledged Maine is struggling to retain its healthcare workforce and its rural hospitals. Bennett and Charles agreed that reimbursement rates need to increase, and Pingree and Bennett agreed that Maine should be working toward universal health insurance coverage.
In fact, Pingree and Bennett agreed on quite a bit: that immigration enforcement has gone too far, that data center development should pause and that the Indigenous tribes in Maine should have sovereignty.
Bennett — ever the middleman — and Charles agreed that the state budget shortfall was due to overspending, and that the state budget deserves a thorough comb-through.
Watch the full debate on Maine Public’s YouTube channel. The candidates will meet on stage again in a CBS13 and FOX23-hosted debate on Tuesday, and on Wednesday in a debate hosted by WMTW.

title: New US indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. authorities charged former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with conspiring to torture his fellow citizens in order to maintain his hold on power. The new indictment, unsealed Thursday, adds pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking offenses.
Maduro, who was previously charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., is now also facing allegations of human rights abuses during his reign as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
“He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition,” says the revised indictment, which newly charges Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, with torture conspiracy.
The revised indictment accuses the couple of staying in power by “terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence,” saying thousands of Venezuelans were “harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed” by people acting at the behest of the government he controlled.
The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro’s behest. The indictment accuses the ex-president of signing off on methods of torture and personally threatening the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.”
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro’s lawyer; Flores’ attorney was due in court for a previously scheduled hearing. Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.
Both have pleaded not guilty in the criminal case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They had already been facing potential life prison sentences if convicted.
Flores was scheduled to be in court Thursday, where her lawyers will urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail, and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she has “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital, when care was needed.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence.”
___

title: Bangor football travels to Portland for rematch of last two A North title games
text:
The rested Bangor High School Rams will try to climb into the Class A North playoff picture when they travel to Portland’s Fitzpatrick Stadium on Friday night to take on Portland High in a rematch of the last two A North championship games.
Kickoff is at 6 p.m., and it is Portland’s Homecoming game.
Bangor, 2-2, was off last weekend while defending two-time regional champ Portland suffered its first loss after four wins as defending state champ Thornton Academy of Saco scored 36 unanswered points en route to a 43-13 triumph.
Thornton blanked Portland 28-0 in the state title game last fall.
Portland had advanced to the state game with a hard-fought 30-22 victory over Bangor in the regional final. Portland had also bested Bangor, 54-14, in the 2024 A North championship game en route to the state title.
Four teams qualify for the Class A North playoffs, and Bangor is currently in fifth place, 12.368 Crabtree Index points behind No. 4 Edward Little of Auburn, which currently owns the last playoff spot.
Bangor and Edward Little are both 2-2 and square off Friday, Oct. 16 at Cameron Stadium in Bangor.
Edward Little is hosting third-place Windham, 2-3, on Friday night.
Windham upended Bangor, 21-14, in Bangor two weeks ago.
Bangor has wins over Lewiston (28-0) and Deering of Portland (32-13) with the other loss being a season-opening 22-18 setback against Massabesic of Waterboro.
Portland rattled off consecutive victories over Lewiston (40-14), Scarborough (25-0), Windham (39-13) and Edward Little (35-7) before Thornton Academy erased a 13-7 deficit by scoring 36 straight points.
Portland’s Alex Martin ran for both Portland touchdowns against Thornton, with one coming on an 86-yard run. He had scored three TDs vs. Edward Little.
Dynamic Gavin Hughes is Bangor’s offensive catalyst, and he produced 172 yards against Windham. But he had only 10 touches as he rushed for 123 yards on seven carries, including an 88-yard TD jaunt, and caught three passes for 49 yards.
Bangor quarterback Alex Tennett completed six of 12 passes for 77 yards vs. Windham, and Obi Okafor rushed for 63 yards on 11 carries.
Among other matchups this weekend, the top two teams in Class D North will collide in Pittsfield at 7 p.m. Friday as No. 1 Winslow, the defending D North champ, will take on second seed Maine Central Institute. Both are 4-1.
Winslow followed a one-point loss to Wells (14-13) with wins over John Bapst of Bangor (26-6), Oak Hill of Sabattus (46-6), Freeport (14-6) and Mattanawcook Academy of Lincoln (44-0).
MCI has victories over Oak Hill (42-8), Mattanawcook Academy (27-25), Hampden Academy (28-13) and Madison (21-12), with its only loss coming to Poland (34-14).
Winslow humbled MCI 63-12 a year ago.
In statewide Class C, 4-1 Foxcroft Academy of Dover-Foxcroft will seek its fifth straight win when it treks to Newport for a 1 p.m. Saturday game against 2-3 Nokomis, which is occupying the eighth spot and the final playoff berth in the 12-team division.
Foxcroft Academy is currently ranked third in the division.
The Ponies followed a season-opening 24-0 loss to second seed Hermon with wins over Oceanside/North Haven of Rockland (28-12), Gardiner (28-0), Madison (41-7) and John Bapst (45-14).
Nokomis has won two of its last three after losing its first two games to Gardiner (37-6) and Hermon (28-6). It has since sandwiched victories over Brewer (42-8) and Hampden Academy (52-0) around a loss to Greely of Cumberland Center (35-7).
Undefeated defending State 8-Player Small titlist and current top seed Stearns/Schenck/Katahdin will be gunning for its sixth victory when it travels to face third seed Bucksport, 2-2, at 7 p.m. Friday.
Stearns/Schenck/Katahdin has beaten Dexter (42-8), the Houlton co-operative team (56-0), Orono (40-20), Lake Region of Naples (32-28) and Washington Academy of East Machias (40-14).
Bucksport has earned victories over Boothbay Region (26-0) and Mount Desert Island (36-24) and has lost to Ellsworth/Sumner (52-26) and Orono (67-28).
Old Town, the No. 1 team in 8-Player North, will try to go 6-0 when it makes the 143-mile one-way trip to Naples to face 1-4 Lake Region, the fifth seed in six-team 8-Player South.

title: Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the US
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to crack down on foreign enrollment.
A proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years.
Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student’s initial application to the program, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal.
Change would be a blow to higher education and some businesses
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. Tech companies and other industries also hire many international students for technical roles.
The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education.
“Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership,” Aw said in a written statement.
In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a “pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it.
Trump administration puts pressure on international students
The proposed rule is part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education. Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them.
This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September.
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, predicted that the fee would be struck down in the courts, as was a $100,000 fee for the H-1B work visas that many tech companies and universities rely on to fill openings for skilled jobs.
The Trump administration is now trying a different way to raise the fee for the visas to more than $100,000.
Rand said fees are not the answer.
“When we educate international students at our universities, and they want to work and apply their talents here after graduating, of course we should embrace them -- not use an exorbitant fee as a pretext to send them packing,” Rand said in an email.
Enrollment concerns mount among education groups
Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said international enrollment has suffered.
Last fall, the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 17%, the sharpest decrease since the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall numbers for this fall are not yet available, but Spreitzer said some individual colleges are reporting drops of 30% to 40%.
She said the new Trump plan will not help.
“We know that OPT is one of the reasons that international students choose to study in the United States because they’re able to have that post-graduation work experience,” she added.
A similar program that allowed international students to participate in internships and practicums also has faced scrutiny from the Trump administration. New guidance from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that the program, Curricular Practical Training, should only be authorized when the work experience is a degree requirement led to a lawsuit Monday.
Education groups, including the Association of American Universities and NAFSA, said that in the past that program was allowed if it was “directly related to the student’s major area of study.” The groups also said ICE was threatening college university officials with criminal prosecution if they did not comply.
“We know the administration has been trying to hinder legal employment-based immigration through numerous means,” said Steven Brown, a Houston-based immigration lawyer. “I think this is the next level of attack, and I think it’s a design to kill the program without killing the program. I don’t see too many schools wanting to pay $70,000 for a student to get OPT.”
___
Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kan.

title: Big brother’s bone marrow donation offers hope to 9-year-old sister with sickle cell disease
text:
ALABASTER, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - An older brother’s bone marrow donation will offer a second chance at life for his 9-year-old sister, who has sickle cell disease.
Alexa Turner, a 9-year-old student at Thompson Intermediate School, is dealing with more than homework. She has sickle cell disease. Her 13-year-old brother, Amari Rose, is a bone marrow match for a transplant surgery set for January.
Now, the siblings are learning to process medical terms including blood transfusion, surgery and lifesaving. Their mother, Jennifer Turner, said she struggles with the vocabulary, too.
“Honestly, the attitude, the positive attitude that they have... they encourage me because I’m the one that needs help when it comes to those big words,” Turner said.
Alexa’s struggle has been difficult for the family
Sickle cell disease causes blood cells to take on an irregular shape, which causes pain and can threaten Alexa’s life.
“When you have sickle cell, it’s not just the one thing that’s being hard. It’s just that you just got to keep on going and keep on walking through that path and let God walk you through it and keep on being brave,” Alexa said.
Amari said watching his sister’s struggle has been difficult.
“It’s been sad to watch my sister get hurt and, like, in pain,” he said.
Alexa’s mother said sickle cell disease brings additional risks beyond blood and pain crises. Her daughter is at risk for acute chest syndrome, a form of pneumonia in the lungs that she experiences every year.
“So, every year, we’re watching her fight for her life with no oxygen. I mean, her lowest is like 70, and we were fighting,” Turner said.
The family is also fighting against silent strokes. Alexa receives monthly blood transfusions to try to restore proper blood flow to her brain and prevent a major stroke.
‘Fight through your fear’
Amari is a bone marrow match for his sister, and the transplant surgery is scheduled for January. The process will include chemotherapy and radiation.
Afterward, the family will need to quarantine. They will isolate for 9 to 12 months to protect Alexa from infection while her immune system rebuilds.
“You have to be brave when anything that you’re afraid of. You have to just fight through your fear and go through it. ‘Cause like how I said with God, if he’s right there beside me... then, I guess he’s just going to be walking me through that path,” Alexa said.
Turner said her daughter’s story underscores the need for people to give blood, which is crucial for Alexa and others with sickle cell disease.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help the family because Turner will not be able to work during the quarantine period.

Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
text:
Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature Thursday for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.
The Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws on themes from classical Greek and Roman literature, modern influences and personal experience for genre-blending works that have ranged from translations of ancient Greek poets to collaborations with dancers and musicians, including Laurie Anderson and Lou Reed.
The Swedish Academy that awards the prize said she won "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature."
The permanent secretary of the academy said the author was in Iceland "listening to the wind" when the academy reached her to notify her of the honor.
"She was very taken by surprise," Ingrid Carlberg said.
Asked how she felt about the award, Carson told the Icelandic public broadcaster RUV: "I think they're all crazy." She described the conversation with the academy as "rather halting."
"They have the usual questions, and I have no answers," she said.
She said poetry is "probably more useful than prose right now because it's faster, and everybody is in a hurry. So basically I think it's good because it's brief. Except Homer. Homer's not brief."
Carson is among the more high-profile recent winners of the literature Nobel, which often honors authors little known outside of the literary world and is sometimes criticized for valuing literary experimentation over the ability to connect with a broad readership.
However, the prize can also introduce readers to writers and works beyond their own languages or reading habits.
Asked how the prize would change her sales, she said: "I'll get a sticker on the front of my book. Stickers help."
Carson's books include "Eros the Bittersweet," a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, the verse novel "Autobiography of Red," as well as "Men in the Off Hours," a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada's Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001, and "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy," which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
She also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the academy said, "may be regarded as independent works in their own right." They include "If Not, Winter," based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles' tragic plays "Electra" and "Antigone" and Euripides' "Bakkhai."
"Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning," said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel Literature Committee.
Carson's wide-ranging influences, from the ancient Greeks to John Keats, Virginia Woolf and Emily Bronte, lead "to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and art forms," Olsson said.
Carson blends genres and styles, offering "different voices that play off against each other," he added.
"Economy of the Unlost," from 1999, sets ancient Greek poet Simonides of Keos against 20th-century poet Paul Celan, he said, while "Men in the Off Hours," published in 2000, "aligns the historian Thucydides with Virginia Woolf."
Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022.
She also has drawn on her own life for works such as "Nox," which was published in 2010 and dealt with the decades-long absence and then death of her brother Michael.
Olsson called it "a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother." It also includes Carson's translation of an elegy by the Roman poet Catullus for his own brother.
Among her most recent work is "Wrong Norma," a wide-ranging 2024 collection of pieces from publications including The Paris Review and The New Yorker, accompanied by Carson's hand-drawn illustrations.
Also that year, Carson wrote in the London Review of Books about being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. She said a "particularly mortifying" symptom was that her handwriting "disintegrated."
"Hard to describe or explain the shame of bad handwriting," she said. "Bad handwriting is ugly. Also it is inauthentic. In the sense it is not you."
The prize was announced in Stockholm. Carson did not immediately respond to emails from The Associated Press.
Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
This week ends with Friday's peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million) per prize.
Italie reported from New York and Lawless reported from London. Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Federal judge to hear request to dismiss Lewiston mass shooting lawsuit
text:
Federal judge in Maine hears request to dismiss Lewiston mass shooting lawsuit
A federal judge heard arguments Thursday afternoon on the U.S. government's request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by survivors of the 2023 Lewiston mass shooting and relatives of those killed.
The motion-to-dismiss hearing was held in Portland before U.S. District Court Judge Lance Walker. Thursday's hearing concerned whether the plaintiffs' claims and case can move forward.
The original lawsuit was filed by 109 survivors and victims' family members in September 2025 and accuses the Army, the Defense Department and Keller Army Community Hospital of failing to adequately respond to warning signs displayed by the shooter and Army reservist Robert Card.
Family and friends of Card say he had displayed warning signs before he killed 18 people and injured 13 others at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar & Grille on Oct. 25, 2023.
The lawsuit alleges that Army personnel failed to follow policies and take steps that could have prevented the shootings.
According to the complaint, the Army violated its own policies by failing to: communicate the warning signs up the chain to the highest levels of command, exercise ongoing jurisdiction over Card until his mental and physical status had been formally adjudicated, and engage available legal processes to restrict Card's access to firearms and communicate all relevant information about Card to law enforcement.
The Justice Department is asking the court to dismiss the case, arguing that federal law shields the government from liability for the kinds of decisions the plaintiffs challenge. The government argued "discretionary" decisions about Card's supervision and medical care involved judgment calls protected by federal law.
Attorneys representing the plaintiffs argued Thursday that the decisions were no longer discretionary after officials admitted Card was a danger to others.
"There is no person, no other agency, no other law enforcement that knew more about the dangerousness and the incredible threat that Robert Card posed to this community," the plaintiffs' attorneys said. "There was no one that was in a better position to prevent this horrible event."
The government's motion also disputes the plaintiffs' claims about Card’s hospitalization and firearm eligibility, arguing that his hospitalization did not qualify as a legal commitment that would bar him from possessing firearms.
In the original motion filed in February, the Justice Department also said the shooting itself, not government action, caused the harm felt by the survivors and victims' family members.
Walker said it could take some time before he comes to a decision on the government's motion to dismiss.
If the case moves forward, the next step in the legal process would be discovery.

title: Case dismissed against 1 of 4 adults after 16 children found in ‘deplorable’ home, looked like ‘feral animals’
text:
VINTON COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - A judge has dismissed the case against one of the four adults charged in an Ohio child endangerment case where 16 children were found in “deplorable conditions.”
The case against Gary Siders Sr. was dismissed after he was found not competent to stand trial, according to court records.
Gary Siders Sr. is one of four adults who were charged after 16 children were found living in an Ohio home that officials called “third world” and “deplorable.”
Gary Siders Jr., Elizabeth Siders and Christina Siders were all indicted by a grand jury in August. Elizabeth Siders and Christina Siders were indicted on 19 charges. Gary Siders Jr. was indicted on 16 charges.
The raid at the home
The adults were arrested after Vinton County Sheriff’s Office and the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation executed a search warrant at the home in Hamden, Ohio.
Officials said they were there for an unrelated investigation when they found the children.
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson said if authorities had waited another 24 hours to raid the home, some of the children may have died.
Conditions of the children
Several of the children were in serious condition and two were flown to hospitals due to the severity of their conditions, Wilson said.
“Some of the children could not even speak and looked like feral animals,” he said.
The children ranged in age from 1 to 18. All 16 of them had to be medically evaluated.
“The number one priority is to make sure that these kids are taken care of physically, mentally and emotionally,” Wilson said.

title: Susan Collins does, in fact, answer the call
text:
Letter writer Earle Wingate of Peru recently asserted that he has written to Sen. Susan Collins “for more than eight years” and that he has “never” received a response from her. (“Country over party means time’s up for Susan Collins,” Sept. 30).
It is true that Wingate has written to the senator many times, but it is false that he has never received a reply to his correspondence.
Our office last received an email from Wingate on Jan. 28, 2025, urging Sen. Collins to oppose the confirmation of certain executive branch nominees.
Wingate received a written response from Collins informing him of her decision to oppose Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel to their nominated positions. Over the past eight years, Wingate has received seven responses to his messages, writing on topics including the following: support for Ukraine (she does), support for convicting Donald Trump during his impeachment trial (she did), opposition to withdrawing U.S. troops from Syria (she did), opposition to the 2019 partial government shutdown (she led the work to end it) and a message approving of her vote to confirm Justice Kavanaugh. Other messages to Collins from Wingate indicated that he did not wish to receive a response.
The truth is that Sen. Collins welcomes hearing from Mr. Wingate and all Mainers and our office strives to respond quickly. We also believe readers deserve an accurate account of the facts.
Katie Brown
Chief of Staff, Sen. Collins
Washington, D.C.

title: Expensive ads don’t make a candidate good
text:
Whoever is orchestrating the media campaigns for Sen. Susan Collins, Bobby Charles and Paul LePage have done an excellent job of embracing misinformation, a deliberate distortion of the facts. They are using classic, well-documented logical fallacies to mislead citizens in every ad that has been released.
While maybe not outright lying, they are still cherry-picking small issues and claiming they are big problems (voter fraud, really?). They’re correlating related issues without looking for actual causes (Hannah Pingree is causing climate change in Maine, really?); attacking their opponents personally instead of addressing the issues; and using classic straw-man arguments, bandwagon appeals and red-herring charges to distract from the fact that massive funding from the billionaire class does not make anyone a good candidate.
Just because they sound momentarily reasonable on air or in our mailbox does not make them true. Checking the actual data will allow everyone to see through the ridiculous arguments in every million-dollar ad backed by those with money and power — who want to keep both.
Patricia Millett
West Farmington

title: AI powered drones are being developed for search and rescue operations
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Personnel from DEEMI say they’re optimistic that new AI-powered technology will be a game changer for search and rescue operations. They’re partnering with the University of Maine and the University of Massachusetts Amherst to develop it.
“Before this emerging technology, what we do is we would fly a pattern with a drone back and forth and take several hundred, sometimes several hundred photos. We’d have to upload them to a server and then we’d have analysts take a look at each individual photo Zooming in, searching back and forth across the photo, looking for an object of interest. You know, hopefully the person that’s lost,” said Vinal Applebee, the Chief Drone Pilot for DEEMI.
But now drones are being developed with artificial intelligence.
The idea is that rescuers can input information about who they’re looking for using things such as what color clothing a person is wearing.
When the drone begins taking photos of the ground below, it will flag images that it believes contains what rescuers are looking for.
Allowing them to look through only a handful of images as opposed to hundreds.
“Our vision is to be able to cut the time from deploying the mission to finding the person from, let’s say, 72 hours down to 7 minutes,” said Xingda Chen, a Postdoctoral researcher at University of Massachusetts Amherst.
“We feel strongly that we’re going to save a lot of time and it will be crucial in the end result,” said Applebee.
But it’s not ready yet, currently the AI is being trained and developed in the field.
“Hopefully we can get this up operational by the end of this year, so I’m trying to push as hard as I could just to make this thing online and be on the server at all times,” said Chen.

title: Father speaks after 1-month-old’s mom accused of slamming baby’s head against the floor
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) — A baby girl is continuing to fight for her life after suffering a number of serious injuries that could have ended it.
The month-and-a-half-old child has been recovering at Children’s Hospital in Omaha.
According to police, the infant suffered life-threatening injuries at the hands of her mother, 20-year-old Kayleigh Lowe.
Court records showed Lowe likely slammed the baby’s head against the floor of their home, threw her in the air and squeezed her ribs.
As a result, police said the baby suffered seven broken ribs and bleeding on both sides of her brain.
The young girl was taken to a Lincoln hospital before being transferred to Children’s Hospital on Sept. 13.
After a few weeks of uncertainty, doctors said they believed the girl would survive, a relief to her father, 20-year-old Cooper Miller.
“She is doing better than she had the last couple of days, so that is giving me better hope,” Miller said. “Her ribs are healing miraculously. Her bruising is gone on her face. She just, she’s so beautiful.”
Miller, who now lives in Hastings, said he was in a relationship with Lowe until the beginning of this year. They learned she was pregnant in late 2025 and the two had kept in touch as she closed in on her due date.
An arrest affidavit showed that Lowe searched “shaken baby syndrome” on her phone on Sept. 2, just 12 days after her daughter was born. She later took the infant to an emergency room on Sept. 10 but left against medical advice, police reported.
A doctor with Children’s Hospital told police that the infant had suffered permanent brain injuries. Miller said that a large portion of his daughter’s brain was full of fluid and threatening to claim her eyesight.
As for a prognosis, Miller said his little girl’s future remained unclear. He is, however, hopeful as doctors expect to know much more by the end of the month.
“They will evaluate from there as to whether or not she’s going to go into rehabilitation, which I am really hoping for because she’s a great candidate for it,” Miller said. “And honestly she could really use it right now given what she’s been through.”
In the meantime, Miller said his daughter has gotten back to eating from a bottle, and he’s eager to see what the future holds.
“There’s been a lot of prayers and a lot of miracles answered. And this one’s one of them,” Miller said. “It’s gonna be a story to tell in the future, too, because the night I got that call I took work off the whole week. I wasn’t going nowhere until I knew my little girl was OK.”
Court filings show the state is working to remove custody from Lowe. Miller expects to know more about his bid for custody this week.

title: Bangor students learn restaurant skills through SOAR Store club visit to Moe’s Barbecue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Fourth- and fifth-graders from Bangor’s Fairmount School got a taste of the restaurant business today.
Members of the SOAR Store after-school club visited Moe’s Barbecue to learn what it takes to run a restaurant, from preparing food to welcoming customers at the register.
The club teaches students about customer service and marketing.
They put those skills to work by selling items to their classmates on Thursday and Friday mornings.
“So we sell items and use the money to help the school. We do snacks, and then there’s a care closet, and then we do a whole bunch of other fun things,” said Duncan Simpson, a Fairmount fifth grader.
“I think it’s fun to be really nice to your customers, like, hey, how are you doing? I think it’s really fun to do that, and I wanted to learn more about it,” said Mirabelle Christopher, a Fairmount fourth grader.
The student-run club uses its profits to restock and support the school.
Students also take on leadership roles, including shift leader.

title: Cornell’s Jane Doe is 'terrified' after swatting incident at her home, lawyer says
text:
Cornell’s Jane Doe is 'terrified' after police swarmed her home in a swatting incident, lawyer says
One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.
Video above: Attorney for Cornell's Jane Doe says she and he family face death threats and swatting call
But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024.
Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents’ home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn.
Doe is increasingly scared for her own safety, Giuffra said in a phone interview with CNN on Wednesday as he detailed his client’s deteriorating mental state after an escalating series of violent threats.
Officers pointed weapons at Jane Doe’s boyfriend, her brother and her father after receiving a bogus tip that “someone was killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening, he said.
Death threats, doxxing attempts and an outpouring of anger online have also been levied at his client, Giuffra added.
“I don’t think she’s in a good spot now,” Giuffra said. “She’s scared.”
Video below: NY AG's office takes over Cornell rape investigation
The public fallout from her allegations have rocked one of the country’s leading educational institutions. The university, its campus police force and the Tompkins County District Attorney’s office have each faced scrutiny over how they initially investigated her claims. Anger among students was palpable during a Wednesday sit-in on the Ithaca, New York, campus.
Doe herself has been following media reports and social media posts on her case, Giuffra told CNN as he described a family reeling from a sudden and terrifying ordeal that punctured their sense of safety.
“Before (this week), it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of,” he said. “Now, it’s somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that’s pretty frightening.”
Doe’s parents are furious after a fake tip to police, lawyer says
At 7 p.m. on Tuesday evening, a police officer in Doe’s hometown was dispatched to respond to a disturbing call: A man had shot and killed his mother and then turned the gun on his sister.
The information was bogus. But the officer, believing an active-shooter situation was unfolding, rushed to Doe’s home, where he saw a car backing out from the driveway, according to a police report from the incident obtained by CNN.
As he apprehended the two men in the vehicle – later revealed to be Doe’s brother and her boyfriend – another figure emerged from the home’s doorway. “I’m the dad. What’s going on?” he yelled, according to the report. The man told police his daughter is Jane Doe of the Cornell case and that the family was “being threatened by numerous unknown people.”
The swatting incident was an escalation in a series of threats to Doe’s safety that have roiled her family this week. The term “swatting” refers to false tips made to law enforcement agencies with the intention of having armed officers deployed to somebody’s home or place of business.
“Luckily, the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up,” Giuffra told CNN on Wednesday, relaying the events of the night. “(Doe’s) boyfriend got thrown on the ground,” and her father also had “guns put in his face,” according to Giuffra. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said.
Police are now investigating the swatting attempt, and the FBI is also looking into the events, according to Giuffra.
According to Doe’s lawyer and two police reports reviewed by CNN, police arrived moments after Doe received a separate phone call from somebody claiming to share a first name with one of the seven men she named in her civil complaint.
According to her account to officers in the reports, Doe “began panicking” when she received the call, “because (her phone) wouldn’t stop ringing.” She informed officers about that previous call while they were at her house following the swatting tip.
Before the night was over, Giuffra’s wife told him that she, too, had received a threatening phone call. “These people have done so much research into (Doe),” Giuffra said. It is not clear whether the separate threats cited in the police reports were connected.
Giuffra said he was in contact with Doe and her family on Wednesday. Her parents are angry and she is terrified, he said.
The lawyer shared with CNN an audio recording of a call he says was placed to his office on Wednesday afternoon. In the recording, a man identifies himself as “the person who called your client.”
The man also is heard saying: “I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed.”
Doxxing attempts also have taken their toll
Tuesday’s swatting attack was an escalation of the potential dangers facing Doe since she filed her lawsuit last month, but it was far from the only threat she’s received, her lawyer said.
Giuffra estimated that dozens of threats have been made against her since mid-September, when his client filed a 101-page complaint alleging she had been sexually assaulted and raped by several members of the Xi chapter of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity.
Doe’s civil suit was filed against the university, the fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that members of the frat drugged and sexually assaulted her in October 2024 and invited other fraternity members in a group chat to join the assault. The suit also alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students, who all deny wrongdoing.
Giuffra detailed to CNN another threat: a text message, sent to Doe’s phone on Monday, with three emojis depicting guns.
Meanwhile, a handful of online personalities with large followings have led a campaign to uncover the identity of Doe, whose name was redacted in legal documents. One wrote on X to 347,000 followers in late September: “If you happen to know who this Cornell ‘Jane Doe’ is, get in touch and I would be happy to publish her name and identifying information.”
He later claimed to have identified her and said he shared that identity online before deleting his post. Such behavior is known as doxxing, or sharing someone’s personal information or identity online without their permission.
It has left Doe frightened and struggling to come to terms with the impact of the lawsuit, which has prompted outrage and scrutiny of how the university and its private police force initially investigated her claims.
On Wednesday, Doe was “taping paper over windows in the house she’s lived at her whole life,” Giuffra said, “so people can’t see into her house to take a shot at her.”
“I don’t get shook up very easily, but this shook me up. I didn’t want to have a body on my hands,” he said.
“The dad is … concerned for his daughter. He can’t believe this has happened out of something where she’s just trying to stand up for herself and be heard,” Giuffra added.
“But the parents are really strong people, and they’re going to protect their daughter.”
Her career dream is 'lost'
Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell’s prestigious Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and it had been her “dream” to attend the school, Giuffra said. Her complaint says she traveled across the country and arrived at the school with the same “hopes, expectations and trepidations of other high school graduates.”
But she left the program without graduating after the alleged assault took place two years ago. Doe initially attempted to begin a career in New York City earlier this year, but after filing the lawsuit – “when everything hit the fan” – she instead returned to her family home, where she has been staying with her boyfriend, her lawyer said.
“The dream is lost,” Giuffra told CNN, referring to her hopes of working in the hospitality industry.
Instead, Doe has been hiding out at her parents’ home, where she has been following the intense media coverage of her case.
“It’s kind of hard to switch it off,” Giuffra said. “She comes from a generation of people who are focused on social media.” CNN is not specifying the location of Doe’s family home at her lawyer’s request.
She has been going on walks but otherwise spends much of her time indoors. She remains in contact with some of the friends she made at Cornell, Giuffra said.
“She’s a little paranoid,” Giuffra said of his client. “If she’s out of (the) safety zone of her family, she just doesn’t seem to function well.” A few friends of the family know she has returned home and have been providing support, and Doe’s mother has taken time off from work to help look after her daughter, he said.
Doe is also aware of the many messages of support that she has received from around the world since filing the lawsuit, according to Giuffra.
Cornell, which recently appointed former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to investigate the school’s handling of sexual assault claims, was the site of a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday to show “solidarity with Jane Doe,” according to flyers for the event.
During a meeting with Cornell’s Graduate and Professional Student Assembly on Monday, university President Michael Kotlikoff acknowledged the mounting frustration across campus as more details and questions emerge about Doe’s 2024 allegations.
“We’re all angry. I understand that anger,” Kotlikoff said, according to the independent student newspaper the Cornell Daily Sun. “People want easy answers to this.”
The school’s president previously released a video statement promising further review of the case, saying it highlights “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”
“The students up there (at Cornell) have been overwhelmingly supportive, and it’s wonderful,” Giuffra said. “They’re trying to effect change, and bringing out to the light something that’s been going on for generations.”

title: Two Loring sites submitted for Aroostook County jail
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - Two sites on the former Loring Air Force Base have been submitted as possible locations for Aroostook County’s new jail.
Loring Development Authority CEO Jonathan Judkins said he and Limestone Town Manager Ed Pocock have discussed the proposal for years, and that it could reduce the tax burden on county residents.
“Loring was incredibly lucky to be considered as one of the sites for the Aroostook County jail,” Judkins said. “Limestone’s town manager Ed Pocock and I have been talking about this proposal for a number of years. It came to me as a simple idea of one taxpayer entity helping another taxpayer entity. We have an opportunity to reduce the tax burden on some of the Aroostook County people.”
Judkins said a centralized location at Loring would cut down on overtime costs for cities and communities outside the range of the current jail.
Two potential sites identified
Judkins said both sites in the proposal meet all requirements for the new jail and have room for expansion if needed.
“So, we have two potential site locations, the crows foot area and then the nose dock area,” Judkins said. “Crows foot features existing structures that could be utilized for administration or housing of the jail personnel. Not to mention world class runway access and ready-made pads of concrete that would support structures of a variety of sizes.”
Past proposal met resistance
Judkins said a county prison had been proposed in Limestone in the past, but back then it was met with backlash.
“Historically, there had been a prison proposed in Limestone. The community did not seem to embrace it. This time it seems like the community can really get behind the idea of the Aroostook County jail being located here for the savings of the taxpayers. You know, we’re all paddling in the same direction. We should try to share resources and utilize the things that already exist,” Judkins said.
Review process underway
The Aroostook County Commissioner’s Office is currently reviewing jail proposals. County voters would have to approve the proposal selected by the Commissioner’s Office before the construction of a new jail can begin.
If Loring is chosen as the new jail site, voters will also need to approve moving the county seat. Any proposal selected will ultimately depend on voter support.
