title: Nearly half of Maine is now in at least severe drought
text:
Experts now estimate that nearly half of Maine is under at least severe drought conditions as the entire state remains mired in a monthslong dry spell that hasn’t been helped by recent rain.
The latest U.S. Drought Monitor map, released Thursday, indicates roughly 46% of the state’s area is in at least severe drought, including 5% — a chunk of coastal Maine — that is experiencing a more dire extreme drought.
No part of the state is yet in exceptional drought, the most serious level.
While the entire state has been under at least moderate drought conditions for multiple weeks, the Drought Monitor reported last week that roughly 19% of the state was experiencing at least severe drought. Now, a large swath of northern Maine has been moved to that designation as well.
That original 19% — an area stretching from northern York County to southern Hancock County, encroaching inward to the Greater Portland, Augusta and Bangor regions — remains virtually unchanged this week. The coastal area of southern and Midcoast Maine under extreme conditions actually shrank slightly.
But a large new zone representing roughly a quarter of the state’s total area — spanning most of Aroostook County, much of northern Penobscot and Piscataquis counties and a slice of Somerset County — is now also under severe drought.
That’s despite recent rain, including a nor’easter that dumped up to 4 inches across the state late last month. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates that, as of Tuesday, Maine needs between 9 and 11 inches of rain within a month to break the drought.
The National Weather Service’s Caribou office said Thursday that water levels are starting to near record lows, while groundwater levels remain below normal. And like the nor’easter, any rain this week won’t provide much relief, the weather service added.
Under extreme drought conditions, rivers, streams and wells dry up, crops widely suffer, and disease breaks out among wildlife, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Even under moderate conditions, honey production can decline, bodies of water drop below average levels, and the risk of wildfires increases.
Maine has battled drought conditions for much of the past two years, with conditions at their worst around this time last year. (More than 40% of the state was in extreme drought last October.)
Conditions steadily improved this spring before a dry, warm summer that was the second-hottest on record in Portland.

title: Midcoast Wood Bank holding meeting to organize volunteer work
text:
Midcoast Wood Bank is holding an open meeting at Topsham Public Library and is inviting community members to help the group decide how to divvy up work and strengthen the wood bank for the coming year.
Since Bruce Wildes founded Midcoast Wood Bank in 2023, volunteers have contributed time, wood, equipment, knowledge, and hard work. In three years, it’s grown to distributing more than 100 cords annually. Now it needs clearer responsibilities and more people involved.
The meeting, running from 9 a.m. to noon on Saturday, Oct. 31, will discuss leadership, create a roadmap for operations — collecting, processing and distributing wood — transportation, fundraising and more.
Anyone can join, no board role necessary. Hands-on volunteers, people with administrative skills, and anyone with ideas about what is working and what needs attention are all welcome.
RSVP by Oct. 14 by emailing [email protected] or calling 207-800-1658. The Topsham library is located at 25 Foreside Road.

title: This daily habit more than doubles your risk of stomach cancer, study says
text:
This daily habit more than doubles your risk of stomach cancer, study says
One sugary drink a day can more than double the risk of stomach cancer, according to a newly published study.
The decades-long study, from Mass General Brigham and published in Gastro Hep Advances, found that people who drank at least one sugary drink each day had about 2.45 times the risk of stomach cancer compared with people who rarely drank them.
Related video above | Cancer cases soar for young people and experts aren't sure why
Researchers studied diet and health information from more than 112,000 U.S. adults.
About 65% of U.S. adults report drinking at least one sugar-sweetened beverage each day, though that figure describes U.S. adults generally, not necessarily the study participants.
The sugary drinks included soda, lemonade, punch and sports drinks.
Over the study period, 278 participants developed stomach cancer. The link appeared in both men and women.
Among women who drank more than one sugary drink a day, the risk was about three times higher than for women who rarely drank them.
Artificially sweetened drinks were not linked to a higher risk.
Researchers also looked at fructose, a common sweetener in sugary drinks, and found that higher overall fructose consumption was associated with more cases of stomach cancer.
The study tracked people’s habits and health, but it did not assign them drinks. Because of that, it cannot prove sugary drinks cause cancer, researchers said.
Researchers say more studies are needed to confirm the findings and understand the connection.

title: Maine heating fund, even with leftover money, won’t go as far this winter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating assistance program plans to use about $4 million left over from last winter to kickstart aid for vulnerable households across the state, MaineHousing announced this week.
This initial round of Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) funding will go to households who applied early to the program with adults over 60 years old, children age 6 and under, and people with disabilities. The $4 million is about 13% of the total heating fuel assistance money expected to be distributed this year.
About 4,400 families will begin receiving credits on their heating accounts in the next week or so, said Scott Thistle, MaineHousing’s spokesperson.
Maine is expecting to receive about $41 million in HEAP funding from the federal government this year — of which about $27 million will be for heating fuel — but that money won’t start arriving until late this month.
“We know this assistance will not fully offset the outsized heating burden many Mainers are facing, but acting now means some of our most vulnerable households can begin the winter with fuel in their tanks,” MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan said in a news release.
Even with the $4 million injection, the heating assistance won’t go as far this winter.
With heating oil costs hovering around a record high, set last month at more than $6 per gallon, the average HEAP award will have less purchasing power than it did last year.
“The benefit amount will just not be as deep,” Thistle said. “It ultimately means less oil for them.”
MaineHousing also used carryover funds to kickstart its HEAP program last year. That was during the six-week government shutdown, when MaineHousing wasn’t sure if the federal government would be providing funding at all, Thistle said.
Last year’s $2 million in extra money provided help for about 4,000 households. This year, $4 million is providing help for 4,400.
The average HEAP award was set this summer at about $700, Thistle said. But after oil costs skyrocketed at the end of the summer and into the fall, the value of that help has fallen significantly, he said.
Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation last week demanding that the federal government allocate more money for heating assistance. Congress kept heating assistance funding level this year.
Prices as high as they are — $5.97 per gallon, as of Monday — demand action from the federal government, Mills said. Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, could be particularly hard-hit if the federal Low Income Heating Assistance Program funds aren’t increased, she said.
Mills blamed record heating costs on President Donald Trump and the war in Iran, where the constriction of the Strait of Hormuz has reduced the worldwide oil supply and driven up costs.
“Federal funding levels appropriated for LIHEAP this winter did not fully consider the drastic impacts of the president’s war that has sent fuel prices skyrocketing and are now insufficient for the circumstances that Maine and other cold-climate states now face,” Mills said.
Meanwhile, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies announced last week their plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, lauded the G7 announcement Friday. She said the release should put “immediate downward pressure on energy prices.”
MaineHousing’s carryover funding will begin with households who applied when the program opened in August, but applications remain open on the agency’s website. Federal funds will go to all eligible applicants as long as there is money available.
Thistle said the number of applications is up about 5% over last year, but are actually substantially far below average in some parts of the state.
Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Person shot during encounter with ICE agents in New York City, officials say
text:
Man shot during encounter with ICE agents in NYC, officials say
A man from the Dominican Republic was shot by federal immigration agents during a targeted enforcement operation in the Bronx on Thursday, according to the Department of Homeland Security, marking the first shooting involving ICE agents in New York City since President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
Federal authorities have not explained what led up to the shooting of the 28-year-old, whose name has not yet been released. DHS said the man has ties to the Trinitarios gang and prior criminal convictions and arrests.
Just after 4 p.m., agents with ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations — a branch of ICE focused on arresting undocumented immigrants — encountered the man when a federal agent discharged a weapon into his vehicle, a law enforcement source told CNN.
The man’s injuries, a graze wound to the neck, were not considered life-threatening, and police transported him to the hospital in a police car and did not wait for an ambulance, according to the law enforcement source.
A 5-year-old was sitting in the back of the car when the shooting occurred and was not injured, the source told CNN. The Associated Press also reports that Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Gov. Kathy Hochul said they had received reports the agents fired at the man while he was inside a vehicle with a 5-year-old child, who was apparently unhurt.
DHS said agents immediately provided aid after the man was shot but did not explain what led to the shooting during the operation.
The man has a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and prior arrests for assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession, according to DHS.
Two agents were also injured in the encounter, according to a law enforcement source, and they also are being treated at a local hospital. One of the agents may have been injured in a car accident, though it’s unclear if the accident was part of the attempted arrest or response, according to a federal official.
CNN asked DHS whether the officers involved were wearing body cameras. The agency referred CNN back to its original statement, which made no mention of body cameras.
At the time of the shooting, witnesses reported to police they saw a man dressed in a bright yellow construction vest holding a gun. Witnesses also told officers they heard five to six gunshots and people screaming, according to police officials.
NYPD were not involved in the incident in the Marble Hill neighborhood just north of Manhattan, the department said in a statement. After the shooting, NYPD officials called for a mobilization to deal with crowd control and evidence at the scene.
Hours after the shooting, agents with Homeland Security Investigations and police officers could be seen walking behind yellow police tape as a group of protesters started gathering at the scene.
HSI responded to the scene to take over the investigation of the shooting, according to a federal source, similar to the law enforcement response to the Sept. 20 ICE shooting in Austin, Texas, which left a man from Venezuela wounded.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement he has “called the President” and “will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city.”
Mamdani and Trump had not yet spoken as of Thursday evening, according to a spokesperson for the mayor.
“Our thoughts are with the injured New Yorker and his family tonight. We are praying for his recovery,” Mamdani said. “Get ICE out of our neighborhoods.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she’s been briefed on the incident.
“We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident,” she said in a statement. “New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why.”
Local leaders and city council members called on DHS to release all available body camera footage and for the state attorney general’s office to launch an independent investigation into the shooting during a Thursday night news conference.
“We want justice for this family, we want it for this neighborhood,” New York Rep. Adriano Espaillat said at the news conference. “And as I said before, I say today, we need to get rid of ICE.”
“Whether you’re in the Bronx or Manhattan, whether you’re documented or not, whether the color of your skin or your religion, you are a New Yorker first, … and New Yorkers stand up for New Yorkers,” Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal said.
____
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Hurricane Hunters fly into Tropical Storm Isaias
text:
BILOXI, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — Hurricane Hunters flew into Tropical Storm Isaias on Wednesday after launching from Keesler Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi. The crew gathered data sent to the National Hurricane Center as the storm moves closer to the Gulf Coast.
The crew flew a WC-130J Hercules about 700 miles southwest of Biloxi, approaching the storm from low altitude.
Second Lt. Andrew Wilson, an aerial reconnaissance weather officer with the 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron, said the data collected during the flights helps forecasters understand what is happening inside the storm.
“If we weren’t out here, we wouldn’t know what this storm is doing,” Wilson said. “You look at satellite imagery and you get an idea of where the storm is, but you don’t really know what exactly is going on inside the storm. We get the data, we send it off to the National Hurricane Center. Then they take all that data, they put it into the weather models and they’re able to give us an idea of what these storms are going to do.”
Lifesaving data
Wilson monitors data collected from instruments on the aircraft’s wings and from dropsondes launched into the storm.
“I’m newer to the squadron. It’s been an amazing thing to do,” Wilson said. “Every storm that I’ve been in, although I’ve only been in a few, has been different. This storm, it has its own things going on, too. We’ve definitely noticed it’s starting to get its act together a little bit.”
From WLOX meteorologist to Hurricane Hunter
Before joining the 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron, Wilson worked as a television meteorologist at WLOX.
“I got to fly with the Hurricane Hunters as a media member,” Wilson said. “It was something I was always interested in. I interviewed for the job in November of 2018. I had just left WLOX. It’s been wonderful.”
Wilson said the public should pay attention to information released by his squadron and the National Hurricane Center.
“It’s really important people pay attention to the information we’re putting out and the National Hurricane Center is putting out, and listen to what they’re putting out. Follow the warnings by local meteorologists,” Wilson added.

title: Exposure to South Portland tank emissions increases cancer, chronic illness risks, report says
text:
South Portland residents living near more than 100 petroleum tanks in the city could be at a higher risk of cancer and other chronic health issues as a result of long-term exposure to carcinogenic emissions, according to a report by the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
The report was based on six years of ambient air monitoring done by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
Monitors placed along the fence line of some of the tank farms regularly logged long-term average benzene concentrations that exceeded state guidelines, according to one and half years of fenceline data collected by the DEP.
Benzene is a known carcinogen, and acute exposure can cause fatigue, dizziness, irregular heartbeat and headaches. High long-term exposures can cause cancers, including leukemia.
The report indicates that the South Portland terminal of the Buckeye Pipeline Corporation, located near Forest City Cemetery, had long-term average benzene concentrations between 2 and 4.5 times the state’s guideline. The Citgo terminal, which is abutted by residential streets, saw levels at twice the state guideline. Levels at Sunoco, Global, Sprague Energy and Portland Pipe Line Corporation (the other petroleum companies with holdings in the city) hovered right around the state’s average guideline.
The tanks are visible from nearby front and backyards. People bike, run and walk by them along the Greenbelt, which sometimes smells like petroleum. Children swing and slide at the new playground in Pleasantdale, a stone’s throw away from tanks.
Acting state toxicologist Thomas Simones, one of the authors of the six-year report, said that the CDC does not know how far from the fence lines the elevated concentrations persist. That will require further investigation, he said.
Representatives from the Maine CDC and DEP will present their results at a South Portland City Council workshop on Oct. 27.
UP IN THE AIR
Simones said residents do not need to worry about air safety for now.
“It’s not to say that if you’re above the guideline, there will be immediate cancer diagnoses in the community or increased rates,” he said. “It’s a theoretical risk that we like to keep low.”
One in three people (or 33,000 out of 100,000) are diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime, he said, based on a combination of family history, diet, alcohol consumption and other environmental factors.
“Here, we’re talking about that number going up to 33,001 or 33,002 out of 100,000 with these increased levels of benzene,” he said. The number is closer to 33,003 near the Citgo terminal, per the report’s modeling.
Rich Campbell is a consultant with Campbell Environmental Group, a firm specializing in remediation work that regularly does work for the state and has worked for many of the oil companies listed in the study. He said he wouldn’t be too concerned if he collected this data for a site they were working on.
Campbell has visited places where people are drinking water contaminated with petroleum, and houses that stink of oil from an underground fuel spill.
“Those are, you know, very high levels,” he said. You don’t reach that level of contamination in ambient air, Campbell said.
“The solution to pollution is dilution,” he said. “That’s the old saying.”
However, other environmental experts disagree.
There is no safe exposure to chemicals like benzene, according to Gail Carlson, an environmental studies professor at Colby College who specializes in the health impacts of pollution.
“If you can see the tanks, you absolutely should be concerned,” she said.
Carlson said the risk of long-term exposure is underestimated in the six-year report, because it doesn’t include the possible carcinogenic chemical naphthalene, which was excluded for data collection and quality concerns. She said the report doesn’t factor in how different chemicals can exacerbate each other’s impacts. (Long-term average concentrations of acrolein, a chemical known to harm the respiratory system, for example, were between 10 and 23 times higher in the city than the state’s guideline.)
The methods of collection, like sensor location and distance from source, could also impact the results, she said.
Some residents worry the findings don’t capture all the risks.
Many of the tank farms in South Portland are not full. The Portland Pipe Line Corp. moved about 5.5 million gallons of crude oil through its South Portland holdings in 2024, although its permit allows the company to move 11 billion gallons per year.
South Portland resident David Hebert wonders whether the emissions would be worse if the tanks were at full capacity. Carlson said that it’s not that simple. Sometimes, a half-full tank can be worse, depending on factors like the ventilation system and age of the tanks, she said.
Carlson thinks the state’s guidelines aren’t protective enough. The Environmental Protection Agency, for example, says that anything higher than a one in a million cancer risk is significant. The state’s guideline is 1 in 100,000 (of 100,000 people breathing the air consistently for 70 years, one person would be expected to get cancer).
“At what level is risk acceptable?” she said. “At what level is risk actionable?”
COMMUNITY IMPACT
For decades, South Portland residents have been worried about the environmental and health impacts of the petroleum tanks that speckle the city.
Three petroleum companies operating in South Portland — Sprague, Global and Gulf Oil — were sued by the EPA in the past 10 years for violating emissions caps for volatile organic compounds dating back decades, the very chemicals that residents are concerned about now. The companies had to pay damages and were ordered to reduce emissions.
Combined, the petroleum companies in the city are permitted to emit more than 550 tons of VOCs per year, according to DEP data.
Global Partners has made operational changes to reduce odors, according to Uri Molina, the company’s community relations manager. He said that Global’s terminal, which stores distillate fuels and asphalt, contains very little benzene compared to other petroleum products.
The other oil companies with holdings in the city did not respond to requests for comments about their contribution to VOC emissions.
Many in South Portland remained concerned about the air in the city, and urged the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and CDC to monitor it. MDEP set up stations across the city by Bug Light, South Portland High School, Redbank, Memorial Middle School and the assessor’s office by city hall. At the urging of residents, they added more locations on Front, Pearl and Mechanic streets, closer to the tanks.
The final six-year report was compiled this fall, and found that risk from exposure increases with time.
Georgia Deveres has lived in South Portland for nearly 40 years, first near Willard Square and now close to Drillen Ace Hardware. She raised her children in the city that she fell in love with.
Her son started getting regular nosebleeds during his freshman year at South Portland High, about 15 years ago, Deveres said. They stopped during the summer, but returned during the school year.
“Was it because he was running track and going to school in a high school that’s basically in a tank farm?” she said. “I’m furious at myself. I sent my kid there.”
When she was 42, Deveres received a scary result on a mammogram of ductal carcinoma, a precursor to breast cancer, even though she didn’t have any family history.
“I’m not saying I got breast cancer because of the tank fumes,” she said. “But I’m not not saying that it couldn’t have contributed.”
Rachel Burger, 89, says she’s has had five different cancers: uterine, vaginal, kidney, bladder and leukemia.
She previously chalked it all up to bad luck, but has started to wonder if they could be related to living near the tanks. Though she can’t see them from her yard, she has smelled them.
Every time there’s a new release of data, there’s a resurgence of public investment, said Chelsea Byun, a nearby resident and former Press Herald editor. She and other concerned residents are organizing a community gathering at 5:30 p.m. at First Congregational United Church of Christ on Meeting House Hill on Oct. 15. Byun is encouraging people to voice their concerns at the city council workshop on Oct. 27.
“We need to get all of our leaders together to actually do something about this now that we have clear evidence that the tank farms are dumping pollution into our neighborhoods,” she said.

title: Watch: Yarmouth cross country is Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Boys Team of the Week: Yarmouth cross country
As the defending Class B state champion, the Yarmouth High boys cross country team knew in preseason it had the returning talent to strive for even higher levels of performance.
On Saturday at the Festival of Champions, the Clippers showed what they could achieve, running to a convincing victory in a field of 79 teams from across New England. Yarmouth also won the event at Belfast’s Troy Howard Middle School in 2025.
Bowen Mitchell (sixth), Jackie Chalmers (eighth), Eli Chalders (13th) and Jesse Canfield (17th) were in the top 20 and just 22 seconds apart in a field with 940 finishers. Yarmouth’s next two runners, freshman Joel Kiander and junior Jasper Keller, finished 72nd and 73rd, providing enough depth to complement the strong top four. Kiander ran fast enough as a solo runner in the freshman race to edge Keller for the Clippers’ final scoring position.
This year’s field was deeper and larger because the New England Championships will also be held on the same course on Nov. 14.
Yarmouth coach Sarah Carrigan said her top four “crushed it.”
“They went in wanting to repeat, but nervous about the competition,” Carrigan said. “But in that top four, all of them PR’d by 20 to 30 seconds. They ran it really strategically, too. That course goes out wicked fast, and they stayed kind of middle of the pack in the first mile and then really turned it on and moved up and executed really well.”
“It obviously feels amazing,” Mitchell said. “I knew all the work we’ve put in was going to pay off. I know that we trusted in the process.”
Yarmouth is the clear favorite to win the Class B championship Oct. 31 at Cony High School in Augusta. Carrigan said the goal for the rest of the season is “taking that pack and moving it up.”
“We definitely have an amazing shot to win states,” Mitchell said. “That doesn’t mean we’re going to stop training. We’re going to train harder, and we want to win.”

title: Randy Cabral's 100th Pavement win highlights NEMA Night at Wiscasset Speedway
text:
While tracks across New England canceled or postponed their racing events on Saturday due to unfavorable weather, Wiscasset Speedway took a chance on the probable window and ultimately won, successfully hosting all Group 1 divisions plus the lightning-fast NEMA Lites and Midgets.
The night kicked off with a 25-lap feature for the County Truss 4-Cylinder Pros. Brody Picard took off with the early advantage, but Chassidy Shorty was on the move, claiming the top spot on lap 5 as Max Parlin followed in succession. Parlin made his way to Shorty's door on lap 8, challenging for the top spot. A lap car slowed the leader shortly thereafter, catapulting Parlin into the lead. While battling for position, Sam Fogg and Darren Miranda made hard contact on lap 22, resulting in a red flag with just 3 laps to go. Max Parlin maintained command on the restart, scoring his second win of the season while Chassidy Shorty and Rowdy Romano rounded out the podium.
Matt O'Brien led the field to green in the night's Pepsi Spotlight feature: a 30-lap bout for the NEMA Midgets. Avery Stoehr was quick to steal it away as Joey Bailey lingered closely behind. Randy Cabral was on the charge early, overtaking second before abruptly coming to a slow on lap 10, resulting in a caution. Avery Stoehr got a good jump on the restart and began to pull away. Meanwhile, third place driver Mike Horn faced mechanical problems, pulling to the infield with just two laps to go. While Avery Stoehr scored his first win of the season, Joey Bailey and Brayden Egan completed the top 3.
Andy Gilbert hopped out to the early lead in the 40-lap feature for the T&L Automotive Modifieds. Kelly Moore was also on the move early, diving to Andy Gilbert's inside on lap 8. The two drivers went door-to-door for a couple of laps before Moore pulled ahead on lap 11. Defending champion Nick Hinkley came to life as the laps wound down, overtaking second on lap 29. Although he was quickly tracking him down, he was unable to catch Kelly Moore, who picked up his third victory of the season. Andy Gilbert followed, completing the podium.
Jeff Farrington took off with the early lead in the 20-lap feature for the Maine Army National Guard Thunder 4 Minis. Ricky Austin made a bold crossover move on lap 2, powering to the top spot just two laps later. Shane Webber was quickly climbing the leaderboard, overtaking second on lap 6 as Derek Cook rode his coattails. Cook got bent out of shape on lap 8, handing third back over to Farrington. He ultimately regained composure, reclaiming the spot on lap 13. Shane Webber was all over Ricky Austin in the closing laps of the race, but Austin was able to hold him off, securing his third straight victory in the division. Derek Cook followed, rounding out the top 3.
Josh Hall took off from the point in the 30-lap feature for the Darling's Brunswick Ford Super Streets. Bubba Pelton peeked to his inside on lap 8 while David Greenleaf joined the fray, making it a 3-way battle for the top spot. Bubba Pelton powered to the lead on lap 11 while David Greenleaf remained glued to his quarter. While duking it out for the top spot, the two drivers made contact on lap 13, catapulting third-place driver Noah Haggett into the lead. It didn't last for long as Greenleaf straightened it out, overtaking the top spot. He sailed into his third victory while Noah Haggett and Bubba Pelton followed, completing the podium.
*Results from the Super Street race are still unofficial and pending engine inspection on the winner's car.
Calvin Bennett took off with the early lead in the 40-lap feature for the NEMA Lites. Randy Cabral was on the move early, overtaking second from Tiana Kibbe on lap 2. Jack Dumas went for a wild ride on lap 13, flipping onto his side in turn 1 after collecting fluid on the track from another competitor. This resulted in an extended red flag and although Calvin Bennett got a strong restart, Randy Cabral seemingly came out of nowhere, clearing him for the top spot. Cabral stretched his lead out to over 2 seconds in clean air, securing his 100th career pavement win as Tiana Kibbe and Zack Martinez rounded out the top 3. Cabral, who was joined by his family in Victory Lane, lovingly dedicated his victory to his dogs, who were also on-site on Saturday.
The night concluded with a 30-lap feature for the Davis Erector Group 207 Crate Modifieds. Ryan Phillips powered to the early lead over Allen Moeller. Travis Buzzell made his way to Moeller's outside on lap 5, challenging for second. Buzzell quickly took over the spot as Nick Hinkley lingered closely behind. Hinkley made way to Buzzell's door on lap 8 and the two drivers battled it out until Hinkley claimed sole possession on lap 12. Travis Buzzell backed down before giving it another go as the laps wound down, stealing the spot back with just two laps to go. Defending champion Ryan Phillips was too far gone at the front of the field, securing the victory as Travis Buzzell and Nick Hinkley completed the podium.
Saturday night's program brought endless excitement and new driver milestones. Team Wiscasset hopes to see even more of this as they host their Group 2 Fan Appreciation Night on Saturday, Aug. 15.
The driver meet and greet will take place on the front stretch at 4 p.m., followed by kid's bike races and qualifying heat races.
As always, adult grandstand admission is just $5 while kids 6 & under get in for free.
For the official track schedule, race results and more, please visit http://www.wiscassetspeedway.com.

title: Loring Celebrates Water Plant Operator’s Legacy
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - Loring in Limestone has renamed their water treatment plant in honor of one man who’s dedicated nearly 30 years to ensuring Loring residents and businesses have had clean, safe drinking water.
Steven C. Gagnon has spent decades working at the Loring water treatment facility and after 29 years he finally took a well-deserved retirement. Now, Loring officials have renamed the plant after him for his years of dedication.
“We changed the name of the Loring developmental water treatment plant from the Madawaska Dam Treatment Facility to the Steven C. Gagnon Water Treatment Plant, and the primary motivation is Steve’s incredible loyalty to it and his craft and his profession in the Loring Development Authority,” said Jonathan Judkins, President & C.E.O. of the Loring Development Authority.
Judkins says Steve has more than deserved the tribute. “Unsung heroes work their lives every day and any tribute that we can give to these guys is a good tribute. Steve served with us for 29 years. You know, the testament to his dedication is the unpaid hours that he’s spent dedicated to trimming grass, cutting trees down. Everything from ensuring that the UV system is operating to give us clean, safe drinking water to going out and shooing wild animals that come up the spillway off. There is no better representative of Loring’s dedication to clean, safe drinking water than Steve Gagnon.”
On Steve’s last day Loring held a celebration. “It was just a matter of keeping it a secret from Steve until his retirement period came. His official last day was last Friday, and we celebrated it and him. He was very emotional and then he was incredibly grateful. He said that was more than he expected and that he is truly honored by the act, and I said, “Steve it’s a small tribute to you who gave us 30 years of work. We were lucky enough to have his family, and his friends join us, as well as Steve’s parents and to see the look of pride on their faces was worth all the effort,” said Judkins.
Now, with his name on the facility he served for nearly three decades, Steve’s commitment to clean, safe water will be part of Loring’s legacy for years to come.

title: GRAPHIC: Bodycam footage reveals moments after 6-year-old boy shot his first grade teacher
text:
NEWPORT NEWS, Va. (CNN) - Newly unsealed body camera footage shows the moments after a 6-year-old Virginia boy shot his elementary school teacher in January 2023. test
Bodycam footage from Newport News Police shows the 6-year-old boy being restrained by a reading specialist at Richneck Elementary School. The boy, who was described by his mother’s attorney as having “extreme emotional issues,” is seen cursing at points in the video.
Abby Zwerner, his first grade teacher, was shot and suffered gunshot wounds to her hand and chest in the January 2023 shooting. Police say the boy had taken the unsecured gun from his mother’s purse and brought it to school in his backpack.
According to prosecutors, the boy stood on a dresser drawer to get the gun from the purse.
The boy’s mother, Deja Taylor, apologized to Zwerner and accepted responsibility for the shooting. She pled guilty to a state charge of felony child neglect and was sentenced to two years in prison in December 2023. She was released from state custody to community supervision in May 2026.
A jury awarded Zwerner $10 million in damages following a civil trial against the school’s former assistant principal, Ebony Parker, who Zwerner said failed to act on concerns that the boy brought a gun to school in the hours before the shooting.
The boy is now in the custody of his great-grandfather. He was not criminally charged in the case, according to Commonwealth’s Attorney Howard Gwynn.

title: AI powered drones are being developed for search and rescue operations
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Personnel from DEEMI say they’re optimistic that new AI-powered technology will be a game changer for search and rescue operations. They’re partnering with the University of Maine and the University of Massachusetts Amherst to develop it.
“Before this emerging technology, what we do is we would fly a pattern with a drone back and forth and take several hundred, sometimes several hundred photos. We’d have to upload them to a server and then we’d have analysts take a look at each individual photo Zooming in, searching back and forth across the photo, looking for an object of interest. You know, hopefully the person that’s lost,” said Vinal Applebee, the Chief Drone Pilot for DEEMI.
But now drones are being developed with artificial intelligence.
The idea is that rescuers can input information about who they’re looking for using things such as what color clothing a person is wearing.
When the drone begins taking photos of the ground below, it will flag images that it believes contains what rescuers are looking for.
Allowing them to look through only a handful of images as opposed to hundreds.
“Our vision is to be able to cut the time from deploying the mission to finding the person from, let’s say, 72 hours down to 7 minutes,” said Xingda Chen, a Postdoctoral researcher at University of Massachusetts Amherst.
“We feel strongly that we’re going to save a lot of time and it will be crucial in the end result,” said Applebee.
But it’s not ready yet, currently the AI is being trained and developed in the field.
“Hopefully we can get this up operational by the end of this year, so I’m trying to push as hard as I could just to make this thing online and be on the server at all times,” said Chen.

title: Isaias is now a hurricane as it surges toward the Gulf Coast. What to know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Isaias strengthened into a Category 2 hurricane as it barreled toward the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday, prompting orders for tourists to abandon beaches for safer spots inland, sending locals scurrying for gas and groceries and leading fishing crews to secure their boats before the potentially destructive storm’s arrival.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season was forecast to intensify rapidly and cause dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Heavy rain and flooding were possible into the weekend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina.
“We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
He added: “Today is the day to prepare and get ready and be in your safe place by tomorrow as conditions will rapidly deteriorate along the northern Gulf Coast as Isaias approaches.”
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph), according to the hurricane center, surpassing the 96 mph (154 kph) threshold for a Category 2 storm.
Isaias was headed northeast at 14 mph (22 kph) and was centered about 260 miles (415 kilometers) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
A hurricane warning was in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida, the hurricane center said. A storm surge warning was in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River.
Preparations underway
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.
At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, while several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida’s Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.
On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Water from the storm surge and high tide could reach heights of 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters) in parts of Alabama and Mississippi, forecasters said. Isaias also could dump up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain on coastal areas and spawn tornadoes overnight Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore.
The National Weather Service warned of possible “long-duration power outages.”
The hurricane formed late in the season
Isaias developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season and was one day short of tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. That record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane. Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, Mexico, and Southern California this weekend.
Isaias is expected to strike a swath of coastline that’s familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism are already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump planned to attend.
In Loxley, a small Alabama community where county officials urged voluntary evacuations, Nichole Eubanks and her husband prepared to ride out the storm on their farm, which is home to dozens of animals, including pigs, donkeys and about 20 rescued cats.
They planned to put contact information on the hooves of their goats, donkeys and pigs in case they got loose.
“It’s definitely scary, and you never really know where these storms are going to go and how bad it’s going to be until it gets there,” said Eubanks, 35.
In the Alabama fishing village of Bayou La Batre, Tony Rice and Lance Connor installed doors on their fishing boat Thursday to protect the vessel. The boat was one of many moored there, and Rice said they planned to move it to a less-crowded spot to decrease the chances of it bumping into others.
In Pensacola, Florida, officials said the airport will close to commercial flights Friday morning. Mayor D.C. Reeves urged residents to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Also contributing were Associated Press reporters Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia; Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas; and Julie Walker in New York.

title: She bought a home in coastal Maine after years spent living at sea
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story is part of the BDN’s Home Buying series that shares stories of Mainers who became homeowners despite the state’s volatile real estate market. Want to share your experience buying a home in Maine? Email kobrien@bangordailynews.com.
A 34-year-old who spent her adult life sailing around New England and the Caribbean has bought her first home in coastal Maine.
Originally from Cape Cod, Annie Kelly spent the past decade in Rhode Island after moving there for school. She bought a three-bedroom, one-bathroom cottage in St. George in August, ending a years-long search for a home base for her nomadic career.
For years she has worked as a boat captain in the charter and yachting industry, which means she travels for work and usually lives on whatever vessel she’s on rather than returning home at the end of each day.
“About three years ago I got tired of not having a mailing address or not knowing where to register my car,” Kelly said.
Kelly’s years-long housing search illustrates how overwhelming looking for a home to buy can be, especially for first-time home buyers with somewhat unconventional careers. Her experience also highlights how challenging it can be when a prospective buyer’s search spans multiple states.
“You can read about the process, but actually being in it is so different and I was really overwhelmed and confused for a lot of it,” Kelly said. “The learning curve you have to do to even understand what’s going on in the process was outrageous.”
She previously rented a small, one-bedroom apartment in Newport for $2,400 a month but otherwise kept most of her belongings, from furniture to souvenirs from her travels, in a storage unit.
“Over the last eight or nine years I didn’t pay rent anywhere, I would just bounce from boat to boat,” Kelly said. “I had a storage unit in Newport for a while that was like my house. I would go there, change out what’s in my duffel bag, then get on the next boat and go wherever the boat was going.”
While this career allowed her to save money for a down payment, as she didn’t pay for housing or food while on board, she lacked a place to call home, she said.
Kelly began looking for a home roughly two years ago. She didn’t look exclusively in Maine at first, but dreamed of living along coastal Maine since 2019 when she began visiting the state during summer sailing expeditions.
“Maine is stunning, beautiful and feels very far away from everything, almost like a retreat,” Kelly said. “It felt like a mythical, magical place and we were always sad to leave.”
However, Kelly wondered if Maine winters would be too dark and cold for her to bear, and whether the midcoast region she loved would be too far from Massachusetts and Rhode Island, where most of her jobs were based.
To test this, Kelly spent last winter in Rockport, where she managed projects on a client’s boat while it was in storage. This was a stark contrast to the many winters Kelly spent on sailing trips to the Caribbean, she said.
At that point, Kelly had looked for a home in Massachusetts or Rhode Island for roughly a year, but shifted her house hunt to Maine in October 2025. She lived in an apartment in Warren that a friend owned while touring at least 20 houses in Maine, she said.
“Before being in Maine, I probably looked at 80 to 100 houses,” Kelly said.
When comparing the housing markets of southern New England and Maine, Kelly said she noticed far fewer open houses in Maine and the buying process in Maine moved slower. However, Kelly’s money stretched farther in Maine than elsewhere, which allowed her to buy more with less.
She wanted a home with at least two bedrooms and a barn or garage while staying under her $350,000 maximum budget, Kelly said. Ideally, Kelly wanted a home within a 30-minute drive to Camden or Rockland and had a preference for older homes with “spooky basements.”
“In my mind, if they’ve been here for 100 years, they’re going to be here for 100 more,” Kelly said. “I think it’s a sign of a good, strong house.”
She found her 1,200-square-foot home this past summer and was drawn to the house’s large backyard and age, as it was built in 1918. The three-bedroom, one-bathroom home sits on 3.5 acres with a barn and spacious back deck.
“It’s the right amount of updated without being flipped,” Kelly said. “As soon as I walked in I knew it was the right one for me.”
The home is also close to the town’s dock and is roughly 20 minutes from downtown Rockland.
Kelly’s $290,000 offer, submitted in July, was accepted and she closed on Aug. 31.
The lower monthly payments allow Kelly to save for larger projects that will be needed in the coming years, such as a new roof. But, Kelly noted she had to spend at least $2,000 on a series of inspections due to the house’s age.
“The biggest relief for me is just having somewhere to be based,” Kelly said. “It’s really nice to just have somewhere to have all my things and to come home in between trips.”
With a place to call home, Kelly said she’s looking forward to advancing her captaining career in a state with a “thriving working waterfront” and “rich history of boatbuilding.”
“Anywhere I’ve sailed into Maine, everyone has been welcoming and lovely,” Kelly said. “It felt like a wholesome place to be where I can come as a young person and continue building a career.”

title: People in addiction often fear law enforcement. In Biddeford, they met on a softball field.
text:
BIDDEFORD — Tia Lavigne stood in the dugout waiting to take the field. At 26, she said it would be the first time she had ever played softball sober.
She said she had played under the influence of substances even as a kid in Buxton. She could throw from home plate to second base without hitting the ground, so she found her place as a catcher. But at just 9 years old, she said, she was given alcohol by an adult and became addicted. Lavigne said she made a lot of “not great choices” and was later arrested on a gun purchasing charge.
By the time she put on the red uniform shirt at Rotary Park in Biddeford on a damp Wednesday night at the end of September, she had been sober for two years, seven months and 16 days, with help from ENSO Recovery in Sanford, and had put herself on a better path by starting her own cleaning business.
“This is the only time I felt comfortable playing ball. All the co-ed teams out there, there are substances around,” she said.
This game, which has become an annual tradition, was unusual: It was built for people in various stages of drug and alcohol recovery to be together — and to play alongside law enforcement officers.
The Recovery Softball BBQ was created by Ryan and Cynthia Paige and their organization AccessDirect Recovery Network in order to break down stigma on both sides.
Lavigne used to see a cop car and bolt in the other direction, she said. On the night of the game, the cars and trucks squeezed into the parking lot and lining the road to the softball field included a lot of police and sheriff’s department vehicles.
“There’s a person out there who might’ve been sober for nine days,” Ryan Paige said, pointing to the field during warmups. “When you look it might be hard to tell who’s who — law enforcement or a person in recovery. That’s the whole point.”
Day to day, he
He stood near the pitcher’s mound before the ceremonial first pitch and said into the microphone that the rate of overdose deaths in Maine was dropping, that recovery was possible and that support from peers mattered. About 150 people stood in the dugouts and along the fences and cheered.
Ryan Paige is in recovery, too, and like some of the people he invited to participate, he said he surprised himself.
“I never thought a life like this was possible for me,” he said, scanning the scene.
He was always social and now he had something productive to channel it toward. So much so that he was too busy to play in the game. He bounced between the barbecue, the vendors and service providers who had set up information tables, the softball field, and the dunk tank, which was a new addition this year.
York County Deputy Sheriff Matthew Cummer, in full uniform, got dunked dozens of times for about an hour. Ryan
QUIETING JUDGMENT
Auburn Police Sgt. Nick Gagnon jogged up to the plate.
“I haven’t hit a ball in 10 years, but I’m hitting this one!” he boldly told the catcher.
Gagnon took a big swing and
He said he’s seen fentanyl and methamphetamine come into Maine over his 17-year career.
“First, like a lot of young officers, you judge people,” he said. “Over time with age and maturity, you learn empathy.”
Asked what he would tell a younger version of himself, he said he would try to explain how important it is to have compassion.
“If you become cynical and judge people in the wrong way,” he said, “ there’s too much hostility between law enforcement and the community.”
By the second inning, the blue team, the Resilient Riders, appeared to be way ahead, though there was no scoreboard and several players said no one was keeping track. It didn’t lessen the effort or enthusiasm in the dugouts.
“It’s so fun to listen to them cheer each other on,” Auburn Police Lt. Matt Dailey said of the players who’d come from sober houses and long-term care facilities to play in the game.
“As law enforcement we need people in recovery to help their friends and get people out of drugs,” he said.
York County Sheriff Bill King walked along the left field fence, blending into the crowd in a sweatshirt.
“I’ve met people who’ve served time in our jail,” he said. “That’s the most fulfilling, to see them working on their substance issues.”
Scott Brockelbank said he played in adult softball leagues for years around Maine and traveled to Disney World for games. During the sixth inning of the game last week, as his team pulled ahead, he said it was the first time he had played sober.
“I always thought I played better messed up, but I actually think I play better sober,” he said. He was proud to play in front of his wife and, in his words, not make a fool of himself.
Brockelbank, who said he first took crack cocaine at age 11 when it was given to him by an adult relative,
“I used to hate law enforcement for a long time. Today I realize they were doing their jobs and I was the problem,” he said. “It’s nice to share the field and not be worried.”
He added that he’d been sober for 90 days.
Brockelbank later said the event may help him get back into softball without it being a trigger to use drugs.
Fog settled onto the field as Gagnon, from the Auburn Police Department, smacked a ball to right center field. His teammate, Austin McAlister, walked up to the plate. McAlister said he got addicted to heroin during his third prison stint, and he used to run away from police and firefighters.
Now he said he’s been sober for 10 months and is in treatment court, where he gets random drug tests.
“Law enforcement changed my life by getting arrested,” he said. “I’m super grateful.”
“When I hear them say going to jail saved my life it feels good,” Gagnon said.
Soaking in the fresh air and freedom of the softball field, McAlister tried out his home run swing and ran down the base path. A few plays later the second baseman fielded a grounder and acrobatically tipped it to the shortstop for an out. Everybody laughed. “It’s like Banana Ball!” someone yelled near home plate, likening it to the wacky, up-tempo baseball that’s getting popular in the U.S..
In the last inning the players decided the red team, the Hope Hustlers, would bat through the order. They were almost certainly losing by a lot but no one was really sure. Dailey, the lieutenant, hit the game’s final pitch a long way out in right field and rounded the bases.
Both dugouts cheered as he came around third, then got tagged out at the plate.
Dailey and his Auburn Police colleagues were the last to leave the field, and they walked away talking about plans for next year’s game.
Nicholas Toth was also thinking ahead. He’d come from a nearby men’s facility in Biddeford to play. At 45, he’d lost toes to frostbite and had other serious health problems, he said. He’s six and a half years sober and credited Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous for helping him.
The night’s game wore him out — he had panted coming around the bases and was emotional as he walked up to Ryan Paige to thank him for organizing everything. Paige had picked him up at a homeless shelter earlier this year.
Just like the players from all backgrounds that night who had whiffed at arcing pitches, lost their footing, and eventually reached base, Toth said his recovery has been bumpy, not linear and not as easy as it looks.
By next year’s game he plans to be living in his own place.
And Ryan Paige has plans to expand the dunk tank.

title: Maine DOT to install temporary supports on Interstate 95 bridge in Benton
text:
The Maine Department of Transportation has closed one southbound lane of Interstate 95 at the overpass that crosses River Road in Benton to install temporary supports.
An inspection showed damage consistent with a vehicle striking the structure. The bridge is located less than a half-mile east of the Kennebec River, just north of Fairfield.
Southbound interstate traffic has been reduced to one lane on the overpass.
The work will also require closing one lane of River Road directly under the bridge. The River Road lane closure will remain in place as Department of Transportation workers complete the project.
Transportation officials advise motorists to use caution and pay close attention when traveling through the work area.

title: Trump repeatedly interrupted by protesters during rally in Texas
text:
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation’s most populous red state.
But Trump’s remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.
Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.
“You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country.”
The president’s message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.
Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.
“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Texas has become an unexpected battleground for Republicans
The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.
Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.
Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.
In a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.
He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.
Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.
“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”
Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primary
While the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.
Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”
“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state’s GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “He’s a fantastic man.”
Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.
He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.
Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.
The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.
The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution.
Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here.”
Trump makes a big announcement, but not about the Senate race
While Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball’s Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.
Trump brought him onstage and said he’d be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame.
Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.
“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. ... You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.”
___
Peoples reported from New York and Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed.

title: Standish-area school district installs new playgrounds after safety concerns
text:
Most students at Maine School Administrative District 6 who started the year without playground equipment will soon be able to climb, slide and swing during recess once again.
Playgrounds at five of six elementary schools in the district, which includes Standish, Buxton, Hollis, Limington and Frye Island, were removed over the summer after an inspection in the spring found “significant safety concerns,” such as exposed rust and nails.
Facilities staff will start installing new playgrounds next week and finish by early November, said Superintendent Brian Campbell. The school board allocated $250,000 of capital reserves to fund the equipment in August.
Campbell said the new equipment, purchased from the Massachusetts-based vendor O’Brien & Sons, closely resembles the previous structures. One added feature is that individual components can be disassembled and replaced when they are worn out so that entire playground removals won’t be necessary in the future, he said.
“We do need to provide good playground equipment so that (kids) can have some fun and get that energy out of them,” Buxton resident Linda Fuller told the school board in August.
Campbell said teachers have found other ways to keep students active with games of four square and large walking groups. He said teachers incentivize students to walk more miles around school buildings with them for raffle tickets for prizes.
Amanda Martin is leading a committee of parents, school board members and staff looking at funding additional equipment that is accessible for children with disabilities.
Martin said she is now homeschooling her kindergartener, who has autism and requires access to a playground to remain calm. She said staff told her the only other option would have been for her daughter to attend Buxton Center Elementary School, which is farther from where she lives in Standish but still has a playground.
“These playgrounds are more than just from bell to bell. They’re actually a shared public resource, and people are using them at all ages and all abilities,” Martin said at the Oct. 5 school board meeting. “Movement is critical to building brains and neurons.”
Martin is working to find pieces of equipment from the vendor building the new playgrounds and fundraising from sponsors. She said game panels, ramps, and a wheelchair-friendly swing are possible amenities, and estimated the total cost of the equipment will come to $50,000-$80,000.
Poland Spring, a Maine-based bottled water company, has expressed interest in sponsoring the additional safety features. It is waiting for proposals on specific pieces of equipment before committing a set amount of money, a company spokesperson said.
Martin also said she is looking into the American Academy of Dermatology’s Shade Structure Grant Program, which gives grants of up to $8,000 to public schools and nonprofit organizations for installing permanent shade structures.
Campbell said any equipment brought forward would need to be inspected by facilities staff to make it sure is up to code before installing it.
“As the new playgrounds are going in, I’m asking the board to ensure that inclusion is part of the design from the beginning,” said Adrienne Paul, owner of Pollywogs to Speckled Frogs Childcare and Preschool in Standish and the Republican candidate for Maine House District 85, at the Oct. 5 school board meeting. “Children need meaningful opportunities to play alongside their peers.”

title: Strawberry farmer hopes steam holds the key to healthy soil and a better crop
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATSONVILLE, Calif. (AP) — Long-time strawberry farmer Rod Koda has rows of plants on his California farm that are still producing fruit well after the harvest would typically end.
The fields brimming with green near the Pacific Coast have produced nearly twice the amount of organic strawberries this year as other plots thanks to steam, he said. The bountiful plots were treated with steam before Koda planted his organic strawberries as part of a project aimed at finding an alternative to chemical fumigants used to kill soil-borne diseases and weeds.
“It’s a very noticeable difference,” Koda said.
Steam has been used for decades in greenhouses, and researchers in California have been working to adapt the technology to the fields where strawberries, one of the state’s key crops, are grown near the Pacific Coast. It’s part of a broader push to help organic farmers become more productive and reduce the use of chemicals that environmental advocates say pose a health risk to farmworkers and those who live near the fields.
Rick Tomlinson, president of the California Strawberry Commission, said researchers have been working on steam for more than a decade and are tinkering with the technology so it can be applied to fields faster. The industry has also been working on other alternatives to chemical fumigants including cutting off oxygen to kill soil disease and developing more resistant plants, he said.
“Fundamentally, there’s this disease in the soil and if you don’t have some solution, you’re just rolling the dice and one of the years you’re going to end up bankrupt,” Tomlinson said, “because it can wipe out the entire field.”
Nine out of 10 strawberries grown in the United States come from California. The berry, which is grown on 35,000 acres (14,000 hectares), was one of the state’s top 10 commodities in 2025.
Strawberry growers have long relied on chemical fumigants because the fruit is grown close to the ground and is soft and fleshy, making it susceptible to disease, farm experts said. Using a machine to inject steam into the soil before planting can kill key soil-borne diseases and weeds and improve crop productivity, said Jenny Broome, a University of California, Santa Cruz researcher working on the project.
Four growers in California participated in the trials last fall, Broome said. On Koda’s farm, the steam-treated plots produced more berries and also suffered less damage from fusarium wilt, a fungal disease, she said.
Steam might also work on fields used for lettuce, carrots and other high-yield crops, she said. A challenge is making steam cost-effective for farmers, and proponents of the technology are trying to speed up the machines used in the process so they can cover more terrain faster.
“We’re going back to the future, where we’re looking back at an older technology but we’re finding more ways to engineer more efficiently and use it,” Broome said.
David Andrews, chief science officer for the Environmental Working Group, welcomed the push for an alternative to traditional fumigants, noting farmworkers in the fields and their families are the ones who have been exposed to the chemicals. He said the technology has improved while concerns about the impact of fumigants have risen.
“The economics are shifting,” Andrews said.

title: Expensive ads don’t make a candidate good
text:
Whoever is orchestrating the media campaigns for Sen. Susan Collins, Bobby Charles and Paul LePage have done an excellent job of embracing misinformation, a deliberate distortion of the facts. They are using classic, well-documented logical fallacies to mislead citizens in every ad that has been released.
While maybe not outright lying, they are still cherry-picking small issues and claiming they are big problems (voter fraud, really?). They’re correlating related issues without looking for actual causes (Hannah Pingree is causing climate change in Maine, really?); attacking their opponents personally instead of addressing the issues; and using classic straw-man arguments, bandwagon appeals and red-herring charges to distract from the fact that massive funding from the billionaire class does not make anyone a good candidate.
Just because they sound momentarily reasonable on air or in our mailbox does not make them true. Checking the actual data will allow everyone to see through the ridiculous arguments in every million-dollar ad backed by those with money and power — who want to keep both.
Patricia Millett
West Farmington

title: Letter to the Editor: No Kings: Vote Early
Trump says US will not resume military strikes on Iran before the midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States.
Trump, while stumping for Republicans this week, has hinted that was confident that at endgame to the war cold come in the days before or after the election, while also hinting that he remained open to resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
But Trump in a social media post on Thursday said the U.S. “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”
Trump added that his team has been “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Negotiations had appeared at a standstill since Trump late last month publicly rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the U.S. met certain conditions.
Iran, however, said last week they had received a U.S. counterproposal. And Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Thursday said he expected Tehran would offer a formal reply within days.
Trump’s post comes as the military has dispatched more resources to the region. U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could arrive as early as the end of October.
Trump’s announcement was made the same day the USS Abraham Lincoln was due to arrive to its home port in San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war. There have been reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
The USS George Washington, which is usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August. The other aircraft carrier in the Middle East, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.
