title: Troy Jackson was being paid by unions throughout his run for governor
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson was paid $138,000 from a pair of unions throughout his previous gubernatorial run over the last two years.
The former Maine Senate president and longtime labor organizer from Allagash challenging five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins, said his main income since early 2025 came from consulting work in a Senate financial disclosure made public this week.
Jackson earned $90,000 from the International Association of Machinists and $48,000 from the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades over most of 2025 through this summer while he was running for governor.
The payments show how closely Jackson’s livelihood has been tied to the labor movement that powers his politics. The same unions that paid him also helped bankroll an outside group backing his bid for governor. Their checks were a major source of income while he ran a demanding statewide campaign that bled into his Senate run.
Jackson’s campaign has offered few details about what the work entailed, describing it only as consulting and organizing services on national and labor issues. The disclosure lists his role with both unions as “general consultant.” Neither union responded to requests for comment.
Both jobs began in March 2025, two months before he entered the governor’s race. The machinists’ job lasted until August, after he’d filed paperwork in July to explore replacing Graham Platner and later secured the Democratic nomination. His past work for the union, which represents Bath Iron Works employees, made headlines after he sent a 2019 letter to the shipyard criticizing hiring practices while being paid as an organizer.
The IUPAT paid Jackson through June 2026, when he placed third in the gubernatorial primary behind nominee Hannah Pingree and runner-up Nirav Shah. Jackson’s payments from IAM were split $50,000 in 2025 and $40,000 in 2026, and $30,000 in 2025 and $18,000 this year from IUPAT. In total, Jackson made nearly $148,000 over 2025 and 2026 and 2025 in “self-employment income.
Painters District Council 35, IUPAT and the Machinists also helped fund the Working Mainers First PAC, an outside group that spent more than $900,000 on advertising to get him elected to the Blaine House. Jackson’s campaign said he did not speak with anyone at the unions about the group’s messaging, plans or funding, which would be illegal under state law.
“Troy’s financial disclosure reflects a lifetime of working for a paycheck,” the Jackson campaign said in a statement that did not answer questions about the nature of his work. “He’s a logger and union member who understands what it means to worry about making ends meet — and he would bring that experience to a Senate dominated by millionaires.”
Filed Monday after Jackson was granted a nearly two-month extension, the disclosure marked the first look at Jackson’s finances. It came as the pivotal battleground race intensified with ads and debates. Both candidates are clashing over claims of financial impropriety and corruption.
The Collins campaign knocked Jackson for taking “the latest extension possible” to file the disclosure. They argued his income from “three unions and a dark money group” was at odds with Jackson’s pledges of transparency.
The Jackson campaign fired back regarding a $4,800 payment in 2025 from Brewer nonprofit Food and Medicine, telling Newsweek, “Only Susan Collins would call a nonprofit delivering food assistance a dark money group while she sits at the center of a pay-for-play scandal.”
Jackson’s team continues to press Collins on a defense contractor who made illegal donations during her 2020 bid and claimed he engaged in a bribery scheme involving the senator and other lawmakers. The Democrat has emphasized that Collins’ husband, former lobbyist Thomas Daffron, was paid as a consultant last year by Chesapeake Enterprises, a firm led by longtime Republican operative and pro-Collins PAC leader Scott Reed.
Collins has vehemently denied any wrongdoing, calling former Navatek CEO Martin Kao a “crook” and liar who spun a tale to the FBI and ProPublica. ProPublica has defended its reporting and says an FBI inquiry only shut down amid President Donald Trump’s crackdown on the agency last year. Collins’ team says the FBI hasn’t talked with the senator or staff on the matter since 2021.
On top of the union payments, Jackson received $4,800 in 2025 as an organizer for Food and Medicine, and $5,100 that year from the Eastern Maine Labor Council. He worked as an organizer for both organizations from September 2021 through February of 2025. A logger for at least 15 years, Jackson has worked as a logger only intermittently after he became a state lawmaker in 2002.
Jackson’s financial disclosure highlighted a stark contrast between the candidates in terms of net worth. Jackson’s and his partner’s assets total between $147,000 and $430,000. His partner has between $100,001 and $250,000 in state retirement benefits, while Jackson’s pension plan is valued between $15,001 and $50,000.
Collins’ assets when combined with her husband’s, former lobbyist Thomas Daffron, were between $4 million and $10 million, largely in mutual funds and stock holdings, in her latest annual financial report.
The senator in 2012 co-wrote the STOCK Act, meant to prevent insider trading and bolster transparency. The STOCK Act has come under scrutiny by both parties and watchdogs for not leading to stronger enforcement.
She has resisted pushes for a congressional stock trading ban, although she voted for a Republican bill that paired one with voter ID requirements. Collins has said members of Congress should not be allowed to buy or sell individual stocks unless the portfolio is managed by an outside advisor without consultation with the lawmaker. Jackson says he’d support a ban.

title: Maine residents could qualify for compensation in generic drug price-fixing settlements
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine residents could qualify for compensation in generic drug price-fixing settlements
Attorney General Aaron Frey has joined a multistate effort to settle allegations that pharmaceutical companies conspired to inflate prescription drug prices.
Maine residents could qualify for compensation in generic drug price-fixing settlements
Attorney General Aaron Frey has joined a multistate effort to settle allegations that pharmaceutical companies conspired to inflate prescription drug prices.
Maine residents who purchased certain generic prescription medications between 2009 and 2019 could be eligible for compensation under settlements that were proposed involving three pharmaceutical manufacturers accused of conspiring to artificially inflate drug prices.
Attorney General Aaron M. Frey announced that Maine is joining a coalition of 45 states and territories that are seeking court approval of settlements involving Ascend Laboratories, Citron Pharma and Mayne Pharma.
Under the proposed agreements Ascend will pay $400,000 to the states, and Mayne will pay $650,000. Citron Pharma's settlement only includes nonmonetary terms because the company no longer exists.
All three companies agreed to reforms intended to promote fair competition and compliance with antitrust laws.
According to the AG, investigators reviewed more than 20 million documents and millions of phone records as part of the multistate investigation.
The latest agreements follow previous settlements with several other pharmaceutical companies totaling approximately $496.5 million.
Maine residents who purchased certain generic prescription drugs between May 2009 and December 2019 may be eligible for compensation.
Consumers can learn more by visiting AGGenericDrugs.com, emailing info@AGGenericDrugs.com or calling 1-866-290-0182.
The settlements proposed still require court approval. The first trial is scheduled for February 2027 in Hartford, Connecticut.

text:

title: Medicare’s $90 premium rebate is rolling out. How much will it offset rising healthcare costs?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Medicare’s $90 premium rebate is rolling out. How much will it offset rising healthcare costs?
The one-time payment comes as premiums are projected to keep climbing in the years ahead.
Medicare’s $90 premium rebate is rolling out. How much will it offset rising healthcare costs?
The one-time payment comes as premiums are projected to keep climbing in the years ahead.
President Donald Trump's one-time $90 Medicare Part B Premium rebate officially rolled out Thursday. Around 20.8 million enrollees are said to benefit from the premium rebate.
According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, most beneficiaries will receive a direct payment of $90 on or around October 8, 2026.
Some beneficiaries will receive a paper check for $90 from the U.S. Department of the Treasury later in October.
Who will receive the $90?
Eligible Medicare beneficiaries include those originally in Medicare part B who are:
- Living in the United States
- Not receiving premium assistance from Medicaid;
- Or not paying an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount.
Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage, who make up more than half of all Medicare recipients, are not eligible.
How much of a dent will $90 make for Part B Premiums?
Each year, the government sets Medicare’s Premiums, deductibles and coinsurance rates. In 2026, the Medicare Part B Premium is $202.90 a month, or $2,434.80 for the year.
The 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projects that the annual premium will rise by $79.20 in 2027, bringing the total to $2,514. The administration’s proposed one-time $90 payment could help offset that increase for one year.
But KFF, a nonprofit health policy research group, said the one-time payment may not go far in offsetting rising costs for healthcare.
Medicare part B Premiums have been growing fast in recent years. The standard monthly premium rose 9.7% in 2026, the second-largest increase in the program's history.
Medicare Part B Premium rates saw the steepest year-over-year increase in 2022, when monthly rates rose 14.5% from $148.50 the previous year to $170.10. The federal government said that increase had to do with the COVID pandemic and uncertainty over a pricey and controversial new Alzheimer's drug, according to a CNN report. Premium rates were rolled back by $5.20 the following year, but have risen steadily since then.
The 2026 Medicare Trustees Report now projects Medicare Part B Premiums will rise by 6% to 7% annually for the next seven years.
Medicare premiums have increased at a far faster rate than inflation and Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustments or COLA.
While the COLA does not directly affect Medicare plan pricing, the increase will be outweighed by rising premiums.

title: Attorney for Lewiston shooting victims urges judge not to dismiss lawsuit against U.S. government
text:
PORTLAND — In a packed courtroom on Thursday, an attorney for the victims of Maine’s deadliest mass shooting said they want to know why the U.S. Army failed several times to seize the firearms belonging to the reservist who killed 18 people and wounded 13.
On Oct. 25, 2023, Robert Card — a 20-year veteran of the Army — opened fire at a bar and a bowling alley in Lewiston. He was found dead two days later.
More than 100 survivors and family members of the victims sued the government a year later, alleging that the Army failed multiple times to seize Card’s firearms despite recognizing an obligation to do so and having a duty under several Army policies identified by the plaintiffs.
They filed their lawsuit under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows lawsuits to be filed against the entire government. The government has requested the lawsuit be dismissed, arguing that it’s covered by several exemptions outlined in the act, including one for “discretionary immunity” in cases where the government’s policies leave decision-making up to its employees.
If the lawsuit is dismissed, there will be no civil discovery process that Jamal Alsaffar, an attorney for the plaintiffs, said would provide his clients with answers.
“There is no person, no other agency, no other law enforcement agency, that knew more about the threat that Sgt. Card posed to this community” than the Army, Alsaffar told a federal judge during a hearing on Thursday. “Let us discover how deep this negligence goes.”
It’s unclear when U.S. Chief District Judge Lance Walker will decide on the government’s motion following the two-hour hearing in the federal court in Portland. Attorneys agreed earlier this year to combine two lawsuits against the government — one filed in September 2024 by 102 plaintiffs, and another filed in April by a sister of one of the victims.
About three months before the shooting, Card had been hospitalized at Keller Army Community Hospital in West Point, New York, after threatening fellow soldiers during a July 2023 training exercise. Despite making further threats of violence and describing what officials later called a hit list, Card was discharged two weeks later.
Recommendations that Card not have access to firearms were discretionary, attorneys for the government argued Thursday. Because medical records state that Card’s hospitalization was voluntary, the government said there was no mandatory requirement that the government take Card’s guns.
“There is no dispute here that Card ultimately consented to hospitalization,” attorney Jocelyn Krieger, from the U.S. Department of Justice, argued in court.
In court records, the DOJ has argued that the plaintiffs cite “no regulation or policy” in their lawsuits that would have required Card’s supervisors to take specific action while he was on duty. Card was not on active-duty orders during the mass shooting, and the government has argued he was “solely responsible” for what happened.
Card had also not been convicted of any crimes that would prohibit him from possessing firearms, DOJ attorney Brandon Capece argued Thursday, after Walker asked how this case was different from a lawsuit in Texas, where the government was ordered to pay $230 million in damages after an Air Force member killed 26 people during a church service in 2017. The government appealed and settled a year later for $144.5 million.
That Air Force member had a domestic violence conviction that legally barred him from having a gun, Capece said.
Alsaffar represented several survivors in the Sutherland Springs church shooting lawsuit. He disagreed with Capece and Krieger in court, saying there are several Army procedures that would have allowed Card’s chain of command to seize his firearms.
The Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Defense found in September that the Army failed to implement several relevant policies when it came to addressing Card in the months before the shooting.
Alsaffar disputed that Card’s hospitalization could be considered voluntary. He said documents show that Card was hospitalized under Army command, with several guards present and restraints.
At Keller and a contracted hospital, Four Winds, Alsaffar said Card expressed he was afraid he would commit a mass act of violence and that he was hearing voices that weren’t there. Keller said Card also consented to letting the government take his guns upon his being discharged.
One of Card’s supervisors failed to open an email about his discharge recommendations, Alsaffar argued, citing testimony to an independent state commission that investigated the shooting. Another captain failed to contact local law enforcement officials about implementing Maine’s yellow flag law, which would have allowed the Sagadahoc County Sheriff’s Office to take Card’s firearms, Alsaffar said in court.
Alsaffar said this was the kind of “garden variety negligence” that the government has been sued and found liable for in other lawsuits.
He said that those Army supervisors testified that they believed officials higher up in the Army would step in, and that the civil discovery process might reveal that.

title: Immigration agents shoot a man during arrest in New York City
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Federal immigration agents shot and wounded a Dominican man while arresting him in New York City on Thursday, in what the Department of Homeland Security called a “targeted enforcement operation.” Protesters decried it as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
The man survived and is being treated at a hospital, the agency said. It did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that “during the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon” and that the man was injured.
The agency described the man as a “criminal illegal alien” with a prior grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests. He was arrested in December 2023 but was released, the agency said, blaming “reckless” policies in Democrat-led cities, such as New York.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani called in a statement for an end to all Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in the city. Demonstrators at the scene chanted, “ICE off our streets now!”
An FBI spokesperson said an evidence response team was responding to the scene “to support our partners at the Department of Homeland Security,” but offered no other details. Messages seeking further information were sent to federal authorities.
The person who was shot was conscious and being treated at a hospital, the New York Police Department said in a post on X, noting that its officers didn’t witness the shooting and weren’t involved.
The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood, a small part of Manhattan attached to the Bronx.
Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, said in a post on social media that she had been briefed on the shooting.
“We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why,” she said.
Videos and photos posted by bystanders on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up an apparently injured man and carrying him into a police vehicle.
Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows.
The videos show agents wearing ICE badges on the scene, including one carrying a rifle.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani said in a statement. Mamdani, a Democrat, said he had called President Donald Trump and planned to demand that the Republican stop all ICE enforcement actions in the city.
“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities,” Mamdani said.
___
Associated Press writers Anthony Izaguirre, Jennifer Peltz and Michael R. Sisak contributed.

title: College football player dies in rollover crash; teammate accused of driving while intoxicated
text:
SHERMAN, Texas (KXII/Gray News) - An Oklahoma football player has died in a rollover crash, with his teammate arrested in connection with the collision.
Dylan Sebock, a Southeastern Oklahoma State University football player, was killed in the crash that occurred early at about 1 a.m. Thursday on U.S. Highway 75.
Sherman police officers said Sebock and the driver of the vehicle, later identified as 23-year-old De’Taurean Johnson, were ejected from the car.
According to police, Sebock was pronounced dead at the scene and Johnson was found lying in the roadway.
Officers said Johnson attempted to take off from the scene before being taken into custody and transported to an area hospital for his injuries from the crash.
Investigators noted that they collected evidence establishing that Johnson was intoxicated while driving, which contributed to the death of the 23-year-old Sebock.
Johnson, listed as a senior linebacker for Southeastern Oklahoma State University, was released from medical care and arrested for intoxication manslaughter.
“We are deeply saddened to confirm that one student has died as a result of the accident. The other student was hospitalized. Our hearts are with their families, friends, teammates, and all those affected by this tragic loss,” the university shared.
Loved ones have since set up a GoFundMe to help support Sebock’s family.

title: One-in-2.9 million Marvel card, with Spider-Man co-creator's cut signature, found at comic shop
text:
One-in-2.9 million Marvel card, with Spider-Man co-creator's cut signature, found at comic shop
A routine stop for Pokémon cards turned into a potentially life-changing discovery for a Pennsylvania man.
Brian Schmidt, a dad of three and bartender in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, was with his kids at 4th Wall Comics when he bought a single pack of new Marvel trading cards on a whim, sister station WGAL reported.
He opened it right away and found a very thick card containing a signature from Steve Ditko, the co-creator of Spider-Man.
"I was like, 'Those look pretty cool. I should get a pack,'" Schmidt said. "And I opened it up, and I had no idea that I pulled, like, a one-in-three-million thing."
The card comes from the 2026 Topps Chrome Marvel Comics collection. Topps calls the subset "The One and Only," which includes one-of-one cut-signature cards featuring Ditko and Spider-Man's better-known creator, Stan Lee.
A cut signature is not an autograph placed directly on the card. It is an authentic signature taken from an existing document and mounted inside a newly manufactured card.
The published odds of pulling a card from that chase are about one in every 2.9 million packs.
At first, Schmidt thought the card might be common.
“I thought it was interesting looking, but I also thought it probably came in every pack,” Schmidt said. “But then, when I got home, I scanned it, and I saw the price, like, ‘Oh, geez.’ And I contacted my friend, and he’s like, ‘You don’t know what you have.’ And I was like, ‘Apparently not.’”
His friend quickly realized the card could be something special.
“He was like, ‘Where’s that?’” Schmidt said. “I was like, ‘In my car.’ He was like, ‘Get it out of your car right now.’ And I was like, ‘OK, OK.’”
Schmidt said he would consider selling it to help with his children’s future.
“I’d love to keep it, but... it might pay for some of college and stuff like that eventually,” he said.
He has contacted Goldin Auctions about possibly consigning the card. It still must be examined, authenticated, and graded before its value is determined.
Store owner reacts
The card was pulled at 4th Wall Comics, where owner James Matheson said he was there when it happened.
“I was just running shipment, and they were looking at this card, and they’re like, ‘Oh, I got a Ditko,’” Matheson said. “OK, cool—awesome pull, Ditko—and I went back to work. But then when I came back up, my brother told me, like, ‘No, dude, that was a signature.’”
Matheson said he was glad it happened in his shop.
“I’m glad I was here to see it, and I’m glad it’s sitting right in front of me,” he said. “It’s cool.”
Who's Steve Ditko?
Ditko, born in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, in 1927, helped define Spider-Man’s look and helped create characters including Doctor Octopus, Sandman, the Lizard and Green Goblin. He died in 2018 at age 90.
Stan Lee is more widely known as the father of Spider-Man, but Marvel credits both men with the creation of the popular character.
The card’s appeal is tied in part to Ditko’s reluctance to seek the spotlight. Unlike many creators, he rarely gave interviews and often declined autograph requests.
A growing card-collecting trend
For collectors, the card is part of a larger trend in the hobby: rare chase cards, autographs and one-of-one inserts hidden inside sealed packs.
Schmidt’s son said the family was excited to be there for the pull.
“It’s just really cool that my dad got to pull it,” he said. “Yeah, they were freaking out when they found out.”
Matheson said the store has seen more interest in trading cards in recent years.
“Ever since, like, COVID, the trading cards, I think, have been getting a little bit more popular,” he said.
Experts say opening packs should be treated as entertainment, not an investment plan.
For Schmidt, though, this one pack was already unforgettable.
"I mean, I'll probably never pull something that cool again," he said.

title: Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts created, White House says
text:
Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts created, White House says
Automatic enrollment added 60 million of the nearly 70 million Trump Accounts. Parents must claim and manage them through the official app.
Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts created, White House says
Automatic enrollment added 60 million of the nearly 70 million Trump Accounts. Parents must claim and manage them through the official app.
The Treasury Department says it has automatically enrolled more than 60 million eligible children into Trump Accounts, a new type of long-term investment account, as of Oct. 1. The White House says that brings the total number of Trump Accounts created to nearly 70 million.
Parents of U.S. citizens under 18 with a Social Security number must claim the accounts to manage them. This process requires downloading the official Trump Accounts app and verifying their identity and relationship to the child. The Treasury Department says auto enrollment eliminated the need for parents to file Form 4547 with their tax return to open an account.
The accounts have drawn attention due to the government's promise of a $1,000 contribution for children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028. However, the Treasury clarified that accounts were opened for all eligible children, not just those qualifying for the $1,000 contribution.
When Trump Accounts launched this summer, the National Consumer Unit asked Fidelity Investments how parents should evaluate them. Fidelity said families should start with their goals, since different accounts serve different purposes.
"Perhaps your next best dollar, because your goal is for saving for your child's education would be a 529," said Rita Assaf, Vice President of Retirement Solutions at Fidelity Investments. She added, "And then retirement, while far away for a lot of children, is still a goal that many have. So, this is where the Trump Account does come up."
Fidelity also advises families to focus on their overall financial health, including building emergency savings and prioritizing their own retirement, especially if they have high-interest debt.
The Treasury Department may contact parents about activating accounts via emails from no-reply@TrumpAccounts.Treasury.gov. Officials emphasized that these emails will never request passwords or sensitive account credentials through email, text, or phone calls.

title: Mills administration allocates funding to keep PCHC afloat
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot Community Health Care is set to receive additional funding to avoid bankruptcy and continue serving nearly 50,000 Mainers, with just over two weeks remaining before a funding deadline.
In a letter sent to Lori Dwyer, PCHC’s president and CEO, Mills said the state will make available $2.8 million in Rural Health Transformation Funds to help preserve access to health care for the Maine people served by PCHC.
In late August, PCHC said it needed roughly $3 million within 30 to 60 days to make it through what it called an “immediate crisis.” Oct. 24 would mark 60 days from that announcement.
Over the last few weeks, PCHC has laid off employees, frozen pay, closed offices and cut services amid other cost-saving measures.
Last month, Mills met with PCHC leadership to learn why the federally qualified health center faces a unique crisis compared to others in Maine.
Her office said at the time the administration was exploring potential short-term state funding to keep operations afloat until the Legislature reconvenes.
Mills’ letter to PCHC
Mills full letter to PCHC:
“I am writing with respect to your request on behalf of Penobscot Community Health Care (PCHC) for additional financial support from the State of Maine given the dire fiscal status of the organization. Specifically, you have requested $7 million from the State — $3 million to protect operations through December 2026 and up to $4 million of additional support over the following eight months in order to effectuate a 12-month turnaround plan for PCHC. Your “Turnaround Strategy and Financial Plan” document outlines this $3 million request as $2.71 million of cumulative operating shortfall in September through December 2026 and a 10 percent contingency request.
“I remain deeply concerned about the extent to which the organization finds itself overextended and underfunded due to a lack of appropriate planning and management. This situation is particularly troubling given the significant investments the State has made in federally qualified health care centers (FQHCs), including PCHC, over the last several years. MaineCare’s total spending on FQHC services has increased by nearly 50 percent over the last three years, totaling over $100 million in calendar year 2025. Regarding PCHC in particular, in those same three years, PCHC’s MaineCare encounter rate has reached $283.89 — an increase of 45 percent.
“It is also important to note that in these times of increased costs and a federal regulatory environment that is creating severe financial and operating pressures, there are a number of health care facilities — hospitals, nursing facilities, behavioral health providers, and other FQHCs — also struggling.
“However, with PCHC being the state’s largest FQHC, serving approximately 50,000 patients, I am committed to doing whatever possible to preserve needed services to the people, particularly the most vulnerable, who currently access care at PCHC. To that end, the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) worked intently to identify funding and increase allotments under the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) to PCHC to support expenses related to Electronic Medical Records (EMR) and for the transition to Alternative Payment Models (APM). Specifically, DHHS has identified an additional $2.8 million beyond the original allotments of $316,324 for APM and $543,276 for EMR. This amount will be paid out monthly in accordance with invoices for expenses from PCHC and in amounts of no more than $1.219 million each in October, November, and December. To the extent additional funding is still sought, that request will need to be made in the next legislative session.
“This request came at a time when my options as Governor are limited. With the Legislature not in session, there is simply no way to appropriate funding without their approval. My Administration’s previous statements about limitations on the use of RHTP still stand. Further, it took great effort to identify funding within RHTP that would not negatively impact other providers, many of whom have made difficult decisions to maintain their operations in the current environment. However, under these exceptional circumstances, and in order to preserve access to services on behalf of tens of thousands of Maine people, my Administration worked collaboratively with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to arrive at this approach. These funds must be used for APM and EMR approved costs, and not for general capital outside of these initiatives.
“Additionally, given this increase in funding to PCHC, and the extremely tentative financial status of the organization, certain reporting will be required as defined in Rider A of the contracts. It is critical to have a full picture of how and why PCHC got into this position and how the management and Board will make changes to restore stability and internal and external trust. The RHTP team will be in touch about next steps toward establishing the contracts with PCHC.
“My top priority has been and remains that the people served by PCHC continue to have access to the health care and other services they need. I appreciate this opportunity to work with PCHC as it pursues long-term sustainability.”
PCHC releases statement
PCHC released this statement Thursday evening:
“We are in receipt of incredible news from Governor Mills and her leadership team. They have identified an additional $2.8 million investment in Penobscot Community Health Care through the Rural Health Transformation Program. These funds will help ensure the future of PCHC and our critical work for the people of Maine. Specifically, they will increase the support for our transition earlier this year to a new electronic medical records system and to alternative payment models. With this investment, PCHC is no longer pursuing an imminent Chapter 11 filing. That is a significant step forward. But the next 12 months will be critical, and we have a great deal of work ahead to put PCHC on solid financial ground.
“On behalf of everyone at Penobscot Community Health Care, I want to thank Governor Mills for her leadership and her commitment to the patients we serve. The Governor, her team, and the Department of Health and Human Services worked tirelessly to find a path forward. They were able to help us efficiently and in a targeted manner while requiring accountability on our part. We know these are public dollars, and we take that very seriously. We look forward to working closely with DHHS, providing regular updates, and being fully accountable for how these funds are used.
“Our work is not finished. In fact, we have asked the following trusted and very experienced Mainers and community health center experts to serve on a Turnaround Advisory Council to help us recover and reinvent how we approach financial strategy so that we can best meet our mission. Among them are Dr. Guy Hudson, CEO, Northern Light Health; Troy Trejo, CEO, Encompass Health Rehabilitation Hospital of Bangor; and Dr. Margaret Flinter, Senior Vice President & Clinical Director, Community Health Center, Inc.
“As we look ahead, I must take a moment to acknowledge PCHC’S incredible staff. Through all of this, their work has not stopped. Every day, they deliver extraordinary care to roughly 50,000 Mainers, many of whom have nowhere else to turn. They should be incredibly proud of themselves for keeping their eye on their mission. I know I am.
“I also want to thank the legislators from across Maine who signed on in support of PCHC and our patients. They stood with us when it mattered. We look forward to continuing that work with the Legislature and the next Governor beginning in 2027 to secure PCHC’s long-term future. Our patients deserve nothing less.

title: Most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast, a new AP-NORC poll finds
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Worries around artificial intelligence cross party lines, with the vast majority of Americans saying the U.S. government should prioritize keeping AI under human control and protecting workers.
A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that most Americans, 64%, think AI is developing “too fast,” while 27% say its development has been “about right” and only 8% say it’s moving “too slow.”
The risk that powerful AI models could evade human control and hurt humanity, once the stuff of science fiction, has been emerging as a more pressing concern. Even leaders of the companies that are developing frontier AI models are calling for a slowdown so that government regulation can catch up. President Donald Trump has pushed back against slowing down AI development because of concerns that China will gain an advantage with the technology. Data centers powering AI projects have also taken a prominent role in major political races as the midterm elections approach.
About 8 in 10 U.S. adults say it’s “extremely” or “very” important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control, and they are about as likely to want the government to prioritize protecting the country’s workforce. Most U.S. adults also think minimizing environmental harm and growing the U.S. economy are highly important. About half say this about promoting technological innovation, and slightly fewer say that about competing with China.
There’s bipartisan concern about the speed of AI’s development, but few Americans think either major political party has an advantage in handling artificial intelligence. Trump, a Republican, also gets a low rating on his handling of the issue, with 67% of U.S. adults disapproving of his performance on AI.
Stephanie Stewart, a junior-high science teacher in Sunset, Utah, said she is frustrated by the president’s opposition to AI regulation.
“There is no handling of the issue except for we’re just going to allow these companies to do whatever they want, and we’re not going to regulate them,” said Stewart, 53.
Most say protecting workers should be a priority for the government
Ron Theusch, a truck driver who lives in rural Alden, Minnesota, said his No. 1 concern with AI is the potential loss of jobs — including his own.
“I can just see a train of self-driving trucks 24/7, just running up and down I-35, loading and unloading. I can just see that happening,” said Theusch, 58.
Most Democrats and Republicans agree on the importance of protecting workers and keeping AI under human control, the poll found.
“There was a movie called ‘Terminator,’ where the robots came back and killed everybody,” Theusch said. “People relate to that … I don’t know where it’s going to land. I really don’t have anything I can do to control it, you know. It’s going to evolve.”
There’s less consensus about the importance of other priorities when it comes to AI. Republicans are more likely than Democrats to say it’s highly important to grow the U.S. economy and to compete with other countries like China. Democrats, on the other hand, are more likely to say it’s at least “very” important to minimize environmental harm.
“I don’t understand how, because they’re doing something as well as us, that we can’t be more human about it and more humane about it than just to say, ‘Well, they’re doing it, so we have to do it,’” Stewart said of U.S. competition with China.
And while about three-quarters of Democrats say AI is developing “too fast,” only about half of Republicans share that worry. People under 30 years old also express higher levels of concern than people 60 or older, the survey found.
“I think I have all the normal concerns, right? I think it’s wonderful for certain applications, but I also feel like it will be overused and can create a lack of personal connections. It can make people lazy because information is just given to them without really having to research things on their own,” said Kelly Opp, a 62-year-old Republican in Albuquerque, New Mexico.
“Like everything else, once you get that ball rolling, it progresses fast on its own, but I think that it will continue to keep progressing. So the speed doesn’t really bother me,” she said.
Americans have little confidence in Democrats or Republicans on AI
As a teacher, Stewart regularly uses AI to help with her work, including with creating assignments or assisting with tests. But she is deeply concerned about AI’s effects on children.
“You’ve got to protect kids. You’ve got to protect teens. You’ve got to protect privacy … we need to try to do something,” she said.
Americans have little trust in either party when it comes to the handling of AI issues. About 4 in 10 Americans say they don’t trust either the Democratic Party or the Republican Party on AI, according to the poll, while nearly 2 in 10 trust both parties equally, and the rest are split between trusting the Republicans and the Democrats.
Even people who identify with the parties are ambivalent about their ability to handle the issue. Only about half of Republicans and Democrats say their party is better equipped to handle AI issues, and roughly 3 in 10 in each case say neither party is.
“I am kind of moderate. And I see that there’s good on both sides,” said Stewart. “Anyone back in Washington is weak on doing anything for anyone but themselves right now. So, no, I don’t think the Democrats would do a better job per se. Maybe they would definitely tout it. But until I see anything coming from anyone, I’m going to be like, ‘Yeah, no. You’re all just sitting there.’”
___
Ortutay reported from Oakland, Calif.
___
The AP-NORC poll of 2,140 adults was conducted Sept. 24-28 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

title: School’s therapy dogs crowned homecoming king and queen
text:
(KCNC) - A Colorado high school crowned two therapy dogs, Polenta and Norene, as its first-ever canine homecoming king and queen.
Evergreen High School created a “puppy homecoming court” for the dogs, who ran uncontested and won.
Dogs support students and staff
Amy Wells, lead counselor at Evergreen High School, said the dogs’ job is simple.
“Their duty is to lie there and just be pet and hang out,” Wells said.
The dogs arrive at school early and stay until after the last bell. Wells said she stands at the front of the building every morning with the principal and lets students greet the dogs.
“I stand in the front of the building every single morning with my principal, and we let the kids come up and pet them or just talk to them,” Wells said.
Jackson Thomas, an Evergreen High School senior, said seeing the dogs affects his mood.
“I light up whenever I see them,” Thomas said.
Support since the shooting
Evergreen was the site of a school shooting one year ago.
“It just felt very vulnerable, you know,” Thomas said.
Wells said research shows cortisol levels can calm with a dog present.
“Research says that cortisol levels will calm down a little bit with a dog,” Wells said.
The dogs can be found in the counselor’s office, walking the hallways or offering support during tests.
Quinn McEvers, an Evergreen High School senior, said students can interact with the dogs without having to talk about what they’re going through.
“You don’t need to talk about what’s going on in your life or how something is affecting you. You can just get the love from the dogs, and it really helps,” McEvers said.
Crowned under the Friday night lights
Thomas said the dogs have made an impact on the school.
“They brought so much joy to this school,” Thomas said.
Polenta and Norene were announced as homecoming king and queen during the homecoming football game.
McEvers said the dogs are more than pets to the school community.
“They make a difference in our community, and I think that it’s really great that they’re getting honored for that because they are a lot bigger than just dogs. They’re really a part of our community,” McEvers said.

title: Worried about election interference? Vote now.
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
We, like many others, hope that the disruptions to voting that President Donald Trump and others have threatened do not happen. Voting is a basic civic right — and responsibility — that should not be interfered with. However, Trump and members of his cabinet have threatened to interfere with that right by stationing military members and Immigration and Customs Enforcement at polling places. Both would be illegal. The president has also tried to use the U.S. Postal Service to delay, and in some cases, stop the delivery of absentee ballots. Some supporters have urged the president to declare martial law to take control of elections.
Many of these moves would be unconstitutional, but that may not matter to Trump and others who want to influence the outcome of the midterm elections. Just talking about troops at polling places and new voting requirements could depress voter turnout. So, it is clear that such efforts are less about securing voting than about deterring some people from voting.
Against this national backdrop, early voting began in Maine this week. It runs through Oct. 29.
Early voting gives Mainers who may be away or busy on Election Day an opportunity to cast their ballots early. It also allows those who are worried about Election Day disruptions the same option.
If you know who you want to vote for, now is a good time to cast your ballot. You can do so in person at your town office when it is open. You can get a ballot at your town office and return it in person, at a secure drop box, or in the mail. If you’re a registered Maine voter but currently live out of Maine for work or school, you can request an absentee ballot and return it by mail.
This year, 70,000 voters have already requested absentee ballots, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
“The election should be business as usual this year because the election laws haven’t changed, but sometimes life gets in the way. We have all unfortunately experienced frustration with the postal service and things from everyday mail to prescriptions not arriving in a timely manner,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said in a press release this week. “That’s why it can be so helpful to vote early.”
It is worth remembering that voter fraud is extremely rare. Despite claims from the president and others who want to restrict voting, it is already a crime for non-citizens to vote in federal and state elections. As a result, non-citizen voting is vanishingly rare. There has never been a conviction for this in Maine. In fact, according to a database compiled by the conservative Heritage Foundation, there have been only two cases of voter fraud that resulted in a conviction or guilty plea since 1982.
Still, Trump and others continue to claim fraud to try to restrict voting.
Earlier this year, Trump ordered the postal service to develop a complex system of verifying voter and citizenship information before absentee ballots were delivered by mail. The scheme was halted by the U.S. Supreme Court, but other disruptions may occur.
So, now is a good time to cast your ballot.
If you need more information before you vote, be sure to watch the debates among the candidates for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House, and follow the BDN’s election coverage. The BDN opinion team also shared your questions with the candidates. You can see their responses at bangordailynews.com/candidates-questions.

title: McDonald’s sued over AI tool that recommends prices to US franchisees
text:
(AP) - McDonald’s is facing a federal lawsuit that alleges its AI-enhanced pricing tool violates antitrust laws because it shares nonpublic data with franchisees who might be competing in the same market.
The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in Illinois, said McDonald’s pricing tool uses artificial intelligence to collect data that competing franchises wouldn’t normally share, like store-level sales. The Chicago-based burger giant has said it makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.
The lawsuit also blames the pricing system for raising McDonald’s U.S. prices.
“McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of U.S. restaurants,” the lawsuit states. “The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”
McDonald’s said Tuesday that the lawsuit is “filled with inaccuracies” and it would vigorously defend itself.
“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” the company said in a statement. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”
The lawsuit was filed on behalf of a consumer, Michael Thomas, of DeKalb, Illinois. According to the lawsuit, Thomas frequently visits McDonald’s and orders a Quarter Pounder with cheese, french fries and a Coke. The lawsuit said Thomas noticed price differences between McDonald’s stores near his home.
McDonald’s said it has used an AI-enhanced pricing tool for more than a decade. The program determines the optimal price for menu items based on a store’s sales, location and other factors, including competitors’ prices.
McDonald’s said that long before adopting the AI-enhanced tool, it collected data and recommended prices to its franchisees, who own and operate 95% of McDonald’s 14,000 U.S. stores.
“All we do is provide the context of what’s going on,” a McDonald’s spokesman told The Associated Press. “We don’t have any way to affect the menu pricing in a restaurant.”
But the lawsuit said McDonald’s has “significant leverage over its franchisees” and can pressure them to follow its pricing recommendations.
The Associated Press left a message Tuesday with the National Owners Association, which represents McDonald’s franchisees.
McDonald’s has been experimenting with various value strategies in the U.S. and other markets for several years as it tries to win back lower-income consumers, whose visits to fast-food chains have dropped.
But franchisees don’t always follow its guidance. During a conference call with investors in August, McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering McDonald’s proposed menu of 10 items for under $3.
“As you know, in our system, that’s not something that we just flip the switch on,” Kempczinski said. “It requires conversations with franchisees.”
The lawsuit asks the judge to certify the case as a class action and to require McDonald’s to pay damages to the class. It also seeks to prevent McDonald’s from enforcing agreements that restrict competition.

title: Harpswell committees hear proposal for solar array on old landfill; may go to voters next year
text:
It’s not exactly trash to treasure, but an old landfill behind Harpswell’s current Transfer Station could be the site of a solar array that powers several nearby municipal buildings.
The person behind the idea, Harpswell Neck resident Jeffrey Wootan, told the Anchor that with electrical costs trending up, “We should be looking seriously at practical opportunities to reduce energy costs.”
His detailed proposal estimates the project would cost about $350,000, but he calculated that it would pay for itself in under nine years and produce almost $1.75 million in revenue over 30 years.
Wootan estimated that electricity rates climb more than 3% each year, based on data from the last two decades. The town also could sell renewable energy credits for the power generated, which Wootan said could produce about $5,000 in annual profit.
Two town bodies, the Energy and Technology Committee and the Resiliency and Sustainability Committee, have heard presentations by Wootan, who has worked in the solar industry for several decades.
Select Board member David Chipman attended those meetings and seemed enthusiastic about the idea. He said he plans to take a proposal to the rest of the board in the hope of getting it to voters at the next Town Meeting, in March 2027.
The proposal is to install five rows of panels on the north end of the capped landfill behind the transfer station.
When a landfill is closed, it is capped, or covered with layers of soil, gravel and other materials. The site looks like a meadow covering a small hill in the middle of dense woods.
Compared to burning fossil fuels, which is how the majority of New England’s power is produced, Wootan said that relying on solar power would avoid releasing about 1,440 tons of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, over 30 years. Wootan compared that amount to what more than 300 cars would emit driving for a single year.
Wootan told the Energy and Technology Committee on Sept. 15 that the location is ideal for a solar array. Its orientation allows panels to face due south, the direction that receives the most sunlight, and the surrounding trees are far enough away that they only block about 1% of the available sunlight. Better still, he said, the town already owns the land, and the site isn’t likely to be used for another purpose.
“It’s a perfect location,” Chipman said at the meeting.
The panels would produce about 200 megawatt-hours of electricity per year, which would cover the electricity usage at the Town Office, the Recycling Center and Transfer Station, and the garage used by on-call paramedics. Wootan arrived at the number after determining from electrical bills that the town uses about 210 megawatt-hours annually. The town currently buys solar credits for its electrical usage, saving 15% on the market rate.
The amount of electricity produced by solar panels decreases as they age. Wootan estimated that the array would lose one-quarter of a percent in efficiency each year, meaning the array would lose almost 8% efficiency over 30 years. But Wootan said many farms continue operating after their planned lifespan, continuing to generate electricity even as the efficiency is slowly declining.
The landfill site has room to add more panels, too, according to Wootan. And there’s a second capped landfill southwest of the Transfer Station that could also house panels. That leaves room to add solar that could be used to power planned town buildings, like the central fire station.
Wootan said electricity from a solar farm on those sites could be sold to households, but Energy and Technology Committee Chair Howard Marshall expressed some hesitation about introducing complications to the discussion at this point.
Wootan believes the project could be completed in 2027 if voters approve the expenditure in March. He offered to write a request for proposals from contractors and to manage the construction.
In 2024, Harpswell voters rejected a proposal from the company ReVision Energy to lease 5 acres of Mitchell Field for 25 years to build a solar farm. The Select Board voted unanimously not to recommend that proposal, citing low revenue potential and an apparent lack of community support for a solar farm in a busy town park.
Sam Lemonick is a staff reporter at the Harpswell Anchor. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: Gardiner soccer is Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week​
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Girls Team of the Week: Gardiner girls soccer
Gardiner High’s girls soccer team is atop the Heal point standings in Class B North, a rare position for a team that has been solid but seldom a title contender.
“It’s honestly a bit of a surprise,” said Jess Prince, the Tigers’ sixth-year head coach.
Gardiner won its first nine games, including crossover games last week against Morse from Class B South (2-1 victory) and Messalonskee from Class A North (3-0 victory). On Tuesday, the Tigers remained unbeaten but settled for a 1-1 tie at Erskine Academy.
After graduating six seniors from a team that went 10-5-1 in 2025, Gardiner spent the preseason working through multiple player combinations, settling on a lineup with three freshmen and several returners in new positions.
When linchpin senior center back Sara Mansir was injured, more juggling followed.
Center midfielder Molly Takatsu shifted to the back line in place of Mansir (who could return later this season). Lexi Dyer moved from outside midfielder to center mid, and senior Kaetlyn Stevens, a key reserve, moved into Dyer’s spot.
Freshmen Olivia Ketner, Evalyn Grover and striker Riley Antognoni have strengthened the lineup. Antognoni leads a balanced scoring attack.
“She’s crazy fast and bothering other team’s backs all day long,” Prince said.
Adela Ricker, a junior first-year starter, has three shutouts and heads a veteran back line of Takatsu, junior Zoey Epperson and seniors Cheyenne Goodman and Lilah Serber that has held opponents to nine goals. Gardiner has scored 25 goals.
The past three seasons, the Tigers have lost on the road in the quarterfinals. This season, they’re looking good for a top-four finish and a home quarterfinal game.
“It’s somewhat of a surprise,” Goodman said. “At the same time, we’re working really hard. We’re excited, because my whole high school career, we’ve never been undefeated this far in.”
Predicting Gardiner’s playoff performance is difficult. The Tigers do not play any of the other current top-six teams in the regular season.
“The past three seasons, we’ve been knocked out by a team that didn’t even have a common opponent,” Prince said. “That’s why that home-field advantage is huge when you get deeper in the playoffs.”

title: Armed man shot and killed by security at federal courthouse in Nashville, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - A man armed with a pistol was shot and killed by security at the federal courthouse in Nashville, Tennessee, according to police.
Nashville Metro Police responded to a “reported shooting call” at the Fred D. Thompson Federal Building and Courthouse Thursday morning.
According to police, the man entered the courthouse and tried to fire his gun but failed. He then pulled out a knife and was subsequently shot by a courthouse security officer.
He was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, where he died.
“This is the first time anything like this has happened at this courthouse,” the police spokesperson said.
The spokesperson confirmed the man did not make it past the courthouse security checkpoint. The checkpoint is a critical measure to protect U.S. senators and other people entering the building.
The suspect’s identity has not been released. Police did say the man is in his 40s and is from out of state but “has ties to Nashville.” They did not elaborate on the exact connection.
Officers and police K-9s searched the suspect’s car and found nothing threatening.
Investigators are speaking with security at the courthouse to better understand the events leading up to the shooting.
The Nashville Public Library’s Main Library branch was being evacuated as a result of the shooting.

title: Hard hats vs. safety helmets: what’s the difference?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For years, hard hats have been the go-to choice for protecting workers from overhead hazards on job sites. They’re familiar, widely used and designed primarily as “Type 1 head protection,” which means they help guard against impacts from above.
But safety helmets are becoming more common, and for good reasons.
As “Type 2 head protection,” safety helmets offer broader protection — not just from overhead impacts, but also impacts from the side, front and rear. That added coverage can make a meaningful difference in environments where head injury risks are more complex.
Of course, more protection often comes with a higher price tag, but that cost may be well worth it when you consider the potential financial and human impact of a traumatic head injury.
According to recent National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI) data, head injury claims average just over $94,000 each.
So, should every workplace switch from hard hats to safety helmets? Not necessarily. The right choice depends on the type of work being done and the specific hazards employees face. That’s why a Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) assessment is so important: it helps determine which option best fits the job.
If your organization is evaluating head protection, make sure you source PPE from a trusted supplier and look for the “ANSI Z89.1” label, which is the universal standard of hard hats in the United States, describing the process of testing the helmets. When possible, aim for Type 2 protection to maximize safety.
Hard hats remain a standard, but safety helmets may offer a stronger layer of protection where the risks call for it.

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was sexually assaulted when repairing campaign signs
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — An Arizona congressional candidate says she was knocked unconscious and sexually assaulted this summer while she was repairing campaign signs overnight.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia told investigators that two men raped her, and she kicked her feet up at one point to try to fight back. She said she felt the weight of one of her attackers on her body and had bruises on her arms from being held down, a bump on her head and other injuries, according to police reports.
“I knew that I had been knocked out,” Greene-Placentia told The Associated Press on Wednesday.
Greene-Placentia, 52, is a Democrat who is challenging incumbent Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh for the 8th Congressional District seat representing parts of metro Phoenix that are reliably red. She said she told her husband and campaign staff about the mid-August attack in Sun City days after it happened. The Phoenix New Times first reported on it.
Greene-Placentia told the AP she was disgusted that two men took control of her body and she had no say in it. She said she decided to speak out publicly when she realized she was telling voters she would advocate for them when she was not advocating for herself.
“My takeaway is that I have a lot more empathy and understanding of why so many women don’t come forward,” she said. “And, and I’m hoping that I can encourage them.”
Greene-Placentia said she could not recall many details of the Aug. 14 assault, including the exact location or a description of the men, though she said one wore black boots and had small feet. She told investigators one of the men used an expletive to describe her, and she believes he referenced her political party.
She said she does not know whether the attack was politically motivated, whether she was followed there or whether it was a crime of opportunity by attackers who saw a woman in a parking lot: “I wish I knew.”
The Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office declined to comment on its investigation.
Hamadeh said in a statement: “I have read the disturbing story and call upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law.”
“No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community,” he added.
Greene-Placentia is a former long-haul trucker who later ran a small transportation company, according to her campaign.
In a social media post supporting Democrat Pete Buttigieg’s 2020 run for the presidency, Greene-Placentia called herself a former Republican and a “never Trumper” and said she voted Libertarian in 2016. Greene-Placentia later became more engaged in Arizona Democratic politics.
She said she often put up and repaired campaign signs overnight because it was cooler than the blistering summer days and there was less traffic.
Arizona Democratic Party treasurer Greg Freeman said he got a call from Greene-Placentia, a friend who ran his 2024 campaign for a county assessor, the morning of Aug. 17. She told him she had been sexually assaulted by two men, Freeman said, and he could tell she was not ready to go to the police or share it publicly.
“Obviously she was processing it on the phone,” Freeman said. “She was just in shock. She was just horrified by what happened.”
Greene-Placentia said she wishes she had called police immediately and gone to the hospital. After the attack she took multiple showers and washed the clothes she was wearing, police reports state.
The embarrassment and anger made it hard for her to come forward, she said. She reported the attack to police in late August.
In an AP interview, Greene-Placentia choked up while explaining that she has had to accept the vulnerable position the attack put her in. “I’ve always considered myself a very strong person, and I hate that somebody used their physical strength to take that,” she said.
The Associated Press does not typically identify people who say they are victims of sexual assault unless they grant permission, which Greene-Placentia has done.

title: Maine Democrats call out Bobby Charles for his views on the war in Iran
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - On Wednesday the Maine Democrats hosted a press conference to call out Republican candidate for governor Bobby Charles on his views regarding the war in Iran.
They say the war has had a negative impact on Mainers citing a survey from the Maine Department of Energy Resources showing the average price of heating oil is up 80% from a year ago.
While Maine Democrats acknowledged the Governor of Maine would have no power to end the war in Iran, they attacked Charles for not staying consistent in his viewpoint on the war.
“For me, what’s the most upsetting about Bobby Charles is he won’t stand by his original comments. Like I said, his values have changed with the wind. And Hannah has been consistent. She has been outspoken against the war. I have been outspoken against the war. Most of my colleagues have been outspoken against the war. I think it’s most important to know that when you’re electing somebody to be governor, you’re electing somebody who has principles that they’re not afraid to stand behind,” said Rep. Amy J. Roeder.
A spokesperson for the Charles campaign responded by stating: “Bobby Charles isn’t running for president. He’s running for governor, to fix what Janet Mills and Hannah Pingree have broken. After eight years of their policies, Mainers pay some of the highest energy costs in the country, their taxes have gone up, and their property tax bills keep climbing. Maine Democrats can’t stop talking about the president because they can’t defend their own record. The question for Maine Democrats is simple: when will they hold Janet Mills and Hannah Pingree accountable?”

title: Four astronauts — and one mustache — return to Earth after eight months in space
text:
Four astronauts — and one mustache — return to Earth after eight months in space
Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
Video above: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket takes off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station
NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France's Sophie Adenot and Russia's Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew's homecoming.
They couldn't wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
"It's a lot of mixed, swirling emotions for all of us," Meir said while still in orbit, noting they would miss "these extraordinary views of our home planet."
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States' 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
"It's kind of become a little bit of my brand up here," Hathaway said in August, "so I don't know if it'll go away right away or I'll end up keeping it for a while."
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.

title: Isaias is now a hurricane as it surges toward the Gulf Coast. What to know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Isaias strengthened into a Category 2 hurricane as it barreled toward the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday, prompting orders for tourists to abandon beaches for safer spots inland, sending locals scurrying for gas and groceries and leading fishing crews to secure their boats before the potentially destructive storm’s arrival.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season was forecast to intensify rapidly and cause dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Heavy rain and flooding were possible into the weekend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina.
“We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
He added: “Today is the day to prepare and get ready and be in your safe place by tomorrow as conditions will rapidly deteriorate along the northern Gulf Coast as Isaias approaches.”
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph), according to the hurricane center, surpassing the 96 mph (154 kph) threshold for a Category 2 storm.
Isaias was headed northeast at 14 mph (22 kph) and was centered about 260 miles (415 kilometers) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
A hurricane warning was in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida, the hurricane center said. A storm surge warning was in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River.
Preparations underway
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.
At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, while several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida’s Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.
On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Water from the storm surge and high tide could reach heights of 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters) in parts of Alabama and Mississippi, forecasters said. Isaias also could dump up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain on coastal areas and spawn tornadoes overnight Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore.
The National Weather Service warned of possible “long-duration power outages.”
The hurricane formed late in the season
Isaias developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season and was one day short of tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. That record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane. Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, Mexico, and Southern California this weekend.
Isaias is expected to strike a swath of coastline that’s familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism are already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump planned to attend.
In Loxley, a small Alabama community where county officials urged voluntary evacuations, Nichole Eubanks and her husband prepared to ride out the storm on their farm, which is home to dozens of animals, including pigs, donkeys and about 20 rescued cats.
They planned to put contact information on the hooves of their goats, donkeys and pigs in case they got loose.
“It’s definitely scary, and you never really know where these storms are going to go and how bad it’s going to be until it gets there,” said Eubanks, 35.
In the Alabama fishing village of Bayou La Batre, Tony Rice and Lance Connor installed doors on their fishing boat Thursday to protect the vessel. The boat was one of many moored there, and Rice said they planned to move it to a less-crowded spot to decrease the chances of it bumping into others.
In Pensacola, Florida, officials said the airport will close to commercial flights Friday morning. Mayor D.C. Reeves urged residents to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Also contributing were Associated Press reporters Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia; Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas; and Julie Walker in New York.
