title: Letter: Rick Bennett is the independent governor Maine needs
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Maine deserves an independent governor. I believe freedom from the rigid ideologies that define the Republican and Democratic parties would allow the governor to address the biggest issues — the high costs of energy, housing, taxes, and health care — without having to appease major party donors and the extreme ends of their base.
What became clear to me after the first televised debate is that Rick Bennett is the right person for the job. His experience as a leader in private business and the Maine Senate were clear in his detailed and thoughtful answers to the moderators’ questions. Leading a state, and finding real solutions, requires dealing with complex problems that often don’t completely align with either party’s platform.
His policy views diverge from Republican Bobby Charles because Bennett believes in protecting our environment (85% score from Maine Conservation Voters) and that government spending should be scrutinized line by line, not DOGE’ed into dysfunction. Compared to Democrat Hannah Pingree, I believe Bennett would bring fiscal responsibility to the state’s budget and real, market-oriented solutions to housing, among other issues. You can see for yourself in the past or upcoming gubernatorial debates.
If you think Maine needs a real change — one that would bring strong leadership, effective solutions, and less partisan bickering and polarization — then vote Rick Bennett for governor.
Nathan Dorn
Ellsworth

title: Hall-Dale girls soccer earns key win over Gardiner in Class B/C crossover game
text:
FARMINGDALE — The Hall-Dale girls soccer team used its speed and dominated possession on the way to its biggest win of the season.
Clare Sturtevant scored two goals and the Bulldogs beat previously unbeaten Gardiner 3-1 in a Class B/C crossover game Thursday night.
“It feels so good, we wanted this game so bad,” said Hall-Dale senior captain Maya Hammonds, who scored with 7:20 remaining. “After seeing their record, we wanted this game so bad. It’s a really great feeling right now.”
The Bulldogs (6-2-2) entered the game ranked fourth in the Class C South Heal point standings and are battling Mt. Abram (11-0) and Maranacook (9-1) for the top spot. A win over the Tigers (9-1-1), who entered as the No. 1 team in Class B North, helps Hall-Dale in its chase for the No. 1 seed.
The Bulldogs led 1-0 at the half and controlled possession in the second half, limiting Gardiner’s offensive opportunities.
“(Possession) is something we’ve been working on and focusing on,” Hall-Dale coach Tatum Hancock said. “To see it be put together to get this result in this game is amazing … We’ve just grown in our camaraderie as a team, building that chemistry and positivity and excitement to be out on the field.”
Hammond received a cross and drilled a shot into the net from about 20 yards to secure the win.
“This (win) is going to give us so much momentum,” Hammonds said. “That’s going to give us a big boost going into the playoffs.”
Here are some other takeaways from Thursday’s game:
Sturtevant showcases her speed
Sturtevant, a sophomore, was the offensive spark plug for Hall-Dale. She gave the Bulldogs a 1-0 lead with 19:19 remaining in the first half when she took the ball on a breakaway and knocked a shot into the bottom right corner of the net.
“She’s really good at facilitating,” Hammonds said. “She finds the open pass and it’s there. She finds those opportunities and takes those open shots, which is really great.”
Sturtevant made it 2-0 with 19 minutes left in the second half.
She showed a different level of speed every time she touched the ball, making life difficult for Gardiner defenders.
“In the last few games, she’s really stepped it up,” Hancock said. “She’s a smart, fast and talented player. We’re really seeing her kind of come into her own, and that’s been great.”
Ricker continues to impress for the Tigers
Junior keeper Adela Ricker is having a strong season in net and kept Gardiner in the match. Fending off a strong Hall-Dale attack, Ricker made 13 saves.
Her best stop came midway through the second half when she stopped the ball in the middle of a scrum directly in front of the Gardiner net.
Unsung hero
Freshman Riley Antognoni gave the Tigers life in the second half. After Sturtevant made it 2-0, Antognoni responded moments later to cut the lead to one.
Statistical leaders
Hall-Dale: Clare Sturtevant (2 goals), Maya Hammonds (1 goal), Audra Schaab (1 assist)
Gardiner: Riley Antognoni (1 goal), Olivia Ketner (1 assist), Adela Ricker (13 saves)

title: UMF project expands snow monitoring across western Maine
text:
FARMINGTON — University of Maine at Farmington researchers are expanding a network of snow-monitoring sites across western Maine to gather real-time information on snow depth, weather conditions and the amount of water stored in the mountain snowpack.
The project will add sensors at remote sites in the Bigelow Mountains and Rangeley area, along with a lower-elevation site in the Pierce Pond watershed, filling gaps in existing monitoring and providing data that could improve flood forecasting and understanding of changing winters.
Rachel Hovel, UMF associate professor of biology, and Julia Daly, professor of geology, said three monitoring locations are in the Bigelows, including two near high-elevation lakes and one near Stratton Brook. Three others are in the Rangeley area near high-elevation lakes, roughly along the Appalachian Trail corridor. Another site is at a lower elevation in the Pierce Pond watershed.
Researchers already have one winter of data from an initial deployment of trail cameras and snow stakes used to track seasonal changes in snowpack. New equipment will be installed this winter and next summer to provide real-time measurements and additional weather information.
Because many of the sites can be reached only on foot, the equipment must be suitable for remote locations. Researchers plan to install snow-depth sensors that will transmit data in real time and help estimate snow water equivalent, a measure of how much water is contained in the snowpack. Sensors will also measure conditions including air temperature and wind speed.
The new sites will complement Maine Climate Center Mesonet stations and other monitoring locations, providing a more complete picture of conditions at different elevations.
Data are expected to be updated several times each day. Researchers are developing standardized deployment methods for the network and plan to make data available through a public dashboard. The dashboard is expected to launch in the third or fourth year of the project.
One goal is to improve forecasting of rain-on-snow flooding, such as the December 2023 event that caused widespread flooding in western Maine. Data from the project will be shared with partners including the Northeast River Forecast Center to improve river forecasts by providing better information about potential water sources.
The project builds on UMF research examining mountain lakes and watersheds in the northern Appalachians. That work has found that high-elevation lakes retain ice later into spring, while the timing of spring ice breakup has been shifting earlier at lower-elevation lakes but has changed less at higher elevations. Researchers began monitoring snowpack in part to better understand its relationship with lake ecology and how snow conditions vary with elevation.
Researchers also hope the expanded network will help answer questions that have been difficult to study because high-elevation data are limited. Those include whether ice layers are becoming more common within the snowpack, the elevation at which rain changes to snow during storms, and changes in the timing of the first snowfall and spring snowmelt.
Those changes can affect wildlife habitat, alpine and subalpine ecosystems and rare plant communities, researchers said. The project also is intended to examine the economic effects of changing winters and improve snow research capacity across the Northeast.
UMF expects to hire about three undergraduate researchers during each of the project’s four years. Students will work during summers and academic years on fieldwork, sensor installation and maintenance, data quality control, database management, analysis and reporting.
The new monitoring will complement the Maine Cooperative Snow Survey, which has collected winter and early spring snow measurements for years but includes relatively few high-elevation sites and generally measures snow weekly during the melt period.
The UMF network will provide more frequent observations from mountain locations, giving forecasters and other decision-makers higher-resolution information while contributing to a coordinated snow-monitoring effort across northern New England.

title: Woman arrested after 6 children found unsupervised in ‘unlivable’ home, barely clothed, police say
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV/Gray News) - A Florida woman is facing several charges after officers say they found a half-dozen children unsupervised and living in deplorable conditions.
Jamie Jakes, 30, was arrested by the Tallahassee Police Department over the weekend on six counts of child neglect.
Authorities said the situation started when patrolling officers noticed a vehicle turn and swerve onto the curve early Sunday morning to barely avoid hitting a child.
Officers said they made contact with the child and took them home. But that’s when they found children who appeared to be unsupervised at the residence, with one wearing only pants and others wearing soiled diapers.
Tallahassee police said they tried to locate clothes, but only found shoes and parts of clothing because the rest were wet and smelled of mildew.
The responding officers reported finding the home to be “unlivable,” with feces, urine and spoiled food, without having anything edible in the refrigerator.
Jakes was said to have left the home a few hours before officers arrived. Police said they came into contact with her when she returned to the house at about 6 a.m.
Jakes told officers she paid someone $150 a week to watch the children, but that person told officers that this was not true, police said.
Court documents stated that Jakes also claimed that the house was clean the day prior, but officers said the feces and urine on the floor did not match that timing.
Jakes was taken into custody and booked into jail by Tallahassee police.

title: 'Incredibly grateful': Mizzou football player recovering after heart transplant, coach says
text:
'Incredibly grateful': Mizzou freshman gets heart transplant after staff saw problem during routine exam
A University of Missouri football player is recovering after receiving a heart transplant, coach Eli Drinkwitz said Thursday.
Earlier this week, Drinkwitz spoke emotionally about the health of freshman Johnnie "DJ" Jones, saying that after routine evaluations for the football program, staff noticed a heart issue.
Jones was later taken to the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, where he and his family learned he would need a heart transplant.
But there's now a positive update to the story.
"Last night, DJ received his heart transplant, and his surgery went well. He is now recovering," Drinkwitz said in a social media post. "We are incredibly grateful for the medical team who cared for DJ and for the donor and donor family whose extraordinary gift made this possible."
Drinkwitz said he will provide updates when possible.
"Please continue to keep DJ, his family, the donor family and his caregivers in your prayers as he begins the recovery process," Drinkwitz said. "We are so thankful for the incredible prayers and support from the entire Mizzou Family."

title: Cooper Flagg and New Balance unveil logo with nod to Maine
text:
After nearly two years of professional partnership, Maine native Cooper Flagg and New Balance unveiled a new logo Thursday that will be used on all collaborative product lines.
The video announcement includes multiple nods to the Pine Tree State, including a shot of the basketball court at Nokomis Regional High School in Newport and a Maine license plate reading “FL4GG.”
The logo itself is a stylized “CF,” with the C resembling a pine tree, another nod to Flagg’s home state.
Flagg attended Nokomis as a high school freshman, earning Maine’s Gatorade Player of the Year in 2022 and helping the Warriors win the school’s first Class A championship. He then played two years at Montverde Academy in Florida and then a year of college basketball at Duke University.
In June 2025, Flagg was selected with the No. 1 overall pick in the NBA Draft by the Dallas Mavericks. He was named Rookie of the Year last season after averaging 21 points, 6.7 rebounds, 4.5 assists and 1.2 steals per contest.
Flagg’s second season tips off Oct. 21 when the Mavericks play at the Houston Rockets.

title: Arts nonprofit to give public access to studios inside Rockland’s Lincoln Street Center
text:
Waterfall Arts invites the public to explore the creative heart of Rockland during the Lincoln Street Center Fall Open Studios from 1-5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, at 24 Lincoln St. in Rockland.
During the free, public event, artists will open their studios and welcome visitors into their creative spaces. Guests will have the opportunity to explore Rockland’s historic high school, now home to more than 40 artist studios and one of the nation’s oldest theaters.
Visitors can get a behind-the-scenes look at working artists’ studios, learn about a variety of artistic mediums, meet artists, and view original artwork.
Participating artists will include:
• Susan Beebe – paintings.
• Gianna Bird – watercolor.
• Gary Briechle – photography and painting.
• Stan Farrell – musician and inventor.
• Katherine Ferrier – quilting and fiber.
• Kathleen Florance – paintings.
• Laura Waller – oil paintings.
Parking is available behind the building. An accessible entrance is located at the side entrance on the south side of the building at the basement level.
A NEW CHAPTER FOR LINCOLN STREET CENTER
The Open Studios event marks an exciting new chapter for the Lincoln Street Center and the broader arts community. Waterfall Arts acquired the Lincoln Street Center on June 30, following a year-long effort by a coalition of organizations and community members to raise the funds needed to secure the building’s future.
The acquisition was made possible through significant community support, including major contributions from The Ellis Beauregard Foundation, The Lesher Family Foundation and two anonymous donors.
Waterfall Arts is a nonprofit based in Belfast whose mission is nurturing and inspiring creative expression across the Midcoast. The organization is proud to have secured the future of one of Maine’s largest community arts facilities, preserving more than 40 working artist studios and ensuring that the historic Lincoln Street Center can continue to serve artists and the community for years to come.

title: Wells football comes back for wild win over Freeport
text:
WELLS — Wells High football coach Tim Roche said he wasn’t sure how his team pulled out a victory on Thursday.
Freeport coach Paul St. Pierre knew all too well why his team suffered a 28-24 loss. The Falcons were done-in by a series of mistakes and failures over the final 4 minutes and 26 seconds, as a 10-point lead and what would have been the program’s first win against the Warriors evaporated.
“We had a chance to win on the road and to finally beat Wells. We were 0-7 as a school, and now we’re 0-8 against Wells,” St. Pierre said.
“We had a chance. But the game’s 48 minutes, not 45.”
Wells, the smallest school in Class C with an enrollment of 400, improved to 4-2. Freeport, a 629-student school that petitions to play in Class D, is also 4-2.
THE BREAKDOWNS, THE COMEBACK
Freeport controlled large chunks of the game with its power running. Backup quarterback Sam Willard was a big part of that, directing two second-half scoring drives. He capped an all-run, 14-play, 65-yard march with a 5-yard run up the middle that put Freeport ahead 17-14 early in the fourth quarter. Willard threw sparingly, but his beautifully lofted 18-yard scoring pass to Ben Gaddis with 5:50 to play put Freeport ahead 24-14.
With 4:26 remaining, Freeport’s series of unfortunate events began when Willard dropped a potential interception that Wells quarterback Noah McDonough threw right to him.
Three plays later, a personal foul gave Wells a first down at the Freeport 12. Jacob Barry scored his second touchdown on a 2-yard sweep, cutting the lead to 24-20 (the 2-point conversion failed) with 2:46 to play.
Knowing an onside kick was coming, Freeport had linemen in the center of the field. Mason Miles’ bouncing straight-ahead kick went between two Falcons as they were descended on by the Warriors’ coverage team, jarring the ball forward, and Robert Stevens of Wells recovered.
“I just saw the ball come out from a bunch of kids. Just jumped on it, you know,” Stevens said.
After a Wells unsportsmanlike penalty and a sack of McDonough by Keegan Haveran, Wells faced third-and-26. As McDonough scrambled for minimal yardage, he was hit out of bounds by Liam Dennison, drawing a 15-yard penalty. Then on fourth down, as Greyson Quigg was on the verge of tackling McDonough for a game-clinching sack, Quigg grabbed the Wells QB’s face mask for another 15-yard penalty and a Wells first down at the Freeport 29 with 1:05 to play.
Wells scored three plays later when McDonough audibled out of a run and threw an 8-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver Dylan Hudnull, who was completely uncovered.
“I saw it and I was hoping that the coach wouldn’t start yelling at it because then they would realize it, but we ended up pulling it off,” McDonough said.
McDonough then completed a 2-point conversion pass to Liam Perkins for a 28-24 lead with 46 seconds to play.
Freeport reached the Wells 11 with a 44-yard kickoff return by Jose Rosquette and a 22-yard pass from Willard to Colby Chipman. Time ran out, though, as Willard’s second-down pass fell incomplete.
UNSUNG HERO
Both teams had numerous players thrust into larger or different roles because of injuries. Wells’ Stevens is one of them. A junior, he’s listed on the roster as a 5-foot-5, 120-pound running back. Thursday night, he was wearing No. 64 and saw snaps at defensive tackle when the already ravaged Warriors line had two more interior players get hurt.
STATISTICS
• Freeport: Sam Willard (25 carries, 118 yards, 1 TD; 4 of 7 passing, 57 yards, 1 TD), Landon Clark (8 carries, 51 yards), Keegan Haveran (9 carries, 27 yards, 1 TD), Bryson Jack (38-yard field goal, 3 for 3 PATs).
• Wells: Jacob Barry (12 carries, 74 yards, 2 TDs), Quinn Finnemore (5 carries, 45 yards, 1 TD), Mason Miles (11 carries, 67 yards), Noah McDonough (2 of 8 passing, 31 yards, 1 TD)
THEY SAID IT
• “I’ll be honest. Everyone doesn’t have a good feeling right now, and they shouldn’t. We had a chance to win that game and we let them off the hook. And we need to learn from this because the playoffs are around the corner.” — Paul St. Pierre, Freeport head coach
• “We started off slow in the first half, but we’ve been working since summer. We’re ready for these kinds of games where we have to push through until the very last minute.” — Noah McDonough, Wells quarterback

title: Expensive ads don’t make a candidate good
text:
Whoever is orchestrating the media campaigns for Sen. Susan Collins, Bobby Charles and Paul LePage have done an excellent job of embracing misinformation, a deliberate distortion of the facts. They are using classic, well-documented logical fallacies to mislead citizens in every ad that has been released.
While maybe not outright lying, they are still cherry-picking small issues and claiming they are big problems (voter fraud, really?). They’re correlating related issues without looking for actual causes (Hannah Pingree is causing climate change in Maine, really?); attacking their opponents personally instead of addressing the issues; and using classic straw-man arguments, bandwagon appeals and red-herring charges to distract from the fact that massive funding from the billionaire class does not make anyone a good candidate.
Just because they sound momentarily reasonable on air or in our mailbox does not make them true. Checking the actual data will allow everyone to see through the ridiculous arguments in every million-dollar ad backed by those with money and power — who want to keep both.
Patricia Millett
West Farmington

title: Belfast to change part of downtown street to one-way traffic
text:
A short stretch of Church Street will become one-way following the Belfast City Council’s unanimous approval Tuesday of ordinance amendments intended to simplify traffic at Post Office Square, improve pedestrian safety and create a van-accessible parking space in front of City Hall.
The amendments to Chapter 58, the city’s traffic and vehicles ordinance, complete the legislative steps needed to implement a street redesign that has been under discussion for several months. The plan will direct traffic north from Main Street toward Market Street, eliminating the southbound approach from that section of Church Street into the downtown five-way intersection.
The accompanying parking arrangement will combine parallel and diagonal spaces, providing 20 on-street parking spaces, a net increase of one, while improving access for people with disabilities.
Councilor Mary Mortier described the proposal as “low hanging fruit” in the city’s effort to relieve congestion at the intersection.
“It makes common sense,” Mortier said. “It’s low cost in budgeting, it adds an ADA parking space, and it adds one more parking space and safety factors on each end. In my book, this is a win, win.”
For motorists, the principal change will be the direction of travel on Church Street between Main and Market streets. Once the new configuration takes effect, drivers will no longer be able to enter that block from Market Street and travel south toward Main Street.
Drivers leaving the shared City Hall and KeyBank parking lot will also need to follow signs directing them toward Market Street. City staff will continue coordinating with KeyBank over the placement of no-left-turn signage at the parking lot exit.
Deputy Economic Development Director Joellyn Warren told councilors the transition would be handled similarly to the earlier traffic change on Miller Street. Signs will warn motorists of the coming change, and the police chief and Public Works director will determine the exact implementation date.
The council’s approval therefore establishes the legal basis for the new traffic pattern, while the physical conversion will follow through installation of signs, pavement markings and related improvements.
Councilor Neal Harkness said he expected the adjustment to offer practical benefits without creating substantial difficulties for drivers.
“I don’t see any significant inconvenience with this change,” Harkness said. “I see it being a safer and more efficient traffic pattern.”
Mayor Eric Sanders acknowledged the adjustment that comes with changing a familiar route.
“Change is hard,” Sanders said, while describing the proposal as common sense.
The amendments make two related changes to Chapter 58. One adds Church Street between Main and Market streets to the city’s list of one-way streets. The other removes the stop requirement for southbound Church Street traffic at Main Street because that approach will no longer be permitted.
The northbound stop requirement at Church and Main remains. Removing the southbound stop requirement accompanies elimination of that traffic movement; it does not authorize drivers to continue south through the intersection without stopping.
The project grew out of the 2025 Belfast Active Transportation Plan, which identified incremental improvements intended to reduce conflicts among turning vehicles and improve safety at Post Office Square.
In a Sept. 29 memorandum to the mayor, council and city manager, Warren described the Church Street proposal as addressing a documented sight-line hazard at the intersection with Main Street.
The goal is to reduce the number of competing movements drivers must anticipate at a complicated downtown junction. Eliminating vehicles approaching Main Street southbound from this block of Church Street removes one source of turning traffic and is intended to make the intersection easier to navigate.
The redesign also changes how the available street space is used for parking.
Although the completed layout will produce a net gain of one space, it includes removal of two spaces in front of the Historical Society near Market Street. Warren’s memorandum identifies that section as a pinch point where the street narrows and cannot accommodate parking on both sides under two-way operation.
Redistributing parking along the block allows the city to address that constraint while providing a combination of parallel and diagonal spaces elsewhere. Residents visiting City Hall, nearby businesses and other downtown destinations will need to follow the new markings when entering and leaving parking spaces.
A central element of the plan is a full van-accessible parking space in front of City Hall, designed to meet Americans with Disabilities Act requirements.
The improvement involves both the parking space and its connection to the sidewalk. Adequate clearance is necessary for people using vehicle lifts or ramps, while a properly positioned curb ramp provides an accessible route from the street.
Public Works will evaluate the existing curb ramp and make any realignment needed to serve the new parking space. The design also preserves access to the fire hydrant in front of City Hall.
New signs will include stop, do-not-enter and no-left-turn signs. The plan calls for two stop signs at Church Street’s intersection with Market Street to improve visibility for approaching drivers.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: The 'glass skin' Korean beauty trend has risks, experts warn
text:
The 'glass skin' Korean beauty trend has risks, experts warn
Greta Costioli was once known as the "glass skin girl" on TikTok. Following the Korean beauty trend, Costioli would layer on product after product — toners, serums, essences and moisturizers — in pursuit of an ultra-dewy complexion.
Related video: Can You Return Opened Makeup?
Costioli, 29, said that ever since she was a teenager, she would apply extra moisturizer for her naturally dry complexion. When the "glass skin" trend became popular on social media, she fully leaned in, including trying one method requiring seven different layers of hydrating toner.
It may sound excessive, but that kind of elaborate skin care routine has become increasingly popular across TikTok and Instagram, where beauty influencers routinely film themselves using skincare products to achieve the glossy, almost reflective complexion known as "glass skin." Celebrities including Kylie Jenner and Hailey Bieber have amplified the trend, posting their regimens that resulted in similar dewy skin.
What it's based on
The glass skin trend has its roots in South Korean beauty culture, where the term is used to describe a complexion that appears exceptionally smooth and poreless. The phrase appears to have first come around in the early to mid-2010s and then saw a major spike at the end of 2025 going into 2026, according to Google Trends. Those who subscribe to the complex routines say their skin benefits from the layers of hydration, and viewers are hooked on the ASMR-like videos as influencers tap their glass-like faces with their fingers and beauty tools.
What we do or don't know
Certain aspects of the glass skin routine, such as moisturizing and using sunscreen, are positive steps toward safe skincare, according to the American Academy of Dermatology. However, problems occur when people use too many products, which can lead to issues such as clogged pores, irritation and breakouts, the association said.
Because of the trend's rising popularity, dermatologists are warning others that the glass skin look may be unrealistic and the skincare routines behind it aren’t suitable for every skin type.
Experts also point out that many of the videos contain advice from non-medical influencers, leading to a lack of basic safety information. New research presented Sept. 29 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 found that nearly 95% of the most viral videos on the trend contained misleading claims.
“We expected to find some gaps in the quality of the information, but I was surprised by how consistent they were,” Dr. Maria Lúcia Paysano, co-lead author of the study and a dermatology resident at the Professor Rubem David Azulay Institute of Dermatology in Brazil, said in an email.
The study authors screened the top videos across five Korean skincare-related search terms. After exclusions, 38 videos were assessed for dermatological claims and safety information using the Global Quality Scale and modified DISCERN, a tool used to assess the quality and reliability of health information.
Out of the 38 videos analyzed, only one video mentioned irritation risk, two addressed sun protection and none mentioned contact dermatitis risk or advised consulting a dermatologist, according to the study. About 45% recommended combining several active ingredients without safety advice, and 32% promised immediate results. Overall, none of the videos were produced by dermatologists, according to the study.
“Problems can arise when complex, one-size-fits-all routines encourage the use of multiple active ingredients without considering individual skin type, tolerance or irritation risk. A skincare routine should prioritize skin health and barrier function rather than simply trying to reproduce a viral appearance,” Paysano said.
Subscribe, like, hide from feed, or report?
The bottom line is you can take it too far. For Costioli, who posts her skincare journey on social media, her glass skin routine initially worked well for her, but soon she started having adverse reactions.
“At first, my skin really loved it, because I have dry skin and my skin absorbs skincare really well. I got a lot of compliments from people online and offline on how great my skin looked,” Costioli said in an email. “However, I kept compromising my skin barrier quite often, because I was simply using too many products.”
For her, a broken skin barrier looked like small red bumps on her face that would last for a few days. But if she continued with the extensive routines, the bumps would get more aggressive. “It wasn’t something I could keep up doing, so I had to reduce the steps in my skincare routine,” she said.
Experts agree that Korean skincare is not the problem. The concern is that social media can turn simple skincare practices into trendy and complex routines that may not work safely for everyone.
“The proof is in the pudding: none of these videos were created by dermatologists, so it should not be a shock that omissions and misinformation are ensued,” Dr. Mona Gohara, a board-certified dermatologist and clinical professor in the department of dermatology at Yale School of Medicine, said in an email. Gohara, who was not involved with the new study, added that many skincare trends, not just the glass skin, have amplified voices that are not medically trained.
Additionally, achieving poreless skin is not possible, as pores are genetic and do not respond to layering products, said Dr. Jane Yoo, a board-certified dermatologist and Mohs surgeon based in New York City.
“When patients try to attain this goal, they may inadvertently be disrupting their skin cycle as the physiologic exfoliation signals are now removed,” said Yoo, who is an assistant clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Yoo was also not involved with the study.
Common skin issues she observes with her patients who have utilized too many products include contact dermatitis, rosacea and acne flares.
Tight, itchy, tender, inflamed, flaky, scaly, and red or darker skin are all signs that someone’s skin barrier may be damaged, added Gohara. To help your skin recover, she recommends pausing scrubs, exfoliating acids and retinoids, and instead cleansing with a gentle, pH-neutral, non-soap cleanser and lukewarm water. She added that barrier repair creams can help, and to keep applying sunscreen during the day.
“It’s great to have patients educated on their skin, but it’s not a one-size-fits-all approach. You have to know your skin type and work with a dermatologist to see if these products are right for you,” Yoo said.
The good news is, “you can pursue the glow while taking care of the skin beneath it,” Gohara said. She recommends moisturizing often, especially as skin can become drier with age and hormone changes. To boost that dewy look, layer from lightest to heaviest with a light, concentrated hydrating hyaluronic acid serum, followed by a moisturizer and then a barrier repair cream.
Yoo, who is a Korean American dermatologist, often tells patients that they do not need a complex routine for their skin. She typically recommends a four-step approach, including a simple cleanser, an active – such as retinol, salicylic acid or vitamin C – a moisturizer and SPF.
“The key is to know thy skin and know what it can tolerate,” Gohara said. “Add one product at a time, start slowly, and wear broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day. Sun damage is one of the biggest vibrance killers, along with stress, smog, smoking, lack of sleep, and yes, sugar.”

title: Former clerk of court accused of bumping his salary on 44 paychecks, police say
text:
LORIS, SC. (WMBF/Gray News) - A former clerk of court in South Carolina is accused of secretly increasing his own pay rate 44 times over about a year and a half.
Todd Keith Massey turned himself in Wednesday morning as he faces charges of breach of trust with fraudulent intent, grand larceny valued at $5,000 or more, and a violation of the state Ethics, Government Accountability and Campaign Reform Act.
From June 2021 through January 2023, Massey, while employed as clerk of court, allegedly gradually increased his own hourly pay rate across 44 consecutive biweekly pay periods, according to the warrants.
The warrants stated that Massey’s real approved salary was $16.98 an hour as of July 2021, but he fluctuated his hourly rate between $22.82 and $46.26 over the following months, without city council or mayoral approval.
This led to him making about $55,183.02 more than his approved salary.
In addition to serving as clerk of court, the city of Loris told WMBF News that Massey held several positions with the city, including police officer, city clerk and city treasurer. The city said it is still working to confirm the dates Massey held each position.
Massey was treasurer of Giving Hope Gardens, a nonprofit in the Loris area that helps support people with disabilities by teaching them life skills.
In April 2025, Massey pleaded guilty to embezzling roughly $70,000 from Giving Hope Gardens.
Massey transferred or wrote $35,000 in checks to “All Star Pest” and nearly $14,000 to “KEM Management.” Both are companies that he owns, according to filings with the South Carolina Secretary of State.
The loss of funds led to staff cuts and fewer interns at Giving Hope Gardens.
A judge then sentenced Massey to five years in prison, suspended to five years’ probation. The 15th Circuit Solicitor’s Office said Massey also paid back $34,000 in restitution.
In December 2025, WMBF News aired an investigation into allegations from customers of Massey’s former North Myrtle Beach business CabinetWorks who say he botched their home remodeling projects.
Multiple complaints of ditching cabinet renovations led to his arrest by North Myrtle Beach police in February 2026.
Arrest warrants stated Massey provided fake invoices, company logos and even staged calls to make customers think their cabinets were on the way but never arrived.
At the time of the February arrest, the news came as a sigh of relief for several customers who shared their complaints during WMBF News’ investigation.
Massey told WMBF News in January that he stepped away from his business to let someone else take over after several customers canceled orders following our investigation.
Massey faces three counts of breach of trust in the North Myrtle Beach case.
WMBF News also learned that Massey previously oversaw finances for Providing Hope VA, another Loris-based charity whose CEO pleaded guilty to money laundering in 2024. Massey was never charged or named in that case.
Massey remains booked at the J. Reuben Long Detention Center as of Thursday morning.

title: Attorney for Lewiston shooting victims urges judge not to dismiss lawsuit against U.S. government
text:
PORTLAND — In a packed courtroom on Thursday, an attorney for the victims of Maine’s deadliest mass shooting said they want to know why the U.S. Army failed several times to seize the firearms belonging to the reservist who killed 18 people and wounded 13.
On Oct. 25, 2023, Robert Card — a 20-year veteran of the Army — opened fire at a bar and a bowling alley in Lewiston. He was found dead two days later.
More than 100 survivors and family members of the victims sued the government a year later, alleging that the Army failed multiple times to seize Card’s firearms despite recognizing an obligation to do so and having a duty under several Army policies identified by the plaintiffs.
They filed their lawsuit under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows lawsuits to be filed against the entire government. The government has requested the lawsuit be dismissed, arguing that it’s covered by several exemptions outlined in the act, including one for “discretionary immunity” in cases where the government’s policies leave decision-making up to its employees.
If the lawsuit is dismissed, there will be no civil discovery process that Jamal Alsaffar, an attorney for the plaintiffs, said would provide his clients with answers.
“There is no person, no other agency, no other law enforcement agency, that knew more about the threat that Sgt. Card posed to this community” than the Army, Alsaffar told a federal judge during a hearing on Thursday. “Let us discover how deep this negligence goes.”
It’s unclear when U.S. Chief District Judge Lance Walker will decide on the government’s motion following the two-hour hearing in the federal court in Portland. Attorneys agreed earlier this year to combine two lawsuits against the government — one filed in September 2024 by 102 plaintiffs, and another filed in April by a sister of one of the victims.
About three months before the shooting, Card had been hospitalized at Keller Army Community Hospital in West Point, New York, after threatening fellow soldiers during a July 2023 training exercise. Despite making further threats of violence and describing what officials later called a hit list, Card was discharged two weeks later.
Recommendations that Card not have access to firearms were discretionary, attorneys for the government argued Thursday. Because medical records state that Card’s hospitalization was voluntary, the government said there was no mandatory requirement that the government take Card’s guns.
“There is no dispute here that Card ultimately consented to hospitalization,” attorney Jocelyn Krieger, from the U.S. Department of Justice, argued in court.
In court records, the DOJ has argued that the plaintiffs cite “no regulation or policy” in their lawsuits that would have required Card’s supervisors to take specific action while he was on duty. Card was not on active-duty orders during the mass shooting, and the government has argued he was “solely responsible” for what happened.
Card had also not been convicted of any crimes that would prohibit him from possessing firearms, DOJ attorney Brandon Capece argued Thursday, after Walker asked how this case was different from a lawsuit in Texas, where the government was ordered to pay $230 million in damages after an Air Force member killed 26 people during a church service in 2017. The government appealed and settled a year later for $144.5 million.
That Air Force member had a domestic violence conviction that legally barred him from having a gun, Capece said.
Alsaffar represented several survivors in the Sutherland Springs church shooting lawsuit. He disagreed with Capece and Krieger in court, saying there are several Army procedures that would have allowed Card’s chain of command to seize his firearms.
The Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Defense found in September that the Army failed to implement several relevant policies when it came to addressing Card in the months before the shooting.
Alsaffar disputed that Card’s hospitalization could be considered voluntary. He said documents show that Card was hospitalized under Army command, with several guards present and restraints.
At Keller and a contracted hospital, Four Winds, Alsaffar said Card expressed he was afraid he would commit a mass act of violence and that he was hearing voices that weren’t there. Keller said Card also consented to letting the government take his guns upon his being discharged.
One of Card’s supervisors failed to open an email about his discharge recommendations, Alsaffar argued, citing testimony to an independent state commission that investigated the shooting. Another captain failed to contact local law enforcement officials about implementing Maine’s yellow flag law, which would have allowed the Sagadahoc County Sheriff’s Office to take Card’s firearms, Alsaffar said in court.
Alsaffar said this was the kind of “garden variety negligence” that the government has been sued and found liable for in other lawsuits.
He said that those Army supervisors testified that they believed officials higher up in the Army would step in, and that the civil discovery process might reveal that.

title: In Winthrop, new helmet tech provides impact data for coaches, medical staff
text:
Thanks to a generous gift, the Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale football program has 50 state-of-the-art Riddell helmets that include impact sensors, giving coaches and athletic trainers access to immediate feedback when a player absorbs a blow to the head.
Coach Joel Stoneton also receives daily emails with an impact report for the entire team. He said that has already helped him correct improper tackling technique for a varsity player who was inadvertently dropping his head during tackling drills, resulting in impacts to the crown of his helmet. Riddell football helmets are considered one of the best in the country.
“I was able to spend extra time with that varsity player, show him the data, and fix it. Get his head up and see your target,” said Stoneton. “More importantly, medically, my athletic trainer can look that up and tell where that impact was on the student.”
Stoneton said he had already worked with the player on his tackling form. But it wasn’t until the player saw the data that his habits changed.
“Sometimes you don’t really understand it until you have a neutral piece of information. Then you can see very clearly that you’re not using the correct part of your body,” Stoneton said.
Stoneton believes having the impact data helps to protect his players this season and widespread use could further the study of how head impacts cause concussions and CTE in football players. CTE is a progressive brain disease caused by repeated blows to the head.
“The more of these helmets that are out there recording data the more we’ll be able to hone in on, maybe get to those thresholds when a concussion happens,” Stoneton said. “It’s just more information to keep our kids safer.”
The Ramblers are using the Riddell Axiom helmet. Those helmets, with an individual retail price just over $1,000, come equipped with five impact sensors. The analytic software that allows coaches to glean the sensors’ information, and is normally an optional add-on subscription, was also part of the gift. The software is sold as a team-wide product. Riddell does not publicize the cost.
Before the season, each helmet was custom fit to individual players’ heads. The helmet will stay with them through their Winthrop career. When new players join the program, they will go through the same fitting process.
“These are fantastic helmets but what takes them further as a coach and working with the trainer are the five different sensors,” said Stoneton, adding that the Riddell rep trained the Winthrop staff on how to utilize and interpret the head impact results.
Riddell is the only football helmet manufacturer that builds impact sensors into their products but the concept is not new. The NFL had a trial, voluntary program it suspended in 2015, citing data inaccuracies and potential infringement on players’ medical privacy rights.
Winthrop’s new helmets were a gift from Walter Wiacek, a part-time Winthrop resident and the chief financial officer of private equity firm Fenway Partners, the primary owner of Riddell. Wiacek and Stoneton were introduced through a mutual acquaintance. Riddell has a community outreach program that includes helmet donations. Wiacek decided Winthrop was a worthy candidate.
“He said he’d been to a couple of our games and liked the local vibe,” Stoneton said. “He donated 50 helmets and wrote a check for $30,000 to cover them.”
As a small-town athletic director, Stoneton said he needed to be sure the helmet fitting and continued use of sensor analytics would be affordable in the future. Football helmets are routinely sent back to the manufacturers after each season to be reconditioned.
Stoneton said the cost of reconditioning and updating the Riddell system for the next season or a new player is “not much different,” than it would be for any other helmet.

title: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt, her attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike has taken her first steps with assistance, just one week after a failed attempt to execute the Tennessee woman left her in critical condition, her lawyers said Thursday.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to put her to death eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn’t kill her, and her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were “limited” and she required some assistance as she walked. She was also able to eat for the first time, her attorneys said.
But they also warned in a statement that there was still uncertainty about her future from both a physical and legal standpoint.
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt.
“While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured,” her attorneys wrote in a statement on Thursday. “Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die.”
Pike regained consciousness on Tuesday, when she awoke and was able to speak, they said.
They initially described Pike as “angry and confused” in the hours after regaining consciousness, and added on Thursday that she continued to have challenges with concentration and memory. Doctors said that it is too early to tell what the long-term affects will be, the attorneys added.
Many questions also remain about Pike’s legal future, and specifically whether Tennessee will seek to make another attempt to execute her. Her attorneys have said that they will push for Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
“She should never be subjected to another execution attempt,” the statement read.

title: Studio Two brings early Beatles sound to Franco Center Oct. 10
text:
LEWISTON, ME – The early Beatles are coming to Lewiston. Studio Two, a four-member tribute band dedicated to recreating the music, look and energy of The Beatles’ early years, will perform at 7 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, at the Franco Center, 46 Cedar St.
The band recreates the sound and experience of the Fab Four with period-appropriate instruments, appearance, and onstage banter. The set features favorite Beatles songs from the group’s early years, including music influenced by the raw sound of The Beatles’ Hamburg era.
Stephen Murray portrays John Lennon, while his brother Robert Murray portrays George Harrison.
“As a trained musician, I never expected to be playing in a Beatles tribute band, but it has been an amazing experience,” Stephen Murray said. “I am humbled to have an opportunity to portray John Lennon, who is one of the most talented musicians and composers of all time, and I am thrilled to bring Beatles music to a multitude of different generations. Best of all, I get to do this with my brother and best friends.”
Robert Murray said authenticity is an important part of the Studio Two experience.
“Playing George Harrison and re-enacting Beatles’ performances from the early years has been a thrill,” he said. “I love the vintage equipment and raw sound of the Beatles’ early era, and we take special care to ensure the look and sound is as close to authentic as possible.”
Studio Two’s musicians are part of a new generation keeping The Beatles’ music and fan culture alive for longtime fans and those discovering the band for the first time.
“Studio Two has been an amazing journey, and every day I look forward to meeting both old fans of The Beatles and new fans of Studio Two!” Robert Murray said.
Franco Center Executive Director Theresa Shanahan said the organization appreciates the support of Androscoggin Bank, sponsor of the concert.
“We are grateful to Androscoggin Bank for sponsoring Studio Two and supporting live music at the Franco Center,” Shanahan said. “Local business support helps us continue to bring a variety of performances to our community and gives audiences another opportunity to enjoy live music in this historic building.”
Doors and the cash bar open at 6 p.m. The concert begins at 7 p.m.
Tickets are $35 in advance and $40 at the door on the day of the show. Tickets are available at francocenter.org, by calling 207-689-2000, or in person at the Franco Center box office from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tuesdays and Wednesdays.
The Franco Center is accessible to people with disabilities from the Lincoln Street Alley entrance. Parking is available on Oxford Street when spaces are available, at the lot at Cedar and Lincoln streets, and at the Lincoln Street lot across from FX Marcotte.
Studio Two is sponsored by Androscoggin Bank.

title: Watch: Yarmouth cross country is Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Boys Team of the Week: Yarmouth cross country
As the defending Class B state champion, the Yarmouth High boys cross country team knew in preseason it had the returning talent to strive for even higher levels of performance.
On Saturday at the Festival of Champions, the Clippers showed what they could achieve, running to a convincing victory in a field of 79 teams from across New England. Yarmouth also won the event at Belfast’s Troy Howard Middle School in 2025.
Bowen Mitchell (sixth), Jackie Chalmers (eighth), Eli Chalders (13th) and Jesse Canfield (17th) were in the top 20 and just 22 seconds apart in a field with 940 finishers. Yarmouth’s next two runners, freshman Joel Kiander and junior Jasper Keller, finished 72nd and 73rd, providing enough depth to complement the strong top four. Kiander ran fast enough as a solo runner in the freshman race to edge Keller for the Clippers’ final scoring position.
This year’s field was deeper and larger because the New England Championships will also be held on the same course on Nov. 14.
Yarmouth coach Sarah Carrigan said her top four “crushed it.”
“They went in wanting to repeat, but nervous about the competition,” Carrigan said. “But in that top four, all of them PR’d by 20 to 30 seconds. They ran it really strategically, too. That course goes out wicked fast, and they stayed kind of middle of the pack in the first mile and then really turned it on and moved up and executed really well.”
“It obviously feels amazing,” Mitchell said. “I knew all the work we’ve put in was going to pay off. I know that we trusted in the process.”
Yarmouth is the clear favorite to win the Class B championship Oct. 31 at Cony High School in Augusta. Carrigan said the goal for the rest of the season is “taking that pack and moving it up.”
“We definitely have an amazing shot to win states,” Mitchell said. “That doesn’t mean we’re going to stop training. We’re going to train harder, and we want to win.”

title: Nearly half of Maine is now in at least severe drought
text:
Experts now estimate that nearly half of Maine is under at least severe drought conditions as the entire state remains mired in a monthslong dry spell that hasn’t been helped by recent rain.
The latest U.S. Drought Monitor map, released Thursday, indicates roughly 46% of the state’s area is in at least severe drought, including 5% — a chunk of coastal Maine — that is experiencing a more dire extreme drought.
No part of the state is yet in exceptional drought, the most serious level.
While the entire state has been under at least moderate drought conditions for multiple weeks, the Drought Monitor reported last week that roughly 19% of the state was experiencing at least severe drought. Now, a large swath of northern Maine has been moved to that designation as well.
That original 19% — an area stretching from northern York County to southern Hancock County, encroaching inward to the Greater Portland, Augusta and Bangor regions — remains virtually unchanged this week. The coastal area of southern and Midcoast Maine under extreme conditions actually shrank slightly.
But a large new zone representing roughly a quarter of the state’s total area — spanning most of Aroostook County, much of northern Penobscot and Piscataquis counties and a slice of Somerset County — is now also under severe drought.
That’s despite recent rain, including a nor’easter that dumped up to 4 inches across the state late last month. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates that, as of Tuesday, Maine needs between 9 and 11 inches of rain within a month to break the drought.
The National Weather Service’s Caribou office said Thursday that water levels are starting to near record lows, while groundwater levels remain below normal. And like the nor’easter, any rain this week won’t provide much relief, the weather service added.
Under extreme drought conditions, rivers, streams and wells dry up, crops widely suffer, and disease breaks out among wildlife, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Even under moderate conditions, honey production can decline, bodies of water drop below average levels, and the risk of wildfires increases.
Maine has battled drought conditions for much of the past two years, with conditions at their worst around this time last year. (More than 40% of the state was in extreme drought last October.)
Conditions steadily improved this spring before a dry, warm summer that was the second-hottest on record in Portland.

title: HBCUs are underfunded. A legal effort starting in Missouri seeks to fix it
text:
HBCUs are underfunded. A legal effort starting in Missouri seeks to fix it
An effort to address decades of underfunding at some historically Black colleges and universities kicked off Wednesday with a lawsuit against the state of Missouri.
Video above: Spelman College is breaking school records with 7 valedictorians
Students and graduates of Lincoln University in the state's capital of Jefferson City allege the lack of financial resources undercut their education and devalued their degrees.
More than a dozen other states are in the crosshairs of a newly formed group called the 1890 Project.
"It is very unfortunate that we still live in a climate where, depending on the color of one's skin, one gets precedence over the other," said Lincoln graduate Jeanneth Johnson, a 54-year-old from the Detroit suburb of Sterling Heights, who is a plaintiff in the lawsuit.
The University of Missouri system and the governor's office both said in written statements that they couldn't comment on pending litigation.
HBCUs missed out on money
Back in 2023, the administration of then-President Joe Biden found HBCUs in 16 states had missed out on $12.6 billion in funding over the last three decades. The finding and an ensuing call for the governors in those states to boost spending came one year after members of Congress also raised concerns. 
At issue is the funding of land-grant universities. The first batch was established in 1862 under the Morrill Act, which gave public lands to states to pay for colleges that focused on educating students in practical fields like agriculture and engineering.
It was a departure from traditional colleges at the time, which focused mostly on classical subjects for the elite, such as Latin, Greek, philosophy and theology. But the law's namesake, Justin Smith Morrill, a senator from Vermont, believed higher education should be accessible to all social classes.
In the wake of the Civil War, Morrill, an abolitionist, called for an update to the act. Passed in 1890, the new law required states either to open their land grants to students of all races or establish separate land grant schools for Black students.
Missouri, a border state that allowed slavery but fought with the Union during the Civil War, wasn't about to open its flagship University of Missouri campus in Columbia to Black students. To meet the new requirement, it looked toward what was then called Lincoln Institute, which a Black Union Army unit started at the end of the war by pooling their wages.
Seventeen other mostly former Confederate states and border states established 18 other land grant schools for Black students. They included Tuskegee University, the only private 1890 land grant.
Federal law requires an equitable distribution of state funding for all of a state's land-grant universities — whether HBCU or otherwise. But the 2023 Biden administration analysis found that only two states funded traditional and HBCU land-grants equitably — Delaware and Ohio. Lincoln University alone was underfunded by $361 million from 1987 through 2020, the newly filed lawsuit says, citing federal numbers.
Today, Lincoln's enrollment has fallen to around 2,200 students, down from around 3,400 in 2011 and just a fraction of the approximately 32,000 enrolled on the University of Missouri's Columbia campus, which was roiled by protests in 2015 over racial injustice, leading to the resignation of two top administrators.
"We're not saying they should be funded equally, but they should be funded on parity," said Don Calloway, a former Missouri state lawmaker who leads the 1890 Project. "And the feds funded Lincoln with the proper parity. The problem is that the state made an intentional choice not to match the federal appropriation. And that's where Lincoln really was cheated."
He blames millions in deferred maintenance on some of Lincoln's enrollment woes.
Calloway said he also is talking to attorneys general in several other states, including Virginia, Arkansas, Maryland, North Carolina, Alabama and Georgia. Over the decades, lawsuits also have been filed in several of those states over underfunding of HBCUs, including one in Maryland that led to a $577 million settlement.
Missouri is the first legal target
But those lawsuits mostly focused on state-level funding disparities between all HBCUs and non-HBCUs. There are dozens of HBCUs that aren't 1890s land grants, often started by nonprofits and religious groups. Calloway said his legal strategy is focused just on the 1890s schools.
"We expect to negotiate and/or litigate in multiple jurisdictions over the next year," he said. "Missouri is the first."
Herbert Kitchen, a plaintiff whose great-great-grandfather, Caleb Lindsey, was one of the soldiers whose pay founded Lincoln, recalled his residence hall frequently was without heat and hot water when he was a student at Lincoln in the 1980s. Rumors were swirling that the school might close, and he said some employers looked at his degree as "second rate."
Kitchen, a retired California community college administrator, thinks of his great-great-grandfather as he fights for Lincoln, a school generations of his family have attended.
"I am," he said, "the hope and dream that my great-grandfather had when he was a slave."

title: Mr. Drew Steps Back From Poland Education Center To Focus On Family, Will Continue Animal Outreach
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Saying Goodbye…For Now…To Mr. Drew & His Animals Too
It's the end of one chapter and the beginning of another for one of Maine's most well-known and well-loved animal attractions.
The History:
Families across Maine have come to know the name Mr. Drew, as the man with all the cool animals.
Aside from the hundreds of talks he's done with his exotic critters to school kids across the Pine Tree State, Drew Desjardins, (know to most of us now as Mr. Drew) has also operated his "Natural Science Hands-on Museum and Exotic Rescue/Reptile Zoo" out of a few different locations in Maine over the last decade.
For years, he was set up in the Lewiston Mall. Most recently, this past January, he and his many volunteers moved the entire operation of the Mr. Drew and His Animals Too Education Center to their latest location of Poland, Maine.
Mr. Drew has not only been educating the public on the animals he has, but he's been rescuing them as well, often taking in animals that humane societies will not.
What's Happening Now?
With his new facility up and running this year, and Mr. Drew appearing at speaking engagements around the state, things seemed to chugging right along.
But, as is often the case in life, sometimes challenges arise and force you to change your focus.
This year has been a tough one for many, economically, and that is certainly affecting many small businesses and nonprofits throughout Maine.
Another thing that often has an impact on people is when a loved one unexpectedly becomes ill. And when it's your child, and they end up in the hospital for an extended period of time, the world just stops, and your priorities shift, as they should.
It is this combination of recent challenges that led Mr. Drew and his team to make the very difficult decision to close the doors to their new facility, permanently.
He made the announcement over the Mr. Drew and His Animals Too Facebook Page earlier this week.
"Mr. Drew and His Animals Too Education Center in Beautiful Poland, Maine is OFFICIALLY CLOSING OUR DOORS FOREVER ON SATURDAY OCTOBER 31st. Please know Mrs. Drew and I have accepted this decision and we are NOT seeking a 'Hail Mary', any public financial support or a GoFundMe...Many of you will suggest other locations like the Auburn Mall but we do not have the finances for another move nor do we have the mental capacity to start over again...With everything going on in our lives, Mrs. Drew and I are getting older and stretched way too thin to continue at this pace."
How Will The Closure Work?
Drew says for the remainder of the month, the facility will stay open from 10 AM to 4 PM, 7 days a week, so that those who have purchased passes can use them, as they will not be able to offer refunds. They will also be open on Indigenous Peoples Day and are planning to go ahead with the Pokemon Event they had planned in advance of the decision to close. They are also in the process of reaching out to those schools and individuals who had book out for parties and field trips past the October 31st date.
What's next for Mr. Drew and His Animals Too?
The Drews sold their home of 20 years to make the move to Poland, so they don't plan to leave the community, especially after all the community did to welcome them in the first place. But they cannot sustain maintaining the facility, all of the animals and their duties to their family all at the same time.
Mr. Drew says that they plan to return to their roots of animal education and outreach, and will continue to book out traveling exhibits for birthday parties, homeschool or scouting functions and community events.
For those who had already booked Mr. Drew for the rest of this year, 2027 or 2028, he plans to honor those engagements, as well.
As for the animals, Mr. Drew says his team is working on that right now, but assures everyone that they will all end up in safe places.
"We cannot move all my animals into my home but many will come with me as I continue to do my outreach, the remaining will be move to educational facilities or sanctuaries that I fully trust. No animal will be euthanized and we are NOT adopting animals out publicly nor taking animals it but you email, I may be able to direct you to other resources."
Mr. Drew says he will be taking a step back from social media for a while, to focus on family and rebrand in a simpler way. If you wish to book him for an event, you can email a request to mr.drewsanimals2@yahoo.com.
We wish Mr. Drew, his family, his crew and all the animals all the best in this next chapter they will write.

title: ‘We are absolutely in a crisis’: The fight to provide access to food in the South
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - In communities across the country, more families are getting pushed farther away from fresh, affordable food.
The USDA calls it “low access.” It’s when a significant share of a neighborhood lives far away from a grocery store. The agency estimates nearly 54 million Americans live in these areas.
When that happens, researchers found that people often rely on convenience store and fast food items. These can be higher in sugar, sodium, and saturated fats. Ingredients which can lead to health problems.
Food deserts impact one in three people in Memphis. Volunteers are working to feed the need through a school pantry and mobile grocery store.
Weekly food distribution
Every week at Winchester Elementary, volunteers pack 60 to 70 boxes of food for students and their families free of charge.
The pantry is the brainchild of Denise Wilson, a fourth-grade math teacher who has been at Winchester for two years.
Two years ago, Wilson noticed a student sleeping in class and complaining of stomach aches.
“We talked to him, the fourth-grade team did. And he explained that, the little bit of food they do have, he made sure his sister got it,” Wilson said.
Wilson created the Bronco Kare Korral Pantry, providing select students and their families’ full meals every week, even during breaks.
“I grew up in this neighborhood,” said Wilson. “I didn’t have the food insecurities that a lot of our kids have, but I did grow up on food stamps. I definitely know that feeling of not having groceries in the house a couple of days before food stamps are supposed to hit.”
Wilson and her team say their work is completely voluntary, providing bags of foods to children every Friday along with carefully crafted boxes of food including meat and veggies for their parents.
Wilson said they depend on donations from the Mid-South Food Bank and donations from the community.
Donations are accepted here: Fundraiser by Denise Wilson : Help Restock the Bronco Kare Korral Pantry
Food desert data
Winchester Elementary sits inside what is commonly known as a food desert, defined by the USDA as an area where the poverty rate is greater than at least 20% of the population and at least 500 people live more than half a mile from the nearest large grocery store.
Many residents in the neighborhood don’t have access to a car and for some, the nearest grocery store is one to three miles away. Many people rely on convenience stores at higher prices with no fresh food options.
Data shows roughly 32% of Memphians live in a food desert.
“We’re absolutely in a crisis,” said Roshun Austin, CEO of the nonprofit The Works, Inc., which focuses on rebuilding communities through affordable housing, fighting blight and food insecurity.
Austin said many Memphis neighborhoods struggle to attract grocery stores.
“A lot of it is due to how we developed our city. We’re very sparsely populated,” Austin said. “We have over 30,000 vacant and abandoned lots in our county. And so, a grocery store is not going into a place next to 10 vacant houses and lots because they have a customer base.”
Mobile grocer expands reach
The Works launched a mobile grocer in 2022. The 20-foot trailer is stocked with fresh produce, meats and dairy.
At a stop in the medical district, most customers no longer drive.
“Sometimes my granddaughter has time to take me or I’ll get one of my neighbors who drive to take me,” said Gloria Thomas, who shops at the mobile store.
Data shows the concept is growing in popularity. The mobile grocer nearly doubled the number of individuals served year over year, from 2,317 people in 2024 to 4,302 people in 2025, according to The Works Impact Report.
“Price of food. Everything is going up,” said BJ Adams, manager of the mobile grocer.
The mobile grocer is not a pantry. Customers must pay for everything inside, but prices are comparable to other full-service grocery stores.
The grocer moves into food deserts across the city at a dozen locations every week from North to South Memphis.
Check out the full schedule here: MOBILE GROCER | The Works.
Cash Saver partnered with The Works, inc. to provide wholesale products in areas where there are no physical stores. The concept is being replicated across the country. Little Rock opened its own mobile market last month after volunteers visited Memphis to learn how to do it.
While mobile grocery stores, community gardens and food pantries help solve some food insecurity issues, Austin said the real solution requires rebuilding neighborhoods.
“It looks like the neighborhoods where you see grocery stores. That means wealth has increased for individuals and their families. That means that it’s an ideal place. It’s a choice neighborhood. People want to live here,” Austin said.
“Because I see the need,” Adams said.

title: These Mainers shined on sailing’s biggest stage
text:
It was perfect sailing weather, blue skies and strong wind. Merritt Carey and Jim Brady weren’t navigating Casco Bay. They sat at a picnic table at SailMaine’s center near the Old Port, navigating memories three decades old.
Thirty-one years ago, Carey and Brady took part in the America’s Cup defender series, the competition to determine who would represent the United States in the prestigious sailing race. Carey was with Mighty Mary, the first all-female America’s Cup crew. Brady, who won a silver medal in the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona, was the navigator for Dennis Conner’s Stars and Stripes during the defender races.
A new documentary has stirred memories, too. “Mighty Mary” tells the story of the race through the eyes of Carey’s team. The film will be screened on Nov. 5 at Hannaford Hall on the Portland campus of the University of Southern Maine, with a panel discussion including Carey to follow. Proceeds from the screening benefit SailMaine’s programs for girls and women, as well as the Hearts of Pine Foundation’s programs for girls and women.
Carey was fresh off taking part in the Whitbread Round the World Race with captain Dawn Riley, who also captained the Mighty Mary team.
“My job was to do the things nobody wanted to do ,” said Carey, who now lives in Yarmouth.
Brady remembered thinking at the time that the Mighty Mary team had a lot of talented sailors, but their overall lack of big boat experience could be a factor.
“I never thought it was going to be a cakewalk,” Brady said. “Right off the bat, we knew we had a battle.”
While Riley and Carey had plenty of racing experience, many of their teammates did not. Some had been Olympic rowers who knew port and starboard, but from a backward perspective because when they rowed, they had their backs to the front of the boat. They were constantly worried they would cause chaos with a mistake, Carey said.
The team was a few races in by the time they received the new Mighty Mary boat. Getting used to the boat’s feel while competing for such high stakes was difficult, Carey said. Their concerns and complaints were brushed off as operator error. If Dennis Connor had the same concerns, they would have been dealt with seriously and fixed, Carey said. But these women?
“They thought, these women don’t know how to sail,” she said, “and they were wrong. We didn’t have any doubts about our ability to handle the boat at all. Everyone on that boat was a hard-driving competitor.”
This was 23 years after Title IX, the landmark law that prohibited sex-based discrimination, Carey noted. Nowadays, each America’s Cup boat is required to have at least one woman on the crew. That requirement shows how slow progress is, Carey said. There are plenty of female sailors qualified for positions who should earn those spots without a requirement.
Later in the competition, Dave Dellenbaugh was added to Mighty Mary’s crew as tactician, ending the team’s all-female status. Carey thinks that was the work of team owner Bill Koch. He won the America’s Cup in 1992 and had a hand in everything, she said. That was the first of three gut punches, Carey said.
The second was what happened after Mighty Mary beat Stars and Stripes in what they thought was an elimination race. Before Carey and her teammates could celebrate, they learned a deal had been struck to make the final a three-boat event. Beating Stars and Stripes that day didn’t matter. Both were moving on.
“I thought we were eliminated,” said Brady, of Portland.
Gut punch three was the final, when Mighty Mary saw a four-minute lead over Stars and Stripes evaporate in tough racing conditions. Stars and Stripes caught a little wind at the right time and eked out the victory.
“There’s no other way to put it. It sucked,” Carey said.
Carey said she hadn’t thought of the experience too much in recent years. The documentary, which she’s seen twice, sparked memories as she reconnected with teammates she hadn’t seen in decades. Taking her three children, son Liam and daughters Madeleine and Grace, to see the film gave her some cool mom cred.
Carey couldn’t recall exactly when during the experience she realized her Mighty Mary team had a real chance to win. Thinking about it, maybe it was from the second they arrived in San Diego to compete. The doubt of others is a deep well. Athletes have drawn from it for motivation for centuries.
It came down to this: Carey and her teammates knew they could race the boat. If you didn’t believe it, that wasn’t their problem.
“Why would you bother if you didn’t think you had a chance?” she said.

title: Gov. Ron DeSantis calls name of Hurricane Isaias ‘weird.’ This is what he’s going to call it instead
text:
(Gray News) - Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the name of Hurricane Isaias “not normal.”
Isaias, which is pronounced “ee-sah-EE-ahs,” is the Spanish form of the name Isaiah.
“I don’t know how to pronounce this, because it’s not normal,” DeSantis said. “I’m calling it Isaiah. You guys can call it what you want. I know that’s not how you pronounce this, it’s something else but it’s weird and I’m just going to keep butchering it for the next 72 hours. And I’d rather just be that — so I’m calling it Isaiah.”
DeSantis made the comments during a news conference about a Florida appeals court tossing parts of a grand jury report on alleged misuse of taxpayer money surrounding Hope Florida.
Hurricane Isaias is continuing to strengthen in the Gulf after becoming the first Atlantic hurricane of the season.
The storm is forecast to make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast later this week as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane.

title: Portland Hearts of Pine eliminated from USL1 playoff chase
text:
The Portland Hearts of Pine are officially eliminated from USL League One playoff contention.
Eight teams in the 17-team league will advance to the quarterfinal round. Wednesday night in Texas, eighth-place Fort Wayne FC beat Corpus Christi, 3-1, to improve to 11-9-9, good for 42 points. Portland (7-12-10) has 31 points with three matches remaining. Even if the Hearts won three straight — something they have not done all season — their maximum point total would be 40.
Portland has been well below the playoff line for most of the season and is 14th in the league standings. In the franchise’s inaugural 2025 season, Portland finished seventh and came within a penalty kick shootout loss of reaching the final.
This season, Portland has been undone by its inability to close out games.
Portland has blown a lead in 10 USL1 matches, mostly because of nine conceded goals in the 90th minute or extra time. Six times Portland settled for a tie. Four times it gave up a second goal and lost. Add in a 2-1 home loss to Chattanooga when they had tied the game with a second-half goal before allowing the winner in the 90th minute, and the Hearts have squandered 25 potential points.
Portland has four comebacks of its own (two ties, two wins), including a 3-3 tie Saturday at Spokane, when it trailed 3-1.
Portland has continued to play in front of packed crowds even in inclement weather. It has averaged 6,234 fans per match at Fitzpatrick Stadium where it is 5-6-3 in league play.
Portland hosts Athletic Club Boise (14-8-7) at 5 p.m. Saturday. Boise, which has announced it will play in USL Championship next season, is in fifth place with a chance to reach the top four and earn a home quarterfinal game. Portland is at third-place Forward Madison (15-7-7) on Oct. 17 and concludes its season Oct. 24, hosting Charlotte Independence (18-5-6), which is one point out of first place.
