title: 5 notable moments from Susan Collins and Troy Jackson’s second debate
text:
Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson ran the gamut from personal attacks to policy disagreements.
It was the second time this week the 73-year-old Collins and the 58-year-old Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president, squared off. Their final two debates will take place next week.
On Tuesday, Jackson put in a strong performance, delivering a couple zingers that took on lives of their own on social media. Those quips included comparing Collins to an arsonist and telling her that “you can’t eat road salt” after she claimed she got the material exempted from tariffs.
Collins was largely on the defensive as she tried to distance herself from President Donald Trump, who is deeply unpopular in Maine, and from corruption allegations amplified by Democrats. But she also displayed her experience and knowledge of the issues.
On Thursday, Jackson was a bit shakier, struggling at times to find his talking points on the fly while Collins continued to hold her own.
Polls continue to show a close race, with Jackson having a slight edge. But Republicans have more money than Democrats and have been flooding the airwaves with ads attacking Jackson in the closing final weeks of the campaign.
Here are five takeaways from their second meeting, which was broadcast on WTMW.
1. Both candidates got personal
The candidates brought each other’s families into the debate.
Collins went on the attack first. She accused Jackson of changing his position on accepting donations from corporations. In his U.S. Senate campaign, Jackson has said he would not — but as state Senate president, his leadership PAC accepted those types of donations.
“It usually has to do with issues that his son has been hired to lobby him on,” Collins said of instances where Jackson has changed his positions over the years.
Later, Jackson took aim at Collins’ husband while discussing high energy prices. Jackson repeatedly blamed the Iran War for increasing fuel and electricity prices, saying that Collins voted five times against stopping it. (Collins noted she has voted nine times to end it.)
“She could use her leverage to stop this war,” he said. “But instead … Sen. Collins and her husband are making money off this war and so is a whole bunch of other people and that’s why this doesn’t stop.”
Jackson was referring to Collins’ husband, Tom Daffron’s, vast stock portfolio, which includes holdings in natural gas and Boeing. (Boeing’s stock price has fallen since the start of the war.)
Collins called Jackson’s charge of her family profiting off the conflict “absolutely outrageous” and demanded an apology.
“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson replied.
2. A rare moment of agreement
When the debate turned to protecting Social Security, Jackson and Collins found a rare point of agreement — both agreed that people who earn more money should pay more into the system.
Social Security taxes are currently capped at a percentage of the first $184,000 you make, regardless of your income. Jackson said that cap should be scrapped so that wealthy people would pay more into the system.
“Here is something where I actually agree with Troy,” Collins said.
But Collins didn’t go as far as Jackson. Instead, she said, she would assemble a panel of independent financial experts to provide recommendations.
“We are simply going to have to adjust the cap,” Collins said.
3. Jackson hits Collins’ strength
Collins has made her experience and seniority a central theme of her campaign. Again, she referenced the $1.5 billion she has helped bring to Maine in recent years as chair of the Appropriations Committee — the first Mainer to hold that position in 92 years.
But Jackson wasn’t impressed. He continued to describe Collins as kowtowing to Trump’s demands.
“She’s powerful during election time but she’s weak every time we need her to stand up and fight for us,” Jackson said.
4. Collins tried to flip the script on abortion
Abortion has been a big issue this campaign, especially Collins’ vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, which led in part to the overturning of Roe v. Wade.
But Collins tried to flip the script by noting that Jackson had been longtime opponent of abortion until he ran for Congress in 2014. She specifically pointed to a bill he opposed that would have allowed for abortions if a pregnancy threatened the mother’s health.
“He was an extremist when it comes to abortion,” Collins said, noting she has always been pro-choice.
Jackson, however, was ready. He acknowledged that he changed his views on abortion after speaking with women — something he said Collins didn’t do when Mainers traveled to D.C. to urge her to oppose Kavanaugh.
“Our records have changed,” said Jackson, who is endorsed by Planned Parenthood. “Mine has gotten better — hers has gotten worse.”
5. Collins recasts voting record with Trump
Jackson has repeatedly accused Collins of voting with Trump 96% of the time. The claim comes from CQ Roll Call analysis of the first seven months of 2025, which found the percentage was closer to 95%.
Collins said using the same approach to analyze her votes under former President Joe Biden would have shown her siding with the Democrat 91% of the time. And a more expansive look at Collin’s voting record in Trump’s second term shows she has sided with him 72% of the time, she claimed.
Collin said she has voted against Trump 137 times.
“But it didn’t matter,” Jackson shot back.

title: 🎃👻 MAINE NOSTALGIA! Remember These Classic LaVerdiere’s Halloween Commercials?
text:
Classic LaVerdiere’s Halloween Commercials Every Mainer Remembers
Now THIS is old-school spooky, Maine!
Any old-school Mainer remembers LaVerdiere’s Super Drug Stores. At its peak, the company operated more than 70 stores throughout Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont.
LaVerdiere’s began in 1922 in Waterville, Maine, starting out as a small newsstand and soda fountain before eventually becoming a full-service drug store.
Aside from the pharmacy, the stores sold general items, as well as toys and Halloween and Christmas decorations. In the 1980s, some LaVerdiere’s locations even featured an arcade called Action Family Arcade. The company was purchased by Rite Aid in 1994.
Read More: Take A Maine Fall Foliage Train Ride On The Leaf Peeper
I spent many a teenage afternoon there at the Action Family Arcade. We always had a plan: Walk from the Tree Streets in Bangor, head up Broadway, hit LaVerdiere’s arcade, fill the air hockey machine with about twenty bucks’ worth of quarters, proceed to do battle and annoy everyone else in the room, then walk up Broadway all the way to Dairy Queen.
Once we got there, we’d fill the jukebox with even more quarters, playing the hits of the day, then order a “Full Meal Deal,” which consisted of a Brazier burger, fries, a soda, and, best of all, a hot fudge sundae.
I also have another fond memory of LaVerdiere’s because one of my childhood buddies, Mark, worked at the downtown location when he was a junior at Bangor High School. Boy, did we give him a hard time whenever he put that lame smock on.
LaVerdiere’s was always famous for its Halloween and Christmas TV ads, and through the magic of YouTube, we found two spooky ads from 1989 and 1992.

OXFORD, Maine (WMTW) —The Maine Secretary of State’s Office confirmed that some incorrect ballots were distributed to voters in Oxford.
The Secretary of State’s Office says a resident contacted the Oxford town clerk on Tuesday after, “receiving an incorrect ballot style, and it was addressed by the clerk.”
State officials say the clerk identified that, due to a packaging error at the printer, “a small number of incorrect ballots were received and sent out.”
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she believed nine wrong ballots distributed.
Town officials were working to contact any voters who may have received an incorrect ballot.
The state said every voter will have the chance to vote the correct ballot. Anyone who receives an incorrect ballot, or who makes a mistake on their ballot, may request a new one.
Voters should have received ballots with the candidates for House District 80, which includes Republican Ernest Fitts.
Azalea Cormier, who is not registered in a party, is also running for the House District 80 seat. There is no Democrat in the race.

title: Study: 1 in 4 NFL players will contract a brain disease. How does this impact Maine high school football?
text:
A recent study revealed that over 90% of NFL players’ donated brains were wracked with CTE, the neurodegenerative disease that leads to depression, mood swings and even dementia, and can only be definitively diagnosed after death.
So why would a co-author suggest youth and high school football players should “play like the pros” if they want to protect their brains?
That’s because NFL players today have strict limits on contact during practices thanks to the league’s collective bargaining agreement with the NFL Players Association.
“We have not seen that trickle down to lower levels of football,” said Charlotte Luster, a co-author of a study published in late August that found CTE in 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021.
A total of 878 NFL players died in that time frame. Lead author Dr. Daniel Daneshvar’s attention-getting takeaway is, at minimum, 1 in 4 NFL players will contract CTE. That rate could be much higher. Previous studies have also found CTE in over 90% of studied brains. But researchers acknowledge there is a bias toward donating brains when a player is suspected to have suffered from brain disease.
Many Maine high school football coaches say they, too, have moved away from full-speed, full-contact practices. The vast majority of Maine high school football coaches have been thinking safety first for more than a decade.
“We go full pads one practice a year, the day before our first scrimmage. And that’s just to try the pants on and make sure they fit,” said Kevin Kezal, who has led Thornton Academy to seven Class A championships since 2012.
First-year Portland coach Dylan Rottkov said, “I think I’ve seen one helmet collision in a practice this season and it was accidental.”
Added Joel Stoneton, head coach and athletic director at Class D champion Winthrop: “In the state of Maine, this is the norm. There are a lot more safety protocols. In my opinion, it is safer now through improvements in equipment, the protocols and what coaches are doing.”
But the coaches do not dismiss the significance of this or other studies. They know there is a direct link between football, at least at the highest levels, and CTE.
“Obviously, our high school players and a group of former NFL players are two very different populations,” Stoneton said. “But I do think the findings reinforce why football programs need to continually look at what we can do better when it comes to reducing unnecessary head impacts and taking care of our players.”
WHAT IS CTE?
CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a progressive brain disease where proteins break down and kill brain cells.The spread of the disease is categorized from Stage 1 (least) to Stage 4 (most).
Common symptoms, based on players’ behaviors and medical reports while they were living, include headaches, depression, changes in behavior or thinking, speech difficulties, mood swings that can be violent, and dementia in late-stage development.
Daneshvar’s most recent study showed a high correlation between players diagnosed with dementia having Stage 3 and 4 CTE. Several high-profile NFL players who died by suicide, including former New England Patriots Aaron Hernandez and Junior Seau, were found to have the disease.
Luster said understanding how CTE is caused — by repetitive head impacts, not isolated concussions — is the important message for high school players.
“Ninety-two percent of football players stop playing in high school. We’re not able to say 1 in 4 high school players will develop CTE. That’s not what we’re studying,” Luster said. “But the exposure of repetitive hits that these NFL players absorbed did not begin when they started playing in the NFL.”
While preventing concussions remains a key safety goal, “CTE forces us to think about repetitive blows,” Luster said.
She called it a dose-response relationship. The head impact is the dose, CTE is the response.
“We did not look at that dose-response relationship in this study, but two studies previously have shown that risk of CTE increases with each additional year you play football,” Luster said.
Another paper published by Daneshvar showed the odds of getting CTE increased 21% with every additional 1,000 head hits.
Dr. Chris Lutrzykowski of MaineGeneral Health is the medical liaison adviser to the Maine Principals’ Association Sports Medicine Committee. Lutrzykowski said, at this point, there is no “established threshold at which risk of CTE is clearly defined.” However, Lutrzykowski agreed that the available data indicates that, when it comes to head impacts, “frequency and duration matter.”
Lutrzykowski added, “reducing the number and amount of time devoted to contact can reduce the number of head impacts considerably.”
WHAT DO PLAYERS KNOW ABOUT CTE?
Before a recent Portland High practice at Deering Oaks, seniors Dom Huntington, a two-way lineman who has been a varsity starter since his freshman season, and receiver/defensive back Maddox Meas said they don’t know a lot about CTE. But they are conscious about their own brain health and safety.
“I want to be able to go to school after high school, be able to get a good job, just to be able to still function normally,” Meas said.
Meas chooses to wear a Guardian cap, an extra padded layer that is attached to the exterior of a helmet. There is debate on whether the caps actually reduce impact levels. But players who wear them say it helps. Guardian caps are increasingly seen in practices and games at all levels of football.
“Sometimes the worst impact is when your head hits the ground. I’ve done that a few times and get a little dizzy sometimes. The Guardian cap, I think it might help out a little bit,” Meas said. “My mom also wants to make sure I don’t get hurt.”
Football helmets have improved in their design, with an emphasis on lessening the force of an impact. Some helmets, like those being worn this season by Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale have impact sensors that send real-time head-impact warnings to athletic trainers and coaches.
Huntington stressed that he doesn’t think he’s absorbed a significant head impact from an on-field hit.
Huntington and Meas both said learning that over 90% of the examined NFL players’ brains show CTE damage is “a little scary.”
They also were both quick to point out that playing high school football is not the same as playing in the NFL.
“Those guys play a lot more, their whole life,” Huntington said. “They practice hard. They go to those big colleges and stuff, so I feel like they’re way more at risk than a high school player. And on our team we don’t have anyone who is going to the NFL, realistically. It doesn’t scare me personally.”
REDUCING HEAD IMPACTS
For more than a decade, coaches in Maine have realized that they need to make their game as safe as possible — especially in practice. It benefits the players’ long-term health. It also assures that schools, many with rosters hovering in low to mid-30s, can actually play their scheduled games.
“At least in my neck of the wood, teams are running with 35 to 45 kids, and for me it has never made sense to go out and bang my kids in practice,” said Stoneton, in his 31st season as a high school coach. “We do a ton of tackling drills, but it’s on pads. We work on technique. One of the first things we do in preseason is to walk through tackling technique.”
This July, the National Federation of State High School Associations called for the elimination of several types of heavy-contact drills, including one-on-one tests of strength in a confined area; blocking, tackling, drills where players begin more than 4 yards apart; and any drill — like the infamous Oklahoma Drill — designed to create head-on collisions. The NFHS statement, posted on the MPA site, is guidance, not mandatory.
Those drills have been long gone in Maine high schools, many coaches and players said.
“Honestly, I don’t think we did drills like (the Oklahoma Drill) back at Livermore Falls in the ’90s because we had about 30 players and couldn’t afford to lose anybody in practice,” said Kezal, who started his coaching career as a Livermore Falls assistant in 1990.
But a quick internet search reveals that high-impact “drills,” with teammates and coaches cheering wildly for big hits, are still common in other parts of the country, particularly at the youth level.
Back in Maine, coaches say there are a variety of ways they can reduce the risk of brain injury. Those include emphasizing better tackling and blocking techniques to “take the head out of the game”; never taking a player to the ground when doing a tackling drill; and avoiding any full-contact drill.
Kezal and Stoneton both stressed the importance of having an athletic trainer at practices and games, and improved concussion protocols.
Rule changes have also helped. Once-accepted practices — like the blind-side crackback block or a defender launching themselves to make a tackle — are now penalized.
“That’s good for the game. Kids know they can’t do that,” Kezal said.
Stoneton has another suggestion, one he knows is unpopular: No tackle football until middle school. At the earliest.
That would eliminate years of unnecessary impacts to developing brains. Stoneton believes it would also increase participation at the high school level.
“Those young kids’ bodies are not ready for that type of play,” Stoneton said. “I’ve seen so many get lit up and it hurt and it didn’t feel good and they decide football’s not for them.”
WILL CHANGES MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
The mean age at death of the NFL players whose brains were studied in the 2016-2021 cohort was 66.5 years.
Most played their final NFL game when artificial turf was more like concrete, helmets were viewed as weapons not protection, and big hits were celebrated and encouraged. As recently as 2008, ESPN ran a weekly segment called “Jacked Up” with studio announcers gleefully glorifying the five most vicious hits of the week.
When a 65- to 70-year-old first started playing football, if a player had his “bell rung,” they might be encouraged to take a couple of plays off. Maybe. In those days, if you weren’t knocked unconscious, you didn’t have a concussion.
In 30 years, will a similar study show a decrease in CTE? It stands to reason that the significant limitations on practice collisions, rule changes, improved equipment and overall awareness of brain injuries will reduce the risk of football players contracting CTE.
“Unfortunately, we don’t know yet,” Luster said. “It could be lower but, at the same time, players are bigger, faster and stronger.”

‘Bridgerton’ Announces Lady Violet Spinoff
text:
‘Bridgerton’ Announces Spinoff for Lady Violet
There are only two Netflix shows with two different seasons in the streamer’s list of its all-time most popular TV series: Stranger Things and Bridgerton.
So if you want to know why they keep making more spinoffs of those shows, uh, that’s why.
Netflix announced today that they are making a new spinoff of Bridgerton, an as-yet untitled limited series focused on the character of Lady Violet, played on the main Bridgerton by Ruth Gemmell.

title: Maine woman turns childhood heart condition into mission to teach kids heart health
text:
Maine woman turns childhood heart condition into mission to teach kids heart health
Ashley Ricker was ten when she knew something was off with her heart. Now, as an adult, she works with the American Heart Association to teach kids how to protect their heart health.
Maine woman turns childhood heart condition into mission to teach kids heart health
Ashley Ricker was ten when she knew something was off with her heart. Now, as an adult, she works with the American Heart Association to teach kids how to protect their heart health.
Life has come full circle for a Maine woman. Ashley Ricker was a child when she was diagnosed with heart disease. Today, she works with kids to teach them about heart-healthy habits.
Ashley Ricker was just ten years old when she knew something was wrong with her heart.
"It felt like my heart was going to jump out of my chest," she said.
She waited a few days, hoping the feeling would pass because she didn't want to worry her mother.
"I just kept having that feeling that my heart was going to come out of my chest because of how hard it was beating and so quickly," Ricker said.
She told her mom she thought she had strep throat because she knew they would check her heart rate, like they do at all doctor visits.
"They get to my heart and they listen to my heart and then they look at my mom and say 'Oh, what kind of heart condition does your daughter have?'" she remembers.
It took some time, but doctors eventually diagnosed her with a rare type of abnormal heart rhythm - ventricular tachycardia.
"I have a really fast heart rate with irregular beats, and if I have too many irregular beats in a row, it makes me prone to cardiac arrest," she said.
Her condition meant she had to limit her physical activity.
"I had to be careful walking up and down stairs, like taking an elevator whenever I could," Ricker said. "There was no swimming. There were no sports teams. There was no running around at recess at all. Those are some of your best memories, I think, when you look back on your childhood, but mine were sitting on the sidelines."
But now, through her work with the American Heart Association, she's reclaiming those missed moments as a kid.
"I get to interact with the kids, and I get to meet little survivors. So, it's definitely very healing and fun and there's not a day that I don't love going to work," Ricker said.
Through the Association's Kids Heart Challenge and American Heart Challenge, Ricker teaches children about their heart health. She says the programs are service-learning fundraising programs centered around instilling whole-child wellness that empower students to build healthy habits, learn lifesaving skills like hands-only CPR and the warning signs of stroke, while raising critical lifesaving funds.
Ricker practices what she teaches, too - she eats well, exercises regularly, doesn't smoke, and limits alcohol.
"One of the biggest things for me is stress management, because I think a lot of people forget your heart rate goes up not just with physical activity but with mental and emotional stress as well," said Ricker.
She says she expects to take beta blockers for the rest of her life. But the healthy habits she chooses don't feel like restrictions.
"They're not restrictions, they're my choice," she said.
The school engagement programs are available throughout the state. School faculty who are interested can reach out to Ashley at Ashley.Ricker@heart.org.
You can find ways to incorporate healthy habits into your daily life through the American Heart Association's website.

title: 'You're resilient': ﻿Long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home
text:
Long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home after more than 200 days at sea
Sailors disembarked the USS Lincoln on Thursday following a deployment that included a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea supporting the Iran war and reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew.
Families waiting for the aircraft carrier’s arrival in San Diego Bay described crying and losing sleep after hearing about the ship’s food shortages and tough conditions. Many said the sailors had sent lists of the food they were craving.
Abel Ramirez, 20, walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
“It feels amazing,” he said while headed out to search for his parents who drove from Texas. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.”
The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.
Dozens of sailors stood atop the Lincoln as it glided past the cityscape of downtown San Diego toward cheering families who were carrying flowers and balloons and ringing cowbells.
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck. "It feels really overwhelming,” she said about being reunited, adding she's glad her mom won't need to eat ramen almost every day.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship’s commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
“She’s our deployment baby,” said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship’s conditions while she was pregnant, she said. “I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn’t sure if he was OK or not,” she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was “pretty bad.”
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
“I couldn’t grasp the reality of it,” he said about coming home. He said he became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, “seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me.”
Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.
He had told his wife about “the lack of food and showers” on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.
The Navy initially downplayed problems on the carrier
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough.”
Hegseth told the crew that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”
The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln’s crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Long deployments can tax service members
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.
Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The deployment didn’t include as many uninterrupted days at sea as the Lincoln’s 265-day stretch.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio.

title: A tradition of service: American Legion yard sale returns
text:
Aug. 8, American Legion Post 36 gathered on Boothbay Common for the organization’s 15th annual community yard sale, bringing residents together while raising money to support veterans and community organizations.
Cathy Moroney, finance officer for Post 36 and president of the corporation, said the event is not primarily about how much money can be raised. “The event is less about making money. It gives the American Legion an opportunity to interact (with the community and tell about) what we’re doing,” Moroney said.
The yard sale was founded by David Patch, a past president of American Legion Post 36, who said giving back to the community is an important part of the organization’s responsibility to the people it serves.
“If we don’t do this stuff and raise money for the community, we’re not doing what we’re supposed to be doing as veterans,” Patch said.
Funds raised through the yard sale help support a variety of causes. The organization provides assistance to veterans in need, donates to community organizations and contributes to scholarships.
For Patch, the event is also a way to keep the importance of local veterans visible. The community has long shown its appreciation for veterans, particularly those who have lived and served locally. That support can be seen throughout the area, including through the banners displayed around town honoring veterans and their service.
“I think we’re all in the mode of making sure the importance of the veterans and their contribution to the country and to the community is always out there,” Patch said.

title: Knowing your family health history matters more than you may think
text:
(Aging Untold) — At almost every doctor’s visit, you’re asked about your family health history. But if you don’t know the answers, or you rush through the form, you might be missing one of the most powerful tools available for predicting and preventing disease.
Why family history matters
“Family history can give you a clue years before disease becomes obvious,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers said people often confuse two different questions when thinking about family history: what diseases run in the family, versus what a relative ultimately died from.
“Are you asking what diseases run in your family? Or are you simply just saying, this is what my relative died from, that disease,” Rogers said. “And those two are not necessarily the same.”
“All those different things can become significant if you see a pattern of them,” Rogers said.
Genes, genomics and epigenetics
Most diseases, Rogers said, are not caused by a single gene, which is why genetic testing can add another layer of information. She pointed to inherited variations such as BRCA 1 and BRCA 2, linked to breast and ovarian cancer, and other pathogenic variations tied to cholesterol.
“We all inherited these different variations in our DNA, and some of those inherited variations can increase our risk for disease,” she said.
Genetic testing can be especially useful for people who don’t have access to their family history, including those who are adopted, Rogers said.
“That’s where genetics might be important, or genomics,” Rogers said. “That’s tells you how is your environment interacting with the genes that you have? How’s your nutrition, lifestyle, all those different things.”
She distinguished between genetics, which she described as a person’s DNA blueprint, and epigenetics, which determines how those genes turn on or off.
“Your DNA is your blueprint. Epigenetics says how those genes turn on or off,” Rogers said.
Environmental exposure plays a role too
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said family health history isn’t only about what’s passed down from parents to children. Environmental exposure during childhood can also affect long-term health.
“Did you grow up with smokers? Did you grow up with somebody that had fried food all the time? Did you grow up in an area where there were chemicals and the pesticides?” O’Rourke said. “What were the other things that you were raised around and with that would also affect your health?”
She said the National Institute on Aging offers a family health history worksheet that can help people begin building a record of their genetic family history, since genetic testing alone may not catch everything.
“People are not familiar with genomics, but these are all the variations that tell you within your blueprint what is your exposure and what is the susceptibility to other things,” Rogers said.
Katherine Ambrose, an aging well coach, said common household and environmental risks include mold, which people are sometimes unaware is present, and radon gas, a naturally occurring radioactive gas. And it is good to test for those.
Lifestyle changes can help offset genetic risk
O’Rourke said while people cannot change their genetic blueprint, they can take steps to reduce risk once they know what they’re predisposed to.
“You can’t change the genetic blueprint, but you can mitigate with a lot of lifestyle, exercise and eating right, and just knowing what you’re at high risk for,” O’Rourke said.
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said knowing a family history of colon cancer or breast cancer, for example, can lead to earlier screening. She also noted that genetic testing is now available for dementia risk.
“If we can circumvent it, then great,” Cradduck said.
A gift for future generations
Ambrose described written family health history as a lasting gift from one generation to the next.
“One of the greatest gifts an older generation can possibly provide to the generations behind them is this knowledge, this written down information that can be accessed when they need it,” she said. “It can be very much more important than an heirloom.”
Resources
Key takeaways
- Family history can reveal disease risk years in advance. Patterns in conditions like heart disease, strokes, cancers, autoimmune disorders, depression and thyroid disease are especially significant, particularly when they occur at an early age.
- Know the difference between “what runs in the family” and “what a relative died from.” These are not always the same thing and confusing them can lead to incomplete health pictures.
- Genetic testing can fill in the gaps, especially for people who are adopted or don’t have access to their full family medical history.
- Environmental exposure during childhood counts too — things like secondhand smoke, diet, pesticides and chemicals in the home can shape long-term health risk alongside genetics.

title: Rubio refuses to address report alleging misconduct by Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle
text:
Rubio refuses to address report alleging misconduct by Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday flatly refused to comment on a new report alleging that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before taking up her post.
Rubio told reporters that he would not discuss the allegations contained in a Wall Street Journal story that said Guilfoyle had asked a donor and supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
He spoke before leaving Greece, where he delivered a speech calling for European countries to return to what he described as their civilizational roots.
Rubio said he was aware of The Wall Street Journal's report, which was published late Wednesday, but had no idea if it was true and he would not address it.
"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," he said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.
At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister on Wednesday, Rubio said he would not address the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but added, "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle, but Rubio would not say if he was prepared to open one.
Congressional Democrats already were looking into claims reported last month by the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle acted improperly while serving as the top U.S. envoy to Greece.
The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing and Rubio has defended her before.

title: Vassalboro wedding venue wins planning board approval
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
VASSALBORO — Keith and Ratesha Rosell have the planning board approval they need to open their Webber Pond Road event center, Rosewood Hills, next spring.
But some think that’s not the end of the opposition to the project, which neighbors say will be loud and disruptive.
After a monthslong review and complaints from neighbors, the planning board spent two hours Tuesday trying to determine if it could impose special conditions on sound regulation to keep the peace.
“I don’t want the neighbors, frankly, calling the town office and saying ‘we have a problem,'” board member Douglas Phillips said.
“That’s what’s going to happen,” board member Paul Mitnik responded. “I can tell you that right now.”
A neighbor sitting among more than a dozen residents at the meeting confirmed this, saying “Yup.”
The town’s site review ordinance requires the venue “not adversely affect the use and
enjoyment of abutting property as a result of noise.” This, per town standards, means sound cannot exceed 55 decibels at the property boundary before 10 p.m., when the venue will close. For reference, 55 decibels is about the volume of a coffee maker brewing or an electric toothbrush.
In September, the planning board asked Code Enforcement Officer Eric Currie to measure the sound levels at the property lines using a decibel meter. The town purchased one, and the Rosells hired a professional DJ and a second code enforcement officer for the test.
Both code enforcement officers found all sound readings below 55 decibels with the speakers aimed directly at the fully open door of the former airplane hangar where the Rosells will host receptions.
At Tuesday’s meeting, Mitnik said he knows from personal experience how much sound can travel through a residential neighborhood, and he didn’t trust the test the planning board requested could give a true picture of how loud events might be.
Neighbors agreed, saying that without the noise of a crowd the test wouldn’t be accurate. But others pointed out that the hangar had no furniture or people to absorb sound, so the noise could have been louder than it would be at a wedding.
Planning board members considered requiring the Rosells to keep the hangar door closed at all times, but ultimately worried how that might impact guests on a hot night. The Rosells said they plan to add insulation to the structure, which the board also considered making a requirement.
Finally, they debated requiring the Rosells to conduct periodic sound tests — which the couple said they already planned to do — but worried how to enforce and regulate such a requirement. Ultimately, the board decided to leave regulation up to the ordinance and to the Rosells.
“I think you have to assume best intent,” board Chair Virginia Brackett said. “They don’t want an event where people are uncomfortable with the sound level.”
The board approved the project on a 4-1 vote, with Mitnik voting no. The Rosells will be required to have no street parking, put signs out during events and comply with its Department of Transportation permit.

title: Acclaimed Western musician to take the stage at Bath’s Winter Street Center
text:
Shinanatu Farm will present Dave Stamey in concert from 7-8:30 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, at the Winter Street Center in Bath. Purchase tickets through the Sagadahoc Preservation website: sagadahocpreservation.org/shop/p/dave-stamey-in-concert.
Stamey is one of the best-known performers in Western music today. The Western Music Association has named him Entertainer of the Year seven times, Male Performer of the Year seven times and Songwriter of the Year five times. He was inducted into the Western Music Hall of Fame in November 2016, and True West Magazine has named him its Best Living Western Solo Musician for four consecutive years.
A Montana native, Stamey worked as a cowboy, mule packer and dude ranch wrangler before turning to music full time. That background shows up in his songwriting, which ranges across the Rocky Mountains, Nevada’s high desert and California’s Pacific Slope, and draws on people and places he actually worked with. Seth Hopkins, director of the Booth Western Art Museum, has called him “perhaps the greatest cowboy balladeer alive today,” and Cowboys and Indians Magazine has described him as “the Charlie Russell of Western music.”
The Saturday show is expected to draw from Stamey’s catalog of fan favorites, including “Buckaroo Man,” “Cowpoke,” “Spin That Pony,” “The Auctioneer,” “Come Ride with Me,” “The Vaquero Song” and “Riding Down the Canyon.”
Shinanatu Farm is a 17.5-acre equestrian property on River Road in Brunswick owned by Kim and Doug Stone. The farm specializes in natural trail riding and horsemanship and is well known for bringing some of the world’s most accomplished Western clinicians to the Midcoast.

title: Lewiston/Auburn affected by potential project delays
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, ME – On Monday September 28, Maine Public Utilities Commission Staff issued a recommended decision denying CMP’s proposed $70 million temporary rate request.
The request is part of the company’s broader rate case currently under review, and any revenues collected through temporary rates would be subject to refund if the Commission ultimately approved a different amount.
This has could have a direct impact on Lewiston and Auburn. There are more than 12,000 customers in the area who receive power from the Deer Rips substation (6,400 customers) and Great Falls substation (6,300 customers).
Both of those substations are planned for upgrades so they can handle more energy, have more capacity to facilitate growth in Auburn and Lewiston and increase reliability for those customers. The Deer Rips substation transformer overloaded on the July 4th holiday weekend due to extreme heat and we had to bring in a mobile transformer that is still in use at that location to keep the power on for those customers. (WMTW toured the Deer Rips substation with the mobile transformer last week: 15,000 Mainers lost power for heat-related issues this summer – WMTW)
Without this rate plan, this work could be deferred causing a delay, including upgrading a Great Falls substation transformer that is more than 50 years old and a Deer Rips Substation transformer that is nearly 50 years old.
In addition to capacity needs in these communities, we are preparing the grid for extreme weather and storms. As noted below in excerpts, CMP has now responded to extreme cold, severe thunderstorms and extreme heat all within a span of roughly nine months.
Central Maine Power (CMP), a subsidiary of Avangrid Inc., reported a record number of heat-related grid events across its 11,000-square-mile service territory as Maine experienced its second-hottest meteorological summer on record.
CMP has proposed upgrades to electrical infrastructure to address capacity and extreme weather challenges. The company has publicly highlighted the need for these upgrades as part of ongoing efforts to strengthen reliability and support growing energy needs. CMP is advancing these solutions to improve reliability, increase system capacity and ensure crews can continue providing safe, reliable service to customers.
“We cannot ignore the reality and challenge in front of us when it comes to the strain that extreme heat is placing on aging components of Maine’s electric grid,” said Linda Ball, President and CEO of Central Maine Power. “We must implement solutions like upgraded substation transformers that are ready to handle the energy demand that comes with extreme heat. We’ve also seen the value of having mobile substations ready to deploy as our crews used these to alleviate equipment that either failed or could have failed on these hottest days.”
High temperatures can increase demand for electricity and place strain on electrical equipment like lines and transformers. CMP grid equipment is designed to operate safely for a limited time above a defined strain threshold. This year, on July 3, prolonged extreme heat on a holiday weekend pushed some of that equipment, like substation transformers in Auburn and in tourism destination Ogunquit, beyond that limit. In several communities, CMP conducted temporary protective outages to prevent damage to critical equipment, an unprecedented measure during periods of extreme heat. Virtually all temporary measures to alleviate demand on these areas of the electric grid were deployed by crews, including the installation of a mobile substation brought to Ogunquit from Augusta with the help of a Maine State Police escort.
CMP’s grid strengthening plans, currently under review by the Maine Public Utilities Commission (MPUC), include replacing two existing transformers at a York County substation with larger units to increase system capacity and backup capability, while upgrading communications technology to support the area’s growing energy needs. CMP’s proposals also include replacing more substation transformers in Cumberland, Franklin, Kennebec, Lincoln, and Penobscot?counties. Additional grid-hardening investments include installing thousands of stronger distribution poles, deploying hundreds of smart devices that enable faster remote restoration, and expanding vegetation management to reduce tree-related outages.
Work to restore power or prevent outages was not limited to teams in the field. CMP Energy Control Center operators and support staff worked around the clock for multiple days, coordinating real-time communications with field personnel and executing critical switching operations to safely manage infrastructure. Previous investments in smart grid technology were instrumental in maintaining service for thousands of customers during periods of extreme demand. This equipment enabled control center operators to find solutions remotely such as shifting how power was flowing on individual lines to alleviate equipment under strain.
CMP’s plans for continued upgrades come as the company reports that approximately 15,000 customers experienced heat-related power interruptions during the summer of 2026. The company anticipates a final decision from the Maine PUC on its proposals subject to the commission’s review and approval.

title: Strike on Ukrainian public buses leaves at least 30 dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv
text:
Strike on Ukrainian public buses leaves at least 30 dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv
A Russian-guided bomb exploded next to public buses filled with passengers in eastern Ukraine, authorities said Thursday, killing 30 people as part of a wave of attacks that also worsened power outages in the capital.
The morning attack occurred next to a bus stop in the war-torn city of Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, prompting public transport to be suspended in the area.
“There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians,” Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the city's military administration, said, adding that the rescue effort had been hampered by subsequent Russian attacks using small drones.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Russia has escalated its aerial attack in recent weeks, putting pressure on Ukraine as it prepares for winter and hitting the infrastructure keeping its war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centers, telecom networks, gas stations and grain exports.
Thursday's attack followed a Russian missile strike a day earlier that killed 22, including five children, in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky. Rescuers were searching the rubble of a residential building. At least 54 people were wounded. Several survivors slept in heavily damaged apartments because they couldn't find anywhere else to stay.
Ukraine appeals for more defense support from NATO
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy traveled to Pryluky on Thursday with visiting British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who announced new sanctions on Russia.
Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries.
“It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine’s defense,” he wrote in an online post. “Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day.”
In audio clips responding to journalist’s questions Thursday evening, Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the U.S. with President Donald Trump’s representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff for two days beginning Friday to discuss strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, among other issues.
Ukraine's energy company DTEK said national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. Regular, rolling outages that occur on a schedule across the country will be halted during these shutdowns.
Officials are urging families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain backup power sources, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks.
Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists defused two unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings. Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said.
Ukrainian attacks damage data center and oil refinery
Russian technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline.
Also Thursday, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.
Ukrainian drones also reached Russia’s Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said most of the drones were shot down by air defenses, but one “reached a northern industrial hub.” He didn’t elaborate. Russian independent news outlet Astra reported that the Omsk oil refinery was on fire after the attack. There was no official confirmation of the report.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his government presented proposals to both Russia and Ukraine aimed at protecting civilian shipping in the Black Sea, while warning that commercial trade and grain exports could be disrupted by escalating military offensives.
Separately, Lithuania deployed about 100 additional soldiers to help secure the NATO member's border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, the Baltic country's defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said. Sandwiched between Lithuania and Poland, Kaliningrad is separated from mainland Russia and remains a major security concern for NATO’s eastern flank.
Associated Press writers Suzan Fraser in Ankara, Turkey; Liudas Dapkus in Vilnius, Lithuania; Derek Gatopoulos in Athens, Greece and Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed.

title: How to eat well in the Maine outdoors
text:
Thanksgiving dinner with gravy and cranberry sauce.
Ramen with foraged mushrooms and green beans.
Corn chowder with seaweed.
Partridge pot pie.
Hot pot.
These meals aren’t from a restaurant or home kitchen. They are on the menus of Registered Maine Guides while they are on trails or in the woods.
“I’ve done everything from Beef Stroganoff to cherry pie,” said Lisa DeHart, of West Gardiner, who has been guiding canoe trips for nearly 30 years.
Camp cooking isn’t just about fun and flavor. A nourishing meal is fuel for a successful adventure, guides said, and safe practices are critical to avoid getting sick in remote places. Experts shared their tips for eating well in the outdoors — whether backpacking or in a campground.
“Things taste better when you’re camping,” said Taylor Boucher, founder and owner of Portage Eats, a new South Portland-based business that makes meal kits for the campsite.
PLAN AHEAD
Candace Sabol of Corinth started cooking at hunting and fishing camps across the state years before she became a guide herself. Sometimes she is working in a lodge, and other times she is cooking in a tent camp without access to electricity or running water.
Preparation is key, she said.
“What comes up with you is what you have for the whole week,” Sabol said.
Chris Toy, a Registered Maine Guide, cooking instructor and cookbook author who lives in Bath, said he often freezes meals, such as shrimp stir fry or chili, for overnight trips to Chimney Pond at Baxter State Park. Not only does that strategy reduce the amount of chopping to be done after a long day of hiking, but he said it also prevents contamination of raw ingredients and reduces the amount of gear to carry up the mountain.
“If you’re not going to be carrying cleavers and cutting boards and ways to clean up, the more you can do at home, the better,” Toy said.
When he is car camping, he still does all the slicing in advance, but more room in the trunk means more equipment. That’s when Toy packs his divided hot pot, which he said is a perfect option for a large group with varied tastes.
“One side could be spicy,” he said. “The other side could be, as I like to joke, wimpy.”
DeHart started a YouTube channel called “3 Minutes with a Maine Guide” in order to archive the skills she learned from her mentors and has used over decades. Many are about camp cooking — how to set up a dishwashing station, how to cook over an open fire, how to choose the right gear, how to make biscuit dough or pie crust in advance.
In a field with so many variables, especially the weather, guides said food is one thing they can control.
“No matter what happens that day on a river for anybody, you can always pull out a day with really good food, and really good food in the middle of nowhere makes a guest feel safe,” DeHart said.
GET CREATIVE WITH CALORIES
Sarah Holman of Portland always checks the nutritional information on her dehydrated meals. She aims for 800 calories for dinner while backpacking and has learned that a package that advertises two servings might really be one.
“I pick snacks that are the highest calorie-to-weight ratio — like nuts,” Holman, who runs a guide service called She Hikes Mountains, said in an email. “They’re heavy, but they provide excellent fat, protein and nutrients.”
Guides make meals that aren’t just about taste. Toy often makes soups for clients, he said, because they offer extra hydration. Holman has recently been adding candied ginger to her almonds in part because it can help settle an upset stomach.
In some cases, guides are sourcing their ingredients on their adventures. Holman said the best ramen she’s ever had was in the woods. She added green beans from her garden and five types of wild mushrooms that she foraged.
Sabol said she doesn’t eat meat except wild game, and often introduces clients to her favorite recipes, such as partridge pot pie.
On Thursdays, Sabol’s camp tradition is to make pizzas with bear heart, barbecue sauce, red onion, mushrooms and jalapenos. Some guests are skeptical, she said, but her recipe wins them over. This week, she planned to use the heart from a bear she shot herself, a milestone she was proud to share with her fellow guides and clients.
“It’s so much more than cooking for people,” Sabol said. “It’s helping people celebrate and share their harvest that they worked so hard for.”
LET SOMEONE ELSE DO THE WORK
Boucher has spent a lot of time thinking about food packaging for the outdoors.
“The packaging really is the most important piece,” she said. “Because you have limited space, and things are being jumbled around.”
When Boucher was planning trips as a Registered Maine Guide, she said she always enjoyed figuring out the food logistics for the group. She now works for the University of Maine and no longer leads trips professionally, but she still wanted to help people figure out those important details.
“My biggest goal is to make it easier for people and help them get outside,” Boucher said.
The meal kits from Portage Eats contain fresh ingredients sourced in Maine and come with instructions for basic cooking. Boucher assembles and distributes the meals at Fork Food Lab in South Portland. She’s about to wrap up her first season and hopes to partner with campgrounds next year to reach more people.
She said her favorites include the seaweed corn chowder and the steak tip kebabs.
Jennifer Scism, who ran a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York and won the TV show “Iron Chef,” said her Kittery-based business Good To-Go started in part because she was experimenting with her tabletop dehydrator and her favorite comfort foods.
Good To-Go can be found in stores nationwide. Most meals only need a little hot water.
Scism said her favorite is the chicken pho. The staff sets aside a bulk bin for her so she can eat it multiple times a week without wasting single-serve packaging, she said.
“No matter what kind of adventure you’re on, whether you’re summiting Katahdin or taking a leisurely walk through the woods,” Scism wrote in an email, “your meal should be something you genuinely look forward to at the end of the day.”

title: Portland Hearts of Pine eliminated from USL1 playoff chase
text:
The Portland Hearts of Pine are officially eliminated from USL League One playoff contention.
Eight teams in the 17-team league will advance to the quarterfinal round. Wednesday night in Texas, eighth-place Fort Wayne FC beat Corpus Christi, 3-1, to improve to 11-9-9, good for 42 points. Portland (7-12-10) has 31 points with three matches remaining. Even if the Hearts won three straight — something they have not done all season — their maximum point total would be 40.
Portland has been well below the playoff line for most of the season and is 14th in the league standings. In the franchise’s inaugural 2025 season, Portland finished seventh and came within a penalty kick shootout loss of reaching the final.
This season, Portland has been undone by its inability to close out games.
Portland has blown a lead in 10 USL1 matches, mostly because of nine conceded goals in the 90th minute or extra time. Six times Portland settled for a tie. Four times it gave up a second goal and lost. Add in a 2-1 home loss to Chattanooga when they had tied the game with a second-half goal before allowing the winner in the 90th minute, and the Hearts have squandered 25 potential points.
Portland has four comebacks of its own (two ties, two wins), including a 3-3 tie Saturday at Spokane, when it trailed 3-1.
Portland has continued to play in front of packed crowds even in inclement weather. It has averaged 6,234 fans per match at Fitzpatrick Stadium where it is 5-6-3 in league play.
Portland hosts Athletic Club Boise (14-8-7) at 5 p.m. Saturday. Boise, which has announced it will play in USL Championship next season, is in fifth place with a chance to reach the top four and earn a home quarterfinal game. Portland is at third-place Forward Madison (15-7-7) on Oct. 17 and concludes its season Oct. 24, hosting Charlotte Independence (18-5-6), which is one point out of first place.

title: Maine’s Jessica Meir, 3 other astronauts return to Earth
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — Maine’s Jessica Meir and three other astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the American, French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
Meir and her NASA colleague Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
“We are so excited to be back on planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down.
While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”
Meir, who is from Caribou, was on her second trip to the space station. Her previous mission, in 2019, lasted 205 days and featured the first all-female spacewalk.
This time, she and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA’s Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA’s first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
Meir’s seventh career spacewalk, on Sept. 1, moved her into third place for total spacewalks by women at NASA and brought her career spacewalk time to more than 49 hours.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef’s toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA’s count.
Meir has been an astronaut since 2013 and was the first Maine woman to travel to space. After graduating as valedictorian from Caribou High School, she studied biology at Brown University. She then earned a master’s degree from the International Space University in France and a doctorate in marine biology from Scripps Institution of Oceanography in San Diego.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: Parents plead to reunite twin baby girls being treated in NICUs at 2 separate hospitals
text:
Parents plead to reunite twin baby girls being treated in NICUs at 2 separate hospitals
A Massachusetts family is facing emotional and logistical challenges as their newborn twins receive care at separate hospitals during a nurses' strike, with local lawmakers stepping in to assist.
The twins, Kendall and Juliette, each weighing just over 2 pounds, are undergoing critical care after major surgeries.
Kendall is at Boston Children’s Hospital following spina bifida surgery, while her sister, Juliette, was transferred to Brigham and Women’s Hospital after heart valve surgery. Their mother is delivering breast milk to both hospitals, while their father described the toll the situation has taken on their family.
"My wife is, she's unbelievably strong, and it's taking a toll on her," dad Michael Kennedy said.
The hospitals are about a half of a mile apart.
The family has also experienced the daily challenges of the neonatal intensive care unit, or NICU.
"We've had days where she [Juliette] pulls tubes out, emergency buttons are hit. A bunch of people have run into the room and got her back," Kennedy said. "And throughout that whole time, my wife was sitting there not knowing what's going to happen to our baby. There was a nurse right there helping us through all of it."
With two older children, 11-month-old Callan and 3-year-old Aurora, to care for at home, the stress of the situation has been overwhelming. The looming nurses strike has added to their concerns.
In a statement, Brigham and Women’s Hospital said, "Decisions regarding transfers are based on multiple factors, including a baby's medical condition and stability, clinical needs, parental wishes, and bed availability."
The parents are seeking help as they navigate this difficult time.
"I received an email from Representative Bill Galvin and also Senator Feeney, and they are trying to help us with this transition, but they know that the strike is coming and they know the severity of that," Kennedy said.

title: Isaias becomes the first hurricane of the Atlantic season as it surges towards US Gulf Coast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Isaias surged towards the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday after strengthening into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, the National Hurricane Center said, prompting mandatory evacuations and school closures in some coastal areas of Florida.
Forecasters warned Isaias could bring damaging hurricane-force winds to parts of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, while also potentially causing a life-threatening storm surge along areas of the northern Gulf Coast. It could also bring heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) across the central Gulf Coast, according to the hurricane center.
The center of the cyclone was about 460 miles (740 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River’s mouth, with maximum sustained winds around 75 mph (121 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center.
After the storm initially formed earlier Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening. Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.
The National Weather Service told communities from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Gulf County, Florida, to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages.”
The hurricane formed late in the season
Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, nearly tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.
Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday about 25% of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
In Alabama, the cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.
Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground. Her family planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta, Collins from Hartford, Connecticut and Golden from Seattle. Associated Press journalists Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia and Julie Walker in New York contributed to this report.

title: Federal government looking to crack down on headlight glare in effort to make driving safer
text:
(NHTSA/Gray News) - The government is updating its standards for LED headlights and other standards related to driver safety.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) made the announcement on Oct. 6. According to the agency, it will consult safety advocates, technical experts, and industry stakeholders to make changes in the following areas:
- Addressing Headlight Glare: Examining the role that modern headlighting technology has on glare for other road users and making appropriate changes
- Modernizing Lighting Technology: Improving rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams, and replaceable light sources
- Improving Performance: Evaluating how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility
- Updating Testing & Materials: Streamlining test procedures for plastic optics and replaceable lenses
- Aligning Global Standards: Harmonizing U.S. vehicle lighting regulations with international safety standards
NHTSA stated this will be the first time in more than 25 years that it will use negotiated rulemaking for vehicle lighting standards.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will appoint up to 18 stakeholders, according to the agency.
NHTSA is asking for the public’s feedback and membership nominations, both of which need to be submitted by Nov. 9.
To leave a comment or nominate someone for membership, visit regulations.gov for docket number NHTSA-2026-1981.

title: In Augusta, the Mill Park Pétanque Club teaches its game to a new generation
text:
AUGUSTA — Eric Ayotte picked up the nuances of pétanque quickly. A golfer, the Mattanawcook Academy junior studied the way the ball spun and broke on the crushed stone court the way he studies a green before a putt.
Where do I want to toss this ball so it not only ends up closest to the cochonet, the smaller target ball, but also prevents my opponents from getting a clean shot? Where’s the break? Is there a divot in the stone that will mess everything up?
“You really have to think about your shot. There’s a lot of moving parts,” Ayotte said between games Thursday morning at Augusta’s Mill Park. “It would be sick to get one of these in Lincoln.”
That’s exactly the kind of thing Raymond Fecteau wants to hear. He calls pétanque, “the best game nobody’s heard of,” and he’s trying to change that.
Fecteau, 82, is one of the founders of the Mill Park Pétanque Club. Since he retired from his career as a barber 17 years ago, Fecteau’s goal has been to play pétanque as much as possible, and pass the game on to anyone who wants to learn how to play.
“What I like best is teaching kids how to do it,” he said, “but we don’t get a lot of kids.”
On this overcast Thursday morning, with the trees along the nearby Kennebec River hitting their fall color peak, that meant giving a lesson to 16 students from a Mattanawcook French class who made the 250-mile round trip from Lincoln.
This was the second time French teacher Melanie Turner brought one of her classes to Augusta for a day of pétanque. It’s a chance for the students to learn a game they can play the rest of their lives, as well as find a touchstone to the Franco culture many of them share, Turner said.
“I think it’s important for them to make that connection,” she said. “I’d like to see if we can bring it back to Lincoln.”
Pétanque’s rules are easy to learn. Standing inside a ring, players try to get their balls closest to the cochonet. The balls are hollow and metal, about the size of a baseball, the perfect size to fit into your palm.
“I think it’s pretty fun,” Gracie Averill, a Mattanawcook junior, said an hour after playing the game for the first time. “We do get competitive. It’s just a fun game that’s not too strenuous.”
At Mill Park, the club has 10 courts, and lighting to play in the evening. Right around the time he retired, Fecteau learned the game on a trip to France. He bought a set of balls and played where he could, introducing friends to the game.
With enough people looking for a place to enjoy a few rounds of pétanque, Fecteau and the club approached the city of Augusta and asked for a space to build courts. The club raised $50,000, and the courts at Mill Park were the result.
The Mill Park Pétanque Club currently has 71 members, Fecteau said. The membership skews older. Seniors come during the day to play. As Fecteau and a handful of club members taught the students, a group of senior women played their weekly games on one of the courts.
Last year, Fecteau had open heart surgery. He thought maybe his pétanque playing days were over. After a couple months of rest of rehab, he was back on the courts. Dan Howard took over as club president, taking a little off Fecteau’s plate.
Teaching the game to younger players, passing the game along, is important.
“I think the baby of our crowd is around 47,” Fecteau said, “but see, these people, they take to it.”
Fecteau pointed to Ayotte and three of his classmates getting instruction from club member Gary Golden. They studied the lay of the court before making their throws. They cheered when somebody made a good throw. He pointed to a court where Howard coached another group of students. The same thing was happening there.
“In the time they’ve been here, you see how much progress they’ve made. It’s satisfying,” Fecteau said.
Fecteau smiled. When you pass on something you love, satisfying isn’t a strong enough description.

title: Brooks woman arrested after months-long drug trafficking investigation
text:
BROOKS, Maine (WABI) - A woman from Brooks is behind bars after officials say she turned over cocaine and fentanyl.

No drugs were found in the vehicle but Brown told authorities that she had drugs on her, officials said.
