title: ‘Genocide’ or not, US must seek an end to the suffering in Gaza
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
Israel’s continuing attacks on Gaza roiled Maine’s U.S. Senate race last week, as Democratic nominee Troy Jackson apologized for remarks he made in a TV interview. He said it was “unfortunate” that there are “people here in Maine that don’t like that term” — genocide — “only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
Like “racism” and “imperialism,” the term “genocide” has become more a weapon used to batter political opponents than anything descriptive of the facts or the truth. It was indeed unfortunate that Jackson indulged his knack for plain-speaking over carefully approaching an issue that, in American as in world politics, has become a powder keg.
As we often do, we’re debating the wrong question. What Israel, led by its longtime leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done in response to the horrific attack by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, has long since degenerated into a campaign of retribution, without any coherent military or political strategy.
Through three long years, Israel has destroyed most of Gaza’s infrastructure, repeatedly put its people to flight and brought the populace to the edge of famine without really settling anything. Some 1,200 Israelis lost their lives on Oct. 7. Since then, an estimated 70,000 Palestinians have died. Depending on your definition of genocide, this may or may not qualify, but surely Israel’s response has been utterly disproportionate, and has gotten us nowhere near a future for the Palestinians that doesn’t produce destitution and endless suffering.
Normally, in a democracy like Israel, these issues would be settled by elections, but that may not be the case here. Just a week before our midterm elections, Israeli voters will choose a new government on Oct. 27, implicitly the first referendum on Netanyahu’s preparedness, or lack of it, for the Oct. 7 attacks — and the absence of any coherent plan for Gaza’s future. We must also recall that Israel withdrew from Gaza in 2005, removing settlers and leaving the power vacuum that Hamas ended up filling.
Americans often complain about our two-party system, but Israel struggles with too many parties, which come and go with each election, often built around a particular political figure. A party with as little as 3.5% of the vote can be represented in the 120-member Knesset, and throughout Netanyahu’s record tenure, serving almost continuously since 2009, his party has never held a majority.
In recent years, Netanyahu’s centrist allies spurned him, forcing him to rely more and more on Orthodox religious parties, which see all the territory now held by Israel as its by right. In reality, the West Bank and Gaza have been, since 1967, Israeli-occupied territories. They also represent the only homeland Palestinians will ever have.
The coalitions of both Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former defense chief, who represents the largest opposition party, are both short of a majority, meaning a half dozen small parties may be needed to form a government. Whether the 2026 election is any more decisive than previous ones isn’t yet known, but if Netanyahu is finally ousted, the atmosphere, if not policies, could shift.
None of Israel’s leading parties favor anything approaching reconciliation with the roughly equal numbers of Palestinians under Israeli rule, let alone negotiations for a two-state solution. Yet suffering in Gaza could be ameliorated, primarily through a U.N. peacekeeping force overseeing restoration of public services while Israel withdraws its troops.
Donald Trump has again done this country a grave disservice by throwing in his lot with Netanyahu’s vainglorious military schemes that imagine Israel subduing Iran. He followed Israel’s lead by bombing suspected nuclear enrichment facilities in June 2025, then launched “Operation Epic Fury” on Feb. 28, which seems to have petered out, despite occasional Trumpian threats of “annihilation.”
Regardless, Congress has a responsibility to bring Trump back to reality, and ensure the U.S. cuts support for Israel’s continuing attacks. Much of the weaponry used in Gaza represents American military aid.
On this issue, Troy Jackson said the U.S. should stop sending “blank checks” to Israel, an entirely sensible idea. Sen. Angus King, no radical, said essentially the same thing months ago, vowing to oppose any further military aid.
We should recognize that nothing Americans do will greatly shape the future of Gaza. Israel, unfortunately, is in control. Demonstrations on college campus won’t make much difference, nor will debating the word “genocide.”
Yet we can stop enabling the excesses of an important ally in the Middle East. We can, as Trump has not, make it clear there are limits — and firmly establish that criticism of Israel’s current government does not equate to antisemitism.

title: Cooper Flagg Pays Tribute to Maine With New Signature Logo
text:

The Newport native and Dallas Mavericks star has just unveiled his new signature logo, giving a nod to his Maine roots.

title: Llewellyn Estes Bridge Removal Work Starts Tuesday, Temporary Crossing Closes For Demolition
text:
Closures Ahead For Temporary Bridge In Old Town; Clean Up Of Collapsed “Llewellyn Estes” Bridge To Begin
It's been two months since the Llewellyn Estes Bridge in Old Town partially collapsed into the water as crews worked to replace it.
The Maine DOT, which has been investigating the bridge failure since it fell as workers began pouring concrete on the deck on August 13th, is now ready to begin removing the collapsed sections of the structure.
How Will The Cleanup Take Place?
To safely remove the debris from the collapse, contractors with Reed & Reed, along with folks from the Maine DOT, will have to close down the temporary bridge for a short while throughout the next two weeks. The temporary bridge was constructed so that motorists could travel along Stillwater Avenue over the river while the original bridge was being replaced.
According to ME DOT officials, the closure is necessary due to how close these two bridges are to one another, and because of the large equipment that will need to be brought in to remove the broken sections, one part at a time.
"Closure timing will depend on demolition operations, construction progress, weather conditions, and other site-specific factors...The work will include crews carefully separating the span from the pier and abutment, reducing it into smaller pieces, and lifting those pieces from the river for processing on land. This work will proceed slowly and carefully to protect workers and the public while minimizing damage to the pier and abutment."
When Will The Bridge Be Closed?
Officials say that the closures will begin Tuesday, October 13th between the hours of 9 AM and 3 PM. It will happen, they say, intermittently throughout that week, and they estimate the work could lead into the next week as well.
What Will Drivers Do When Llewellyn Estes Temporary Bridge Is Closed?
With plenty of messaging via message boards in the vicinity, motorists will be guided along a familiar detour (this is the same one that's been used in former instances when the bridge has been closed).
This will take them up Bennoch Road to North Main Street and connect them with College Ave in Orono, which will hook back up with Stillwater, just past the bridge. The detour does add about an extra 10 minutes max to that drive, so folks should plan accordingly.
Read More: Maine Musician Writes Song About Stillwater Bridge Collapse
Maine DOT officials say they hope that if the weather, the demolition and deconstruction efforts all line up, and no other major challenges arise, the temporary bridge will reopen to a regular traffic pattern by the end of the week of October 19th.

title: Susan Collins does, in fact, answer the call
text:
Letter writer Earle Wingate of Peru recently asserted that he has written to Sen. Susan Collins “for more than eight years” and that he has “never” received a response from her. (“Country over party means time’s up for Susan Collins,” Sept. 30).
It is true that Wingate has written to the senator many times, but it is false that he has never received a reply to his correspondence.
Our office last received an email from Wingate on Jan. 28, 2025, urging Sen. Collins to oppose the confirmation of certain executive branch nominees.
Wingate received a written response from Collins informing him of her decision to oppose Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel to their nominated positions. Over the past eight years, Wingate has received seven responses to his messages, writing on topics including the following: support for Ukraine (she does), support for convicting Donald Trump during his impeachment trial (she did), opposition to withdrawing U.S. troops from Syria (she did), opposition to the 2019 partial government shutdown (she led the work to end it) and a message approving of her vote to confirm Justice Kavanaugh. Other messages to Collins from Wingate indicated that he did not wish to receive a response.
The truth is that Sen. Collins welcomes hearing from Mr. Wingate and all Mainers and our office strives to respond quickly. We also believe readers deserve an accurate account of the facts.
Katie Brown
Chief of Staff, Sen. Collins
Washington, D.C.

title: What a shot! Maine high school student kicks a full-court basket
text:
What a shot! Maine high school student kicks a full-court basket
Kickball is popular on playgrounds and in phys ed classes. A student at Mt. Abram High School in Strong just did something in her class that could get her the attention of ESPN SportsCenter.
During a game of kickball in the gym during phys ed class, Lydia Lojas was the batter and kicked from home plate at one corner of the basketball court - and the ball went off the backboard and through the hoop at the far end, more than 80 feet away.
In video shared by Mt. Abram Athletics, several people could be seen celebrating and cheering for the incredible shot.

title: Barack Obama boosts Troy Jackson in Maine Senate race against Susan Collins
text:

On Thursday, the Democrat’s campaign released video of the former president urging voters to pick Jackson, a former state Senate president.
Obama, speaking directly to the camera while sitting in a chair, said he’s “proud to be on board” as a Jackson supporter, citing the candidate’s prior work as a logger and a political leader.
“In this economy, we need a fighter like Troy,” Obama said. “A fifth-generation logger, Troy worked 80 hours a week and still struggled to get by. So as Maine’s Senate president, he fought to raise wages, lower the cost of prescription drugs and provide free lunch to every student in the state. After Roe was overturned, Troy helped protect the right to an abortion in Maine.”
“And now we need Troy to deliver for us in the Senate,” Obama continued. “So do not sit this one out. Get out there and vote for Troy Jackson.”
The 50-second video is one of about two dozen Obama has recorded in key battleground races for U.S. Senate and governor. Politico reported that Obama — arguably the most prominent spokesperson for the Democratic party — is targeting races where he can “move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters, particularly in states with key races.”
The video seeks to consolidate moderate Democrats and independent voters behind Jackson by focusing on economic issues.

“The momentum we’re seeing in Maine is something I’ve never seen before,” Jackson said. “Working people are sick and tired of a government that works for the wealthy and well-connected while they struggle to get by. They’re ready for change, and together, we’re going to bring that change to Washington.”

title: Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from green card program, alleging fraud
text:
Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from green card program, alleging fraud
President Donald Trump's administration is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using H-1B visas as it accuses the company of fraud.
Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like the one Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans.
In a wide-ranging announcement Thursday, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms.
The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies.
Vance says US workers are replaced with ‘foreign indentured servants’
Vance said that the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft."
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, near Seattle, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. "Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers."
Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position.
H-1B program has been scrutinized
The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
Trump also has targeted foreign students
The Vance announcement came a day after Trump's administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practical Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.
Vance also called out universities that he suggested were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT. The universities did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Trump says US will not resume military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections
text:
Trump says US will not resume military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections
President Donald Trump said Thursday that he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States.
Trump, while stumping for Republicans this week, has hinted that he was confident that an endgame to the war could come in the days before or after the election, while also hinting that he remained open to resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has been threatening that a post-midterm election escalation in the seven-month-old war remains a viable option, despite his initial promises to Americans of a military campaign that would last a matter of weeks.
But Trump in a social media post on Thursday said the U.S. “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”
Trump added that his team has been “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
The U.S. and Iran signed a short-lived interim agreement in June, intended to establish a 60-day ceasefire and framework for a permanent peace deal.
The deal signed by Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian collapsed within weeks amid renewed military actions and disputes over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical water that one-fifth world's oil flowed through before the war.
Negotiations had appeared at a standstill since Trump late last month publicly rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the strait within seven days if the U.S. met certain conditions.
Iran, however, said last week they had received a U.S. counterproposal. And Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi earlier on Thursday said he expected Tehran would offer a formal reply within days.
Trump on Wednesday during a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, said that his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, has continued indirect negotiations with Iranian officials.
But at the same time, Trump suggested he had mixed feelings about ending the war at this point.
“I think the deal isn’t really something that I want to do, but they’re willing to offer us anything to stop,” Trump said.
Trump believes that the U.S. is gaining leverage as the U.S. military is having greater success in helping oil tankers traverse the Strait of Hormuz and get Gulf allies’ oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.
Iran has lost its near chokehold over oil flows through the vital waterway with U.S. Central Command shepherding oil tankers through the strait at night with their location systems turned off.
That, with the help of Gulf pipelines that skirt the strait, has allowed Gulf countries to export oil at nearly prewar levels.
But Iran has ramped up attacks on tankers passing through the strait in recent days. And overall, ship traffic remains well below prewar levels, as are shipments of liquid natural gas and fuel products.
Tanker operators willing to risk running the gauntlet under Central Command’s protection are in some cases charging rates of $1 million a day or more, shipping analysts say.
The situation has become further complicated as Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government have launched a military campaign aimed at driving Iran-backed Houthi rebels from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another critical Mideast trade route for oil and other goods. The Houthis, in turn, are targeting Saudi airports and key infrastructure in the kingdom with drone and missile strikes.
Trump's post comes as the military has dispatched more resources to the region. U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could arrive as early as the end of October.
Trump’s announcement was made the same day the USS Abraham Lincoln was due to arrive to its home port in San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war. There have been reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
The USS George Washington, which is usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August. The other aircraft carrier in the Middle East, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

title: Man with a gun fatally shot by security at Nashville federal courthouse, police say
text:
Man with a gun fatally shot by security at Nashville federal courthouse, police say
A man armed with a pistol and knife was fatally shot by a security officer Thursday just inside the busy entrance of a federal courthouse in Tennessee’s largest city, authorities said.
The man in his 40s tried to fire his gun but failed and then pulled out a knife at around 9:30 a.m., said Don Aaron, spokesperson for Metro Nashville Police.
“The security individual fired on the armed individual,” Aaron said, adding that the man was taken to a hospital where he was pronounced dead.
The man was from out of state. Investigators didn't immediately know why he was at the courthouse, and a search of his car found “nothing threatening,” Aaron said.
Courthouse visitors must go through a security checkpoint, which is common at all federal courts. The entrances are typically staffed by armed former police officers contracted by the U.S. Marshals Service.
“That’s the entrance that most people in this courthouse use," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Rob McGuire told reporters outside.
The library next door was closed as a result, and officers with dogs were circling the perimeter while workers in nearby buildings gathered to watch.
McGuire noted that the local U.S. Attorney's Office is inside the courthouse, as are the offices of Tennessee's U.S. senators.
There have been “security instances where a person acts up or acts inappropriately and has to be removed from the premises, but nothing even approaching this kind of situation,” he said.
Reports of the shooting immediately stirred anxiety and concern.
“People are calling their families to let them know they're OK,” McGuire said. “I called my wife, called my son, called people that I knew were wanting to know if I was OK. We're all doing that.”

title: He retired as a town manager 13 years ago. He keeps coming back to guide towns in crisis.
text:
At least three days a week before the sun rises, Dan Foster pulls out of his driveway in Fort Fairfield and makes the hour-and-20-minute trek north to Madawaska, where he is — for the moment — the town manager.
Foster spent a good portion of his career in municipal government. He was Fort Fairfield’s town manager for 15 years beginning in 1998. When he retired in 2013, he never thought he would return to the job.
But inexplicably, at 75 years old, here he is. Foster was hired in mid-September as the interim manager of the Canadian border town that has been in turmoil for the last month as its Select Board works to fire the town’s full-time manager over financial transgressions, among other controversies.
It’s not the first crisis Foster has navigated. In fact, it’s the fourth time he’s been an interim manager in the last four years.
“My brother goes, ‘You’re going to do this again? Seriously?’” Foster said in an interview Wednesday.
In an era where political polarization has permeated every level of Maine politics, town managers — who are unelected nonpartisan public servants — have been pulled into the fray. Foster has acted as a single-man bullpen for communities in need of a stopgap.
“I really enjoy the challenges of problem solving, of working with the department heads, with the employees, with the board, with community members. I find it energizing,” he said. “At 75, it gives me purpose. And that’s pretty cool.”
To the world of municipal managers, Foster is Dennis Eckersley, a successful starting pitcher who became a dominant reliever in the later stages of his career.
When he stepped back onto the mound in 2022, it was to help Fort Fairfield out of a bases-loaded, no-outs jam. The town faced more than $1.2 million in short-term debt and had less than $200,000 in the bank. Property taxes had increased by an average of 36% and threatened to climb higher.
Over more than a year, he guided Fort Fairfield out of the red. The town made drastic, “painful” budget cuts to its library, parks and recreation department, and EMS services — a source of the debt. But at the end of the 2022-23 fiscal year, it reached a budget surplus, an audit found.
“Dan really kind of took on the crisis and made it so that it didn’t feel like everything was absolutely on fire,” said Timothy Goff, a former Fort Fairfield town manager who was both preceded and succeeded by Foster. “I think that was really the key for me transitioning into that role.”
Six months after Foster stepped aside in Fort Fairfield, Madawaska’s Select Board was looking for an interim leader. The town’s manager, and a selectman, had resigned in quick succession following tumult over pay for public works employees and an ensuing staffing crisis. Their solution? Foster.
“We owe a lot of credit [to] Mr. Dan Foster over here for taking Madawaska under his wings and doing so much,” former Select Board Chair Jason Boucher said at a meeting five months later, after the town hired a permanent manager. “Dan came here, and it wasn’t just to fill a seat. It wasn’t just to help us along. Dan came here and he took Madawaska personally.”
Early last year, Goff resigned as Fort Fairfield’s manager. The town again hired Foster, who worked in the interim from March to June of 2025. He went back to his retired life on Monson Pond, a quiet neighborhood in southern Fort Fairfield that he calls “the most amazing place.”
That lasted more than a year. But this fall, Madawaska needed him for a second stint, and Foster heeded the call.
“I really thought that, ‘You know, Foster, maybe it’s time to frickin’ slow down. I mean, you’re really getting up there in age,’” Foster said of himself. “But I couldn’t say no to Madawaska. I just couldn’t.”
Foster, who owned a furniture store and worked as commercial loan officer, among other careers, didn’t enter government until he was 47, but said he felt like he was “made for” the job of town manager.
“To me, it’s never about how much I know. It is, ‘Who do I know that knows, and do I have the brains to go to somebody who has the expertise and take their damn advice,’” Foster said.
In an interim role, that principle remains the same, albeit with a slightly different focus.
“I’m not here to set policy or to look at long-term goals and objectives for the community,” Foster “I’m here to maintain the status quo, keep things running smoothly.”
He is cognizant of the vitriolic political climate that has caused some of Maine’s manager turnover, but the partisanship doesn’t get to him. As Goff put it, “Dan’s got pretty tough skin.”
Foster stays off social media, he said. And as an interim manager, he’s willing to wade into difficult issues that may create residual fallout for himself, in order to set up the next permanent manager in a better position.
“I have never found it that emotionally wearing on me as a person,” Foster said. “I’ve had people mad to hell at me. It’s OK. It doesn’t impact me that way … even taking into consideration how contentious the world is, my experience dealing with people one-on-one is fine.
“I find the vast majority of the people good people. They’re just trying to get by, and we have so many things coming at us, from so many different directions.”
Foster enjoys his retired life. But he also appreciates coming out of the bullpen from time to time to fill an increasingly challenging public service role. He’s even OK with ridiculous baseball analogies. “Just don’t compare me to [Bill] Buckner,” he said.
“I don’t know how much longer it’s going to be before I’m over in Riverside Cemetery,” Foster said. “But in the meantime, I want to enjoy every single waking moment that I have.”

title: Gov. Ron DeSantis calls name of Hurricane Isaias ‘weird.’ This is what he’s going to call it instead
text:
(Gray News) - Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the name of Hurricane Isaias “not normal.”
Isaias, which is pronounced “ee-sah-EE-ahs,” is the Spanish form of the name Isaiah.
“I don’t know how to pronounce this, because it’s not normal,” DeSantis said. “I’m calling it Isaiah. You guys can call it what you want. I know that’s not how you pronounce this, it’s something else but it’s weird and I’m just going to keep butchering it for the next 72 hours. And I’d rather just be that — so I’m calling it Isaiah.”
DeSantis made the comments during a news conference about a Florida appeals court tossing parts of a grand jury report on alleged misuse of taxpayer money surrounding Hope Florida.
Hurricane Isaias is continuing to strengthen in the Gulf after becoming the first Atlantic hurricane of the season.
The storm is forecast to make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast later this week as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane.

title: Watch tonight’s high stakes debates for governor, senate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The candidates running in Maine’s two highest profile races are debating tonight, back-to-back.
First, at 7 p.m., the candidates for governor — Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and Independent Rick Bennett — will meet in Bangor for a debate hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public, and NEWSCENTER Maine.
Then, at 8 p.m., Senate candidates Troy Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins will square off in their second debate in three days on WMTW.
We will stream both debates, back-to-back, right here — along with live updates starting at 6:30.
We’ll see you there.
And just like that, it’s over!
Thanks so much for following along with us tonight. It was a marathon double debate session. See you at the next one.
-Kirby Wilson
-Both candidates essentially said they don’t use artificial intelligence for major daily tasks
-The candidates said they disagree on term limits for senators and Supreme Court justices. (Jackson is in favor of both, Collins is opposed to both.)
-Kirby Wilson
Collins countered by saying appropriations doesn’t have jurisdiction over tariffs, but she’s working with the Trump administration to try to get some of them lifted.
-Drew Johnson
Collins said ICE does need reforms, including restrictions on where the agency should conduct arrests. But she said the agency shouldn’t be abolished. A similar exchange happened last debate as well.
-Kirby Wilson
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better, hers has gotten worse.”
“She’s made sure that, I think she’s put 55 anti-abortion judges onto the courts, including Brett Kavanaugh, that she knew that he was anti-abortion and that was what he was going to do when he got there, and he did.” Jackson continued.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
“When Donald Trump wants something, Sen. Collins will not stop him,” he said.
-Kirby Wilson
The candidates agree on something!
Jackson and Collins agree that high earners should pay a greater share of their income to Social Security. This may be the first moment of agreement all night.
-Kirby Wilson
This is another familiar theme: Collins says Jackson and Augusta leaders are to blame for Maine’s cost-of-living woes. Jackson says D.C. politicians and Collins are.
-Drew Johnson
Collins shot back that policies that Jackson advocated for have caused premiums to spike in Maine.
-Kirby Wilson
“To say that my husband and I are making money off the war in Iran is absolutely outrageous,” Collins said.
This was one of the most striking moments of the debate so far.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
“I have been the leading proponent” of the program in Congress, argued Collins, and said they could expand the program.
Collins also emphasized that “we have a supply problem” and that the United States needs to become “energy independent.”
-Drew Johnson
“People are going to freeze to death this winter because they can’t afford to heat their home,” Jackson said.
-Kirby Wilson
“He’s in jail today, where he belongs,” Collins said.
Jackson insisted the allegations aren’t false, before turning to what he said was Collins’ proximity to Donald Trump, who he emphasized is “a convicted felon.”
-Drew Johnson
Collins keeps it much more positive, noting some of her signature legislative accomplishments, and saying they came because of her seniority and her connections.
-Kirby Wilson
The Senate debate is underway!
We don’t have a moment to rest. It’s time for Troy Jackson vs. Susan Collins, round two.
Bennett and Pingree played their closing statements much straighter, asking viewers for their vote.
-Kirby Wilson
Charles said he opposed late-term abortions but attempted to sidestep the question somewhat, saying “there are a ton of issues that are confronting us” and that “this is not the number one issue.” When pressed for an answer, he again said he opposes late-term abortions.
“There is only one Bobby Charles, and he is perfectly consistent,” Charles said, noting that he’s long been critical of Trump’s Canada tariffs, for example.
Then he pivoted to criticizing Pingree some more. He’s staying on the attack.
-Kirby Wilson
Bennett on why he left the GOP
When asked why he left the Republican party to run as an independent, Bennet said he once believed that parties were “a vehicle for participation” in the political process, but that is no longer the case.
“Both parties are more interested in keeping us fighting with each other than actually resolving issues,” Bennett said.
“Hannah talks more about Trump than Trump talks about himself,” Charles said.
-Kirby Wilson
A $1 billion budget shortfall?
This part of the night could make news: What are the candidates’ plans to fight the state’s potential $1 billion budget shortfall? Not sure we’ve heard from the candidates on this point.
-Kirby Wilson
Charles said he does not support the expansion.
“I would say we made a fundamental error,” Charles said of expanding MaineCare, noting that able-bodied Mainers are taking advantage of the program, which has become underfunded.
-Kirby Wilson
“I would argue that Biddeford probably wouldn’t have had happened if the sanctuary state law didn’t exist here, because the comms, they were sidelined. The comms between local and state and feds would have been clear,” Charles said.
-Kirby Wilson and Drew Johnson
He argued that “Biddeford probably wouldn’t have had happened” if the various law enforcement agencies involved if there were better lines of communication.
-Drew Johnson
The candidates start with substance
Quite a substantive start, so far! Bad times for those who want to see name calling.
-Kirby Wilson
Among other priorities, Pingree said DEP permits should get a 90-day “shot clock,” noting that Maine needs to incentivize more housing on the supply side. She plugged her housing plan, which you can find here.
And Bennett said the state should reduce down payments for first time home buyers. He also said the state should assist with mortgage payments.
He addressed the supply side challenges of housing as well, arguing the state should increase factory-build housing.
-Kirby Wilson
And we’re off!
The gubernatorial debate has started. This debate is brought to you by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine.
-Kirby Wilson

title: Atlantic hurricanes starting with ‘I’ typically bring death and destruction. Here’s why
text:
(AP) - Be wary of hurricanes that start with the letter “I.”
The ninth letter of the alphabet leads all others in the number of named Atlantic storms that have been retired over the decades due to their destruction or high death tolls. The names may be out of circulation, but storms including Ian, Ida, Igor, Ike, Inez, Ingrid, Iota, Irene, Irma, Isabel and Ivan left lasting legacies.
Next up is Isaias, which became the first hurricane of the Atlantic season on Wednesday night. Whether it lives up to the misery of others whose first letter it shares remains to be seen. The latest forecast suggested Isaias could be less dramatic, but still “extremely dangerous.”
“It’s the ‘I’ storm, which usually we have a lot earlier in the year,” said Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of atmospheric and environmental sciences at the University at Albany. “It’s always the ‘I’ storms that seem to cause problems.”
Isaias was expected to make landfall on the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
Atlantic hurricanes have been given names since 1953, and 100 of them are no longer used. There have been 14 storms with “I” names retired, including 12 this century. When eastern and central Pacific hurricanes are considered, that retired “I” list grows to 20.
Ten Atlantic storm names starting with “F” have been retired, followed by “C” with nine, and “D” and “M” with eight apiece, according to a list compiled by the hurricane center.
Why I is such a foreboding letter
Hurricanes starting with “I” typically occur in the middle of the June 1-Nov. 30 season, when warming ocean waters can supercharge a storm’s energy.
The timing of Isaias is an exception to this trend, due to the current super El Niño weather pattern, which stunted Atlantic hurricane formations through September while cranking out storms throughout the Pacific region.
Isaias came one day shy of tying a 121-year-old record for the latest-forming initial hurricane of the Atlantic season.
‘I’ storms prove to be costly
Of the 55 costliest hurricanes to hit the United States, a dozen began with the letter “I”, including four in the top 10.
Category 4 Ian in 2022 came in at No. 3 with $119.6 billion in damage. Ian hammered Florida with such ferocity that it wiped out whole neighborhoods, tossed boats onto highways, swept away beaches and swamped homes in roof-deep waters.
Category 4 Ida, devastating parts of Louisiana in 2021, was the sixth-costliest hurricane at $84.6 billion. Category 4 Irma tore through the Florida Keys in 2017 for No. 8 at a cost of $64 billion. Category 2 Ike made landfall near Galveston, Texas, in 2008 for No. 10 at $43.2 billion. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said it based these figures on the 2024 Consumer Price Index adjusted cost.
In 2020, they ran out of names. Then came Iota
The 2020 hurricane season exhausted that year’s alphabetical list of storm names by mid-September, so later storms were identified using Greek letters, including Iota, the 30th named storm of that record-breaking year.
Category 4 Iota decimated Nicaragua and Honduras in November 2020 only two weeks after another hurricane had passed through the region.
The World Meteorological Organization, which oversees storm naming, later decided not to use the Greek alphabet for future storms, citing potential confusion when translated into other languages. Instead, a supplemental list of names will be used when the standard list is exhausted in a particular season.
Ivan spawned 118 tornadoes in a destructive loop
Ivan tore through Grand Cayman island in 2004, damaging or destroying an estimated 95 percent of the buildings there, the National Weather Service said. Then it slammed into the United States, spawning 118 tornadoes from Florida to Pennsylvania, more than any other tropical system since modern-day records have been kept starting in 1950, the weather service said. The storm was blamed for 124 deaths, including 57 in the United States.
Ivan formed during an El Niño, and churned a loopy path. After coming ashore near Gulf Shores, Alabama, it went up to Virginia, then back down through southeast Florida, returning into the U.S. Gulf and to Texas.
Irene was among the costliest in its category
In 2011, Hurricane Irene sent cars bobbing down rivers, swept away covered bridges, put millions in the dark and killed dozens of people. It made landfall along the North Carolina coast, then veered north along a densely populated corridor. New York City took a direct hit, but the heaviest rains were further inland.
In Vermont, the storm killed six people, washed homes off their foundations and damaged or destroyed more than 200 bridges and 500 miles (805 kilometers) of highway. It was the costliest Category 1 U.S. hurricane on record since at least 1980, with estimated total damage of $18.8 billion.
___
AP Science Writer Seth Borenstein in Kensington, Maryland, contributed to this report.

title: Armed man shot and killed by security at federal courthouse in Nashville, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - A man armed with a pistol was shot and killed by security at the federal courthouse in Nashville, Tennessee, according to police.
Nashville Metro Police responded to a “reported shooting call” at the Fred D. Thompson Federal Building and Courthouse Thursday morning.
According to police, the man entered the courthouse and tried to fire his gun but failed. He then pulled out a knife and was subsequently shot by a courthouse security officer.
He was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, where he died.
“This is the first time anything like this has happened at this courthouse,” the police spokesperson said.
The spokesperson confirmed the man did not make it past the courthouse security checkpoint. The checkpoint is a critical measure to protect U.S. senators and other people entering the building.
The suspect’s identity has not been released. Police did say the man is in his 40s and is from out of state but “has ties to Nashville.” They did not elaborate on the exact connection.
Officers and police K-9s searched the suspect’s car and found nothing threatening.
Investigators are speaking with security at the courthouse to better understand the events leading up to the shooting.
The Nashville Public Library’s Main Library branch was being evacuated as a result of the shooting.

title: Animal hospital owner accused of using dead dog’s name to obtain prescription drugs
text:
LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) — The owner of an animal hospital and an alleged accomplice have been indicted in what prosecutors describe as a prescription drug scheme that used a dead dog’s name to obtain narcotics.
A Lorain County grand jury indicted Dr. Kris L. Taylor, 62, of Strongsville, and Camile Nieto, 29, of Avon, on seven counts, according to an indictment obtained by 19 News.
The two are accused of taking part in a scheme at Landings Animal Hospital to repeatedly write and fill prescriptions for oxycodone and the anti‑anxiety drug Alprazolam in the name of “Punkin,” a dog that was already dead, the indictment says.
According to the Landings Animal Hospital website, Taylor is the owner and a veterinarian at the Avon Lake hospital on Avon Belden Road. It is unknown whether Nieto was also a staff member.
Investigators say the alleged conduct happened between August 10, 2024, and June 7, 2025. The indictments list more than 20 prescriptions for Oxycodone and Alprazolam allegedly written for “Punkin” and filled at pharmacies across Northeast Ohio, including locations in Avon and Avon Lake.
Taylor and Nieto are each charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, a first-degree felony; deception to obtain a dangerous drug and possession of oxycodone, both second-degree felonies; illegal processing of drug documents involving oxycodone, a fourth-degree felony; deception to obtain a dangerous drug and illegal processing of drug documents involving alprazolam, both fifth-degree felonies; and possession of alprazolam, a first-degree misdemeanor.
Court records show both appeared in court Thursday and were each given a $500,000 bond.
Landings Animal Hospital told 19 News it remains open.

title: Trump’s government payout plans, ranging from $90 to $5,000, face huge hurdles
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Trump’s $90 to $5,000 payout promises face hurdles
Trump has promised payments from $90 to $5,000, but the biggest payout faces major hurdles and isn’t guaranteed
President Trump’s $90 to $5,000 payout promises face hurdles
Trump has promised payments from $90 to $5,000, but the biggest payout faces major hurdles and isn’t guaranteed
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
With less than a month until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump has promised Americans a trio of government payments, with amounts ranging from $90 to $5,000.
If a government payout sounds good, you should first know that not everyone is guaranteed to benefit — and the biggest payment is far from certain.
Polls show the economy and affordability are top of mind for voters as they prepare to cast ballots in the Nov. 3 elections. At the same time, Trump’s approval ratings are low, with survey respondents reporting displeasure with his economic policies.
The White House’s plans aim to buffer some of that sentiment. Here’s what to know about the payments:
The $5,000 dividend check
This might have garnered the most headlines when Trump first announced it, but making the $5,000 checks a reality faces enormous obstacles. Trump said every adult U.S. citizen would receive the payment if Republicans win control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. But the administration has announced no formal plan for such checks and fiscal experts cast doubt on the plan during a time of existing economic challenges.
When will I receive it? That’s unclear. Aside from this promise being tied to an election’s outcome, the White House press release about this dividend provided no details on how Americans would receive it.
Where will the money come from? Trump cited tariff revenues as a potential funding source, but lawmakers did not include a separate tariff dividend in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tax and spending bill that became law in 2025. The payout first would require Congress’ approval. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said he would introduce legislation to fund the proposal. But political analysts say such legislation is unlikely to attain the required 60-vote supermajority in the Senate. The payment could cost the federal treasury more than $1 trillion.
One-time $90 payment for some people on Medicare
On Oct. 2, the administration said it will send one-time $90 payments to certain enrollees in the Medicare Part B government insurance program. The program covers medically necessary services and preventive services — such as ambulance use and medical equipment — for people 65 and older and others with certain disabilities. Part B eligibility requirements vary based on whether a person has to pay a premium for Part A, which covers hospital insurance.
Trump said the money is to help ease the cost of rising Medicare Part B premiums, which cost about $203 for most people.
Do I qualify? More than 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible, according to the White House. People are not eligible if their premiums are covered by Medicaid, if they pay income-related adjustments or if they are enrolled in Medicare Advantage. In 2026, around 64.2 million people are enrolled in Part B.
When and how will I receive the money? The payments are expected to go out in October, through direct deposit or by check through a Medicare-registered mailing address, the White House said.
Where will the money come from? The Medicare Improvement Fund, a fund Congress created in 2008 to make improvements to the original Medicare.
How can I check my eligibility and payment status? To check eligibility, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). To check payment status, call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213.
$500 for some Affordable Care Act enrollees
On Sept. 10, the White House said the government would issue a $500 per person “refund” to some Affordable Care Act enrollees.
Where will the money come from? The White House says the payments will be drawn from what it called "overcharges." It said the Biden administration charged excess "user fees" passed on to consumers in the form of higher premiums, meaning consumers were charged more than what was needed to operate the federal exchange. User fees cover the expenses of services such as the Healthcare.gov website and its call center, Reuters reported, citing the healthcare think tank KFF.
The Biden administration finalized a 1% rate increase from 2025 to 2026 to offset a projected drop in enrollees following the government’s discontinuation of certain subsidies, Reuters said.
Nearly 1 million Americans will receive the $500 payment, the Trump administration said. The payments come as ACA marketplace health insurance premiums rose by hundreds or thousands of dollars this year.
When will the refunds be issued? October 2026, through checks.
Am I eligible? People who do not receive Affordable Care Act premium assistance, specifically in 30 federal-exchange states: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
The White House told PolitiFact the recipients will mainly be people above 400% of the federal poverty line.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Norway Savings Bank donates $2,500 to Spurwink
text:
PORTLAND — Each year, over 10,000 people of all ages, abilities and backgrounds are served by Spurwink through a wide variety of programs and services aimed at helping participants lead engaged, connected and meaningful lives in their communities.

“We value NSB’s dedicated investment in our mission,” Eric Meyer, president and CEO of Spurwink, said. “When we step back from our individual roles, we see the whole of a mosaic taking shape: a vision of children, adults, and families affected by behavioral health challenges and developmental disabilities living healthy, engaged lives in their communities. NSB’s role is a critically important piece of our mosaic.”
For more information about Spurwink, its services and opportunities to help the organization, visit www.spurwink.org.

title: Maine Supreme Judicial Court hears arguments over deadly fall at Prouts Neck Cliff Walk
text:
BATH, Maine (WMTW) - The Maine Supreme Judicial Court heard arguments Wednesday over whether the Black Point Inn can be held responsible for a Georgia woman’s deadly fall from the Prouts Neck Cliff Walk in 2022.
The oral arguments were held at Morse High School in Bath.
The case is before Maine’s highest court after a Cumberland County Superior Court judge granted summary judgment to the owners and operators of the Black Point Inn.
The appeal centers on whether an innkeeper can owe its guests a duty of care on nearby property the inn does not own or maintain.
Both sides acknowledged that the Black Point Inn does not own or control the Prouts Neck Cliff Walk, but the attorney for the woman’s estate argued that the hotel heavily marketed the Cliff Walk as an amenity.
“It’s disingenuous for the Black Point Inn to have advertised this amenity, to have policed its parking lot to make sure that anyone there was paying money to it, to invite their guests to use it, to hand them maps,” said attorney Charles King.
King also said the inn had a heightened duty to warn the woman of danger.
Tiffany Ottenga, the attorney representing the Black Point Inn, said the hotel “indisputably” did not owe a duty to the appellants.
“(The hotel) did not own, control, maintain or possess the cliff walk,” Ottenga said.
It is unclear when the Supreme Judicial Court will make a decision.
Four years since a woman’s deadly fall
The question is being asked by the family of Ramona Gowens, who was vacationing in Maine with her sister, Sonia Hall, in September 2022 when she died. According to court records, the pair walked from the inn on the Cliff Walk and stopped to take photographs near a fence overlooking the coast. When Gowens leaned against the fence, it gave way, and she fell backward through brush and into a steep, 30-foot-deep chasm. She later died from her injuries.
Claims of negligence and a “duty to warn of dangers”
The estate and Hall sued BPI Partners, LLC, which owns the property and buildings where the inn is located, and Migis Hotel Group, LLC, which operates the inn. The defendants initially sought dismissal, arguing they had no duty to the plaintiffs because the accident occurred off the inn’s property. That motion was denied. After discovery, the defendants again argued they owed no duty regarding the Cliff Walk, and the Superior Court granted summary judgment in their favor. The plaintiffs appealed in February 2026.
The plaintiffs are now seeking to reverse that decision and allow their claims to proceed to trial.
Their attorneys argue Maine law recognizes a heightened duty between an innkeeper and its overnight guests and that the duty should extend to the Cliff Walk because of the way the Black Point Inn promoted it and provided access to it.
The inn’s attorneys are asking the Law Court to uphold the Superior Court’s ruling.
What the inn is arguing
In their brief, BPI Partners and Migis Hotel Group argue that the Cliff Walk is separate from the inn, is not necessary to access or use the hotel, and has traditionally been accessible to the public. They say the Prouts Neck Improvement Association, a voluntary homeowners association, maintains the Cliff Walk, not the inn.
The defendants’ brief concludes that the Superior Court’s decision should be affirmed and that the inn did not “owe its guests a duty of care while using the Cliff Walk.”
The Law Court’s calendar identifies the case as involving negligence, whether a “special relationship” creates a duty to warn of dangers and the question of control over premises.
The court heard several appeals at Morse High School on Wednesday as part of its effort to bring oral arguments to Maine schools.

title: Trump tries to smooth over controversial remarks about Iran striking San Diego, Los Angeles
text:
(Gray News) – President Donald Trump fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton Wednesday night, but his remarks were not only focused on Paxton.
Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.
“You want to see trauma? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country.”
People at the rally cheered when the president clarified the controversial statements he made earlier in the week at a political rally in Nebraska.
How are California leaders responding?
“Trump thinks he will scare people into voting for MAGA candidates by threatening the bombing of over 16 million Americans. He has lost his mind,” Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X in response to Trump’s most recent comments at the rally in Texas.
Los Angeles is the most populous city in California and the second most populous in the United States. It has one of the busiest container ports in the Americas and is home to the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command Headquarters.
LA Mayor Karen Bass reacted to Trump’s statement on X saying, “We should not be in a position where we are questioning whether or not the President of the United States is threatening cities in his own country.”
Bass said on X that she called Congressman Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, “to investigate the dangerous threats the President has encouraged this week against Angelenos.”
“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” Bass said on X earlier in the week.
“Seriously, again? How many times do we have to say it? San Diego is not a prop. San Diego is not a target. San Diego is not your applause line,” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote on X in response to Trump’s remarks in Texas.
“We are a proud military city full of real people. Stop using us in your reckless war talk.”
San Diego is home to Naval Base San Diego, where the Navy SEALs train. There is a large military presence in the city with 70,000 civilians and active-duty service members living and working in the area.
The president’s message was interrupted in Texas repeatedly by protesters, including one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.
Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.
“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”

title: Obituary: Jane Charlotte Day Wheeler
text:
SOUTH PARIS – Jane Charlotte Day Wheeler, 92, of South Paris, Maine, passed away on Sept. 4, 2026. Jane was born on May 28, 1934, in West Paris, Maine, where she grew up and developed a lifelong love of her hometown. She graduated from West Paris High School in 1952 and attended Auburn Maine School of Commerce, earning a two-year business degree.
On July 27, 1953, she married Glenn A. Gurney. They had three children, Peter, who predeceased her, Denise E. Gurney and Melissa J. Gurney. Glenn passed away in 1974. Jane later married Harvey S. Wheeler on April 30, 1977. Harvey had two grown children, Shirley and Nancy. Harvey passed away in 2012.
Jane spent her adult life in South Paris. She was an active and devoted member of the Unitarian Universalist Church of South Paris, serving on its board for many years. Her faith and values were expressed through her care for others and support of community causes.
Family was at the heart of Jane’s life. She especially cherished her grandchildren, Patrick, Derek, Christopher, Brandon, Alyssa, James, Jennifer and Becky. She has many grandchildren who she adored. Jane loved camping, picnics, trips to the ocean, gardening, cooking and baking, exercise classes, eating out and, perhaps most especially, ice cream. She was also known for having a story to accompany the items she baked or presents she gave away, a tradition that became part of the family’s memories of her.
She will be remembered for her love of family, her generosity, her sense of humor, her connection to community and the many stories she shared around the table. She leaves behind a family who will continue to tell those stories, and love her through them.
A memorial service will be held at 1 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, at the Unitarian Universalist Church, 36 Pine St., South Paris. A committal service will follow at Riverside Annex Cemetery, Paris Hill Rd., South Paris.
Online condolences may be shared at http://www.chandlerfunerals.com.

title: Federal government looking to crack down on headlight glare in effort to make driving safer
text:
(NHTSA/Gray News) - The government is updating its standards for LED headlights and other standards related to driver safety.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) made the announcement on Oct. 6. According to the agency, it will consult safety advocates, technical experts, and industry stakeholders to make changes in the following areas:
- Addressing Headlight Glare: Examining the role that modern headlighting technology has on glare for other road users and making appropriate changes
- Modernizing Lighting Technology: Improving rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams, and replaceable light sources
- Improving Performance: Evaluating how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility
- Updating Testing & Materials: Streamlining test procedures for plastic optics and replaceable lenses
- Aligning Global Standards: Harmonizing U.S. vehicle lighting regulations with international safety standards
NHTSA stated this will be the first time in more than 25 years that it will use negotiated rulemaking for vehicle lighting standards.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will appoint up to 18 stakeholders, according to the agency.
NHTSA is asking for the public’s feedback and membership nominations, both of which need to be submitted by Nov. 9.
To leave a comment or nominate someone for membership, visit regulations.gov for docket number NHTSA-2026-1981.

title: A Maine guide pulled 200 tires from a river last year. Yesterday, he pulled his 700th.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Over the last couple of years, Brandon Bichrest has brought attention to the number of tires sitting in our rivers. I first wrote about him last September, after he started removing tires from the Androscoggin River. A lot has changed since then.
The more I look into river cleanups, the more I realize how many different people and groups are doing them around the country. Some are groups that have been cleaning rivers for years. Others are individuals who simply decided to do something about the trash they were seeing.
And, just like when you decide you want to buy a red 4Runner and suddenly see red 4Runners everywhere, I have started noticing river cleanups all over Instagram and Facebook that I never noticed before.
I have been in the fishing industry for 25 years and have been a member of Trout Unlimited for a long time. I have seen plenty of river cleanups over the years, but I don’t remember seeing this much attention being given to them.
It got me wondering how many other people across the country were doing the same thing and whether individuals can sometimes accomplish more by simply taking it upon themselves to make something happen.
I remember when I was part of the Sunkhaze Trout Unlimited group. We had more than 100 members, but it seemed like only five people would show up for meetings. Events could be tough to organize when everything was being done by just a handful of people.
So is it better to have a large organization behind something, or can one person who is passionate enough actually get more done?
I started thinking about that question when I came across the Delaware River Club and its Pig Farm Ink “Get Trashed” event, where people get together to clean up the Upper Delaware River. They have been doing it for 10 years.
If you look at the pictures from these cleanups, you see tons of tires and other trash being removed. It’s amazing to see how much people can accomplish, but it also makes me wonder: How and why is there still so much trash in the river after 10 years of cleanups?
Maybe that is part of the problem. We are dealing with decades of trash that was put into rivers long before most of us ever thought about it.
Another example is the owner of Mossy Creek Fly Fishing. He rows his boat down the Shenandoah River and fills it with tires. He calls it the “Tire Barge.” He has been doing it since 2019.
He even turns it into a little contest. People try to guess the total number and weight of the tires, and the winner gets a $100 gift card to the fly shop. Battle Creek Landfill disposes of the tires for free.
I think that’s a great example of taking an idea and making it something people want to participate in.
Brandon’s tire mission
I recently reached out to Bichrest to see how the tire removal was going. When I asked him why he started pulling tires out of the river, his answer was pretty simple.
“Because they’re everywhere and unsightly. Then I did research and learned how bad tires are for the water and for bug life.”
He also pointed me toward a shocking YouTube video about the history of using tires as fish habitat across the country.
Last year, Bichrest had removed around 200 tires. Yesterday, he pulled his 700th.
Think about that for a minute. Seven hundred tires pulled out of a river.
Bichrest explained that this isn’t a project for someone who is inexperienced or not prepared for hard work. Pulling a 50-plus-pound tire off the bottom of a river in five feet of water while dealing with current is not easy. After trying to remove one myself, I can tell you he isn’t exaggerating.
I also asked Bichrest what happens to the tires after he gets them out. Once he gets around 100, he contacts a company that comes and takes them away. The tires are then ground up and used for things such as driveways.
He is showing what just one person can accomplish.
So I tried it myself
I see Bichrest’s posts all the time, and I talk to him almost every week. I also tease him about his posts from time to time.
So this year, with the Penobscot running low, I happened to find an area with a few tires. I had clients with me, and we decided to try to pull one out.
The first tire was in about three feet of water, which is roughly waist deep. I couldn’t even move it, so I eventually gave up.
As I moved farther downstream, I found another tire sitting in about a foot of water. It was completely full of dirt, which made it much harder to remove.
We eventually got it moving, but as I was pulling it out, the inner tube hit my hand.
I jumped.
I knew there were eels in the river.
When Bichrest says removing tires isn’t for the weak, I now understand exactly what he means. I can also see why you would probably need a couple of people working together if you wanted to remove any real number of tires.
What about the Penobscot?
Will I start removing tires from the Penobscot? I’m not sure.
Maybe Stac and I could make it part of our 2 Fly Bug Bumper. We are going to look at it.
Is there a major tire problem in the Penobscot? No, I wouldn’t say that. But there are tires in the river, and if they can be safely removed, why not?
Maybe this is where these grassroots cleanups can make a difference. You don’t necessarily need a huge organization, a big budget or hundreds of volunteers. Sometimes you just need one person who looks at a problem and says, “I’m going to do something about it.”
I didn’t notice these efforts before. But now that I am looking, I see them everywhere.

title: Darlene T. Little

Darlene Teresa Little passed away July 22, 2026 after a short illness surrounded by her children.
Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Feb. 17, 1955 to Joan L. Andrews and Paul H. Little, she went to school in Philadelphia and moved to Boothbay with her parents after Paul retired in 1992.
Darlene worked at the Seagate Motel and loved working for the Friants. She also did home care helping the elderly with household chores, and she was a member of the Boothbay Region Miss Fires for several years.
She loved camping and going to the jamborees at the Ponderosa campground with her friend Ray Guyon, and in recent years camping at Lake Pemaquid campground with family.
She loved the holidays, summertime cookouts, and just enjoying being around family and friends. She always considered everyone her friend as she could spark up a conversation with anyone.
She was pre-deceased by her parents Paul, Joan, and friend Ray.
She is survived by her children Rocchina Ruffin, her husband Lorenzo children Lorenzo, Shavonn and Marcus, Kimberly Appenzeller, children Julianna and David William Little, children Mathew and Madison; sisters April husband Clarence, Tracy husband Marc, Paula and brother-in-law Roland; brother John; along with many cousins, nieces, and nephews.

title: Glenburn man allegedly broke windows at Bangor business and threw apples at passing cars

A Glenburn man allegedly broke windows at a Bangor business and threw apples as passing cars Wednesday night.

title: Maine attorney files ethics complaint against Sen. Susan Collins
text:
Maine attorney files ethics complaint against Sen. Susan Collins
8 Investigates reviewed U.S. Senate Ethics Committee data to see how often complaints result in formal action
Maine attorney files ethics complaint against Sen. Susan Collins
8 Investigates reviewed U.S. Senate Ethics Committee data to see how often complaints result in formal action
A Maine attorney has filed a complaint with the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics against Sen. Susan Collins, hoping the committee will investigate allegations reported by ProPublica that Collins accepted campaign donations in exchange for government contracts.
The bipartisan committee, which is composed of three Democrats and three Republicans, provides ethical guidance and investigates complaints against senators and Senate staff members.
"I believe that it's important to demand the best of our elected officials," said Valerie Adams, who filed the complaint. "I believe that these are issues that we as voters should pay attention to, and I hope that the committee will act on it and open an investigation."
Anyone can file a complaint. The committee receives dozens of allegations each year, but according to annual reports reviewed by 8 Investigates, most are dismissed, either because of a lack of evidence or because the alleged conduct does not violate Senate rules.
Over the last five years, 91% of complaints were dismissed without an investigation.
"I believe the issue needs media attention in order to put pressure on the committee to open an investigation," Adams said.
Complaints that are not dismissed proceed to an initial inquiry. Over the past five years, 63% of complaints that reached this stage were ultimately dismissed.
For minor violations, the committee can issue a public or private letter telling a senator they violated Senate ethics rules. It issued three letters over the past five years.
If the committee finds serious ethical concerns, it may open a formal review, which could result in disciplinary action. The committee opened one review over the past five years. The review was closed after its subject, New Jersey Sen. Robert Menendez (D), resigned.
The committee has not issued any formal sanctions in recent history.
"I don't think we should ever lose hope that what we're doing will matter, and whether or not an investigation is opened, I think it's important that the issue is getting attention and I think it's important to request that an investigation be opened," Adams said.
In response to the complaint, a Collins campaign spokesperson wrote: "This is getting to be pathetic. For the third consecutive week, a recently failed Democratic candidate has parroted false charges that they know nothing about, against Susan Collins."
Adams previously worked as an assistant district attorney for Cumberland County. This spring, she lost her primary race against incumbent District Attorney Jacqueline Sartoris.
Because of confidentiality requirements, much of the committee’s work takes place behind closed doors.
