title: If Susan Collins wins, Donald Trump wins
text:
Earlier this week, Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign summed up Tuesday’s debate between her boss and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson: “It was clear from the beginning that Sen. Collins is running to serve Maine, and Troy Jackson thinks he’s running against Donald Trump.”
It doesn’t bother me at all if Jackson thinks he’s running against the president. You know who else shares that notion? The president.
The way I see it, Jackson also has an agenda to serve Maine that’s at least as good as what Collins envisions, even if, as a new senator, he would have far less ability to deliver on his priorities.
More important, though, is that hindering President Trump is the best thing any Maine senator can do for our state, nation and the wider world.
There are many reasons to retire Collins. And just as many to keep her on Capitol Hill funneling federal dollars back home to Maine. But looming over every calculation is a more stark reality: an unfettered president who is enabled by a spineless Congress.
Collins has occasionally offered polite objections to Trump’s most egregious actions but she has failed to rally her party to stand for something beyond loyalty to a would-be tyrant.
For Collins supporters, her civility and seniority are what’s crucial. They insist, correctly, that her presence and status in the nation’s capital benefits Maine.
We need to ask ourselves: At what point does her institutional clout come at the expense of the democracy we cherish? Voters have to weigh whether Collins has grown too entrenched, too distant from her constituents and too beholden to her party and the president.
That’s what matters.
During last month’s Republican Midterm Convention in Texas, Trump said at least three times that voters this fall need to pretend “I’m on the ballot.”
What Trump meant by his insistence that he is “on the ballot” is that voters should send GOP politicians — including Collins — to the Capitol to continue to do his bidding … or at least stay out of his way. For him, sadly, the measure of a senator is how compliant she is to the whims of the White House.
During this week’s debate, Collins said she is “not exactly” Trump’s favorite senator, to which there is some truth.
It is equally true, however, that the president wants her to secure another term. Like everyone else, Trump recognizes that a “concerned” Collins is far better for him than a dedicated foe like Jackson.
Collins wants Mainers to see her as a moderate, reasonable and independent leader in the mold of former Sens. Olympia Snowe and William Cohen. That vision has grown ever more hollow as Collins faced the difficult task of dealing with Trump. As he runs amok in Washington, she has, sadly, proved that she isn’t up to the challenge of protecting the prerogatives of the Senate and defending the laws it has enacted.
We can appreciate that Collins has delivered plenty of federal help to Maine without sending her back into a crucial fight in which she has already capitulated.
If Collins wins, Trump wins.

title: What's driving up Maine electric bills
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rising natural gas prices and increasing costs to repair and upgrade electric infrastructure are driving Maine’s eye-popping power bills, according to a new analysis from Maine’s Office of Public Advocate.
Renewable energy projects, and particularly subsidies for Maine’s now-retired community solar development program, are the smallest factor in ballooning prices, according to the agency.
Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said in an interview that the intent of the analysis was to give consumers a more complete picture of the complicated and varied forces pushing up electric bills. Her office is Maine’s public watchdog for utility consumers.
“If people are frustrated and they just want it to go down, but they’re blaming it all on one bucket of these price drivers, they’re going to continue to be frustrated,” Sanborn said. “No one policy solution and no one backward-looking blame game is going to explain where we are at right now and how to drive prices down in the future,” Sanborn added.
A typical residential bill for a Central Maine Power customer increased 72% in the last six years, to $157 per month, according to the analysis.
Almost half that increase — $30 — was due to increases in electric supply prices, largely due to surging natural gas prices after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
New England relies on natural gas power plants, but supply is constrained in the winter when fuel is directed for home heating instead. That leaves power plants to rely on burning more expensive liquified natural gas or oil to keep the lights on.
Electric distribution — poles, wires and other infrastructure that brings power to homes and businesses — was the second biggest driver, adding about $18 to bills according to the public advocate. Much of that increase came from the cost of responding to and recovering from storms, the agency said.
Transmission charges to bring power from power plants, hydro dams and other generators to local communities added about $9 to the overall cost, Sanborn’s office said.
“Stranded costs,” which include funding for some renewable energy projects, such as the controversial community solar net energy billing program, added another $9, according to the agency’s analysis.
And even if everything had stayed equal, Maine customers would have expected to pay about $27 more per month just from inflation, according to the analysis.
Sanborn said her office is working on multiple policy angles to bring down costs.
“We think it’s important to show the various different drivers in those increases, because each of those different drivers is going to require a different solution,” Sanborn added.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Former President Obama backs Troy Jackson in Senate race
text:
Former President Barack Obama backs Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race
Former President Barack Obama shared his support for Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Maine, in a new video released on Thursday.
Former President Barack Obama backs Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race
Former President Barack Obama shared his support for Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Maine, in a new video released on Thursday.
Former President Barack Obama is throwing his support behind Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate in Maine's race for U.S. Senate.
Obama made the announcement in a video posted Thursday morning by Jackson's campaign on YouTube.
"In this economy, we need a fighter like Troy," Obama said. "So do not sit this one out. Get out there and vote for Troy Jackson."
Obama highlighted Jackson's "working-class roots," as well as his focus on lowering prescription drug costs, raising wages, providing free school lunch and protecting abortion rights in Maine.
Watch Obama's full announcement in the video player below.
Obama has announced support for two dozen candidates in either U.S. Senate or gubernatorial races in 2026. In 2020, he endorsed Democrat Sara Gideon in her race against Sen. Susan Collins.
Jackson has pointed to those same issues as major parts of his legislative record. He sponsored legislation in Maine aimed at expanding access to free school meals, and his campaign has highlighted his work on prescription drug costs and workers' rights.
Obama also pointed to abortion rights, saying Jackson helped protect abortion access in Maine after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Jackson supported legislation signed by Gov. Janet Mills in 2022 that expanded abortion access in Maine. His position on abortion has evolved over the course of his political career. On Monday, at a campaign event alongside Planned Parenthood, Jackson has said he was wrong to oppose abortion earlier in his career and now believes that reproductive rights are part of healthcare.
"I'm honored to have President Obama standing with us in this fight," Jackson said in a statement released with the endorsement. He said Maine voters are looking for a government that works for working people rather than "the wealthy and well-connected."
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, became the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in July after Graham Platner withdrew from the race. 
He is challenging Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is seeking a sixth term.
"If Senator Collins had President Obama's character, we wouldn't be in this mess right now," Jackson said during a visit at the Augusta Food Bank on Thursday.
The Collins campaign released a statement on Thursday in response to Obama's announcement.
"The fact that Troy Jackson is endorsed by Obama, funded by Chuck Schumer, and campaigning with Bernie Sanders this weekend tells you how much the national Democratic machine wants to control Maine’s Senate seat," the campaign said. "Susan is supported by Mainers like Denise, a retired teacher, who has more money in her monthly Social Security check and Mark, whose son has better access to lifesaving insulin, all thanks to her work. Those are the people who matter to Senator Collins."
The announcement of support comes on the same day that Jackson and Collins are scheduled to face each other in WMTW's Senate debate, which starts at 8 p.m. Thursday. You can watch the debate live on Channel 8. The debate will also be livestreamed on WMTW.com, the WMTW app (iOS and Android) and Very Local, as well as the WMTW-TV YouTube channel and the WMTW-TV Facebook page.

title: Aging Untold: Knowing your family health history matters more than you may think
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how family health history can help doctors spot medical risks early and shape a more personalized path for your care.
Plus, find out how creating an “anti-bucket list” can help you let go of guilt, grudges and obligations as you age.
Later, we meet a 95-year-old Vermont volunteer whose decades of preserving plants earned her the ultimate living legacy.
Your family health history could provide your doctor with important clues years before disease becomes obvious, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She said it’s important to identify patterns in conditions such as heart disease and strokes, particularly when they occur at a very early age, as well as cancers, autoimmune disorders, depression and thyroid diseases.
Genetic testing can be especially useful for people who don’t have access to their family history, including those who are adopted.
Saying “no” might be one of the most powerful tools for a freer, more joyful life after 60.
The idea of a bucket list is pretty common — a list of everything you still want to do. But what about an “anti-bucket list” — the things you want to stop doing, stop caring about or stop apologizing for?
“One of the privileges of getting older is subtraction,” Rogers said. “What can I do to subtract that’s going to give me more peace, more sleep, more joy. And it’s OK.”
Read the full article and see how to create your own anti-bucket list.
The number of cases of traumatic brain injury is rising, and older adults 75 and up account for nearly a third of TBI-related hospitalizations, largely due to fall risk.
Despite the widespread impact, federal funding for TBI research, education and awareness has lapsed — and advocates say the consequences could be severe.
Hilda White has carefully preserved more than 50,000 plant specimens at the University of Vermont’s Pringle Herbarium, which is like a library of plants.
The 95-year-old presses the plants and affixes them to archival paper so they can be studied and referenced for generations to come.
For her 95th birthday, the herbarium gave White a gift unlike any other.
A newly discovered fern, found in Colombia in 2023, was officially named for her.

title: ‘We are absolutely in a crisis’: The fight to provide access to food in the South
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - In communities across the country, more families are getting pushed farther away from fresh, affordable food.
The USDA calls it “low access.” It’s when a significant share of a neighborhood lives far away from a grocery store. The agency estimates nearly 54 million Americans live in these areas.
When that happens, researchers found that people often rely on convenience store and fast food items. These can be higher in sugar, sodium, and saturated fats. Ingredients which can lead to health problems.
Food deserts impact one in three people in Memphis. Volunteers are working to feed the need through a school pantry and mobile grocery store.
Weekly food distribution
Every week at Winchester Elementary, volunteers pack 60 to 70 boxes of food for students and their families free of charge.
The pantry is the brainchild of Denise Wilson, a fourth-grade math teacher who has been at Winchester for two years.
Two years ago, Wilson noticed a student sleeping in class and complaining of stomach aches.
“We talked to him, the fourth-grade team did. And he explained that, the little bit of food they do have, he made sure his sister got it,” Wilson said.
Wilson created the Bronco Kare Korral Pantry, providing select students and their families’ full meals every week, even during breaks.
“I grew up in this neighborhood,” said Wilson. “I didn’t have the food insecurities that a lot of our kids have, but I did grow up on food stamps. I definitely know that feeling of not having groceries in the house a couple of days before food stamps are supposed to hit.”
Wilson and her team say their work is completely voluntary, providing bags of foods to children every Friday along with carefully crafted boxes of food including meat and veggies for their parents.
Wilson said they depend on donations from the Mid-South Food Bank and donations from the community.
Donations are accepted here: Fundraiser by Denise Wilson : Help Restock the Bronco Kare Korral Pantry
Food desert data
Winchester Elementary sits inside what is commonly known as a food desert, defined by the USDA as an area where the poverty rate is greater than at least 20% of the population and at least 500 people live more than half a mile from the nearest large grocery store.
Many residents in the neighborhood don’t have access to a car and for some, the nearest grocery store is one to three miles away. Many people rely on convenience stores at higher prices with no fresh food options.
Data shows roughly 32% of Memphians live in a food desert.
“We’re absolutely in a crisis,” said Roshun Austin, CEO of the nonprofit The Works, Inc., which focuses on rebuilding communities through affordable housing, fighting blight and food insecurity.
Austin said many Memphis neighborhoods struggle to attract grocery stores.
“A lot of it is due to how we developed our city. We’re very sparsely populated,” Austin said. “We have over 30,000 vacant and abandoned lots in our county. And so, a grocery store is not going into a place next to 10 vacant houses and lots because they have a customer base.”
Mobile grocer expands reach
The Works launched a mobile grocer in 2022. The 20-foot trailer is stocked with fresh produce, meats and dairy.
At a stop in the medical district, most customers no longer drive.
“Sometimes my granddaughter has time to take me or I’ll get one of my neighbors who drive to take me,” said Gloria Thomas, who shops at the mobile store.
Data shows the concept is growing in popularity. The mobile grocer nearly doubled the number of individuals served year over year, from 2,317 people in 2024 to 4,302 people in 2025, according to The Works Impact Report.
“Price of food. Everything is going up,” said BJ Adams, manager of the mobile grocer.
The mobile grocer is not a pantry. Customers must pay for everything inside, but prices are comparable to other full-service grocery stores.
The grocer moves into food deserts across the city at a dozen locations every week from North to South Memphis.
Check out the full schedule here: MOBILE GROCER | The Works.
Cash Saver partnered with The Works, inc. to provide wholesale products in areas where there are no physical stores. The concept is being replicated across the country. Little Rock opened its own mobile market last month after volunteers visited Memphis to learn how to do it.
While mobile grocery stores, community gardens and food pantries help solve some food insecurity issues, Austin said the real solution requires rebuilding neighborhoods.
“It looks like the neighborhoods where you see grocery stores. That means wealth has increased for individuals and their families. That means that it’s an ideal place. It’s a choice neighborhood. People want to live here,” Austin said.
“Because I see the need,” Adams said.

title: Maine’s Jessica Meir, 3 other astronauts return to Earth
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — Maine’s Jessica Meir and three other astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the American, French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
Meir and her NASA colleague Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
“We are so excited to be back on planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down.
While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”
Meir, who is from Caribou, was on her second trip to the space station. Her previous mission, in 2019, lasted 205 days and featured the first all-female spacewalk.
This time, she and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA’s Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA’s first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
Meir’s seventh career spacewalk, on Sept. 1, moved her into third place for total spacewalks by women at NASA and brought her career spacewalk time to more than 49 hours.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef’s toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA’s count.
Meir has been an astronaut since 2013 and was the first Maine woman to travel to space. After graduating as valedictorian from Caribou High School, she studied biology at Brown University. She then earned a master’s degree from the International Space University in France and a doctorate in marine biology from Scripps Institution of Oceanography in San Diego.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: Man killed, 2 people injured after vehicle crashes into Ellsworth homes
text:
Maine man killed, two people injured after vehicle crashes into Ellsworth homes
A Maine man died and another was seriously injured after the vehicle they were traveling in crashed into two homes in Ellsworth early Thursday morning, leaving a third person hurt, according to authorities.
The crash happened just before 1:30 a.m. on Main Street, near the intersection of Bucksport and Surry roads, according to WMTW media partner WABI.
Police said the driver, identified as Landon Rockwell, 19, of Dedham, was approaching the intersection when he lost control of the vehicle. The vehicle went off the road and hit a house on the opposite side of Main Street and then struck a second home.
A passenger in the vehicle, Paul Meservey, 23, of Orrington, was killed in the crash.
Rockwell was thrown from the vehicle as a result of the crash. He was taken by ambulance to a local hospital and then flown to a hospital in Bangor.
Police said the first home was unoccupied at the time of the crash, but there were people in the second house. One person who was in the second home was taken to Maine Coast Hospital after they complained of pain.
The circumstances surrounding the crash are under investigation, and the Hancock County District Attorney's Office has been notified.

title: Family demands answers after video display board falls on 5-year-old boy at school, killing him
text:
PALM BAY, Fla. (WESH) - A Florida family is demanding answers after a 120-pound video display board fell on a 5-year-old boy at school, killing him.
The victim was identified by his family as 5-year-old Bellamy Dawkins-Morris, who had autism.
Brevard Public Schools says Bellamy was seriously injured after a Promethean video display board fell on him around 11:36 a.m. Wednesday at Riviera Elementary School. School staff called 911 and began lifesaving measures before the boy was taken to the hospital, where he later died.
Family members say they are devastated by Bellamy’s death and searching for answers.
“We’re expecting him to be safe. He didn’t return to us,” said Bellamy’s great-aunt, Miriam Rodriguez. “My emotions, my sadness has subsided, and I am angry. We need answers, and we need them immediately.”
Brevard Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Mark Rendell says he met with Bellamy’s family shortly after the boy’s death.
“We lost a life today, a precious young life. There are no words to describe that loss,” Rendell said. “I’ve been doing this for over 30 years, and I really couldn’t find the words to share with them my grief and the grief that all of us have.”
According to Bellamy’s family, his mother was told he was moving the display board back and forth before it tipped over and fell on him. The family is now questioning whether the board was properly secured and whether enough supervision was provided.
Another great-aunt, Melissa Rodriguez, says they believe Bellamy’s death could have been prevented.
“I’m angry because it could have been prevented if they were paying attention to him. I’m not saying he doesn’t do things that he shouldn’t do, but this child did not deserve to not be here anymore,” she said.
The Palm Bay Police Department’s Special Victims Unit and Major Case Unit are investigating.
As investigators work to determine exactly what happened, Bellamy’s family says they are seeking accountability and legal counsel.

title: Maine House speaker says lawmakers will aim to ease federal healthcare cuts, heating oil spikes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
House Speaker Ryan Fecteau on Thursday said that lawmakers will try to lessen the impact of federal healthcare cutbacks and the spike in heating oil prices.
Work requirements for Medicaid are set to start in 2027 and are expected to result in over 31,000 additional uninsured Mainers, according to state estimates. Those cutbacks stem from the 2025 budget bill, which also cut into the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Thousands of Mainers are also paying much higher Affordable Care Act premiums after some of the program’s subsidies expired at the end of 2025.
Fecteau and Rep. Gary Friedmann, D-Bar Harbor, participated in a news conference on Thursday with Defend America Action, a progressive advocacy group.
“We’re going to have to stand ready to provide some immediate relief when we return to Augusta,” said Fecteau, referring to heating oil cost increases and also possibly tapping into a $30 million SNAP contingency fund. The legislative session will begin in January.
The contingency fund was set up this year to continue SNAP payments during government shutdowns. Fecteau said presuming the government doesn’t shut down this winter, the state money could be used to boost the SNAP program, formerly known as food stamps.
Meanwhile, heating oil prices have reached $6 per gallon. Politicians including Gov. Janet Mills, and all three major gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett, have called for helping Maine residents afford heating oil this winter.
Friedmann said that when the Legislature convenes in January, a top priority will be figuring out “how to keep our constituents from freezing.”
The federal Low Income Heating Assistance Program helps about 40,000 Maine people with their heating costs. But the roughly $27 million in heating oil funding expected this winter won’t begin arriving until late this month and about $4 million leftover from last winter will be used to jumpstart the program for those who are most vulnerable and applied early, MaineHousing announced this week.
About 23,000 fewer Mainers had SNAP benefits in August 2026 compared with July 2025, when the budget bill was passed, according to an analysis by the Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Friedmann said Maine will do what it can to help, but state government will not be able to restore cuts made by the federal government to programs like Medicaid and SNAP.
“The state of Maine doesn’t have the resources of the federal government,” Friedmann said. “We can’t make up for the billions in healthcare cuts that the feds are passing on to us.”
James Myall, policy analyst for the Maine Center for Economic Policy, said the state is facing about $350 million in cutbacks to Medicaid and SNAP.
Myall said the state can do some things to reduce negative impacts, such as providing a few extra months of SNAP benefits for people who are about to lose SNAP eligibility.
“It’s a matter of trying to find a way to provide extra help for people, and balancing that with the state having enough money to do it,” Myall said.
Fecteau said state lawmakers are also looking at ways to help hospitals, which are struggling financially, cutting services like birthing centers or closing. That’s before funding losses begin next year under the Medicaid cutbacks.
Fecteau said “we obviously need serious help from Washington,” but there’s also a “real urgency” for the state Legislature to help Maine’s hospitals.
“We need to have all parties at the table having a real earnest conversation about what the future of healthcare delivery looks like across the state,” Fecteau said.
Medicaid work requirements that start in January 2027 will mandate that some recipients work, volunteer or attend school 80 hours per month or lose their Medicaid insurance.
Fecteau said one of his priorities will be to ensure that people who are eligible for Medicaid maintain their benefits and “don’t get discouraged and don’t walk away from the process because they can’t make sense of these new requirements.”
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services hired 35 staffers to help administer the new work requirements, with a goal of ensuring eligible people maintain Medicaid enrollment, state officials have said.

title: Wife of ex-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro seeks release from US jail
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The wife of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was set to be back in court Thursday, where her lawyers will urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.
Both have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They face potential life prison sentences if convicted of being part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail, and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she also suffers from “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital, when care was needed.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence.”

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
text:
Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
A U.S. congressional candidate in Arizona, Bernadette Greene-Placentia, says she was raped by two men while she was repairing one of her campaign signs.
Greene-Placentia said it happened Aug. 14 around 2 or 3 a.m. in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City, according to an incident report from the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office shared by her campaign.
Greene-Placentia reported the alleged rape to the sheriff's office more than two weeks later on Aug. 31, according to the report.
"When it first happened, I didn't want to tell anybody," she told The New York Times on Wednesday. "I was embarrassed that I couldn't defend myself," she said.
CNN has sought comment from Greene-Placentia. The sheriff's office is investigating the case, it said Wednesday.
The Democratic candidate for Arizona's 8th congressional district, which includes parts of Phoenix and nearby areas including Sun City, was out putting up and fixing political signage and was hit in the back of her head by two unknown men while walking back to her vehicle, the incident report says.
Greene-Placentia lost consciousness and does not recall how she was hit in the head or how many times, according to the report, which says she and investigators have not been able to determine the exact location of the attack.
She woke up to the pain of one of the men raping her while holding her down, according to the report. She "described having bruises on her arms from being held down."
The other man then raped her, the report says. She said she also recalls seeing her feet as she fought back by kicking.
Greene-Placentia does not remember what the men looked like or what they were wearing, according to the report.
"She only recalled one of them wearing black boots and having small feet," the incident report reads.
She recalled to investigators that one of the men said "Democratic b----" at some point during the incident, the report states. But, on Wednesday, she said she could not be sure what she had heard, according to The New York Times.
The incident report says that she did not take any pictures of the bruises on her body or the bump on her head following the incident.
She told deputies that "immediately after the sexual assault, she went home and took three showers and a bath." Greene-Placentia did not go to a hospital or get a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) exam.
"I asked Bernadette if there was any DNA left on her clothing, which she stated she has washed the clothes since then," an investigator wrote in the incident report.
Both men remain "truly unknown," the report adds.
"I look back and it's like, why didn't I go to the hospital?" she told CNN affiliate KNXV. "I'd always considered myself a strong person, and so I was embarrassed."
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office followed up with Greene-Placentia on Sept. 1, and she provided more details of her injuries.
She explained she was struck on the left side of the back of her head, which had a significant bump on it. She also had three vertical bruises that appeared to be in the shape of a hand on her left arm, according to the report.
Greene-Placentia also stated she experienced vaginal bleeding for two to three days following the assault. She also told the sheriff's office her assailants may have been white men.
"She did not recall if the male subjects left by foot or got into a vehicle," the incident report says.
According to the report, she did not tell anyone of the incident until two to three days later, when she talked to her husband, Alexander Placentia, and two campaign staff members.
After the initial reluctance to speak out, Greene-Placentia felt she would be a "hypocrite" if she didn't go public, she told The New York Times.
"I don't want my campaign to be about this," she said to the newspaper, "but women need to know it's OK to come forward."
The New York Times reported that Greene-Placentia was concerned coming forward would be viewed as a political gambit. A former long-haul trucker, she "feared that her campaign’s messaging around affordability and health care would be overshadowed," the article said.
"Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette," campaign spokesperson Craig Beckman said in a statement to CNN on Wednesday. "She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone."
The Times said Greene-Placentia "no longer installs or repairs campaign signs alone after dark, a habit she had adopted to avoid the punishing Arizona summer heat."
Greene-Placentia's political opponent, incumbent U.S. Rep. Abraham Hamadeh, said in a statement to the Times that law enforcement should "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place, in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law."
Greene-Placentia told KNXV she hopes speaking out will help other survivors.
"I believe very strongly in women's bodily autonomy, and I was angry that these men used their physical size to take that autonomy from me," Greene-Placentia said. "Speaking up was me taking it back."

title: Cornell gang-rape accuser has been receiving death threats, attorney says
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — The woman accusing several men of raping her at a Cornell University fraternity party was “misled” about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday.
Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell’s internal disciplinary process, the university’s police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press.
In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police.
Van Houten has said that he asked Cornell’s police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer.
Giuffra said the woman was told that the criminal investigation was ongoing.
“I think she was misled. She was told it was still — they weren’t going to prosecute, but they were still investigating,” Giuffra said. “I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren’t doing anything.”
Giuffra added that at the time, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.
“But nothing was being done, and we didn’t know that,” Giuffra said.
A message seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell’s media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university’s police department.
The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident that no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman’s account, written by a police officer.
Summary left out key details, lawyer says
Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman’s participation in drug use and sex was “voluntary, conscious and consensual.”
That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month.
Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available.
Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, The New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten’s office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed.
“At first I thought these police were incompetent,” Giuffra said. “It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down.”
Giuffra said that while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support, including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults.
Students rally against sexual violence
Some Cornell students staged a sit-in at a dining hall and vowed not to spend money on campus Wednesday to protest sexual violence and how the university has handled complaints, in the latest expression of outrage over an alleged 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
A handwritten sign reading “Justice for Jane Doe” — the name under which the accuser is suing — was propped on an empty table in the dining hall in the afternoon. Some students sat around the room without eating, while others lunched. Another small group sat outside holding signs with messages such as “we are Jane Doe.”
The demonstrations were meant to spotlight complaints that the university is slow to respond to reports of sexual assault while quick to protect its reputation. Among other demands, the groups want the university to retool disciplinary procedures for addressing complaints and expel or revoke the degrees of anyone involved in the alleged October 2024 sexual assault.
Jane Doe, who was a student then, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month.
Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.
Man in lawsuit wants attorney general removed
The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, Van Houten said he was reopening the investigation. Days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul took the case away from him and appointed the state’s attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor.
Giuffra applauded the move, saying he was troubled by Van Houten’s plan for conducting the reopened investigation and “didn’t think he was up to the task.” Giuffra said the district attorney wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel within two weeks.
That timeline, leaving little time to review evidence or interview witnesses, suggested that Van Houten may have been trying “to go take a dive and not really give it his best effort and not do any investigation,” Giuffra said.
James hasn’t said how long her investigation might take, but she suggested it would take months.
On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit filed a court petition seeking James’ removal from the case, arguing she showed bias by posting on social media a few days before her appointment: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.”
A spokesperson for James declined to comment.
Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.
This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.
___
Sisak reported from New York.

title: Maine Supreme Judicial Court hears arguments over deadly fall at Prouts Neck Cliff Walk
text:
BATH, Maine (WMTW) - The Maine Supreme Judicial Court heard arguments Wednesday over whether the Black Point Inn can be held responsible for a Georgia woman’s deadly fall from the Prouts Neck Cliff Walk in 2022.
The oral arguments were held at Morse High School in Bath.
The case is before Maine’s highest court after a Cumberland County Superior Court judge granted summary judgment to the owners and operators of the Black Point Inn.
The appeal centers on whether an innkeeper can owe its guests a duty of care on nearby property the inn does not own or maintain.
Both sides acknowledged that the Black Point Inn does not own or control the Prouts Neck Cliff Walk, but the attorney for the woman’s estate argued that the hotel heavily marketed the Cliff Walk as an amenity.
“It’s disingenuous for the Black Point Inn to have advertised this amenity, to have policed its parking lot to make sure that anyone there was paying money to it, to invite their guests to use it, to hand them maps,” said attorney Charles King.
King also said the inn had a heightened duty to warn the woman of danger.
Tiffany Ottenga, the attorney representing the Black Point Inn, said the hotel “indisputably” did not owe a duty to the appellants.
“(The hotel) did not own, control, maintain or possess the cliff walk,” Ottenga said.
It is unclear when the Supreme Judicial Court will make a decision.
Four years since a woman’s deadly fall
The question is being asked by the family of Ramona Gowens, who was vacationing in Maine with her sister, Sonia Hall, in September 2022 when she died. According to court records, the pair walked from the inn on the Cliff Walk and stopped to take photographs near a fence overlooking the coast. When Gowens leaned against the fence, it gave way, and she fell backward through brush and into a steep, 30-foot-deep chasm. She later died from her injuries.
Claims of negligence and a “duty to warn of dangers”
The estate and Hall sued BPI Partners, LLC, which owns the property and buildings where the inn is located, and Migis Hotel Group, LLC, which operates the inn. The defendants initially sought dismissal, arguing they had no duty to the plaintiffs because the accident occurred off the inn’s property. That motion was denied. After discovery, the defendants again argued they owed no duty regarding the Cliff Walk, and the Superior Court granted summary judgment in their favor. The plaintiffs appealed in February 2026.
The plaintiffs are now seeking to reverse that decision and allow their claims to proceed to trial.
Their attorneys argue Maine law recognizes a heightened duty between an innkeeper and its overnight guests and that the duty should extend to the Cliff Walk because of the way the Black Point Inn promoted it and provided access to it.
The inn’s attorneys are asking the Law Court to uphold the Superior Court’s ruling.
What the inn is arguing
In their brief, BPI Partners and Migis Hotel Group argue that the Cliff Walk is separate from the inn, is not necessary to access or use the hotel, and has traditionally been accessible to the public. They say the Prouts Neck Improvement Association, a voluntary homeowners association, maintains the Cliff Walk, not the inn.
The defendants’ brief concludes that the Superior Court’s decision should be affirmed and that the inn did not “owe its guests a duty of care while using the Cliff Walk.”
The Law Court’s calendar identifies the case as involving negligence, whether a “special relationship” creates a duty to warn of dangers and the question of control over premises.
The court heard several appeals at Morse High School on Wednesday as part of its effort to bring oral arguments to Maine schools.

title: Jails, prisons can now bill MaineCare for some clinical services, including addiction treatment
text:
Maine’s jails and prisons will finally have a way to pay for addiction treatment and other services for incarcerated individuals before release, thanks to a federal waiver granted late last month.
Androscoggin County Sheriff Eric Samson said Thursday he was looking forward to being able to take advantage of the waiver next year and reduce the financial burden on the jail, but didn’t yet know how much help it would provide.
The Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services approved Maine’s request to allow correctional facilities to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for certain clinical services provided up to 60 days from an individual’s expected release date.
Those services include medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorder, physical and behavioral health case management, treatment for HIV and hepatitis C, family planning services, diagnostic services and a 30-day supply of prescription medications provided upon release.
It’s a turning point for the jails, which have been required to provide medication-assisted treatment since a 2019 ruling, but shoulder the costs for those services on a local level.
Many jails have leaned on grants, opioid settlement funds and local fundraising, according to a January 2026 report from the Maine County Corrections Professional Standards Council.
Maine’s counties spent more than $12.6 million on medication-assisted treatment and mental health services across 15 correctional facilities last year, the report said.
Samson is among the state’s county sheriffs who have been struggling with rising costs and pressure from the towns and cities ultimately paying those costs. He said Thursday his department has been preparing for the federal waiver since 2024, meeting with federal agencies and state representatives as they prepare for the roll out.
That roll out will initially involve county jails that are most ready for the new system, Samson said, and it is expected Androscoggin County Jail will be among the first.
Samson said he is cautiously optimistic about the arrangement.
“It should provide savings due to the reimbursement, but until we get this implemented, we won’t know how advantageous it will be,” he said. “But it should provide some relief financially.”
MaineCare officials say correctional facilities will start billing for services on July 1, 2028.
Staff Writer Mark LaFlamme contributed to this report.

title: Mamdani's Oct. 7 commemoration outrages supporters and critics of Israel
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tried to thread a needle on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks by condemning Hamas’ “horrific war crimes” and denouncing Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza. It did not go well.
Instead, his comments further angered some Jewish critics who consider his strong opposition to Israel antisemitic, and pro-Palestinian protesters interrupted a Wednesday night vigil for victims of Hamas’ attack to confront the mayor and cast him as a traitor to their cause.
Mamdani, a Democrat and the city’s first Muslim mayor, has long been a fierce defender of Palestinian human rights and is one of the country’s most prominent political critics of Israel’s military actions in Gaza. His stance has drawn scrutiny in a city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel, while at times some on the far-left have bashed him for not doing enough to hold Israel to account.
On Thursday, Mamdani appeared to take the protest in stride, telling reporters: “I am the mayor of New York City and this is what I signed up for.”
A parsed statement
The maelstrom began when Mamdani commemorated the victims of Hamas’ surprise attack on Israel with a statement that began with a solemn recognition of the “unthinkable loss” suffered by Israelis but then castigated Israel’s military response.
“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” the statement read. “It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children.”
The statement reignited criticism that Mamdani harbors antisemitic views — a claim he has vehemently denied — and was blaming Israel for the attack.
“This is a reprehensible statement on the anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack by a Palestinian terrorist organization against innocent Israelis,” U.S. Rep. Dan Goldman, a Jewish Democrat in New York, wrote on X. “In the guise of ‘grieving’ with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with.”
Ofir Akunis, consul general of Israel in New York, who had invited Mamdani to a Wednesday screening of footage documenting the attack, called the mayor’s statement a “disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered on October 7.” Akunis later posted an image of an empty chair reserved with a placard for the mayor along with the caption “guess who didn’t show up.”
Simmering tensions
Mamdani, who took office in January, has moved to assuage concerns that his criticism of Israel does not amount to antisemitism, courting high-profile Jewish political allies and late last month debuting a sweeping plan to address antisemitism and hate crimes in the city.
At the same time, he has continued to employ, and defend, heated rhetoric toward Israel, which includes calling for the arrest of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he calls a “war criminal” and “the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people.”
Netanyahu, in an address at the United Nations General Assembly last month, called Mamdani “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and charged that “many Jews no longer feel safe in New York.”
Mamdani also marked the anniversary by attending a candlelight vigil at Union Square in Manhattan organized by Israelis For Peace, which describes itself as a group of Israeli anti-occupation activists. The vigil was disrupted by protesters who waved Palestinian flags and chanted.
Mamdani, who did not speak at the vigil, appeared somber while protesters booed and yelled: “Zohran, your hands are red!”
At one point, Brad Lander, a Jewish politician who struck up an alliance with Mamdani when they were both running for mayor last year, denounced the violence overseas, saying “no matter what country or nationality or religion, every mother, every mother gives birth to her children and wants the best for them, wants life for them.” Protesters jeered.
“We refused to compromise on anyone’s humanity. No amount of shouting stopped us,” Lander, the Democratic nominee for a House seat in Manhattan and Brooklyn, later wrote on X with a photo taken at the vigil. “May their memory be for a blessing.”

title: Indian actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar dies at 75
text:
Indian actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar dies at 75
Indian actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar dies at 75
Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker, died Thursday at his home in the western state of Goa. He was 75.
Patekar died of a suspected cardiac arrest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported, citing a doctor at the hospital where he was pronounced dead.
Born in 1951 in India’s western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built a career spanning nearly five decades in Hindi- and Marathi-language cinema. He was known for intense performances and roles that often portrayed complex or unconventional characters.
Patekar made his film debut in the 1978 Hindi film “Gaman,” and later earned acclaim for “Parinda” and “Krantiveer.” Patekar became popular in mainstream Bollywood films, while also working in India’s “parallel cinema” movement, known for its focus on realism and social issues. He gained wider international recognition with filmmaker Mira Nair’s Oscar-nominated “Salaam Bombay!”
He won three National Film Awards, India’s highest film honors, and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honors.
In 2018, during India’s #MeToo movement, a Bollywood actress accused Patekar of sexual harassment on a film set. Patekar denied the allegation. The case was among several that drew attention as women publicly spoke about sexual misconduct in India’s film industry.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi mourned Patekar’s death, praising his “intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence” as an actor.
“He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations,” Modi wrote on X.
Patekar is survived by his wife and son.

title: A cautionary tale of unexpected costs (and 3 great things, too)
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I strongly dislike skewing negative in my columns and communications. I find negativity to be predictably easy to manifest, as finding how any particular thing could have met your expectation better is a simple task requiring little creativity and an overabundance of cynicism. It’s one of my tenets as a writer, in that, writing a sad story or song isn’t as hard as writing a happy song, or a hopeful story that inspires. In short, making someone genuinely cry is easier than making someone genuinely laugh; which is to say, manifesting genuine positivity is harder than manifesting negativity. Cynics may say positivity is immature, or unrealistic — nay my friends, it is the oxygen we all need to breathe. Inhaling smoke leads to dying, inhaling oxygen leads to life.
In short, I really don’t want the end of this column to be perceived as negative, even though it describes a negative experience. Please use it as an instructive way to avoid the same mistakes we encountered (by relatively no fault of our own, as you will see).
Before that, though, I do want to share three incredible things I’m excited for that may excite you, too. It’s a small way of me balancing the column, too, to provide a little oxygen.
CHAMBER TOWN HALL, BATH
This is our first of three town halls that the chamber is running to bring business leaders in these communities up to speed on the new business laws they need to know about. We are setting up the next two editions of these in Topsham and Brunswick and will release those dates soon, but we start next week at J.R. Maxwell’s in Bath at 5 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15. We will do a 20-minute presentation on several new business laws. Then we will open the floor until 6:30 (or beyond if questions warrant) to hear about the biggest concerns business leaders have so we can find a way to help. RSVP at MidcoastMaine.com.
CANDIDATE 1-ON-1 INTERVIEWS
Bi-annually we do recorded video interviews with all of the candidates running for statehouse races in our region. We got a late jump on this, with other projects running simultaneously, but we’re hoping to have all interviews recorded and distributed at least 10 days before the election. (Legislators, check your inbox for your invitation, or e-mail [email protected].)
MERRYMEETING TREE FEST SIGN-UPS ARE LIVE
We’re well underway in organizing the Merrymeeting Tree Fest at the Brunswick Landing Y and we’re looking for numerous volunteers and tree/event/wreath sponsors! We’re spinning up some new branded documents this week, that we’ll add to the chamber website with more info (MidcoastMaine.com) or you can follow the Merrymeeting Tree Fest Facebook page for more updates.
Now, for the cautionary tale. It involves credit card processing fees.
Wait! Don’t stop reading!
I get it — not a sexy topic, and most business owners say “I can’t even look at those, I just get so upset.” Which is precisely the point. Here’s our story.
We have a credit card processor that has a payment portal we are required to use for online transactions. The link to paying the chamber online is on our website, but once you click on it, you are sent to their payment portal.
Card testing is the act of hackers or bots getting a list of credit cards, and trying up to ring up phony transactions to see which cards go through — if the transactions go through, they know they can max out that card somewhere else. The credit card processor’s payment portal for the chamber has been a victim of card testing over the past 10 months, and it has seen hundreds of phony transactions per day.
To be clear: no legitimate transactions were harmed in any way. You’re safe. Your info is safe. We did all that the credit card processor’s site recommended for reposting a new portal link and adding filters to the account. Unfortunately, the hackers attempted transactions have continued. Yet, the filters catch them, much like a spam filter on an email inbox — legit ones come through, phony ones are filtered out. I assumed at some point the company would find out why they are being bombed by card testing and let us know when the issue was resolved.
Unfortunately, what we discovered (unlike spam in an email inbox), we have been charged for each phony transaction attempt, even though the technology issue allowing the card testing is with the credit card processor’s payment portal that we are required to use. Though we implemented their suggested filters, which ensured the payments not processing, it did not stop the attempts. It has resulted in hundreds of dollars in fees each month that the credit card processor is saying is our responsibility. They direct-draw their monthly fees, thus it’s not a bill we have to pay — it’s money already taken.
Here’s the point: As money gets tight this winter, and people get desperate, we are likely to see a rise in fraudulent transactions, whether it be credit cards, email scams, social media catfishing, and even phone scams. We must be hyper aware of this threat. As AI continues to develop, these schemes will get harder to detect.
Which is to say, don’t let your credit card processing fees go through every month unchecked. Check all bills for added fees and question anything that looks off. Ours was an additional fee that our team just assumed was because of an increase in credit card payments, and thus an increase in fees. It was not. It was fraudulent transactions that we are unknowingly responsible for despite the transactions not generating us any income. It’s so easy to have direct draws come out of your account and to not scrutinize them — but take the time to check. You may find enough extra fees to cover other expenses that are great investments for your business — you know, like annual chamber dues. Be safe out there.
Cory King is executive director of the Bath-Brunswick-Topsham Regional Chamber of Commerce.

title: Fatal Ellsworth crash damages recovery home, displacing six men early Thursday
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - A man died and another was seriously injured early Thursday after authorities say their vehicle crashed into two homes in Ellsworth.
One of the homes was vacant. The second was home to six men with Refuge Recovery Housing.
Nobody in the recovery house was injured, but the crash left the home uninhabitable.
“That was my first thought, just the safety of the people in the program,” said Daniel Stewart, executive director of Refuge Recovery Housing.
Stewart said he searched overnight for hotel rooms during peak leaf-peeping season.
“I was up all night trying to find a hotel. This time of year is a very difficult thing to do in that in this area. So, we were actually after picking them up at 1:00 in the morning, we probably spent several hours driving to every hotel motel that we could find in the area and every single place was booked up,” Stewart said.
Stewart said he eventually found a hotel on Mount Desert Island and later found a temporary place for the men to stay while the organization rebuilds.
“I think that as terrible as this is, I do believe that things, the good things can come from this and seeing the community come together is just, it’s always good to see even under the worst circumstances,” Stewart said.
Stewart said he is nearing 10 years sober and that incidents like this remind him why his work matters.
“I mean, sometimes I just wonder how am I one of the lucky ones, right? Because so many people don’t make it. And so my takeaway that I hope that the people in recovery, especially the men in our program who are seeking recovery right now is just that this really is, this is a life or death. Our decisions matter,” Stewart said.
Stewart said the damage to the house is a setback for the organization but called it a motivator to continue its work.
“We’re not going to let this stop us or even slow us down. If anything, we’re going to use this to motivate us, to open up more homes, to provide more resources, to get the community even more involved in supporting one another because we know this can happen. But, it’s going to take everybody coming together and saying, we’ve had enough of this. We’ve had enough of just watching just addiction and all of just the drugs and alcohol running rampant in our communities, just the destruction and everything that it’s caused. We’ve had enough, and we’re going to do everything we can and save as many people as possible,” Stewart said.
Police said a passenger in the car that hit the house, 23-year-old Paul Meservey of Orrington, was killed in the crash.
The driver, 19-year-old Landon Rockwell of Dedham, was flown to a Bangor hospital. There has been no update on his condition.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Meet the 95-year-old university volunteer who has a fern named for her
text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (Aging Untold) — For 28 years, Hilda White has shown up at the University of Vermont’s Pringle Herbarium to do a job most people have never heard of: mounting plants.
The 95-year-old has carefully preserved more than 50,000 plant specimens at the herbarium, which is kind of a library for plants.
“I can’t draw, but this is my artistic outlet,” she said.
She presses and affixes them to archival paper so they can be studied and referenced for generations to come.
“If I mount the plants, the plants will be around for hundreds of years, barring any unforeseen accidents or anything,” White said.
Birthday gift unlike any other
For her 95th birthday, the herbarium gave White a gift unlike any other: a newly discovered fern, found in Colombia in 2023, was officially named for her.
The plant is a Christmas fern.
Wes Testo, who is now the director of the Pringle Herbarium collection, discovered it during a research trip to South America.
“I was walking through the forest there, and I saw this just spectacular fern,” Testo said. “I knew immediately it was something I hadn’t seen before.”
Testo and his colleagues decided to name it for White: Polystichum hildae.
“Oh, I was absolutely blown away,” White said when she learned of the honor. “You can’t imagine, I cried all afternoon.”
Preserving history
Testo said White’s contributions have been essential to the research conducted in the collection.
The collection’s survival is something neither White nor Testo take for granted.
In 2017, a fire broke out at Torrey Hall, where the collection was housed at the time. Testo was in South America doing research when he received word.
“All I could see from an email in Colombia — the roof on fire. I thought my whole Ph.D. was going up in flames along with the rest of the collection here,” Testo said.
White was on her way to work when the fire broke out. Staff and volunteers, including White, worked to restore and remount the damaged plants.
No plans to stop
White says she has no plans to stop volunteering at the university.
“Oh no! I’ll be here as long as I can,” she said.
