text:
Classic LaVerdiere’s Halloween Commercials Every Mainer Remembers
Now THIS is old-school spooky, Maine!
Any old-school Mainer remembers LaVerdiere’s Super Drug Stores. At its peak, the company operated more than 70 stores throughout Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont.
LaVerdiere’s began in 1922 in Waterville, Maine, starting out as a small newsstand and soda fountain before eventually becoming a full-service drug store.
Aside from the pharmacy, the stores sold general items, as well as toys and Halloween and Christmas decorations. In the 1980s, some LaVerdiere’s locations even featured an arcade called Action Family Arcade. The company was purchased by Rite Aid in 1994.
Read More: Take A Maine Fall Foliage Train Ride On The Leaf Peeper
I spent many a teenage afternoon there at the Action Family Arcade. We always had a plan: Walk from the Tree Streets in Bangor, head up Broadway, hit LaVerdiere’s arcade, fill the air hockey machine with about twenty bucks’ worth of quarters, proceed to do battle and annoy everyone else in the room, then walk up Broadway all the way to Dairy Queen.
Once we got there, we’d fill the jukebox with even more quarters, playing the hits of the day, then order a “Full Meal Deal,” which consisted of a Brazier burger, fries, a soda, and, best of all, a hot fudge sundae.
I also have another fond memory of LaVerdiere’s because one of my childhood buddies, Mark, worked at the downtown location when he was a junior at Bangor High School. Boy, did we give him a hard time whenever he put that lame smock on.
LaVerdiere’s was always famous for its Halloween and Christmas TV ads, and through the magic of YouTube, we found two spooky ads from 1989 and 1992.

title: Groom carries bride to altar after she suffers rare artery tear, stroke on wedding day
text:
'Let's sit down, marry, let's go to the ER': Groom carries bride to altar after she suffers stroke on wedding day
What was supposed to be the start of a new chapter for Anna and Connor Lasco turned into a medical emergency on their wedding day.
The couple said Anna began feeling dizzy while getting ready for their Sept. 5 wedding in Rochester, New York. Her symptoms quickly worsened.
"I had this loud buzzing noise in my left ear," Anna Lasco said. "And suddenly my leg, left leg specifically, like, gave out under me."
She said her vertigo became severe and her speech was affected.
"It sounded like I was intoxicated," Anna Lasco said. "People actually asked me if I was intoxicated."
Connor Lasco said he knew something was wrong when he saw her.
"When I did arrive at that venue and was called in there… her eyes were very wide," Connor Lasco said. "And that's really when I kind of felt something wasn't normal."
Couple still gets married, then heads to hospital
The couple still got married, but Connor carried Anna to the altar because she could no longer walk reliably. After the ceremony, they went straight to the hospital.
Doctors diagnosed Anna with a left vertebral artery dissection, a tear in an artery that supplies blood to the brain. She was later flown by helicopter to another hospital, where doctors said she had suffered a stroke.
Doctor explains rare condition
Dr. Faisal Aziz, chief of vascular surgery at Penn State Health, said a dissection is essentially a tear inside a blood vessel.
He said vertebral artery dissections can be difficult to recognize because symptoms may start with dizziness, nonspecific headaches, vertigo or feeling off balance.
"Usually in the beginning, they may start off as dizziness, nonspecific headaches at the back, vertigo or feeling off balance," Aziz said. "If the symptoms get worse, they can lead to double vision, blurred vision, sometimes even loss of vision in severe cases. And they can progress to slurred speech or trouble swallowing."
Aziz said the condition is rare, affecting roughly one to two people out of every 100,000 each year, but it can happen in younger adults.
He said dissections can follow obvious injuries, such as a car crash, fall or sports contact, but they can also happen after sudden or forceful neck movement — and sometimes without a clear cause.
"We have seen it with roller-coaster rides or sometimes with yoga, extreme stretching of the neck during an exercise, sometimes even with severe cough or vomiting — and sometimes without any clear causes," Aziz said.
He said people should not ignore sudden symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo or eye symptoms.
"It is fortunate that these neck accidents or traumas don't happen that often," Aziz said. "But the key thing is that when they happen and symptoms — dizziness, vertigo, eye symptoms — happen, one should not ignore that."
Read up on the Cleveland Clinic's information on vertebral artery dissections here.
Recovery and rehabilitation
Doctors say many dissections heal with medical care and monitoring.
"The natural history is actually very good," Aziz said. "Most of them, they heal pretty quick, and most of the symptoms resolve on their own."
Doctors stress that dizziness or a headache alone does not necessarily mean someone has an artery dissection. But sudden or severe symptoms — especially vision changes, weakness, facial drooping, difficulty speaking or trouble walking — should be treated as an emergency. They say to call 911 rather than drive yourself to the hospital.
Anna spent 18 days in the hospital and is now recovering at home. She said even simple movements now take concentration.
"It takes a lot of mental strength," Anna Lasco said. "It's like I actually am trying to walk."
Connor Lasco said the couple is taking recovery day by day.
"We're going to get better," Connor Lasco said. "This is the journey we're walking together."
To support the Lascos, visit their GoFundMe page here.

title: Phillips-area school district discusses possible school consolidation at forum
text:
Maine School Administrative District 58 residents were presented Oct. 6 with three options that could decide which district campuses stay open in the coming years.
At a community forum on future planning at Mt. Abram High School in Salem Township, representatives of Oak Point Associates, an architecture firm, explained their findings on possible renovations, consolidations or closures for its campuses across the district.
The district includes Avon, Kingfield, Phillips and Strong, with elementary schools in Kingfield and Phillips, an elementary and middle school in Strong, and a high school in Salem Township.
Voters in Kingfield and Strong will decide Nov. 3 whether to withdraw from MSAD 58, with many citing gaining local control of their schools.
The architect said the firm’s projections assume all four towns will remain as members.
Tyler Barter, an architect and principal at Oak Point Associates, presented three potential options, from the least expensive to the most.
None of the options came with exact costs associated with them.
Under option one, the district would move students pre-K through third grade to Kingfield Elementary School. Fourth through eighth graders would attend Day Mountain Regional Middle School in Strong. Mount Abram High School would remain, but the district’s central offices in Phillips would relocate to the school.
Option two would also reconfigure the schools, with additional renovations. Kingfield Elementary would see renovations and an addition of the main offices serving pre-K through fourth grades. Day Mountain and Mount Abram schools would remain largely as is with some renovations to update the buildings.
Option three would see a single, combined pre-K through grade eight school next to Mount Abram High School. This option would carry the highest cost.
Barter said although it would certainly be the most expensive in up-front costs, in the long term, a single campus could be the least expensive when deferred maintenance and other costs associated with options one and two were taken into account.
In every option, Oak Point recommended the closure of Phillips Elementary School due to the cost of upkeep compared to Kingfield and Day Mountain schools.
Barter said if one or both towns did withdraw … “we would have enough data now to help the district with that discussion in November.”
Closing one of the schools would act as a cost-saving measure by immediately ceasing the daily operational costs. Oak Point did not calculate the exact savings made by closing each school, but Barter said it would be significant.
“This is the very beginning of kind of a longer process, so as we start to get more information, we will work with your school board to really refine these,” Barter said.
The three options will be presented at the next school board meeting Oct. 15 for feedback.

title: Gardiner soccer is Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week​
text:
Girls Team of the Week: Gardiner girls soccer
Gardiner High’s girls soccer team is atop the Heal point standings in Class B North, a rare position for a team that has been solid but seldom a title contender.
“It’s honestly a bit of a surprise,” said Jess Prince, the Tigers’ sixth-year head coach.
Gardiner won its first nine games, including crossover games last week against Morse from Class B South (2-1 victory) and Messalonskee from Class A North (3-0 victory). On Tuesday, the Tigers remained unbeaten but settled for a 1-1 tie at Erskine Academy.
After graduating six seniors from a team that went 10-5-1 in 2025, Gardiner spent the preseason working through multiple player combinations, settling on a lineup with three freshmen and several returners in new positions.
When linchpin senior center back Sara Mansir was injured, more juggling followed.
Center midfielder Molly Takatsu shifted to the back line in place of Mansir (who could return later this season). Lexi Dyer moved from outside midfielder to center mid, and senior Kaetlyn Stevens, a key reserve, moved into Dyer’s spot.
Freshmen Olivia Ketner, Evalyn Grover and striker Riley Antognoni have strengthened the lineup. Antognoni leads a balanced scoring attack.
“She’s crazy fast and bothering other team’s backs all day long,” Prince said.
Adela Ricker, a junior first-year starter, has three shutouts and heads a veteran back line of Takatsu, junior Zoey Epperson and seniors Cheyenne Goodman and Lilah Serber that has held opponents to nine goals. Gardiner has scored 25 goals.
The past three seasons, the Tigers have lost on the road in the quarterfinals. This season, they’re looking good for a top-four finish and a home quarterfinal game.
“It’s somewhat of a surprise,” Goodman said. “At the same time, we’re working really hard. We’re excited, because my whole high school career, we’ve never been undefeated this far in.”
Predicting Gardiner’s playoff performance is difficult. The Tigers do not play any of the other current top-six teams in the regular season.
“The past three seasons, we’ve been knocked out by a team that didn’t even have a common opponent,” Prince said. “That’s why that home-field advantage is huge when you get deeper in the playoffs.”

title: In Winthrop, new helmet tech provides impact data for coaches, medical staff
text:
Thanks to a generous gift, the Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale football program has 50 state-of-the-art Riddell helmets that include impact sensors, giving coaches and athletic trainers access to immediate feedback when a player absorbs a blow to the head.
Coach Joel Stoneton also receives daily emails with an impact report for the entire team. He said that has already helped him correct improper tackling technique for a varsity player who was inadvertently dropping his head during tackling drills, resulting in impacts to the crown of his helmet. Riddell football helmets are considered one of the best in the country.
“I was able to spend extra time with that varsity player, show him the data, and fix it. Get his head up and see your target,” said Stoneton. “More importantly, medically, my athletic trainer can look that up and tell where that impact was on the student.”
Stoneton said he had already worked with the player on his tackling form. But it wasn’t until the player saw the data that his habits changed.
“Sometimes you don’t really understand it until you have a neutral piece of information. Then you can see very clearly that you’re not using the correct part of your body,” Stoneton said.
Stoneton believes having the impact data helps to protect his players this season and widespread use could further the study of how head impacts cause concussions and CTE in football players. CTE is a progressive brain disease caused by repeated blows to the head.
“The more of these helmets that are out there recording data the more we’ll be able to hone in on, maybe get to those thresholds when a concussion happens,” Stoneton said. “It’s just more information to keep our kids safer.”
The Ramblers are using the Riddell Axiom helmet. Those helmets, with an individual retail price just over $1,000, come equipped with five impact sensors. The analytic software that allows coaches to glean the sensors’ information, and is normally an optional add-on subscription, was also part of the gift. The software is sold as a team-wide product. Riddell does not publicize the cost.
Before the season, each helmet was custom fit to individual players’ heads. The helmet will stay with them through their Winthrop career. When new players join the program, they will go through the same fitting process.
“These are fantastic helmets but what takes them further as a coach and working with the trainer are the five different sensors,” said Stoneton, adding that the Riddell rep trained the Winthrop staff on how to utilize and interpret the head impact results.
Riddell is the only football helmet manufacturer that builds impact sensors into their products but the concept is not new. The NFL had a trial, voluntary program it suspended in 2015, citing data inaccuracies and potential infringement on players’ medical privacy rights.
Winthrop’s new helmets were a gift from Walter Wiacek, a part-time Winthrop resident and the chief financial officer of private equity firm Fenway Partners, the primary owner of Riddell. Wiacek and Stoneton were introduced through a mutual acquaintance. Riddell has a community outreach program that includes helmet donations. Wiacek decided Winthrop was a worthy candidate.
“He said he’d been to a couple of our games and liked the local vibe,” Stoneton said. “He donated 50 helmets and wrote a check for $30,000 to cover them.”
As a small-town athletic director, Stoneton said he needed to be sure the helmet fitting and continued use of sensor analytics would be affordable in the future. Football helmets are routinely sent back to the manufacturers after each season to be reconditioned.
Stoneton said the cost of reconditioning and updating the Riddell system for the next season or a new player is “not much different,” than it would be for any other helmet.

title: Maine attorney general’s office accidentally shares confidential case information
text:
The Office of the Maine Attorney General on Thursday accidentally sent a report containing sensitive details about active criminal cases to an external mailing list that includes local media outlets.
The 45-page Criminal Division Report contains information on homicides, missing person cases, financial crimes and more. Many of the details contained are confidential and have not been previously disclosed.
The incident raises questions about the potential implications on the cases — which include some of the state’s most high-profile homicides — as well as how such sensitive material was inadvertently sent to dozens of people outside the attorney general’s office. Danna Hayes, a spokesperson for the office, said in a written statement Thursday evening that the report was accidentally sent to a media distribution list.
“The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that. … We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine,” Hayes said.
Frayla Tarpinian, executive director for the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services, said in an interview that she was “shocked to hear about a release of this magnitude.”
“I don’t know exactly what’s on it,” Tarpinian said of the document, “but if it involves precharge information or investigatory information that has not yet been brought forward … that information is very sensitive.”
The document contains updates on active cases, recent pleas and sentences. It’s broken into numerous categories, including: murder and manslaughter cases; drug, tax and healthcare crimes; and election and public corruption violations. The first page notes in all capital letters that it “may contain confidential information including attorney work product.”
While much of the information has been included in public court records and police reports, some of the case descriptions in the document include explicit descriptions of causes of death in homicides, specific dollar amounts in financial cases, and names of suspects not yet charged in missing persons investigations.
For example, cases involving a healthcare company disclose “potential” amounts of money involved, including an instance where more than $1.5 million is suspected of being stolen. One missing person case notes that a relative was interviewed multiple times and describes their demeanor with investigators. Some case updates also include anticipated outcomes, such as how a defendant is expected to plead.
Such sensitive details becoming public can impact active investigations in a variety of ways, Tarpinian said.
“It could make pursuing a suspect harder, it could make collecting evidence more difficult and it could make it, ultimately, more difficult to bring cases forward,” she said.
It can also raise issues surrounding the justice system’s integrity, she added, by disclosing the names of individuals who may eventually be determined to have not been involved in a crime.
Kristy Winslow, a senior paralegal and supervisor for the criminal division of the attorney general’s office, sent the email at about 2:50 p.m. Thursday. A follow-up email attempted to recall the message several minutes later.
About half an hour after the original email was sent, Hayes, the attorney general’s spokesperson, asked anyone who received it to delete the message and destroy any printed copies of the report.
“Any disclosure could endanger the integrity of the criminal investigations and the safety of the individuals,” she wrote.
The list of recipients included dozens of state employees — but also journalists and email addresses for the Portland Press Herald, Morning Sentinel, Kennebec Journal, Sun Journal and Bangor Daily News, as well as WGME, WVII and WMTW owner Hearst.
Tarpinian said she feels for those involved in Thursday’s incident.
“I think we all can sympathize with sending information that we didn’t intend to,” she said. “This is just on a larger scale than I think usually happens.”

title: Wilton board approves $70,407 police truck purchase
text:
WILTON — The Wilton Select Board unanimously approved the purchase of a 2027 Ford F-150 police truck for $70,407 on Tuesday, Oct. 6, replacing an aging patrol cruiser and providing the Police Department with additional capabilities for training, towing and emergency response.
The purchase includes $48,841 for the truck from AutoFair and $21,566 for police equipment and installation through ITS. The money will come from the town’s Vehicle Capital Improvement account.
Police Chief Ethan Kyes recommended the pickup over a Ford Police Interceptor, citing its ability to transport equipment, tow heavier loads and support off-road operations. The truck will also be used for routine patrol duties.
The department received bids for both vehicle types, with some alternatives carrying lower purchase prices. During the meeting, board members questioned the additional expense of choosing a truck.
Kyes said the department relies on officers’ personal vehicles to transport equipment for firearms training because the equipment does not fit easily into cruisers.
“When we go to training, firearm training, we will take a personal truck that someone owns and put the equipment in it and drive it to the range,” Kyes told the board.
The truck would also be able to tow a speed trailer expected to arrive in late November. Kyes identified disaster response, evidence transportation and higher resale value as additional reasons for choosing the pickup.
The new vehicle will replace a black 2017 cruiser with about 132,000 miles and 16,000 engine hours. According to Kyes, the next-highest engine-hour total among the department’s vehicles is about 6,000, despite that vehicle having about 163,000 miles.
The four-door F-150 will enter the department’s regular patrol rotation and be equipped with a partition for transporting people in custody.
Board members also questioned the visibility of the department’s vehicles, particularly dark-colored cruisers with markings that can be difficult to distinguish.
Kyes said the department intends to add more visible, reflective lettering to several vehicles. He explained that lettering decisions had been delayed while the department awaited developments concerning a possible merger with the Jay Police Department.
Installation scheduling and costs have also contributed to the delay. Kyes said one vendor quoted about $1,300 to letter a single cruiser, not including the time required for officers to transport the vehicle.
The board approved Kyes’ recommendation without opposition.

title: Delta passenger stole airport tug and drove around tarmac before crashing, official says
text:
Delta passenger stole airport tug and drove around tarmac before crashing, official says
A Delta Air Lines passenger went out a terminal door at a Southern California airport Tuesday night, stole a vehicle on the tarmac, crashed it, and then tried to commandeer an airline truck before he was arrested, an airport official said.
Related video: Audio between the Delta pilot and Atlanta Hartsfield Air Traffic Control amid report of fumes
The passenger, who was scheduled to fly to Seattle, went out an access door at gate 12 at John Wayne Airport in Orange County around 5:30 p.m. PT, airport spokesperson AnnaSophia Servin told CNN.
The man then stole an Alaska Airlines tug, a type of vehicle used for moving luggage trailers or planes around the airfield, and drove it to gate 7, where he crashed into another vehicle, the airport said.
The Delta passenger then attempted to steal a lavatory service truck belonging to American Airlines before he was arrested by airport police, Servin said.
"There was a security breach at the airport. Looks like someone stole a tug so they pretty much shut down," an air traffic controller told pilots of planes waiting on the tarmac in audio recorded by the ATC.com app.
Airport crews inspected the man's route down a taxiway between gates 7 and 12 for any debris or other hazards, and planes quickly resumed moving around the airfield.
"Delta has zero tolerance for unlawful behavior, and we take all incidents seriously," the airline said in a statement. "Nothing is more important than the safety and security of our customers and people, and we are cooperating fully with law enforcement."
Jay Barr, 26, was arrested on charges of vehicle theft, trespassing and vandalism, the Orange County Sheriff's Department said. He currently remains in custody and CNN could not locate legal representation for him.
CNN has reached out to Alaska Airlines and American Airlines for more information.
John Wayne Airport, in suburban Los Angeles, serves more than 11 million passengers a year and has flights to 50 destinations.

title: Man arrested in connection with incident at US-run military base in England released on ﻿bail
text:
Man arrested in connection with incident at US-run military base in England released on bail
A 22-year-old British man arrested on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England has been released on bail, authorities said Thursday.
Related video: Trump criticizes UK for releasing suspects in alleged terror plot targeting base used by US
The suspect, who was not named, is the seventh man bailed in the investigation of an apparent plot aimed at RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.
British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident that led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday.
The Trump administration believed the base faced Iranian threats intended to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible, according to a U.S. official, who was not authorized to comment publicly on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide details about what the suspects were planning or why the U.K. thinks Iran was involved.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
Police are continuing to investigate the incident that led to scores of residents being evacuated from their homes near the base on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area.
Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the initial five suspects, but no explosives.
All the suspects arrested have been in their 20s and six have been British nationals while one is a dual U.K.-Iranian citizen.
The U.K.-owned base, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, was used by American B-1 and B-52 bombers during the Iran war.
The British government allowed the U.S. military to use RAF Fairford for what it called defensive strikes on Iranian missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf.

title: Maine’s top court turns Kennebunk High into a courthouse for a day
text:
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court became a unique classroom on Thursday when it traveled to Kennebunk High School to hear two cases.
In a yearly tradition meant to connect with high school students throughout the state, the court travels to several high schools to hear oral arguments in actual ongoing cases. This year, the court was in Kennebunk for the first time.
The program, which began in 2005, brings the court to schools each October to give students a first-hand look into how the court works, as well as giving students an opportunity to ask the lawyers questions about their case.
Each visit requires an invitation from a local legislator. This year, state Rep. Dan Sayre invited the court to Kennebunk.
“It’s an incredible opportunity for us and our students to see how the justice system works,” said Scott Tombleson, principal of Kennebunk High School. “I mean, I’m 56 years old and I haven’t gotten to see something like this before.”
Students packed the auditorium Thursday morning as the court, led by Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill, heard two cases: Bree A. Blalock et al. v. Birchlane LLC, and State of Maine v. Darrel Sproul.
The first case tackled questions about leasing contracts regarding a rental property in Portland. Bree Blalock filed a small claims complaint against Birchlane LLC for a return of payment after she no longer wished to move into the apartment unit in question.
According to Blalock’s lawyer, Regan Sweeney, Blalock was dissatisfied with the condition of the apartment when she arrived to move in.
Students Elliot French and Catie Thombs, both 16, said they were a bit surprised with how conversational the hearing was.
“It was a lot more emotionally charged than I thought it was going to be,” said French. “When I think of the law, I think of it as very logical and very technical.”
At one point during the Q&A portion of the second trial, two of the lawyers, Anya Sproule and Rory McNamara, agreed that the location of the trials affected the tone of the proceedings.
Both lawyers took turns explaining that, since the trial was taking place in front of students and was intended to teach them about the court system, there was more explaining of the law than would take place in a typical courtroom — not to mention a bit more of an effort to be cool.
A third case that was initially supposed to be heard was canceled, leaving time for students to ask questions of the justices directly, an opportunity they initially would not have had.
One student asked, “Do you actually get to bang the gavel?”
“This is my favorite question,” said Justice Andrew Mead. “But we do not have a gavel.”
“What?” the student frowned. “But that’s the best part!”
Another student asked what each justice’s hardest case was. The court agreed it was hard to say, but that any sentencing decisions or decisions involving children were among the most difficult.
“I’ll admit it, there have been times where I’ve cried up here,” said Stanfill. “We make a lot of tough decisions.”
Thombs, French and another student, Isabelle Westlander, 15, are not planning careers in law after high school, but all agreed that the presentation was more interesting than they expected.
“I have an interest in the way that people handle these kinds of criminal cases,” said French, who’s considering being an art teacher. “I do think that now I might want to go and look a little bit more into that.”
“I’m not sure I would want to be a part of it though,” laughed Thombs.
Westlander agreed. “I don’t think I’d be able to come up with responses from the judges as quick as that.”

title: The FBI has seized tools used by Chinese hackers for cyber operations, officials say
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by a group of hackers that officials say is associated with the Chinese government and responsible for disruptive cyber operations in the United States and abroad, including against the power industry, academia and critical infrastructure.
The seizure of the tools, announced Wednesday by the FBI and Justice Department, represents the latest law enforcement effort in recent years to go after a broad-based hacking campaign known to the private sector as Flax Typhoon.
The tools at issue, called “Microscan” and “FishHub,” were used by the hackers to scan, phish and hack targets that included U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure. The tools were used to target, among other entities, an unnamed power company in the U.S., Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese universities, a multinational, nongovernmental organization and Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies.
The latest operation has rendered the tools inoperable in what FBI and Justice Department officials said was a blow to the hacking operation.
“We aim to remove the capability from the threat actors. We target their infrastructure, their money, and their tools,” FBI Cyber Division Deputy Assistant Director Jason Bilnoski told The Associated Press, calling the hacking operation “indiscriminate and reckless.”
The tools were operated by a Chinese-based information security company called Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has said is closely associated with the Chinese government and is the actual identity of Flax Typhoon.
In September 2024, the FBI announced that it had disrupted a botnet associated with Flax Typhoon that installed malicious software on more than 200,000 consumer devices, including cameras, video recorders and home and office routers, to create a massive botnet — a network of infected computers. The botnet was used to facilitate cyber crimes, such as the theft of sensitive information from victims’ networks.
FBI San Diego Supervisory Special Agent Brett Lally said that the department would continue to monitor for ways that the company might rebuild its infrastructure.
“It’ll be interesting to see what this round of disruption actions have in terms of their ability to operate as a company in China,” Lally said.
____
Tucker reported from Washington.

title: Judge says search warrants used to seize property from former Prince Andrew were unlawful
text:
Judge says search warrants used to seize property from former Prince Andrew were unlawful
Police investigating former Prince Andrew's links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein unlawfully searched his homes, a London judge said Thursday.
Related video:
Justice Nicholas Hilliard said significant errors were made by Thames Valley Police in applying for search warrants, and by a judge in granting them in the investigation into the disgraced former prince now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor.
Mountbatten-Windsor was not in court, but he was already aware of the partial legal victory because police had previously conceded in July that the warrants were improper.
Police, however, had tried to keep the matter out of the public eye while the investigation continued, leading to a delay in its revelation.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and police searched two of his homes.
His lawyers had asked the High Court judge to invalidate the warrants that allowed those searches.
Attorney Mark Stephens, who wasn’t involved in the case, said the development "opens a door to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s lawyers to start to chisel away at some of the fruits of that unlawful warrant.”
The judge, however, said “the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful.”
Hilliard said he still needs to rule on whether to return Mountbatten-Windsor’s property because there’s a provision by which police can retain unlawfully seized property for evidence.
Stephens said that under English law, there will be further hearings to determine exactly what, if any, evidence would be thrown out.
“The judge will make that decision based on whether or not it’s likely to be probative,” Stephens said. “But, of course, it’s very different in other countries. For example, in America, if you have the fruits of an unlawful warrant, then all that evidence is out. But that’s not the case in the U.K., so we’ve got a few more rounds to go here.”
The judge said the warrants were unlawful because the judge who issued them had not considered whether items being seized were subject to legal privilege or another protection known as “special procedure material.”
Thames Valley Police said in a statement that it accepted that the warrants must be quashed, but said the investigation was continuing.
The former prince's ties with Epstein have long troubled the royals
King Charles III stripped his younger brother of his princely title last year as he sought to shield the rest of the royal family from the continuing fallout from Mountbatten-Windsor's links to Epstein.
While Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, continues to receive a stipend from the king’s private funds, Buckingham Palace has made it clear that those funds may not be used to fund his effort to challenge the search warrants.
The police investigation initially focused on allegations that Mountbatten-Windsor shared sensitive information with Epstein when the former prince was a U.K. trade envoy, but police later said they could also consider other matters.
Police questioned Mountbatten-Windsor for 11 hours before releasing him under investigation, meaning he was neither charged nor exonerated.
It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal was placed under arrest.
The allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor came to light when the U.S. Justice Department released millions of pages of documents from its investigation into sex trafficking by Epstein and his connections to a network of wealthy, powerful men around the world.
Mountbatten-Windsor’s ties to Epstein have been a source of embarrassment to the royal family for more than a decade.
Lawmakers questioned the relationship as far back as 2011, when the then-prince was forced to give up his globetrotting role as the U.K.’s special trade envoy. Eight years later, he failed to explain his continuing ties to Epstein in a disastrous interview with the BBC, ending his career as a working member of the royal family.

title: Susan Collins’ campaign needs to be more forthcoming
text:
In his recent op-ed column (“Susan Collins’ donors are the people we need to be worrying about,” Nov. 9) Maurice Cunningham makes a valid point that the bigger scandals in politics are the perfectly legal pay-to-play dark money contributions.
Cunningham cites, among others, Peter Thiel’s Palantir, which he characterizes as “a virtual partner of the government” with millions in contracts, including $200 million with ICE, and whose employees have given $117,000 to Collins’ political committees.
But legal scandals should not deter us from scrutinizing and holding accountable illegal ones.
Collins’ campaign officials object to reports of a $150,000 illegal campaign contribution from the CEO of the defense contractor Navatek and alleged reciprocation through government contract awards worth millions, claiming that the FBI investigated and dropped its inquiry. But they tend to fail to note that Trump’s FBI later backed off, and, meanwhile ProPublica’s reporting has presented receipts, including in the form of a check to a Collins-affiliated entity.
The Collins campaign needs to be more forthcoming. Voters heading to the ballot box have a right to know whether this “Navagate” scandal is real and what is says about who Collins’ true constituents are.
Nelson Checkoway
Ogunquit

title: At the Harbor Theater
text:
‘The Uprising’
(R; 2 hours, 8 minutes)
Based on the true story of the uprising that inspired the legend of Robin Hood, Andrew Garfield stars as the leader of a rebellion against the tyranny of King Richard II in a fight for justice.
In 1831 plague sweeps across Europe, killing half the population of England. As King Richard II and the oligarchs impose a brutal tax on the poorest members of society, a farmer’s simmering discontent erupts into full-blown anger. Within days, he leads a ferocious rebellion as thousands of commoners march on London in the name of justice and freedom.
Final showing Thursday, Oct. 8 at 7 p.m.
‘Primetime’
(R; 1 hour, 50 minutes)
In 2006, television journalist Chris Hansen sets out to make television history with “To Catch a Predator,” the enormously popular series that turned hidden-camera sting operations into must-see TV. Robert Pattinson stars as Hansen in “Primetime,” a provocative new crime thriller inspired by the real-life phenomenon and the complicated legacy it left behind.
As ratings climb and the operation grows increasingly ambitious, the film turns its attention to the people behind the cameras and the increasingly blurred lines between journalism and entertainment, justice, and spectacle.
Directed by Lance Oppenheim and also starring Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers, Matthew Maher, and Bokeem Woodbine, “Primetime” is a darkly compelling look at an era of television that captivated millions while raising questions that feel even more relevant in today’s true-crime-obsessed culture.
Showings Friday, Oct. 9 at 7 p.m., Saturday, Oct. 10 at 7 p.m., Sunday, Oct. 11 at 2 p.m., Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 2 p.m., and Thursday, Oct. 15 at 7 p.m.
‘Four Rational People’
(NR; 1 hour, 53 minutes)
After nearly 50 years, nine Grammy Awards, and thousands of concerts, the acclaimed Emerson String Quartet prepares to play its final notes. “Four Rational People” follows the legendary ensemble through its farewell season, weaving together memories from an extraordinary career with intimate glimpses of life on the road as longtime friends and collaborators confront the difficult decision to walk away from the music they love — and from one another.
Both a celebration of an extraordinary musical legacy and a poignant reflection on friendship, aging, and knowing when it is time to pass the torch, the documentary culminates in one final Emerson String Quartet performance and the bittersweet reality of what comes after the curtain falls.
“Four Rational People,” part of Harbor Theater’s “Arts on Film Series,” plays for one show only Friday, Oct. 16 at 2 p.m.
Finally
Harbor Theater is open for 2 p.m. matinees on Wednesday and Sunday and at 7 p.m. Thursday through Saturday. Tickets are $12 for adults and $8 for children. Member prices are $8 for adults and $6 for children under 18. For more information about the theater, membership, and other upcoming films, go to boothbaycinema.org or facebook.com/boothbaycinema, or call 633-0438. Harbor Theater is a nonprofit cinema located at 185 Townsend Ave., at the junction of Routes 27 and 96, in Boothbay Harbor, across from Hannaford Supermarket.

title: Less fighting, more Matt Dunlap
text:
If people were around for Paul LePage’s time as Maine’s governor, they will remember that he was in the news constantly for getting into fights with one person after another — sometimes even in his own party. The last thing we need in Maine’s 2nd District is an angry politician making enemies instead of working together to get things done.
While revenue shortfalls resulting from former Gov. LePage’s tax cuts created severe economic disparities that directly harmed low-income families, and stripped away their ability to purchase basic life necessities, Matt Dunlap is a champion of Medicare, Social Security and Medicaid. The last thing we need is for more of our local hospitals to close or lose services like maternity wards.
Matt Dunlap has the integrity and experience to lead during these challenging times.
Christopher Wright
Belfast

title: If Susan Collins wins, Donald Trump wins
text:
Earlier this week, Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign summed up Tuesday’s debate between her boss and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson: “It was clear from the beginning that Sen. Collins is running to serve Maine, and Troy Jackson thinks he’s running against Donald Trump.”
It doesn’t bother me at all if Jackson thinks he’s running against the president. You know who else shares that notion? The president.
The way I see it, Jackson also has an agenda to serve Maine that’s at least as good as what Collins envisions, even if, as a new senator, he would have far less ability to deliver on his priorities.
More important, though, is that hindering President Trump is the best thing any Maine senator can do for our state, nation and the wider world.
There are many reasons to retire Collins. And just as many to keep her on Capitol Hill funneling federal dollars back home to Maine. But looming over every calculation is a more stark reality: an unfettered president who is enabled by a spineless Congress.
Collins has occasionally offered polite objections to Trump’s most egregious actions but she has failed to rally her party to stand for something beyond loyalty to a would-be tyrant.
For Collins supporters, her civility and seniority are what’s crucial. They insist, correctly, that her presence and status in the nation’s capital benefits Maine.
We need to ask ourselves: At what point does her institutional clout come at the expense of the democracy we cherish? Voters have to weigh whether Collins has grown too entrenched, too distant from her constituents and too beholden to her party and the president.
That’s what matters.
During last month’s Republican Midterm Convention in Texas, Trump said at least three times that voters this fall need to pretend “I’m on the ballot.”
What Trump meant by his insistence that he is “on the ballot” is that voters should send GOP politicians — including Collins — to the Capitol to continue to do his bidding … or at least stay out of his way. For him, sadly, the measure of a senator is how compliant she is to the whims of the White House.
During this week’s debate, Collins said she is “not exactly” Trump’s favorite senator, to which there is some truth.
It is equally true, however, that the president wants her to secure another term. Like everyone else, Trump recognizes that a “concerned” Collins is far better for him than a dedicated foe like Jackson.
Collins wants Mainers to see her as a moderate, reasonable and independent leader in the mold of former Sens. Olympia Snowe and William Cohen. That vision has grown ever more hollow as Collins faced the difficult task of dealing with Trump. As he runs amok in Washington, she has, sadly, proved that she isn’t up to the challenge of protecting the prerogatives of the Senate and defending the laws it has enacted.
We can appreciate that Collins has delivered plenty of federal help to Maine without sending her back into a crucial fight in which she has already capitulated.
If Collins wins, Trump wins.

title: Mama bear mode: Video shows bear charging into car while protecting cub
text:
Mama bear mode: Video shows bear charging into car while protecting cub
A driver in Japan had a terrifying encounter with a brown bear and its cub near a bear habitat.
It happened near a bear habitat in Hokkaido Prefecture, NHK News reported.
Just seconds after the driver encountered the brown bear and its cub, video provided by Nayoro Police showed the larger bear charging into the front of the car, slamming into it and onto part of the hood.
The attack happened not once, but twice, as the driver remained safely inside the vehicle.
After the attack, the bear finally backed off and disappeared into the darkness with the cub.

title: Nearly half of Maine is now in at least severe drought
text:
Experts now estimate that nearly half of Maine is under at least severe drought conditions as the entire state remains mired in a monthslong dry spell that hasn’t been helped by recent rain.
The latest U.S. Drought Monitor map, released Thursday, indicates roughly 46% of the state’s area is in at least severe drought, including 5% — a chunk of coastal Maine — that is experiencing a more dire extreme drought.
No part of the state is yet in exceptional drought, the most serious level.
While the entire state has been under at least moderate drought conditions for multiple weeks, the Drought Monitor reported last week that roughly 19% of the state was experiencing at least severe drought. Now, a large swath of northern Maine has been moved to that designation as well.
That original 19% — an area stretching from northern York County to southern Hancock County, encroaching inward to the Greater Portland, Augusta and Bangor regions — remains virtually unchanged this week. The coastal area of southern and Midcoast Maine under extreme conditions actually shrank slightly.
But a large new zone representing roughly a quarter of the state’s total area — spanning most of Aroostook County, much of northern Penobscot and Piscataquis counties and a slice of Somerset County — is now also under severe drought.
That’s despite recent rain, including a nor’easter that dumped up to 4 inches across the state late last month. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates that, as of Tuesday, Maine needs between 9 and 11 inches of rain within a month to break the drought.
The National Weather Service’s Caribou office said Thursday that water levels are starting to near record lows, while groundwater levels remain below normal. And like the nor’easter, any rain this week won’t provide much relief, the weather service added.
Under extreme drought conditions, rivers, streams and wells dry up, crops widely suffer, and disease breaks out among wildlife, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Even under moderate conditions, honey production can decline, bodies of water drop below average levels, and the risk of wildfires increases.
Maine has battled drought conditions for much of the past two years, with conditions at their worst around this time last year. (More than 40% of the state was in extreme drought last October.)
Conditions steadily improved this spring before a dry, warm summer that was the second-hottest on record in Portland.

title: Maine Republican Party continues to take jabs at Pingree
text:
Maine GOP continues to take jabs at Pingree
In a press conference on Thursday morning, the Maine Republican Party says Maine can't handle four more years of Democratic control in Augusta.
Maine GOP continues to take jabs at Pingree
In a press conference on Thursday morning, the Maine Republican Party says Maine can't handle four more years of Democratic control in Augusta.
The Maine Republican Party is once again taking aim at the Democratic nominee for governor, Hannah Pingree. This time, they're criticizing the Maine Department of Health and Human Services under the Mills Administration, an administration that Pingree worked for.
"Four very young children died in a few short months, followed by years of scrutiny of Maine's child protection system," Rep. Katrina Smith, R-Palermo, said. "Our Child Welfare Ombudsman repeatedly found serious problems. The federal government found that Maine was violating rights of children with disabilities, and our children's educational outcomes fell dramatically."
The Maine GOP said these failures are a result of eight years of Democratic leadership in Augusta.
Pingree was the director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 until May of last year.
The role of that office is to find policy solutions to issues facing Maine, including climate change, workforce development, housing, issues facing youth and older Maine people, the opioid crisis, and Maine's long-term economic prosperity.
"These problems did not happen overnight. They happened over a series of years, and during those years, Hannah Pingree was not standing on the outside of the government. She was leading an office specifically designed to coordinate agency and tackle long-term problems," Smith added.
Child welfare and autism services fall under the Maine Department of Health and Human Services and test scores fall under the Maine Department of Education.
This isn't the first time Pingree has come under fire by Republicans in recent weeks. They also said that she has used her position to distribute money to benefit her community of North Haven and her family.
The Island Institute disputes the claim that the state grant money paid Pingree's husband for a film project.
The Bobby Charles campaign also pointed to the grant that the island of North Haven received. This was an $840,000 forgivable loan while Pingree was involved in housing initiatives.
This funding, distributed by MaineHousing, is available to build rental housing in 15 Maine island communities, including North Haven.
Pingree's team did not wish to comment on these allegations.

title: Don’t miss the Draconid meteor shower, a celestial event that won’t take all night
text:
Don’t miss the Draconid meteor shower, a celestial event that won’t take all night
The shower peaks around 9 p.m. on Oct. 8
Don’t miss the Draconid meteor shower, a celestial event that won’t take all night
The shower peaks around 9 p.m. on Oct. 8
The Draconid meteor shower will briefly light up the sky Thursday night — and it won’t even keep onlookers out past midnight.
Related video above: See the moment a meteor lights up the sky above an erupting volcano
The shower is expected to peak at 9 p.m. ET Thursday, but depending on viewers’ location, meteors will be visible into the wee hours of Friday morning, according to EarthSky.
The Draconids are best seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but sky-gazers in the Southern Hemisphere might glimpse a few meteors by looking near the horizon just after darkness falls.
Fortunately, a waning crescent moon isn’t expected to be bright enough to obscure the shower, in which 10 meteors can streak across the sky per hour. The Draconid meteors move more slowly than those witnessed during other showers, clocking about one or two seconds of visibility rather than a fraction of a second.
Unlike most other meteor showers that peak early morning, the Draconids are best seen just after nightfall and throughout the evening hours because of the location of the shower’s radiant point — where the meteors appear to come from in the night sky.
The Draconids could bring a meteor storm
The shower gets its name because the meteors look like they arc from the direction of the constellation Draco the Dragon. Eltanin and Rastaban, stars that make up the head of the dragon, are in the far northern sky in October, according to EarthSky.
Meteor showers occur as our planet passes through debris trails left behind by comets and asteroids, which eject bits of rock and ice as they orbit the sun. The Draconids are the result of Earth intersecting with a trail from the comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, and occur in October each year when the planet nears the comet’s orbit.
The Draconids are also referred to as the Giacobinids in honor of that comet’s discoverer, Michel Giacobini, who spotted the celestial object in 1900.
While the Draconid meteor shower is considered much smaller when compared with larger ones later this year, sky-gazers favor this celestial event due to the possibility of a meteor storm.
Meteor storms can happen when a comet’s debris is concentrated close to the comet, rather than spread out, as Earth passes through the trail, and can depend on how close the comet comes to our planet during its orbit around the sun. Hundreds or thousands of meteors can be visible per hour during a meteor storm.
The comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner completes its orbit of the sun about every seven years, with scientists reporting increased meteor activity in September 2018 when the comet came closest in its orbit to Earth. The comet also neared Earth in March 2025 and remains relatively close this year — which means that for this unpredictable shower, an outburst is always possible, according to EarthSky.
The best way to watch the meteor shower is to sit in a reclining lawn chair or lie on your back and look up at the sky with a wide view. No special equipment is needed, but if you want the best viewing conditions, it helps to be as far from artificial light as possible.
Upcoming meteor showers
There are more meteor showers to look forward to as the end of the year approaches. Here are the peak dates to glimpse these dazzling celestial events, according to the American Meteor Society.
- Orionids: Oct. 21-22
- Southern Taurids: Nov. 4-5
- Northern Taurids: Nov. 11-12
- Leonids: Nov. 16-17
- Geminids: Dec. 13-14
- Ursids: Dec. 21-22

title: Study: 1 in 4 NFL players will contract a brain disease. How does this impact Maine high school football?
text:
A recent study revealed that over 90% of NFL players’ donated brains were wracked with CTE, the neurodegenerative disease that leads to depression, mood swings and even dementia, and can only be definitively diagnosed after death.
So why would a co-author suggest youth and high school football players should “play like the pros” if they want to protect their brains?
That’s because NFL players today have strict limits on contact during practices thanks to the league’s collective bargaining agreement with the NFL Players Association.
“We have not seen that trickle down to lower levels of football,” said Charlotte Luster, a co-author of a study published in late August that found CTE in 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021.
A total of 878 NFL players died in that time frame. Lead author Dr. Daniel Daneshvar’s attention-getting takeaway is, at minimum, 1 in 4 NFL players will contract CTE. That rate could be much higher. Previous studies have also found CTE in over 90% of studied brains. But researchers acknowledge there is a bias toward donating brains when a player is suspected to have suffered from brain disease.
Many Maine high school football coaches say they, too, have moved away from full-speed, full-contact practices. The vast majority of Maine high school football coaches have been thinking safety first for more than a decade.
“We go full pads one practice a year, the day before our first scrimmage. And that’s just to try the pants on and make sure they fit,” said Kevin Kezal, who has led Thornton Academy to seven Class A championships since 2012.
First-year Portland coach Dylan Rottkov said, “I think I’ve seen one helmet collision in a practice this season and it was accidental.”
Added Joel Stoneton, head coach and athletic director at Class D champion Winthrop: “In the state of Maine, this is the norm. There are a lot more safety protocols. In my opinion, it is safer now through improvements in equipment, the protocols and what coaches are doing.”
But the coaches do not dismiss the significance of this or other studies. They know there is a direct link between football, at least at the highest levels, and CTE.
“Obviously, our high school players and a group of former NFL players are two very different populations,” Stoneton said. “But I do think the findings reinforce why football programs need to continually look at what we can do better when it comes to reducing unnecessary head impacts and taking care of our players.”
WHAT IS CTE?
CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a progressive brain disease where proteins break down and kill brain cells.The spread of the disease is categorized from Stage 1 (least) to Stage 4 (most).
Common symptoms, based on players’ behaviors and medical reports while they were living, include headaches, depression, changes in behavior or thinking, speech difficulties, mood swings that can be violent, and dementia in late-stage development.
Daneshvar’s most recent study showed a high correlation between players diagnosed with dementia having Stage 3 and 4 CTE. Several high-profile NFL players who died by suicide, including former New England Patriots Aaron Hernandez and Junior Seau, were found to have the disease.
Luster said understanding how CTE is caused — by repetitive head impacts, not isolated concussions — is the important message for high school players.
“Ninety-two percent of football players stop playing in high school. We’re not able to say 1 in 4 high school players will develop CTE. That’s not what we’re studying,” Luster said. “But the exposure of repetitive hits that these NFL players absorbed did not begin when they started playing in the NFL.”
While preventing concussions remains a key safety goal, “CTE forces us to think about repetitive blows,” Luster said.
She called it a dose-response relationship. The head impact is the dose, CTE is the response.
“We did not look at that dose-response relationship in this study, but two studies previously have shown that risk of CTE increases with each additional year you play football,” Luster said.
Another paper published by Daneshvar showed the odds of getting CTE increased 21% with every additional 1,000 head hits.
Dr. Chris Lutrzykowski of MaineGeneral Health is the medical liaison adviser to the Maine Principals’ Association Sports Medicine Committee. Lutrzykowski said, at this point, there is no “established threshold at which risk of CTE is clearly defined.” However, Lutrzykowski agreed that the available data indicates that, when it comes to head impacts, “frequency and duration matter.”
Lutrzykowski added, “reducing the number and amount of time devoted to contact can reduce the number of head impacts considerably.”
WHAT DO PLAYERS KNOW ABOUT CTE?
Before a recent Portland High practice at Deering Oaks, seniors Dom Huntington, a two-way lineman who has been a varsity starter since his freshman season, and receiver/defensive back Maddox Meas said they don’t know a lot about CTE. But they are conscious about their own brain health and safety.
“I want to be able to go to school after high school, be able to get a good job, just to be able to still function normally,” Meas said.
Meas chooses to wear a Guardian cap, an extra padded layer that is attached to the exterior of a helmet. There is debate on whether the caps actually reduce impact levels. But players who wear them say it helps. Guardian caps are increasingly seen in practices and games at all levels of football.
“Sometimes the worst impact is when your head hits the ground. I’ve done that a few times and get a little dizzy sometimes. The Guardian cap, I think it might help out a little bit,” Meas said. “My mom also wants to make sure I don’t get hurt.”
Football helmets have improved in their design, with an emphasis on lessening the force of an impact. Some helmets, like those being worn this season by Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale have impact sensors that send real-time head-impact warnings to athletic trainers and coaches.
Huntington stressed that he doesn’t think he’s absorbed a significant head impact from an on-field hit.
Huntington and Meas both said learning that over 90% of the examined NFL players’ brains show CTE damage is “a little scary.”
They also were both quick to point out that playing high school football is not the same as playing in the NFL.
“Those guys play a lot more, their whole life,” Huntington said. “They practice hard. They go to those big colleges and stuff, so I feel like they’re way more at risk than a high school player. And on our team we don’t have anyone who is going to the NFL, realistically. It doesn’t scare me personally.”
REDUCING HEAD IMPACTS
For more than a decade, coaches in Maine have realized that they need to make their game as safe as possible — especially in practice. It benefits the players’ long-term health. It also assures that schools, many with rosters hovering in low to mid-30s, can actually play their scheduled games.
“At least in my neck of the wood, teams are running with 35 to 45 kids, and for me it has never made sense to go out and bang my kids in practice,” said Stoneton, in his 31st season as a high school coach. “We do a ton of tackling drills, but it’s on pads. We work on technique. One of the first things we do in preseason is to walk through tackling technique.”
This July, the National Federation of State High School Associations called for the elimination of several types of heavy-contact drills, including one-on-one tests of strength in a confined area; blocking, tackling, drills where players begin more than 4 yards apart; and any drill — like the infamous Oklahoma Drill — designed to create head-on collisions. The NFHS statement, posted on the MPA site, is guidance, not mandatory.
Those drills have been long gone in Maine high schools, many coaches and players said.
“Honestly, I don’t think we did drills like (the Oklahoma Drill) back at Livermore Falls in the ’90s because we had about 30 players and couldn’t afford to lose anybody in practice,” said Kezal, who started his coaching career as a Livermore Falls assistant in 1990.
But a quick internet search reveals that high-impact “drills,” with teammates and coaches cheering wildly for big hits, are still common in other parts of the country, particularly at the youth level.
Back in Maine, coaches say there are a variety of ways they can reduce the risk of brain injury. Those include emphasizing better tackling and blocking techniques to “take the head out of the game”; never taking a player to the ground when doing a tackling drill; and avoiding any full-contact drill.
Kezal and Stoneton both stressed the importance of having an athletic trainer at practices and games, and improved concussion protocols.
Rule changes have also helped. Once-accepted practices — like the blind-side crackback block or a defender launching themselves to make a tackle — are now penalized.
“That’s good for the game. Kids know they can’t do that,” Kezal said.
Stoneton has another suggestion, one he knows is unpopular: No tackle football until middle school. At the earliest.
That would eliminate years of unnecessary impacts to developing brains. Stoneton believes it would also increase participation at the high school level.
“Those young kids’ bodies are not ready for that type of play,” Stoneton said. “I’ve seen so many get lit up and it hurt and it didn’t feel good and they decide football’s not for them.”
WILL CHANGES MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
The mean age at death of the NFL players whose brains were studied in the 2016-2021 cohort was 66.5 years.
Most played their final NFL game when artificial turf was more like concrete, helmets were viewed as weapons not protection, and big hits were celebrated and encouraged. As recently as 2008, ESPN ran a weekly segment called “Jacked Up” with studio announcers gleefully glorifying the five most vicious hits of the week.
When a 65- to 70-year-old first started playing football, if a player had his “bell rung,” they might be encouraged to take a couple of plays off. Maybe. In those days, if you weren’t knocked unconscious, you didn’t have a concussion.
In 30 years, will a similar study show a decrease in CTE? It stands to reason that the significant limitations on practice collisions, rule changes, improved equipment and overall awareness of brain injuries will reduce the risk of football players contracting CTE.
“Unfortunately, we don’t know yet,” Luster said. “It could be lower but, at the same time, players are bigger, faster and stronger.”

title: Meet the 95-year-old university volunteer who has a fern named for her
text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (Aging Untold) — For 28 years, Hilda White has shown up at the University of Vermont’s Pringle Herbarium to do a job most people have never heard of: mounting plants.
The 95-year-old has carefully preserved more than 50,000 plant specimens at the herbarium, which is kind of a library for plants.
“I can’t draw, but this is my artistic outlet,” she said.
She presses and affixes them to archival paper so they can be studied and referenced for generations to come.
“If I mount the plants, the plants will be around for hundreds of years, barring any unforeseen accidents or anything,” White said.
Birthday gift unlike any other
For her 95th birthday, the herbarium gave White a gift unlike any other: a newly discovered fern, found in Colombia in 2023, was officially named for her.
The plant is a Christmas fern.
Wes Testo, who is now the director of the Pringle Herbarium collection, discovered it during a research trip to South America.
“I was walking through the forest there, and I saw this just spectacular fern,” Testo said. “I knew immediately it was something I hadn’t seen before.”
Testo and his colleagues decided to name it for White: Polystichum hildae.
“Oh, I was absolutely blown away,” White said when she learned of the honor. “You can’t imagine, I cried all afternoon.”
Preserving history
Testo said White’s contributions have been essential to the research conducted in the collection.
The collection’s survival is something neither White nor Testo take for granted.
In 2017, a fire broke out at Torrey Hall, where the collection was housed at the time. Testo was in South America doing research when he received word.
“All I could see from an email in Colombia — the roof on fire. I thought my whole Ph.D. was going up in flames along with the rest of the collection here,” Testo said.
White was on her way to work when the fire broke out. Staff and volunteers, including White, worked to restore and remount the damaged plants.
No plans to stop
White says she has no plans to stop volunteering at the university.
“Oh no! I’ll be here as long as I can,” she said.

title: Bucksport council candidates differ on data center potential
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Three candidates are facing off for two three-year seats on Bucksport’s town council: Ralph Chapman, Jon Goss and incumbent Mark Eastman.
Councilor Tracey Hair is not seeking reelection.
Councilors elected this year are likely to face continued discussions about budget reductions following cuts made after property tax bills ballooned in 2025.
The town is also navigating negotiations with American Iron & Metal, which bought the former Verso paper mill site and its holdings in 2015, including the Silver Lake dam.
AIM is petitioning the state to abandon the dam, which holds back the municipal water supply. Bucksport wants to ask voters whether to take ownership of it if AIM eventually agrees.
The mill site itself mostly belongs to Whole Oceans, which proposed a fish farm there nearly a decade ago. Officials say the project is still moving ahead, but the company has taken meetings with other companies interested in the site, including data center developers, Bucksport’s Economic and Community Development Director Rich Rotella said last week.
The current council is set to vote Thursday on a six-month moratorium to allow Bucksport to update its regulations around the projects, which has met with a mixed response.
Ralph Chapman
Chapman, a former industrial engineer, scientific researcher and scientific educator, has lived in Hancock County for 36 years and Bucksport for seven.
He represented Brooksville in the state legislature for eight years and served on committees there, and currently chairs Bucksport’s community resilience committee.
Chapman is civic-minded and thinks his previous experience could help Bucksport. That’s motivated him to run for council for the last three years, he said, and he’s focused on livability for young families.
“If the town cannot provide a way for young families to live and thrive here, then the town has no future,” he said, citing issues including the housing crisis and unaffordability, and opportunities including recreation and childcare.
Several years ago, Chapman belonged to a citizens group that successfully urged the town not to partner with AIM to reopen its landfill. That potentially saved Bucksport millions in liability for closure costs, he said.
Chapman also suggested two months ago that councilors discuss the data center moratorium on the table now.
While he supports the temporary ban and is skeptical of data centers, he’s not necessarily against one. He’d listen to a proposal, but developers would need to explain how it would benefit both Bucksport and society, he said.
He suspects the town taking ownership of the dam to be the least expensive choice, and would likely support that unless new information surfaced, he said.
Chapman supported some budget cuts and questioned others this year, such as the reduction of town funding to nonprofits and social service agencies. He said he’d look for ways to lower expenses and increase revenue, pointing to the outside funding he seeks out on the resilience committee as an example.
The committee recently won a roughly $75,000 grant for initial work to create an energy coaching program for residents to save on their energy bills.
Chapman also thinks the council could pursue property tax relief by advocating for state revenue sharing and universal single-payer healthcare, which he said would significantly cut down municipal and school employee expenses.
Mark Eastman
Incumbent Mark Eastman, currently deputy mayor, has held his seat since 2017. He’s been on the town’s economic development committee since 2012, belonged to its comprehensive planning committee in 2015 and helped found local community nonprofit Main Street Bucksport.
Born and raised in Bucksport, Eastman owns Ocean’s Edge Realty.
Every town has its challenges, he said, but Bucksport has a bright future and is headed in the right direction – attracting population for a year-round community where people can afford to work and live.
Eastman is seeking reelection to help see through projects such as a 2028 Main Street upgrade through the Maine Department of Transportation’s Village Partnership Initiative and potential mill site redevelopment.
Improvements to Main Street – with $9 million in outside funds and a $1 million town match – could also add appeal at the mill property, he said.
Today’s industry can’t replace the jobs that were lost when the mill closed, Eastman said, but he thinks the tax base can be replaced.
He supports a moratorium, but isn’t broadly against data centers.
Scale is important, he added, saying a “hyperfacility” wouldn’t suit Bucksport but a smaller project – which the state has generally defined as under 20 megawatts – might. Eastman also supports adopting decommissioning or abandonment requirements.
As for the dam, he’d rather inherit it and funding for maintenance from AIM than deal with an abandoned structure.
“I don’t see an avenue that we don’t eventually end up with this dam,” he said.
Eastman doesn’t see room for more steep budget cuts without driving off experienced town staff and cutting services. He expects to stay the course unless there’s major public sentiment otherwise.
“If people want a full service town, this is what it takes to have a full service town,” he said.
Eastman plans to make this his last term if elected. He said he has stayed to provide continuity with relatively new town manager Jacob Gran, but feels new energy is important for organizations.
Jon Goss
Goss is a local volunteer sports coach, Little League leader, parent of two recent Bucksport High School graduates and employee of Sprague Operating Resources. He serves on the town’s climate resiliency committee.
He’s been asked to run before, he said, and decided this is the time.
Goss wants to attract business while prioritizing environmental responsibility, he said. He’s from Milford but with local family and has lived in Bucksport for 25 years.
“I just want a seat at the table to help be part of the team and help carry some of the weight that the current and past councilors have had to do,” he said.
He supports preparing for a possible data center and thinks the town should hear all proposals. Bucksport needs to approach all project ideas with an open mind, he said while acknowledging the limits of direct council involvement.
He’s also interested in raising Bucksport’s waterfront in preparation for higher tides. Goss said that would also be an opening to increase accessibility and replace existing pavers with asphalt, which is cheaper to maintain.
Goss describes himself as a fiscal conservative while a strong advocate for keeping the public safety budget intact. Police presence protects the town from the looming opioid epidemic, he said, and current addiction resources aren’t adequate.
He said it’s up to residents to decide on the dam’s future when the time comes and information is available on the most economically feasible option.
But Goss, who lives along the lake, doesn’t see maintaining the water level as a priority without major demand from a paper mill. He suggested a rock spillway as a less costly alternative.
The only way to preserve Bucksport’s character and community pride in it is to help residents avoid being pushed out by rising property taxes, he said. At the town level, the only remedy is economic development for the tax base, in his view.
“At the end of the day, if we don’t attract business to town, then we can’t sustain certain programs,” he said.
Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Nov. 3 at the G.H. Jewett School.
