title: Lewiston boys soccer wins top-2 showdown with Brunswick in overtime
text:
BRUNSWICK — Lewiston boys soccer coach Dan Gish said, in a game like this, all a player needs is one opportunity.
Blue Devils midfielder Khalil Ibrahim capitalized on his opportunity Thursday against Brunswick.
After an Abdirauf Hersi free kick from midfield, Ibrahim controlled the ball in the box and fired a shot that deflected off a Dragons defender into the goal with 1:39 remaining in overtime to give Lewiston a 1-0 win.
“It was slow motion for me,” Ibrahim said. “As soon as I heard my teammate Nathan (Dimandja) say shoot, everything was in slow motion. I took a touch (and) shot it. I didn’t really know what to do. I just shot it, and it took a huge deflection.”
Brunswick became the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll after defeating the second-ranked Blue Devils 3-2 last week in Lewiston. The Blue Devils (10-1) returned the favor Thursday, dealing the Dragons (9-1) their first loss of the season on their home field, in what was another classic Lewiston-Brunswick hard-fought showdown.
“One opportunity and having the composure to finish it, and not backing off for a single minute by either team,” Gish said. “So, it’s a great confidence booster. If you can win away, especially in overtime, that’s quite a feat. And we’re not done by any means.”
Corner chances
Both teams had plenty of corner-kick opportunities throughout the game. Lewiston finished with eight and Brunswick had six. On the Dragons’ second chance, in the 15th minute of the first half, the ball was loose in the box and went toward the goal, but a Lewiston defender stopped it.
Dimandja almost finished on a corner kick in the 25th minute, but his header went over the crossbar.
“He finds a way to get open,” Gish said. “He is great at tracking the ball and putting shots on target (and) headers on target.”
Both teams had several more corner kicks opportunities throughout the game, but neither capitalized. For the Dragons, even getting shots on goal was difficult.
“We were spinning (our) wheels a little bit,” Brunswick coach Mark Roma said. “I feel like we started the game well. We had a grip. Then we got away from it a little bit, which happens sometimes.”
What it means
Lewiston is first in the Class A North Heal point standings by more than 20 points over Brunswick. The Blue Devils have three games remaining, while the Dragons have four. Both teams face No. 3 Edward Little (sixth in the Varsity Maine poll) — Brunswick on Saturday in Auburn, while the Blue Devils host the Red Eddies in the regular season finale Oct. 20.
Unsung hero
Hersi took many of Lewiston’s free kicks, including the one in overtime that set up the game-winning goal. Hersi said the Blue Devils were determined to bounce back from last week’s loss to the Dragons.
“I was just thinking of putting it in a dangerous place … last (week against Brunswick), I did the same thing and we almost capitalized,” Hersi said. “But, thank God, this game, we capitalized off this long ball. All game, I’ve been trying to create something, a goal or assist. I’m happy I’m able to contribute to my team.”
Statistical leaders
Lewiston: Khalil Ibrahim (goal), Abdirauf Hersi (assist), Farhan Mohamed (three saves)
Brunswick: Declan Theberge (four saves)

title: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed
text:
Firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had described it as being “public.”
The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice on Wednesday, said, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the U.S., especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Experts offer mixed reactions on the plan
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike's botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.
When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, “I don’t recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government,” she said.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Trump has spoken out against public executions in Iran
Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on Feb. 28.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on Jan. 14. “It’s stopping, and there’s no plan for executions.”
In his State of the Union address just days before launching the Iran war, Trump reiterated, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on Dec. 3.”
It's not clear if Hasan will try to appeal
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan began his portion of the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence.
The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed him telling military mental health workers that he could “ still be a martyr ” if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, spoke with Hasan on Wednesday but is barred from offering much detail about that conversation. He is not representing Hasan in his criminal case but said he’s worried about his physical health under the plan laid out by officials, and that Hasan has not yet had access to legal counsel.
Galligan said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain but no attorney from either the Trial Defense Service or from his civilian defense when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution. Galligan called that a breach of Army regulations.
A spokeswoman for the Army said Thursday that multiple attempts were made to contact Trial Defense Service attorneys, saying they made every reasonable effort and adhered to policy.
“The civilian counsel was not reasonably available to be physically present for the notification on the 5th,” the spokeswoman said, adding that counsel was located in Virginia but did not provide a name.
The spokeswoman also said Hasan has not been kept from contacting and communicating with his counsel.
Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Amnesty International said in its report on executions in 2025 that it knew of at least 17 public executions — 11 in Iran and 6 in Afghanistan.
___
Lauer reported from Philadelphia. Associated Press writers Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix, Josh Boak and Michelle L. Price in Washington, and Gene Johnson in Seattle contributed to this report.

title: Trump honors Microsoft's CEO after Vance drops an H-1B visa hammer on the company
text:
Trump honors Microsoft’s CEO after Vance drops an H-1B visa hammer on the company
President Donald Trump celebrated tech billionaires for their contributions to America on Thursday only hours after a company run by one of them, Microsoft, was accused by his vice president of abusing the visa system to bring in more foreign workers.
It so happens five of the six leaders he honored are immigrants.
Before the ceremony that recognized Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Vice President JD Vance announced at a news conference that the tech company was being suspended from a program that allows companies to apply for green cards for skilled foreign workers with H-1B visas.
The crackdown on Microsoft revealed the tension between the companies that power U.S. economic growth and the administration's efforts to reduce immigration. Trump's team insists it's possible to spot the superstar immigrants who could lead groundbreaking companies and says hiring unexceptional foreigners has hurt U.S. workers.
"Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," Vance told a news conference. He said the company had abused the visa system. "You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."
Vance said Microsoft last year fired 6,000 U.S. workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
The tech company, based in Redmond, Washington, has 223,000 employees worldwide. It said in a statement that the majority of its H-1B visa applications last fiscal year were "to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees."
In presenting the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft's CEO, Trump took a more flattering approach and made no statements about the company's hiring of foreign workers.
"For more than three decades, Satya Nadella has been a key figure in the transformation of Microsoft, revolutionizing the company and empowering businesses, students and consumers from all over the world with some of the most capable software ever built," Trump said.
When Vance was asked about the seeming contradiction, he said, "We're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft."
Of the six tech leaders who received an award for scientific and technological achievement from the president, five came from abroad.
The president gave the National Medal of Science to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Lisa Su, CEO of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices. Each of them was born overseas — South Africa for Musk, Russia for Brin and Taiwan for Huang and Su.
In addition to Nadella, Trump also gave the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, who has sponsored the government's special investment accounts for children known as Trump Accounts. Dell was born in Texas, while Nadella immigrated from India.
On social media, Nadella thanked Trump.
"I'm humbled to stand alongside so many giants of American innovation and looking forward for what we can continue to do together to advance technology and drive American prosperity," he posted.
They're praised as 'national treasures'
Trump called the group of billionaires "national treasures," comparing them to his uncle, John Trump, an electrical engineer and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who received the National Medal of Science in 1983.
"Such a big day in the world of science and the world of technology — this is the biggest day there is," Trump said. "You're going to go down in the annals of history as being great."
The honors — part of a summit celebrating a new "golden age" of science — build on Trump's already lavish praise toward the entrepreneurs for their work accelerating the development of artificial intelligence technology, which he refers to as super intelligence. He has increasingly counted on the technology to deliver on his economic agenda and pushed for the U.S. to lead its development while resisting calls for guardrails that he worries will stifle growth.
"We have an extremely high IQ audience, for a change," Trump joked to the event's attendees.
Past winners of the National Medal of Science, which was established in 1959, have mainly been academics and research scientists rather than business leaders. The ceremony honoring the business leaders overlaps with the awarding this week, separately, of Nobel Prizes.
The tech leaders have been frequent visitors to the White House in recent weeks. Musk, Huang and Su sat at the head table with Trump at the lavish state dinner for China's leader, Xi Jinping. Also attending were Brin, Nadella and Dell, who on Wednesday was in the Oval Office to talk about Trump Accounts.
Last week, Huang and Musk were among the tech leaders at the White House to sign a voluntary agreement on developing AI after recent models raised national security and safety concerns.
With November's midterm elections less than a month away, Trump has also sought to drive home to voters how investment in AI data centers and related computer equipment has helped to boost a record-high stock market, swelling the net worth of wealthier Americans. But the message hasn't always landed. Polls show bipartisan concerns about AI developing too quickly, and high costs for everyday items like gas and groceries are dampening the economic outlook for many Americans.
Vance also said that several universities including Stanford and MIT should be investigated for visa fraud. Huang and Brin have degrees from Stanford and Su has multiple degrees from MIT.
The White House praised the contributions of Thursday's honorees.
"These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation," said Liz Huston, a White House spokesperson.

title: Obituary: Joï»¿hn P. “Jack” Flynn
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – John P. “Jack” Flynn, born on Jan. 27, 1938, in Danvers, Mass., passed peacefully on Oct. 2, 2026, surrounded by family. In between, he left an indelible mark on his children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews, and the countless people he coached, counseled, and mentored.
He attended Danvers schools, graduating from the former Holten High School where he lettered in football, basketball, and track. He captained or co-captained a number of teams, and was mentored by multi-sport coach George Radulski, who served as an important and lasting influence.
In June 1960, freshly graduated from Bates College as the first college attendee in his family, he married Carol (Heldman). Their 66 years together were filled with devotion, adventure, and a deep commitment to family. Their journey included many countries but was always uniquely local.
From 1960 through 1993, he served South Portland High School as a teacher, guidance counselor, football coach, and athletic director. Upon retirement from South Portland, he joined his college teammate, Howard Vandersea, as an assistant coach at Bowdoin College and later came out of retirement again to coach Scarborough High School to its inaugural state football championship. He never stopped coaching.
He was an accomplished athlete and coach and was inducted into the sports halls of fame at Danvers, Mass. high school, along with his sister, Anne, the South Portland Football Hall of Fame, the Maine Sports Hall of Fame, and was recognized by the Maine Chapter of the National Football Foundation and College Football Hall of Fame. He was selected to the Sunday Telegram All Maine Team while at Bates. He was awarded Coach of the Year multiple times. His teams won, but greater satisfaction came from the enduring connection he had with former players and counselees during their ensuing lives. He remained in regular contact with so many of them.
Jack’s faith was his compass. As a devoted parishioner of Holy Cross Roman Catholic Church, he lived his values with humility, kindness, and steadfast purpose.
Notwithstanding his many individual accolades, he would say his greatest accomplishments were his children and especially his grandchildren, Jennifer, Kiely, Christopher (Ellery), Tyler, Andrew, Elizabeth, Josiah, and Mary. He took great pride and satisfaction from each of their accomplishments but was never surprised by any of them. The arrival of great-grandchild, George, on New Year’s Day in 2025 brought him immeasurable joy. Jack and Carol made it a point of emphasis to be present for every baptism, confirmation, graduation, and most concerts, recitals, and athletic events of their grandchildren, regardless of where they were occurring. Jack and Carol loved skiing with them at Mt. Abram in winters and spending summers with them at Higgins Beach.
Jack was predeceased by his parents, John and Rose; his sister, Patricia; his in-laws Lloyd and Blanche Heldman, John and Patricia Monahan, Bob Nowak, Stanley Michalski, Carol Heldman, Lloyd “Mike” Heldman, and Lorrain Heldman.
He is survived by his beloved wife, Carol; their four children and their spouses, Deborah Racine (Kevin), Catherine Solario, Brian (Gervaise) and John; his grandchildren; great-grandchild; his beloved sister, Anne Michalski, brother-in-law Dan Heldman; cousin and “little brother” Len Johnson (Janice); and a wide circle of nieces, nephews; friends; former players; and counselees. who have been grateful for his influence. A better friend couldn’t be found. He will be missed greatly, but his example will not be forgotten.
Although there were too many friendships to mention all, those that spanned 50 years or more included their Bates College fellow alumni, Will and Bev Callendar, El and Eileen Guthrie, Joe and Anne Murphy, Pete and Maryellen Gartner, and Jim and Audrey Flanagan, as well as Lee and Pat Akerley, Tige and Sandy Curran, Connie and Louise Nisbet, John and Jean Sullivan, Bill and Beverly Cunnane, and Jay and Martha Vance.
The family extends heartfelt gratitude to the compassionate care teams who supported Jack in recent months, and to the Gosnell House.
Visiting hours will be held on Thursday, Oct. 15 from 4 to 7 p.m. at the Conroy-Tully Walker Funeral Home of South Portland, 1024 Broadway, South Portland. A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated on Friday, Oct. 16 at 11 a.m. at Holy Cross Church, 124 Cottage Rd., South Portland. Interment will follow at Calvary Cemetery, Broadway, South Portland. The family will host a celebration reception following the committal. To view Jack’s memorial page or to share an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to a charity of your preference.

title: Attorney for Lewiston shooting victims urges judge not to dismiss lawsuit against U.S. government
text:
PORTLAND — In a packed courtroom on Thursday, an attorney for the victims of Maine’s deadliest mass shooting said they want to know why the U.S. Army failed several times to seize the firearms belonging to the reservist who killed 18 people and wounded 13.
On Oct. 25, 2023, Robert Card — a 20-year veteran of the Army — opened fire at a bar and a bowling alley in Lewiston. He was found dead two days later.
More than 100 survivors and family members of the victims sued the government a year later, alleging that the Army failed multiple times to seize Card’s firearms despite recognizing an obligation to do so and having a duty under several Army policies identified by the plaintiffs.
They filed their lawsuit under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows lawsuits to be filed against the entire government. The government has requested the lawsuit be dismissed, arguing that it’s covered by several exemptions outlined in the act, including one for “discretionary immunity” in cases where the government’s policies leave decision-making up to its employees.
If the lawsuit is dismissed, there will be no civil discovery process that Jamal Alsaffar, an attorney for the plaintiffs, said would provide his clients with answers.
“There is no person, no other agency, no other law enforcement agency, that knew more about the threat that Sgt. Card posed to this community” than the Army, Alsaffar told a federal judge during a hearing on Thursday. “Let us discover how deep this negligence goes.”
It’s unclear when U.S. Chief District Judge Lance Walker will decide on the government’s motion following the two-hour hearing in the federal court in Portland. Attorneys agreed earlier this year to combine two lawsuits against the government — one filed in September 2024 by 102 plaintiffs, and another filed in April by a sister of one of the victims.
About three months before the shooting, Card had been hospitalized at Keller Army Community Hospital in West Point, New York, after threatening fellow soldiers during a July 2023 training exercise. Despite making further threats of violence and describing what officials later called a hit list, Card was discharged two weeks later.
Recommendations that Card not have access to firearms were discretionary, attorneys for the government argued Thursday. Because medical records state that Card’s hospitalization was voluntary, the government said there was no mandatory requirement that the government take Card’s guns.
“There is no dispute here that Card ultimately consented to hospitalization,” attorney Jocelyn Krieger, from the U.S. Department of Justice, argued in court.
In court records, the DOJ has argued that the plaintiffs cite “no regulation or policy” in their lawsuits that would have required Card’s supervisors to take specific action while he was on duty. Card was not on active-duty orders during the mass shooting, and the government has argued he was “solely responsible” for what happened.
Card had also not been convicted of any crimes that would prohibit him from possessing firearms, DOJ attorney Brandon Capece argued Thursday, after Walker asked how this case was different from a lawsuit in Texas, where the government was ordered to pay $230 million in damages after an Air Force member killed 26 people during a church service in 2017. The government appealed and settled a year later for $144.5 million.
That Air Force member had a domestic violence conviction that legally barred him from having a gun, Capece said.
Alsaffar represented several survivors in the Sutherland Springs church shooting lawsuit. He disagreed with Capece and Krieger in court, saying there are several Army procedures that would have allowed Card’s chain of command to seize his firearms.
The Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Defense found in September that the Army failed to implement several relevant policies when it came to addressing Card in the months before the shooting.
Alsaffar disputed that Card’s hospitalization could be considered voluntary. He said documents show that Card was hospitalized under Army command, with several guards present and restraints.
At Keller and a contracted hospital, Four Winds, Alsaffar said Card expressed he was afraid he would commit a mass act of violence and that he was hearing voices that weren’t there. Keller said Card also consented to letting the government take his guns upon his being discharged.
One of Card’s supervisors failed to open an email about his discharge recommendations, Alsaffar argued, citing testimony to an independent state commission that investigated the shooting. Another captain failed to contact local law enforcement officials about implementing Maine’s yellow flag law, which would have allowed the Sagadahoc County Sheriff’s Office to take Card’s firearms, Alsaffar said in court.
Alsaffar said this was the kind of “garden variety negligence” that the government has been sued and found liable for in other lawsuits.
He said that those Army supervisors testified that they believed officials higher up in the Army would step in, and that the civil discovery process might reveal that.

title: Darlene T. Little
text:
Darlene Teresa Little passed away July 22, 2026 after a short illness surrounded by her children.
Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Feb. 17, 1955 to Joan L. Andrews and Paul H. Little, she went to school in Philadelphia and moved to Boothbay with her parents after Paul retired in 1992.
Darlene worked at the Seagate Motel and loved working for the Friants. She also did home care helping the elderly with household chores, and she was a member of the Boothbay Region Miss Fires for several years.
She loved camping and going to the jamborees at the Ponderosa campground with her friend Ray Guyon, and in recent years camping at Lake Pemaquid campground with family.
She loved the holidays, summertime cookouts, and just enjoying being around family and friends. She always considered everyone her friend as she could spark up a conversation with anyone.
She was pre-deceased by her parents Paul, Joan, and friend Ray.
She is survived by her children Rocchina Ruffin, her husband Lorenzo children Lorenzo, Shavonn and Marcus, Kimberly Appenzeller, children Julianna and David William Little, children Mathew and Madison; sisters April husband Clarence, Tracy husband Marc, Paula and brother-in-law Roland; brother John; along with many cousins, nieces, and nephews.
A celebration of life will be at Evergreen Cemetery on Saturday, Aug. 22 at 1 p.m. with a gathering following.
In lieu of flowers the family requests donations be sent to the Lincoln County Animal Shelter in Darlene’s name.

Benjamin Brigman, 24, is a transient from Presque Isle.

title: One Bangor spa is blending witchcraft with wellness
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - When you think of witches, brooms, black cats and pointy hats may come to mind.
Instead of a bubbling cauldron, one Bangor witch is using a spa basin to put patrons under a spell of serenity.
The Beauty Artist, located at 268 State Street, offers services including red-light therapy, infrared sauna and a head spa.
What sets these services apart from their TikTok-viral counterparts is the infusion of owner Crystal French’s witchcraft practice.
“I’ve identified as a witch for quite some time, but not necessarily public-facing. And about three years ago was when I decided that I wanted to, we call it, ‘coming out of the broom closet.’ So, I came out of the broom closet and incorporated it into my work,” French describes. “I was a little nervous at first because of a lot of like misconception with what a witch is and a lot of it’s like Hollywood stereotypes unfortunately.”
As witchcraft spans centuries and continents, French calls the practice “a very personal experience.”
“What it means to me is that everything is with intention. The energetic part is what resonates the most with me,” explains French. “How that translates to my services is the same concept, with everything is energy, helping people understand their bodies better energetically and looking at traditional beauty services is something significantly deeper than surface level.”
For French, offerings like the Enchanted Head Spa or Ember Room red-light therapy sauna transcend one-time treats. Instead, she promotes them as rituals, another term she says is frequently misunderstood.
“Rituals can be everyday things that we do just by habit, but it’s the intent that we have behind it that’s important. So, creating these rituals, it gives people a place to feel seen,” French says.
Since incorporating her witchcraft practices into her services, French says the spa has helped her feel seen, too.
“I wouldn’t even have to necessarily outwardly label myself as a witch to have had that experience, but allowing myself permission, I connected so much deeper with the work that I was doing, and the people that were receiving the work,” reflects French. “It’s just been really beautiful.”
French says the practices can benefit anyone, regardless of belief. Through guided meditations and giving clients crystals to hold during facials and massages, she says her magic touch lies in giving patrons the tools and space to truly relax.
The Beauty Artist is open for spa appointments Monday through Friday with an occasional Saturday.
Upstairs at the same address, The Ember Room is a self-serve infrared sauna with red light therapy and a massage chair. This is open seven days a week.

title: Manson Family member Patricia Krenwinkel gets third parole recommendation in California
text:
Manson Family member Patricia Krenwinkel gets third parole recommendation in California
Krenwinkel had been denied parole by Gov. Gavin Newsom last year
Manson Family member Patricia Krenwinkel gets third parole recommendation in California
Krenwinkel had been denied parole by Gov. Gavin Newsom last year
Patricia Krenwinkel, one of the women convicted of murder in the Tate-LaBianca murders in 1969, has been recommended for parole. This is the third time Krenwinkel has been recommended for release.
After the release of fellow Manson Family member Leslie Van Houten in 2023, Krenwinkel is now the woman with the longest term in California state prison. She has been incarcerated for 57 years.
Krenwinkel, along with other followers of Charles Manson, murdered seven people under orders from Manson. He believed he could start a race war with the murders.
Among those killed was actress Sharon Tate, who was 8 1/2 months pregnant at the time.
Five people were tried: Tex Watson, Susan Atkins, Leslie Van Houten, Charles Manson, and Krenwinkel. They were all sentenced to death, but a 1972 Supreme Court decision put a moratorium, nationwide, on the death penalty. As such, all sentences were commuted, and Krenwinkel, along with Watson, Van Houten, Atkins and Manson, had their sentences commuted to life.
Krenwinkel had been granted parole last year, but Gov. Gavin Newsom overturned the decision. He did the same for Leslie Van Houten in 2023, but the full board overturned his decision, and Van Houten was released.
Attorneys representing Krenwinkel with UnCommon Law say that she has a spotless disciplinary record and that evaluations over the past 40 years have found her to be a low risk to public safety.
The attorneys point out that she was just 19 when she came under Manson's influence and was searching for belonging.
They say that Manson "exploited that vulnerability through manipulation, drugs, and psychological abuse. Over the decades since, Pat has worked to understand how she became capable of causing such profound harm and to take responsibility for the consequences of her actions."
The firm claims that political pressure "is increasingly threatening the integrity of parole decisions in California."
Sister station KCRA reached out to the governor for comment on Krenwinkel's parole decision.
The governor's office referred KCRA to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, which noted Krenwinkel was preliminarily granted parole at her 17th suitability hearing on Tuesday.
"All grants of parole are proposed decisions and become final only after a thorough and comprehensive review by the Board of Parole Hearings and the Governor," CDCR said.
In cases where the incarcerated person was convicted of murder, the governor has an additional 30 days after the board's 120-day period for reviewing the decision to review the parole decision.
The governor could choose to allow the decision to stand or reverse it. Should the governor reverse the parole decision, the person would be scheduled for a new hearing within 18 months of the person's previous hearing.
KCRA asked Newsom's office for additional comment on whether he would allow the release.
CDCR said that the Board of Parole's record in granting parole only to those who are not likely to recidivate is among the best in the country, with more than 96% of people released after a parole hearing not convicted of another crime within three years.
The board's standard for parole involves "numerous steps and use of validated risk assessment tools, including evaluation by forensic psychologists," according to CDCR.

title: Hurricane Hunters fly into Tropical Storm Isaias
text:
BILOXI, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — Hurricane Hunters flew into Tropical Storm Isaias on Wednesday after launching from Keesler Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi. The crew gathered data sent to the National Hurricane Center as the storm moves closer to the Gulf Coast.
The crew flew a WC-130J Hercules about 700 miles southwest of Biloxi, approaching the storm from low altitude.
Second Lt. Andrew Wilson, an aerial reconnaissance weather officer with the 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron, said the data collected during the flights helps forecasters understand what is happening inside the storm.
“If we weren’t out here, we wouldn’t know what this storm is doing,” Wilson said. “You look at satellite imagery and you get an idea of where the storm is, but you don’t really know what exactly is going on inside the storm. We get the data, we send it off to the National Hurricane Center. Then they take all that data, they put it into the weather models and they’re able to give us an idea of what these storms are going to do.”
Lifesaving data
Wilson monitors data collected from instruments on the aircraft’s wings and from dropsondes launched into the storm.
“I’m newer to the squadron. It’s been an amazing thing to do,” Wilson said. “Every storm that I’ve been in, although I’ve only been in a few, has been different. This storm, it has its own things going on, too. We’ve definitely noticed it’s starting to get its act together a little bit.”
From WLOX meteorologist to Hurricane Hunter
Before joining the 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron, Wilson worked as a television meteorologist at WLOX.
“I got to fly with the Hurricane Hunters as a media member,” Wilson said. “It was something I was always interested in. I interviewed for the job in November of 2018. I had just left WLOX. It’s been wonderful.”
Wilson said the public should pay attention to information released by his squadron and the National Hurricane Center.
“It’s really important people pay attention to the information we’re putting out and the National Hurricane Center is putting out, and listen to what they’re putting out. Follow the warnings by local meteorologists,” Wilson added.

title: One man dead, another seriously injured after vehicle hits two homes in Ellsworth
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) — A man died and another was seriously injured after authorities say their vehicle crashed into two homes in Ellsworth early Thursday morning.
The crash happened just before 1:30 a.m. on Main Street near the intersection of Bucksport and Surry roads.
How the crash happened
According to police, 19-year-old Landon Rockwell of Dedham was approaching the intersection when he lost control of the vehicle. It went off the road and hit a house on the opposite side of Main Street, then a second residence.
A passenger in the vehicle, 23-year-old Paul Meservey of Orrington, was killed in the crash.
Rockwell was ejected from the vehicle. He was taken by ambulance to a local hospital, then flown to a hospital in Bangor.
According to police, the first house is unoccupied; however there were people in the second house. One person was taken to Maine Coast Memorial for a complaint of pain.
The Hancock County District Attorney’s Office was notified as the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash continues.

title: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports. Her 237 days in orbit set an endurance record for the European Space Agency.
“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”
All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX’s recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston.
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA’s Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA’s first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef’s toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA’s count.
SpaceX is now gearing up for a space station supply run next week. Elon Musk’s company will launch more than 6,000 pounds (2,700 kilograms) of cargo, including the last of a series of solar panel additions, toilet pump, spacewalking suit, and fresh fruit and other goodies.

title: Christa Pike 'up and walking' after surviving execution attempt, lawyer says
text:
Christa Pike 'up and walking' after surviving execution attempt, lawyer says
Christa Pike is "up and walking" just a week after surviving two lethal injections, her lawyer now says.
Speaking to BBC, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said Thursday that the 50-year-old Pike was walking around her hospital room, taking her first steps after the failed Sept. 30 execution.
Ferrell said Pike's arms remain swollen and barely functioning, adding his client is still trying to regain function.
Turning to her mental state, Ferrell tells BBC, "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Related video above | Christa Pike's attorneys speak after court hearing
Ferrell added that much is still unknown about what comes next, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Pike has been hospitalized for a week after being injected with two ostensibly fatal doses of pentobarbital.
On Tuesday, her attorneys said, she was finally conscious and speaking.
"I was not in the room when she woke up, so I don't want to speculate too much," said Randy Spivey, another of Pike's attorneys. "Our understanding was the first thing she said when she woke up were 'Where am I?' and 'Who are you?' There's still a lot of cognitive confusion."
Spivey said they had believed that she was brain dead as of Monday night, but woke up on Tuesday "to the shock of everyone."
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
At a hearing Wednesday, a judge told the state that the Tennessee Department of Correction needs to save evidence including “anything that was in the actual room.”
Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles said she plans to issue a sweeping order that will direct the state to maintain recordings, witness accounts, emails, drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.
The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office had argued a court order was unnecessary. John W. Ayers, assistant attorney general, said some evidence from the death chamber already had been collected and logged. He declined to comment after the hearing.
Pike’s attorneys accused the state of carrying out the attempted execution in secrecy, saying more transparency is needed. They also repeated their calls for clemency for Pike. Republican Gov. Bill Lee has not yet indicated how he’ll respond.
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Federal judge in Maine to hear request to dismiss Lewiston mass shooting lawsuit
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - A federal judge heard arguments Thursday afternoon on the U.S. government’s request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by survivors of the 2023 Lewiston mass shooting and relatives of those killed.
The motion-to-dismiss hearing was held in Portland before U.S. District Court Judge Lance Walker. Thursday’s hearing concerned whether the plaintiffs’ claims and case can move forward.
The original lawsuit was filed by 109 survivors and victims’ family members in September 2025 and accuses the Army, the Defense Department and Keller Army Community Hospital of failing to adequately respond to warning signs displayed by the shooter and Army reservist Robert Card.
Family and friends of Card say he had displayed warning signs before he killed 18 people and injured 13 others at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar & Grille on Oct. 25, 2023.
The lawsuit alleges that Army personnel failed to follow policies and take steps that could have prevented the shootings.
According to the complaint, the Army violated its own policies by failing to: communicate the warning signs up the chain to the highest levels of command, exercise ongoing jurisdiction over Card until his mental and physical status had been formally adjudicated, and engage available legal processes to restrict Card’s access to firearms and communicate all relevant information about Card to law enforcement.
The Justice Department is asking the court to dismiss the case, arguing that federal law shields the government from liability for the kinds of decisions the plaintiffs challenge. The government argued “discretionary” decisions about Card’s supervision and medical care involved judgment calls protected by federal law.
Attorneys representing the plaintiffs argued Thursday that the decisions were no longer discretionary after officials admitted Card was a danger to others.
“There is no person, no other agency, no other law enforcement that knew more about the dangerousness and the incredible threat that Robert Card posed to this community,” the plaintiffs’ attorneys said. “There was no one that was in a better position to prevent this horrible event.”
The government’s motion also disputes the plaintiffs’ claims about Card’s hospitalization and firearm eligibility, arguing that his hospitalization did not qualify as a legal commitment that would bar him from possessing firearms.
In the original motion filed in February, the Justice Department also said the shooting itself, not government action, caused the harm felt by the survivors and victims’ family members.
Walker said it could take some time before he comes to a decision on the government’s motion to dismiss.
If the case moves forward, the next step in the legal process would be discovery.

title: Former President Barack Obama endorses Troy Jackson in Maine Senate race
text:

Obama cites Jackson’s record

“The fact that Troy Jackson is endorsed by Obama, funded by Chuck Schumer, and campaigning with Bernie Sanders this weekend tells you how much the national Democratic machine wants to control Maine’s Senate seat,” the campaign said.“Susan is supported by Mainers like Denise, a retired teacher, who has more money in her monthly Social Security check and Mark, whose son has better access to lifesaving insulin, all thanks to her work. Those are the people who matter to Senator Collins.”
Debate scheduled Thursday

title: UMaine men’s hockey prepares for challenging test in home opener against Quinnipiac
text:
The University of Maine men’s hockey team will receive a valuable barometer this weekend when it plays its home opener in year 50 of the program against perennial NCAA national championship contender Quinnipiac at 7 p.m. Friday and Saturday at the Alfond Arena in Orono.
UMaine is 1-1 after splitting a two-game series in Worcester, Massachusetts, against Atlantic Hockey America’s Holy Cross Crusaders, winning 4-1 before losing 3-2 in overtime.
The sixth-ranked Bobcats are coming off a 10-2 thrashing of New Hampshire and a 6-3 win over reigning Hockey East tournament champion Merrimack College.
They were the preseason favorites to win the ECAC title.
Saturday night will be Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center Lafayette Family Care Institute Cancer Awareness Night.
As a special remembrance of Deena Renwick, mother of former UMaine two-time alternate captain Nolan Renwick, who died of cancer in July 2025, the Black Bears will wear Number 24 jerseys, Nolan Renwick’s number, during the pre-game skate.
Those jerseys will be signed by the player who wore them and then put up for auction with all proceeds going to support the Lafayette Champion the Cure Challenge. The bidding will end at 11 p.m. Saturday.
The No. 24 jerseys will also be available at the Bear Necessities Fan Shop.
Nolan Renwick is currently playing for the ECHL’s Maine Mariners.
This will be the fifth consecutive year the Black Bears and Bobcats have met for a two-game nonconference series and the Black Bears hold a 4-3-1 advantage.
Quinnipiac rallied from 3-0 and 4-1 deficits to earn a 4-4 tie and a shootout win thanks to two extra-attacker goals in their first meeting a year ago before Quinnipiac blanked the Black Bears 4-0 in the second game in Hamden, Connecticut.
The previous year in Orono, UMaine earned 2-1 and 6-5 (overtime) victories.
UMaine leads the all-time series 12-10-2 including an 8-5-1 record at Alfond Arena.
Head coach Rand Pecknold’s Bobcats have won the last six ECAC regular season championships and have gone to the NCAA Tournament the last seven campaigns. They won the NCAA title in 2023.
They went 27-10-3 last season with a 5-2 win over Providence in the Sioux Falls Regional followed by a 5-0 loss to North Dakota.
They have returned nine of their top 10 scorers led by right wing Ethan Wyttenbach, who was the Tim Taylor National Rookie of the Year and a first team East All-American. He had 25 goals and 34 assists and his 59 points tied the program record.
He was chosen to the league’s All-Preseason team along with teammate Elliott Groenewold, who was selected the league’s best Defensive Defenseman last season. He was a first team All-ECAC selection with seven goals and 13 assists in 40 games and a plus-39 rating in plus-minus, which was the highest mark by a Quinnipiac defenseman in over 20 years.
Players receive a plus-one if they are on the ice when their team scores an even-strength or shorthanded goal and a minus-one if the opponent scores one.
And Wyttenbach and Groenewold didn’t waste any time putting their footprint on the 2026-27 season with a team-high four points apiece last weekend. Wyttenbach was one of five Bobcats with two goals, and he also had two assists while Groenewold had four assists.
Quinnipiac has five returnees who had at least 34 points a year ago in Wyttenbach, left wing Antonin Verreault (16 goals, 24 assists), centers Markus Vidicek (20 goals, 15 assists) and Chris Pelosi (18 goals, 16 assists) and left wing Mason Marcellus (8 goals, 26 assists).
Matej Marinov and Dylan Silverstein, who combined to start all 40 games, have both left, leaving newcomers Rorke Applebee, a transfer from Lake Superior State, and freshman Christian Kirsch to man the nets and each earned a win last weekend.
UMaine head coach Ben Barr is embracing the challenge.
“They are always one of the best teams in the nation, and this may be one of the best teams they have ever had,” Barr said. “What a great opportunity for us to play a team like this, especially at home. It should be a lot of fun. We’ll see what we have.”
UMaine has 15 newcomers and 12 of them made their UMaine debuts last weekend.
Two of those newcomers, Robert Morris transfer left wing Tanner Klimpke (2 goals, 1 assist) and Bemidji State transfer defenseman Isa Parekh (1 goal, 2 assists) are two of UMaine’s top point-getters, along with sophomore defenseman Lukas Peterson (3 assists).
“It’s going to be a challenge and I’m excited for it,” said Klimpke. “I’m looking forward to seeing what this rink is all about. It will be sweet. I’ve heard there is no other place like it. The energy, everything is unbelievable.”
“We definitely get a lift when we come on the ice here,” said Barr. “This is the best place to play in college hockey.”
He said they are going to have to play a tight-checking game and be disciplined.
“They are extremely skilled and we don’t want to give them tons of power play looks,” said Barr. “When we have the puck, we have to be poised with it and hold onto it. We can’t give them anything free. We have to make good decisions. We can’t panic with the puck.”
“They are definitely a good team and they’re highly-ranked,” said UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler. “But we are going to play our game and we will go into the weekend with some confidence.”
One of the things they need to work on is getting pucks to the net and doing a better job capitalizing on their scoring chances at the net front.
“We need to be dogs around the net,” said Fowler, who added that it doesn’t matter how pucks go into the net as long as they go in.
“If you keep getting pucks to the net, they’re going to go in. You have to trust the process,” he said.

title: Maine AG’s office mistakenly shares 45 pages of sensitive information on pending cases
text:
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey’s office mistakenly sent a confidential 45-page document to multiple news organizations on Thursday afternoon.
The first page of the document says “May contain confidential information including attorney work product” in all capital letters. It details evidence in cases, including listing manslaughter or homicide cases in which suspects, named in the document, have not yet been criminally charged.
The cases have explicit, unreleased details about how the person was killed, additional injuries and evidence police have gathered in the cases.
The sharing of such confidential investigative details could jeopardize uncharged cases by tipping off suspects named in the document. It also raises the question of how the document was sent to 76 people, including a public works director and the sister of a murder victim.
It can also taint juries for the cases that have been charged, Maine Commission on Public Defense Services Executive Director Frayla Tarpinian said when told about the email.
“Oh my god,” Tarpinian said. “That’s a huge issue. I’m sure they’re scrambling right now.”
The email was sent by senior paralegal Kristy Winslow, seemingly intended for lawyers and investigators connected to the cases. The email asked people to update their cases for a criminal division report and she attached an example from August.
In response to the initial email, Deputy Attorney General Lisa Bogue replied to all email recipients, telling people to update the list for any changes since July.
Both Winslow and Bogue tried to recall their emails after they were originally sent.
Frey’s office sent another email 32 minutes later instructing recipients to delete the documents. Any disclosure of information from the documents could endanger the investigations and safety of people, spokesperson Danna Hayes said.
“The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that,” Hayes said in a statement. “Unfortunately, a distribution list reserved to push public information out to the media was accidentally used. We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine.”
There are legal protections around what documents are released while investigations are ongoing to protect the process as well as to shield people who may be accused but not actually involved, Tarpinian said.
“From a defense standpoint, I would love to know what the police have about somebody who’s going to be my client,” Tarpinian said. “My client having information about what the police know or have is incredibly helpful in shaping defense.”
For cases already going through the legal system, the defense attorneys should in theory already have all the evidence contained within the document, Tarpinian said. She was concerned to hear that homicide cases in which juveniles are charged are included in the document.
If a case remains in juvenile court, the person is supposed to be rehabilitated and released, which could be jeopardized by these details, she said. However, that concern lessens if the person is bound over to adult court.

title: InvestigateTV+: Finding solutions for food deserts
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an inside look at food deserts, where fresh groceries are out of reach, healthier options are limited, and prices can be even higher.
Also, a dementia patient’s disappearance before dawn sparks a massive search, highlighting the wandering risk caregivers fear and resources that can be activated.
Fighting for food access
In communities across the country, more families are getting pushed farther away from fresh, affordable food.
The USDA calls it “low access.” It’s when a significant share of a neighborhood lives far away from a grocery store. The agency estimates nearly 54 million Americans live in these areas.
Food deserts impact one in three people in Memphis. Volunteers are working to feed the need through a school pantry and mobile grocery store.
The people who help search
For families caring for someone with dementia, it’s a constant concern that they may get disoriented, walk out of their house, and struggle to get home or find safety.
That behavior is known as “wandering.” It’s an umbrella term that can mean everything from escape to repetitive pacing or getting lost.
If a person isn’t found within 24 hours, half are either severely injured or found dead.
In many states, officials use emergency alerts and resources for missing, at-risk adults like silver alerts. In Georgia, it’s known as Mattie’s Call. It was named after 67-year-old Mattie Moore, who had Alzheimer’s and wandered from her home and was found dead months later.
Escaping quicksand
As kids playing outside, a lot of us were afraid of running into quicksand. But as it turns out, quicksand is not a bottomless pit like in the movies. It is a mixture of sand and water that appears solid.
According to Scientific American, quicksand can look solid, but the moment a person steps on it, the sand grains lose their grip and the ground turns “soupy.”
Letting kids celebrate birthdays
A nonprofit is bringing birthday parties to children experiencing homelessness so they can celebrate their special day while living in shelters.
Extra-Ordinary Birthdays organized a party for Yalina, who turned 7, at a shelter in Washington, D.C. The celebration included a cake, a personalized card, decorations and gifts chosen in her favorite color, pink.

title: Jails, prisons can bill MaineCare for some clinical services, including addiction treatment
text:
Maine’s jails and prisons will finally have a way to pay for addiction treatment and other services for incarcerated individuals before release, thanks to a federal waiver granted late last month.
Androscoggin County Sheriff Eric Samson said Thursday he was looking forward to being able to take advantage of the waiver next year and reduce the financial burden on the jail, but didn’t yet know how much help it would provide.
The Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services approved Maine’s request to allow correctional facilities to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for certain clinical services provided up to 60 days from an individual’s expected release date.
Those services include medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorder, physical and behavioral health case management, treatment for HIV and hepatitis C, family planning services, diagnostic services and a 30-day supply of prescription medications provided upon release.
It’s a turning point for the jails, which have been required to provide medication-assisted treatment since a 2019 ruling, but shoulder the costs for those services on a local level.
Many jails have leaned on grants, opioid settlement funds and local fundraising, according to a January 2026 report from the Maine County Corrections Professional Standards Council.
Maine’s counties spent more than $12.6 million on medication-assisted treatment and mental health services across 15 correctional facilities last year, the report said.
Samson is among the state’s county sheriffs who have been struggling with rising costs and pressure from the towns and cities ultimately paying those costs. He said Thursday his department has been preparing for the federal waiver since 2024, meeting with federal agencies and state representatives as they prepare for the roll out.
That roll out will initially involve county jails that are most ready for the new system, Samson said, and it is expected Androscoggin County Jail will be among the first.
Samson said he is cautiously optimistic about the arrangement.
“It should provide savings due to the reimbursement, but until we get this implemented, we won’t know how advantageous it will be,” he said. “But it should provide some relief financially.”
MaineCare officials say correctional facilities will start billing for services on July 1, 2028.
Staff Writer Mark LaFlamme contributed to this report.

title: How to eat well in the Maine outdoors
text:
Thanksgiving dinner with gravy and cranberry sauce.
Ramen with foraged mushrooms and green beans.
Corn chowder with seaweed.
Partridge pot pie.
Hot pot.
These meals aren’t from a restaurant or home kitchen. They are on the menus of Registered Maine Guides while they are on trails or in the woods.
“I’ve done everything from Beef Stroganoff to cherry pie,” said Lisa DeHart, of West Gardiner, who has been guiding canoe trips for nearly 30 years.
Camp cooking isn’t just about fun and flavor. A nourishing meal is fuel for a successful adventure, guides said, and safe practices are critical to avoid getting sick in remote places. Experts shared their tips for eating well in the outdoors — whether backpacking or in a campground.
“Things taste better when you’re camping,” said Taylor Boucher, founder and owner of Portage Eats, a new South Portland-based business that makes meal kits for the campsite.
PLAN AHEAD
Candace Sabol of Corinth started cooking at hunting and fishing camps across the state years before she became a guide herself. Sometimes she is working in a lodge, and other times she is cooking in a tent camp without access to electricity or running water.
Preparation is key, she said.
“What comes up with you is what you have for the whole week,” Sabol said.
Chris Toy, a Registered Maine Guide, cooking instructor and cookbook author who lives in Bath, said he often freezes meals, such as shrimp stir fry or chili, for overnight trips to Chimney Pond at Baxter State Park. Not only does that strategy reduce the amount of chopping to be done after a long day of hiking, but he said it also prevents contamination of raw ingredients and reduces the amount of gear to carry up the mountain.
“If you’re not going to be carrying cleavers and cutting boards and ways to clean up, the more you can do at home, the better,” Toy said.
When he is car camping, he still does all the slicing in advance, but more room in the trunk means more equipment. That’s when Toy packs his divided hot pot, which he said is a perfect option for a large group with varied tastes.
“One side could be spicy,” he said. “The other side could be, as I like to joke, wimpy.”
DeHart started a YouTube channel called “3 Minutes with a Maine Guide” in order to archive the skills she learned from her mentors and has used over decades. Many are about camp cooking — how to set up a dishwashing station, how to cook over an open fire, how to choose the right gear, how to make biscuit dough or pie crust in advance.
In a field with so many variables, especially the weather, guides said food is one thing they can control.
“No matter what happens that day on a river for anybody, you can always pull out a day with really good food, and really good food in the middle of nowhere makes a guest feel safe,” DeHart said.
GET CREATIVE WITH CALORIES
Sarah Holman of Portland always checks the nutritional information on her dehydrated meals. She aims for 800 calories for dinner while backpacking and has learned that a package that advertises two servings might really be one.
“I pick snacks that are the highest calorie-to-weight ratio — like nuts,” Holman, who runs a guide service called She Hikes Mountains, said in an email. “They’re heavy, but they provide excellent fat, protein and nutrients.”
Guides make meals that aren’t just about taste. Toy often makes soups for clients, he said, because they offer extra hydration. Holman has recently been adding candied ginger to her almonds in part because it can help settle an upset stomach.
In some cases, guides are sourcing their ingredients on their adventures. Holman said the best ramen she’s ever had was in the woods. She added green beans from her garden and five types of wild mushrooms that she foraged.
Sabol said she doesn’t eat meat except wild game, and often introduces clients to her favorite recipes, such as partridge pot pie.
On Thursdays, Sabol’s camp tradition is to make pizzas with bear heart, barbecue sauce, red onion, mushrooms and jalapenos. Some guests are skeptical, she said, but her recipe wins them over. This week, she planned to use the heart from a bear she shot herself, a milestone she was proud to share with her fellow guides and clients.
“It’s so much more than cooking for people,” Sabol said. “It’s helping people celebrate and share their harvest that they worked so hard for.”
LET SOMEONE ELSE DO THE WORK
Boucher has spent a lot of time thinking about food packaging for the outdoors.
“The packaging really is the most important piece,” she said. “Because you have limited space, and things are being jumbled around.”
When Boucher was planning trips as a Registered Maine Guide, she said she always enjoyed figuring out the food logistics for the group. She now works for the University of Maine and no longer leads trips professionally, but she still wanted to help people figure out those important details.
“My biggest goal is to make it easier for people and help them get outside,” Boucher said.
The meal kits from Portage Eats contain fresh ingredients sourced in Maine and come with instructions for basic cooking. Boucher assembles and distributes the meals at Fork Food Lab in South Portland. She’s about to wrap up her first season and hopes to partner with campgrounds next year to reach more people.
She said her favorites include the seaweed corn chowder and the steak tip kebabs.
Jennifer Scism, who ran a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York and won the TV show “Iron Chef,” said her Kittery-based business Good To-Go started in part because she was experimenting with her tabletop dehydrator and her favorite comfort foods.
Good To-Go can be found in stores nationwide. Most meals only need a little hot water.
Scism said her favorite is the chicken pho. The staff sets aside a bulk bin for her so she can eat it multiple times a week without wasting single-serve packaging, she said.
“No matter what kind of adventure you’re on, whether you’re summiting Katahdin or taking a leisurely walk through the woods,” Scism wrote in an email, “your meal should be something you genuinely look forward to at the end of the day.”

title: Leavitt field hockey tops Cony for key Class B North win
text:
TURNER — For all the good field hockey the Leavitt Hornets have played this year, moving up the Heal point standings in a strong Class B North field has proved difficult.
A win over another top squad in the region, then, was just what fifth-ranked Leavitt needed. The Hornets got one Thursday against second-ranked Cony.
Leavitt owned the game from start to finish and claimed a 4-0 victory. Calee Libby, a senior, scored three goals for the Hornets, who remain unbeaten against Class B teams, having lost only to Class A powerhouse Skowhegan.
“It was a really important win,” Libby said. “I think it’s a game that really shows what we’ve got and what we’re going to put out for some of the hard games we have coming up. … We have a lot of grit, and when we want something, we’re really going to put it forth.”
HOW THEY DID IT
• Possession dominance: Leavitt (9-1) didn’t really let Cony see much of the ball in the first half. The game was played primarily in Cony’s defensive zone, allowing the Hornets to launch a barrage of shots.
• Structure: Leavitt’s offensive success, coach Cathy Marston said, was due in part to the Hornets’ ability to keep their shape in attack. With players in the right place at the right time, Leavitt made the most of its opportunities.
“When we’re locked in, we really do keep the structure well, and the girls can finish,” Marston said. “They get a little feisty in the circle, and when they’re on, they’re on. We had our sticks down and out in front of our bodies, and we were ready.”
WHAT IT MEANS
• Leavitt jumped from fifth to second in Class B North. With two of the Hornets’ four remaining games against other contenders — Belfast and Gardiner — there’s room for them to cement their position near the top of the region.
• Cony (7-3-1) had a four-game winning streak — all via shutouts — and a six-game unbeaten streak snapped. Although the four goals allowed were the most by the Rams this season, coach Jenny Evans said a game against one of the region’s top teams was what her squad needed.
“I’m glad we had a team like Leavitt as we get geared up for the playoffs, because we can’t come off these 6-0 or 7-0 wins and expect it to be given to us,” Evans said. “It’s definitely a good reminder that we have to work for all of the balls that we need.”
UNSUNG HERO: AINSLEY BARRY
Libby’s hat trick will get the most acclaim, but fellow senior and forward Ainsley Barry was no less impactful for Leavitt. The Hornets’ second goal came on an assist from Barry, who caught the Cony defense napping with a speedy run and found Libby for a tap-in.
“She’s really the rock to our whole team,” Libby said. “She’s always looking for us and doing a great job of watching the field and knowing what’s best. It really shows how selfless she is that she passed it to me. We have a good connection going on.”
NOTABLE QUOTABLE
“We have a core of four or five who have been with us for a while, but we’ve added (four) freshmen (Grace Bilodeau, Aquinnah Chretien, Kameo Cote and Adalyn Williams) to the mix. They’ve really stepped up this year, and I’m grateful for that.” — Cathy Marston
STAT LEADERS
• Cony: Courtney Ramage (seven saves)
• Leavitt: Calee Libby (three goals), Brylee Emmons (goal), Ainsley Barry (assist), Savannah Boulay (assist), Riley Millett (two saves)

• Leavitt: at Belfast, 3:30 p.m. Tuesday

title: Juniper and McKown Points: Tasty happenings on Juniper Point
text:
One of the most enjoyable components of summer on Juniper Point is the coming together of families who have been returning for years and who also invite friends and family to partake in this thriving community. As we begin the second week of August it is paramount to acknowledge that JPVIS activities and events contribute to the camaraderie and joy of building friendships. It is something to cherish and share as summer’s end is approaching too quickly.
It’s worth repeating that August activities at our wonderful Community House began with a weekend of delicious fare—the annual Pancake Breakfast and Tennis Exhibition followed by the annual Chowder Cook-Off. I believe this year’s event was the best attended ever by chowder chefs and tasters alike since the first competition in 2018. The twelve earnest chowder cooks arrived and set up their crock pots and served samples to close to 100 people that had come to taste their creations. The joy created by this event was palpable from the enthusiastic cheers for the winners.
No question that an important part of gathering is eating, especially after a fun evening of Round Robin or Triples Tennis that fill the courts. Dave Taylor and Susan Kirby have done a masterful job keeping the courts alive all summer with evening tennis tournaments to include all levels of players and ending with an occasional potluck affair. Coming up this week on Aug. 12 is the “Maine Bean Suppah.” Even if you don’t play tennis, you’re invited to attend to enjoy eating a bowl of traditional slow cooked baked beans. A contribution of a side dish of your choice to round out the fare is welcome. Note: Bean Suppers date back to the 1800s in New England. Stuart McGillivary, longtime year-round resident who spent the summers here with his parents and grandparents, shared that the Community House was always the local gathering spot for bean suppers.
Among other tasty happenings, Becky Taylor celebrated her birthday on Aug. 3, and to honor her, Becky’s niece, Meg Taylor prepared Becky’s birthday breakfast, lunch and dinner. Eggs Benedict was served to start Becky’s day, followed by a delicious lunch of a grilled cheese sandwich with fresh pesto, and the finale for dinner--delicious fish tacos creatively composed with fish sticks. Birthday dessert was a mouthwatering Harbor Bar made with vanilla ice cream sandwiched between two big chocolate chip cookies and dipped in chocolate!! What a gift!
Summing up the latest on the very busy tennis tournament scene are notes from Dave and Susan of last week’s winners. Congratulations to:
Ladies Singles Champion: Jackie Browne. Finalist: Eleanor Hutcheson
Men’s Open Singles Champion: Chris Hewett. Finalist: John Armstrong
Senior Men’s Singles: Charlie Hutchinson. Finalist: Curtis Hutcheson
Junior Girls’ Singles Champion: Claire Taylor. Finalist: Aria Snyderman
Junior Girls’ Doubles Champions: Katherine Taylor, Aria Snyderman. Finalists: Claire Taylor, Abby Taylor
Other tasty happenings on the calendar this week are:
The Junior’s Weekly Ice Cream Social on Aug. 16 from 6:30 to 8:00 p.m.
The Summer Salad Send-Off—the women of Juniper Point are invited to come for lunch and fun at the Community House from 11:30 a.m. to 1p.m. on Aug. 19. Bring a salad that you love to share. Iced tea and sparkling water will be provided.
Also, on the evening calendar for Aug.19 at 6:30 p.m. is the JPVIS History and Story Telling Potluck. The 1972 JPVIS Community Cookbook put together by Kit Andrews’ mother, Lib, consists of recipes contributed by long time Juniper Point residents. It is the motivation behind this gathering. Sign up for this fun evening of conversation and eating and make one of the many recipes included in the cookbook.
Before closing many thanks to the kind and thoughtful people I begged to talk with me about their summer food memories here on the Point. Thanks to Rick Barton, who shared the story of his grandmother who loved to bake for him and his brothers and other kids on the Point as they passed by her kitchen door following the aroma of fresh baked cookies and Johnny cakes with blueberries; to Stuart McGillivary, who shared the stories of his mother who also loved to bake but loved to go out to lunch with her lady friends by boat driven by a local boat boy; to Don Snyder for a delightful conversation about his love of recipe testing for Cooks Illustrated as well as his pleasure in cooking chicken--perfectly fried with a crispy golden brown panko crust -when family come to visit; to Annie Siracusa, who shared the stories of her Italian born parents who kept the tradition of cooking Italian family dinners in their summer home here, and how she now prefers to keep meal preparation less complicated with two teenagers who enjoy local fare like hot dogs and chili dogs from Dutton’s.
Do keep the memories you make here on the Point close. Happy Summer.
