title: The Lincoln County News
text:
After wet weather forced the cancellation of what would have been Wiscasset Speedway’s Group 2 season finale and Strictly Shootout two weekends ago, track management decided to pull an audible and add those racing events to their season-ending “Fall Fury” program, which was appropriately renamed “Fall Fury XL” following the change.
Due to the schedule becoming supersized, the start time was moved up by two and a half hours. Much to the track’s surprise, the turnout on Saturday was absolutely phenomenal, with nearly 200 competitors showing up to compete across all divisions. This was completely new territory for the track, but they welcomed the challenge and opened a never-used area of the pits to successfully accommodate and fit all of the drivers.

title: How to eat well in the Maine outdoors
text:
Thanksgiving dinner with gravy and cranberry sauce.
Ramen with foraged mushrooms and green beans.
Corn chowder with seaweed.
Partridge pot pie.
Hot pot.
These meals aren’t from a restaurant or home kitchen. They are on the menus of Registered Maine Guides while they are on trails or in the woods.
“I’ve done everything from Beef Stroganoff to cherry pie,” said Lisa DeHart, of West Gardiner, who has been guiding canoe trips for nearly 30 years.
Camp cooking isn’t just about fun and flavor. A nourishing meal is fuel for a successful adventure, guides said, and safe practices are critical to avoid getting sick in remote places. Experts shared their tips for eating well in the outdoors — whether backpacking or in a campground.
“Things taste better when you’re camping,” said Taylor Boucher, founder and owner of Portage Eats, a new South Portland-based business that makes meal kits for the campsite.
PLAN AHEAD
Candace Sabol of Corinth started cooking at hunting and fishing camps across the state years before she became a guide herself. Sometimes she is working in a lodge, and other times she is cooking in a tent camp without access to electricity or running water.
Preparation is key, she said.
“What comes up with you is what you have for the whole week,” Sabol said.
Chris Toy, a Registered Maine Guide, cooking instructor and cookbook author who lives in Bath, said he often freezes meals, such as shrimp stir fry or chili, for overnight trips to Chimney Pond at Baxter State Park. Not only does that strategy reduce the amount of chopping to be done after a long day of hiking, but he said it also prevents contamination of raw ingredients and reduces the amount of gear to carry up the mountain.
“If you’re not going to be carrying cleavers and cutting boards and ways to clean up, the more you can do at home, the better,” Toy said.
When he is car camping, he still does all the slicing in advance, but more room in the trunk means more equipment. That’s when Toy packs his divided hot pot, which he said is a perfect option for a large group with varied tastes.
“One side could be spicy,” he said. “The other side could be, as I like to joke, wimpy.”
DeHart started a YouTube channel called “3 Minutes with a Maine Guide” in order to archive the skills she learned from her mentors and has used over decades. Many are about camp cooking — how to set up a dishwashing station, how to cook over an open fire, how to choose the right gear, how to make biscuit dough or pie crust in advance.
In a field with so many variables, especially the weather, guides said food is one thing they can control.
“No matter what happens that day on a river for anybody, you can always pull out a day with really good food, and really good food in the middle of nowhere makes a guest feel safe,” DeHart said.
GET CREATIVE WITH CALORIES
Sarah Holman of Portland always checks the nutritional information on her dehydrated meals. She aims for 800 calories for dinner while backpacking and has learned that a package that advertises two servings might really be one.
“I pick snacks that are the highest calorie-to-weight ratio — like nuts,” Holman, who runs a guide service called She Hikes Mountains, said in an email. “They’re heavy, but they provide excellent fat, protein and nutrients.”
Guides make meals that aren’t just about taste. Toy often makes soups for clients, he said, because they offer extra hydration. Holman has recently been adding candied ginger to her almonds in part because it can help settle an upset stomach.
In some cases, guides are sourcing their ingredients on their adventures. Holman said the best ramen she’s ever had was in the woods. She added green beans from her garden and five types of wild mushrooms that she foraged.
Sabol said she doesn’t eat meat except wild game, and often introduces clients to her favorite recipes, such as partridge pot pie.
On Thursdays, Sabol’s camp tradition is to make pizzas with bear heart, barbecue sauce, red onion, mushrooms and jalapenos. Some guests are skeptical, she said, but her recipe wins them over. This week, she planned to use the heart from a bear she shot herself, a milestone she was proud to share with her fellow guides and clients.
“It’s so much more than cooking for people,” Sabol said. “It’s helping people celebrate and share their harvest that they worked so hard for.”
LET SOMEONE ELSE DO THE WORK
Boucher has spent a lot of time thinking about food packaging for the outdoors.
“The packaging really is the most important piece,” she said. “Because you have limited space, and things are being jumbled around.”
When Boucher was planning trips as a Registered Maine Guide, she said she always enjoyed figuring out the food logistics for the group. She now works for the University of Maine and no longer leads trips professionally, but she still wanted to help people figure out those important details.
“My biggest goal is to make it easier for people and help them get outside,” Boucher said.
The meal kits from Portage Eats contain fresh ingredients sourced in Maine and come with instructions for basic cooking. Boucher assembles and distributes the meals at Fork Food Lab in South Portland. She’s about to wrap up her first season and hopes to partner with campgrounds next year to reach more people.
She said her favorites include the seaweed corn chowder and the steak tip kebabs.
Jennifer Scism, who ran a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York and won the TV show “Iron Chef,” said her Kittery-based business Good To-Go started in part because she was experimenting with her tabletop dehydrator and her favorite comfort foods.
Good To-Go can be found in stores nationwide. Most meals only need a little hot water.
Scism said her favorite is the chicken pho. The staff sets aside a bulk bin for her so she can eat it multiple times a week without wasting single-serve packaging, she said.
“No matter what kind of adventure you’re on, whether you’re summiting Katahdin or taking a leisurely walk through the woods,” Scism wrote in an email, “your meal should be something you genuinely look forward to at the end of the day.”

title: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports. Her 237 days in orbit set an endurance record for the European Space Agency.
“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”
All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX’s recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston.
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA’s Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA’s first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef’s toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA’s count.
SpaceX is now gearing up for a space station supply run next week. Elon Musk’s company will launch more than 6,000 pounds (2,700 kilograms) of cargo, including the last of a series of solar panel additions, toilet pump, spacewalking suit, and fresh fruit and other goodies.

title: National report underscores how UMaine Cooperative Extension is tackling the state's workforce challenges
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine faces an urgent challenge: growing its skilled workforce by tens of thousands of people over the next several years. According to the state’s 10-year Economic Development Strategy, this will require flexible ways for adults to build on what they already know, develop new skills and continue learning while working and supporting their families.
A new national report shows how Cooperative Extension will be a key player in that effort.
The National Center for Higher Education Management Systems recently released “Recognizing Extension Learning: Pathways to Credit and Career Advancement”, a report examining how universities can better connect learning gained through non credit workshops and certifications, to academic credit and career advancement. NCHEMS worked closely with University of Maine Cooperative Extension to explore how credit for prior learning and skills validation were driving the organization’s efforts to develop an increasing array of micro-credentials.
“These are exactly the kinds of challenges Extension is built to address,” Hannah Carter, deputy provost and dean of UMaine Extension, said. “We’ve always focused on providing practical, applied learning for people in their communities, workplaces and at different stages of life.
Every year, thousands of Mainers engage in Extension programs, from improving farm management practices and earning food safety certifications to building business skills, developing leadership through 4-H and learning to adapt to climate and economic changes.
These programs are designed to be practical and accessible. They don’t currently provide an automatic path to college credit, but the report describes how such pathways could be developed.
At the center of the report are two key concepts: skills validation and Credit for Prior Learning. Skills validation helps document what learners know and can do. CPL allows universities to evaluate that learning and, when appropriate, award academic credit toward certificates or degrees. Together, these approaches create pathways that allow learners to build on what they’ve already accomplished rather than starting over.
“Because we are part of the University of Maine, we’re well positioned to connect that learning directly to academic systems and turn experience into credit,” Carter said.
For Maine, this approach aligns directly with the state’s goal of helping more adults earn credentials while staying in the workforce.
“Many of the learners we serve are already working, raising families and contributing to their communities,” Laura Wilson, director of non-credit learning at Extension, said. “They don’t necessarily have the time or resources to step into a traditional degree program full-time. But they are still learning and that learning has value.”
Wilson said the opportunity lies in making that value visible, “If we can clearly define the skills people gain through our programs and align those with academic frameworks and workforce needs, we can create more flexible, step-by-step pathways into credentials valued by employers. That’s what makes education more accessible and more relevant to today’s workforce.”
NCHEMS identified the University of Maine as a model not only because of the scope of its Extension programming, but because of how the university is rethinking the relationship between noncredit and credit learning.
The report highlights UMaine’s expanded CPL framework and its work designing stackable learning experiences, which are programs intentionally structured so that learners can build knowledge over time and apply it toward higher level credentials.
This approach reflects a shift from viewing education as a single, linear path to recognizing it as a continuum.
“Extension is often the first point of contact people have with the university,” Carter said. “By creating clearer pathways from those initial learning experiences into additional education and credentials, we’re opening doors for people who may not have seen higher education as an option for them.”
That model has particular importance in Maine, where rural geography and workforce demands require more flexible approaches to education. With educators and programming staff spread across the state, Extension is already structured to support the state’s workforce goals at a local level.
Grounded in community relationships and local needs, Extension bridges non-credit learning with higher education. This connection is critical to addressing workforce gaps in key sectors identified in the state’s economic strategy, including agriculture, natural resources, small business development and community resilience. For example, Extension recently expanded its horticulture offerings to train clients ranging from volunteers to entering professionals.
“We created the Maine Horticulture Training Program in partnership with Maine’s horticulture industry to respond to a well-documented need for more skilled workers,” Rebecca Long, coordinator of horticulture training programs at Extension, said. “Together, we designed a program that gives participants the knowledge, hands-on experience and confidence to enter the field without committing to a full degree. We also found that, for some participants, the training sparked an interest in continuing their education, making a pathway to academic credit a natural next step.”
The report underscores a broader shift in higher education that places increasing value on demonstrated skills alongside traditional degrees. For Maine, that shift represents an opportunity.
“Workforce development isn’t just about bringing new people into the state,” Carter said. “It’s about investing in the people who are already here, helping them build skills, advance in their careers and contribute to their communities in new ways.”

David Pastrnak scores twice to lead Bruins past Mammoth
text:
BOSTON — David Pastrnak scored his first two goals of the season and added two assists as the Boston Bruins routed the Utah Mammoth 6-1 on Thursday night.
Matthew Poitras, Casey Mittelstadt, Mason Lohrei and Morgan Geekie also scored for the Bruins, who led 3-0 after one period and 6-0 after two. Jeremy Swayman made 36 saves.
Pastrnak scored his first goal with 5:38 left in the first period on a power-play wrist shot, assisted by Frederic Brunet and Geekie. He tacked on a power-play slap shot 4:40 into the second period, assisted by Geekie and Hampus Lindholm.
Jack McBain scored for the Mammoth midway through the third period to spoil Swayman’s shutout bid.
Karel Vejmelka stopped 11 of 14 shots he faced before he was replaced by Sebastian Cossa, who made five saves.
The Bruins scored three power-play goals, while the Mammoth went scoreless on the power play. The Bruins blocked 23 shots.

Utah: Visits the Buffalo Sabres on Saturday night.
Boston: Hosts the Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday.

title: Trump says he’ll award pitcher Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom
text:
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump announced Wednesday night that he would award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to fireballer Roger Clemens, calling the seven-time Cy Young winner “maybe the greatest pitcher of all time.”
Addressing a rally in San Antonio, Trump renewed his calls for Clemens to be inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame. That’s an honor the pitcher known as “The Rocket” has yet to receive because of suspicions he used steroids during a 24-year career that featured time with the Boston Red Sox, Toronto Blue Jays, New York Yankees and Houston Astros.
“We’re giving him the Presidential Medal of Freedom,” Trump said. “And, along with the Congressional Medal of Honor, it’s the highest award bestowed upon anyone.”
The president continued: “He’ll be in the Hall of Fame someday, but he deserves it. One of the greatest athletes, and maybe the greatest pitcher, of all time.”
He added that the medal “is a big step up from the Hall of Fame.”
Trump has given the medal to various athletes during his two terms in the White House, including golfing legend Tiger Woods, former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Roger Staubach, famed Yankees closer Mariano Rivera and Lou Holtz, former coach of Notre Dame football.
He’s bestowed the same honor on Elvis Presley posthumously and on Rush Limbaugh the year before the conservative radio host died.
Wednesday’s surprise revelation came near the end of a Trump speech that lasted more than 100 minutes, and with the crowd having lost some of its enthusiasm. Clemens was attending the event, and the president called him to the stage, where the retired right-hander offered, “Well, I’m stunned.”
“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” Clemens said. “And to get it from this man, this president, there wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from.”
Clemens, who was raised in Houston, said he was honored that the announcement came in Texas and added of Trump: “You’re talking about a winner. That’s a winner right there.”
Clemens, like slugger Barry Bonds and many other stars widely suspected of using performance-enhancing drugs, was repeatedly rejected by baseball writers in his bid for the Hall of Fame. There are other avenues where Clemens and others could eventually make it, but the road is not easy.
Clemens isn’t the first star baseball player Trump has made a Hall of Fame case for. The president issued a posthumous federal pardon last year for the late Pete Rose, which led to Major League Baseball lifting its ban on the all-time career hits leader.
Trump has called for Rose to be inducted in the Hall of Fame too — also, so far, unsuccessfully.
__
Weissert reported from Washington.

title: Bangor Police Respond To Six Incidents Involving Glenburn Resident Over Two Days
text:
Glenburn Man Becomes ‘Frequent Flier’ At Penobscot County Jail After Multiple Arrests In One Week By Bangor PD
Officers from the Bangor Police Department were kept quite busy by the alleged antics of one Glenburn man this week.
Read More: Ellsworth, Maine Crash Kills Orrington Man, Injures Dedham Man
38-year-old Ryan Sawyer was arrested twice and involved in no less than six criminal incidents after his arrival in the Queen City, having been transported to Bangor after giving another law enforcement agency some trouble.
According to Sgt. Jeremy Brock of the Bangor PD, these incidents ranged from disorderly conduct to obstructing a public way.
The first encounter Bangor PD had with the man was Tuesday evening (October 6th) when they received calls from a local hospital that a man was taking his clothes off and acting aggressively. Officers, in the process of issuing him a trespass warning, watched him move out into the roadway, when he had to be told to move out of the way of traffic. He was issued a criminal trespass warning, left for a while, but then came back and blocked the emergency entrance to the hospital. Because this meant ambulances could not safely enter that space, cops were called back to the scene, and Sawyer was arrested.
He was out of jail by the next day, and allegedly spent Wednesday evening causing issues for Bangor residents and business again.
The first call Bangor PD received was on Clinton Street, just after 7:30 PM "for a disorderly complaint of a man throwing apples at a car whilst screaming. Sawyer
was warned for disorderly conduct." He received another warning from the police and moved on from there.
Sawyer ended up, less than an hour later, at a business on Hammond Street, where he was allegedly screaming profanities, scaring patrons and those around the business, and breaking windows. So the police were called out again.
"The business owner was still visibly upset from the encounter and told officers that she had asked Sawyer to leave when he began asking patrons of the store to use their phones. The owner said Sawyer then began hitting the windows with his fists and yelling vulgarities at the business owner. Others who witnessed the outburst were
also frightened by it."
Officers caught up with Sawyer, who had moved away from that scene after the alleged chaos he created, and arrested him again.
Read More: Fatal Crash On Bar Mills Road In Hollis Claims One Life
Ultimately, Sawyer was arrested twice in two days, and charged with 3 Bail Violations, Obstructing a Public Way, Aggravated Criminal Mischief, Disorderly Conduct and Terrorizing.

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was sexually assaulted while fixing campaign signs
text:
SUN CITY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - A Democratic candidate for Arizona’s 8th Congressional District reported she was knocked unconscious and sexually assaulted by two men while fixing campaign signs in August.
A police report obtained by Arizona’s Family states Bernadette Greene-Placentia was fixing campaign signs Aug. 14 in Sun City. While walking back to her car, she was hit in the head and knocked unconscious, according to the report.
Greene-Placentia reported when she woke up, she was being held down and sexually assaulted by a man. She said another man then sexually assaulted her while she fought back by kicking her feet.
During the assault, the report states Greene-Placentia heard one of the men saying “Democratic b---h.” She reported the two men left her face down in the parking lot, and she doesn’t remember much afterward.
Greene-Placentia told her husband about the assault two or three days later and reported the assault to law enforcement two weeks later, according to the report. She told investigators she did not get a medical exam after the assault.
Authorities were not able to collect DNA or other physical evidence in the case.
The investigation is ongoing.
Political leaders respond
Greene-Placentia is running against Trump-backed GOP incumbent Abraham “Abe” Hamadeh in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District. Hamadeh’s campaign gave the following statement regarding his opponent’s reported assault and called for an investigation:
“I have read the disturbing story and call upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law. No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community.”
Several other Arizona political leaders also expressed their support for Greene-Placentia after news of the reported attack, including Gov. Katie Hobbs and Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego.
“Governor Hobbs is outraged by the sexual assault against congressional candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia,” a statement from Hobbs’ office read. “This was a cruel and cowardly attack, and it has no place in Arizona. No one should have to fear for their safety, or the safety of the people they love, while serving their community. Violence of any kind, against anyone, will not be tolerated in our state. Our hearts are with Bernadette and her loved ones.”
“What happened to Bernadette Greene-Placentia is an outrage,” Kelly posted on social media. “It took real courage for her to speak publicly about something so painful. The criminal who did this must be found and held fully accountable.”
“I’m absolutely heartbroken to hear this news, and I’m thinking of Bernadette and her loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” Gallego said. “We cannot tolerate political or sexual violence in any form. Those responsible must be held accountable. Thank you for speaking out, Bernadette. We’re with you.”
Note: Arizona’s Family does not typically name victims of sexual assault, but Greene-Placentia has publicly come forward with her claims.

title: Less fighting, more Matt Dunlap
text:
If people were around for Paul LePage’s time as Maine’s governor, they will remember that he was in the news constantly for getting into fights with one person after another — sometimes even in his own party. The last thing we need in Maine’s 2nd District is an angry politician making enemies instead of working together to get things done.
While revenue shortfalls resulting from former Gov. LePage’s tax cuts created severe economic disparities that directly harmed low-income families, and stripped away their ability to purchase basic life necessities, Matt Dunlap is a champion of Medicare, Social Security and Medicaid. The last thing we need is for more of our local hospitals to close or lose services like maternity wards.
Matt Dunlap has the integrity and experience to lead during these challenging times.
Christopher Wright
Belfast

title: PCHC gets $2.8M from the state, warding off bankruptcy
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Penobscot Community Health Care announced Thursday that it will receive $2.8 million from the state. As a result, the organization is no longer considering bankruptcy.
The money for the struggling nonprofit healthcare organization will come from the Rural Health Transformation Program. PCHC said the funds will “help ensure the future of PCHC and our critical work for the people of Maine.”
“Specifically, they will increase the support for our transition earlier this year to a new electronic medical records system and to alternative payment models,” the organization said.
PCHC is Maine’s largest federally qualified health center, serving roughly 50,000 patients.
The organization, which is considered a safety net provider for low-income Mainers, announced in August that it needed $3 million in the next two months to avoid drastically cutting services or declaring bankruptcy.
On Thursday, PCHC said it is no longer pursuing an imminent Chapter 11 filing.
“That is a significant step forward. But the next 12 months will be critical, and we have a great deal of work ahead to put PCHC on solid financial ground,” the organization said.

title: Wells names Brian Pellerin police chief
text:
The town of Wells has announced the appointment of a new police chief.
Brian Pellerin, chief deputy of the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office, will take on the post starting Nov. 10, the town said in a news release Thursday afternoon.
Pellerin succeeds longtime Chief Jo-Ann Putnam, who retired in June after nearly 20 years in the role. Town Manager Michael Pardue has acted as interim chief since then.
In a written statement, Pellerin said he believes the town’s goals align with his.
“The Town of Wells’ vision for a collaborative, community-centered police chief aligns closely with my leadership philosophy and the experience I have gained throughout my career,” Pellerin said. “Wells is especially meaningful to me. Wells is a respected coastal community that values professionalism, community engagement and thoughtful leadership.”
In a social media post, the town touted Pellerin’s extensive experience, including his 34 years in law enforcement and 12 years on the Maine Criminal Justice Academy’s board of trustees.
“The town is confident that Chief Pellerin’s extensive law enforcement background and executive leadership experience will help build upon the Wells Police Department’s long-standing commitment to public safety and community service,” the town’s post reads.
Earlier this year, Pellerin mounted an independent campaign for York County sheriff before dropping out of the race last month. At the time, Pellerin said he had “decided to pursue a different professional path that better aligns with where I believe I can make the greatest contribution.”

title: York Village revitalization effort breaks ground after years of planning
text:
York Village is getting a long-awaited facelift, which will require more than a year of work, the relocation of a Civil War monument and the removal of a beloved tree in the center of the village.
The York Village Revitalization Project aims to modernize the area, which officials say will make the intersection in the center of the village safer for pedestrians and cyclists.
“It was designed back when there were horse-and-buggies going through there, so it’s not a modern type of intersection,” Town Engineer Dean Lessard said this week. “It’s kind of confusing for people.”
Work finally began in late September after years of planning. Here’s what’s going on.
CUTTING PAVEMENT
On Sept. 28, crews from Gorham construction company R.J. Grondin & Sons broke ground. So far, workers have placed signs for traffic control and started cutting pavement to prepare to reconfigure the road.
Right now, the intersection at York Street and Long Sands Road is a triangle shape with narrow streets surrounding it. Lessard said that design has been confusing for people who don’t frequent the area.
Making it a modern “T” design will help to eliminate visual confusion and make it safer.
“It’s not a high accident intersection necessarily, but there’s a lot of close calls that make people feel uncomfortable, both walking and driving,” Town Manager Peter Joseph said. “We get complaints.”
There aren’t any bike lanes at the intersection now, and there still won’t be when the project is completed, Lessard said. The road will remain narrow — widening it would be a much lengthier and more expensive process — but there will be clear marks in the pavement that indicate where the road becomes a “share lane” for cars and bikes.
Lessard said the town will also prioritize making the area more presentable by hardscaping and adding vegetation to make it a place where people can gather. He hopes it’ll give a boost to the surrounding businesses.
Crews will start excavating once drainage pipes get delivered so they can start replacing and improving the existing drain.
The Civil War monument will have a new home, too, but it isn’t going far — just 25 feet to the east side of the intersection at a new pedestrian plaza.
“Those are the big improvements: bicycle, pedestrian, make it more driver-friendly and safe,” Lessard said.
YEARS OF PLANNING, SECURING FUNDS
The York Village Revitalization Project has been floated several times since Lessard began as engineer in 2011. But it’s been in the works for far longer.
“I think there was a plan back in the ’60s that talked about doing something for the village that never made it very far,” Lessard said. “It’s been talked about for decades.”
By 2016, it became clear to officials that the town should reconsider after watching tourists become confused by the area in the summer months. The issue was finally brought to the ballot in May of that year, when voters approved $400,000 for the project — a 10% local match to state and federal transportation funds.
Joseph said the project encountered a few roadblocks that delayed the project significantly, including struggles to secure funding since voters approved it years ago.
Construction costs have been subject to significant inflation since 2016, which created a shortfall — a little over $100,000 — in the town’s 10% match, Joseph said. Officials had to secure that additional funding before work could start.
“It was not anything that we were surprised by at all, and nobody should be surprised that 10 years later, you know, the cost would be more,” he said.
The planning phase also took a few years to sort out.
Lessard said there were five possible options that were voted on when the revitalization idea was originally revived 10 years ago. The winning plan hasn’t changed much from the original conceptualization, but the Civil War monument posed some issues.
It was dedicated to the town by Gov. Joshua Chamberlain in 1906. For it to be moved, the state had to determine if a monument with such historical significance could be relocated, and that took longer than anticipated, Joseph said.
The monument’s new home will come with a plaque, acknowledging that it was moved as part of the revitalization project.
“It’s moving, like, 30 feet, but that was a major, major roadblock in the project,” Joseph said.
SOME RESIDENTS WARY OF CHANGE
Joseph said residents’ feedback has been a bit of a mixed bag. Some are excited about added safety measures, and officials are looking forward to hearing fewer complaints about the area, Joseph said.
Others, though, are wary of change, even though the project has been in the works for a decade.
At a joint select and planning board meeting Monday, a few residents raised concerns about the large honey locust tree towering over the monument, which will likely be removed by early November.
“It all starts with a tree,” said James Kences, a member of the town’s conservation commission. He expressed concern that removing the tree will pave the way for developers to build without regard for the character of the town.
“It will be toppled without ceremony by an individual who won’t even break a sweat, and that will be its end after many decades,” Kences said.
The tree grew there on its own, without being planted by anyone, and has become a beacon in the center of town for some residents.
For Lessard, the town engineer, the invasive tree is more of a weed.
“I’ve been here for a while, and I understand that people get attached to it,” he said. “But unfortunately, that one tree will have to be removed for the project to make that intersection safer.”
The project is expected to be completed by late October 2027.

title: Animal hospital owner accused of using dead dog’s name to obtain prescription drugs
text:
LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) — The owner of an animal hospital and an alleged accomplice have been indicted in what prosecutors describe as a prescription drug scheme that used a dead dog’s name to obtain narcotics.
A Lorain County grand jury indicted Dr. Kris L. Taylor, 62, of Strongsville, and Camile Nieto, 29, of Avon, on seven counts, according to an indictment obtained by 19 News.
The two are accused of taking part in a scheme at Landings Animal Hospital to repeatedly write and fill prescriptions for oxycodone and the anti‑anxiety drug Alprazolam in the name of “Punkin,” a dog that was already dead, the indictment says.
According to the Landings Animal Hospital website, Taylor is the owner and a veterinarian at the Avon Lake hospital on Avon Belden Road. It is unknown whether Nieto was also a staff member.
Investigators say the alleged conduct happened between August 10, 2024, and June 7, 2025. The indictments list more than 20 prescriptions for Oxycodone and Alprazolam allegedly written for “Punkin” and filled at pharmacies across Northeast Ohio, including locations in Avon and Avon Lake.
Taylor and Nieto are each charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, a first-degree felony; deception to obtain a dangerous drug and possession of oxycodone, both second-degree felonies; illegal processing of drug documents involving oxycodone, a fourth-degree felony; deception to obtain a dangerous drug and illegal processing of drug documents involving alprazolam, both fifth-degree felonies; and possession of alprazolam, a first-degree misdemeanor.
Court records show both appeared in court Thursday and were each given a $500,000 bond.
Landings Animal Hospital told 19 News it remains open.

I am writing to express my concerns regarding Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection campaign receiving at least $50,000 from Marc Rowan, CEO of Apollo Global Management, through supporting PACs.

Timothy Stevens
Kennebunk

title: 3 takeaways on the 2nd Maine gubernatorial debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The second of four debates in Maine’s three-way race for governor was mostly a substantive affair — and, to some extent, a repeat of the candidates’ first meeting last week.
The debate was hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine at the Gracie Theatre on Husson University’s campus in Bangor. The three candidates went back and forth for an hour on housing, immigration, healthcare and more.
Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree remains the race’s strong favorite, having dominated fundraising and holding a steady double-digit lead in polling since she won a competitive ranked-choice primary this summer.
Bobby Charles, a Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, won the Republican nomination in a similarly competitive — but more bruising — primary. His campaign has tried to link Pingree to higher electricity prices and property taxes under Democratic Gov. Janet Mills.
Rick Bennett, the independent, is a state senator from Oxford County who left the Republican Party when he joined the race last summer. He’s tried to position himself as a middle-ground candidate, but has failed so far to pick up widespread support, polls show.
After the trio’s second debate, here are a few takeaways.
1. Charles talked about Pingree about as much as himself.
Charles began his participation in the debate, and ended it, by attacking Pingree.
The first question posed to the candidates was about housing affordability, and — before spinning into a list of policy proposals that included reducing property taxes for disabled veterans and raising the Homestead Exemption — Charles said housing costs have doubled under Mills and Pingree, who served in Mills’ administration.
That’s been his strategy since he won the Republican nomination: Link Pingree to Mills, and point the finger.
And this approach was typified by Charles’ closing statement. After a brief moment of emotion, Charles pointed the finger at Pingree once again.
“Who in their right mind, charged with affordable housing by a governor, would give $840,000 to her own nonprofit, one that employs her husband and her family?” Charles said, alluding to state funding awarded to a nonprofit Pingree once led, before being cut off by Maine Public host Jennifer Rooks.
Charles’ time was up.
2. The second debate was pretty similar to the first.
As in the first debate, Charles, behind in polls by double digits, went on the attack and positioned himself as an outsider with new ideas. He again attempted to distance himself from President Donald Trump on tariffs and said he has appealed to Trump to return to the negotiating table, calling Canada a “friend.”
As in the first debate, Pingree stuck to her message, avoided addressing Charles’ constant attacks and linked Charles on tariffs and the war in Iran to Trump — whose approval ratings are well underwater in Maine, recent polling shows.
And as in the first debate, Bennett swung with his independence. He called the two-party system, which he abandoned last year, the “political industrial complex,” calling out both Democrats and Republicans for stifling debate and encouraging the explosion of campaign money.
3. There were a few areas of policy agreement.
On the first question of the night, all three candidates acknowledged housing production in Maine is too slow, and that rolling back regulations may help ease the state’s 80,000-unit shortfall.
Pingree called for a 90-day environmental permitting “shot clock,” Charles said he would encourage municipalities to speed up permitting and Bennett said he would audit the state’s housing bottleneck to understand where delays are coming from.
All three candidates acknowledged Maine is struggling to retain its healthcare workforce and its rural hospitals. Bennett and Charles agreed that reimbursement rates need to increase, and Pingree and Bennett agreed that Maine should be working toward universal health insurance coverage.
In fact, Pingree and Bennett agreed on quite a bit: that immigration enforcement has gone too far, that data center development should pause and that the Indigenous tribes in Maine should have sovereignty.
Bennett — ever the middleman — and Charles agreed that the state budget shortfall was due to overspending, and that the state budget deserves a thorough comb-through.
Watch the full debate on Maine Public’s YouTube channel. The candidates will meet on stage again in a CBS13 and FOX23-hosted debate on Tuesday, and on Wednesday in a debate hosted by WMTW.

title: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration announced Thursday it was suspending Microsoft and several other firms from a program allowing foreign workers to apply for green cards as it also lashed out at universities that bring international students to the U.S. on exchange programs.
The announcement by Vice President JD Vance marks the latest swing from the Trump administration at employers and universities that welcome foreign students and workers into the country.
Such programs have frequently been targeted by some Trump supporters who argue they undercut American students and workers. Supporters say they allow the U.S. to attract the best talent from around the world and fill important hiring gaps.
Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like H-1B visas — which Vance accused Microsoft of abusing — essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In the wide-ranging announcement, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms.
The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies.
Vance says US workers are replaced with ‘foreign indentured servants’
Vance said the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.”
Microsoft is No. 5 among U.S. employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No. 1.
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.” Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, the company said 80% were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“These were not to hire new people,” Microsoft said in a statement. “The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.”
The company added that it only files H-1B petitions for “those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category.”
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at USCIS during the Biden administration, called Vance’s announcement “incoherent.”
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” he said. “Once you have a green card, you’re no longer dependent on your employer for your immigration status — you’re a permanent resident who can change jobs and negotiate higher wages without fear.”
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position.
H-1B program has been scrutinized
The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
Trump last year attempted to ratchet up the fee for H-1B work visas to $100,000, saying it would protect American workers from losing their jobs to lower-paid foreigners, but a federal judge struck that down in June.
The administration has since tried a different tack, announcing plans in August for a $103,265 fee. The proposed regulation described the new fee as a “dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system.” The rule isn’t yet final and is expected to face a legal challenge, like the one before it.
Ron Hira, a Howard University political science professor and longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.” Hira noted the White House last month issued a little-noticed executive order directing government agencies to “implement appropriate measures to protect American workers from abuse of the H-1B program and ensure that the program serves the national interest.’’
“There are supposed to be protections for U.S. workers that say: If you hire an H-1B, you are promising that you are not adversely affecting similarly employed U.S. workers,’’ Hira said. “That’s never been enforced.’’
Besides Microsoft, Vance said the government was similarly suspending Adobe and tech consulting firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. The companies did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
Trump also has targeted foreign students
The Vance announcement came a day after Trump’s administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practical Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.
Vance also called out universities, suggesting that they were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. In most cases, to get the visa, students must receive the majority of their funding from an institution, such as a fellowship-granting organization, rather than paying for their tuition personally.
Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT. Stanford said it would cooperate with the investigation. The other universities did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ___
Associated Press writers Heather Hollingsworth in Mission, Kansas and Paul Wiseman and Annie Ma in Washington D.C. contributed. Ortutay reported from Oakland, Calif.

title: Letter: Debate questions for Susan Collins
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Mainers are watching the Susan Collins/Troy Jackson debates, with hope and trepidation. An informal gathering of questions from neighbors over the weekend turned up these priorities we hope moderators will put to our senior senator:
You opposed final passage of last year’s budget reconciliation law but voted to let it advance. Why move forward a bill you said would hurt Maine’s Medicaid recipients and rural hospitals?
As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, what have you done to stop the administration from withholding money Congress approved?
Tariffs on Canada hit Maine’s loggers, lobstermen and border towns. Will you vote to return tariff authority to Congress?
What are you doing to help Mainers whose access to healthcare has been lost or imperiled thanks to your vote to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill?
You voted to confirm Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. Do you stand by that vote?
Will you rule out raising the Social Security retirement age?
Name one instance since January 2025 where your objections changed an outcome, not just the record.
You tout your 10,000 consecutive votes as a positive attribute of your service in the Senate. Why should Mainers thank you for the votes for Brett Kavanaugh, RFK Jr., expanded funding for ICE, and the One Big Beautiful Bill?
You voted to confirm Justice Kavanaugh, saying you believed Roe was settled law. Knowing what followed, would you cast that vote again?
To justify returning you to the Senate we want direct answers, not just “concern.”
Joline Godfrey
Saint George

title: 🚆🏀🏒 MAINE FANS, LET’S GO! Take Amtrak to Celtics & Bruins Games This Season!
text:
Maine Fall Fun: Take Amtrak to Celtics & Bruins Games
For me, the best part of this time of year is fall! Every major sport is going on at once, and it’s pretty darn exciting.
If you’re from Maine and just happen to be a huge Celtics or Bruins fan, there’s a pretty easy way to get to TD Garden without spending hours behind the wheel.
This past spring, I headed to TD Garden to see the final regular-season Boston Celtics game. Normally, that would mean the usual stress-filled four-hour drive from Maine, but this time, we decided to switch things up and try something different: the Amtrak Downeaster. After the quick 90-minute drive from Bangor to Brunswick, I got to kick back, relax, and leave the stress of driving behind.
And honestly? I’m glad we did.
The Downeaster runs between Brunswick and Boston, with stops along the way in places like Portland, Saco, Exeter, New Hampshire, and Haverhill, Massachusetts. The final stop is Boston’s North Station, which just happens to be right underneath TD Garden.
That makes it pretty hard to beat if you’re heading to a Celtics or Bruins game. ??????
Our round-trip ticket was about $50, and the ride took around 3 hours and 20 minutes. Yes, that’s a little longer than driving from Brunswick, but for me, it was absolutely worth it.
Instead of worrying about traffic, parking or navigating Boston, we could sit back, enjoy the scenery, grab some food and a drink, and let someone else do the driving.

And there’s another cool option for game nights:
They offer an Event Night Train for select Celtics and Bruins games and TD Garden concerts. For qualifying events that start at 8 pm or later, the special train can leave Boston North Station at 11:25 pm, for the trip back toward Maine.
One important thing to remember: the train won’t wait if your game runs late, so check the schedule carefully before making your plans.
Schedules can change, so be sure to check the Amtrak Downeaster website for the latest information before your trip.
For Maine sports fans, though, this is a pretty fun alternative: no Boston traffic, no downtown parking headache, and you can step off the train practically underneath TD Garden. Not a bad way to spend a fall game day!

title: Trump points to Brazil vote count in latest election-rigging claim
text:
Brazil election results don't prove President Trump's claims of election fraud in the US
Trump pointed to Brazil's fast vote count as proof of U.S. election fraud — but PolitiFact says that claim lacks evidence.
Brazil election results don't prove President Trump's claims of election fraud in the US
Trump pointed to Brazil's fast vote count as proof of U.S. election fraud — but PolitiFact says that claim lacks evidence.
President Donald Trump pointed to quick results in the first round of voting in Brazil's presidential election to denounce the pace of ballot counting in Democratic U.S. areas as "corrupt."
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of Brazil's former president who was sentenced to prison following an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election — was leading Oct. 4 in the first round of voting ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 47% to 45%. They will proceed to a runoff Oct. 25.
Trump posted Oct. 4 on Truth Social, "125 Million People voted today in the first round of Brazil’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the SAME DAY! In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other U.S. Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is CORRUPT!!!"
In a different late-night post that is no longer available, Trump made the same statement about India, which did not hold a presidential election over the weekend.
By the time of Trump's Brazil post, it was clear the candidates were headed to a runoff and nearly all votes were cast.
The pace of vote counting is not a sign of election rigging. Brazil and the U.S. have different voting systems and election laws.
For years, Trump has repeatedly spread falsehoods about "rigged" elections, including in California. Officials abiding by state law is not a sign of fraud.
How Brazil administers elections
Brazil has no mail-in voting. Voting is in person, at electronic voting machines, and it is mandatory for citizens between ages 18 and 70, said Pablo Ortellado, a University of São Paulo professor of public policy. Voting takes place on a single day that is a national holiday.
Elections are run by a specialized branch of the judiciary, the Electoral Justice system. At the top is the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), a national court that sets the rules and coordinates 27 regional electoral courts that handle elections on the ground.
"It is a single, nationally standardized system: the same machines, the same procedures and the same counting process across the whole country," Ortellado said. "That is a big part of why results come out within hours."
Brazilian officials have worked to increase transparency. In 2021, the Superior Electoral Court created the Electoral Transparency Commission, which includes experts, civil society entities and public institutions in inspecting and auditing the electoral process.
The country has used electronic voting machines since 1996. Voters cast ballots on dedicated machines protected by multiple layers of testing and auditing.
"Curiously, Brazil's electronic voting system, which is indeed very fast and quite secure, draws heavy criticism precisely from the Brazilian right that is sympathetic to Trump," Ortellado said. "Critics argue, among other things, that because there is no printed record of each vote deposited in a ballot box for physical verification, the system cannot be properly audited."
Since the late 1990s, the nation's election results have been available quickly.
As soon as the polls close at 5 p.m., results are gathered, said Paulo Valle, a political scientist and researcher at the University of Central Florida and FGV in Brazil. "By the end of the evening, we have 99.9% of the ballots counted."
Brazil has a completely paperless system, said Eduardo Repilloza Fernández, coordinator general for Transparencia Electoral, an organization that encourages elections held according to internationally recognized integrity standards.
"There's no signatures to check, no physical paper-ballot tabulation systems. Voters do not get an individual receipt of their vote," Fernández said.
How the U.S. administers elections
In the U.S., each state sets its own election laws, and cities and counties administer elections.
State laws cover the deadline for receipt of mail ballots, when election officials can open mail ballots and prepare them for tabulation and the dates by which they must certify official results. All of those laws play a role in how long it takes to complete the official count.
Some contests have wide enough margins between top candidates that media outlets can project a winner based on partial results. But the final official results are often certified weeks later. If the vote is close, even an election with little mail balloting can take time to call. Some elections with lots of mail balloting can be called quickly if a candidate is far ahead.
No state completes an official count on election night.
Trump singled out California, which often takes longer than the rest of the country because nearly everyone votes by mail and it counts ballots postmarked on or before Election Day and received not later than seven days after Election Day.
Expansive voting by mail is convenient for voters — even Trump frequently votes by mail. But it takes longer for local election officials to process and verify mail ballots.
We asked the White House for Trump's evidence that the pace of counting ballots in California or the cities of Detroit, Philadelphia or elsewhere is a sign that people are rigging the election. We did not get an immediate response.
Falsehoods followed Brazil's 2022 election
President Jair Bolsonaro, father of Flávio Bolsonaro, narrowly lost in 2022 and claimed the election was fraudulent, sparking protests by his supporters.
More than 1,000 people stormed Brazil's government buildings, including those of Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential offices on Jan. 8, 2023, smashing windows and setting fires. In March 2026, Bolsonaro received permission to serve his sentence for the coup attempt at home because of poor health.
The Atlanta-based Carter Center, which sent observers to Brazil for the election, said it was not aware of any evidence of fraud in the 2022 election, and none of the international or Brazilian observers reported any evidence of significant fraud. The center similarly sent experts to watch the 2026 election.
Cesar Zucco, a Columbia University professor of Brazilian studies, told PolitiFact that voter registration, voting and counting “are electronic and safe” and that “the only people that ever questioned the mechanics of the elections were Bolsonaro and his allies in the recent past."
Our ruling
Trump said Brazil's same-day election results are proof that places like Detroit, Philadelphia and California "take weeks to rig" their elections.
His frequent critique after other countries' speedier election results still lacks evidence.
Brazil and the U.S. have different voting systems and laws. Brazil has a nationally standardized system that uses the same machines, the same procedures and the same counting process across the whole country, and doesn't have voting by mail, which is expansive in some U.S. states, including California. Voting by mail takes longer for local election officials to process mail ballots and verify they were cast by the voters whose names are on the envelopes.
The pace of vote counting is not proof of election rigging.

title: Will Trump attend the Alabama-Georgia game amid Hurricane Isaias threat? Here’s what he said
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The midterm elections are looming and the first hurricane of the Atlantic Season is menacing the Gulf Coast.
But President Donald Trump is really, really hoping the weather doesn’t stop him from going to another big college football game — this one in Alabama on Saturday night.
“Well, hurricane and football? I love Alabama. I gotta go to the game. It’d be awfully hard,” Trump said Wednesday, when asked if Hurricane Isaias — and a forecast track which has parts of Alabama, Mississippi and Florida bracing for significant impacts — might alter his plans.
Trump had been set to visit Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa when Alabama hosts Georgia in a Top 10 matchup, following an afternoon rally in Tennessee.
Officials are still discussing how the storm might affect the game. But if it happens and Trump is there, it would be the 10th college football game he’s attended as president since 2017 — including the late September game in Knoxville when Texas topped Tennessee 20-17.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday “if there’s a hurricane, I don’t want to do anything” to take the focus of first responders and law enforcement away from the storm, saying he wanted people to be safe.
“We’ll have to see,” he said.
It’s unusual to mix football and midterm politics
A president trying to give his party a midterm boost typically wouldn’t even contemplate going to two college football games so close to Election Day. But Trump’s longtime love of sports — and big crowds — are often key factors in his travel schedule.
Live sports — especially big games that attract casual fans nationwide — are one of the few televised programs that can still draw large, real-time audiences. But mixing sports and politics can be tricky: Trump received cheers but also boos when he was shown on Tennessee’s jumbotron, despite being in a deep red state.
“I think what they’re trying to do is get this broadcast: trying to raise enthusiasm, particularly among young men,” said University of Richmond political scientist Dan Palazzolo, who has researched, written and taught about the intersection of politics and sports.
Tennessee and Alabama are “safe turf,” Palazzolo said, and Trump “clearly sees sports as a kind of way to connect with a certain part of the base.”
While presidents usually visit key swing states leading up to elections, Trump’s sinking approval ratings mean some GOP candidates may be looking to distance themselves from the increasingly unpopular Iran war and the higher gasoline prices it’s caused.
The White House says Trump attending football games — even in reliably Republican states — can energize his core supporters around the country. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers described the president as “the greatest champion of college sports in American history” and said that Trump has used his executive powers and championed congressional efforts to try to overhaul how the sport is governed.
Trump is now a week into what he said would be 32 days of travel ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3 — including a visit last week to Alabama and other stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Ohio and Nebraska. Swings in coming weeks will take him to Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Kansas and Alaska, among other places.
Presidents have used sports for political gains before. But not like this
Richard Nixon publicly leaned into his fierce love of football to ”make a difference politically by capturing the Midwest, working class values," Palazzolo said. His successor, Gerald Ford, was a standout University of Michigan center and used his playing days as a key component of his folksy personal style when campaigning.
But Trump has made sporting events a big part of his second term. A onetime owner of the USFL’s New Jersey Generals, Trump recently attended the Presidents Cup and flew to his golf course for the Irish Open.
He was at the World Cup final, the NBA finals and the NCAA football championship game, while marking his 80th birthday with a UFC extravaganza on the White House lawn.
In 2025 alone, Trump went to the Super Bowl, the Daytona 500, the Ryder Cup, a New York Yankees game and the U.S. Open men’s final, as well as UFC fights and the NCAA wrestling championships.
“I think it helps the brand more than anything else. Because, I think his brand is ‘Sports Guy,’” said Dave Mowery, an Alabama-based consultant who has worked on campaigns for both parties.
“I know everything is political,” Mowery said. “But it almost puts him above politics and into that type of guy that is seen in the box with the people.”
In some states, there’s the risk of backlash
Mowery, a Georgia fan who plans to attend Saturday’s game against Alabama, said a presidential visit means fans have to cope with additional security and arriving early to sit in the stands long before the game begins.
He said not everyone there will support Trump, though few will be frustrated enough about the disruptions to vote for Democrats on that issue alone. Seeing the president flash on the scoreboard, or wave to the crowd from a private box, probably won’t win him votes from the crowd, either, Mowery said.
Palazzolo said he thinks it’s a “time-drain” for a president to go to a football game when there’s no evidence it can sway voter behavior — and he said it risks backlash, especially in parts of the country where football remains bipartisan with “conservatives and liberals finding common ground at the ballpark.”
Mowery said the difference between attending a big game in the South versus other parts of the country is that college football is the top attraction. That’s in contrast to NFL games, which might be bigger draws in other, more northern battleground states.
He also said it’s no accident that Trump has stuck to attending marquee college matchups.
“If ‘Sports Guy’ helps drive the brand, then you want to be at the top of that food chain,” Mowery said. “He wants to go to the best game on the board. He wants to go to the top of the pops.”

title: Aging Untold: Knowing your family health history matters more than you may think
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how family health history can help doctors spot medical risks early and shape a more personalized path for your care.
Plus, find out how creating an “anti-bucket list” can help you let go of guilt, grudges and obligations as you age.
Later, we meet a 95-year-old Vermont volunteer whose decades of preserving plants earned her the ultimate living legacy.
Your family health history could provide your doctor with important clues years before disease becomes obvious, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She said it’s important to identify patterns in conditions such as heart disease and strokes, particularly when they occur at a very early age, as well as cancers, autoimmune disorders, depression and thyroid diseases.
Genetic testing can be especially useful for people who don’t have access to their family history, including those who are adopted.
Saying “no” might be one of the most powerful tools for a freer, more joyful life after 60.
The idea of a bucket list is pretty common — a list of everything you still want to do. But what about an “anti-bucket list” — the things you want to stop doing, stop caring about or stop apologizing for?
“One of the privileges of getting older is subtraction,” Rogers said. “What can I do to subtract that’s going to give me more peace, more sleep, more joy. And it’s OK.”
Read the full article and see how to create your own anti-bucket list.
The number of cases of traumatic brain injury is rising, and older adults 75 and up account for nearly a third of TBI-related hospitalizations, largely due to fall risk.
Despite the widespread impact, federal funding for TBI research, education and awareness has lapsed — and advocates say the consequences could be severe.
Hilda White has carefully preserved more than 50,000 plant specimens at the University of Vermont’s Pringle Herbarium, which is like a library of plants.
The 95-year-old presses the plants and affixes them to archival paper so they can be studied and referenced for generations to come.
For her 95th birthday, the herbarium gave White a gift unlike any other.
A newly discovered fern, found in Colombia in 2023, was officially named for her.

title: AARP Maine van tour spreads Social Security message in Aroostook County
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - AARP Maine is taking its Social Security message on the road with a statewide van tour making stops in Aroostook County, encouraging voters and candidates to pay attention to the program ahead of the election.
The tour launched in Bath and headed north, with stops in Houlton, Presque Isle and Caribou.
AARP Maine State Director Noel Bonam said the group is talking with residents about what Social Security means to them. The organization expects to reach nearly 100 Maine communities by the end of the month.
Bonam said those conversations matter for younger adults, too.
“And I think for younger adults, they really need to start paying attention to Social Security and not just push it to the side saying that something I’ll worry about when I get older. But you have to start making sure that it’s protected now, that the folks you’re voting for are going to protect it,” Bonam said.
Bonam said the campaign aims to remind voters of their influence and make sure candidates hear their concerns about Social Security.
The van will continue south, with planned stops in Bangor and Waterville. Anyone who spots it is encouraged to stop and share why the program matters to them.

title: We need a public, nonprofit universal healthcare system now
text:
Paul F. Kando lives in Damariscotta.
Maine’s newspapers are full of articles and reader comments about the terrible shape of our healthcare. Not only is our business-modeled “healthcare” expensive, lately it has been even difficult to find a doctor; and essential hospital departments are being closed, based on their lack of profitability.
I am afraid capitalist ideology is at the root of what, in these United States, including Maine, passes for “healthcare.” But health, illness and knowledge are not commodities on which to legitimately profit.
At age 90, I still miss the “circuit doctors” of my teenage years. As a teenager in postwar Europe, my family and I were beneficiaries of a simple, decentralized universal healthcare alternative — which could serve as an alternative model to our failing system.
My whole native country was divided into circuits, to each of which a resident “circuit doctor” was assigned. At his/her disposal, as needed, were a pool of home visiting nurses and other assistants, as well as other doctors to consult.
The circuit doctor was paid a decent salary plus expenses and provided an office and subsidized family housing in the community. His job was to keep visiting his circuit, to (1) counsel healthy ways of living, (2) diagnose illnesses, (3) distribute or prescribe (no cost) medicines as required, (4) treat and help heal sick people in their homes and (5) arrange for pubic, nonprofit hospital or sanatorium care (including transportation), if needed.
Our family’s beloved circuit doctor routinely stopped by to see us once or twice every week. Our healthcare was free from a public nonprofit system. It was also economical: with people’s homes doubling as healthcare facilities, the cost of most hospital/nursing home rooms was eliminated. Even very ill people were cared for at home by our circuit doctors who often taught family members to do home care.
Of course, such a free public healthcare system was made possible in part by universal access to housing and tuition free education. We had no homeless people, and our doctors received their education without becoming indebted. But the most important feature was the absence of (capitalist) ideology. And in such a nonprofit system insurance companies had no legitimate role— certainly not in selecting medical procedures.
Such a system could be painlessly tax-financed through fair, progressive taxation that set the income tax rate according to a person’s real income (the standard throughout the sadly bygone, civilized era of the post-World War II liberal consensus in American politics). Alternatively, everyone could be charged a given percentage (say 2-3%) of his/her income.
Having lived with much better options in several civilized countries, I consider corporate “business” healthcare an oxymoron. Civilized countries have affordable, universal healthcare systems. Americans seem to be intellectually paralyzed when it comes to alternatives to our own failing health system, even though good alternatives abound.

title: Lapse in federal funding for traumatic brain injury research leaves millions without support
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Aging Untold) — A traumatic brain injury, or TBI, can change a life in seconds.
Between 1 and 3 million people visit emergency rooms each year with a concussion — a mild form of TBI — according to the Cleveland Clinic. While TBIs are especially common in young athletes, experts say they often occur far outside of sports.
The number of TBI cases is rising, approaching 3 million per year. Older adults 75 and up account for nearly a third of TBI-related hospitalizations, largely due to fall risk.
Despite the widespread impact, federal funding for TBI research, education and awareness has lapsed — and advocates say the consequences could be severe.
A law that expired
The Traumatic Brain Injury Act, first signed in 1996, provided federal funding for research, resources and advocacy. But the act expired in 2024.
“The pause in federal funding is very scary,” Maureen Cunningham, executive director of the Brain Injury Association of America’s Missouri chapter, said. “There’s going to be limited research, so the advances that have been made in research related to brain injury and living life with brain injury are going to stop.”
Survivors speak out
At a TBI survivor camp in Kansas City, the stakes are personal. Mike Caton, who survived a workplace accident in 2005 when a rod went through his head, lost much of his memory and can no longer work. His wife, Mary, said the injury changed him profoundly.
“They tell me it went through his brain and came back out,” she said.
Steven Garman, 39, sustained his TBI in a car crash and still deals with seizures and speech difficulties. His mother, Barbara, said the camp offers her a rare moment of relief.
“I can relax. I don’t have to be on guard all the time,” she said.
Kate Hwang, a former Kansas City, Missouri, police officer, suffered a TBI in 2003 after being attacked while writing a ticket. The injury forced her into early retirement.
“I had seizures, headaches, there was personality change in the beginning and depression,” Hwang said. “These programs mean a lot to people like me, the people behind me, and we need assistance past the initial injury.”
A bill in Congress
Rep. Frank Pallone is sponsoring the TBI Reauthorization Act, which he introduced in February 2025. Despite bipartisan support, it did not pass. He is hopeful it will advance in 2026.
“I think a lot of it is that people don’t recognize this as a disorder,” Pallone said. “And so an important part of it is not only providing services to people and advocacy, but also recognizing that traumatic brain injury exists as a phenomena.”

title: ‘Cyberpunk 2077’ Movie in Development
text:
‘Cyberpunk 2077’ Movie in Development at Paramount
The new Skydance company combining the old Paramount and Warner Bros. movie studios sure has a lot of movie projects in the news this week. (I’m sure it’s just a coincidence.)
Today comes word that the studio is developing a film based on the Cyberpunk 2077 video game. According to Variety, “Transformers producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura is attached to the project. CD Projekt Red, video game developer and the franchise rights holder, also serves as producer on the project.”
First released in 2020, with a DLC that went on sale in 2023, Cyberpunk 2077 has gone on to sell more than 40 million copies and is among the top-selling video games of the century.
READ MORE: Every Video Game Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
The game is a futuristic RPG set in the dystopian world of Night City, where a mercenary named V finds himself mysteriously stuck with the memories of a dead man named Johnny Silverhand. Non-gamers may know the title because it’s the one that features Keanu Reeves (very much looking like Keanu Reeves) in that key supporting role as Johnny Mnemonic Silverhand.
Whoa.
After several decades in which video game movies were borderline toxic and doomed from the get-go, Hollywood has finally seemed to crack the code on turning these massive popular interactive franchises into successful films and television series. The fifth biggest film of 2026 is The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, while one of the biggest hits of the fall was Zach Cregger’s reboot of Resident Evil, which outgrossed all the previous cinematic adaptation of the horror games.
Next year will bring a new Sonic the Hedgehog and a live-action Legend of Zelda film, among others. On television, The Last of Us, Fallout, and Twisted Metal have all become multiseason hits on various streaming services. We’ve come a long way from Double Dragon.
